0.title: The Cross at the Centre: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
0.overview:
Of all the churches Paul founded, none gave him more grief — or more glory — than the church at Corinth. Corinth was one of the great cities of the ancient world: a rebuilt Roman colony on the narrow isthmus of Greece, sitting athwart the trade routes of the Mediterranean, a cosmopolitan, polyglot, ferociously commercial city where every culture, every religion, and every vice was for sale. The Greek verb korinthiazesthai — to live like a Corinthian — had become a byword for sexual immorality. Into this city Paul came on his second missionary journey around AD 50, stayed eighteen months (Acts 18:11), and planted a church that would make him simultaneously the most celebrated and most embattled apostle in his own lifetime.

He wrote this letter from Ephesus around AD 54–55, provoked by reports from Chloe’s household and a letter from the Corinthians themselves. What he had heard was alarming: the church had fractured into personality factions (“I follow Paul”; “I follow Apollos”; “I follow Cephas”; “I follow Christ”); a man was openly sleeping with his stepmother and the church was arrogant about it; members were suing each other in pagan courts; spiritual gifts had become instruments of status and one-upmanship; the Lord’s Supper had been turned into a class exercise in social humiliation; and some were denying the bodily resurrection entirely. This is a church in crisis — not the crisis of persecution from outside, but the far more dangerous crisis of pride, worldliness, and theological confusion from within.

Paul’s answer to every single one of these crises is the same: the cross. The word of the cross (1:18) is the only wisdom that addresses human arrogance. The crucified Christ (1:23) is the only foundation (3:11) on which a community can be built. The resurrection of Christ (15:20) is the only ground on which the resurrection of the dead makes sense. Every pastoral problem in the letter — from church discipline to spiritual gifts to the collection for the Jerusalem poor — is resolved by returning to the gospel of the crucified and risen Lord. This is why Martin Luther set the theology of the cross (theologia crucis) against the theology of glory (theologia gloriae), and why this letter is the most searching diagnostic of the church’s recurrent temptation to dress the gospel in the clothing of worldly wisdom and power.

The governing conviction is that this letter was written to the twenty-first century as much as the first — because the Corinthian church is every church, and the Corinthian heart is every heart, that has tried to hold the gospel and the values of the world simultaneously.

1.title: Divisions, the Cross, and the Wisdom of God
1.overview:
Corinth in the 50s AD was a boom town. Destroyed by Rome in 146 BC, it was refounded by Julius Caesar in 44 BC as a Roman colony, settled largely with freed slaves, and grew rich on trade between its two harbours on either side of the isthmus. It was full of people climbing the social ladder: one inscription found there records that a man called Erastus paved a street at his own expense in return for public office, perhaps the same Erastus, “the city treasurer”, who sent greetings in Romans 16:23. Status, eloquence and success were prized. Paul spent eighteen months planting the church (Acts 18), and a few years later wrote from Ephesus after hearing of serious problems.

The first problem is division: members were lining up behind favourite teachers as though they were rival schools of philosophy. Paul answers it at the root, with the message of a crucified Messiah that overturns human ideas of wisdom and status, and with the God who chose ordinary people so that no one could boast except in the Lord.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, writing with a colleague called Sosthenes, introduces himself as an apostle by God’s calling. He addresses the church in Corinth as God’s own people, made holy in Christ and called to be saints, together with believers everywhere who call on the name of Jesus, the Lord of all, and wishes them grace and peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Called by the Will of God

Paul calls himself an apostle “by the will of God”, and that is theology, not modesty: his commission rests on God’s will, not on his gifts or a church’s vote. When the Corinthians question Paul, they are questioning the God who sent him. The same is true of their own standing: they are saints because they were called (v. 2), not because they volunteered.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s authority was contested at Corinth by people who preferred Apollos’s polish or Peter’s prestige. Now: In a church culture that prizes celebrity and charisma, the ground of ministry is still God’s calling, not human talent. A pastor who rests his authority on his own gifts has little to stand on when people turn against him.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and our brother Sosthenes,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Chapter 1 opens with greeting and thanksgiving: the Corinthians are God’s church, sanctified in Christ, enriched with every gift, and God will keep them to the end (vv. 1–9). Then Paul takes up the first problem, a church splitting into fan clubs around favourite leaders (vv. 10–17), and goes to the root: the message of the cross, foolish and weak to the world, is the power and wisdom of God (vv. 18–25); God chose the nobodies so that no one can boast before him (vv. 26–29); everything is found in Christ, so let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord (vv. 30–31). The chapter that begins with a quarrel over men ends with every eye on one Man.

The setting. Paul wrote from Ephesus, about AD 54, a few years after founding the church (Acts 18:1–18; 1 Corinthians 16:8). Since then he had written an earlier letter (5:9), heard reports from Chloe’s people (1:11), and received a letter with questions (7:1). 1 Corinthians answers both: divisions, sexual immorality, lawsuits, marriage, food offered to idols, worship, the Lord’s Supper, spiritual gifts and the resurrection.

Called by the will of God. Three phrases carry the weight, and each takes something away from Paul: called; by the will of God; and apostle (apostolos), one sent with authority, a man under orders carrying somebody else’s message. He does not write that he became an apostle, trained for it, or was appointed by a church; any of those would have located the commission in Paul. He puts it outside himself entirely (Galatians 1:15).

Not an application he submitted. Whatever else the Damascus road was, it was not a job interview. Paul was travelling with warrants in his luggage to arrest Christians when he was knocked to the ground and blinded by the very person he was persecuting (Acts 9:3–9). So he can open a letter to a church questioning his authority (4:3; 9:3) by saying, in effect: the appointment was not mine to make and is not mine to resign.

Why it matters for this letter. Sixteen chapters of correction are coming, for people who do not want to be corrected. If Paul’s standing rests on his personality, eloquence or track record, the Corinthians can simply prefer somebody else’s, and that is precisely what they have done (v. 12). If it rests on the will of God, their preferences are beside the point.

An apostle of Christ Jesus. The title is itself a confession of the resurrection. Nobody is sent by a dead man, and Paul’s whole claim rests on having seen the risen Lord and been commissioned by him (9:1; 15:8). And the sending did not begin with Paul. Christ is the Apostle of our confession, sent by the Father (Hebrews 3:1), and on the evening of the resurrection he told his disciples that as the Father had sent him, so he was sending them (John 20:21). Paul’s authority is borrowed authority, the risen Son extending his own commission through a man he had arrested on a road. That is why it cannot be voted down: to receive the one Christ sends is to receive Christ (John 13:20).

And our brother Sosthenes. The second name is easy to read past, and it may be one of the quietest miracles in the New Testament. When the Corinthian Jews dragged Paul before the proconsul Gallio and the case was thrown out, the crowd seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal (Acts 18:17). He held the office Crispus had held before he became a Christian (Acts 18:8), the leadership of the opposition. We cannot be certain it is the same man; Sosthenes was not a rare name. But if it is, the head of the opposition became the co-sender of the letter, and the Christians at Corinth opened it and saw a name they remembered from the wrong side of a courtroom.

The gospel recruits its opponents. Hold on to that when you pray for someone who seems entirely closed: the relative who mocks, the colleague who has heard it all. Paul was among the most dangerous enemies the early church had, and Sosthenes may have been another. Both names head this letter. The gospel does not merely survive its opponents; it has a long history of enlisting them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean apostles still exist today in Paul’s sense. The eyewitnesses sent by the risen Lord laid the foundation of the church once (Ephesians 2:20), and their authority continues in their writings: when we want to hear an apostle, we open this letter. If some churches call pioneering missionaries apostles, meaning sent messengers, the word can bear it (2 Corinthians 8:23), but no one now adds to the foundation or speaks with Paul’s authority.

Is my job a calling in the same sense? Not quite, though it is not nothing. When Paul says called here, and of all Christians in verses 2, 9 and 24, he means God’s effectual summons into Christ: the call that saves. That call is the same for the apostle and for you. Paul’s particular office was a further, unrepeatable commission. Your work, family and church responsibilities are callings in a secondary sense: the place where God has put you to serve him (7:17–24). So you need not hunt for a dramatic sense of vocation before your life counts. The first call, the one that made you his, is already the greatest thing that will ever happen to you; everything else is lived out of it.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote this letter from Ephesus, around AD 53–55, a few years after founding the church. Sosthenes may be the synagogue ruler beaten at Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: To the church of God that is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both their Lord and ours: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Corinth was a wealthy Roman colony and trading city on the isthmus between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese, with ports on two seas. It was proud, competitive, status-conscious and famous for its immorality; the Greeks had coined a verb from its name, korinthiazomai, to Corinthianise, meaning to live immorally. It was full of new money, competitive display and imported religion.

To the church of God that is in Corinth. The little word of is doing more work than any other in the sentence. The church (ekklēsia, in the Greek Old Testament Israel gathered before the LORD) belongs to God, not to Paul or Apollos or any faction; it merely has an address. And every reader in the ancient world knew what Corinth was. To write “the church of God in Corinth” was very nearly a contradiction in terms, and Paul writes it without a flicker of embarrassment. If God can have a church in Corinth, he can have one anywhere.

To those sanctified in Christ Jesus. A great deal of Christian anxiety turns on this phrase. “Sanctified” (hagiazō, set apart as holy) is a perfect passive: something that was done to them, at a point in the past, with results that continue (6:11). It is not a report on their conduct but a statement about their location: they are set apart for God because they are in Christ, who is holy. To be in Christ means to be joined to him by the Spirit through faith, so that God now deals with you as belonging to his Son: he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him (6:17). And the Son made that holiness available at a cost. On the night before the cross he said that for their sake he consecrated himself, that they also might be sanctified in truth (John 17:19). He set himself apart for the altar, so that a church in Corinth could be set apart for God, once for all.

Remember who is being described. This is the church that will shortly be rebuked for factions, for a man living with his father’s wife, for lawsuits in pagan courts, for drunkenness at the Lord’s Supper while the poor went hungry, and for chaos over spiritual gifts. Paul has already had the report (v. 11), and he still calls them sanctified saints. He does not withdraw the title to motivate them to earn it. He states who they are, and then spends sixteen chapters telling them to become it. That order is the gospel. The world says: behave, and you will belong. Paul says: you have been set apart, therefore live like it.

Called to be saints. Saints (hagioi, holy ones) is what all believers are, not a special class. In the New Testament it is never a rank awarded to the exceptional but the ordinary word for a Christian, and Paul applies it happily to perhaps the worst-behaved congregation in his correspondence. The question is not whether your record has earned the description, but whether you are in Christ, because the description follows the location. And called, here as everywhere in this letter, means more than invited. It is not an invitation slipped under the door that you may or may not open; it is like Jesus at the tomb calling Lazarus by name, a word that creates the response it asks for (John 11:43–44).

Call upon the name. The address opens outward: Corinth is one congregation inside something worldwide. And the phrase call upon the name of the Lord is lifted straight out of the Old Testament, where it means to invoke and worship the LORD, Yahweh himself (Genesis 4:26; Joel 2:32; Romans 10:13). Paul applies it to Jesus without argument or apology. To call on Jesus is to worship him as God: a strong statement of Christ’s deity, and it arrives disguised as an address label.

Grace and peace. The greeting fuses grace, a Christian reshaping of the ordinary Greek greeting, with peace, the Hebrew shalom. And they come from the Father and the Son together, one preposition governing both, as the single source of the gift. Paul is not arguing for the deity of Christ here. He is assuming it, in a passing line, which is a far stronger indication of what the earliest church believed than any formal argument would be (Romans 1:7; 2 Corinthians 1:2).

If I am already sanctified, why must I still grow in holiness? Because the Bible uses the word in two ways, and both are true of you. Definitively, you were set apart for God the moment you were joined to Christ; that is finished and does not fluctuate (6:11; Hebrews 10:10). Progressively, the Spirit is now making your actual life match that status, a lifelong work that is real but never complete in this life (2 Corinthians 3:18; the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, 13.1–2). The first is the ground of the second, never its reward. You do not pursue holiness to become God’s; you pursue it because you are his. So when you fail, you have not lost the first; you have found another place where the second still has work to do.

On a Tuesday. When you have sinned badly, not a slip but the real thing, what is your first instinct about your standing before God? Do you assume you must work your way back in before you can pray properly? That instinct is common, and it is not the gospel. The letter that says you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified (6:11) says it to people who were still getting it badly wrong. Go to him today as what he has made you, and ask him to make your life match your name.
verseByVerse.note: Corinth was a wealthy Roman colony and trading city on the narrow isthmus of Greece, with two ports and a mixed, mobile population. “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God constantly for the grace given to the Corinthians in Christ. They have been enriched in every way, especially in their speech and knowledge, because the message about Christ took firm root among them, and so they lack no spiritual gift as they wait for Christ to be revealed. Christ will keep them firm to the end, so that they will be blameless on his day. God is faithful, and it was he who called them into fellowship with his Son.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Faithfulness of God as the Ground of Perseverance

Verse 9 is one of Paul’s great texts on perseverance. The guarantee that the Corinthians will be kept to the end (v. 8) is not their grip on Christ but God’s grip on them. The calling, the fellowship and the keeping are all God’s work, and the saints persevere because he is faithful.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians had turned their spiritual gifts into status symbols, measuring their standing by the quality of their tongues and the depth of their knowledge. Paul’s thanksgiving quietly corrects them: they “were enriched” in these things; the gifts were given, not earned. Now: The same pride can attach to theological sophistication or spiritual experience. Paul’s corrective is the same: it is all grace. What do you have that you did not receive? (4:7).

verseByVerse.quote: I give thanks to my God always for you because of the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus, that in every way you were enriched in him in all speech and all knowledge—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thanks first. Paul already holds Chloe’s report (v. 11): the quarrelling, the immorality, the lawsuits, the disorder. He has a list that would justify opening with anger, and the first thing he does is thank God for them. This is not flattery or a sweetener before the medicine. He is thanking God for something God did, so he can do it with complete sincerity about a church he is about to take apart. Nor does thanksgiving cancel correction: he simply refuses to let the problems be the first or the truest thing he says.

Enriched in him. Enriched (a passive: the wealth arrived as a gift) belongs to the word family Paul uses in his best-known sentence about Christian wealth: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). That is where the Corinthian riches came from. Their wealth is the measure of his poverty; what they have in their hands is what it cost him to put it there.

In all speech and all knowledge. Speech and knowledge are the two things that have gone most badly wrong at Corinth. Speech is the arena of the tongues problem that will occupy chapters 12 to 14. Knowledge is the source of the arrogance Paul confronts at 8:1, where he says flatly that knowledge puffs up. So Paul thanks God for the very gifts that are currently doing the damage, because they were real gifts.

Tracing the gift to the Giver. Our instinct when a gift is misused is to disparage it. Paul traces each gift back to the Giver, gives thanks, and then spends the letter putting it back in its place. The trouble at Corinth was never that they had too much of God’s grace. It was that they had forgotten it was grace.

How can I thank God for someone without pretending his sin is fine? By thanking God for what God has done in him, not for what he is doing wrong. The two are different columns, and Paul keeps them separate: thanks for grace in verses 4–9, correction from verse 10 on. Thanksgiving is not a verdict that the problem is small; it is a confession that God is at work even there. It also changes the correction. You will speak more gently, more hopefully and more accurately to someone whose gifts you have honestly thanked God for that morning, and he is far more likely to hear you, because he can tell you are not his enemy.
verseByVerse.note: The Corinthians prized eloquent speech and knowledge — the very gifts later misused.

verseByVerse.quote: even as the testimony about Christ was confirmed among you— so that you are not lacking in any gift, as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The testimony confirmed. The testimony about Christ is the gospel Paul preached, and “confirmed” (bebaiōthē) is a word from contracts and guarantees: ratified and made secure. The gifts at Corinth were not decorations. They were God’s signature under the apostolic message, so that nobody could say it was merely one man’s opinion.

Not lacking in any gift. A congregation deficient in love, humility, unity, self-control and basic decency is told it lacks no spiritual gift whatever. Both are true at once. Gifting is not maturity, and one is no evidence of the other. That is a warning to the gifted, who may read their usefulness as God’s approval of their character, and a relief to everybody else, who may have assumed that the gifted must be the godly.

For the Christian who thinks he has no gift. You watch people who teach, or organise, or know what to say in a hospital room, and find nothing comparable in yourself. Paul later applies this to each believer: to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good (12:7). Not to some; to each. Gifts are ordinarily discovered by serving, not by introspection. Take the job nobody wants, and see what God does with it.

The revealing. “Revealing” (apokalypsis) is the drawing back of a curtain on someone who is already there: Christ’s return in glory. The gifts are issued for the waiting, equipment for the interval between his going and his coming, provisions for a journey rather than trophies for a cabinet. Some Corinthians acted as if they had already arrived (4:8); Paul reminds them they are still waiting (13:8–12).

Gifts from an ascended King. The gifts the Corinthians were quarrelling over were not native talents. Paul says elsewhere that when Christ ascended on high he led a host of captives and gave gifts to men (Ephesians 4:7–8, citing Psalm 68:18): they are the spoils of his victory, handed out by a King who has gone up to the Father and will come again. So every gift looked back to a Saviour who had died, risen and ascended, and forward to the same Saviour unveiled. A gift that becomes a reason to admire its holder has forgotten both ends of its own story.

Possession or equipment? That single clause would have solved most of the Corinthian problem if they had believed it. A gift understood as a possession becomes a measure of standing; standing invites comparison; and comparison produces the factions of the next paragraph. A gift understood as equipment for a job raises a different question: not what does this say about me, but what is this for? The same gift, held in two ways, builds a church or splits one.

Where Christians differ: do all the gifts continue today? Some hold that the revelatory and sign gifts, prophecy, tongues and gifts of healing, belonged to the apostolic age and ceased once the foundation was laid and the New Testament complete, pointing to the apostles and prophets as a foundation laid once (Ephesians 2:20) and to the signs as God’s attestation of the apostolic message (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). Others hold that they continue until Christ returns, reading the perfect of 13:10 as his appearing rather than the closing of the canon, and noting that this very verse ties the gifts to the period of waiting for the revealing of the Lord, which is plainly not over. This commentary’s view: the first is the better view. The sign gifts authenticated the apostles and their message, and with a closed canon God speaks to his church through Scripture, sufficient for all of life (2 Timothy 3:16–17). This is held charitably: both positions are taken by people who love Scripture and submit to it, and what Paul says here, which neither side disputes, is the main thing. Whatever gifts God has given you were given for the waiting, will not be needed when he appears, and were never intended to tell you or anyone else how you are doing (Romans 8:23–25; 1 Peter 4:10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every individual had every gift (12:29–30). The church as a whole lacked nothing.

If the sign gifts have ceased, does God still heal? Yes. Cessationism is not the belief that God has stopped acting; it is the belief that he no longer gives individuals the apostolic gift of healing or new revelation as signs authenticating a message. God still hears prayer for the sick and often answers it, sometimes through doctors, sometimes beyond them, and James tells the sick to call the elders to pray (James 5:14–15). So pray boldly for healing, and give thanks when it comes. What you should be wary of is anyone who claims to heal at will or to bring a new word from God that binds your conscience. Test everything by the Scripture God has already given.

For worship. The one we wait for is not absent but hidden, already there behind the veil, and the curtain will be drawn back. On that day every gift will be laid down like a lamp at sunrise, because the Light himself will have come, and the tongues that argued at Corinth will have only one thing left to say. The gifts were tokens of his care for the interval; the unveiling will be the Giver himself, seen face to face (13:12).

verseByVerse.quote: who will sustain you to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who will sustain you to the end. The one who sustains is named at the end of verse 7: our Lord Jesus Christ, certainly not the Corinthians. The word is bebaiōsei, the same root as “confirmed” in verse 6, the language of a legal guarantee: as God confirmed the gospel among them, he will confirm them to the last day. The comfort is in the tense: not that he may, or will if you hold on tightly enough, but a plain future about something already guaranteed.

Guiltless. This is the word the whole verse is built to deliver. Anenklētous is a courtroom term. It does not mean never having done anything; it means unaccused: no charge standing, no case to answer. The day of the Lord is the day of judgement and Christ’s return, and on that day believers will stand without accusation, because Christ’s righteousness is theirs (Romans 8:33–34; Colossians 1:22). Paul’s word for it is justification: the Judge pronouncing a guilty person in the right with him, for Christ’s sake and not for any goodness he has reached (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

How can that be true? Paul is about to spend fifteen chapters on what is wrong with them, and before he names a single item he tells them how judgement will go for them. Only one way, and the letter will say it plainly at 15:3: Christ died for our sins. The charges are not being ignored, waived, or quietly dropped for lack of evidence. They were transferred. Every accusation that could be brought against a Corinthian believer on that day was brought against Christ on a Friday afternoon outside Jerusalem, and answered there. The sheet is clean because someone else’s was filled in.

For the Christian who is afraid of the last day. You believe in the forgiveness of sins in general, and are not sure it will hold for you in particular, because you know things nobody else knows: the thing you have never told anyone, the pattern you have confessed a hundred times and returned to, the person you damaged who never got an apology. You expect that day to be the moment it all comes out. But look at what Paul says will be true of you then: guiltless. Not forgiven with a permanent asterisk. Not acquitted after a difficult hearing. No charge standing. If a single accusation could still be brought against a believer on that day, then Christ’s death dealt with most sins and not all, and the letter that says he was raised on the third day would be describing a job half done.

Where Christians differ: perseverance. Some teach that true believers may fall away and be finally lost. This is the view of Arminian Christians (who hold that saving grace can in the end be resisted and lost), and they hold it out of a sincere desire to take Scripture’s warnings seriously. This commentary’s view: Paul says God will sustain them to the end. If it were up to the Corinthians, with all their failings, they would not stand. But God keeps his people. True believers may fall into serious sin, as the Corinthians did, and must be corrected; but God will not let them go (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29; Westminster Confession 17.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 17.1). The warnings are real, and they are one of the ways he keeps them.

What about people who seemed to be Christians and then walked away? Scripture gives two answers that must be held together. Some who leave were never truly joined to Christ, however real it looked: they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). Others are true believers in a long and grievous backsliding, as Peter was for a night and the Corinthians were for a season, and God will bring them home. From the outside we often cannot tell which, so we do not pronounce; we pray, we keep the door open, and we keep calling. What you can know is your own case: if you are still coming to Christ with your sins today, that coming is the evidence that he is keeping you.

verseByVerse.quote: God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is faithful. Three short words in the Greek, and they are the floor under everything Paul has just promised, the reason for the confidence of verse 8. It is a key phrase in this letter (10:13).

But what if I let go? A reader who has taken verse 8 seriously will already have asked it. It is very well to say that God will sustain me to the end, but I have let go before. I know how thin my grip is on a bad week, and I have watched people who seemed far stronger than me walk away. What happens then? Paul’s answer is not to reassure you about your grip. He changes the subject away from your grip altogether, and puts the entire weight on the character of God. The guarantee is not that you are faithful; it is that he is. That is the only guarantee worth anything, because a promise is exactly as reliable as the person making it, and you already know what yours are worth.

By whom you were called. The calling is his act: God called them, effectively, into union with Christ. The fellowship is his gift. And the faithfulness that will keep them in it is his character. There is no point in that sentence at which the Corinthians contribute anything, which is a remarkable thing to say about a church whose behaviour is about to be dismantled for fifteen chapters. What God begins, he finishes (Philippians 1:6). The most dangerous thing in the world is not a God who might abandon you; it is a God of infinite faithfulness who has committed himself to you. Dangerous, because such a God will not leave you as you are; and safe, for exactly the same reason.

What perseverance does and does not claim. It does not claim that a Christian cannot sin badly or drift for years; the Corinthians are the proof of that. The name perseverance of the saints can sound like a statement about their stamina. It is first a statement about their preservation by God: Christians persevere because they are being kept.

Into the fellowship of his Son. Koinōnia means sharing, partnership, common life. They were not called into a religion or a moral improvement scheme but into a shared life with the Son of God, and since every believer shares in Christ, they share in one another. The Corinthians, divided into parties over which teacher they prefer, are told in the last line of the thanksgiving that they were all called into partnership with the same Person. That quietly makes absurd the factions Paul is about to name (vv. 10–12).

What does fellowship with Christ look like on an ordinary day? It means that what is his is yours, and what is yours he has taken. His righteousness covers you, his Spirit lives in you, his Father is your Father, and his future is your future. In return he has taken your sin, your burdens and your griefs as his concern. You enjoy it by using it: speaking to him in prayer as one who is welcome, listening to him in Scripture, receiving him at his table, and sharing your life with others who share his. It is not a feeling you must manufacture. It is a relationship you are already in, and feelings tend to follow when you act on it.

For worship. He has never broken a promise. Not to Abraham, waiting twenty-five years for a son; not to Israel, kept through four centuries in Egypt; not to David, whose throne stood empty for nearly six hundred years before a child was born in Bethlehem to fill it. Each of those promises looked, for a long time, like one that had failed, and each was kept, and kept at last in the same Person: all the promises of God find their Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). That Son is the one into whose fellowship you have been called, and the God who kept every word to the fathers will not let go of what he has called.

parallels.desc: the faithful God

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul appeals to them, in Christ’s name, to agree with one another and end their divisions. Chloe’s household have reported quarrels over favourites: Paul, Apollos, Peter or Christ. Is Christ split into pieces? Was Paul crucified for them? He is glad he baptised only a handful, so no one can claim to be his disciple. Christ sent him not mainly to baptise but to preach the gospel, and not with clever rhetoric, which would empty the cross of its power.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cross Against Personality Cults

The Corinthian factions show what happens when a leader’s personality becomes the centre of a church. The preacher is a herald, announcing a message that does not belong to him. Paul’s refusal of “eloquent wisdom” is not a dislike of learning; it is a choice to let the gospel speak with its own power instead of dressing it in borrowed clothes.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The ancient world ran on patronage and on travelling orators: you attached yourself to an impressive teacher and measured your standing by his. The Corinthian factions were the church doing what Corinthian culture always did. Now: Celebrity culture is the modern version. A church member who follows a famous preacher online in place of his own pastors, or a church that divides over which tradition’s champion to follow, is repeating the Corinthian mistake.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment. For it has been reported to me by Chloe’s people that there is quarreling among you, my brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I appeal to you. Paul does not command here, though as an apostle he could. He pleads (parakalō). And he pleads by the name of Christ: by his authority, and by the one name in Corinth that belongs equally to every person he is writing to, which is exactly the point he is about to make. Christ has been named ten times in the first ten verses. Before Paul mentions a single faction, he has filled the room with the one Person they all share.

In the flow. With verse 10 the body of the letter begins. The factions run to the end of chapter 4, and Paul answers them not with a plan for managing the church but with the cross (1:18–2:5), the Spirit’s wisdom (2:6–16), and a right view of ministers as servants (3:1–4:21).

No divisions. Literally, that you all say the same thing: one voice rather than rival slogans (v. 12). Schismata (schisms) are tears, the word used of a torn garment (Mark 2:21): not a difference of opinion but the sound of fabric giving way. The church had not yet split into separate congregations, but there were cliques and rivalries. And what makes it worse is what the fabric is: this letter will shortly call the church a body (12:12–27), and a tear in a body is not an untidiness. It is a wound.

United in the same mind. Katartizō means mended, restored, put in order; it is the word used of the fishermen mending their nets (Mark 1:19). Paul wants the torn garment mended, a shared mind and purpose. This is not a demand that every Christian hold identical views on every question. Paul himself makes room for genuine disagreement on real matters, food, days, disputable things (Romans 14), and this same letter will spend chapter 8 handling a question on which believers landed differently. What he is after is a shared orientation: a church so fixed on the same Lord that no rival loyalty can organise a party.

One loaf, one name. Paul does not ask the Corinthians to manufacture a unity they lack. He asks them to stop tearing one they already have. They were all baptised into the one name of Christ; they all eat from one loaf, which is a sharing in his body (10:16–17); they are all members of the one Christ (12:12). That unity was made at the cross, where he broke down the dividing wall in his own flesh and created one new people in place of two (Ephesians 2:14–16). A party at Corinth is not a difference of taste. It is a hand raised against something Christ died to make.

Chloe’s people. They were probably members of her household or business, perhaps slaves or freedmen travelling between Corinth and Ephesus: exactly the sort of witnesses a status-conscious congregation would discount. Paul takes the report seriously and says openly where it came from. He will not build a rebuke on gossip he cannot attribute.

What does this ask of me on Sunday? Most readers are living somewhere inside this passage. Your church has a fault line: a leadership dispute, a music argument, two families who no longer speak, a slow separation into those who liked the last minister and those who wanted the change. Four things are asked of you, and none of them is dramatic. Refuse the party: the factions at Corinth were sustained by people saying I follow, and every division needs recruits; declining to take a side is a positive act, not cowardice. Stop repeating it: much of what tears a congregation is not the original disagreement but its retelling, and the sentence that begins I probably shouldn’t say this has done more damage in more churches than any heresy. Speak to the person, not about them, which is what Paul is doing here, at some cost. And keep eating together: this letter treats a shared table as a theological act, and people who eat together find it much harder to caricature each other.

Unity is not the same thing as quiet. A call for unity is not a call to suppress genuine concern, and “you are being divisive” is the standard reply of anyone who wishes an uncomfortable question would go away. Paul himself opposed Peter to his face when the gospel was at stake (Galatians 2:11). Nor does unity ever mean covering up sin or abuse; this very letter demands that serious sin be dealt with openly (5:1–13). The unity commanded here is unity around the crucified Christ. The test is whether the thing dividing your church is Christ or preference. If a congregation is splitting over the gospel, that is a grief and may be a necessity. If it is splitting over anything else, and it usually is, then Paul’s plea applies without qualification.

When is it right to leave a church? Rarely, and never casually. There are real reasons: the gospel itself is denied or obscured; serious sin or abuse is protected rather than dealt with; you are required to act against Scripture; or you have moved away. Preference about style, music or personality is not one of them, and even real concerns should first be raised humbly, privately and with the elders (Matthew 18:15). If you must go, go openly and peaceably, without recruiting others or leaving a trail of grievance, and join another faithful church promptly. Leaving Christ’s people altogether is never an option Scripture offers.

For worship. On the night he was betrayed, with the cross a few hours away, the Lord Jesus prayed for people who did not yet believe in him, that they would all be one, as he and the Father are one (John 17:20–21). Corinth was inside that prayer, quarrels and all, and so is every divided congregation since. The Son has never asked the Father for anything in vain. His church still tears, and he still mends it, and on the last day there will be one flock and one Shepherd (John 10:16), with not a seam showing.
verseByVerse.note: Chloe’s people were probably members of her household or business who had travelled to Ephesus.

verseByVerse.quote: What I mean is that each one of you says, “I follow Paul,” or “I follow Apollos,” or “I follow Cephas,” or “I follow Christ.” Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four slogans. Literally, I belong to Paul. Each name is a real attraction. Paul’s party was probably the loyalist old guard, proud to follow the founder. Apollos, an eloquent Jew from Alexandria (Acts 18:24–28), was the polished speaker, a considerable draw in a city that paid to hear orators. Cephas is Peter’s Aramaic name; his party, perhaps Jewish believers, claimed the leading apostle of the Twelve, with a prestige Paul could not match.

Or “I follow Christ”. Some think this is Paul’s own retort, but it reads most naturally as a fourth slogan. Perhaps the most dangerous party, because it looks like the right answer, and it is rebuked alongside the others. It is the claim to have risen above the mess: I have no time for your teachers and your traditions and your squabbling church; I have Christ, directly, and I need nothing else. It sounds like maturity and is a subtler form of the same pride, because it has still turned Christ into a party badge, and it has done it by using his name to look down on his people.

Good material, bad division. Nothing here is a heresy; as far as we can tell, nobody is teaching error. Every one of these men is a genuine servant of God, and Paul will insist two chapters later that Apollos and he are simply servants through whom the Corinthians believed (3:5). That is what makes it so hard to see from the inside. A congregation dividing over false teaching at least knows what it is doing; a congregation dividing over preferences believes it is defending something important.

Is Christ divided? Then come three questions, and each one is a hammer. Has Christ been split up and shared out among factions? If the church is his body, then a factional church is a dismembered Christ. The image is grotesque, and it is meant to be. There are not four Christs to distribute among four parties. Every believer at Corinth has the whole of him, which means no group holds a portion the others lack. To divide the church is to tear him.

Was Paul crucified for you? Here is the only credential that could justify a Christian naming himself after someone. Loyalty of this depth belongs to a person who died for you, and exactly one person qualifies. Paul is not being modest. He is pointing out that the Corinthians have offered him something he has no right to receive, and he refuses to be the head of a party.

Or were you baptized in the name of Paul? Baptism names your owner. To be baptised into the name of someone is to be publicly transferred into his possession, and every Corinthian was baptised into the name of Christ, whoever happened to be standing in the water with him. These are absurd questions with obvious answers: only Christ died for them, and they belong to him alone.

For the one who has withdrawn into a private faith. You have been hurt by a church, or simply exhausted by one. You have watched Christians behave in ways that embarrassed you, and you have quietly withdrawn: you love Christ, you read your Bible, and you have concluded you can do without the rest. Nothing in this passage doubts the hurt, and a church that damaged you owes you an apology it may never offer. But look where the fourth slogan sits. Paul does not put it above the others as the one healthy option. He puts it in the same sentence and lets the same three questions fall on it, because Christ has attached himself to a body, and no one can take the Head and decline the rest of him. The eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you (12:21).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should have no preferences among teachers, or that denominations are always sinful. Paul does not rebuke anyone for learning more from Apollos than from Cephas, and churches that hold distinct convictions about baptism or church order are not what he is attacking. The sin is boasting in a human leader and treating your own side as the measure of who really belongs (3:21). A loyalty has become a party spirit when you can no longer gladly receive Christ’s gifts through someone outside it.

Can I just listen to my favourite preacher online instead of my own church? Listen to him gladly, but not instead. Christ gives his gifts through the gathered church you actually belong to: the pastor who knows your name, the elders who will visit you in hospital, the table you share, the people who can see your life and speak into it (Hebrews 10:24–25; 13:17). A celebrity preacher cannot shepherd you, and he will never know if you drift. And comparing your pastor unfavourably with a man edited for an online audience is exactly the Corinthian habit Paul is rebuking. Thank God for both, and give your loyalty to the local body where Christ has placed you.
verseByVerse.note: Apollos had taught at Corinth after Paul. Cephas is Peter’s Aramaic name.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name. (I did baptize also the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Glad he baptised few. He is not disparaging baptism. Christ commanded it (Matthew 28:19), Paul assumes every Corinthian has received it (v. 13), and he treats it in this very letter as bound up with the moment believers were joined into one body (12:13). What he is glad about is narrower and shrewder. Paul probably left most baptisms to others, and the fewer people who could claim a personal bond with him through baptism, the fewer could build a party on it.

Who these people were. Those he remembers were people of standing. Crispus was the ruler of the synagogue (Acts 18:8), probably the most prominent convert in the city. Gaius later hosted the whole church (Romans 16:23). Stephanas and his household were the firstfruits of Achaia (16:15–17). These are exactly the people a personality cult would be built around, and Paul knows it.

Not in my name. The reason goes deeper than tactics. Baptism belongs to Christ because what it pictures belongs to him. To be baptised into his name is to be publicly marked as joined to him in his death, burial and rising (Romans 6:3–4; Colossians 2:12). No apostle died for the Corinthians and no apostle rose for them, so no apostle may have his name written over their baptism. Crispus the synagogue ruler and Gaius the wealthy host went down into the water on the same terms as the poorest believer beside them, with nothing to bring, buried with a crucified Lord and raised with him into one body (12:13).

Stephanas too. The little parenthesis is the sound of a real man dictating a real letter and remembering something halfway through.

I do not know. A man writing Scripture has just admitted, in Scripture, that he cannot remember. The difficulty assumes that inspiration means dictation, God using Paul as a pen. That is not what Scripture claims for itself. Luke opens his Gospel by describing research and eyewitnesses (Luke 1:1–4). The human authors are not bypassed; they are used.

What inspiration does mean. The Spirit so superintended what these men wrote that the result is precisely what God intended to say, without suppressing their vocabulary, temperament or memories (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21). This verse truly asserts that Paul, at the time of writing, was not certain whether there had been others. Nothing false has been affirmed. And a forger inventing an apostolic letter would hardly leave his author groping after a detail and correcting himself mid-sentence.

Where Christians differ: household baptisms. Paedobaptists (Christians who baptise the infants of believers) argue from household baptisms (here, and Acts 16:15, 33) that believers’ children should be baptised, seeing baptism as the sign of God’s covenant promise, which like circumcision includes children (Genesis 17:7; Acts 2:39; Colossians 2:11–12). This commentary’s view: the New Testament never mentions an infant in any household baptism. The text here does not say who was in the household or how old they were, but at the end of the letter this same household is described as devoting themselves to serving the saints (16:15), which describes believers old enough to serve. Elsewhere the households that were baptised are households that heard the word and believed (Acts 16:32–34; 18:8). Baptism in the New Testament follows repentance and faith (Acts 2:38, 41; 8:12). So this commentary holds believer’s baptism (1689 London Baptist Confession 29), while warmly recognising paedobaptist brothers and sisters as faithful Christians who read the covenant differently.

I was baptised as an infant and have since come to faith. Should I be baptised? On the view this commentary holds, yes: the baptism the New Testament describes is the public confession of a believer, and since you did not make that confession as an infant, the step of obedience is still before you. That is not a slight on your parents, who very likely acted in faith and love, and it is not a judgement on paedobaptist churches, which are true churches of Christ. Talk it through with your pastor or elders, read the passages for yourself, and act with a clear conscience. If your church holds the other view, raise it humbly; this is a matter on which godly Christians differ, and love must govern the conversation.
