verseByVerse.quote: For Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not sent to baptise. On this sentence the opening argument turns. But first, the half that sounds wrong: the risen Christ sent his apostles to make disciples, baptising them (Matthew 28:19). How can Paul say he was not sent to do it?

What he cannot mean. Paul was not against baptism. He was baptised himself as soon as his sight returned (Acts 9:18), he has just named the people he baptised (vv. 14–16), and his teaching on what baptism signifies (Romans 6:3–4) is among the richest in the New Testament. Whatever this sentence means, it cannot mean that baptism is optional.

Not this but that. The shape of the sentence is a Hebrew way of stressing priority: not this but that, meaning that first. God says through Hosea, I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6), though he had commanded the sacrifices. Paul is telling the Corinthians what his commission was chiefly for. Christ sent him to preach (euangelizō, to announce good news). Baptising was not the centre of the assignment, and it did not need an apostle’s hands.

The Great Commission was given to the church. In Matthew’s Greek there is a single command, make disciples; baptising and teaching describe how it is carried out, and the church has obeyed it together, never assuming each apostle must perform every part in person. Jesus set that pattern himself: John notes that Jesus himself did not baptise, but only his disciples (John 4:2). Paul describes the same division of labour two chapters later: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (3:6).

Paul’s particular commission. The risen Christ appointed him a servant and witness and sent him to the Gentiles to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light (Acts 26:16–18). He was a planter of churches, and the preaching was the part only he had been sent to do. So Paul is not contradicting Matthew 28; he is describing his place in obeying it. Disciples are made first by the announcement of Christ crucified, and baptism follows faith, as it did at Pentecost, where those who received his word were baptised (Acts 2:41).

Does it matter who baptised me? It does not. A baptism does not take its value from the reputation of the minister, from how well you knew him, or from whether he later disgraced himself. You were baptised, as every Corinthian was, into the name of Christ (v. 13), and that name is the whole of it.

Eloquent wisdom. Literally wisdom of word (sophia logou): clever rhetoric and human philosophy. In Corinth travelling orators, the sophists, were celebrities, paid for their performances, judged by their style, compared and followed by rival fans. To preach the cross in that register is to enter the competition, and the moment you do, the audience starts assessing the performer. They may leave impressed. They will not leave undone.

Emptied of its power. The verb is kenoō, the word used in Philippians 2:7 of the Son’s glorious self-emptying; here the emptying is a disastrous one. The cross can be hollowed out, not by attack but by presentation. A preacher can leave every doctrine formally intact and still drain the thing of power, simply by making the message a vehicle for the messenger. What saves is not a well-delivered idea but a Person who died and rose, met in the plain word about him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean preachers should be careless or dull, or that learning and clear speech are bad. Paul himself argued and reasoned (Acts 17:2; 19:8), was trained under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), and plainly took enormous trouble over words. A muddled sermon is not thereby more spiritual; it is merely worse. It means preachers must not rely on technique or try to make the gospel attractive by hiding its offence.

Two powers. What Paul is against is the substitution of one power for another. Two things can produce a response to preaching: the speaker’s persuasive skill, and the Spirit of God working through the message of a crucified Saviour. Both produce visible results; only one produces conversions. A herald carries a message that does not belong to him, and the moment the herald becomes interesting in his own right, the message has a rival.

How can I tell whether I am moved by the preacher or by Christ? Ask what you take home. If on Monday you remember chiefly how good the sermon was, the turn of phrase, the story, the cleverness, the preacher may have become the subject. If you remember Christ, what he has done, what he asks of you, and find yourself praying about it, the message has done its work. Another sign is what happens when the gifted preacher is away: if you stay home, you were following him. None of this means you should prefer dull preaching. It means you should pray for your pastor to be clear, and pray for yourself to listen for the Lord behind the voice.

For worship. God has arranged it this way on purpose. He could have chosen a method that rewarded eloquence, and the gospel would have travelled through the ancient world on the strength of its orators. Instead he chose a message that no amount of skill can make respectable, a crucified man, so that when it saves anybody at all there is no possibility of mistaking whose power did it. The weakness is not a defect in the method; it is the method. And the crucified Lord at its centre needs no polish from us, because he is himself the power of God, and his cross has never once been emptied by anything but our attempts to improve it.
verseByVerse.note: Greek culture prized polished rhetoric; travelling orators were admired like celebrities.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — Christ the Wisdom and Power of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The message of the cross seems foolish to those who are perishing, but to those being saved it is the power of God. Scripture foretold that God would confound the wisdom of the wise. Since the world in its wisdom did not come to know God, God was pleased to save believers through the apparent foolishness of preaching. Jews want miraculous signs and Greeks want wisdom, but Paul preaches a crucified Messiah, an offence to Jews and nonsense to Gentiles, yet to those God calls, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ is God’s power and God’s wisdom.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Theology of the Cross

Luther distinguished a theology of the cross from a theology of glory, and 1:18–25 is its clearest ground. The theology of glory looks for God in power, success and wisdom that make sense on human terms. The theology of the cross finds God revealed in weakness, foolishness and the apparent defeat of Good Friday. The cross was never a fallback plan but God’s plan from eternity, the place where his justice and his love were both satisfied in the same event and in the same Person.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Crucifixion was the ultimate mark of shame and criminal status. The early Christians were staking their standing and their lives on an executed man. Now: The pressure is to make the gospel more palatable: to lead with Jesus as life coach rather than sin-bearer, with personal fulfilment rather than atonement. The cross still offends the wisdom of the age, and the answer is still to preach it.

verseByVerse.quote: For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the cross. It is not the cross considered as an event, but the message about it, spoken out loud by somebody: the message that God saves through a crucified man. God has chosen to save people through an announcement, and the announcement is about an execution. The word for folly is mōria, nonsense (it later gave English its word moron). To the perishing, the cross is not merely unconvincing; it is idiotic, and Paul says so without defensiveness, because he expects it. A message that the natural mind found reasonable would not be this message.

In the flow. For links verse 18 to verse 17: if the message itself is God’s power, dressing it up can only hide it. From here to 2:5 Paul sets out three exhibits of one truth, the message (1:18–25), the people God called by it (1:26–31), and the preacher who brought it (2:1–5), each weak by the world’s measure and full of God’s power.

Being saved. Two present participles, those who are perishing and us who are being saved: two directions of travel, and the same message lands differently depending on which road you are on. And the cross is not merely a message about power; it is God’s power at work, saving people (Romans 1:16).

When your family thinks it is beneath you. You have a brother, or a daughter at university, or a colleague, who is not hostile but kind and faintly embarrassed on your behalf, as if you were an intelligent person with one inexplicable exception. This verse tells you three things. First, it is predicted; you have run into precisely what Paul said would happen. Second, it is not that you explained it badly; Paul explained it better than you, and the folly verdict came in anyway. Third, and this changes how you pray, the difference between the two responses is not intelligence. Both hear the same words; what separates them is which road they are on, and that is God’s business. So answer as well as you can, kindly and without heat, and then pray for him, because what he needs is not a cleverer you but an opened eye.

Isaiah’s word. The quotation is from Isaiah 29:14, about people who honoured God with their lips while their hearts were far from him, and about the wise men of Judah who thought they could manage the Assyrian crisis by clever alliances. Their wisdom perished, not because it was outargued, but because God did something outside its categories.

God has done this before. The cross completes a pattern. He gave Abraham a son at a hundred, took Israel out of Egypt with no army, and brought them home from Babylon by a pagan king’s decree; every time, the experts had established that it could not be done (Isaiah 55:8–9). Then the pattern reached its centre. The scribes and chief priests of Jerusalem and the officials of Rome examined Jesus, weighed him and disposed of him, and they were right on their own terms: he died. On the third day God raised him, and every calculation that had finished him was overturned. That is where Paul sees Isaiah’s word come true at full scale.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is irrational or that Christians should despise thinking. This letter is itself a sustained piece of careful argument. The foolishness is in the content, a crucified Saviour, not in the manner of the people who believe it. We are to be always ready to give a reason (1 Peter 3:15). We are simply told not to be shocked when the reason is found absurd.

Does “being saved” mean I am not saved yet? You are saved, you are being saved, and you will be saved, and all three are true at once. The moment you trusted Christ you were justified, forgiven and adopted, and that can never be undone (Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:8). Now God is working that salvation out in you, freeing you from sin’s power day by day (Philippians 2:12–13). And at Christ’s return he will complete it, raising your body and removing sin altogether (Romans 13:11; 1 Peter 1:5). Paul uses the present tense here because salvation is begun and continuing, to be completed at Christ’s return. It is not uncertain. It is unfinished, and the one who began it will finish it.

parallels.desc: the wisdom of their wise men shall perish

verseByVerse.quote: Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Three questions, and each names a recognised professional. The wise (sophos): the Greek philosopher, the man with an account of reality. The scribe (grammateus): the Jewish scholar of the law, master of the sacred text. The debater of this age (syzētētēs): the professional arguer of the lecture hall, a man who could take either side and win. Between them they represent every avenue by which the ancient world thought truth might be reached: reason, expert handling of revelation, and rhetoric. Where are they? Their wisdom could not save.

The taunt after the battle. The form is borrowed from Isaiah’s taunts: where then are your wise men? (Isaiah 19:12; 33:18). It is the language of a battlefield after the fact, when the confident men who explained beforehand why it would go the other way are nowhere to be found.

Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? By the cross, God showed that all human wisdom was foolish in the matter of knowing him. He did not argue with it. He simply did what it said could not be done, and left it standing in the empty field.

Two wisdoms. The sentence contains two wisdoms, and everything turns on keeping them apart. It was God’s wisdom that arranged matters so that human wisdom, with all its philosophy and religion, would not be able to find him (Romans 1:21–22). The failure is not an accident God worked around; it is the design, so that salvation would be by grace. To know God here means more than knowing that he exists. It means knowing him as he is and trusting him, the knowledge Jesus calls eternal life (John 17:3), and that is exactly what philosophy and religion never reached.

Why would God arrange such a thing? Not because knowledge of him is unavailable. Paul argues elsewhere that the creation broadcasts it continuously, so plainly that nobody is left with an excuse (Romans 1:19–20). The barrier was never a shortage of evidence. It is that the mind doing the looking is not neutral. Human beings do not merely fail to find God; they suppress what they find, because the God who is actually there is not one we would have chosen, and he does not leave us in charge. The problem is moral before it is intellectual, which is why more information alone has never yet converted anybody.

The folly of what we preach. So God closed the route that would have let the clever arrive first, and opened one that anybody can walk: it was his good pleasure. Kērygma is the content of the message, not just the act of preaching. Paul does not say God saves through folly, but through the message the world files under nonsense. The instrument is preaching; the condition is believing. Neither requires a degree.

The Son who makes the Father known. If the world could not know God through its wisdom, how is he known at all? Jesus answered that himself, in a prayer that reads like a commentary on this verse. He thanked his Father for hiding these things from the wise and understanding and revealing them to little children, and then said that no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (Matthew 11:25–27). The road closed in verse 21 has one door, and the door is a Person, which is a mercy with a wide reach: if philosophy were the road, the woman running a household on no sleep and the man whose schooling ended at fourteen would be shut out; instead a professor and a child stand at the same distance from the door. What we preach is not a better philosophy. It is Christ, the only one who has seen the Father and made him known (John 1:18).

Then what about people who never hear the gospel? Scripture is plain that salvation comes through conscious faith in Christ, and faith comes by hearing the word of Christ (Romans 10:13–17; Acts 4:12). Creation and conscience leave everyone without excuse, but they cannot tell anyone that God has given his Son for sinners (Romans 1:20; 2:14–16). That is why this verse is a missionary verse: it pleased God to save through preaching, so the church must send preachers. We do not need to be anxious that God is unjust; the Judge of all the earth will do right, and those who perish are judged for the light they had and rejected. Infants who die in infancy are in a different case: we hold that elect infants are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, 10.3). Parents who have lost a little one may rest their grief on that mercy, and on the Lord who took children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16).

verseByVerse.quote: For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Jews demand signs. Two cultures, two currencies, and the cross is legal tender in neither. Many Jews wanted miraculous proofs of power (Matthew 12:38; John 6:30), not unreasonably: God had authenticated Moses with plagues and Elijah with fire, and they were waiting for a Messiah who would do something visible about Rome. Greeks sought wisdom: a philosophy that satisfied the mind, beautifully argued.

But we preach Christ crucified. Paul gives neither. The verb is present: he kept doing it. He did not lead with the resurrection to soften the entrance, and he did not translate the cross into something more presentable. He went into the most status-obsessed city in Greece and announced an executed criminal. “Crucified” is a perfect participle: the one who was crucified and remains so. The cross is the heart of the message, not an embarrassing detail.

A stumbling block to Jews. Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world, reserved for slaves and rebels. For Jews it also meant being under God’s curse, for a man hanged on a tree is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). A crucified Messiah was not merely a failed one; by their own law he was under God’s curse, a contradiction in terms. So Paul uses the word skandalon, scandal: not an intellectual objection, but a stumbling block, something you trip over and go down.

And folly to Gentiles. The Greek objection was different and just as total. Crucifixion was not a subject for polite society; Cicero said the very word cross should be kept far from a Roman citizen’s thoughts, eyes and ears. Worshipping a crucified Jew was not merely false but tasteless, too grotesque to merit a rebuttal. One of the earliest surviving pictures of the crucifixion is a mocking graffito scratched on a wall in Rome, showing a man worshipping a crucified figure with a donkey’s head, and the caption: Alexamenos worships his god.

To those who are called. Then the sentence turns. Not to those who worked it out, or were open-minded or better educated: called, effectively summoned by God. To some the same Christ crucified is a stumbling block, to others nonsense, and to a third group the identical message is the power and wisdom of God. Nothing about the sermon changed. What changed was that God called them.

Where Christians differ: the general call and the effectual call. Many Christians, Arminians among them (those who hold that God’s grace enables every hearer to believe but can be finally resisted), understand God’s call as an invitation that grace makes it possible to accept or refuse; they want to guard the genuineness of the offer and human responsibility, and those are real concerns. This commentary’s view: the gospel is offered to all who hear it, genuinely offered, and all are commanded to believe (the general call). But Paul here speaks of those who are called as distinct from the rest who hear and stumble. This is the effectual call, God’s inward work by the Spirit that makes the gospel powerful in the elect, so that they come freely (Romans 8:30; Westminster Confession 10.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.1). The first can be refused, and constantly is. The second is God doing in a man what the man could not do in himself. The difference between those who believe and those who mock is God’s calling, not human cleverness.

Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. The cross does not abolish the Jewish hunger for power or the Greek hunger for wisdom; it satisfies both, in the last place either would have looked. They wanted power: here is the true power of God that saves, in a man led out after a flogging, whose crossbeam a passer-by was forced to carry (Mark 15:15, 21). They wanted wisdom: here is the wisdom of God that planned salvation, in an event that looks like the collapse of every plan. The categories were not wrong; they were pointed in the wrong direction. Our own age has the same two hungers, a faith that works and a faith that is intellectually respectable, and both can be ways of staying in charge of what God must be like. The cross refuses both demands on our terms and meets both on God’s: the power that raises the dead, and the wisdom by which a holy God is just in forgiving sinners (Romans 3:26).

If only the called believe, why should I evangelise or pray? Because the call comes through the preaching. God does not call people in a vacuum; he calls them through the message of Christ crucified, spoken by ordinary believers (Romans 10:14–17). The effectual call is not a reason to stay silent but the reason to speak with hope: you do not have to produce faith in anyone, and you cannot, but God can, and he has chosen to do it through words like yours. So pray, because the calling is his; and speak, because the calling comes by the word. Without the effectual call, evangelism would be hopeless. With it, no one is beyond reach.

For worship. Consider what he did. He could have come with the signs they demanded; he had done greater things with a word, and twelve legions of angels were available for the asking (Matthew 26:53). He chose instead the one form of death designed to make a man contemptible, and went to it deliberately, in public, outside a city wall, between two criminals, for people who were at that moment shouting for it. The Jews asked for a sign and were given the only one that could save them. The Greeks asked for wisdom and were handed the wisdom of God with nails through it. There has never been a moment in the history of the universe when God looked less like God, or was more fully himself (Colossians 2:14–15).
verseByVerse.note: Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world, reserved for slaves and rebels; for Jews, a crucified man was under God’s curse.

verseByVerse.quote: For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The foolishness of God. Read flatly, the sentence is close to blasphemy, and Paul knows exactly what he is doing. He speaks ironically, from inside the world’s verdict: very well, take your own categories and follow them where they lead. What looks like foolishness on God’s part, saving through a crucified man, is wiser than all human wisdom combined.

The comparison is not close. Set the cross against the accumulated wisdom of the human race, every philosophy, every ethical system, every scheme for making people good, and ask which of them has actually dealt with guilt. Not managed it, or explained it away: dealt with it. The wisest scheme the world has devised leaves a man with his record and his conscience intact and no remedy for either. What the world calls foolish removed the record.

The weakness of God. The cross looked like weakness: the Son of God helpless, mocked, dying. Rome’s machinery of force was employed that Friday to full effect, and it worked: the man died. Three days later he was alive, and nothing in Rome’s armoury could put him back in the tomb. By the cross God defeated sin, death and Satan (Colossians 2:15). What was operating in that tomb was not weakness with a good result but strength of a kind the categories had no room for.

Into your own weakness. Take this verse into your own weakness. There is a persistent assumption in us that God works through our strong points: that he will use the areas where we are competent and impressive, and that our weaknesses are the parts of us he has to work around. This verse says the opposite about him, and Paul will later say the opposite about himself: it was in his weakness that Christ’s power rested on him, which is why he stopped asking for the thorn to be removed (2 Corinthians 12:9–10).

So should I not bother developing my abilities? No. Your abilities are gifts from God, and you should develop them and use them gladly (Matthew 25:14–30). The point is where you put your trust. Strength used in dependence on God is a tool in his hand; strength trusted in instead of God is an idol, and he will often break it. And weakness is not a virtue in itself; it is the place where we stop pretending and lean on him, which is why he does so much there. Work hard, and pray as one who knows the results are his.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells them to look at their own church. Not many of them were clever, powerful or well-born by worldly standards. God deliberately chose what the world thinks foolish, weak and contemptible to shame the proud, so that no human being can boast before him. It is God who has placed them in Christ Jesus, and Christ has become for them wisdom from God: their righteousness, their holiness and their redemption. So, as Scripture says, anyone who boasts should boast in the Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
Boasting and Grace Alone

Verses 28–29 carry the logic of grace into the life of a church. If salvation depended even partly on wisdom, power or birth, some people could boast. When God saves fishermen, tax collectors, former persecutors and people the world overlooks, the only boast left is in the grace that did what merit never could. God’s choice of the lowly is not a preference for lowliness for its own sake; it removes every ground of pride.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinth’s social ladder was steep: citizens over freed slaves over slaves, the educated over the illiterate, patrons over clients. The church crossed every one of those lines, and the crossing came from the gospel of the cross. Now: A church that quietly copies the class and status lines of its surrounding culture denies in practice what it confesses in its creed. The cross makes a community where the only boast is in the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider your calling. Blepete: look at it. Paul has argued the point theologically for eight verses; now he tells them to check it against the evidence in the room. The proof of God’s method is sitting in their own congregation.

According to the flesh. That is the literal phrase behind worldly standards. The three terms are the standard triad of ancient status: education, influence and birth, which determined where you sat and who returned your greeting. Many of the Corinthian believers were probably slaves, freedmen and workers.

Not many, not none. He does not say none, and the church at Corinth proves that too: Crispus the synagogue ruler, Gaius who was host to the whole church, and Erastus the city treasurer (Romans 16:23), a man holding public office. The gospel is not a movement of the poor that excludes the comfortable; God saves treasurers as well as slaves. But they were the exceptions, and everybody in the room knew it.

What the critics said. The outside world certainly knew it. More than a century later the pagan critic Celsus was still sneering that Christianity was a religion of wool-workers, cobblers and laundry-workers, who would say nothing in front of educated men but got hold of children and women in back rooms. He meant it as a demolition; he was describing what Paul says God did on purpose.

To shame the strong. God chose (the verb comes three times in verses 27–28) the people the world overlooks, on purpose: not to bypass the strong but to shame them, by the simple fact of the outcome. By saving the weak, God shows that salvation has nothing to do with human strength. When the people who could not have found God by wisdom are manifestly full of God, the whole apparatus of wisdom stands exposed as useless for the one thing that finally mattered.

For the ordinary Christian. You are not a leader, you have no platform and no obvious gift, your life has been spent on work nobody records, and you have settled into believing that the real work of God is done by other people and your part is to make up the numbers. The verse is not a description of your limitations but of God’s preference. He did not accept the unimpressive because nobody better applied. He chose them, for a reason that has nothing to do with their inadequacy and everything to do with what he intends to show.

Not a new policy. He picked a childless couple to found a nation, a shepherd boy over seven older brothers, a young woman in a village of no reputation to carry the Son of God, and fishermen and a tax collector to take the gospel to the world (1 Samuel 16:7; Luke 1:52; Matthew 11:25).

The Lord came by the same road. When God sent his own Son, he sent him by this road too: born to parents who could offer only the poor family’s sacrifice of two birds (Luke 2:24; Leviticus 12:8), raised in a town people sneered at (John 1:46), known in his own village as the carpenter (Mark 6:3), and in the end despised and rejected by men (Isaiah 53:3). The church at Corinth looked like its Lord. God did not choose weak people in spite of having a strong Saviour; he chose them because his Saviour came weak, and the shaming of the wise that began in a manger was finished on a cross.

Should the church then not bother reaching the educated and influential? It should reach everyone, and Paul himself reasoned with philosophers in Athens and spoke before governors and kings (Acts 17:22–31; 26:1–29). Not many is not none, and the gospel is for the powerful as much as the poor. What this verse forbids is courting people because of their status, giving the rich man the good seat (James 2:1–4), or thinking the church will be strengthened chiefly by attracting impressive people. A church that only seeks the influential has forgotten how it began. Reach everyone, honour everyone, and expect God to fill his house mostly with people the world overlooks.

For worship. He is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). The Son who could have gathered the wise and the well-born around his throne has filled his house with wool-workers and cobblers, slaves and freedmen, and people like us, and he presents them to his Father without a trace of embarrassment: behold, I and the children God has given me (Hebrews 2:13). The world looked at the church in Corinth and saw a back room full of nobodies. The Father looked and saw the brothers and sisters of his Son, chosen before they were born, called by name, and already his.

verseByVerse.quote: God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Low and despised. The language intensifies: not merely the foolish and the weak now, but the low (agenē, without family, of no birth) and the despised (exouthenēmena, treated as nothing).

Things that are not. Then a phrase that goes past every social category: ta mē onta, the things that do not exist, the people whose names are on no list and whose absence would alter nothing. In a Roman colony obsessed with rank this was no metaphor: a slave had almost no legal personality. Things that are not are the nobodies; things that are are the somebodies. God uses nobodies to nullify (katargeō) the somebodies.

God’s signature. The phrase is God’s signature. He is the God who calls into existence the things that do not exist (Romans 4:17). So when he builds a church out of nobodies, he is not making the best of poor material; he is doing what he has always done, in the way he has always done it.

The God who raises the dead. Romans 4:17 sets the two halves of God’s method side by side: he gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist. And Paul goes on to say where that power was finally shown: in the God who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Romans 4:24–25). At the cross the world counted Christ among the things that are not, a dead man in a borrowed tomb. On the third day God called him out of it. The church of nobodies at Corinth is the same power at work again, people the world counts as nothing raised with Christ into a life the somebodies of Corinth could never buy.

No boasting before God. This is the sentence the whole chapter has been walking towards. This is the purpose of election: God’s free choice, before the foundation of the world, of particular people to be saved in Christ, a choice grounded in his own love and not in anything he found in them (Ephesians 1:4–5). If he chose people for their wisdom, power or birth, or saved by achievement, effort or sincerity, somebody would arrive with a contribution and a reason to be pleased with himself. By choosing nobodies, he excludes all boasting (Romans 3:27; Ephesians 2:8–9). When Isaiah, a prophet and a master of words, saw the Lord high and lifted up, he did not mention his gifts; he cried woe to himself, because he was a man of unclean lips (Isaiah 6:1–5). Nobody boasts in that light, and the only people who can stand there at all are people brought in by grace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God chose people because they were lowly. Lowliness is not merit either. God chose freely, and the lowliness of those chosen displays that freedom.

For the one who feels like a nothing. Some readers struggle not with pride but with the settled sense of being a nobody: years that produced nothing anyone could point to. This verse is addressed to you. First, God did not choose people despite their being nothing, as if he had to overlook something; the nothings are what he chose. Second, he chose them to bring to nothing things that are. He is not collecting the overlooked in order to keep them safely at the back. He is deploying them to dismantle everything the world has been impressed by. That is not a consolation prize. It is a commission.

If no one may boast, is it wrong to feel pleased with something I have done well? No. Paul himself rejoices over the work God did through him (15:10; 2 Corinthians 1:12). There is a right gladness in work well done, a child well raised, a kindness that landed. The difference is where the credit goes. Boasting before God treats the thing as my ground of standing, my reason to be accepted, my proof that I am better than others. Gratitude receives it as his gift, worked through me, and gives him the praise. A simple check: can you rejoice just as much when God does the same through someone else? If so, you are probably giving thanks, not boasting.

verseByVerse.quote: And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of him. Literally from him (ex autou): God is the source of your being in Christ, not your searching. Union with Christ is God’s work, not yours, and every one of the four gifts that follow arrives by that route.

Became to us. Paul does not write that Christ gives us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. He writes that Christ became them to us. These are not commodities dispensed from a distance; you do not receive four parcels; you receive him, and he turns out to be all four.

The end of shopping. That is the cure for Corinth. They were shopping: wisdom from Apollos, status from their gifts, standing from their faction. Paul’s answer is that the shopping was over before it began. Everything they were assembling piecemeal was already theirs in one Person.

Wisdom. The city was full of wisdom for sale, and it was standing in front of them, in Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). That does not mean a Christian knows more about everything. It means he knows the one thing on which everything else finally depends: who God is, and how a guilty man may stand before him.

Righteousness. Christ is our right standing before God. His righteousness is counted to us: justification (Romans 3:22; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). Not that God has made you a good person and now accepts you, but that in Christ his record is credited to you and yours charged to him. Luther called it an alien righteousness: it comes from outside you, not produced in you, but reckoned to you, and therefore not subject to how your week has gone. It answers the question underneath all religion: how can I possibly be right with God? You cannot. He became it for you.

Where Christians differ: imputed righteousness. Some deny that Christ’s righteousness is counted to believers, saying instead that God makes us righteous inwardly, and accepts us on that basis. This commentary’s view: Christ became our righteousness. Our right standing with God is not our own inner goodness but Christ’s obedience counted to us, received by faith alone (Romans 4:5–6; 5:19). Sanctification, which follows, is the inward renewal; it is distinct from justification but never separated from it. Those who hold the other view, including the Roman Catholic Church, rightly insist that grace really changes people, and Paul agrees; he simply will not let the change become the ground of our acceptance. Both are found in Christ, so the one who has Christ has both.

And sanctification. Christ is our holiness, the word of verse 2. In him we are set apart for God, before ever we begin to grow holier, and from him we receive the Spirit who makes us holy. That is why this letter can call the Corinthians sanctified while telling them to stop visiting prostitutes (6:15–20). The status comes first and the change follows from it; a Christian does not become holy in order to be accepted, but works out a holiness he has already been given.

And redemption. Apolytrōsis: release, especially release secured by a ransom, as when a slave or captive was set free. Christ is our release, bought by the price of his blood (Ephesians 1:7). It looks back to a price paid, and it looks forward to a deliverance not yet complete, when the body itself is finally free at the resurrection (Romans 8:23).

The whole of a Christian’s life. Set them side by side and they cover the whole of a Christian’s existence: wisdom for the mind that could not find God, righteousness for the guilt that could not be removed, sanctification for the life that could not be cleaned, redemption for the body that will not last. All four in one place.

If Christ is my sanctification, do I need to make any effort? Yes, and gladly. Paul tells the same Corinthians to flee sexual immorality, to discipline the body, and to be steadfast and immovable (6:18; 9:27; 15:58). Christ being your holiness does not make you passive; it makes your effort hopeful. You work out your salvation because God is at work in you (Philippians 2:12–13), and the Spirit you received from Christ is the power by which you fight. The difference from religion is the direction: you are not striving to become acceptable, you are striving because you are accepted, and every step of growth is drawn from him. Effort without Christ is self-improvement; Christ without effort is a misunderstanding.

parallels.desc: the LORD is our righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boast in the Lord. Paul cites Jeremiah 9:24 in shortened form, and the full sentence (Jeremiah 9:23–24) is the whole argument of this chapter written six centuries earlier. Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows the LORD.

Wisdom, might, riches. Set that beside verse 26, wise, powerful, of noble birth, and you can see why Paul reached for this text. He has been preaching Jeremiah’s sermon to Corinth, and the three grounds of human boasting have not altered since; only the vocabulary moves.

Not stop boasting, but boast in the right thing. The verse does not say: stop boasting. The instinct to have something to point to, some answer to whether your life amounts to anything, is not removed when a person becomes a Christian. It is redirected; Paul glories freely in the cross (Galatians 6:14). The question is never whether you will glory in something, but in what. And Jeremiah’s right boast is not that you have achieved anything, but that you understand and know the LORD. Even the boast is not about you.

The LORD is Jesus. In Jeremiah the one to be known is the LORD, the covenant name of God, the name later generations would not even pronounce. Paul condenses the whole sentence to boast in the Lord and applies it, without a syllable of explanation and in a context that points to Christ, to the crucified man he has been preaching since verse 18. It is simply where the sentence lands: the Lord in whom we boast is the Lord Jesus, Yahweh come in the flesh.

In the flow. Boasting runs through the whole letter (3:21; 4:7; 5:6), and the next paragraph applies the same rule to the preacher himself (2:1–5). A church that has learned to boast only in the Lord has nothing left to build a faction with.

What does boasting in the Lord sound like in real life? It sounds like telling people what God has done rather than what you have done: how he found you, how he carried you through the illness, how he answered a prayer, how Christ forgave a sin you thought unforgivable. It sounds like giving the credit away when you are praised, not with false modesty, but with honest thanks. It sounds like speaking of Christ with the same warmth you would use for a person you admire. And on the bad days it sounds like this: I have nothing, but I have him. Boasting in the Lord is not a religious technique. It is what people naturally do about the thing they treasure most.

On a Tuesday. Recall the last time you felt diminished and what your mind reached for to restore itself: a qualification, a child doing well, a theological position more rigorous than the other person’s. That reserve is your boast, whatever you would say in church, and time can take every one of them from you. The boast Jeremiah names cannot.

For worship. The chapter that began with people boasting in Paul, in Apollos, in Cephas, in their own eloquence and knowledge and rank, ends by taking every one of those props away and putting a single name in the empty space. And the name will bear the weight. Wisdom fades, might is buried and riches pass to someone else, but the Lord we boast in has been raised from the dead and will never die again (Romans 6:9). Nothing that happens to us can make him less worth boasting about. A church with nothing to bring him has been given the one boast that will still be true on the last day, and will still be ringing after it.

parallels.desc: let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me

2.title: The Spirit, the Cross, and True Wisdom
2.overview:
Paul continues his answer to a church that prized clever speech and secret wisdom. He first came to Corinth not as a dazzling orator, but weak, nervous and resolved to speak of nothing except Jesus Christ and him crucified, so that their faith would rest on God’s power. Yet the gospel is not anti-intellectual. There is a wisdom Paul speaks among the mature: God’s wisdom, hidden and now revealed, which the rulers of this age did not grasp.

This wisdom cannot be discovered; God has revealed it by his Spirit, who knows God’s depths and taught the apostles their words. A person without the Spirit cannot accept these things, but believers have the mind of Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul recalls his arrival in Corinth. He did not come with impressive rhetoric; he had made up his mind to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ, crucified. He came in weakness, fear and great trembling, relying not on persuasive technique but on the Spirit’s power, so that their faith would rest on God’s power.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Theology of Proclamation

Paul’s plain preaching is not only a pastoral strategy; it comes from what he believes. The power of the gospel is the Spirit working through the word of the cross, not the preacher’s skill, the brilliance of the argument or emotional pressure on the audience. The preacher is the instrument, not the cause. If people are not converted by the preaching of Christ crucified, they will not be converted by anything the preacher can add.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In first-century Corinth the travelling orator was a celebrity who could hold an audience spellbound, charge a fee and move on. Paul refused to compete on those terms. Now: The modern pressure is to make church “compelling” through production values, platform charisma and emotional manipulation. Paul’s answer is not to be deliberately dull, but to trust the cross to do what polished performance cannot: save people.

verseByVerse.quote: And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with lofty speech or wisdom. For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Chapter 2 carries on the argument against worldly wisdom. Paul first preached Christ crucified, in weakness, so that their faith would rest on God’s power (vv. 1–5). There is a true wisdom, God’s plan of salvation in Christ, hidden and now revealed, which the rulers of this age did not grasp, or they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (vv. 6–9). It is known only by the Spirit, who searches the depths of God and teaches the apostles the very words (vv. 10–13). The natural person cannot receive these things; the spiritual person can, and has the mind of Christ (vv. 14–16). It is one of the Bible’s key passages on revelation, inspiration and illumination.

When I came to you. Paul goes back to his first visit, about AD 50 (Acts 18:1). The church has since heard Apollos and would have preferred more polish. And I ties this to the end of chapter 1: foolish message, unimpressive converts (1:26–31), unimpressive preacher; from first to last the power was plainly God’s.

Lofty speech. Hyperochē means superiority, excellence: the elevated style of the professional orator. Some manuscripts read mystery of God instead of testimony of God; the ESV notes this. Either way, the content is God’s message about Christ.

I decided. Ekrina, I reached a verdict: Paul did not drift into a plain style; he weighed it and decided. A popular reading says he had tried philosophy at Athens (Acts 17), found it a failure, and arrived at Corinth chastened. It is probably wrong: Luke does not present Athens as a failure (Acts 17:34), and Paul still quotes a pagan poet in this letter (15:33). He is describing a settled resolve about content.

The centre that governs everything. Nothing except Jesus Christ and him crucified cannot be taken woodenly: this very letter deals with lawsuits, marriage, food offered to idols, worship, spiritual gifts and the resurrection body. The cross was not one topic among many but the lens for all of them. When the Corinthians squabble over food, he ends with the brother for whom Christ died (8:11). When they abuse the Supper, he takes them back to the night he was betrayed (11:23). Every practical problem in this church is finally settled at a cross.

And him crucified. Not Jesus Christ alone, who could have been made respectable as a great teacher or moral example: him crucified. Paul deliberately keeps the offensive part in the centre of the frame, because the moment you remove it you have a religion the world can admire and nobody needs saving by.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul preached only on the crucifixion and nothing else. He taught the whole counsel of God (Acts 20:27), and all of it flowed from the cross. Nor is it a defence of anti-intellectualism: the man writing it was trained under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3) and is in the middle of a sustained argument. And a congregation fed only on the mechanics of justification, never told how to be a husband or handle money or forgive, is not being fed the way this letter feeds.

What is the message of Christ crucified? That Jesus, the eternal Son of God made man, lived the perfect life we have not lived, and then died on the cross in the place of sinners, bearing the punishment our sins deserved, so that God is just in forgiving us (Romans 3:25–26; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24). That he was buried and raised on the third day, proving the payment accepted (15:3–4). And that everyone who turns from sin and trusts him is forgiven, counted righteous and made a child of God, freely, without any contribution of his own. If you can say that clearly to a friend, you can do what Paul did at Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: And I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling, and my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Weakness, fear and trembling. This should not be made more dignified than it was. Paul had just been beaten with rods and jailed at Philippi, run out of Thessalonica and then Berea by mobs, and met polite mockery at Athens (Acts 16:22–17:34). He arrived alone. And during that stay the Lord appeared to him in a vision at night and said: do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent (Acts 18:9–10). You do not say that to a man who is not afraid. The fear was real, and Paul puts it in writing to a church that preferred more impressive speakers. He is not embarrassed by it; he is arguing from it.

Not in plausible words. Peithos, persuasive, means the techniques of rhetoric designed to win over an audience. Paul refused to compete with the sophists on their terms. The KJV’s enticing words of man’s wisdom follows later manuscripts; the earliest lack of man’s, and the sense is the same.

Demonstration of the Spirit. Apodeixis was a technical term in rhetoric: a compelling proof, a demonstration that settles a matter. Paul claims something better than persuasion, and locates it outside himself. The proof of his message was not his technique but the Spirit’s power: convicting hearts, bringing new birth, and in the apostolic ministry accompanied by signs (2 Corinthians 12:12; 1 Thessalonians 1:5).

Resting on God’s power. This is the point of the paragraph, and it is about foundations. A faith produced by a persuasive man lasts exactly as long as that man remains persuasive, and a cleverer speaker can undo it, which is precisely what has begun to happen at Corinth. And when a preacher falls, or turns out to be ordinary, everyone whose faith was built on him finds nothing underneath. Faith that rests on God’s power stands.

Weak in him. Paul’s trembling was not an accident that the message happened to survive. It matched the message. The gospel he carried was about a Lord who was crucified in weakness but lives by the power of God, and Paul says that he and his companions are weak in him too, yet live with him by the power of God (2 Corinthians 13:4). A swaggering herald of a crucified King would contradict his own announcement. The weakness of the preacher was a small copy of the weakness of the cross, and the power that raised Christ from the dead was at work in both.

Fear is not disqualifying. It is easy to assume the people God uses are the confident ones, and that if you were less prone to going dry-mouthed when the conversation turns to Christ, you would be useful. The founding missionary of the Gentile world arrived at Corinth shaking. Fear is not the opposite of usefulness, and confidence is not the qualification.

What does the Spirit’s demonstration look like today? Chiefly what it looked like at Corinth: people convicted of sin, turning to Christ, and being changed. The church at Corinth was itself the proof: idolaters, thieves and drunkards washed, sanctified and justified (6:9–11). In the apostolic period the Spirit also confirmed the message with signs, and this commentary holds that those sign gifts belonged to that foundational time, because Scripture presents them as the marks that authenticated the apostles and their message (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many faithful Christians believe they continue, and both sides agree on what matters most here. But the greatest miracle has never ceased: a dead heart made alive through a plain message. Look for that, pray for it, and do not despise it because it is quiet. Every conversion is the power of God on display.
verseByVerse.note: Paul came to Corinth after the cool reception at Athens.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Yet Paul does teach wisdom among the mature: not the wisdom of this age or its passing rulers, but God’s secret wisdom, planned before time for our glory. Had the rulers understood it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. God has revealed it by his Spirit, in words the Spirit teaches; the unspiritual person cannot receive it, but believers have the mind of Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit and the Knowledge of God

Verses 10–16 are the main ground for what is called the inward witness of the Holy Spirit. Calvin rested the believer’s certainty about Scripture not on outside proofs but on the Spirit’s own witness in the heart, and Paul’s argument here is the foundation: the things of God are spiritually discerned, the Spirit alone reveals them, and he has been given to those who are in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians’ preference for polished rhetoric over Paul’s plain preaching was at root a preference for a wisdom they could judge by their own natural abilities. Now: It is tempting to judge the gospel by academic or cultural standards, as if the question were whether Christianity can hold its own in a university seminar. Good reasons matter, and apologetics serves evangelism, but it cannot replace it: only the Spirit can open eyes to see the Lord of glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet among the mature we do impart wisdom, although it is not a wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are doomed to pass away. But we impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which God decreed before the ages for our glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Among the mature. After a chapter and a half of demolishing wisdom, Paul says the Christian message is wisdom after all, just not of a kind the world can recognise or reach.

Not two tiers of Christian. Read carelessly, the sentence sets up an inner circle trusted with deeper material, as in the mystery religions of Corinth. Two things rule it out. The first is the word itself: teleioi, the mature, the grown-up. Here it means all who have the Spirit and accept the gospel, as opposed to the natural person (v. 14). It is not a rank but an age: Paul’s contrast a few lines later is between adults and infants in Christ (3:1), one category at different stages.

The sting. The second is the sting. The Corinthians regarded themselves as the mature elite. Paul says among the mature we impart wisdom, and a few lines later tells them he could not do it with them, because they were still on milk and squabbling like children (3:1–3). It is a rebuke delivered by holding the door open and observing that they cannot yet walk through it.

Doomed to pass away. The rulers of this age, who crucified Jesus (v. 8), are being brought to nothing, passing away with this age.

A hidden wisdom. Literally, God’s wisdom in a mystery. Paul’s word is mystērion, and in his hands a mystery is never a puzzle to be solved but a secret God has decided to tell (Romans 16:25–26; Ephesians 3:4–6), disclosed not to an elite few but to the whole church. And the secret has a name. Paul calls it God’s mystery, which is Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:2–3), and sums it up for Gentile believers as Christ in you, the hope of glory (Colossians 1:27).

Decreed before the ages. Proorizō means predestined, determined beforehand. Before time began, God planned salvation through Christ crucified. The cross was not God’s recovery from an unexpected disaster but the arrangement made in eternity, before there was anybody to be saved by it (Ephesians 1:4; Revelation 13:8).

For our glory. Not merely our rescue: the eternal decree had our glory in view, the glorification of believers, sharing the glory of the Christ who is in them (Romans 8:30; Colossians 1:27). This letter will spell out later what that means: a body raised imperishable, in glory, in power (15:42–43). God intended not simply to get us out of trouble but to bring us somewhere.

Does “for our glory” put us at the centre instead of God? No. Our glory is the glory of sharing his: being made like Christ, seeing his face, reflecting his likeness (Romans 8:29; 2 Corinthians 3:18). It is the glory of a mirror catching the sun, not of a lamp lit by itself. And Scripture says the whole plan is to the praise of his glorious grace (Ephesians 1:6, 12, 14). God’s glory and our good are not rivals. He is most glorified in giving his people the greatest gift, which is himself, and we are most glad when we receive it. So you may long for the glory to come without any embarrassment. It is God’s idea, and it will be all of his doing.

On a Tuesday. If God settled this before the ages, then the thing you are most anxious about is happening inside a plan that was complete before the world was made. That does not tell you how it will go. It tells you that it is not being improvised, and that the same decree which reaches back before time reaches forward to a glory you have not yet seen (Ephesians 1:4; Romans 8:29–30).

verseByVerse.quote: None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
None of the rulers. Who are the rulers? Some take them as the human authorities: Pilate, Herod, Caiaphas, the Sanhedrin. Others take them as the spiritual powers working behind them (Ephesians 6:12). The best reading is probably both; the New Testament shows Satan operating through named human beings at exactly this point (Luke 22:3; John 13:27). They thought they were getting rid of a troublemaker; they were carrying out God’s plan.

Was the cross a blunder? If they had known, they would not have done it. Does that mean Satan miscalculated, and that if the powers had been better informed the atonement would never have happened? The New Testament will not let us rest there, and the answer is one of the most important things a Christian can grasp about how God governs the world. Peter puts both halves in a single sentence at Pentecost: Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and you crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). Not one clause qualifying the other. The plan was fixed, and the men who executed it were lawless and guilty. The believers in Jerusalem say the same when they pray, naming Herod, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered to do whatever God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:27–28). They freely did what they wanted. What they wanted had been decreed.

Blind because they were evil. So the ignorance here is real, and it is culpable. The powers were not victims of insufficient briefing; they were blind because they were evil, and their blindness was the very thing God used. This is the pattern of Joseph and his brothers written across cosmic history: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). The devil got exactly what he wanted, and it destroyed him: through death the Son destroyed the one who has the power of death (Hebrews 2:14).

When someone has wronged you. Here is comfort for anyone on the receiving end of malice. You are not obliged to believe that what was done to you was good, or that the person who did it meant anything but harm. The cross settles that God does not require evil to be innocent in order to make it serve him. The worst act in the history of the world is the one he used to save it. So bring what was done to you to the cross. Do not call the evil good, and do not tell yourself God was absent. Tell him what was done, and then, when you are able, say with Joseph: you meant it for evil, but God meant it for good. It may take years before you see how.

The Lord of glory. Lord of glory echoes the Old Testament’s names for God: Psalm 24 asks who this King of glory is, and answers: the LORD of hosts (Psalm 24:7–10; 29:3). Paul attaches that title, without a word of explanation, to a man his readers knew had been flogged and nailed up outside a city wall between two criminals. The one they crucified was God the Son. It is a stunning phrase and an exact one: because Christ is one person with two natures, what is true of either nature may be said of the person.

Did God die on the cross? The person who died was God the Son, so in that sense yes, and the Bible says so (Acts 20:28). But he died in his human nature, not his divine nature. His body died and his human soul was separated from it; his divine nature, which cannot die, did not cease, and the Trinity was never broken apart. That is not a technicality. It means the one who bore your sin was not a lesser being but God himself, so the sacrifice has infinite worth; and it means he truly died as a man, so he could stand in a man’s place. Only one who is both God and man could do both.

For worship. The King of glory came to his own gates and they did not lift up their heads; they crucified him. He made the wood and the iron in the nails, and held the hearts of the men who drove them beating through every hour of it. And he did not come down, because coming down would have saved him and lost us (John 1:10–11). The Lord of glory was crucified for us, and his glory was never brighter than in that hour (John 12:23; 17:1).

verseByVerse.quote: But, as it is written, “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him”— these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No eye has seen. This sentence is often quoted on its own, at funerals and on cards, as a statement that heaven is beyond imagining, and that turns it inside out. It loosely quotes Isaiah 64:4, with echoes of 65:17, but the main clause is in verse 10: God has revealed these things. Quoting verse 9 without verse 10 makes Paul say the opposite of what he wrote.

Three faculties ruled out. The citation closes every route: observation (eye), tradition (ear), and the religious imagination at full stretch (heart). That leaves one possibility: God had to say it himself.

Prepared for those who love him. What God has prepared includes salvation in Christ now as well as glory to come: the hidden wisdom of a crucified Lord of glory. Isaiah had prayed for a God who would rend the heavens and come down (Isaiah 64:1). Many eyes saw Jesus of Nazareth and many ears heard him, and still they did not see who he was. When Peter confessed him as the Christ, the Son of the living God, Jesus told him that flesh and blood had not revealed this to him, but his Father in heaven (Matthew 16:16–17). That is this verse in a single scene: the thing prepared is Christ, and only God can show him.

Revealed to us. Apokalyptō means unveiled. Us refers first to the apostles, through whom God gave the revelation that became the New Testament, and then to all believers who receive it.

The depths of God. Searches does not mean the Spirit is exploring a God he does not yet fully know; it is the language of complete access to God’s inmost thoughts and purposes. Only someone who is himself God can know the depths of God: a strong text for the Spirit’s deity.

The same Spirit in ordinary believers. The Spirit with full access to the interior life of God is given to ordinary believers. That is how a person with no education can read a page of Scripture and genuinely meet God there, while a hostile expert reads the identical page and finds nothing but literature.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we know everything about heaven. Much remains unseen (1 John 3:2). But the heart of God’s plan is revealed.

Is the Holy Spirit a person or a power? A person, and God. Only a person searches, knows, teaches and can be grieved (v. 13; Ephesians 4:30), and only God knows the depths of God. He is not an influence God sends out, like warmth from a fire; he is the third person of the Trinity, equal with the Father and the Son, who comes to live in believers himself. So we speak of him as he, not it. And we may pray to him, worship him and rely on him as we do the Father and the Son, while knowing that his delight is to point us to Christ (John 16:14).

For worship. Standing at a graveside, we are not reduced to saying that we cannot imagine what has happened to the one we loved. We can say a great deal, because God has told us: that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8); that the dead in Christ will rise (1 Thessalonians 4:16); that this perishable body will put on the imperishable (15:53); that he will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4). The Christian at a funeral is the one person in the room who has been told. God did not leave us guessing; he sent his own Spirit out of his own depths to tell us what he has prepared.

parallels.desc: from of old no one has heard or perceived

verseByVerse.quote: For who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might understand the things freely given us by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? Paul supplies an analogy so ordinary that it is easy to miss how much it settles. No one can know what you are thinking unless you tell them. Consider someone you have lived alongside for thirty years: you can predict how they will react, and they still surprise you. There is a room in every human being that no one else has entered, and the only occupant is the person himself. God sees into it (Psalm 139:1–4), but no other human being does.

So also the Spirit of God. Now scale that up. If one finite creature is closed to another, there is no route from the outside into the interior life of God: however clever the investigator, he is standing at a door with no handle on his side. Only God’s Spirit knows God’s thoughts. The Spirit is one with God, sharing his inner life, yet is also a distinct person who reveals (v. 10) and teaches (v. 13).

Not the spirit of the world. It is the mindset and wisdom of fallen humanity, and behind it, perhaps, the evil spirit at work in the disobedient (Ephesians 2:2). It is the outlook a person absorbs simply by living here: the instincts about what matters, what success looks like, what is faintly ridiculous. It is competent within its own range, assessing a career or a reputation, but it has no equipment for the things of God.

But the Spirit who is from God. Believers have received the Spirit from God (Romans 8:9): the door was opened from within. God has not merely sent information about himself; he has given the one person who has always been inside, and he has given him to ordinary believers in a quarrelsome congregation in a port city.

Freely given. Charizomai, from the same root as grace: the things graced to us. Here is the double gift: God gives, and then God gives the capacity to know what he has given. Without the second gift the first would sit unrecognised, like a man holding a deed in a language he cannot read.

All that the Father has is mine. Jesus described this verse before Paul wrote it. On the night before the cross he told his disciples that the Spirit of truth would glorify him, because he would take what was Christ’s and declare it to them; and he added that all the Father has is his (John 16:14–15). The things freely given us by God are the Father’s things, held by the Son and opened to us by the Spirit. The Spirit never shows us a God behind Christ’s back. Every depth of God he opens turns out to have Christ at the centre of it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers have private revelations beyond Scripture. The Spirit helps us understand what God has given and revealed in his word.

If I have the Spirit, why does my Bible reading so often feel dry? Because illumination is not the same as excitement. The Spirit’s work is to make you understand and believe what is there, and he often does it slowly, like rain soaking into soil rather than a flash flood. Dryness can come from tiredness, distraction, unconfessed sin, or simply a season God uses to teach you to keep going by faith. Keep reading, ask him before you open the page, read slowly enough to notice what it actually says, and talk to him about it as you go (Psalm 119:18). Many believers find that a passage which seemed dull on Tuesday is the one that holds them up on Friday.

verseByVerse.quote: And we impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Words taught by the Spirit. The claim moves a step further: not merely that the Spirit gave the message, but that he was involved in the wording. This is a key text for verbal inspiration: the Spirit guided the apostles’ very words (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21).

Why the words matter. Inspiration does not mean that God gave the apostles a general impression which they then dressed in whatever language came to hand; the Spirit superintended the expression as well as the substance. That is why Scripture can be studied at the level of a single word. If the ideas alone were inspired, the words would be packaging.

The promise of the upper room. Paul’s claim rests on a promise Jesus made: the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father would send in his name, would teach them all things and bring to their remembrance all that he had said to them (John 14:26), and would guide them into all the truth (John 16:13). So the New Testament is not the church’s memories of Jesus, slowly improved. It is Christ himself keeping his word to teach his people through the men he sent, and to hear them is to hear him (Luke 10:16).

Real men, God’s words. The human authors were not suppressed: Paul’s Greek does not read like Luke’s, and this same letter has its author failing to remember whom he baptised (1:16). The Spirit used real men, with their own styles and limitations, and the result is exactly what he intended to say.

Interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual. The last clause is genuinely difficult. The Greek is compressed (pneumatikois pneumatika synkrinontes): literally, combining spiritual things with spiritual. It may mean explaining spiritual truths to spiritual people (the ESV text), comparing spiritual things with spiritual things, or expressing spiritual truths in spiritual words. The ESV notes these alternatives. What is not in doubt is the direction of Paul’s argument: the Spirit’s truths are conveyed in the Spirit’s words and received by the Spirit’s people.

Scripture interprets Scripture. The second rendering describes something Christians do constantly, whether or not Paul meant it here: an obscure verse is read in the light of a clear one (Westminster Confession 1.9). That is why the person who has read all of it will understand any part of it better than the person who knows three favourite chapters very well.

Where Christians differ: inspiration. Some say the Bible contains God’s word but that its words are merely human, and may contain errors. This commentary’s view: Paul says the words, not only the ideas, were taught by the Spirit. Scripture is God-breathed in all its parts, without error in all it affirms, while using the personalities and styles of its human authors (Westminster 1.4–5, 8; 1689 1.4–5, 8). The Spirit did not dictate mechanically, but guided the writers so that what they wrote was exactly what God intended.

If the very words are inspired, which translation is the real Bible? Inspiration belongs strictly to the words as the prophets and apostles first wrote them in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek. But God has preserved those words with remarkable care, and a faithful translation into your language is truly the word of God to you, because it carries what God said (Westminster 1.8; 1689 1.8). The differences between good modern translations are mostly about style and readability, not doctrine. So read a reliable translation with full confidence, compare another when a verse puzzles you, and leave the arguments about manuscripts to those trained for them, knowing that no doctrine of the faith hangs on a disputed reading.

verseByVerse.quote: The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The natural person. One of the hardest sayings in Paul. The natural person (psychikos anthrōpos, soulish, living only by natural human life) is the human being equipped with everything natural birth supplies and nothing more: someone without the Spirit. He can be a brilliant philosopher. The issue is not intellect but spiritual life.

Does not accept, and not able. Paul says two things about him. He does not accept (dechomai) these things: he may understand the words, but the gospel seems foolish to him (1:18). And he is not able (ou dynatai): a lack of ability, not just of willingness, the more uncomfortable claim. Spiritual truths can only be discerned (anakrinō, examined, judged) rightly with the Spirit’s help.

Stating it carefully. Paul is not saying that unbelievers are less intelligent, or that an atheist cannot give an accurate account of Christian doctrine; many can do it better than most churchgoers. He is saying that such a person cannot receive these things as true and desirable, cannot see them for what they are, because he has no organ for that discernment. It is like describing a colour to a man born blind. The damage of sin is not only to the will, so that we will not come; it reaches the understanding, so that we do not see anything worth coming for. And the root is moral rather than intellectual: the cross looks foolish to a man not because he has thought hard and found a flaw, but because he is estranged from the God it reveals.

The teacher of Israel. Jesus met this verse in person. Nicodemus, the teacher of Israel, was as learned and devout as the natural man ever gets. Jesus told him that unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God (John 3:3), and when Nicodemus asked how these things could be, he pointed him to the Son of Man lifted up as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so that whoever believes in him may have eternal life (John 3:14–15). The cure for the natural man is not a better argument but new birth, and the new birth brings a man to look at the crucified Christ and live. This regeneration is the Spirit’s act of giving life to someone dead in sin, as little earned as his own birth was (Ephesians 2:4–5; Titus 3:5).

Where Christians differ: total inability. Some teach that unbelievers have the natural ability to receive the gospel if they choose to, and God’s grace only assists them; many Arminian Christians hold instead that God’s grace restores to every hearer the ability to accept or refuse. Both views are held by sincere believers who want to honour human responsibility. This commentary’s view: Paul says the natural person is not able to understand the things of the Spirit. Sin has darkened the mind and enslaved the will (Ephesians 4:18; Romans 8:7). This is total inability: not that unbelievers are as bad as they can be, but that they cannot turn to God by their own power. Only the Spirit, by regeneration, opens the heart (Acts 16:14; Westminster Confession 9.3, 10.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 9.3, 10.2).

Then why say anything to anybody? This verse always raises the question, and it deserves a straight answer. If my brother-in-law cannot receive it, what am I doing at Christmas dinner? The answer is that God has appointed the message as the very instrument by which he gives the capacity. He does not wait for people to become able and then send a preacher; he sends the preacher and makes them able. Luke records it in one line about a businesswoman at Philippi: Paul spoke, and the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said (Acts 16:14). Two things happened, and only one of them was Paul’s. Ezekiel is the picture. Told to preach to a valley of dry bones, the least promising congregation in Scripture, he is not asked whether they are capable of responding. He is told to prophesy, and while he is prophesying the bones come together (Ezekiel 37). The preacher’s job was never to produce life. It was to speak, while God produced it.

The weight comes off your shoulders. So this verse makes evangelism bearable. It explains why your relative is not persuaded by evidence he cannot fault: not because you argued badly, but because argument was never the missing ingredient. Keep speaking when the door opens, and ask God by name for the one thing you cannot supply (2 Corinthians 4:4–6).

Is this not just a way of saying that anyone who disagrees is blind? Not unless Paul used it to avoid arguments, and he does not: this letter answers objections at length and sets out the witnesses to the resurrection one by one (15:3–8). Paul is not saying reasons do not matter. He is saying reasons alone are not enough, because the deepest resistance to the cross is not in the head. A sceptic can test that honestly: if the gospel were true, would I want it to be? Whoever finds the answer is no has learned that his problem is not only the evidence. Many honest doubters do want it to be true and still struggle; to them Christians owe patience and good reasons, and they may bring even their doubt to God in prayer.

If unbelievers cannot understand, how can God hold them responsible? Because their inability is not like a missing limb; it is the inability of a heart that does not want God. A man who hates his brother so much that he cannot bring himself to forgive him is not excused by his cannot; the cannot is the guilt. So with the natural person: he cannot receive the things of God because he loves darkness rather than light (John 3:19–20; Romans 1:18–21).
