No one will stand before God and say he wanted Christ but was not allowed. Everyone who wants him may come, and is welcome (John 6:37). The wonder is not that some are lost but that any are saved.

For worship. You were the natural person once: unwilling, unable, and sure the cross was foolish. Then the God who said let light shine out of darkness shone in your heart, to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6), and the face you had found foolish became the one you love most. The same Spirit is able to open any heart, and the hardest case you know is not too hard for him.
verseByVerse.note: The “natural person” is someone without the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself to be judged by no one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The spiritual person. Pneumatikos means anyone who has the Spirit: every true believer, not a superior class, as some Corinthians thought.

Judges all things. The same word as verse 14: discerns, examines, evaluates. With the Spirit, a believer can evaluate everything rightly in the light of God’s truth, including the world’s wisdom. This is not a claim to be right about politics or medicine or his own motives. He is given the capacity to see what the world is, what a life is for, and what the cross means, and no amount of natural brilliance supplies that.

Seeing everything by the cross. What does the spiritual person see that others miss? Paul’s own letter is the answer. He looks at sin tolerated in a church and sees Christ our Passover lamb, sacrificed (5:7). He looks at the human body and sees a temple of the Spirit, bought with a price (6:19–20). He judges all things because he measures all things by Christ crucified.

Judged by no one. The natural person cannot properly evaluate the spiritual person, any more than a blind person can judge colours. The point is not the Christian’s superiority but the world’s incompetence in this particular court.

A sentence often abused. This sentence is often misused, nearly always in one direction. It has been used by leaders to place themselves beyond accountability, by teachers to dismiss every objection as carnal, and by ordinary Christians who do not wish to be corrected: you are not in a position to assess me; I am spiritual. Used that way it has protected a great deal of harm. The proof that it cannot mean this is in this very letter. Three chapters later Paul pronounces judgement on a Corinthian believer’s conduct (5:3), and he tells them to weigh one another’s prophecies (14:29) and to settle disputes between brothers (6:5). Believers are not above correction; it is unbelievers who are not qualified to judge spiritual truth.

When your family thinks you have thrown your life away. Some Christians’ families think they have wasted themselves: the son who turned down the career for the mission field, the woman whose relatives regard her faith as a phase she should have outgrown, the man his colleagues have filed under harmless and rather sad. Paul’s word is that on this subject they are not competent to reach a verdict. That is not arrogance: they are assessing a spiritual matter with instruments that do not extend to it, and their conclusion tells you about the instruments rather than about you.

Does “judges all things” mean Christians should have a strong opinion on everything? No. The spiritual person discerns the things of God: what is true about God, sin, Christ and the life that pleases him. On the many questions Scripture does not settle, the best car, the right investment, much of politics and science, a Christian may be no wiser than his neighbour, and should say so humbly. Spiritual discernment shows itself less in having opinions than in seeing ordinary things in God’s light: recognising an idol in a good thing, noticing pride in your own heart, hearing the gospel distorted. It grows by soaking in Scripture (Hebrews 5:14), not by speaking first.

On a Tuesday. The world’s opinion of your faith is not the final word. Your brother’s opinion of your behaviour very often is, and a Christian who uses this verse to deflect correction from other believers has turned a sentence about the world’s incompetence against the very people God gave him for the purpose. When you last reached for the idea that people do not understand you, was your critic outside the faith, or a Christian who loves you and had noticed something true?

verseByVerse.quote: “For who has understood the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For who has understood the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him? Paul closes the argument with a question from Isaiah and an answer that ought to be impossible. The quotation is Isaiah 40:13 (also Romans 11:34), and its setting matters. Isaiah is at his most soaring, describing a God who measures the waters in the hollow of his hand and weighs the mountains in scales, before whom the nations are a drop from a bucket and dust on the balance. Into that he drops the question: who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel? (The Greek translation Paul quotes renders Isaiah’s Spirit of the LORD as the mind of the Lord.) The expected answer is nobody, ever. No human can know God’s mind by his own wisdom, much less teach him.

But we have the mind of Christ. A breathtaking claim. In Isaiah, the mind of the Lord is the mind of Yahweh; Paul equates it with the mind of Christ. We cannot reach God’s mind ourselves, but we have Christ’s mind given to us by the Spirit: his way of thinking, revealed in the apostolic gospel. We is first the apostles, then all believers who receive their teaching. The unreachable has been given.

What it looks like. This is a real participation, and it has a recognisable shape. To have the mind of Christ is to begin valuing what he values and to be unimpressed by what impressed you before. It is to look at a difficult person and see someone he died for, to ask what would be honest rather than what would be advantageous, to feel the pull of the poor and the unimportant in a way that has no natural explanation. It grows, because someone else’s mind has been given to you.

The mind of Christ is a servant’s mind. Paul at once turns this on the Corinthians, whose jealousy showed they were thinking like the world (3:1–3), and the phrase is still used to end arguments. It does not mean your convictions are automatically his, and it is not a weapon against other Christians. Paul describes the mind of Christ elsewhere not as a set of superior opinions but as a disposition: he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:5–8). A man chiefly using the mind of Christ to win is describing something else.

How do I grow in the mind of Christ? By keeping company with him where he speaks. Read the Gospels and watch how he thinks: whom he notices, what angers him, what he refuses, how he prays. Let Scripture correct your instincts, especially where it surprises you, and ask the Spirit to renew your mind (Romans 12:2). Then practise it in small things: choose the lower place, forgive quickly, speak the truth kindly, serve someone who cannot repay you. Spend time with mature Christians in whom you can see it. Growth is slow, and you will often notice it only looking back, but it is sure, because the one who gave you his mind is at work to form it in you.

For worship. Nobody has instructed him, or improved his plan, or contributed a single thought he did not already hold. Then he came, and was not recognised, and was crucified by the men he was dying for. And he has given his own mind to a church at Corinth that could not stop arguing about which preacher it preferred, and to every frightened preacher and ordinary believer since. Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God (Romans 11:33–36).

parallels.desc: who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel?

2.text: <sup>1</sup>And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with lofty speech or wisdom.<sup>2</sup>For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.<sup>3</sup>And I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling,<sup>4</sup>and my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power,<sup>5</sup>so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God.<sup>6</sup>Yet among the mature we do impart wisdom, although it is not a wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are doomed to pass away.<sup>7</sup>But we impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which God decreed before the ages for our glory.<sup>8</sup>None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.<sup>9</sup>But, as it is written, “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him”—<sup>10</sup>these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.<sup>11</sup>For who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God.<sup>12</sup>Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might understand the things freely given us by God.<sup>13</sup>And we impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual.<sup>14</sup>The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned.<sup>15</sup>The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself to be judged by no one.<sup>16</sup>“For who has understood the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.

3.title: God’s Field, God’s Building, God’s Temple
3.overview:
The Corinthians thought of themselves as spiritual and wise. Paul tells them bluntly that their quarrelling over leaders shows they are still spiritual infants. Their leaders are only servants: in a farming picture, Paul planted and Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. In a building picture, Paul laid the only possible foundation, Jesus Christ, and the day of judgement will test by fire what others build on it.

The church is God’s temple, where his Spirit lives, and God will destroy whoever destroys it. So no one should boast about human leaders, because everything already belongs to believers, and they belong to Christ, and Christ to God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul could speak to them only as infants in Christ, as their jealousy and quarrels prove. Paul and Apollos are only servants, each doing the job the Lord assigned: one planted, one watered, and God gave the growth. The church is God’s field and God’s building.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of God in Ministry

The repeated point that God gives the growth is not a platitude; it is sovereign grace applied to the fruit of ministry. Neither Paul nor Apollos converted a single soul. So a minister cannot take credit for results, cannot treat apparent fruitlessness as simply his own failure, and cannot be ranked against another minister as if their different “results” measured their different abilities.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian factions measured Paul and Apollos by their outputs, and Paul refuses that measure. Now: Churches are still tempted to judge ministry by attendance, conversion numbers and cultural impact, and to credit these to the leader’s skill. Paul’s answer: plant faithfully, water patiently, and trust the God who gives the growth.

verseByVerse.quote: But I, brothers, could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ. I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not ready for it. And even now you are not yet ready,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Chapter 3 applies chapters 1–2 to the divisions. Their quarrelling proves they are still infants (vv. 1–4). Paul and Apollos are only servants: one planted, one watered, but God gave the growth (vv. 5–9). The only foundation is Jesus Christ, and the Day will test by fire what each builder puts on it (vv. 10–15). The church is God’s holy temple (vv. 16–17). So boast in no man: all things are yours, because you are Christ’s (vv. 18–23). The chapter opens by calling them infants and ends by telling them they own the universe, and what turns it is not their growth but whose they are.

Not as spiritual people. The Corinthians thought of themselves as spiritual (pneumatikoi), wise and mature; they had the gifts, the knowledge, the tongues. Paul takes the label off them in his first sentence: you were not acting like it.

Infants in Christ. Sarkinos, of the flesh, means made of flesh: believers still governed too much by the old ways of thinking. Nēpioi are babies: truly in Christ, but immature.

Growing up into him. Both words matter: infants, but in Christ. In Christ: their standing rests on him, not on their progress; a slow believer is as safe as a mature one. Infants: that union is meant to grow, and grown up looks like this: no longer children tossed about by every wind of teaching, but growing up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ (Ephesians 4:14–15). Maturity is not becoming more impressive, which is what Corinth wanted, but more like Jesus. The milk and the solid food are the same Christ crucified (2:2), taken in more deeply until he is formed in us.

Milk, not solid food. Milk is the basic truths of the gospel; solid food is deeper teaching and application (Hebrews 5:12–14). When Paul first came, they could only take milk, and that was normal. But the Christian who moves on from the cross has not advanced; he has wandered off.

Even now. What stings is the tense: not that they were immature when he arrived, since everybody is, but that years have passed and nothing has changed. An infant is delightful. A man who has been an infant for years is a tragedy.

How would you know? You cannot see your own growth directly, and in this chapter the people most confident of their maturity are the ones who do not have it. Paul’s measurement, in the next verse, is jealousy and strife (3:3), and it is plainly not knowledge: the Corinthians were enriched in all knowledge (1:5), and it had not made them adults. A person can accumulate information about God for thirty years and remain a spiritual toddler.

Where Christians differ: the carnal Christian. Some teach that there are two kinds of Christians: spiritual Christians, who have surrendered to Christ as Lord, and carnal Christians, who have accepted Christ as Saviour but live permanently as if unconverted. This commentary’s view: Paul is rebuking immaturity in true believers, not describing a permanent, acceptable category of Christian. The Corinthians were in Christ, and some still behaved in fleshly ways, which Paul calls them to leave behind. The real contrast in these chapters is between the natural person, who does not have the Spirit at all (2:14), and the believer who has the Spirit and is not yet living like it. All true believers have the Spirit (Romans 8:9) and are being changed (2 Corinthians 3:18), though at different speeds. A profession of faith that never produces any change is not saving faith (James 2:17; 1 John 3:9–10; Galatians 5:19–21). That warning is not aimed at the believer who grieves over slow growth: the grief itself is the Spirit’s work. Those who teach the two-category view usually want to explain real Christians who are struggling, and they are right that believers can be immature. Christ is received as both Saviour and Lord.

How do I move from milk to solid food? Not chiefly by learning harder doctrines, though that has its place, but by putting into practice what you already know. Hebrews says the mature are those whose powers of discernment have been trained by constant practice (Hebrews 5:14). So read Scripture steadily, not just favourite passages; sit under faithful preaching and ask how it applies to you; obey the thing you were last convicted about; and spend time with older believers whose lives show the fruit. Above all, let the gospel go deeper rather than leaving it behind. Mature Christians do not need the cross less; they see more of it, and it shapes more of them.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you were like ten years ago in the one area where you are hardest to live with: your temper, your tongue, your resentment. Growth shows up there, and the person best placed to judge is whoever shares your house. If you are not growing, your standing in Christ has not slipped; ask the Spirit for growth, and feed on his word (1 Peter 2:2).

verseByVerse.quote: for you are still of the flesh. For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Still of the flesh. Here the word is sarkikos, fleshly: governed by sinful human nature. And the measurement is startlingly ordinary.

Jealousy and strife. Jealousy (zēlos) is the heat of wanting what someone else has, of not being able to be glad about another person’s advantage. Strife (eris) is the quarrelling that follows. This is not exotic wickedness but the ordinary weather of a church committee, and Paul treats it with complete seriousness: in his list of the works of the flesh these two sit beside idolatry and sorcery (Galatians 5:20). We rank them low because they are respectable.

The measure they never thought to use. The Corinthians assessed spiritual maturity by spiritual phenomena: who could speak in tongues, who had the deeper knowledge, whose teacher was most impressive. Paul assesses it by whether they can get on with each other. That is not Paul’s invention. It is what Jesus said would identify his disciples to a watching world: not their doctrine or their gifts, but their love for one another (John 13:35). And it is what the love chapter of this letter will say: gifts without love are noise (13:1–3).

Was Paul crucified for you? Paul has already given the cure for this jealousy, in the questions that opened his whole argument: Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? (1:13). Rivalry needs a scoreboard, and at the cross there is none. Every person in that church stood there with the same debt and was bought with the same blood, so the ground for envy is gone before it starts. And the love that is to replace it is not vague niceness. It has a measure, which Jesus gave on the night he was betrayed: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another (John 13:34). Envy wants another person’s place. Christ gave up his own for people who had wronged him. Underneath, envy shows that my worth has come to depend on my ranking, so that every rise in someone else feels like a fall in me. The cross settles a believer’s worth outside every ranking, in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20), and a person whose worth is settled there can afford to be glad when others are blessed.

Are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way? Literally, walking according to man. It is the sharpest phrase in the verse. They are behaving just like unbelievers, like the competitive culture of Corinth around them. The church was running on ordinary human operating principles: rank, rivalry, the instinct to be associated with the winning side. Nothing was happening in that congregation that could not be equally observed in a trade guild or a political faction. Fan clubs and rivalries are normal in the world; they should not be normal in the church. The Spirit had been given to them, and you could not tell from the outside.

Is every disagreement in church fleshly? No. Christians can disagree honestly about real questions, and Paul himself argues hard in this letter. What makes a disagreement fleshly is the spirit of it: envy, the need to win, taking sides around personalities, contempt for the other person, refusing to listen, spreading the quarrel to others. You can test yourself by asking whether you could pray warmly for the person you disagree with, and whether you would be glad if God blessed him. A disagreement held in love, aimed at the truth and the good of the church, is not strife. A disagreement that has become about me is.

On a Tuesday. Put a name to the person in your church whose success you find hardest to be glad about, whose name you are slightly relieved to hear criticised. You have just located the exact point at which, on Paul’s measurement, you are still an infant. That is not said to condemn: a diagnosis is the first mercy. Confess the jealousy to God by name, knowing he forgives it (1 John 1:9), and then pray for that person’s good today (James 3:14–16).

For worship. There is no envy in God. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand; the Son delights to glorify the Father; the Spirit does not speak on his own authority but takes what is Christ’s and makes it known (John 3:35; 16:13–14). From eternity the life of God has been a life of glad giving, with no rivalry anywhere in it, and that same Spirit has been given to us to replace our envy with his love.

verseByVerse.quote: For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not being merely human? What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you believed, as the Lord assigned to each.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For when one says, “I follow Paul”, and another, “I follow Apollos”, are you not being merely human? Paul names only himself and Apollos now, perhaps because they were the two who had worked in Corinth. The tragedy of a personality faction is that it is so unremarkable. A church divided this way is not guilty of some unusual sin. Its failure is that it looks exactly like everybody else.

What then is Apollos? What is Paul? What, not who. Paul asks what their function is, not their personal importance. Asking what a person is rather than who he is reduces him, deliberately, to a function. Paul is refusing to be a personality.

Servants through whom you believed. His answer is one word: diakonoi, servants, often the one who waits at table: the person who brings the food and is not the reason anyone came. The Corinthians have organised their church around a debate about waiters. And “through whom” makes them instruments, not sources.

As the Lord assigned to each. Even the differences the Corinthians are quarrelling over were handed out by the Lord. That removes the ground from both factions at once: Apollos’s polish and Paul’s founding are facts about what God gave each man, not reasons to prefer him. You cannot build a hierarchy out of gifts that were distributed rather than earned.

The ascended Lord who hands out the gifts. The Lord who assigned is Christ himself. Paul tells the Ephesians that grace was given to each one according to the measure of Christ’s gift, and that the risen Christ, having ascended, gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers to his church (Ephesians 4:7–11). So boasting in one of them is so strange: it is like quarrelling over which of a friend’s gifts you prefer while forgetting the friend. The Corinthians believed through these men; they believed in him, and he is the one who sent the men.

Comparison is an argument with God. You hear a gifted preacher and come away diminished or quietly competitive; you watch another ministry flourish while yours does not. Paul’s cure is not to try harder at humility but to remember the word assigned: envying what another was given is a complaint about the distribution. Comparison, followed all the way down, always turns out to be an argument with God about what he decided to hand out.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers deserve no honour. Elders who labour in preaching and teaching are worthy of double honour (1 Timothy 5:17). But they are servants, not masters.

What if I really do benefit more from one preacher than another? That is natural and not sinful. God gives different gifts, and some will help you more than others; Paul himself speaks warmly of particular co-workers. Receive the help gratefully. The danger comes when preference turns into partisanship: when you belittle the other preacher, stay away when your favourite is not speaking, or treat your liking as a measure of spirituality. Thank God for the servant who feeds you best, and be equally willing to be fed by the one who does not suit your taste, because both are bringing food from the same Master’s kitchen.

verseByVerse.quote: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I planted, Apollos watered. Paul brought the gospel to Corinth first (Acts 18:1–11); Apollos came later and built up the young church (Acts 18:27–19:1). But God gave the growth: planted and watered are completed past actions, gave is imperfect: God was continually causing growth all along.

What no farmer can do. A farmer can prepare the ground, choose the seed, water at the right intervals and keep the weeds down, and a lazy farmer produces a poor crop. But no farmer has ever made a seed germinate. He creates conditions; life is not among the things he supplies. That is the exact shape of Christian ministry. Preaching, hospitality, patient friendship, years of prayer: all worth doing well, and not one of them can produce spiritual life in another human being.

A growth that is from God. Jesus used the same picture of his kingdom: a man scatters seed, sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows, he knows not how (Mark 4:26–27). And Paul tells the Colossians where the growth comes from: the whole body, holding fast to the Head, grows with a growth that is from God (Colossians 2:19). The life God gives in a church is the life of the risen Christ flowing from the Head into his members. That is why no preacher can produce it. He can describe Christ; only God can make a dead heart alive together with him (Ephesians 2:4–5).

Neither is anything. The conclusion is more severe than we usually let it be: literally, neither of them is anything at all. Paul gives his own life’s work the value zero in the column that matters. He does not mean the work was pointless, for each will receive wages (3:8). He means it contributed nothing to the one thing that had to happen. And if both men are nothing, the argument is over.

For those who have prayed for years. This is the verse for the parent whose adult child has walked away, the wife whose husband remains politely unmoved, the person who has explained, invited, wept, and watched nothing happen, and has begun to suspect the failure is theirs. You were never able to give the growth, and neither was the apostle Paul. That does not make your planting and watering worthless. God ordinarily uses exactly such means, for people cannot believe in one of whom they have never heard (Romans 10:14), and your years of faithfulness are the seed and the water. So name the person to God and ask him for the one thing only he does, and go on planting. It removes a burden you were never given and could not carry.

If God gives the growth, should a church bother to plan, train and evaluate? Yes. Farmers who trust God for the harvest still plough straight furrows. Paul planned his journeys, trained co-workers and thought hard about how to reach people (9:19–23). Careful planning, good teaching and honest review of what you are doing are part of faithful planting and watering. What the verse rules out is thinking that the right method guarantees results, measuring faithfulness by numbers, or taking credit when things grow. Plan carefully, work hard, and pray as people who know that without the Lord nothing will come up at all.

For worship. The God who gives the growth gave the first growth of the new creation on a Sunday morning: his Son was laid in the ground like a seed, and God raised him, the firstfruits of a harvest still coming in (15:20). Every believer since belongs to that harvest: a dead heart made alive, a green shoot where nothing grew. God did it for his Son, he does it again each time a sinner believes, and he has never once needed his gardeners to be clever.

verseByVerse.quote: He who plants and he who waters are one, and each will receive his wages according to his labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who plants and he who waters are one. Hen eisin: they are one thing, one in purpose, serving the same Lord, aiming at the same harvest. The Corinthians made them rivals; there is no gap between them for a faction to occupy.

Wages according to labour. Each worker will be rewarded individually by God, not according to success, which belongs to God, but according to labour (kopos): toil, the kind of work that wears you out. Results cannot be the measure of the servant, because they were never his to produce. The Corinthians compared outputs, as every generation since has done with attendance figures and reach. The ledger God keeps has a different column heading.

For the faithful who saw little. The missionary who gave forty years to a hard field and saw a handful of converts; the pastor of a small village congregation while the church in the next town filled up; the mother whose children do not believe. Each may have done the arithmetic and concluded the life was wasted. This verse says the arithmetic is wrong, not because results do not matter, but because they were never the thing being weighed. The Lord who gives the growth does not charge his servants for the growth he chose not to give.

My recompense is with my God. The Lord Jesus walked this road before any of his servants. In Isaiah the Servant of the Lord says that he has laboured in vain and spent his strength for nothing, yet his right is with the Lord and his recompense with his God (Isaiah 49:4), and the New Testament hears that Servant’s voice in Christ (Luke 2:32, echoing Isaiah 49:6). By the measure of results his ministry ended badly. He left the verdict with his Father, and the Father answered by raising him and giving him the nations. Every servant who labours with little to show stands where his Master stood, and is paid by the same God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is earned by labour. Salvation is a gift (Romans 6:23), and Paul will shortly say that the man whose work burns is saved anyway (v. 15). What is being paid for is not your entrance but your labour, and even the reward is gracious, God crowning his own gifts.

Will some believers have more in heaven than others, and will that not cause envy? Scripture does speak of differing rewards (Luke 19:17–19; 2 Corinthians 5:10), but it never pictures heaven as a place of rivalry. Every believer will have all of Christ and will be perfectly satisfied, as a small cup and a large cup may both be full. And envy will be impossible, because sin will be gone and love will be perfect: we will rejoice in every other believer’s reward as gladly as in our own, since every reward will be a display of God’s grace. In the vision of Revelation the elders cast their crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:10). Whatever we receive, we will give back to him.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s field, God’s building.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s fellow workers. God’s is emphatic, three times in one short verse: God’s fellow workers, God’s field, God’s building, and the point is ownership. Synergoi can mean fellow workers with God, but the context favours his workmen, labouring side by side in a field that is his. That is no demotion worth grieving over. The dignity of Christian work never came from our importance to it, but from whose work it is.

You are God’s field. The church belongs to God, not to Paul or Apollos. A field is not divided into plots belonging to different farmers. The Corinthians have been marking out territory in ground that belongs to somebody else.

God’s building. Paul switches pictures, and not carelessly. A field is forgiving: if a crop fails you sow again. A building goes up in a fixed order, every course resting on the one beneath. The stakes have just risen.

I will build my church. The builder has spoken for himself. When Jesus first promised the church, he said: on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18). My church: it is his. I will build: he is not a distant patron funding the work but the builder on site, using his servants as his tools. So the church is God’s building because it is Christ’s, and every true addition to it, every person brought to faith and every life built up, is work he is doing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church belongs to anyone but God. A church is not a voluntary society belonging to its members, a platform belonging to its minister, or a heritage belonging to the families who have been there longest. None of them holds the title deeds; God does.

Then who makes the decisions in a church? Christ does, through his word, and every church structure is a stewardship under him. Christians differ on how that works out: some churches are led by elders with the congregation’s consent, some by a congregational vote, some by a wider presbytery or by bishops, and faithful believers hold each of these views from Scripture. Whatever your church’s order, the principle of this verse applies to all of them: leaders are servants answerable to the owner, members are workmen and not shareholders, and every decision should begin with the question, what does the Lord of this field want? A meeting that forgets that question has forgotten whose meeting it is.

parallels.desc: the planting of the LORD

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: By God’s grace Paul laid the foundation, Jesus Christ, and others build on it with lasting or worthless materials. The day of judgement will test each person’s work by fire: lasting work is rewarded, and worthless work burns, though the builder himself is saved. The church is God’s holy temple, where his Spirit lives, and God will destroy anyone who destroys it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as the New Temple

In a city full of pagan temples, Paul claims that the living God now lives, by his Spirit, not in a building of stone but in a community of flawed, quarrelsome people. This is the new covenant fulfilment of the Old Testament temple: God with his people, through the Spirit given to all who belong to Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The divisions at Corinth were more than social trouble. The factions were demolition work on the place where God had chosen to live. Now: A church split or a deliberate campaign against a congregation is an attack on the dwelling of the Holy Spirit. That gives church unity a weight that mere niceness cannot: we are protecting the home of God.

verseByVerse.quote: According to the grace of God given to me, like a skilled master builder I laid a foundation, and someone else is building upon it. Let each one take care how he builds upon it. For no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
According to the grace of God given to me. Paul’s apostleship and skill were gifts of grace (15:10). He neither boasts nor pretends to a modesty he does not feel: he states the skill and assigns its origin in the same breath.

A skilled master builder. Architektōn (architect) is the chief builder, who lays the foundation and hands the site on to others. And someone else is building on it: Apollos, and every generation of teachers since.

Take care how he builds. This warning governs the rest of the chapter. It is addressed first to teachers, and it is not whether but how: everyone in a church is building something, and the quality of it will be exposed by fire.

No other foundation. The foundation is not open for discussion. Christ crucified, as preached by the apostles, is the only foundation (Isaiah 28:16; Ephesians 2:20), and a church built on anything else is not a church of God. What does it mean for a church to rest on him? That everything it is depends on who he is and what he did. Its peace with God rests on his death for sinners; its life rests on his resurrection; its message is his gospel; its hope is his return. Take any of those away and nothing else can bear the weight, which is why Peter told the rulers in Jerusalem that there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:11–12). Even Paul did not choose it: it is laid, by God.

How foundations shift. Churches rarely announce a change of foundation. They shift by degrees, always onto something good: their history and families; a personality, the Corinthian version; a cause; an experience; a doctrinal system held so tightly that Christ becomes a topic within it. Every one of those can coexist with an impeccable statement of faith. Ask what would have to be removed before your church noticed something essential had gone, and how long it would take anyone to notice if Christ were quietly no longer at the centre (Matthew 7:24–27).

What should I look for in a church? First, the foundation: is Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, clearly at the centre of what is preached, sung and prayed, and is the Bible taught faithfully as God’s word? Then the building: is the gospel shaping how people live and love one another, are baptism and the Lord’s Supper observed, is there loving care and discipline, are the leaders godly and accountable? Style, size, music and programmes come far lower. No church is perfect, and if you wait for one you will never join one. Look for one built on Christ and trying, imperfectly, to build well, and then commit yourself to it.

parallels.desc: a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation

verseByVerse.quote: Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw— each one’s work will become manifest, for the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gold or straw. Six materials, in two groups of three. Gold, silver and precious stones were what David gathered for the house of God (1 Chronicles 29:2); wood, hay and straw were the stuff of ordinary huts, thrown up quickly. They stand for sound, faithful ministry or shallow, worldly ministry, and the difference that matters is behaviour under fire: wood, hay and straw do not merely char, they vanish.

The Day will disclose it. The Day is Christ’s return and judgement (1:8; 4:5). Now the difference is largely invisible: a straw building can be more impressive than a gold one if it is bigger, and two ministries can produce identical statistics while made of entirely different substances. A Christian might be found to have done a great deal of the wrong kind: a life of visible activity, admired at the time, that turns out to have been made of hay.

Revealed by fire. Fire here is a picture of God’s searching judgement (Malachi 3:2–3; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–8), and it tests the work, not the person’s salvation. What sort: quality, not quantity. And the fire is not an arbitrary test. It is what the holiness of God does to everything that comes near him, for our God is a consuming fire (Hebrews 12:29). Nothing false can stand in the presence of the Holy One, and nothing true has anything to fear from it.

What makes a work gold? Paul does not give a list, and we should be careful about inventing one. But the letter itself supplies the direction. Work genuinely built on the foundation: Christ crucified, not merely mentioned but load-bearing. Work done in dependence on the Spirit rather than on technique. Work aimed at people’s good rather than at the builder’s standing, which is the very thing that has gone wrong at Corinth. And work done in love, since gifts exercised without it are nothing (13:1–3).

Tested by the one it rests on. Paul calls it the day of our Lord Jesus Christ (1:8), so the one who examines the building is the one it stands on. The fire asks one question of every piece of work: does it belong on this foundation? Whatever came from Christ, his truth taught, his love shown, work done by his Spirit and for his name, shares the nature of the stone beneath it and stands. Whatever came only from us, our cleverness, our ambition, our need to be seen, burns.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only full-time ministers will be judged. Paul speaks first of teachers in the church, but the principle applies to every believer’s service.

Will my sins be exposed in front of everyone on that Day? What this passage says will be revealed is your work, so that it can be rewarded or lost. Your sins, if you are in Christ, have already been judged at the cross; there is no condemnation left for you (Romans 8:1), and God has cast them behind his back (Isaiah 38:17; Micah 7:19). Scripture does say that all will give account and that hidden things will be brought to light (4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:10), so believers should live seriously. But whatever is shown of a believer on that Day will be shown as a sinner fully forgiven, and the point of it will be the glory of the grace that saved him, not his shame.

On a Tuesday. Take anything you are doing for God this week and ask whether you would still do it, and as carefully, if nobody ever knew you had done it (Matthew 6:1–4). No one’s motives are wholly pure, even in his best work; but Christ obeyed perfectly in our place, his obedience is counted as ours, and for his sake the Father accepts the imperfect work of his children (Romans 5:19; Westminster 16.6).
verseByVerse.note: Fire tests metals; wood and straw burn up.

parallels.desc: like a refiner’s fire

verseByVerse.quote: If the work that anyone has built on the foundation survives, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as through fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A reward, or loss. Two outcomes, stated without softening. Faithful work will stand and be rewarded (Matthew 25:21); otherwise there is loss of reward, as if a lifetime’s labour went up in smoke.

He himself will be saved. The builder is a true believer. His salvation does not depend on the quality of his work but on the foundation, and the foundation is Christ, whose work on the cross is finished and cannot burn. The clause is unqualified: his life’s work is gone and he is not. This verse does not put a single believer’s salvation in question, and it was never meant to be read by an anxious Christian as a threat.

But only as through fire. Like a man escaping a burning house with nothing but his life. He is out, he is alive, he is not going back in, and everything he spent forty years accumulating is behind him in the flames. Saved, but with empty hands.

Where Christians differ: purgatory. The Roman Catholic Church has used this passage to support purgatory, a place of temporal purifying punishment after death for believers before entering heaven. From the medieval period onwards it became a principal text for that doctrine, and the reading is not foolish: there is a fire, there is a Christian, and he passes through it and comes out saved. This commentary’s view: the passage does not teach purgatory. The fire tests works, not people; verse 13 says so twice. What burns is the work; the man is not being purified, he is being rescued from a blaze consuming what he built. It happens on the Day of judgement, not over a period after death; nothing suggests duration, degrees or satisfaction for sin. And it is about the work of teachers, not punishment for sins. Behind that lies the deeper reason: Christ became our righteousness (1:30). If the cross dealt with sin, there is nothing left for a fire to deal with; if a fire is still required, the cross did not finish. Christ’s sacrifice fully paid for his people’s sins, so there is no punishment left for them (Hebrews 10:14; Romans 8:1). At death, believers go immediately to be with Christ (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Westminster Confession 32.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1).

Sobering enough without additions. A Christian can reach the end of his life, undoubtedly saved, with nothing to show for it, because what he built was made of the wrong stuff. Paul writes it to frighten people out of it while there is time.

What is the reward? Its heart is the Lord’s own commendation (4:5; Matthew 25:21), with wider service in the age to come and an imperishable crown (9:25); salvation is the same for every believer, reward is not, and even the reward is grace (Revelation 4:10). (See Mark 9:41 for the fuller answer.)

What it does not mean. It does not mean faithfulness does not matter, since we are saved anyway. Loss of reward is real loss, and there is shame in it (1 John 2:28). But the way back is open while you live, as the next paragraph says.

I have wasted years. Is it too late to build with gold? No. As long as you are alive, you can start building on the foundation with materials that last. The thief on the cross had hours, and Christ welcomed him. Paul himself spent his early years destroying the church, and then laboured more than all the apostles by the grace of God (15:9–10). God does not ask how late you started but whether you are faithful now. Confess the wasted time, refuse to waste more on regret, and give yourself to what lasts: loving people, teaching truth, serving in Christ’s name. Work begun late in faith is still gold.

parallels.desc: a brand plucked out of the burning

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know. A phrase Paul uses ten times in this letter, always with an edge: you have been told, and have forgotten. “You” is plural: the congregation together is God’s temple (in 6:19 it will be each believer’s body). And temple here is naos, the sanctuary itself, the house where God dwelt.

In a city full of temples. Corinth had temples to Apollo, to Asclepius, to Aphrodite on the mountain above the town, with priests and sacrifices and processions. Paul tells ordinary people meeting in somebody’s dining room that they are where the living God has taken up residence. The temples on the skyline are empty.

And that God’s Spirit dwells in you? As the glory-cloud filled the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:10–11), so God’s Spirit lives among his gathered people. The church is where God is.

Something greater than the temple. The church is God’s temple only because of Christ. Jesus said that something greater than the temple was here (Matthew 12:6), and he called his own body the temple that would be destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19–21). The Spirit who now lives in the church is the Spirit poured out by the risen and exalted Lord (Acts 2:33), and the church is a temple because it is joined to him: built on him as cornerstone, it grows into a holy temple in the Lord (Ephesians 2:20–21). To tear at the congregation is to tear at the body of Christ.

God will destroy him. The same verb comes twice (phtheirō, ruin, corrupt): you ruin it, he will ruin you. Whoever wrecks the church, by factions, false teaching or corrupting influence, God will ruin. This is not a builder who builds badly but a wrecker. So a church split is not a management problem or a personality clash; it is demolition work on the house where God lives, and he defends his property.

Holy. Not because the members are impressive, for Paul has just called them infants, but because of who lives there. You may think very little of your congregation; God has chosen to live in it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a true believer who causes trouble will lose salvation. It describes those who destroy the church, showing they were never truly of it (1 John 2:19), and warns all of us how seriously God takes the unity and purity of his church. The warnings are real, among the means God uses to keep his people. The person in view is not someone who has been difficult, or held an unpopular position, or raised a hard question, but one set on wrecking the church.

Is this verse about looking after my body? Not directly. People often quote it against smoking or overeating, but here the temple is the church, the gathered people of God, and the sin is damaging that community. Paul does teach that the individual believer’s body is a temple of the Spirit, three chapters later, where the issue is sexual immorality (6:18–20), and caring for your body honours God for that reason. But the first application of this verse is to how you treat your church: your words, your loyalties, your influence. Wrecking a congregation is a far graver thing than most of us realise.

Is it not harsh for God to destroy someone over trouble in a church? If the church were a club, perhaps. But Paul’s point is that it is the place where the holy God lives, among people he obtained with his own blood (Acts 20:28). A father who saw someone setting fire to the house where his children slept would not be harsh to stop him; he would be unloving if he did not. The warning is aimed at the one set on wrecking the church, not at the struggling member, and it is given in advance, while there is still time to turn back. God’s severity here is the other side of his love: he will not let anyone tear down what his Son died to build.

On a Tuesday. Go back over the last conversation you had about someone in your church who was not present, and ask whether it was building or quietly taking something down. Much demolition in churches is done a sentence at a time, by people who would be horrified to be told what they are standing in. Where you find it, confess it to the Lord who bought this house, and go and build (Ephesians 2:21–22).

For worship. The God whom heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain (1 Kings 8:27) once filled Solomon’s temple with a cloud. Then the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and the glory walked the roads of Galilee (John 1:14). Now by his Spirit the same holy presence has made its home among forgiven sinners in an ordinary room, and he guards that home as jealously as he ever guarded Zion. The Holy One is not far off. He has moved in.
verseByVerse.note: “You” is plural: the church together is God’s temple.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — The Folly of Boasting in Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Anyone who thinks he is wise by this world’s standards should become a fool in the world’s eyes, so as to become truly wise, because God sees through the world’s wisdom. So no one should boast about human leaders: everything belongs to believers, and they belong to Christ, and Christ to God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Everything in Christ, Nothing Apart from Him

Verses 21–23 are one of the great lists of what it means to be in Christ. Every apostle, every circumstance, every horizon of time, even death itself, belongs to the believer. Because they are joined to Christ, they share in all that is his. They need not cling to Paul or Apollos; they have all of them, and far more besides.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians were each claiming a third of the apostolic inheritance when they could have had the whole. Their factions were a self-imposed poverty in the middle of great wealth. Now: A Christian who defines himself by his tradition (Calvinist, Arminian, Baptist, Anglican) rather than by Christ is doing the same thing. The traditions are real and valuable, and they are yours in Christ. But Christ is not yours in the tradition.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. For it is written, “He catches the wise in their craftiness,” and again, “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let no one deceive himself. Self-deception is the danger of the clever, and the hardest kind to detect, because the deceiver is entirely trusted by the person being deceived.

Become a fool. To become wise, you must accept being thought a fool by the world, by embracing the message of the cross (1:18–25). This is not a recommendation to stop thinking but a verdict on your thinking: to agree that the equipment you have relied on cannot reach God, and to receive from him what you could not work out.

The door marked fool. Every Christian does this, and for some it costs more. The person whose standing rests on being the one who understands things, the academic, the man used to being the most informed person in the room, is being asked to walk into the kingdom by a door marked fool, and to keep walking through it afterwards.

Wisdom with a name. The wisdom on the other side of that door is not a better philosophy. It is a person. Christ became to us wisdom from God (1:24, 30). To become a fool in order to be wise is to stop trusting the wisdom you brought and to receive him instead: the crucified Lord whom the rulers of this age did not recognise (2:8). The world’s wisdom could not find God. God’s wisdom came looking for us, and hung on a cross.

He catches the wise. From Job 5:13: God traps the clever in their own schemes. And there is a fine irony here: Paul is quoting Eliphaz, one of Job’s comforters, whose confident wisdom God himself exposes before the book ends (Job 42:7). The man who said it was caught by it. Yet Paul introduces the line with it is written: Scripture records Eliphaz faithfully, mistakes and all, and this sentence is true.

The thoughts of the wise. From Psalm 94:11, where the psalmist writes the thoughts of man; Paul sharpens it to the wise, since that is the group in question at Corinth. Futile (mataios) means empty, leading nowhere. God does not outwit the clever in argument; he knows their reasoning goes nowhere, a heavier verdict than being contradicted.

A permanent posture. Becoming a fool is not a one-off act but a lasting posture: letting Scripture correct your categories rather than trimming Scripture to fit them. Every serious reader meets passages that offend his instincts, and at that point either he bends or the text does.

In the flow. With verse 18 Paul ties the argument together: the factions were the world’s wisdom (1:18–2:16) in action, and the cure is to become a fool in the world’s eyes again, which leads to the conclusion: let no one boast in men (3:21).

Should Christians study at university or work in science and scholarship? Yes, gladly. All truth is God’s truth, the world is his to explore, and Christians have done some of the finest thinking in history in every field. Daniel learned the literature of Babylon without bowing to its gods (Daniel 1:17). What this verse forbids is not learning but letting learning sit in judgement over God. So study hard, think carefully, and take your faith into the lecture room rather than leaving it at the door. Find Christian friends who will help you think, and when a teacher’s claims clash with Scripture, test them humbly and patiently, remembering that the fear of the Lord is where wisdom starts.

parallels.desc: he catches the wise in their own craftiness
the LORD knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath

verseByVerse.quote: So let no one boast in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future—all are yours,
verseByVerse.commentary:
So let no one boast in men. The conclusion of chapters 1–3, and the logic is unexpected. Paul does not say you have nothing to boast about, but that you are far too rich to boast in men. The Corinthians are behaving like people fighting over scraps, and Paul’s answer is to open the accounts.

For all things are yours. A glorious reversal. You said, I belong to Paul. Paul says: no, Paul belongs to you.

Whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas. These are the very men the factions were dividing over, all given to serve you (Ephesians 4:11–12). The faction was a self-imposed poverty, each clinging to a third of an inheritance that was entirely theirs.

Or the world. Then the list jumps. The whole created world is yours, for the meek shall inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5; Romans 4:13). What does that mean on an ordinary day? Not that you hold the title to anything, but that nothing in the world is finally against you: all of it, even its losses, is put to work for the good of those who love God, and the whole of it will be theirs in the new creation (Romans 8:28; Revelation 21:7).

Or life or death. Life is yours: a possession, not a predicament. And then a word nobody would put in a list of assets: death. The last enemy has been so defeated that it now serves the believer, for it brings him to Christ (Philippians 1:21). The thing every human being organises his life around avoiding has become an item on a list of possessions.

The present or the future. Present circumstances and future events: all work together for your good (Romans 8:28, 38). The present, this month, with its unresolved situation, belongs to you as much as the glory does.

The heir of all things. None of this is ours by nature. Scripture names one heir of all things, the Son, through whom God made the world (Hebrews 1:2), and we are heirs only as fellow heirs with him (Romans 8:17). Through his own death Christ destroyed the one who has the power of death and delivered those who through fear of death were held in lifelong slavery (Hebrews 2:14–15). Death is ours because it was first his, and he walked out of it. The whole inventory, apostles, world, life, death, present and future, is the estate of Christ, settled on the people he has made his own.

Not a prosperity gospel. The words all things are yours have been used to underwrite a gospel of prosperity, which has little to say about death, on the same list. Paul is writing to a church that is mostly poor and socially insignificant (1:26), and is about to say that the apostles themselves are hungry, poorly dressed and homeless (4:11).

If death is mine, why am I still afraid of dying? Because death is still an enemy, the last one (15:26), and the process of dying can be hard. Jesus himself wept at a grave and was in anguish in Gethsemane. Fear of dying is not unbelief; it is being human in a fallen world. What Christ has removed is the sting: death can no longer separate you from God, condemn you or keep you (15:55–57; Romans 8:38–39). So bring the fear to him honestly. Read what he has promised about the other side. Ask to be with believers who have died well. And remember that he has gone through death ahead of you, and will be with you in it.

On a Tuesday. If you feel spiritually poor, name what you think you are short of: standing, security, a future, someone in your corner. Then read the list again. It is possible to be an heir of everything and live like a man counting coins, and the only thing that has to change is that somebody tells you what is in the account (Romans 8:32; Psalm 24:1).

verseByVerse.quote: and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you are Christ’s. These words hold the chapter together: all things belong to you because you belong to Christ. This is the true slogan: I am Christ’s.

Owner and owned. All things belong to you, but you are not the top of the chain, and that keeps the words all things are yours from becoming a fantasy of self-importance. You own everything, and you are owned. A man who says I am Paul’s has swapped an infinite estate for a small allegiance, and got the direction of ownership wrong.

And Christ is God’s. Christ, as the Son and Mediator (the one who stands between God and us), belongs to God the Father and serves his glory (11:3; 15:28). Read carelessly, the clause sounds like a demotion, as the fourth-century Arians (who taught that the Son was created) argued from sentences like this.

Equal in nature, ordered in relation. The church’s answer, set out at Nicaea, is that Scripture speaks of the Son in two registers. As to his being, he is fully and equally God: this same Paul calls him the Lord of glory (2:8) and applies to him the covenant name, the LORD, from Jeremiah 9:24 (1:31). As to his mission, he willingly took a place of submission: sent by the Father, doing the Father’s will, and at the end handing the kingdom over to the Father (15:24–28). The submission is not evidence of a lesser deity (John 14:28; Philippians 2:6–11); it is the shape divine love took when it came to fetch us.

What does it mean in practice to belong to Christ? It means your life is not your own: your time, body, money, gifts and future are his to direct (6:19–20). That is a claim, and it is also a comfort. Because you are his, he takes responsibility for you: he feeds, guards, corrects and keeps what belongs to him (John 10:27–29). It means your identity is settled not by your job, your politics, your tribe or your failures, but by whose you are. And it means every other loyalty, to family, church, nation or leader, is real but secondary, held under him. When you are unsure what to do, ask the simple question: what would my Owner want?

For worship. A squabbling congregation was handed the world, life, death, the present and the future, not because it had grown up but because it belonged to Christ. And Christ is God’s. He did not seize his place; he received all things from the Father, gave them away to us, and at the end will hand the kingdom back, so that God may be all in all (15:28). There is no grasping anywhere in the Godhead. Everything the Son has, he has from the Father; everything we have, we have from the Son; and the whole vast movement runs outward from a God who has never needed anything and has never stopped giving (John 17:10).
