4.title: Servants of Christ, Spectacles to the World
4.overview:
Paul finishes his answer to the factions. Apostles are Christ’s servants and the managers of God’s revealed truth, and what counts for a manager is faithfulness. The Lord alone will judge it, at his coming, so the Corinthians must stop judging early and stop puffing themselves up over one teacher against another, for everything they have is a gift.

Then, with biting irony, Paul sets the Corinthians’ sense of already reigning beside the apostles’ real life: hungry, beaten, homeless, treated as the scum of the earth, yet blessing those who curse them. He writes as their father in the gospel, sends Timothy, and asks whether he must come with a rod or with love and gentleness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Servants and Stewards: The Judgment That Matters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul and his fellow workers are Christ’s servants and stewards, and the one thing required of stewards is faithfulness. Paul does not trust the Corinthians’ verdict, or even his own clear conscience: the Lord is his judge, who at his coming will reveal the purposes of every heart and give each servant his commendation. So they must not judge before the time, or boast in one leader against another, since everything they have was received.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Last Judgement and Its Present Implications

Paul’s refusal to pass judgement early on himself or others (vv. 3–5) is not relativism. The final judgement has not yet been given, so every present judgement, including our verdict on ourselves, is provisional. That guards against both false confidence (I know I am right) and false despair (I know I am condemned), because both claim a verdict that belongs to God. The practical result is freedom from being crushed by criticism or puffed up by praise.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians were judging Paul and finding him wanting, not by faithfulness but by eloquence and visible success. Now: Judging ministers by attendance, public approval or conference invitations is the modern version. A minister who shapes his ministry around his peers’ praise has chosen the wrong judge.

verseByVerse.quote: This is how one should regard us, as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Chapter 4 finishes Paul’s answer to the divisions. Ministers are servants and stewards; what matters is faithfulness, which only the Lord can judge, at his coming (vv. 1–5). Everything they have was received, so they have no ground for pride (vv. 6–7). With biting irony Paul sets their sense of already reigning beside the apostles’ real life: hungry, beaten, homeless, the scum of the world (vv. 8–13). Then, as their father in the gospel, he sends Timothy and asks whether he must come with a rod or with gentle love (vv. 14–21). The chapter of servants who own nothing ends by pointing to the Servant who had every right to come with a rod and came to bear it instead.

This is how one should regard us. The Corinthians had been viewing their teachers as Corinth viewed its orators: celebrities to be followed and ranked. Paul hands them another lens with two humbling words ground into it.

As servants of Christ. The first word is hypēretēs, an assistant or attendant: the officer who carries out a superior’s orders, the synagogue attendant who handed Jesus the scroll and took it back (Luke 4:20), the servants of the word on whom Luke relied (Luke 1:2). The assistant does not set the orders, and nobody cheers him by name. And they are servants of Christ, not of the Corinthians, who were treating their ministers as hired entertainers. A man who takes his orders from Christ cannot also take them from the people who prefer him.

Stewards of the mysteries. The second word is oikonomos, the steward: the household manager, very often a slave, who ran the estate, kept the accounts and dispensed the stores to the rest of the household (Luke 12:42). He handled a great deal of wealth and owned none of it. What he distributes is not his, and he cannot alter the terms on which it is given out. And a mystery, for Paul, is not an esoteric secret but the thing once hidden and now announced (2:7).

The mystery is a person. And the thing announced has a name: God’s mystery, which is Christ (Colossians 2:2). So what the steward carries out of the storeroom is Christ himself, crucified and risen, offered whole to everyone in the house. A steward of Christ fails if he hands out something else in his place, however attractive: himself, a method, a mood, a cause. He succeeds when the household is fed with Christ, undiluted and unaltered, whether or not anyone remembers who served it.

Found faithful. Then the single criterion. Not gifted, not effective, not admired: faithful (pistos), trustworthy with something that is not his. A steward is not assessed by how much the household admired him, but by whether the accounts balance when the master comes home.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers are a priestly class who dispense grace through rituals. They are stewards of a message, not keepers of a sacred store that only they can unlock. Nor does it mean gifts and effectiveness are worthless; God gives gifts to be used. It means that none of them is the test.

Is this only about pastors? No. Paul is speaking first of himself and Apollos, but every Christian is a steward of something (1 Peter 4:10). Money, time, a gift, a position, a family, a piece of knowledge somebody trusted you with: all of it is held rather than owned, and the question in each case is the same. The parable of the talents is told to ordinary disciples, and its verdict is not well done, good and successful servant, but good and faithful (Matthew 25:21). So the mother at home with small children, the man in an office no one will ever write about, the elderly saint who can only pray: each is managing the master’s goods, and each will be asked the same single question.

What should I look for in a pastor, then? Look for faithfulness before flair. Does he preach what Scripture actually says, including the parts that are unpopular, or does he edit the stores to suit the household? Does he live what he preaches, at home and in private as well as on the platform (1 Timothy 3:1–7)? Does he point to Christ rather than to himself? Is he the same man in a small meeting as in a large one? A gifted speaker is a gift from God, and you may thank God for one. But a church that chooses or rates its ministers by charisma alone is repeating Corinth’s mistake, and it usually ends up with stewards who own the house.

What if a faithful minister’s church stays small? Then he has not failed. Faithfulness and visible results are not the same thing, and Scripture is full of faithful servants with thin harvests. Noah was a herald of righteousness, perhaps for many years, and eight people entered the ark (2 Peter 2:5). Jeremiah preached for forty years to a nation that did not listen. Some of the most faithful pastors in history laboured in obscure villages and are known now only to God. Numbers are not unimportant, because God wants his house full, but growth is God’s work (3:6–7), and the steward is responsible only for what is in his hands. Pray for your pastor, and do not measure him by a scale the Lord does not use.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you would change if you genuinely believed it was not yours: the money, the diary, the children. The change required is usually not in how hard you work but in whose interests (Luke 12:42–44). None of us will be found perfectly faithful. Christ was, in our place, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), so a steward who has failed may come back to his Master unafraid and begin again.
verseByVerse.note: A steward was a trusted household manager, often a slave, put in charge of his master’s goods.

verseByVerse.quote: But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself. For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A very small thing. The Corinthians were evaluating their teachers, comparing Paul unfavourably with others. Judged is anakrinō: examined, cross-examined, as in a preliminary hearing. And human court is literally a human day, set against the Day of the Lord (3:13). Paul is not saying their opinion is worthless but that it is not the verdict: the court they had set up has no jurisdiction.

Not even myself. Then he removes his own assessment from the court as well: not low self-esteem but accurate self-knowledge, since no man has full access to his own motives. His conscience is clear about his ministry among them: no doctrine watered down, no money taken, no flattery used.

But I am not thereby acquitted. And he refuses to treat that as a verdict of innocence. Acquitted is dedikaiōmai, from the great word of justification, here used in its courtroom sense: declared in the right. A clear conscience is not the final verdict. Conscience can be wrong, or blind, or badly taught, and the heart lies not only to others but to its owner (Psalm 139:23–24; Jeremiah 17:9). Paul is not saying his salvation is uncertain. He is saying that his faithfulness as a servant will be assessed by the Lord, not by his own feelings.

It is the Lord who judges me. Christ alone is qualified to evaluate his servants, because he alone sees everything, including the motives Paul cannot see in himself. This produces not anxiety but a strange freedom: you need not manage your reputation, nor run a permanent internal tribunal. For the believer the verdict that matters most has already been given in Christ, so he can stop trying to win one from everybody else, and from himself.

The Lord who judged him faithful. The Lord who judges Paul is the Lord Jesus, to whom the Father has given all judgement (John 5:22), and Paul knew his Judge before he ever stood before him. Years later he wrote that Christ Jesus our Lord had judged him faithful, appointing him to his service, though formerly he was a blasphemer, persecutor and insolent opponent (1 Timothy 1:12–13). The Judge’s first word to Paul was spoken on the Damascus road, in mercy, to a man with blood on his hands. A servant who answers to that Lord knows what kind of Judge he is.

If a clear conscience does not acquit me, how can I have any assurance? A guard is needed at once, because this verse can land on an anxious Christian like a sentence. Am I to go through life suspecting myself? No, and the answer is in the same clause. Paul’s point is not that he is secretly condemned but that the verdict is not his to give, in either direction. He refuses to acquit himself and equally refuses to condemn himself. Both are the Lord’s business, and the Lord has already spoken about those who are in Christ: there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Assurance does not rest on the quality of your self-examination. It rests on Christ’s finished work and God’s promise, sealed to you by the Spirit (Romans 8:16). John writes the same comfort to people whose hearts were accusing them: God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything (1 John 3:19–20).

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers are above accountability or criticism. Elders can be rebuked for sin (1 Timothy 5:19–20), and churches are told to test what they hear (1 Thessalonians 5:21). It means the final evaluation of a servant’s faithfulness belongs to Christ, and ministers should not live for human approval. Nor does it mean self-examination is pointless: Paul commands it before the Lord’s Supper (11:28). Examine yourself, by all means; just do not mistake your findings for the Judge’s verdict.

So should I ignore criticism? No: listen to it, but do not bow to it. Criticism is often a gift, and the Lord frequently uses other people to show us what we cannot see (Proverbs 27:6). Ask honestly whether it is true, whether it agrees with Scripture, and whether people who love you are saying the same thing. If it is true, repent and be grateful. If it is false, you may let it go without bitterness, because the person who said it was never your judge. The difference Paul is drawing is between taking criticism seriously and treating it as a verdict. The first is humility. The second is slavery to opinion, and it will leave you either crushed or defensive.

On a Tuesday. Bring to mind the last criticism that stayed with you for days, and the last praise you replayed, and ask what authority you granted to each. When the voice in your own head starts its familiar hearing, acquitting you too quickly or condemning you without mercy, you may say to it what Paul said: you are not the judge either. Then rest in the Lord’s judgement, which for those in Christ is already given.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart. Then each one will receive his commendation from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the time. The fault Paul names is not judging as such but the timing of it: a verdict delivered before the evidence is complete and before the Judge has taken his seat. The Corinthians were ranking their ministers before the court had sat.

Not a ban on all judging. This verse is often quoted to shut down any moral assessment. But one chapter later Paul pronounces judgment on a man’s conduct (5:3), instructs the church to judge those inside it (5:12), and asks incredulously whether they are really unable to settle a dispute between brothers (6:5). Whatever this verse forbids, it cannot be the thing Paul does immediately afterwards.

What is reserved. What it forbids is the verdict only God can reach: the assessment of another person’s heart and final standing. You may say that an action is wrong; you may not say what a man is before God, or what he was really after, because you do not have the file. It is the difference between “what he said was untrue” and “he is a liar through and through”; between “this decision was unwise” and “he only did it for the credit”. The first is observation. The second is a ruling on the purposes of the heart, and it is reserved.

Before the Lord comes. The time of judgement is the return of Christ, and the Judge who comes is no stranger to his servants. God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed, and has given assurance of it by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31). The man is Jesus, who was himself condemned by a hasty human verdict. That is why the Corinthians can wait: everything until then is the preliminary hearing.

Things now hidden. Not necessarily evil things, but everything hidden from human view, including the reasons behind what was done in the light. The charity done to be noticed will be disclosed, and equally the kindness done anonymously, the temptation resisted in private, the prayers no one heard.

Purposes of the heart. Boulai are counsels, motives, the reasons a person acts. Two ministers may do the same thing, one for Christ’s glory and one for his own, and from the pew they look identical; only the Lord knows which.

Commendation from God. Here the verse becomes unexpectedly wonderful. The Day will expose every heart, and Paul expects the outcome for God’s servants to be epainos, praise spoken aloud: not a bare acquittal but commendation, from God, to each one. It is the note of the master in the parable saying well done, good and faithful servant (Matthew 25:21), and it is from God that praise matters (Romans 2:29). That God should forgive us is grace beyond calculation. That he should then intend to praise us, having himself supplied everything he is praising, is something else again. Augustine said that when God crowns our merits he crowns nothing but his own gifts. The judgment Christians most instinctively dread is described here as the occasion on which their Father speaks well of them out loud (1 Peter 1:7).

Will everything I have hidden come out on that day? Scripture says plainly that nothing will stay hidden (Luke 12:2–3; 2 Corinthians 5:10), and it does not give us the details of how that disclosure happens. But two things are certain for the believer. First, your sins were already judged, in full, at the cross; whatever is brought to light on that day is brought to light as forgiven, covered by the blood of Christ, and no charge can be laid against God’s elect (Romans 8:33). Second, the emphasis of this very verse is not exposure but commendation. The Day that uncovers everything is, for those in Christ, the Day of their Father’s praise. You need not dread it. You may long for it.

Is it wrong to want God’s praise? No; it is the right ambition, and Paul holds it out to us as a motive. What is wrong is wanting people’s praise instead of God’s (John 12:43), or wanting God’s praise as a wage that puts him in our debt. Jesus told his disciples to do their giving and praying in secret, precisely so that the Father who sees in secret would reward them (Matthew 6:4, 6). Children of a good father want to hear him say “well done”, and he wants to say it. The desire becomes healthy when we remember that every good thing he will praise in us, he first put there.

On a Tuesday. Catch yourself this week at the moment you move from “that was unkind” to “she is that sort of person”. Stop at the first sentence. And if you are the one whose motives are being questioned unfairly, whose faithfulness nobody sees, take heart: the Lord who sees in secret has a word of praise prepared, and nobody else’s verdict can cancel it.

verseByVerse.quote: I have applied all these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, brothers, that you may learn by us not to go beyond what is written, that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another. For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For your benefit. Paul explains what he has been doing: applied (metaschēmatizō, to transfer a figure). He has used himself and Apollos as the worked example, so that he would not have to name the leaders the Corinthians were actually quarrelling over. It is a pastor’s tact: he puts himself and his friend in the dock, two men plainly not rivals, so that no one in Corinth is humiliated by name.

Not beyond what is written. The phrase is genuinely obscure, perhaps a proverb or a schoolroom expression about tracing letters inside the lines. What is written is Scripture, which Paul has quoted again and again in chapters 1–3 (1:19, 31; 2:9; 3:19–20), and the Corinthians had wandered outside it. Their factions, rankings and worldly standards of eloquence were inventions with no warrant in anything God has said. The instinct is permanent: stop at the line, and do not build convictions on ground Scripture has not given you.

Where Christians differ: Scripture and tradition. Some churches hold that tradition or church authority has equal standing with Scripture, and so add doctrines Scripture does not teach. This commentary’s view: Not going beyond what is written expresses the principle the Reformers called sola Scriptura: Scripture alone is the final authority for faith and life. Teachers and traditions are useful servants, but nothing may be required of Christians as necessary that is not taught in Scripture or drawn from it by good and necessary consequence, that is, what plainly follows from what it says (Westminster Confession 1.6, 1.10; 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.6, 1.10).

Puffed up. The word is physioō, inflated, swollen with air: Paul’s favourite word for this church, six times in the letter and only once elsewhere. Nobody in Corinth was boasting in himself outright. They were boasting in their teacher: I am of Paul, I am of Apollos. It is a respectable form of pride, because it feels like loyalty, but it was really a claim that I, who chose the better teacher, am the better Christian.

For who sees anything different in you? Now verse 7, a sentence that has humbled proud Christians for centuries. Three questions, and there is no way through them. The first: what distinguishes you from the person you feel superior to? Who has made you differ? The question expects the answer: nobody, except God.

What do you have that you did not receive? The second question, and the honest answer is nothing whatever. Not your intelligence, which was in your genes before you could form a preference. Not your upbringing, or the country you were born in, or the family that told you about Christ, or the health that let you work, or the temperament that makes you easier to like. Not your knowledge, which came from teachers and books other people wrote. Not your faith, which Paul elsewhere says is the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8). Not your salvation, which was planned before the world began. Not one item on the list was generated by you. This is the doctrine of grace pressed down to the level of daily pride: the God who chose you, called you and kept you is the God who gave you every single thing you might be tempted to compare. Augustine said it was this very verse that finally convinced him that even the beginning of faith is God’s gift.

If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it? The pride is not merely unattractive; it is a false claim. It presents a gift as an achievement, which is dishonesty as well as ingratitude. At bottom, pride is a refusal to be in anyone’s debt, even God’s. Grace invites us to live gladly in his debt for ever, and it is a far happier place to live. Boasting in a gift is absurd: you boast in the giver. And see how completely this removes the ground for comparison, which is what the whole chapter has been about. You cannot rank yourself against another Christian on the basis of gifts you were both handed. It would be like two beggars quarrelling over which of them was the more distinguished for having been given a coat.

Boast in the Lord. The list of things received has a summit: Christ, who became to us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption (1:30–31). The greatest thing any Corinthian had received was not a gift or a teacher but Christ himself, and in him a righteousness that was never theirs to earn. Pride in a teacher boasts in a man who was only a servant, and forgets the Lord who was given to us whole.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may never use books, confessions or creeds. These are helpful as long as they serve and agree with Scripture, and Paul himself handed on what he had received (15:3). Nor does verse 7 mean that gifts are imaginary or that we should pretend to have none. False modesty denies the gift and so dishonours the Giver just as surely as pride does.

Does this mean I should not feel good about hard work? No. Receiving everything does not make you passive. Paul worked harder than all the apostles, and in the same breath said it was not he but the grace of God that was with him (15:10). So you may be glad when you have worked hard and done well; gladness is not boasting. The difference is where the gladness goes. Pride stops at itself: look what I did. Gratitude travels on: look what God has given and done through me. When someone praises your work, you do not need to deny it or deflect it awkwardly. Thank them simply, and then, in your heart, hand the praise straight on to the One it belongs to.

On a Tuesday. The next time you feel the small internal lift of being further on than another believer, ask Paul’s question: what do I have that I did not receive? What is left when it collapses is not humiliation but relief, and gratitude, and a strange new warmth towards the person you were just measuring (Romans 12:3; John 3:27).

For worship. Every good thing in every believer has a single address of origin. All of it came down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change (James 1:17). Even the Son gives away what he received. In his last prayer before the cross he said to his Father, The glory that you have given me I have given to them (John 17:22). Glory passes from the Father to the Son, and from the Son to sinners who had nothing, and heaven will be full of people who received everything and boast in no one but the Giver.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — Apostles as Spectacle: The Cruciform Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to irony. The Corinthians act as if they are already rich and reigning, while God has put the apostles at the end of the procession, like men condemned to die in the arena, a spectacle to the world and to angels. The apostles are hungry, beaten and homeless, blessing when cursed and treated as the world’s rubbish.
verseByVerse.theology:
Which Age We Live In

The Corinthians’ problem was not only social pride but confusion about which age they were in. They lived as if the resurrection age had fully arrived. Paul answers that we live between Christ’s first and second coming, and in this time the Christian life is shaped by the cross. Suffering, weakness and apparent defeat are not failures of faith but a share in Christ’s own path, in which resurrection comes through the cross, not around it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Behind verse 9 is the arena, where condemned criminals were brought on at the end of the show. Paul had been beaten and imprisoned, and would eventually be executed. Now: The prosperity gospel is the modern form of Corinthian triumphalism, treating health, wealth and success as the normal marks of Spirit-filled Christianity. Paul’s hungry, homeless fools for Christ’s sake stand against any teaching that makes suffering a sign that something has gone wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings! And would that you did reign, so that we might share the rule with you!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Already you have all you want! Three exclamations, all irony. “All you want” is korennymi, to have eaten your fill, and the repeated “already” names their error: they believed they had arrived.

Already you have become rich! Rich in gifts and knowledge (1:5), and proud of it. They had taken the gift Paul thanked God for and turned it into a status. A congregation can be genuinely blessed and use the blessing as evidence that it no longer needs anything, least of all correction.

Without us you have become kings! They behaved as if they were already reigning, as believers will in the age to come (6:2–3; Revelation 5:10), and as if they had got there without the apostles. They had claimed the age to come as a present possession. Paul does not deny that Christians are rich; all things are theirs (3:21–22). What he denies is the timing. The inheritance is certain, and it has not yet been paid out.

Holy irony. Scripture is not embarrassed by sarcasm: Elijah suggesting that Baal might be asleep (1 Kings 18:27), the Lord himself on men who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel (Matthew 23:24). Irony is a legitimate instrument when someone is so pleased with himself that a straight statement will simply be absorbed. But it is a sharp tool, never for sport, and Paul says a few lines later why he used it: not to shame them but to warn them as his beloved children (4:14).

Would that you did reign! Then the irony breaks, and the wistfulness is real: I wish the kingdom had come, because I am hungry and cold, and if you were really reigning then so would I be. His complaint is not that they are too hopeful. It is that they have taken delivery of a hope that has not yet arrived, and have therefore stopped needing the cross.

The order of the King’s own road. The Corinthians wanted the crown without the cross, and their King went the other way. On the road to Emmaus the risen Jesus asked, Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? (Luke 24:26). Suffering first, then glory, is the shape of his story (1 Peter 1:11). He reigns now at the Father’s right hand, and must reign until all his enemies are under his feet (15:25), but his people share his reign the way they share his life, by first sharing his sufferings (Romans 8:17). To claim the throne early is to step off the road he walked.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers have nothing now. We have every spiritual blessing (Ephesians 1:3), and the kingdom has truly arrived in Jesus, but the full glory is future. Christians live between the already and the not yet, and the error at Corinth was to erase the second half.

So is it wrong to pray for healing or provision? No. Jesus taught us to ask for daily bread, and James tells the sick to call the elders to pray (James 5:14). God often heals and often provides, and we should ask him boldly and thank him gladly. What this verse rules out is the teaching that health, wealth and victory are guaranteed now to anyone with enough faith, so that suffering becomes a sign that something has gone wrong with you. That is Corinthian triumphalism in modern dress. Paul’s answer to it is not a better argument. It is the next five verses, in which he lists what the apostles were actually enduring while the Corinthians reigned (4:9–13). Ask God for good things; do not tell him he owes them to you before the time.

For worship. There is a King who really does reign already, and he is not keeping his throne to himself. The one who conquers, he says, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne (Revelation 3:21). Paul’s wish will be granted after all, because its Lord is generous. The crowns are real, the date is fixed, and the King who will give them out won them by wearing a crown of thorns.
verseByVerse.note: Paul speaks with irony: they acted as if the kingdom had already fully come.

verseByVerse.quote: For I think that God has exhibited us apostles as last of all, like men sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Last of all. The imagery is from the arena. At the end of a day at the games the condemned were brought out, with no weapons and no chance, not to compete but to die in front of people; condemned prisoners were also paraded last in a Roman triumph, on their way to execution. God has exhibited the apostles in that slot.

Like men sentenced to death. Epithanatios: condemned to die. Paul faced death every day (15:30–31) and was always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake (2 Corinthians 4:11). The Corinthians are reigning as kings; their founding apostle describes himself as the closing act of an execution. Those are not two styles of Christianity. One of them mistakes what age we are in.

A spectacle. The word is theatron, theatre. Paul assumes that what happens to Christians is watched by the unseen order: the same assumption behind the angels who long to look into these things (1 Peter 1:12), and behind the claim that God intended his manifold wisdom to be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places through the church (Ephesians 3:10).

The first man on that stage. The apostles were not the first to be put there. Luke tells us that when Jesus died, all the crowds that had assembled for this spectacle went home beating their breasts (Luke 23:48). He was the condemned man led out last, stripped and lifted up where the whole city could see. The apostles stand in his place because they belong to him. A servant is not greater than his master, Jesus said; if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (John 15:20). Paul’s slot at the end of the procession is the one his Lord occupied first.

A lit stage. That puts a strange dignity on the least impressive Christian life. The believer quietly humiliated for his faith is on a lit stage, watched by beings who understand what they are looking at. What the angels see in the church is a creature who is losing and is not bitter, who blesses the people taking everything from him and does not stop trusting God. That is the life of the crucified Christ in his servant.

Are there still apostles like the ones God put on display? Not in the sense Paul means here. An apostle in this sense was a witness of the risen Christ, commissioned by him in person (Acts 1:21–22; 1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:8), and the apostles were part of the church’s foundation, which is laid once (Ephesians 2:20). The word is used more loosely in the New Testament of messengers sent out by churches (2 Corinthians 8:23; Philippians 2:25), and missionaries today stand in that line. But no one now can meet the qualifications of the Twelve and Paul, and no one should claim their authority. What the apostles taught is in Scripture, and that is how their office continues. And look at the mark Paul gives here: not a platform and a following, but being led out last into the arena, which is the very opposite of what many who claim the title today look like.

Are angels really watching me? Scripture says they are, though it does not tell us how much they see or understand. They rejoice over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10), they serve those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), and they are learning the wisdom of God by watching the church (Ephesians 3:10). That is not meant to make you self-conscious, as if you were performing. It is meant to tell you that your faithfulness is not wasted. When you forgive someone who has not apologised, or keep trusting God in a hospital corridor, it is not happening in an empty room.

For worship. On that first stage the spectacle was turned inside out. The man the crowd watched die was disarming the rulers and authorities, putting them to open shame, triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15). The condemned man at the end of the procession was the Conqueror leading it. From that hour every follower made a spectacle for his name has been walking in a victory parade, not a funeral, and the road ends where his ended: on a throne.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned prisoners were paraded last in a Roman triumph, or sent into the arena at the end of the games.

verseByVerse.quote: We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are held in honor, but we in disrepute.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fools for Christ’s sake. Three contrasts, and in each the apostles get the worse half. Paul is not claiming that Christians are unintelligent, nor recommending eccentricity for its own sake. The foolishness is entirely derived: it is what you look like when you have staked everything on a crucified man, in a world that measures by power and success (1:18).

Weak and strong. The apostles are weak: Paul came to Corinth in weakness and fear and much trembling (2:3). The Corinthians think they are strong, and the irony is that this very sense of strength is their weakness.

In disrepute. Atimos: dishonoured. The Corinthians had managed to hold the gospel and their social standing at once, respectable in Corinth and confident in church. Paul’s implication is quiet and pointed: if the message is genuinely offensive, how have you avoided all the offence?

Outside the camp. Each half of these pairs that Paul takes for himself was worn first by Christ. His own family said he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21). He was crucified in weakness (2 Corinthians 13:4). He died the death Rome kept for those it most despised, outside the city gate. Hebrews draws the conclusion: let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured (Hebrews 13:13). The disgrace is not a detour from following Jesus. It is where he is.

The question that has not aged. Christian convictions can be held in a way that costs nothing, making sure nobody at work or in the family ever has occasion to think one odd. And this verse is also for the Christian already paying the cost in small ways: the colleague whose views are treated as a harmless quirk, the relative the family has kindly decided has become a bit much. That is not persecution as the early church knew it, and should not be dressed up as martyrdom. But it wears people down because it is so ordinary. Being thought a fool for Christ’s sake is not a sign you have handled things badly. It is a sign you are in the apostolic line.

How do I know whether I am a fool for Christ or just foolish? Ask what the offence is attached to. If people think you odd because you will not lie for the company, because you go to church, because you believe Jesus rose and is the only way to the Father, that is the foolishness of the cross. If they think you odd because you are harsh, preachy, careless about your work or quick to take offence, that is your own foolishness, and it is a burden to the gospel, not a badge (1 Peter 4:15–16). Paul was courteous, hard-working and wise in how he spoke (Colossians 4:5–6). The goal is that if they reject you, they should be rejecting Christ in you, not the rough edges round him.

verseByVerse.quote: To the present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly dressed and buffeted and homeless, and we labor, working with our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat. We have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the present hour. Now the catalogue, deliberately physical, his condition as he writes. Buffeted is kolaphizō, struck with the fist, the very word used when Jesus was struck in the high priest’s house (Matthew 26:67). The apostle carries in his body the bruises his Lord received first.

Working with our own hands. Among the educated Greeks manual work was looked down on, and the professional speakers who toured Corinth were paid handsomely for talking. Paul made tents (Acts 18:3; 20:34), and part of the Corinthian embarrassment was straightforwardly social: their founder had calloused hands. He accepted it so as not to put an obstacle in the way of the gospel (9:12).

When reviled, we bless. Here is the heart of the passage: no retaliation, no campaign to set the record straight. And these responses are not passive. To bless is actively to ask God’s good for the man who has just insulted you. To endure is to stay put under the pressure rather than escape it. To entreat (parakaleō) is to speak kindly, to appeal, to keep the door open towards someone spreading lies about you. It is exactly what Paul had been taught: bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you (Luke 6:28). And it is what he knew of his Lord, who when he was reviled did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23), and who from the cross asked the Father to forgive the men who had nailed him there (Luke 23:34).

Scum of the world. Then the two ugliest words available: perikatharma, the filth in the bucket after cleaning, and peripsēma, what is scraped off. Both were used of the lowest criminals, sometimes thrown out or sacrificed to purge a city in disaster. This is how Paul lists his credentials, not the visions or the churches planted. When Paul wants to prove he is a genuine apostle to a church impressed by success, he produces his hunger and his ruined reputation.

Does blessing those who revile me mean I must let people abuse me? No. Paul is describing how to answer insult, slander and persecution for the gospel’s sake: with blessing instead of revenge. He is not telling anyone to remain under abuse at home, at work or in a church. Paul himself appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen when he was being illegally beaten (Acts 22:25), and when his life was threatened he escaped (Acts 9:25). Abuse should never be tolerated, and the right response to it includes getting to safety, telling those who can protect you, and reporting crimes to the authorities, who are God’s servants for that very purpose (Romans 13:4). You can pray for God’s good for an abuser, and refuse to retaliate, from a place of safety. Blessing is not the same as staying.

Should pastors then work for a living instead of being paid? Not necessarily. Paul says plainly that the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (9:14), and he accepted gifts from other churches (Philippians 4:15–16). He chose to work in Corinth so that no one could accuse him of preaching for money in a city full of paid speakers (9:12, 15–18). Some ministers today rightly work a trade, and others are rightly supported by their churches. The principle is not the payslip but the heart: a minister must never preach for gain, and a church must never let its minister go in need.

On a Tuesday. These responses can be learned, because the Spirit of the Christ who blessed his executioners lives in you. When somebody misrepresents you and the answer is drafted in your head at once, Paul’s three verbs are the alternative: ask God to do that person good, by name; stay where God has put you rather than withdrawing in a sulk; keep speaking to them rather than about them (Romans 12:14, 20–21; 1 Peter 3:9). And pray this week for Christians treated as the refuse of the world in places where faith can still cost a life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — A Father’s Warning and Appeal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul writes not to shame them but to warn them as his beloved children. Through the gospel he became their father, so he urges them to imitate him and sends Timothy to remind them of his ways in Christ. Some have grown arrogant, as though he were not coming. He will come soon, if the Lord wills, to see not their talk but their power, and asks whether he must come with a rod or with gentleness.
verseByVerse.theology:
Spiritual Fatherhood and Learning by Imitation

Paul’s fatherhood rests on the gospel: “I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel” (v. 15). That is about formation, not control. Paul asks to be imitated not as an authority but as a living picture of the gospel he preached: not his person but his pattern, the pattern of the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In Paul’s absence some at Corinth had grown arrogant and dismissed him. Timothy is sent to show by his life what Paul had taught. Now: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (11:1) is among the most demanding things a minister can say, and among the most necessary. Disciples need examples, not only doctrines, and a church with correct theology but no Christlike character has missed the point.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not write these things to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children. For though you have countless guides in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not to shame but to admonish. The irony stops. The sarcasm (4:8–13) was not injured pride but a father who could not get through to his children. Shaming and admonishing feel similar from the outside and are opposite in intent. Shame attacks the person: it aims to make him feel small, and it produces either compliance or resentment and never growth. Admonition (noutheteō, to put in mind, to warn and counsel) attacks the problem. It aims at change, and it can only be received from someone the hearer is sure loves him.

Countless guides. Literally ten thousand. The word for guides is paidagōgoi: the household slave who walked the children to school, kept them out of trouble and enforced the rules (Galatians 3:24). Useful, necessary, and not a parent. Paul is not sneering at the many teachers; he is naming a different kind of bond.

You do not have many fathers. Guardians can be replaced; a father is unique. Egennēsa: I begot you. Through Paul’s preaching God gave them new birth, and the man through whose preaching you were born cannot be replaced by a better speaker. The polished man may well teach you more. He will never be the one who told you first.

Those whom I love. Paul’s order, hard words first and love stated plainly, is the risen Christ’s own. To a church that said, I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing, almost exactly the Corinthians’ boast (4:8), Jesus gave a rebuke as sharp as anything in this chapter, and then explained it: those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent (Revelation 3:17, 19). The one who rebukes his churches is the one who died for them, and his warnings come from the same heart as his wounds.

Where Christians differ: calling ministers father. Jesus said to call no one on earth your father (Matthew 23:9), yet Paul calls himself their father. Some use this to justify the title Father for priests. This commentary’s view: Jesus forbade giving any human the place of ultimate spiritual authority that belongs only to God. Paul is describing a relationship, not claiming a title or rank. He brought them to new birth through the gospel, and cares for them with a father’s love (1 Thessalonians 2:11; Philemon 10). The word describes affection and responsibility, not a priestly office, and he uses it to plead, not to rule. The verse gives no warrant for making Father an honorific for ministers. Many who use the title mean by it the pastoral affection Paul describes, and the point is not to scorn them but to keep the Father in heaven without a rival.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul has authority over their faith in place of Christ: not that we lord it over your faith, he says, but we work with you for your joy (2 Corinthians 1:24). He is a father in Christ, through the gospel, and the life he passed on was never his own.

How to correct someone. Paul speaks the hard thing first, without softening it, and then makes the affection explicit: beloved children. It is easy to go wrong either way: the love assumed and never stated, so the rebuke lands as shame; or the love stated at such length that the correction never gets said. So ask whether the person you need to correct knows, because you have told them, that you are for them. Paul could call the Corinthians puffed-up infants playing at kings because they had watched him work with his hands among them and knew what he had spent on them (2 Corinthians 12:14–15).

What if the person who led me to Christ later fell away or hurt me? Then grieve, but do not doubt what God did. The new birth is God’s work, not the messenger’s; Paul was only the instrument, and God can use a cracked vessel to carry living water (Philippians 1:15–18). Your faith does not depend on the one who brought it to you, but on the Christ he pointed to. If that person sinned against you, you are not bound to stay close or to pretend nothing happened, and if they did harm, it should be dealt with honestly. But you may still thank God for the gospel you heard through them, and pray that he would restore them.
verseByVerse.note: The word for “guides” was used of the household slave who took charge of children on their way to school.

verseByVerse.quote: I urge you, then, be imitators of me. That is why I sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, to remind you of my ways in Christ, as I teach them everywhere in every church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Imitators of me. It sounds breathtakingly presumptuous. Paul supplies the qualification later: be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (11:1). So the imitation is not of a personality but of a direction; he is a man pointing, and he is asking them to follow the pointing. Children learn by copying their father, and our discomfort with the sentence may say more about us than about him.

What he is asking them to copy. He has just described it (4:9–13), and it is not his eloquence, his authority or his success. It is hunger, disrepute, manual labour, and blessing people who revile you. Imitate me, in this context, means: take the lower place, work with your hands, be thought a fool, and do not retaliate. Nobody builds a personality cult on that material. And many of these people could not read, so Christianity was passed on the way a trade is, by watching somebody do it; few people become patient by reading about patience.

Christ’s before it was Paul’s. Every item on that list was Christ’s first. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58); he worked with his hands as a carpenter (Mark 6:3); he took the lowest place and washed feet; when he was reviled, he did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23). Paul’s life is a copy because Christ lives in him (Galatians 2:20), and that is why the appeal is not arrogant. The risen Christ, by his Spirit, was producing his own humility and love in Paul’s ordinary days. He is not asking the Corinthians to become like Paul. He is asking them to become like the Lord they can see, imperfectly but truly, in Paul.

I sent you Timothy. Paul’s spiritual son (1 Timothy 1:2) was on his way (16:10), bringing not new doctrine but a reminder of Paul’s ways (hodoi, paths) in Christ. Paul does not send a letter alone; he sends a man formed by exactly the pattern under dispute. The argument travels in a document; the pattern travels in a man.

Everywhere in every church. Paul had no special teaching for Corinth; he taught the same in all the churches (7:17; 11:16; 14:33). It answers the pride that thought Corinth could be an exception: there is one gospel and one pattern of life, the same in Ephesus and Philippi and here.

Is it arrogant for me to say “follow my example”? Not if it is said in Paul’s spirit and about Paul’s pattern. Every parent, elder and older believer is already being imitated whether they like it or not; the only question is whether they will own it. Elders are told to be examples to the flock (1 Peter 5:3), and older women to train younger women by their lives (Titus 2:3–5). You do not need to claim perfection. You can say: watch how I bring my failures to Christ, how I handle money, how I speak about people who are absent. That is not boasting. It is the honest admission that Christianity is caught as well as taught.

What if there is no one in my church I can imitate? There almost certainly is, but they may not be where you are looking. The people worth imitating are rarely the most visible. Look for the faithful rather than the impressive: the couple who have quietly loved each other for forty years, the widow who prays, the man who never speaks badly of anyone. Ask to spend time with them. Read the lives of faithful Christians from the past, too (Hebrews 13:7). And remember that the final pattern is Christ himself, whom every human example only points to.

verseByVerse.quote: Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you. But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some are arrogant. The diagnosis is shrewd and universal: people behave differently when they believe they will not be met. Puffed up again, and the cause was distance: some were saying Paul would not dare return, and a confidence had grown up of the sort that always grows in the absence of the person who might answer back.

If the Lord wills. Paul simply announces that the absence is temporary (16:5). If the Lord wills is not a verbal tic but the settled habit of a man who does not consider his own plans self-executing, the same instinct James insists on: you ought to say, if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (James 4:15). A man who says that about a journey has already settled something about who runs the world, and it shows up in his diary rather than only in his theology.

Not talk but power. Talk (logos) is the impressive speech Corinth prized; power (dynamis) is the real working of God’s Spirit in a life. Paul is not coming to compare rhetoric; he is coming to see whether the gospel these people discuss so fluently has produced in them what it always produces where it is real. Jealousy and strife were the evidence of the flesh (3:3), and gifts without love are nothing (13:1–3). So the power Paul means to look for is not first the spectacular. It is whether these people have begun to love each other.

My master is delayed. Jesus described this exact arrogance. A servant says to himself, My master is delayed, and begins to beat his fellow servants and to eat and drink with drunkards, and the master comes on a day he does not expect (Matthew 24:48–50). Puffed-up confidence grows wherever the Lord seems far away, and the cure is the same: the one who is absent is coming, and a church lives well only when it lives as the household of a returning Lord.

Must I always say “if the Lord wills”? It is not a formula you must attach to every sentence; Paul often speaks of his plans without it (16:8). It is an attitude of the heart that should be visible in how you plan. Make plans, work hard at them, and hold them with an open hand, knowing that you do not know what tomorrow will bring (James 4:13–16). Saying the words aloud now and then is a good discipline, because it reminds you and others who is in charge. What matters is that you would not be shocked, or bitter, if God redrew the map.

On a Tuesday. A man can talk about grace fluently for thirty years and be no easier to live with. So ask those who live with you, not those who hear you teach, whether they see love, patience and holiness behind your words, and ask God for the power, which only his Spirit supplies.

verseByVerse.quote: For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power. What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom of God. The kingdom of God is God’s rule, present now through Christ and the Spirit, and it shows itself not in eloquent religious talk but in changed lives (Romans 14:17; 1 Thessalonians 1:5). Against the Corinthians: fluency is not evidence of anything.

Not a demand for the spectacular. But power here is not a promise of the spectacular, to be conscripted to demand signs and wonders as proof of a genuine church. The power this letter has described is the power of God that saves through a message about an execution (1:18), that will raise the dead (6:14), and that turns a jealous congregation into people who love each other. That is not less than miraculous; it is simply harder to photograph.

What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod? Then the final question, and Paul leaves it hanging as a question rather than a threat. The rod is a father’s rod of discipline (Proverbs 13:24). The rod is real: Paul has apostolic authority and will use it, as chapter 5 is about to show. Nothing in this chapter’s tenderness cancels the discipline. A father who can never be firm is not being kind, and a church that can never act is not being loving.

Or with love in a spirit of gentleness? Gentleness is prautēs: meekness, mildness, strength under control. Both the rod and gentleness are love; but gentleness is what Paul longs to use. And the choice is not his. He has put it in their hands: what do you wish? This is the strangest kind of authority, a man with the right to compel, asking. He would rather arrive as a father with nothing in his hand, and whether he can depends entirely on what they do between receiving this letter and seeing him. That is exactly how God deals with his people throughout Scripture. He warns before he acts, at length, and the warning is itself the mercy: a rod described in advance is a rod trying not to be used. Turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die (Ezekiel 33:11)?

The meekness and gentleness of Christ. Paul’s gentleness is borrowed. Writing to this same church later, he opens his sternest section: I, Paul, myself entreat you, by the meekness and gentleness of Christ (2 Corinthians 10:1). The King entered his capital mounted on a donkey (Matthew 21:5), and called the weary to himself because he was gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29). The kingdom’s power does not cancel that gentleness; it travels in it. When Paul hopes to arrive with love and a gentle spirit, he hopes to arrive looking like his Lord.

In the flow. Verses 20–21 bring to rest the first great section of the letter, begun with the plea that there be no divisions (1:10), and the rod opens chapter 5, where Paul must deal with a sin the proud church had tolerated (5:1–2).

Does God still come to his children with the rod? Yes, but always as a Father, never as an executioner. The Lord disciplines those he loves, and the discipline of believers is not punishment for sin, which Christ has already borne, but training for holiness (Hebrews 12:5–11). It can come through hardship, through the loss of comfort, through the exposure of sin, or through the discipline of the church. It is painful, and it is always for our good, that we may share his holiness. The quickest way to be spared the rod is to respond to the word: when God speaks gently, listen.

Is church discipline really loving? It is, when it is done in the right way, and the next chapter shows why. Discipline is meant to bring a sinner to repentance, to protect the church, and to honour Christ’s name (5:5–7). It must be carried out by the church in a patient, ordered way (Matthew 18:15–17), with humility and with the aim of restoring, not removing. A church that never disciplines is not kinder than one that does; it is simply leaving people to wander towards danger without a warning. But discipline must never be harsh, hasty or used to protect leaders, and it never replaces calling the police when a crime has been committed.

On a Tuesday. Is there a correction God has been making gently, through a verse that keeps coming back or a friend’s word, that you have been putting off? Respond while it is still the gentle word. And if you have authority over others, follow Paul’s order: warn clearly, show your love plainly, give time to respond, and only then use the rod, and even then with sorrow rather than satisfaction.

For worship. The One who had every right to come with a rod to a world in open rebellion came instead as an infant, worked with his hands, was reviled and blessed, and was made a spectacle last of all. The only rod that has yet fallen in full fell on him: he was pierced for our transgressions, and with his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). The King holds all power, and he comes to his people in gentleness, because the rod has already been spent on his own back.

5.title: The Leaven of Immorality: Church Discipline and the Holiness of God
5.overview:
Paul now deals with a scandal. A man in the church is living with his father’s wife, probably his stepmother, a relationship forbidden by the law of Moses and condemned even by Roman society. Worse, the church is proud of itself instead of grieving. Paul, though absent, has already made his judgement: when they assemble with the Lord’s power, they must hand this man over to Satan, putting him outside the church, so that his sinful nature may be destroyed and he may be saved on the day of the Lord.

Paul uses a Passover picture. Just as Jewish households swept every scrap of yeast out of the house before the feast, the church must get rid of the old yeast of sin, because Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed. Then he corrects a misunderstanding of an earlier letter. He meant not that they should avoid all immoral people in the world, but that they must not share fellowship with a professing believer who persists in serious sin. God judges outsiders; the church must judge those inside.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A case of open sin, and a church proud of tolerating it. Paul calls for grief and for action taken by the gathered church in the Lord’s name, aimed at the man’s salvation. Then the Passover picture: because Christ our lamb has been sacrificed, the church must clear out the old yeast and keep the feast with sincerity and truth.
verseByVerse.theology:
Church Discipline as a Gospel Act

Calvin grounds church discipline in the same logic Paul uses here: the church’s holiness is not its own achievement but a share in the holiness of Christ who dwells in it. Excommunication is not the last word against the sinner; it is meant to bring him to repentance. A church that will not discipline, in the name of grace or of avoiding conflict, is less gracious than it thinks: it lets unrepentant sin spread through the whole body, and it withholds from the sinner the painful mercy of being confronted.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The church’s pride may reflect the influence of members with status and polish who had turned gospel freedom into permissiveness. Now: Many churches never practise discipline at all, and a church afraid to confront unrepentant sin can end up shaped more by the fear of conflict than by love for the sinner.

verseByVerse.quote: It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans, for a man has his father’s wife. And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn? Let him who has done this be removed from among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 5 turns from divisions to a case of open, scandalous sin, and to the church’s failure to deal with it. The scandal is not only the man but a congregation proud of its tolerance. This is the New Testament’s clearest teaching on church discipline, and at its centre stands not a rule but a Lamb.

Actually reported. The word can mean actually or generally: this is common knowledge. The thing is talked about across the region. “Sexual immorality” is porneia, the broad word for any sexual sin outside marriage.

Not tolerated even among pagans. This is the sting: it breaks not only the law of Moses but the standards of pagan Corinth. Roman law prohibited such a marriage outright, and Cicero treats a comparable union inside a family as a crime almost beyond belief. Corinth was famous across the Mediterranean for vice, and the church had managed to be more permissive than Corinth.

His father’s wife. The wording is careful: not his mother but his stepmother, the father probably dead or divorced. The law of Moses forbade it explicitly (Leviticus 18:8; Deuteronomy 22:30). “Has” is a present tense, which suggests an ongoing relationship, perhaps living together or even married, settled rather than a single lapse. And since Paul says nothing about disciplining the woman, she was probably not a believer; the church has authority only over its own members (v. 12).

And you are arrogant! Here is the real subject of the chapter: not the man, but the congregation. They were not ashamed of it; they were proud, puffed up, the word Paul has used against them all through chapter 4. Probably it prized its own spiritual sophistication and had a theology of freedom it was pleased with: the body did not matter spiritually (6:12–13), grace was large enough to accommodate even this, and a church that took it in its stride proved how far beyond ordinary scruples it had travelled. The shape is permanent. There is a kind of tolerance that presents itself as maturity and is actually cowardice with a theology attached. Underneath it is usually a hunger to be thought well of: to be the church nobody could call narrow. But a church that needs the world’s approval more than its Lord’s has already chosen whose verdict it fears (Galatians 1:10).

Ought you not rather to mourn? The word is pentheō, the verb for grieving a death, the word used of mourners at a funeral. This is the turning point of the passage, because it names the right emotion, and it is one we rarely reach for. There are two other responses available when serious sin surfaces in a church. One is what the Corinthians did: absorb it, explain it, be relaxed about it. The other is what churches more often do: outrage, gossip, the energetic circulation of the details, and a certain relish. Paul asks for neither. He asks for grief, the response of people who have lost something they loved and are standing at a graveside. Grief cannot be faked and cannot be enjoyed. Outrage is pleasurable; that is why it is so popular. Indifference is comfortable. Mourning is neither, and it is the only one of the three that has any love in it: you do not grieve over someone you were not attached to.

Proud of what the Lamb died for. The Corinthians were boasting about the very kind of sin for which Christ, their Passover lamb, was sacrificed (v. 7). A church that thinks grace makes sin small has forgotten what grace cost. Their only glory was a crucified Saviour (1:30–31), and no one can glory in the cross while being proud of the sins that put him there. And mourning is not a gloomy alternative to joy. It is the posture Christ himself blessed: blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matthew 5:4).

Removed from among you. Mourning does not replace action; it is the only right soil for it. The grief Paul asks for is not a feeling that leaves everything as it was, but the sorrow of people who love the man and the Lord too much to pretend.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church should expel members for every sin. All believers sin, every day. Church discipline is for serious, open sin persisted in without repentance, after patient warning (Matthew 18:15–17).

Why was the woman not disciplined too? Almost certainly because she was not a member of the church. Paul says plainly that the church’s responsibility is for those inside it, and that God judges those outside (vv. 12–13). That does not make her sin less serious, and it does not mean she is beyond the reach of the gospel. It means the church’s formal discipline applies only to those who profess Christ and have joined themselves to his people. Toward her, as toward every unbeliever, the church’s task is to proclaim the gospel and pray.

What should an ordinary member do when there is a scandal in the church? First, do not spread it. Talking about the details with people who are not part of the solution is gossip, however concerned it sounds (Proverbs 16:28). Second, pray, both for the person caught in the sin and for the leaders who have to handle it. Third, if you know something your leaders need to know, tell them directly and privately. Fourth, check your heart: aim for the grief Paul asks for, not the interest or superiority that comes so easily. And if the sin is a crime, especially any abuse, it must be reported to the police; the church’s discipline never replaces the law.
verseByVerse.note: “His father’s wife” probably means his stepmother. The law of Moses forbade it, and Roman law condemned it too.

verseByVerse.quote: For though absent in body, I am present in spirit; and as if present, I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did such a thing. When you are assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Absent in body, present in spirit. Paul means what any of us mean by being with someone in spirit, in thought and concern, but with an added weight: his apostolic authority genuinely travels in the letter being read aloud (Colossians 2:5). When they hear this document, they are hearing him.

Already pronounced judgment. Paul can give the verdict from a distance because the facts are not in dispute: a man is living with his stepmother in plain sight.

When you are assembled. Paul has pronounced the verdict, but carrying it out waits until the congregation gathers. The apostle with unquestioned authority does not remove the man by letter. Discipline in the New Testament is a corporate act of the gathered church, not a private decision taken by a leader, and this cuts both ways. The congregation cannot hand this to the minister and then complain about him. And the leader who decides a case privately and announces the outcome finds no cover here. The Lord built the same safeguard into the procedure: the steps of Matthew 18 end with tell it to the church, not tell it to the pastor (Matthew 18:17).

With the power of our Lord Jesus. Two things make such a gathering more than a disciplinary hearing. It is in the name of the Lord Jesus: convened on his authority, not the church’s own. And it proceeds with the power of our Lord Jesus, which is exactly the promise attached in Matthew: where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them (Matthew 18:20). That sentence is, in its context, a guarantee given to a church doing this very thing, and the most sobering reason for doing it carefully. It does not make a church’s vote infallible. It means that when a congregation acts by his word, the warning the man receives is not only from his neighbours but from his Lord (Luke 10:16).

Who actually carries out discipline, the elders or the whole church? Christians organise this differently, and honest believers disagree. Congregational churches, including many Baptists, read this verse and Matthew 18:17 as giving the final act to the gathered membership, led and guided by its elders (2 Corinthians 2:6 speaks of a punishment by the majority). Presbyterian churches see the elders, the church’s representatives, acting on behalf of the congregation. Others mix the two. But the common ground is wide and it is the point of this verse: discipline is never the act of one man alone, it is done before the Lord with his authority, it involves the church, and it is done openly and carefully, not in secret.

verseByVerse.quote: you are to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deliver this man to Satan. Paul’s own final clause forbids reading this alarming sentence as damnation. The whole letter has been describing two spheres: the community where Christ dwells by his Spirit (3:16), and the world outside, which lies in the power of the evil one (1 John 5:19; Ephesians 2:2). To be excluded from the assembly is to be put out of the first and into the second: removed from the protection, the fellowship, the Lord’s Table and the prayers of God’s people, and left in the open. Paul uses the same phrase once more (1 Timothy 1:19–20).

For the destruction of the flesh. This phrase is genuinely disputed. Some take it of physical suffering, even death, on the pattern of the judgments in Acts 5 or later in this letter (11:30). Others take “flesh” (sarx) in Paul’s usual moral sense, the sinful nature, so that what is to be destroyed is the appetite itself, by being allowed to run to its own bitter end. The second fits Paul’s vocabulary and the purpose clause far better. A man protected from the consequences of what he is doing will continue; a man who is left to feel what it actually costs may come to his senses. It is the road of the prodigal, who needed the pigs before he wanted the father (Luke 15:14–17).

So that his spirit may be saved. This clause governs everything. This is not the church washing its hands of a man. It is the last available means of grace, applied because everything gentler has failed. Excommunication, the formal removal of a professing believer from the membership and the Lord’s Table of a church, is not in the New Testament the opposite of seeking someone’s salvation; it is an instrument of it, the surgeon’s knife, used with the intention of a cure.

The day of the Lord. In this letter it is the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, and Paul has promised this church that Christ will sustain them to the end, guiltless in that day, because God is faithful (1:8–9). That is what makes so severe a step thinkable. The church can put a man outside its fellowship without putting him outside the reach of Christ, because his salvation never rested on the church’s grip. The Lord leaves the ninety-nine to go after the one that is lost (Luke 15:4). Discipline is the church’s part; bringing the sheep home is his. And the Judge on that day will be the Shepherd who went looking.

What happened next. No treatment of this verse is honest without the sequel. Writing to the same church later, Paul deals with a disciplined man, perhaps this one, though commentators are divided. The discipline had worked, and Paul told the church to forgive and restore him, so that we would not be outwitted by Satan (2 Corinthians 2:5–11). In 1 Corinthians 5 Satan is the instrument God uses to bring a man home; in 2 Corinthians 2 he is the danger of a church that will not let a repentant man back. The second failure is the commoner one.

Where Christians differ: church discipline. Many churches today never practise discipline, thinking it unloving or judgmental. Others practise it harshly, for minor issues. This commentary’s view: Church discipline is commanded by Christ and the apostles (Matthew 18:15–17; 2 Thessalonians 3:6, 14–15; Titus 3:10). It is one of the marks of a true church, alongside the preaching of the word and the right use of the sacraments (Belgic Confession 29). Its purposes are the restoration of the sinner, the purity of the church, and the honour of Christ (the Westminster Confession 30.3). It should be done carefully, in stages, with love and prayer, and only for serious, persistent, unrepentant sin.

The guard against cruelty. This text has been used to justify real cruelty. Shunning as punishment, families broken apart, people pursued for years, the machinery of control: all of it has claimed this verse. The test is the purpose clause. If a church disciplines without longing for the person’s return, without a route back, without telling him plainly what repentance would look like and how gladly he would be received, then whatever it is doing, it is not this. Paul’s aim is a man saved in the day of the Lord, and everything that does not serve that aim is somebody else’s idea.

Can a true Christian be put out of the church? Yes. Paul’s hope that the man’s spirit will be saved suggests he may be a genuine believer in serious, stubborn sin. True Christians can fall grievously for a time, as David did (Westminster 17.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 17.3). But God does not let his own go. One of the ways he brings them back is through the discipline of his church, which he uses to make them feel the misery of their sin and to turn them home. So the doctrine that God keeps his people to the end does not make discipline unnecessary; discipline is one of the means by which he keeps them. Whether a particular person is truly born again is finally known to God, and will be shown by whether he returns.

Can someone who has been put out ever come back? Yes, and the church should long for it and make it easy to see the way. The door in this passage opens both ways. In 2 Corinthians a disciplined man walked back through it and the church was told to forgive him, comfort him and reaffirm its love (2 Corinthians 2:7–8). Restoration should follow real repentance, which shows itself in turning from the sin, not merely in regret at the consequences. When it comes, the church should welcome the person as the father welcomed the prodigal, without probation by suspicion and without endless reminders of the past.

What if I was disciplined unfairly? Churches are made of sinners, and they can be wrong. A church can act hastily, without proper process, for things Scripture does not condemn, or to protect its leaders. If that has happened to you, remember chapter 4: it is the Lord who judges you (4:4). A wrong human verdict does not change your standing before God. Seek to understand what was said, examine yourself honestly before the Lord, and, if you can, ask for the matter to be reviewed or talk with wise believers from outside the situation. If reconciliation is impossible, it is right to find a faithful church elsewhere. And ask God to keep you from bitterness, which can do more harm than the injustice.
verseByVerse.note: To “deliver to Satan” means to put the man out of the church into the world, where Satan rules, in the hope that he will repent.

verseByVerse.quote: Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your boasting is not good. A church that is congratulating itself while one of its members is destroying himself has its eyes in the wrong place.

Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? A proverb, which Paul uses also in Galatians 5:9. Leaven is not the dried yeast in a modern packet but a lump of old fermented dough kept back from the last baking and worked through the new. The image is domestic and exact, and it explains why Paul will not let this pass as one man’s private business. Leaven works invisibly and it works completely. You cannot put a small piece in one corner of the dough and have the rest unaffected; given time it is through everything, and there is no way of taking it out again. Paul is describing what tolerated sin does to a congregation.

How the leaven spreads. The danger is not that everyone in the church will commit that particular sin. It is that the standard moves. Once something serious has been publicly accommodated, it becomes the new floor. How do you raise a small matter in a church that has swallowed a large one? A single unaddressed case does not produce one hypocrite; it produces a congregation in which nothing can be said about anything. And the young believer watching learns that the church’s words about holiness are not meant.

Cleanse out the old leaven. Then Paul reaches for Passover. Before the feast every Jewish household removed all leaven from the house (Exodus 12:15, 19; 13:7). In later practice this became a search by lamplight through every room for any crumb. Not a general resolve to be purer: a search, room by room, because a lamb was about to be killed.

As you really are unleavened. This clause is the engine of New Testament ethics, and it reverses how we naturally think. Not: purify yourselves in order to become clean, but: you are unleavened, so get the leaven out. The status comes first and the effort follows from it. In Christ they are already holy, sanctified (1:2), and they are told to become what they are. God has already counted them clean in Christ and claimed them as his own (6:11), and the command is to let the house match the owner. A son is not told to behave well so that he can join the family; he is told to behave like the family he already belongs to (Ephesians 5:1). A Christian who reverses the order will spend his life trying to earn a thing he was given at the start.

Christ, our Passover lamb. Everything in the chapter rests on this clause. Consider what stood behind the original feast. A night in Egypt; a lamb chosen and killed in every house; blood struck on the doorposts; and death moving through the streets, and passing over every door where the blood was (Exodus 12). Nobody inside was safer because of his character; the blood was on the door or it was not. Every Passover afterwards was a rehearsal, with a lamb on the table that could never actually take away anything. Then John saw Jesus walking by the Jordan and said, behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). He died at Passover (John 19:14; the Gospels date the Last Supper in ways that are not easy to align, but all four place his death at the feast), and not a bone of him was broken, as the law required of the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46; John 19:36). The lamb was always him.
