What does it mean that Christ is our Passover lamb? It means that he died in our place, so that the judgment we deserved passed over us. In Egypt, the firstborn in a house marked with blood was spared, not because he was innocent, but because a death had already taken place in that house: the lamb had died instead. That is what happened at the cross. God’s just judgment against our sin fell on Christ, our substitute, and everyone sheltering under his blood by faith is spared (1 Peter 1:18–19; Romans 3:25). And the Passover was not only rescue from death; it was the beginning of a journey out of slavery. Christ’s blood frees us from the guilt of sin and also brings us out from its rule.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we keep the Jewish Passover, or must clear our kitchens of yeast. Christ has fulfilled it. The Lord’s Supper is the new covenant meal (11:23–26), and the old leaven we put away is sin, not bread. (The KJV’s sacrificed for us follows later manuscripts; the earliest lack for us, though the verse plainly means it.)

On a Tuesday. Is there one sin in your life you have quietly accommodated: a habit, a resentment, a way of handling money or truth, that you no longer even fight because it has become the floor? Leaven is never content with one corner. Go looking for it the Passover way, specifically, room by room, and bring it to Christ. A sin you are still fighting is not the floor; it is the battle, and the fight itself is the Spirit’s work in you (Galatians 5:17). You are not cleaning the house to earn the lamb; the lamb has been sacrificed, and that is why you clean.

For worship. There was never any leaven in him. The Passover lamb had to be without blemish (Exodus 12:5), and the Son of God lived the one human life with nothing that a search by lamplight would ever find. Then he gave that spotless life for a leavened people, and his righteousness was counted as theirs (2 Corinthians 5:21). The Lamb without spot has made a stained people into new dough, and he will present them to himself without blemish at the last (Ephesians 5:27).
verseByVerse.note: Before Passover every Jewish household removed all leaven (yeast) from the house.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us therefore celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven, the leaven of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us therefore celebrate the festival. It is an unexpected way to finish a paragraph about excommunication, and it tells you how Paul understood the Christian life. The Passover lamb was killed, and then came the seven days of the Feast of Unleavened Bread (Exodus 12:15–20): a whole week of feasting flowing out of the sacrifice. Paul applies that structure. Christ has been sacrificed, once, finished; what follows is not a fast but a festival, and the festival is now.

The feast he set at Passover. It was on the day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed, that Jesus took bread and said it was his body, given for them (Luke 22:7, 19). The old feast ended at that table and the new one began there. So Paul is speaking to people who gather at the Lord’s Supper, where the bread is a participation in the body of the true Lamb (10:16). That is why malice is so out of place among them, and later he will rebuke them for bringing their divisions to that very table (11:17–22). No one can bring a grudge against a brother to the meal at which Christ gave himself for both of them.

Malice and evil. Then a surprise. After seven verses on a case of gross sexual immorality, the leaven Paul names is not immorality but malice. The word is kakia, ill will, the settled disposition to want someone’s harm; and evil is ponēria, active wickedness. He names the sin the congregation had not thought to look for, the sin of the respectable. The malice was general, and it is what had made the church proud rather than grieving in the first place. It is possible to be scrupulous about the sins one has no appetite for.

Sincerity and truth. Against that Paul sets two words. Eilikrineia, sincerity, means unmixed, with no second layer. And alētheia, truth, is the match between what a person is and what he appears to be. That makes the cleansing far more searching than the removal of one man. A church can conduct discipline impeccably and still be full of the leaven this verse names: it can put out the immoral member and go on with its factions and its long-running grudges.

What does malice look like in ordinary life? Rarely like open hatred. More often it is the small pleasure you feel when someone you dislike stumbles; the story you tell that makes another person look slightly worse; the grudge you keep fed by rehearsing it; the cold silence that punishes; the joke with an edge. It is wanting, even a little, for someone else not to do well. Paul lists it among the things to put away (Ephesians 4:31; Colossians 3:8), and the way to put it away is not only to stop but to replace it: to ask God for that person’s good, to speak well of them when they are absent, and to forgive as God in Christ forgave you (Ephesians 4:32).

How can holiness be a feast when it feels so hard? Because what you are putting away is the stale bread, and what you are given is better. The fight against sin is real, and it can be painful. But it is the struggle of someone clearing the table for a banquet, not of a prisoner breaking stones. Every sin you put away was a thief at the feast, taking your joy. The Lord who commands holiness is the Lord who spread the table, and he invites you to it with the words of the old prophet: come, buy and eat without money and without price (Isaiah 55:1). Duty and delight are not opposites here. The command is to enjoy what Christ has done in the way that fits it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul corrects a misreading of an earlier letter. The separation he asked for is not from the sinners of the world, which would mean leaving it, but from a professing believer who lives in open sin. God judges outsiders; the church is responsible for its own.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church’s Jurisdiction and God’s Jurisdiction

Paul’s distinction between inside and outside (vv. 12–13) sets the scope of church discipline. The church is not called to police the world but to keep its own fellowship true. Its mission to the world is the gospel, and its care for its own members is part of what makes that witness credible.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul had already written a previous letter (now lost) on this subject, and the Corinthians had misapplied it. They managed to be withdrawn from the world and undisciplined within at once. Now: Churches still drift into one or the other. Paul’s answer is a third way: engaged with the world in love, honest with the community in accountability.

verseByVerse.quote: I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people— not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters, since then you would need to go out of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My earlier letter. Paul had written to Corinth before this, and that letter is lost. “Associate” means to mix together with: close, ongoing fellowship.

In the flow. Having told the church to put the man out (vv. 2–8), Paul heads off the obvious evasion so that his command cannot be dodged. His distinction, inside and outside, carries straight into chapter 6, where the Corinthians are doing the reverse: taking the disputes of insiders to be judged by outsiders.

Not the immoral of this world. They had apparently applied it to Corinth at large, perhaps deliberately, so that the instruction became impossible and could be ignored. He meant something nearer home.

The greedy and swindlers. The greedy always want more, at others’ expense; swindlers are robbers and extortioners, people who grab. Paul sets sins of money and of worship alongside sexual sin, and that should stop us from ever treating sexual sin as the only kind that counts. A church that would discipline adultery but never greed has not read this verse.

Out of the world. The policy is unworkable. In that city, a rule of no contact with immoral people would empty the market, the workshop, the street and most families. You would have to leave, as separatist movements have attempted in some form. Paul rules that out as a misunderstanding of the command. The Lord prayed not that his disciples should be taken out of the world, but kept from the evil one in it (John 17:15). He himself was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners, which was intended as an insult and was simply an accurate description of how he spent his time (Matthew 11:19). And Paul will shortly tell this church to accept dinner invitations from pagan neighbours (10:27).

Strict and open in the wrong places. They were strict where they should have been open, and open where they should have been strict: rigorous, in theory, with outsiders who had never professed anything, and relaxed about a member living in public sin. A church can still be indignant about the sins of the surrounding culture and unable to have a hard conversation with one of its own.

Where Christians differ: the lost letter. Some argue that if an apostolic letter was lost, the New Testament canon must be incomplete. This commentary’s view: Not everything an apostle wrote was meant by God to be Scripture for the whole church in all ages. God, in his providence, preserved exactly the books he intended to be the canon (the Westminster Confession 1.2, 1.8; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.2, 1.8). The canon is closed and complete, sufficient for all faith and life (2 Timothy 3:16–17). The lost letter’s point is preserved here anyway.

Does a lost letter mean part of the Bible is missing? No. Paul, like any pastor, wrote a great deal that was true and useful and not meant to be Scripture: notes, arrangements, greetings, earlier instructions. Inspiration is not a claim that every sentence Paul ever wrote was meant for the canon. What God intended his church to have, he gave and preserved, and nothing we need for salvation or for godly living has been lost. You can open your Bible with full confidence that it is the complete word God meant you to have.

Can I have close friends who are not Christians? Yes, and you should. Jesus did. Friendship is one of the main ways the gospel travels. What Scripture warns against is being bound together with unbelievers in ways that pull you away from Christ: being unequally yoked (2 Corinthians 6:14), which applies most clearly to marriage, and letting bad company corrupt good morals (15:33). So ask two questions about any friendship. Am I influencing them toward Christ, or are they drawing me away from him? And would I be free to speak of Christ, and to say no to sin, in their company? If the answers are good, enjoy the friendship and pray for your friend.
verseByVerse.note: The earlier letter Paul mentions has not survived.

verseByVerse.quote: But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is guilty of sexual immorality or greed, or is an idolater, reviler, drunkard, or swindler—not even to eat with such a one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bears the name of brother. These are the decisive words: not the immoral of the world, who have professed nothing, but the person inside, who calls himself a Christian and whose life publicly contradicts it.

The name of brother. The name this man bears was not his to invent. Christ is not ashamed to call his people brothers (Hebrews 2:11): he took their flesh, died for them, and made them one family with himself as the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29). To be called brother in the church is to carry his family name. The man in this verse wears the name that belongs to the household of the Son of God while living in the very things the Son died to free him from, and expects the family to say nothing. Withdrawing fellowship refuses to let Christ’s name be used as a cover, and it calls the man back to the Brother whose name he bears.

Reviler and drunkard. Paul adds two names to his earlier list, and sitting in the middle of the catalogue, between an idolater and a drunkard, is the reviler, the man with a vicious tongue, a verbal bully. He sits in the same list as the man in verse 1, with greed beside them both. A congregation will act on scandal and will tolerate a reviler for thirty years.

Not even to eat. In that world a shared table was not a casual arrangement. It was the public sign of acceptance, friendship and common life. The reference probably includes the church’s own meal, the gathering at which the Lord’s Supper was taken, as well as ordinary social meals. The man is to find that the fellowship whose signs he has been receiving is closed to him, precisely so that he notices that something is wrong and feels the seriousness of his sin (2 Thessalonians 3:14–15).

About the unrepentant, not the struggling. Two guards are essential here. The first: this is about the unrepentant, not about the struggling. Nothing here touches the Christian who is fighting a sin and losing, who is ashamed, who keeps confessing and keeps failing. That person is not a candidate for this passage; he is a candidate for Galatians 6:1, restoration by the spiritual in a spirit of gentleness. The category Paul is describing is settled, public and defended: a man who has decided, and who expects the church to accommodate it. If you are reading this with a guilty conscience about a sin you hate, this verse is not about you, and the fact that you hate it is itself a sign of the Spirit’s work in you (Romans 7:22–25).

The church’s table, not the family’s bonds. The second guard: this concerns the church’s corporate fellowship, and it is not a licence to destroy natural bonds. Paul is regulating the assembly’s table, not the duties of a parent, a child or a spouse. When he writes about a similar case elsewhere he gives the tone explicitly: do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother (2 Thessalonians 3:15). That sentence should govern the whole practice, carried out by the church’s proper process, never by one member’s private decision to shun someone. The aim is to make the contradiction unmistakable: to withdraw the signal that everything is fine, while leaving no doubt that he is wanted back.

Must I stop having meals with a grown-up child who professes faith and lives in serious sin? No. Paul is speaking about the church’s fellowship, not about the bond between parent and child, which God himself made. You may and should go on loving your child, having them in your home, and caring for them. What changes is that you cannot pretend all is well with their walk with Christ. Speak honestly, and more than once, but not at every meal; pray without ceasing; and keep the door wide open. If the church has acted, support its discipline by not treating it as unimportant, while showing your child that your love has not moved an inch. That is the very balance Paul asks for: warn him as a brother.

Am I a “reviler” if I lose my temper? Not in the sense Paul means. Every Christian sins with his tongue (James 3:2), and a believer who loses his temper, is grieved, apologises and fights it is not the person in this list. The reviler is someone whose pattern of life is verbal abuse: who habitually belittles, demeans, intimidates or rages at others, and who sees nothing wrong with it. That pattern is serious enough to call for discipline, and it is especially serious in a home, where words can be a form of abuse. If you recognise yourself in that description, do not wait to be confronted. Confess it to God and to those you have hurt, seek help, and put it away.

On a Tuesday. Pray for anyone you know who calls himself a Christian but lives in open sin, and ask whether your friendship has quietly signalled to him that everything is fine. Only mourners can be trusted with this. Anybody who finds it satisfying should not be doing it (Galatians 6:1).

verseByVerse.quote: For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge? God judges those outside. “Purge the evil person from among you.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Paul settles the jurisdiction in a single sentence. Outsiders are unbelievers, and it is not the church’s job to discipline the world. The world is answerable to God directly, and he needs no assistance. This is not indifference to the world’s sin: the same apostle will describe the judgment of God on human wickedness at length in Romans 1. It is a recognition that the church has not been appointed the world’s magistrate. Our commission to those outside is announcement, not enforcement: we tell them what God has done in Christ. Their accounts are not ours to audit.

Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge? The church is responsible for its own members. “Judge” here means to exercise discipline, to assess conduct by God’s word and act on it, not to condemn anyone eternally. Belonging to a church is not a private arrangement between a believer and God; it is joining a family that has promised to watch over one another.

God judges those outside. Unbelievers are in God’s hands, and he will judge them rightly at the last day. Energy spent keeping a running commentary on the sins of people who never claimed to be anything else is spent in a court that is not ours.

Purge the evil person from among you. The closing citation comes from Deuteronomy, where the phrase recurs like a refrain (Deuteronomy 17:7; 22:21), used when Israel had to remove a serious offender. In Israel the purging was often capital. Paul keeps the seriousness and changes the penalty. The church is not a state, holds no sword, and executes nobody; what it can do is exclude. The new covenant form is as grave as the old and far more merciful, because a man put outside the camp can come back, and a man stoned outside the camp cannot. The whole of discipline in the New Testament is a death sentence commuted to a temporary exclusion, with the door left unlocked.

Outside the gate. That mercy is a consequence of the sacrifice Paul has just named: Christ, our Passover lamb (v. 7). The reason the church does not need to purge anybody with a stone is that the death the covenant required has already been died, by someone else, once. In Deuteronomy the evil is taken outside the camp and the people are made clean. And there was a day when someone was led out of the city, in the name of the community’s purity, and executed outside the walls between two criminals. He was not the evil person. He was the only one in the story who was not, and he went out anyway, in the place of the man in verse 1 and the arrogant congregation in verse 2 and every reader of this page. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should not speak out about sin in society, or that the church has no prophetic voice. Christians may and should speak for justice, for the unborn, for the poor, for marriage, and they may vote and serve as citizens. It means church discipline applies only to church members, and that the church does not try to govern the world by its own discipline.

How does this fit with “Judge not”? They are about different things. In 4:5 Paul forbids passing verdicts on the hidden purposes of the heart, which only the Lord can see. Jesus forbids the hypocrite’s censorious judging, and tells him to take the log out of his own eye so that he can see clearly to help his brother (Matthew 7:1–5). Here Paul requires the church to deal with the open, unrepentant conduct of someone who claims to be a brother. Christians must not judge hearts; they must judge conduct by Scripture, inside the church, humbly and for the sinner’s good. And a church that does this is not claiming to be better than the person it disciplines. Every member, the leaders first, stands under the same word and is a forgiven sinner, and the one who restores another is told to keep watch on himself, lest he too be tempted (Galatians 6:1).

So how should I treat a non-Christian who lives in the sins on Paul’s list? With love, honesty and patience, as someone who needs the same Saviour you needed. Do not expect him to live by a standard he has never accepted, and do not make his morals the first subject you raise. His deepest problem is not his behaviour but that he does not yet know Christ, and the gospel is what changes behaviour. Be his friend, be honest when he asks what you believe, and pray for him. If he comes to faith, then he will come under the church’s care and its call to holiness, and he will find, as every Christian has, that the Lord who calls us to purity also gives the power for it (6:11).

For worship. God judges those outside, and every one of us was once outside: separated from Christ, strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world (Ephesians 2:12). The Judge of outsiders is the God who brings outsiders in. In Christ Jesus those who once were far off have been brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13),. The church judges its own only because it is a family of former outsiders, and the Father who welcomed them has room at his table for many more.

parallels.desc: so you shall purge the evil from your midst

5.text: <sup>1</sup>It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans, for a man has his father’s wife.<sup>2</sup>And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn? Let him who has done this be removed from among you.<sup>3</sup>For though absent in body, I am present in spirit; and as if present, I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did such a thing.<sup>4</sup>When you are assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus,<sup>5</sup>you are to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.<sup>6</sup>Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump?<sup>7</sup>Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.<sup>8</sup>Let us therefore celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven, the leaven of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.<sup>9</sup>I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people—<sup>10</sup>not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters, since then you would need to go out of the world.<sup>11</sup>But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is guilty of sexual immorality or greed, or is an idolater, reviler, drunkard, or swindler—not even to eat with such a one.<sup>12</sup>For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge?<sup>13</sup>God judges those outside. “Purge the evil person from among you.”

6.title: Lawsuits, Liberty, and the Temple of the Spirit
6.overview:
Two more problems show the Corinthians living by the standards of their city rather than of Christ. First, church members were suing each other in the public courts. In Roman Corinth, civil litigation was a contest of status that the well connected usually won. Paul is appalled that believers, who will one day judge the world and even angels, cannot settle disputes among themselves, and that they would rather drag one another before unbelieving judges than suffer wrong. He reminds them that the unrighteous, including thieves and swindlers, will not inherit God’s kingdom, and that some of them used to be exactly that, before they were washed, made holy and justified in Christ by the Spirit.

Second, some were using slogans like “all things are lawful for me” and “food for the stomach and the stomach for food” to justify sleeping with prostitutes, as if what the body does did not matter to the soul. Paul answers that the body belongs to the Lord and will be raised. A believer’s body is a member of Christ, and union with a prostitute makes the two one flesh. So they must run from sexual immorality. Their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit; they are not their own; they were bought at a price, and must honour God with their bodies.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Believers were taking one another to pagan courts. Paul argues from their future to their present: the church should settle its own disputes, and a lawsuit between brothers is a defeat whoever wins. Better to suffer wrong than to do it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Saints Will Judge the World: Present Implications

Paul argues here from the last things, from what is coming: “do you not know that the saints will judge the world?” (v. 2). What believers will be shapes how they behave now. Those who will share in Christ’s judgment at the end (Daniel 7:22; Revelation 20:4) already have, by their union with him, a dignity that makes taking small disputes to pagan courts absurd.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Roman legal culture in Corinth was a social arena where disputes were used to assert status and damage opponents. Paul refuses the framework: the cross makes a community in which being willing to absorb loss shows more strength than winning in court. Now: Paul’s question, “Why not rather suffer wrong?”, still cuts against every instinct.

verseByVerse.quote: When one of you has a grievance against another, does he dare go to law before the unrighteous instead of the saints? Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you incompetent to try trivial cases?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 6 deals with three more failures that show the Corinthians had not grasped what it means to belong to Christ: lawsuits between believers (vv. 1–8), the unrighteous and the washing that changes them (vv. 9–11), and the slogans that excused sexual sin (vv. 12–20). Everything hangs on what Christ has made his people: future judges, washed sinners, limbs of his body, a purchased home for God.

The setting. Roman civil courts in a provincial city were public, costly and often corrupt, and the man with connections and a hired advocate generally won. Taking a brother to court was a way of using your position against somebody with less of it.

In the flow. Chapter 5 closed with a question: is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge? (5:12). The Corinthians were doing the opposite. They would not judge the immoral man inside the church, and they were handing their own quarrels to judges outside it. In verses 9–11 Paul shows what joins the two failures: those who wrong their brothers and those who live in sexual sin are on the same list, and the same washing is offered to both.

A grievance against another. The word means a matter, a case: a civil dispute, probably about property or money (v. 7). Taking it to court was not merely choosing an inconvenient venue. It imported into the church the mechanism by which the powerful of that city kept the weak in their place (1:26).

Does he dare go to law before the unrighteous instead of the saints? “Dare” is tolmaō: to have the audacity, the nerve. Paul is not opening with an argument; he is opening with astonishment that anyone would think of it. “The unrighteous” is not name-calling. It is Paul’s standing category for those outside Christ, unbelieving judges outside God’s people, and he uses it to make a point about competence. These judges do not share the standard by which the case ought to be decided. They can apply Roman law. They cannot ask what love requires, or what the cross makes fitting between two brothers. The saints, fellow believers in the church, can.

Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? Then the argument from the greater to the lesser. This is one of six times in this chapter that Paul asks, do you not know? (vv. 2, 3, 9, 15, 16, 19). It is a startling claim, and Paul assumes they have been taught it. Its roots are in Daniel’s vision, where the saints of the Most High receive the kingdom (Daniel 7:18, 22, 27), and in the Lord’s own promise that his followers would sit on thrones (Matthew 19:28; Revelation 20:4). At the last day believers will share in Christ’s judgment of the world. Their part in it is not independent authority but a consequence of union with Christ. Union means that believers are so joined to him by faith that what is his is shared with them. His death counts as theirs, and so will his reign (Romans 6:5; 2 Timothy 2:12).

One like a son of man. In Daniel’s vision one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and is given dominion and a kingdom; then judgment is given for the saints of the Most High, and they possess the kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14, 22). Jesus took that title as his own (John 5:22, 27). So the saints judge only because they belong to him: where he sits, those who are in him sit (Revelation 3:21). Their dignity is borrowed from his. A man who will share the throne of the Son of Man was asking a pagan magistrate to settle a debt between two of Christ’s own people.

And if the world is to be judged by you, are you incompetent to try trivial cases? The word for trivial is the smallest available: everyday disputes, tiny compared with the last judgment. Paul’s logic is simple and unanswerable. People appointed to a share in the final judgment cannot plausibly claim they are unqualified to sort out a disputed debt. And that quietly exposes the real problem, which was not competence. A church that could produce men wise enough to settle the matter was choosing not to, because at least one party did not want a fair settlement. He wanted to win, and the court was where winning was available.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should never use the courts, or that crimes should not be reported to the authorities (see on v. 7). Paul is speaking of civil disputes between believers.

What about legal processes that are not one brother suing another? Paul condemns a believer taking another believer to court to win a private grievance without first letting the church settle it. An insurance claim, the legal formalities of a divorce that has biblical grounds, probate and similar matters are not what he is describing. And if a fellow member refuses every attempt at reconciliation and church judgment, Jesus says he is to be treated as one outside the church (Matthew 18:17); the believer is then no longer suing a brother who is acting as a brother. Even then, verse 7 still asks whether it might be better simply to suffer the wrong.

Does “the saints will judge the world” mean believers decide who is saved? No. Salvation and condemnation belong to God alone, and Christ is the Judge (John 5:22; Acts 17:31). Scripture does not give us the details of how the saints share in his judgment. It most likely means that, united with Christ, they will reign with him, agree with his verdicts and take part in them as his people, the way the twelve are promised thrones (Matthew 19:28). It is not a licence to pronounce on anyone’s eternal destiny now. Its purpose here is to show the Corinthians how great their calling is, and how small their quarrels look beside it.

On a Tuesday. If you have a dispute with a fellow Christian, go to them first, and then to wise believers, before going public. And ask whether you are looking for a resolution or for a verdict: you can usually tell by noticing whether you would accept an outcome in which nobody was declared right. The Corinthians had access to brothers who could have helped them. They preferred a venue that would produce a loser.
verseByVerse.note: Roman civil courts were public, costly and often corrupt; lawsuits were a way for the powerful to win status.

parallels.desc: judgment was given for the saints of the Most High

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that we are to judge angels? How much more, then, matters pertaining to this life!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know that we are to judge angels? Paul drops it in as though it were common knowledge, which tells us it had been part of his teaching at Corinth. It is an extraordinary line to drop in passing, and he does not stop to explain it. Which angels? Most likely the fallen ones: the beings Peter describes as committed to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment, and Jude in the same terms (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). There is a day appointed for their sentencing, and Paul says believers will have a part in it. It is an astonishing dignity.

The measure of it. Angels are creatures older than we are and, as Peter says, greater in might and power (2 Peter 2:11). The Corinthians were being intimidated in a provincial courtroom by men with money; they are destined to sit in judgment on beings beside whom a Roman magistrate is nothing.

Matters pertaining to this life! The ordinary business of living: money, property, contracts, boundaries. Paul uses this vast claim not to make them feel important, since the whole letter assaults their sense of importance, but to make their behaviour look absurd. A man who genuinely believed he would one day share in the judgment of angels would find it very hard to keep up a two-year grievance about a boundary wall.

Made for a little while lower than the angels. How could creatures of dust sit in judgment on beings of a higher order? The answer is a man. The Son of God did not take hold of angels but of the offspring of Abraham (Hebrews 2:16): he became one of us, not one of them. Hebrews reads Psalm 8 of him: made for a little while lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:7–9). In him human nature has been seated far above all rule and authority (Ephesians 1:20–21). The saints will judge angels for one reason only: they are joined to the Man who is on the throne.

Will we judge the holy angels too? There is no hint of that. The holy angels have never sinned, and they serve God’s people now (Hebrews 1:14). Paul is most probably thinking of the fallen angels who await judgment. Some think the word “judge” here also includes the idea of ruling, so that redeemed humanity, in Christ, will have a place of honour over the whole created order. Either way, Scripture does not give us details, and it is wise not to build theories on one sentence. The point is clear without them: your future is so great that your present quarrels should look small.

verseByVerse.quote: So if you have such cases, why do you lay them before those who have no standing in the church? I say this to your shame. Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between the brothers, but brother goes to law against brother, and that before unbelievers?
verseByVerse.commentary:
So if you have such cases, why do you lay them before those who have no standing in the church? “Those who have no standing” translates exouthenēmenoi: the despised, those counted as nothing in the church. In the ESV reading they are the pagan judges, whose values the church does not share and to whom it does not look for wisdom. Why, then, would Christians hand them their family quarrels?

Question or command? Verse 4 can be read two ways. The ESV takes it as a question: why do you lay them before those who have no standing in the church, that is, before pagan judges? Older translations, the KJV among them, read it as a command, perhaps ironic: appoint even the least regarded members of the church to judge. The ESV reading is the more likely, because Paul goes straight on to ask whether there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute (v. 5). Either way the point is the same: the church should be able to settle these matters itself.

I say this to your shame. Earlier he wrote, I do not write these things to make you ashamed (4:14). Here he does.

Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between the brothers? The irony would have been unbearable, and it is the whole point. This is the church that has spent four chapters congratulating itself on its wisdom (1:5; 3:18). They had factions organised around competing teachers; they prided themselves on knowledge and eloquence; they thought of themselves as the mature. Now Paul simply asks them to produce one wise man for a practical purpose, and the answer, evidently, is that they cannot. It is the standing test of whether wisdom is real. Wisdom that can discuss the deep things of God and cannot help two brothers settle a debt is not wisdom in any sense the Bible recognises. James makes the same point from the other end: the wisdom from above is peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy, and where there is jealousy and selfish ambition, whatever else is present, it is not wisdom (James 3:14–17).

The mind of Christ. This church had been told that Christ crucified is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1:24), and that we have the mind of Christ (2:16). Wisdom, in this letter, has the shape of a cross. A church that has the mind of Christ ought to be full of people able to settle a dispute between brothers, because the whole gospel is the story of a quarrel settled at the expense of the one who was in the right. The wise man Paul is looking for is not the cleverest member, but the one who thinks like the cross.

But brother goes to law against brother, and that before unbelievers? The last phrase carries the second injury. Double shame: brothers fighting, and doing it in public, in front of exactly the people the church exists to reach. Think of what a Corinthian pagan would have seen. A new movement claiming that its God had reconciled enemies and made one body out of Jew and Greek, slave and free, and two of its members in the basilica, arguing about money, using the same lawyers and the same tactics as everybody else. Every claim the church had made about itself was being tested in that courtroom, and it was failing.

The modern courtroom. Congregations now split in public, and Christians savage one another in writing before thousands, over matters two people of goodwill in one room could have resolved in an afternoon. The watching world does not weigh the arguments. It concludes that their message of reconciliation does not work.

What it does not mean. It does not mean church leaders have the power of a civil court. The church can mediate and advise, and discipline members who refuse to be reconciled. It cannot fine, imprison or enforce, and it must never try to handle crimes itself.

What does settling a dispute inside the church look like in practice? Paul assumes the church should have a working way of settling disputes between its members. Not a court, but wise people the parties are willing to be bound by. In practice, the two people first talk privately (Matthew 18:15). If that fails, they agree together to bring in one or two mature, impartial believers, often elders or people they both trust, and they agree in advance to accept their counsel. Some Christians use trained Christian mediators or arbitrators, whose agreements can also be recognised in law. The aim is not merely a ruling but reconciliation, with honesty about wrongs done on both sides.

parallels.desc: able men to judge the people

verseByVerse.quote: To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? But you yourselves wrong and defraud—even your own brothers!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Already a defeat. The outcome was settled the moment the case was filed: whoever wins, the church has already lost, because love has already failed.

Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? Then two questions that cut sharply against the instincts of every age. Paul is not asking them to pretend the wrong did not happen. The words are blunt: be wronged, be cheated. They assume a real injury and a real loss. What he is proposing is that a Christian might decide to absorb it. The logic is not passivity but a different arithmetic. The Corinthian litigant has calculated that the disputed sum is worth more than the brother. Paul says the calculation is wrong, and that a man shaped by the cross will reach a different total, because the one he follows absorbed infinite wrong without retaliating, and when he was reviled did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23). It is the Sermon on the Mount applied to a courtroom: if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well (Matthew 5:39–40). Better to lose money than to lose a brother and dishonour Christ. It is a radical, cross-shaped answer.

You yourselves wrong and defraud! Paul now turns from the plaintiffs to the defendants. Some of them were the cheaters, defrauding their own brothers, perhaps using the courts to do it.

Where Christians differ: may a Christian ever sue a Christian? Some say never, under any circumstances. Others say the courts are open to Christians like anyone else. This commentary’s view: Paul’s rule is that disputes between believers should be settled within the church, and that it is often better to accept loss than to sue a brother. But this assumes both parties are willing to submit to the church. Where a professing believer refuses church correction, he is to be treated as an unbeliever (Matthew 18:17), and there may be cases where legal protection is necessary, especially for the vulnerable, or where crimes are involved. Abuse, violence and fraud should be reported to the authorities whom God appointed to punish evil (Romans 13:4).

A guard against misuse. This passage has been used to do real harm. These verses are about property and money disputes between Christian brothers. They are not a rule that Christians must never use the law, and they cannot be stretched into one without contradicting Scripture and Paul himself. Paul invoked his Roman citizenship when he was about to be flogged (Acts 22:25) and appealed to Caesar rather than be handed over (Acts 25:11). In Romans he says the civil authority is God’s servant, who bears the sword to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), which is not something God instituted so that his people should never use it. So this text has nothing to say against reporting a crime, nothing against protecting a child, nothing against a victim of abuse or assault going to the police, or an employee taking a genuine grievance to a tribunal. Any leader who quotes “why not rather suffer wrong?” to persuade a victim to stay silent and keep it in the church has taken a verse about a money dispute and used it as a lid. That is the opposite of what the passage intends, since the whole point is that the strong should stop using their advantage against the weak.

Does suffering wrong mean I must let someone go on cheating me? No. Choosing to absorb a loss, rather than sue a brother, is not the same as enabling ongoing wrong. You may forgive a debt and still decline to lend again. You may let go of a grievance and still end a business partnership with someone who has been dishonest. You may, and sometimes must, warn others or bring the matter to the church, so that the person is called to repent and others are protected (Matthew 18:15–17). Love does not pretend that wrong is right. It simply refuses revenge, and it cares more about the brother’s soul and Christ’s honour than about winning.

On a Tuesday. This cuts both ways. If you are the one who has been wronged, could you absorb it, genuinely, without keeping a running account, as Christ keeps none against you (Colossians 2:14)? And if you are honest, is there anyone with a legitimate grievance against you: money owed, a promise not kept, an advantage taken because you could? Put it right this week. Both men in the courtroom may need the same verdict (Romans 12:17–19).

For worship. Jesus is the one man who never wronged anyone and was wronged by everyone. He was defrauded of his clothes at the foot of a cross, and he did not sue. He was tried by an unrighteous court, and he did not appeal. He suffered wrong, not because he could not defend himself, but because he was buying back the very people who had wronged him. We were the ones who defrauded God of the honour we owed him, and he did not take us to court. He took our place in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–11 — The Unrighteous Will Not Inherit the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A warning and a welcome. Those who live unrepentant in the sins Paul lists have no share in God’s kingdom; and some of the Corinthians had lived exactly so, until they were washed, sanctified and justified.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification, Sanctification, and the New Identity

The three verbs of v. 11, washed, sanctified, justified, cover the whole of what God does in saving a sinner: cleansing from sin’s pollution, claiming him as his own, and declaring him righteous. All three are done “in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God”: the work of Father, Son and Spirit together.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The list in vv. 9–10 describes the Corinthian street: not distant behaviour but the lives many in the congregation had lived before the gospel reached them. Now: Every church contains people whose past is on this list. For them the three words of v. 11 are the truest thing that can be said about that past: it was real, and so is what Christ has done.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who practice homosexuality, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? There is a link with verses 1–8 that English hides. The “unrighteous” (adikoi) are the same word as the pagan judges of verse 1, and those who wrong their brothers in verse 8 are doing adikeō, acting unrighteously. Paul is saying: you are behaving like the very people you took your case to, and you know where they are heading. To inherit the kingdom is to have a share in God’s coming reign, eternal life in the age to come. “Will not inherit” does not mean less reward; it means no share at all.

Do not be deceived. The warning implies that someone was doing the deceiving. The likely message was that grace is so complete and freedom so total that how you lived did not matter if you had knowledge or gifts. Paul says that is a lie. It is still being told.

The sexually immoral and adulterers. The sexually immoral are those who commit any sexual sin outside marriage; adulterers are those unfaithful to their marriage.

Nor men who practice homosexuality. The ESV notes that the two Greek terms behind this phrase refer to the passive and active partners in consensual homosexual acts. Malakoi means literally soft ones; in sexual contexts it could denote the passive partner in male same-sex intercourse. Arsenokoitai is a compound of arsēn (male) and koitē (bed), literally male-bedders, and appears to have been coined from the Greek Old Testament of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, where both words appear in the prohibition of a man lying with a male. Together they cover both roles in the act, and Paul uses the terms to cover homosexual acts generally.

Thieves and the greedy. The list is broad: nine items in the ESV, and only three of them sexual. Alongside them sit theft, greed, drunkenness, verbal abuse and dishonest dealing: sins present in every congregation and rarely preached with this seriousness. Nearly everybody appears somewhere, so no one can look down on others. A church that reads it as a description of outsiders, or of one particular group, has misread it.

Will not inherit. Those whose lives are characterised by these sins, unrepentant, show they are not God’s people. Every item in this list is a settled way of life, not an experience of temptation: the thief who steals, the drunkard who drinks, the reviler whose tongue is his weapon.

The kingdom is the Son’s inheritance. Before it is ever ours, the kingdom belongs to Christ. God has appointed the Son heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2), and no one inherits anything except by being joined to the Heir: we are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). The list is not an entrance exam to pass before God will look at you. It describes lives that show no sign of belonging to the Heir, because no one can be joined to Christ and settled in the very things he died to remove. The question the verse presses is not, have I been good enough? but, am I his? Paul at once tells the Corinthians that people with exactly these pasts had become his (v. 11). The respectable person who has kept clear of every item on the list is no nearer the kingdom for it if he is trusting his record rather than the Heir; Paul counted his own spotless record as loss in order to gain Christ (Philippians 3:7–9).

Where Christians differ: homosexuality. Some argue that Paul condemned only exploitative relationships, such as pederasty or prostitution, not loving, committed same-sex relationships. This commentary’s view: The terms Paul uses draw directly on Leviticus, which forbids homosexual acts as such, without reference to exploitation. Paul also names both partners rather than only the exploiter, which an argument about exploitation would not require. Elsewhere Paul grounds his teaching in creation (Romans 1:26–27), and Jesus defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman (Matthew 19:4–6). The historic Christian teaching is that sexual relations belong only within marriage between a man and a woman. This must be held with deep compassion. Same-sex attraction is a real and often painful experience, not chosen, and believers who experience it and live faithfully are brothers and sisters to be loved and supported. Homosexual sin is listed alongside greed, drunkenness and slander, sins all of us need forgiveness for. And verse 11 shows the gospel’s welcome to all.

Temptation is not practice. If you are a Christian who experiences same-sex attraction and is not acting on it, who has perhaps fought this for years, told almost nobody, and reads this verse with dread every time it is preached, understand that you are not the person described here. A desire resisted is not a life lived. The man in this list is not fighting; he has settled. And a believer who is fighting is doing exactly what the gospel produces in those it washes (v. 11). The same distinction applies right along the list: being tempted to greed is not greed. What Paul is warning against is not the presence of a struggle but the absence of one: the comfortable conviction that a person may practise what he likes and inherit the kingdom anyway. That is the deception, and it is why he opened with do not be deceived (Galatians 5:19–21; Ephesians 5:5–6).

Can a true believer fall into these sins? Yes, and Scripture records it: David committed adultery and arranged a murder, and the man in chapter 5 was a member of this church. But Paul is describing a way of life, not a single fall, and the believer who falls is brought back to repentance, as David was (Psalm 51). What cannot be true of someone born of God is that he goes on in these things, unrepentant, to the end (1 John 3:9–10). The warning is real, and it is one of the means God uses to keep his people from that road. The God who keeps his own to the end keeps them through warnings like this one, not in spite of them.

How should I treat a gay friend or family member? With the same love and honesty you would show anyone on this list, which includes you. Keep the friendship, keep eating together, keep listening; Jesus was a friend of sinners, and so should you be. Do not make one sin the whole of the person or the first thing you talk about. Their greatest need, like yours, is Christ, not first a change of behaviour. If they ask what you believe, tell them gently and truthfully, including what you believe about your own sin and your own need of grace. And if a Christian friend confides that they experience same-sex attraction, count it an honour that they trusted you, keep their confidence, and walk with them.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the two Greek terms behind “men who practice homosexuality” refer to the passive and active partners in homosexual acts.

verseByVerse.quote: And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And such were some of you. Four words in the Greek change the temperature of the chapter. The most severe list in the letter describes the people he is writing to. The congregation contained former idolaters, former drunkards, former thieves, former practising homosexuals, men who had lived what verse 9 describes. And the tense is the gospel. Such were: past, finished, no longer the case. Paul does not write: such are some of you, but you are forgiven. He says the description has stopped being true.

But you were washed. Then three verbs, and every one of them describes something done to them. Washed clean: cleansed from sin’s filth. This answers what sin leaves behind after the guilt is dealt with. A man may believe he is forgiven and still feel unclean, and this word is aimed at exactly that.

You were sanctified. Set apart as holy to God, transferred into his own possession: a once-for-all claiming, as distinct from the lifelong growth in holiness. This is stated as an accomplished fact, not a target, the same thing Paul said in his opening greeting, addressing this troubled church as those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints (1:2). The daily work of growing in holiness follows, but it grows out of this: they already belong to God.

You were justified. Declared righteous before God: the legal word. Their guilt removed, Christ’s righteousness counted to them, nothing can be brought against them (Romans 5:1; 8:33). Paul puts sanctification before justification, though logically God declares before he transforms; all three happen together at conversion. He seems to move from what is most felt to what is most decisive.

In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God. All three verbs hang on that name. Paul has already told this church that Christ Jesus became to us righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1:30): what was done to them is what Christ himself is for them. They were justified because he was delivered up for their trespasses and raised for their justification (Romans 4:25). They were washed because his blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). And the Spirit of our God is the one who takes what Christ did and makes it theirs. Nothing here was self-administered.

The verse for the person carrying a past. Something specific: the years you do not talk about, the pattern you were in before Christ found you, which surfaces at three in the morning to tell you what you really are. Paul does not say it was not serious. He says that it is in the past tense, that three things have happened to you since, and that not one of them depends on your assessment of yourself. The accusation uses the true past to establish a false present. The reply is not a denial of the history but a statement about the tense. Such were some of you. You were washed. You were sanctified. You were justified.

Does “such were some of you” mean that the old desires disappear? Paul is describing a changed standing and a changed direction: these people are washed, set apart and declared righteous, and those sins are no longer who they are. He does not promise that temptation ends. Some believers find old desires greatly weakened; many, including those who experience same-sex attraction, go on being tempted and go on fighting, and that fight is the normal Christian life (Romans 8:13; Galatians 5:17), not evidence that the gospel has failed. And “you were washed” points to the cleansing of the new birth (Titus 3:5), which baptism pictures (Acts 22:16) but does not itself accomplish. Reformed Christians, Baptist and Presbyterian alike, agree on that, though they differ over whom to baptise.

Should a church welcome people with pasts like these? Yes, with open arms, because the church at Corinth was made of them. A church that is shocked by former thieves, addicts, adulterers or people who have lived a gay life has forgotten what it is. Every member is a former something. Welcome does not mean pretending sin does not matter; it means telling the truth Paul tells here, that Christ washes and changes sinners, and then walking with people as he changes them. If your church would struggle to welcome a person with a story like those in verse 9, ask what that says about how you understand your own story.

For worship. The washing was not a rinse; it cost the blood of the Son of God. He did not tidy up the guilty; he bought them. He paid for the people of verse 9 knowing every item on the list, and he has never once suggested he overpaid. The Father chose, the Son shed his blood, the Spirit applied it, and a congregation of former idolaters and thieves became saints. Such were some of us. But we were washed, and the God who washed us will never call us dirty again (Titus 3:3–7; Romans 8:33–34).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–20 — Flee Sexual Immorality: The Body as Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul takes apart the Corinthian slogans that excused sexual sin, and puts in their place the truth about the body: it is for the Lord, it will be raised, it is joined to Christ, the Spirit lives in it, and it was bought at a price. So flee sexual immorality, and glorify God in your body.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection and the Significance of the Body

Paul grounds sexual ethics in the resurrection: “God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power” (v. 14). The body is not a shell to be discarded but the self that God will raise, the same body, transformed. That is why what we do with it matters for ever. The resurrection of the body is the ground of a Christian ethics that takes the body seriously.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Visiting a prostitute was widely accepted in Corinth, part of the city’s social and sometimes religious life. Some Corinthians may have thought it religiously meaningless and biologically natural. Now: The sexual ethics of any age follow from what it thinks the body is. Paul’s answer is that the body is the Spirit’s home, bought at the cross and bound for resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be dominated by anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All things are lawful for me. These words are almost certainly a slogan used at Corinth, which Paul is quoting. Perhaps they had twisted his own teaching on freedom into a licence to do anything. He does not simply deny the slogan; he lets it stand and puts two limits round it. Christian freedom is real; what he refuses is the idea that freedom is the only question worth asking.

In the flow. Sexual immorality headed the list in verses 9–10, and now Paul goes back to it, because the Corinthians had arguments ready to excuse it. This is also the root of the pride in 5:2, a theology of freedom that made sin look small, and the same slogan will come back over food offered to idols (10:23).

But not all things are helpful. The first limit: helpful means beneficial, of real advantage. A thing may be entirely permitted and still be a bad idea. Is this allowed? is the question of a man looking for the edge of the territory he can occupy without penalty. Is this helpful? is the question of a man who wants to get somewhere.

But I will not be dominated by anything. The second limit goes deeper, with a wordplay. The slogan says all things are exestin, permitted, within my authority. Paul replies that he will not be exousiasthēsomai, brought under the authority of, anything. Same root, turned round: I have authority to do all things, but I will not let anything have authority over me. A man who insists he is free to do a thing, and cannot stop doing it, is not describing liberty. He has simply found a theological vocabulary for his slavery.

The one man nothing mastered. Only one person has ever been completely free in Paul’s sense. Jesus had authority over all things, and nothing had authority over him. Hungry after forty days in the wilderness, he refused to turn stones into bread at the devil’s suggestion, because man does not live by bread alone (Matthew 4:2–4). He said of his own life that he had authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again (John 10:18), and he used that authority not to please himself but to give himself (Romans 15:3). The Corinthian used his liberty to feed his appetite; Christ used his to go to the cross.

What are the things God has left free? They are the many matters Scripture neither commands nor forbids: what you eat and drink in moderation, how you spend your leisure, what music you enjoy, which job you take, whether you own a television. Older writers called them things indifferent. In these, you have real freedom, and other Christians must not bind your conscience with rules God has not given (Romans 14:1–4; Colossians 2:20–23). But even here Paul gives you three questions to ask: is it helpful, to me and to others? Is it mastering me? And, as he will add later, does it glorify God (10:31)? Freedom is a gift to be used for Christ, not a fence to see how close you can stand to the edge.

On a Tuesday. Is there something permitted that has started to master you: your phone, food, entertainment, alcohol? Take whatever you would defend on the grounds of Christian freedom, and instead of arguing about whether it is permitted, put it down for a month. What happens next is the answer. If it goes without much difficulty, the freedom was real. If you find yourself negotiating or rationalising, you have discovered which way the authority is running (2 Peter 2:19). That discovery is not a reason for despair. Finding the chain is the first step to having it broken: bring it into the light with a trusted believer, and ask the Lord who sets captives free to do it.
verseByVerse.note: The words in quotation marks are probably slogans used at Corinth, which Paul quotes and then corrects.

verseByVerse.quote: “Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food”—and God will destroy both one and the other. The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Food for the stomach. Another slogan, and its reasoning is still in use. Hunger is met with food and nobody considers it a moral event; therefore sexual desire may be met wherever it is convenient, and it is no more significant than a meal. Many Greeks thought the body unimportant beside the soul.

God will destroy both. Possibly also part of the slogan: the body will perish anyway, so what we do with it does not matter. Paul grants that food and the stomach belong to an order that is passing away, but he rejects the conclusion.

The body is for the Lord. The body is not like the stomach. It is not one organ among many but the whole person in bodily existence, and it belongs to the Lord.

And the Lord for the body. Not merely that the body is for the Lord, which we might have guessed, but that the Lord is for the body. God is committed to your physical self. He is not tolerating it, waiting for the real you to be released from it at death. He made it, he took one himself, he redeemed it, and he intends to raise it.

A doctrine of the body. The ancient world held that the material was inferior and the spiritual was what mattered. The faith whose central claims are an incarnation, a bodily resurrection and a coming new creation cannot regard flesh as an embarrassment. That is why sexual ethics in the New Testament are never arbitrary restrictions. They follow from this account of your physical self: that God became one, died in one, rose in one, and intends to give you one that will not decay.

Does God care about my sleep, my health and how I treat my body? Yes, though not in the way our culture worships the body. If the Lord is for the body, then what you do with yours is never spiritually neutral: not the sleep you refuse it, not the way you speak about it, not the contempt some Christians carry for their own physical selves and mistake for humility. Rest is a gift (Psalm 127:2), and bodily training is of some value (1 Timothy 4:8). But the body is not an idol to be perfected; it is a servant to be cared for and offered to God (Romans 12:1). Look after it as you would look after something precious lent to you by a friend.

Will we have bodies in eternity? Yes. When a believer dies, his soul goes at once to be with Christ, conscious and at rest, while his body waits in the grave (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). At Christ’s return the body will be raised, the same body and yet transformed, made imperishable and glorious like Christ’s own (15:42–44; Philippians 3:21). We will not float as spirits for ever. We will live, body and soul, on a renewed earth. That is why the body matters now: it is not a husk to be thrown away but the seed of what will be raised.

verseByVerse.quote: And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Never!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God raised the Lord. Paul answers the food-and-stomach argument with the resurrection. The body has a future. The same power that brought Jesus out of the tomb is going to be applied to your physical self, and what will stand in the new creation is not a disembodied spirit but a raised person (15:20–23). What will be raised matters now.

Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Then the second argument, moving from the future to the present. Members (melē) is the ordinary word for limbs and organs. This is not a metaphor about belonging to a club. Paul means that by union with Christ, the believer’s physical self is joined to him as a hand is joined to a body. Believers are united to Christ, body and soul. Your hands, eyes and whole body are parts of Christ.

Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Having said that, he draws the conclusion with deliberate bluntness. Prostitution was common in Corinth, sometimes connected with temples, and banquets and festivals often ended with it. To have sex with a prostitute is to take what belongs to Christ and join it to her. It is meant to shock, and it should. Paul refuses to let the sin be pictured privately, as a transaction between two consenting people in a room. He insists that Christ is not absent from it. The Christian does not leave his union with the Lord at the door and pick it up on the way out; there is no such door. Whatever a believer does with his body, he does as a limb of Christ.

Never! One of Paul’s strongest negatives, the expression he reserves for a suggestion so appalling it does not deserve an argument.

The modern form. The modern form of the same transaction, a screen, an image, another human being reduced to a function, is private, deniable and available at any hour, and every defence of it depends on its being nobody else’s business: it harms no one, it is only an image. Paul’s answer is that the Lord is present at it, because the man doing it is a limb of Christ. And the image on the screen is a person too, often exploited, sometimes trafficked, made in God’s image and used as a product.

If I have fallen into this, has Christ let go of me? No. That is precisely why it matters so much what you take him into: he does not withdraw when you sin. That is a heavier thought than shame, and it is also more hopeful, because shame merely tells a man what he is and leaves him there. This tells him whose he is. The argument for purity here is not that you are dirty and must clean yourself up. It is that you are joined to Christ, already, now, in the body. So come back to him at once, confess it plainly (1 John 1:9), bring it into the light with a trusted believer, and take practical steps against it. His hold on you is the ground of your fight, not the prize for winning it.

On a Tuesday. Before you open the app, enter the room or click the link, ask the plain question: am I about to take a limb of Christ here? And then use those same limbs for him today: hands that help, eyes that look on others with honour, feet that go where love sends them (Romans 6:12–13; 12:27).

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, as it is written, “The two will become one flesh.” But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? Paul now shows why the comparison with food fails: sex does something that eating never does. “Joined” is kollaō, glued, cleaved to. Sex is never merely physical. It unites two persons. Even a casual encounter creates a real union.

The two will become one flesh. The citation is Genesis 2:24, the charter of marriage, spoken in Eden before the fall. God designed sexual union to express and seal the lifelong covenant union of husband and wife (Matthew 19:5–6). Paul applies it to a paid encounter with a stranger: the bond forms regardless. It was built into the act by God at creation, and it does not wait to be authorised by the intentions of the people involved. Neither of them meant a union. A union occurred.

Why casual sex is not casual. So sex can never be what every generation insists it can be: a thing done with the body alone and walked away from. Paul’s claim is not merely that casual sex is emotionally unwise, though it is. It is that there is no such thing: the act is a covenant-shaped act whether or not a covenant exists, and doing it outside one does not neutralise it but tears it. People discover, to their own surprise, that someone they were assured meant nothing turns out to be lodged in them years later. Something was joined that was designed not to come apart.

One spirit with him. Paul uses the same verb both times, setting the two unions side by side to make them contradictory. The man is already joined to Christ, and he is proposing to be joined to somebody else. One spirit with him means that the Holy Spirit who rests on Christ lives in the believer, so that Christ’s own life flows into his, as the vine’s life flows into the branches (John 15:5). That union is deeper than marriage; it is the reality to which marriage itself points (Ephesians 5:31–32). Sexual immorality sets up a rival union.

A rival intimacy, and a greater one. Paul’s final answer to sexual sin is not a rule. The believer is one spirit with the Lord: a union closer than the one being contemplated, permanent where that is momentary, and satisfying at a depth the other cannot reach even when it delivers everything it promises. The fight is usually lost at the level of desire rather than of information. What holds is knowing what you already have. Purity that is only refusal is a starvation diet, and starvation diets do not last. The Christian is not being asked to want less. He is being asked to notice that he is already joined to Someone, and to want that more, which is the only appetite strong enough to displace the other one (Psalm 63:1–5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean a sexual encounter creates a marriage. It means sex has a meaning that cannot be emptied out, which is why it belongs in marriage.

I have a sexual past. Am I bound for ever to the people I slept with? No. The union Paul describes is real, and its wounds can be real, but it is not a marriage and it does not own you. Christ’s union with you is stronger, and his blood washes every sin of the past (v. 11). Confess it to God, receive his forgiveness as fully as he gives it, and ask him to heal the memories and attachments that remain; often it helps to talk with a wise pastor or counsellor. Many believers with painful sexual histories go on to know deep joy in Christ, and in a faithful marriage. The past is real, but it is not the strongest bond in your life.

What if I was sexually abused? Then you did not sin; you were sinned against. Paul is speaking here about what people choose to do with their bodies, not what was done to them by force or manipulation. Nothing done to you without your free consent has joined you to your abuser in the sense of this verse, and none of the guilt is yours. Your body remains a member of Christ and a temple of his Spirit, and he is not ashamed of you. Please tell someone safe, seek help, and, where a crime has been committed, report it. Christ, who was himself stripped and shamed by cruel men, stands with the wounded, and he promises to bind up the broken-hearted (Psalm 147:3).

parallels.desc: they shall become one flesh

verseByVerse.quote: Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Flee from sexual immorality. One word, and it is the whole strategy. The tense is continuous: keep fleeing, make it a habit rather than an emergency measure. Not argue with it, but run. Elsewhere Christians are told to stand, to resist the devil, to put on armour and hold their ground (James 4:7; Ephesians 6:13). In this particular fight, standing your ground to prove you can is not courage. It is how people lose. The model is Joseph, who does not debate with Potiphar’s wife. He runs out of the house and leaves his garment in her hand (Genesis 39:12; 2 Timothy 2:22). It cost him his reputation and his liberty, and it was the right decision.

Every other sin a person commits is outside the body. The clause is genuinely difficult, and commentators divide over it. Some think Paul is again quoting a Corinthian saying, every sin is outside the body, and then contradicting it. Others take it as Paul’s own statement, meaning that sexual sin is unique in its relation to the body.

Against his own body. The second reading is the more likely. Drunkenness and gluttony also harm the body, but they act on it from outside. In sexual sin the body itself is given to another and the two become one flesh (v. 16), so the sin is committed with the very body that is joined to the Lord (vv. 15, 17). It is not the worst sin, but it defiles the body that is the Lord’s temple, and the damage lands on the person committing it.

Sin in the body, borne in his body. The sin Paul singles out is committed in and against the body, and the remedy God provided came in a body too. He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, Peter writes, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness (1 Peter 2:24). Every sexual sin of every believer was carried to the cross and judged there, and that is where the power to flee comes from. A Christian does not run from sexual sin in order to make himself clean. He runs because that sin has already been condemned in the body of his Lord, and the life now open to him is life to righteousness.

What fleeing looks like. The modern form of this battle is often a device in a pocket. It is tempting to resist only at the point of temptation, using willpower at the very moment it is least available: late, tired, alone, discouraged. That fight is rarely won for long. Fleeing happens earlier, and it is structural rather than heroic. The decision is taken at ten in the morning, not eleven at night: the filter installed, the device out of the bedroom, the friendship that has begun to warm quietly cooled before anyone has said anything they cannot unsay. And it means telling somebody. Sin that has to be reported to a friend on Thursday loses much of its power on Wednesday.

Does fleeing mean avoiding everyone of the opposite sex? No. Paul worked closely with women in the gospel (Romans 16:1–7; Philippians 4:2–3), and Jesus spoke alone with a Samaritan woman. Fleeing is not fear of people; it is wisdom about situations. It means knowing your own weaknesses and setting sensible boundaries: being careful about privacy and secrecy, about emotional intimacy with someone who is not your spouse, about the moments and places where you know you are vulnerable. Treat older women as mothers and younger women as sisters, in all purity (1 Timothy 5:2). The aim is honour toward others, not suspicion of them.

What if I keep falling, even after I have tried to flee? Then do not stop fleeing, and do not stop coming back to Christ. Repeated failure tempts you to give up, either by concluding you can never change or by deciding it does not matter. Both are lies. Confess it honestly to God, who is faithful and just to forgive (1 John 1:9). Tell a mature Christian and let him help you see where the battle is actually being lost, which is usually earlier than you think. Strengthen the barriers, and ask for help if it has become an addiction. Many have walked out of long patterns of sin by God’s grace, often slowly. The Spirit who lives in you is stronger than the habit.

parallels.desc: Joseph fled

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A temple of the Holy Spirit. Earlier the temple was the congregation (3:16); here it is each believer’s body. Temple is naos: not the whole complex of courts but the inner sanctuary, the place where God dwells. What made a temple a temple was the occupant. The argument is not that your body is impressive. It is that Someone lives there. In Israel the inner sanctuary was the most guarded place in the land: one man, once a year, with blood, lest he die (Leviticus 16:2, 34). The same holy God now lives in the body of every believer, and that should make us tremble as well as rejoice. Sexual sin brings the Holy One into the brothel.

Whom you have from God? The Spirit is God’s gift (2:12). You did not earn him. He is a gift, not an achievement, and therefore not something any believer can claim to be too unworthy to have received.

You are not your own. Five words that cut across the deepest assumption most people hold about themselves, the opposite of the modern slogan, my body, my choice. It is a claim of ownership over the one thing every human being reserves. The sceptic hears the end of freedom. But no one is truly his own: everyone is ruled by something, an appetite, an ambition, the opinion of others (Romans 6:16). Everyone will have a master; what matters is whether your master gave his life for you.

Bought with a price. The ground changes everything. “Bought” is the language of the slave market. Somebody paid, and the payment transferred ownership. The price was the cross: not silver or gold, but the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19; Revelation 5:9). You belong to your new master, and he is a master who bought you to set you free. That makes the sentence the most reassuring in the chapter.
