If you are not your own, then you are not finally at the mercy of your own failures, your own assessment of yourself, or your own capacity to hold on. The body you have treated badly, the self you are ashamed of, the life you suspect you have wasted: none of it is yours to write off, because none of it is yours.

So glorify God in your body. The chapter ends not on a prohibition but on what the body is actually for. Hands that work honestly, a tongue that blesses rather than reviles, arms that pick up a child, a body spent in service and eventually worn out in it: all of that is what this verse asks for. All of it is the work of the Spirit who lives there.

A textual note. Some later manuscripts add “and in your spirit, which are God’s”; the shorter reading is original. The addition is true, but Paul’s point in this chapter is deliberately about the body.

Does this verse forbid smoking, tattoos or unhealthy food? Its first meaning is narrower: Paul is writing about sexual immorality, and a body that belongs to the Lord must not be joined to a prostitute. But the principle reaches further, because the body is not ours. We are to care for it as belonging to God, and other texts plainly forbid drunkenness and gluttony (Ephesians 5:18; Proverbs 23:20–21). What the verse does not do is settle every question of habit or appearance; the ban on tattoos in Leviticus 19:28 belonged to Israel’s separation from pagan mourning rites. Where Scripture does not forbid, Paul’s own test from verse 12 applies: is it helpful, and am I being mastered by it?

If I am not my own, must I let others do what they like with my body? No; the very opposite. You are not your own because you belong to Christ, not because you belong to anyone else. No husband, wife, boyfriend, employer or church leader owns your body, and no one has the right to use, hurt or control it. Belonging to Christ is your protection. If someone is abusing or coercing you, it is right to say no, to get to safety and to seek help, including from the police. The Lord who bought you at the cost of his own blood is not indifferent to what is done to his temple, and he calls his church to protect the vulnerable, not to hand them back.

For worship. The true temple once walked the streets of Jerusalem. Jesus spoke of the temple of his body; men destroyed it on a cross, and in three days he raised it up (John 2:19–21). From that risen and exalted Lord the Spirit was poured out (Acts 2:33), and the God who had filled the house on Mount Zion moved into people, men and women who had been on the list in verse 9, washed, sanctified, justified, and now inhabited. The Spirit of the living God has made his home in jars of clay, and he will not leave until he has raised them in glory.
verseByVerse.note: “Bought with a price” uses the language of the slave market.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>When one of you has a grievance against another, does he dare go to law before the unrighteous instead of the saints?<sup>2</sup>Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you incompetent to try trivial cases?<sup>3</sup>Do you not know that we are to judge angels? How much more, then, matters pertaining to this life!<sup>4</sup>So if you have such cases, why do you lay them before those who have no standing in the church?<sup>5</sup>I say this to your shame. Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between the brothers,<sup>6</sup>but brother goes to law against brother, and that before unbelievers?<sup>7</sup>To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded?<sup>8</sup>But you yourselves wrong and defraud—even your own brothers!<sup>9</sup>Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who practice homosexuality,<sup>10</sup>nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of God.<sup>11</sup>And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.<sup>12</sup>“All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be dominated by anything.<sup>13</sup>“Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food”—and God will destroy both one and the other. The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.<sup>14</sup>And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power.<sup>15</sup>Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Never!<sup>16</sup>Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, as it is written, “The two will become one flesh.”<sup>17</sup>But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him.<sup>18</sup>Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body.<sup>19</sup>Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own,<sup>20</sup>for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.

7.title: Marriage, Celibacy, and the Calling of God
7.overview:
From chapter 7 Paul answers questions the Corinthians had sent him in a letter. The first concerns sex and marriage. Some in Corinth had swung to the opposite extreme from the immorality of chapter 6: they said it was better for a man not to touch a woman at all, even in marriage, and perhaps that believers should divorce unbelieving spouses or not marry. Roman society, by contrast, pressed people to marry. Paul steers between both pressures.

Married couples should not deny each other sexually, except briefly by agreement for prayer. Singleness is good and Paul himself prefers it, but it is a gift, and those without it should marry. Believers should not divorce, as Jesus taught; a believer married to an unbeliever should stay if the unbeliever is willing, but is not bound if the unbeliever leaves. Each person should serve God in the situation in which he was called, though a slave who can gain freedom should take it. Because the time is short and because of a present crisis, Paul advises the unmarried to consider staying single, so as to serve the Lord without divided concerns. But marriage is no sin, and a widow may remarry, only to a believer.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul answers the ascetic slogan from their letter. Marriage is God’s provision, and within it husband and wife owe themselves to each other on equal terms. Singleness and marriage are both gifts; those who burn with desire should marry.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Goodness of Marriage and the Gift of Celibacy

The Reformers resisted the medieval church’s view of celibacy as the spiritually higher state. They read 1 Corinthians 7 as honouring both callings as gifts of God, neither superior in itself, and Luther’s own marriage was a public statement that marriage is not a second-class state.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian ascetics may have shared the same low view of the body that produced the “food for the stomach” argument in chapter 6, turned the other way: if the body is spiritually inferior, why give it what it desires? Paul refuses both extremes. Now: Sexuality is still treated either as a dangerous force to be suppressed or as an identity that cannot be questioned. Paul makes it neither: a good gift, shaped by covenant promises, and not the last thing about anyone.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.” But because of the temptation to sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 7 is the Bible’s longest discussion of marriage and singleness. Some in Corinth had swung away from the immorality of chapter 6 into the opposite error: sex itself was unspiritual. Paul answers their letter point by point, honouring both marriage and singleness as gifts. Behind every line stands a Lord who assigns each of his people a life, calls them in it, and goes with them there.

Now concerning the matters about which you wrote. With this sentence the letter changes shape. Until now Paul has answered reports (1:11; 5:1); from here he answers a letter the Corinthians sent him, and “now concerning” marks each new topic: marriage (7:1), the betrothed (7:25), food offered to idols (8:1), spiritual gifts (12:1), the collection (16:1) and Apollos (16:12). The apostle takes their questions seriously, in their order, as a pastor answers a letter from people he loves.

Not to have sexual relations. Literally, not to touch a woman, a polite expression for sexual relations. Because Paul is now quoting their letter, this is very probably their slogan, not his, and the ESV puts it in quotation marks for that reason (older translations such as the KJV print it as Paul’s own words): the watchword of ascetics who said that even married couples should abstain. Paul spends the rest of the chapter qualifying it. Read as Paul’s own view, it makes the chapter a grudging concession, and much unhappy teaching about sex has been built on that misreading.

Two errors that are really one. Chapter 6 dealt with a party for whom the body did not matter because it was disposable: so do what you like with it. Here is a party for whom the body did not matter because it should be denied: so give it nothing. They are the same error, a contempt for the body God made and Christ redeemed, and Paul refuses both (6:13). And the ascetic error has a pull of its own: giving up good things can feel like a holiness we have earned. But rules of do not handle, do not taste, do not touch have no value against the indulgence of the flesh (Colossians 2:21–23), and no one is made acceptable to God by refusing what he gave.

Because of the temptation. Literally, because of immoralities, plural: the many forms of it on every street of a port city like Corinth. Enforced abstinence inside marriage would not produce saints. It would produce sin. And God does not treat that sin lightly: the marriage bed is to be kept undefiled, because God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterous (Hebrews 13:4). Marriage is his holy provision, not a loophole.

His own wife, her own husband. “Have” here probably means have sexual relations with, within marriage. One wife, one husband, his own and her own, in perfect parallel: monogamy and complete mutuality, before Paul has even begun to argue.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the only reason to marry is to avoid sin. Scripture gives many purposes for marriage: companionship, for it is not good that the man should be alone (Genesis 2:18); children (Genesis 1:28); a living picture of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:32); and the prevention of immorality. Paul is answering a specific question here, not writing a full theology of marriage.

The Lord who went to a wedding. The ascetics thought they honoured Christ by despising what he had made. But when the Pharisees asked Jesus about marriage, he took them back to the beginning: the Creator made them male and female, and the two shall become one flesh (Matthew 19:4–6). He was defending his own handiwork (John 1:3). And John tells us that Jesus began his signs at a wedding in Cana, turning water into wine so that the feast would not fail (John 2:1–11). The Son of God did not keep his distance from marriage as a lesser thing. He made it, he defended it, and he blessed it with his presence.

Realism without shame. Paul does not tell the Corinthians to aspire to a purity they will not sustain. He tells them, in effect: you are not made of iron, you live in Corinth, and God has provided for this. There is no shaming in it, and that note holds for the whole chapter, which married readers can hear as calling them second-rate and single readers as calling them deficient. The strongest thing in Paul’s answer is a refusal to bind anyone’s conscience where God has not (1 Timothy 4:1–5).

Is sexual desire itself sinful, then? No. Desire for one’s husband or wife is part of the good creation; God made the man and the woman, brought them together, and they were naked and not ashamed (Genesis 2:25). A whole book of the Bible, the Song of Songs, celebrates married love without embarrassment. What is sinful is desire turned toward someone who is not your spouse, or desire allowed to rule rather than serve. Paul’s point is that God has given a holy place for this desire, and that pretending to be above it does not make a person more spiritual; it makes him more vulnerable.
verseByVerse.note: From here Paul answers questions the Corinthians had sent him in a letter. The ESV notes that “to have sexual relations” is literally “to touch.” The quoted saying was probably a slogan of some at Corinth.

parallels.desc: it is not good that the man should be alone

verseByVerse.quote: The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband. For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Conjugal rights. Literally what is owed, a debt word. Paul is describing an obligation each spouse owes, not a right to be seized. And the husband is addressed first: in a world where a man’s desires were assumed to be the point, Paul begins with what a husband owes. And likewise the wife to her husband: complete mutuality, each owing the other in the same terms.

The wife does not have authority over her own body. “Have authority” (exousiazō) is the same verb Paul used in 6:12, where he refused to be dominated by anything. In marriage each gives the other a claim on their body. In the Greco-Roman world this first half was unremarkable: a wife’s body was understood to be at her husband’s disposal.

Likewise the husband. The second half was startling. A husband’s body was his own; his liberties outside the marriage were assumed and largely unpoliced, with slaves, prostitutes and mistresses all quietly allowed for. The single word likewise gave a wife the same claim on her husband, with the same force, that he had on her. And it means the passage cannot be read as a charter for a husband’s demands, because whatever it grants him it grants her in the same breath and the same sentence.

What it does not mean. It does not mean either spouse may force or coerce the other. The passage is about giving, not taking. Love does not insist on its own way (13:5), and husbands must love their wives as Christ loved the church (Ephesians 5:25). These verses have been quoted to wives, usually by husbands and occasionally by pastors who should have known better, to argue that a woman has no right to refuse, that her consent is not required, that saying no is a sin. It will not carry the weight. The whole framing is mutual: two people who have each given themselves away, each responsible for the other’s good. And Paul at once adds that even abstaining must be by agreement (v. 5). A man who uses verse 4 to override his wife’s no has taken a verse about mutual self-giving and turned it into a lever, and he has quietly ignored the half of it that binds him.

If this verse was used against me, what do I do? First, hear it plainly: forced or pressured sex in marriage is not what Paul is describing, and it is not your duty to submit to it. It is a sin against you, and where it involves force or threat it is also a crime. You are not to blame for refusing it. Tell someone you trust, a pastor or elder, a wise friend, a doctor or counsellor, and if you are in danger, seek safety first and contact the authorities. A church that hears this should protect you, not send you back to explain yourself. And if you have carried guilt for years because a verse was twisted against you, lay it down. The Lord who wrote these words is the one who binds up the broken-hearted (Psalm 147:3), and he never handed anyone a lever.

The mind of Christ in marriage. The obligation is to give, and neither spouse is anywhere given permission to take. Paul did not invent that pattern. It is the mind of Christ, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself (Philippians 2:5–7). The husband who loves his wife as Christ loved the church follows a Lord who handed over his own body for his bride. A debt owed and gladly paid: that is the shape of the cross carried into the most private room of a Christian home.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not deprive one another. “Deprive” (apostereō) means rob or defraud, the same verb Paul used a chapter earlier of the Corinthians cheating their brothers in the law courts (6:7–8). To withhold yourself from your spouse is treated here as a kind of theft. Withholding is a common instrument in an unhappy marriage and it is rarely named. It is deniable, requires no words, and can be maintained for years while both people pretend nothing is happening. Paul calls it fraud.

By agreement for a limited time. Then the single exception, with three conditions. By agreement: both, freely, for Paul’s picture is never one spouse deciding for the other. For a limited time: with an end agreed in advance, not an indefinite drift. And that you may devote yourselves to prayer: a season of special prayer, a positive spiritual purpose (some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read fasting and prayer; the earliest have prayer alone), not leverage, punishment, or the slow retreat that such withdrawals often are.

Come together again. Paul assumes the resumption. Abstinence in marriage is the exception, not the rule: a parenthesis in a normal life, not a higher state to be aspired to.

So that Satan may not tempt you. Paul names the danger without embarrassment. A marriage in which this has been allowed to lapse is a marriage with a door left open, and there is somebody who tries doors. And he says not because of your sin but because of your lack of self-control: a statement about how human beings are made, offered without condemnation.

A Bridegroom who does not defraud. Why is withholding called robbery? Because marriage was made to show something. Paul quotes Genesis, the two shall become one flesh, and then says, This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). A husband and wife who give themselves to each other are telling a true story about a Bridegroom who never holds himself back. Christ does not ration his love to his church or go quiet in a grievance. He gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25), and he gives himself still (Hebrews 7:25). A marriage that defrauds has stopped telling that story; a marriage that gives goes on telling it.

Two readers, two words. To the one who has been quietly withholding, perhaps for reasons that felt justified, hurt, exhaustion, or a grievance never resolved, it is a summons to say so out loud: not to comply resentfully, which Paul asks for nowhere, but to stop conducting the argument in silence and have it in words. And to the one who has been going without and has begun to feel foolish for minding: it is not foolish. A verse of the Bible exists to say that this matters. And pray together, even briefly, even awkwardly: Peter tells husbands to live with their wives with understanding, so that their prayers are not hindered (1 Peter 3:7).

What if one of us cannot, through illness, pain, trauma or age? Then this verse is not a rule to be enforced against a suffering spouse. Paul is addressing the deliberate withholding of a gift that could be given, not the inability to give it. Where there is physical illness, pain, the after-effects of childbirth, depression or past abuse, love will be patient and gentle, will seek medical and pastoral help, and will find other ways of tenderness. A husband who presses an unwell or traumatised wife is not obeying this verse; he is breaking the one before it. And the spouse who goes without for such reasons should take that longing to God honestly, and to a trusted counsellor if needed, rather than let it harden into resentment or wander elsewhere.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as a concession, not a command, I say this. I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A concession, not a command. Paul marks the status of what he has just written, as he does all chapter (vv. 10, 12, 25). Most likely “this” is the permission to abstain for a time for prayer (v. 5): allowed, not required. Some take it more broadly of the marriage counsel in general. Either way, Paul is scrupulous about not binding consciences where God has not bound them.

I wish that all were as I myself am. Paul was unmarried as he wrote; whether he had never married or was a widower, he does not say. He found singleness a freedom for ministry, because the single person can give undivided attention to the Lord (vv. 32–35).

Each has his own gift from God. This sentence stops Paul turning his preference into a rule. The word is charisma, a grace-gift, the same word he uses of the gifts of the Spirit in chapter 12. Marriage is a gift and singleness is a gift: not one gift and one deficiency, but two gifts, differently distributed, both from God. A married Christian is not the standard from which single Christians are a variation, and a single Christian is not someone waiting in a corridor for real life to begin. Both have been handed something.

Both gifts meet in Christ. The surest proof that singleness is no deficiency is the life of Jesus. The one perfectly whole human being who ever lived never married, and his life lacked nothing; he was full of grace and truth (John 1:14). It was Jesus who first spoke of a gift like this (Matthew 19:11–12). Yet this single man is also the Bridegroom, and the Bible’s story closes with his wedding (Revelation 19:7; 21:2). In him neither state is second-rate: he honoured the one by living it and the other by making it the picture of his love.

Where Christians differ: is celibacy holier? The medieval church came to treat celibacy as a higher, more spiritual state, and required it of clergy. This commentary’s view: Paul values singleness highly, but he calls both singleness and marriage gifts from God. Neither is holier. Forbidding marriage is described as a teaching of demons (1 Timothy 4:1–3), and church leaders may be married (1 Timothy 3:2; 1 Corinthians 9:5). The Reformers rightly restored the honour of marriage, including for ministers. Each believer should seek to serve God in the calling he has given.

What it does not mean. It does not mean singleness is a gift only for those who feel no desire. Single Christians are often told they must have the gift of singleness, and therefore should not mind, so that wanting marriage becomes a failure to accept their gift. But Paul describes the state itself as the gift, given by God for now, to be used for him. The single Christian who longs to be married has not forfeited anything. He is a person in the condition God has him in, wanting something good that he does not have, which is the ordinary experience of married and unmarried alike.

How do I know whether I have the gift of singleness? If you are single today, you have it today; that is what Paul means by gift. The question is not a hidden feeling you must detect in yourself, which is unanswerable and produces only anxiety. It is the one Paul will put in verse 17: what is the life the Lord has assigned me now, and what does faithfulness in it look like? You may pray for marriage, look for it wisely and gladly receive it if God gives it; that too would be his gift. Some people find over years that God has given them a settled freedom in singleness (Matthew 19:11–12), and they may embrace it with joy. Neither path needs to be decided on a feeling.

verseByVerse.quote: To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them to remain single, as I am. But if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the unmarried and the widows. The unmarried may mean widowers here, paired with widows, or all unmarried people. Paul repeats his own preference, again as counsel rather than command.

If they cannot exercise self-control. The word is used of athletes in training (9:25). There is no virtue in a heroic celibacy you cannot sustain.

Better to marry than to burn. Some have taken it of the fire of judgment, but the sense here is almost certainly the ordinary one: consuming desire that will not leave a person alone. Strong desire is a legitimate reason to marry, and that is part of what marriage is for.

Marriage will not put the fire out. Nor is the verse a promise that marriage will solve the problem. Some have married quickly to resolve their desires and discovered that marriage does not extinguish desire, and adds a second person with her own history, tiredness and struggles. A married man can still look at a woman with lustful intent (Matthew 5:28). Marriage is a God-given place for desire, not a cure for sin.

The Spirit’s fruit of self-control. If marriage is not the cure for the heart, what is? The word Paul uses for self-control in this verse belongs to the same family as the last fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:23. It is not a talent some Christians are born with but what the Spirit of Christ grows in the people Christ has bought. He bore on the cross the guilt of every lustful look, and he now lives in his people by his Spirit, so that the fight against desire is no longer fought alone, or fought to earn his favour. Because he himself suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18). Married or single, the help for the burning comes from him.

And what if marriage is not open to me? There is an honest word owed to the reader for whom this verse offers no route at all. Paul’s advice presupposes that marriage is available. For many it is not: through circumstance, through a lack of anyone godly to marry, through same-sex attraction, or through a spouse who is present but with whom this part of life has ended through illness. Such a reader can find this verse almost mocking: the remedy is named and the door is shut. Scripture does not pretend that is easy, and neither should we. What it does say is that no one has been promised the fulfilment of every legitimate desire in this life; that the Lord who requires this of some was himself a single man, tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15); and that his grace is said to be sufficient precisely where the thorn is not removed (2 Corinthians 12:9). That is not a tidy answer, and it is not meant to be. But it is better than the two things such readers are usually offered, which are a demand to feel differently and a promise God has not made. And God has a word for those the world counts as without a future: to the eunuchs who hold fast his covenant he promises a name better than sons and daughters, an everlasting name that shall not be cut off (Isaiah 56:4–5).

How strong does desire have to be before I should look to marry? Paul is not setting a threshold; he is giving permission. If you find that the desire for intimacy is a constant pressure, that it drives you toward pornography or fantasy or compromise in relationships, that is a clear sign that you should prayerfully and actively seek marriage, and there is nothing unspiritual about doing so. Talk to mature believers, pray, and take sensible steps to meet godly people. At the same time, fight the sin now: marriage is not a reward for those who first become pure, but neither is the struggle a reason to marry the first person who is willing. Marry in the Lord (v. 39), and marry someone you can love for a lifetime.

On a Tuesday. If you are single and struggling, do not fight alone: tell one trusted Christian friend. And if you are married, ask how you can make your church a place where single people are neither pitied nor pressured, but welcomed into homes, prayed for by name, and trusted with real work.

For worship. The Lord knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14), and he does not sneer at desire or demand that it vanish. Every good longing for love was put there by him, and every one is a small sign pointing to the love that will at last fill it. He has promised a marriage to every one of his people, the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9), where no believer will be single and none will be alone. Whatever fire is burning now, it is burning in someone already betrothed to Christ, and the Bridegroom is coming.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On divorce Paul first gives the Lord’s own command to believing couples, then his apostolic ruling for marriages to unbelievers: stay if the unbeliever is willing; if he leaves, the believer is not bound, for God has called us to peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Command and Apostolic Judgment

Paul’s distinction in vv. 10 and 12 (“not I, but the Lord” and “I, not the Lord”) shows how an apostle handled the words of Jesus. It does not make vv. 12–16 less authoritative; Paul writes under inspiration. Verses 12–16 extend the principle of Jesus’ saying to a situation he did not address.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Divorce was common and easy in the Roman world. What to do in a mixed marriage, especially if the unbeliever wanted out, was an urgent question for many in the church. Now: Verse 15 (sometimes called the “Pauline privilege”, the freedom of a deserted believer) is still much debated and much needed, in cases of desertion and of abuse that amounts to it. God has called you to peace is a pastoral starting point, not a blank cheque.

verseByVerse.quote: To the married I give this charge (not I, but the Lord): the wife should not separate from her husband (but if she does, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband), and the husband should not divorce his wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not I, but the Lord. Paul is citing the teaching of Jesus, the teaching the Gospels record (Mark 10:9–12; Matthew 5:32; 19:6–9). Where Paul has a word from Christ he says so and rests on it. “Married” here means where both spouses are believers; he will deal with mixed marriages in verse 12.

The Lord of the beginning. Paul expects the words of a teacher from Galilee to settle the matter in a Greek city twenty years later, because of who spoke them. When Jesus was asked about divorce, he did not merely choose between the rabbis. He went behind Moses to creation: from the beginning it was not so, and what God has joined together, let not man separate (Matthew 19:6–8). He was restoring his own design. The command on marriage comes from the Lord of marriage.

Should not separate. “Separate” was a common word for divorce at that time; there was little legal distinction in Greek and Roman practice between walking out and divorcing. Paul addresses the wife first: under Roman law at Corinth a woman could initiate divorce, which she ordinarily could not do under Jewish law, so Paul speaks to her directly, as a person with agency and responsibility. Some Corinthian women may have wanted to leave their husbands for a celibate life (v. 1).

Remain unmarried or be reconciled. A practical parenthesis. A believing wife who leaves without biblical grounds is not free to marry someone else. Paul states the rule and in the same breath deals realistically with its being broken: there will be separations, and here is what to do when there has been one. And the door he leaves open is reconciliation.

The husband should not divorce. “Divorce” means send away. Divorce was easy in that world, and among Jews the school of Hillel allowed it for almost any reason. Christ forbids it. The passage will not support the common assumption that a marriage may be ended because it has failed: because the love has gone, or the two have grown apart, or one of them is unhappy.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul is ignoring the exception Jesus gave for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9). He is giving the general rule. And Paul is about to add another in verse 15, where a believer is deserted by an unbelieving spouse. So the historic Protestant position, that Scripture permits divorce on those two grounds and no others, adultery and wilful desertion (the Westminster Confession 24.5–6), is built from the whole of what is written rather than from any one text, and it is the reading followed here (on abuse, see below).

Is it not cruel to keep someone in an unhappy marriage? It can sound that way, but think about what a marriage vow is. Nobody needs a promise for the happy days; the vow was made for the days when feeling fails, for better and for worse. A love that may leave whenever it stops being rewarded is closer to a contract than a covenant, and it leaves the weaker partner, the ill, the ageing, the one who has disappointed, with no security at all. God binds a husband and wife together as he has bound himself to his people, and he did not leave us when we were unlovable (Romans 5:8). The command does not abandon an unhappy couple to their misery: it sends them to repentance, to help and to the church, and an unhappy marriage is often a marriage on the way to being mended. Danger is a different matter: no one is required to stay where they are unsafe. Abuse is never to be tolerated; a spouse who is being abused should seek safety at once, and the church must stand with them and protect them.

What about abuse? The charge that a wife should not separate does not require anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. Abuse is never to be tolerated in a Christian home or excused by a Christian church. Leaving to be safe is not the separation Paul forbids, and a church must never send a victim back to an abuser or counsel her to submit to violence, threats or cruelty. Abuse is a crime as well as a sin; it should be reported to the authorities, and the abuser should face the church’s discipline. Whether persistent, unrepentant abuse ends the marriage itself is a harder question. The grounds for divorce remain the two Scripture gives, adultery and desertion. But this commentary holds, with many Reformed pastors and church courts, that persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion: a spouse who makes the home unsafe and will not repent has in fact deserted the marriage while remaining under the same roof, abandoning every promise he made. That is a judgement about whether desertion has occurred, not a third ground, and it is weighty enough that it should be made with the elders of the church, never alone and never in a hurry. What is never in doubt is the first step: get safe.

May the innocent party remarry after adultery? Paul’s instruction to remain unmarried or else be reconciled is given to the one who has separated without grounds. Where a marriage has been broken by a spouse’s adultery, Jesus’ words in Matthew 19:9 imply that the innocent partner who divorces and remarries does not commit adultery, and the historic Protestant confessions conclude that remarriage is then permitted, as if the offending party were dead (Westminster 24.5). Others hold that remarriage is never allowed while a former spouse lives, appealing to verse 39 and to Mark 10:11–12. The first view is the more likely, because Jesus’ exception would mean little if the marriage bond remained intact. Even then divorce is permitted, not commanded; forgiveness and reconciliation after adultery are often possible and always beautiful.

I have already remarried after a divorce that did not fit these grounds. What now? Do not break up the marriage you are in. A second wrong does not undo the first, and the vows you have now made are real vows before God. Repent honestly of any sin in how it began, without excuses and without endless self-punishment; receive Christ’s forgiveness, which is as full for this as for anything else; and set yourself to keep the vows you have made, faithfully, for life. If there are children or a former spouse affected, ask what you can still do to act justly and kindly toward them. Your pastor can help you think it through.

If you are divorced. If you are divorced, and particularly if you know your own sin was part of why, this passage is telling the church what marriage is. It is not a sentence passed on you, and it does not put you outside the reach of what this letter has already said: such were some of you, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (6:11). Justified means declared righteous by God, not because of our record but because of Christ’s. Divorce is not the one sin left outside the reach of forgiveness, and a repentant divorced believer is not on a permanent second tier before God. The command in verse 10 is for a marriage you are in. The mercy in 6:11 is for a life you have already lived.

For worship. Behind this charge is the faithfulness of God himself. He is the husband who did not divorce his people when they played the harlot; he sent Hosea to buy back an unfaithful wife as a picture of what he would do (Hosea 3:1). He is the God who keeps covenant, and he kept his with a bride who broke it every day (Malachi 2:14–16). At the cross the Bridegroom paid for his bride’s unfaithfulness in his own body, so that she could be presented to him without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27). And every Christian whose marriage has broken, by their own fault or another’s, is held by a Husband who has never yet let go of anyone he took.
verseByVerse.note: Paul cites Jesus’ own teaching on divorce.

verseByVerse.quote: To the rest I say (I, not the Lord) that if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I, not the Lord. Jesus, teaching within Israel, had left no saying about a marriage in which one partner came to Christ and the other stayed a pagan. So Paul gives his own apostolic ruling. That does not make it a private opinion the church may take or leave. Paul cannot quote a saying of Jesus, but he speaks with the authority Christ gave him, and he ends the chapter claiming that he too has the Spirit of God (v. 40; 14:37). The distinction is about the source of the teaching, not its authority, and it is a mark of Paul’s honesty.

An unbelieving wife. In a city like Corinth people were converted out of pagan households, and very often one spouse believed and the other did not. Some new believers may have thought they must leave, fearing they were defiled by the union. Paul’s answer runs in one direction: the believer is not to initiate the ending.

An unbelieving husband. The same words for the woman, whose situation was the harder. In the ancient world a wife was expected to follow her husband’s religion; a woman who turned from his household gods to Christ might be seen as disloyal or even subversive.

Ezra reversed. There was an Old Testament precedent for exactly this situation, and it went the other way. When the returned exiles were found to have married foreign wives, Ezra had them put away, wives and children both, as an act of covenant faithfulness (Ezra 10:1–3). A Jewish believer at Corinth might have concluded that the holy thing was to end a marriage to a pagan. Paul reverses it. Under the new covenant the direction of contamination has changed: the believer’s presence sets the household apart for God, rather than the household defiling the believer (v. 14). Holiness is no longer a fragile thing to be protected by separation. It is a stronger thing that spreads.

Sent into the house. The reason: the Holy One has come into the world without being defiled by it, and he does not take his people out of it. Hours before his arrest, Jesus prayed for his disciples: I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one; as you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world (John 17:15, 18). The believer married to a pagan is not to be lifted out of the house. He is kept in it, and sent there, as Christ was sent among sinners, to be the Lord’s light at that table.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers may marry unbelievers. Paul forbids that (v. 39; 2 Corinthians 6:14). He is speaking of those already married when one came to faith. Nor does it mean anyone must remain where he or she is being abused (see on v. 11).

What if my unbelieving spouse opposes my faith, but does not leave? Then stay, and be wise. Opposition is not desertion, and mockery or coldness, painful as they are, do not end a marriage. Paul assumes many believers were living with spouses who disliked the new faith. Keep worshipping and keep loving; do not use your faith as a weapon in arguments, and do not hide it either. Where your spouse forbids something Scripture does not require on a particular day, be flexible; where he or she demands what God forbids, gently and firmly obey God (Acts 5:29). Ask your church to stand with you in prayer and practical help. And if opposition becomes threats, control or violence, that is abuse, and you should seek safety and counsel at once.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus had not addressed marriages where one partner became a believer; Paul applies his authority as an apostle.

verseByVerse.quote: For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Made holy because of his wife. This is the reason the believer is to stay, and it is widely misunderstood. It does not mean the unbelieving spouse is saved. Paul settles that himself when he wonders whether the believer may yet save the spouse (v. 16). Nobody is redeemed by marriage. “Made holy” is the ordinary word for sanctified: set apart. The believer was probably worried that sharing a bed and a table with someone outside the covenant made the marriage unclean, and the children with it. Paul says the influence runs the other way. The marriage is sanctified, acceptable to God, and the unbeliever is set within the sphere of God’s blessing, exposed every day to the gospel and to a godly spouse.

Your children are holy. If the marriage were unclean, the children would be too. But the children of a believing parent are holy: set apart, under the influence of the gospel and a believer’s care, and in that sense distinct from the children of two unbelievers. They are not outsiders.

The direction of transfer. That reversal runs all through the Gospels. Under the old order, touching a leper made you unclean. When Jesus touched one, the leper was made clean (Mark 1:40–42). The direction of transfer changed when he arrived. In the new covenant, holiness is not a delicate condition that contamination destroys; it is the stronger force in the room. If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump (Romans 11:16).

Where Christians differ: holy children and baptism. Some argue from this verse that the children of believers are in the covenant and should therefore be baptised as infants. This commentary’s view: The verse says the unbelieving spouse is also made holy, yet no one would baptise an unbelieving spouse. So holy here cannot mean qualified for baptism. It means set apart in a special relation to God’s people and blessing. Baptism in the New Testament is for those who repent and believe (Acts 2:38–41; 8:12). This commentary holds this credobaptist reading (baptism for those who profess faith), while recognising with charity that paedobaptist brothers and sisters, who baptise the infants of believers, read the covenant signs differently. The verse was not written to settle that question, and it should not become the thing this chapter is about.

What it does not mean. It does not mean children of believers are automatically saved. They need to be born again and believe, like everyone else. But they are greatly privileged: they hear the gospel from their earliest days, are prayed for by name, and see what a Christian life looks like up close.

What about my children if my spouse is not a Christian? This verse was written for exactly your fear. Your children are not disadvantaged before God because only one parent believes; they are set apart, because you are there. Teach them the Scriptures as Timothy’s mother and grandmother did, apparently with a father who was a Greek (Acts 16:1; 2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15). Pray with them, take them to church where you can, and let them see the faith lived gently rather than argued with their other parent. Be honest that you and their father or mother see things differently, without belittling your spouse. And pray for their salvation, and for your spouse’s, with real hope.

The comfort of an anxious believer. That is what the verse is for. If you are the only Christian in your house, your marriage is not a compromise God tolerates rather than blesses. Your presence there is not a problem to be managed; it is the reason the place is holy.
verseByVerse.note: “Made holy” does not mean saved, but set within the sphere of God’s blessing through the believing partner.

verseByVerse.quote: But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. God has called you to peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let it be so. Now Paul deals with the case where staying is not in the believer’s power. “Separates” means divorces, departs. The believer is not to pursue, obstruct or fight to hold a marriage the other person has ended. That is a permission, not an instruction to give up easily; the whole preceding paragraph assumes the believer wants the marriage to continue.

Not enslaved. Bound as a slave is bound: it is a strong word, and the believer is free. At minimum the deserted believer is freed from any duty to chase the one who left, or to wait in limbo indefinitely.

God has called you to peace. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read us. This clause governs the whole verse. Where reconciliation is genuinely impossible, where the other person has gone and will not come back, God is not requiring you to conduct a war, or to keep hold of something being pulled out of your hands. There is a pious tenacity that looks like faithfulness and is actually a refusal to accept a loss God has permitted. Paul releases the deserted believer from it. So far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18); and when it does not depend on you, peace is still your calling.

The peace of the call. God’s call in this letter is always a call into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord (1:9), and the first peace it brings is peace with God, made by the blood of Christ’s cross (Romans 5:1; Colossians 1:20). That is why a deserted believer can be called to peace even when the house is in pieces. The one you promised your life to has walked out; the One who called you has bound himself to you, and nothing in all creation can separate you from his love (Romans 8:38–39). It is the peace of someone whose deepest belonging was never in the hands of the one who left.

Where Christians differ: desertion and remarriage. Some say a deserted believer may separate but never remarry while the former spouse lives. This commentary’s view: Not enslaved means the marriage bond is broken, and the deserted believer is free to remarry, in the Lord. Paul uses similar language about being free to remarry after a spouse’s death (v. 39; Romans 7:2–3). Scripture recognises two grounds for divorce with freedom to remarry: sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9) and wilful desertion by an unbelieving spouse that cannot be remedied by the church or civil authority (the Westminster Confession 24.6). Divorce is always a tragedy, and churches should handle each case with care and wise counsel. To say a deserted person is not enslaved while still holding them to a bond they cannot escape and did not break would be a strange kind of freedom; the Reformers read it this way, and that reading is followed here. Those who read it more narrowly are not to be dismissed, but the deserted should not be left in limbo by a church afraid to say anything.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer may push an unbelieving spouse to leave, or use this as an excuse to end a hard marriage.

What counts as desertion, and what if the one who left calls himself a Christian? Desertion is a settled, wilful abandonment of the marriage: leaving and refusing to return, or refusing to live as husband or wife at all, despite patient efforts at reconciliation. A row, a few weeks apart, or a spouse who is difficult but present is not desertion. And if the one who leaves professes faith, the church should treat it as a matter of discipline (Matthew 18:15–17): call him to return, and if he persists, he is to be treated as an unbeliever, and the same freedom follows. This commentary holds, with many Reformed churches, that persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion: a spouse who makes the home unsafe and will not repent has deserted the marriage while still living in it. In every such case the victim should seek safety first, and the counsel of the elders, and the church should not leave the deserted to decide alone.

The loneliest seat in church. The person who has been left often carries a double burden: the desertion itself, and a persistent sense that a better Christian would have held the marriage together. Paul does not treat the departure as evidence about you. He addresses you as someone who has had something done to them, releases you from the obligation to fix what you did not break, and tells you that the God who called you called you to peace, which is precisely what you have been unable to feel, and precisely what he intends you to have.

On a Tuesday. If you have been left, let the church carry some of it with you: ask your elders for counsel, accept the meals and the help with the children, and let one or two friends ask how you really are. If someone in your church has been left, do not avoid them because you do not know what to say. Say that you are sorry, and then show up, again and again. Sometimes making peace means helping someone carry a loss they did not choose.

For worship. God does not abandon the abandoned. He says, I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5), and he says it as the Lord who was himself forsaken. Christ was deserted by every friend he had, and on the cross he cried, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? He went through the darkest desertion there has ever been, so that no one who belongs to him would ever be left by God. He is still in the empty house, and he is not leaving.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “God has called us to peace.”

verseByVerse.quote: For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? The sentence can be read two ways, and both are grammatically possible. Commentators have divided over it for centuries, and the pastoral force differs. Read hopefully, it is an argument for staying, attached to verses 12–14: who knows, you might win him to Christ, so stay if he is willing (1 Peter 3:1–2). Read soberly, it is a comfort for letting go, attached to verse 15: how can you know that you will save him? You cannot, so do not hold a departing spouse hostage to a hope you have no way of guaranteeing. The second fits verse 15 more closely; the first fits the whole passage’s encouragement to stay. Paul may well have intended both to be heard by the two different readers who would need them.

Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife? “Save” here means be God’s instrument in bringing them to salvation, as Paul says he became all things to all people that by all means he might save some (9:22). What is beyond dispute is the astonishing thing the verse takes for granted: that a Christian may be the human means by which their own husband or wife comes to Christ. Paul does not say it is likely. He says it is possible, and he says it in a way that assumes his readers had seen it happen.

Likewise, as Christ did. The instrument God most often uses in such a house has a shape. When Peter tells wives that unbelieving husbands may be won without a word by their conduct (1 Peter 3:1–2), he begins with Likewise, and the word points back to Christ: when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). The believing spouse wins by becoming a little like the Lord who won them: patient under contempt, gentle without being silent, leaving the outcome to God.

A question, not a promise. How do you know? does not guarantee that a faithful wife will win her husband. Some do; some pray for forty years and bury a man who never came. But it also forbids the opposite conclusion, the one it is easy to drift into after years: that it is settled, that he will never change, that after this many years there is no point. You do not know that either.

If my spouse dies without believing, did I fail? No. You were never given the power to save anyone, and Scripture does not lay that weight on you. The question in this verse is meant to free you from it. Grief over a spouse who died without professing Christ is real and deep, and you should not pretend otherwise. But you may leave that person with the Judge of all the earth, who will do what is right (Genesis 18:25), and who knows things about the last hours and the hidden heart that you do not. Your faithfulness was not wasted. It was seen by God, it was a witness, and it was the obedience he asked of you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Live as You Were Called
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The principle beneath the whole chapter: live the life the Lord has assigned, in which God called you. Paul tests it on the two great divisions of his world, Jew and Gentile, slave and free.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Relativisation of Social Status by the Gospel

Paul’s refrain, remain as you are, is not social conservatism but a matter of what comes first. The gospel puts every earthly status beneath a higher one: in Christ. That does not make social structures indifferent (Paul does not say slavery is good); the gospel works from the inside out, changing what every condition means before it changes the condition. This was the seed from which the abolition of slavery grew: not a political revolution, but the recognition that the slave is Christ’s freedman, which in time made the institution intolerable to Christian conscience.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: First-century Christianity attracted people across the entire social spectrum, from Lydia the merchant to Onesimus the slave. Paul guards against two errors: treating a change of status as spiritually necessary, and treating it as forbidden. Now: “Remain as you are” answers the anxiety that serving God requires a different job or a different place. God’s providence put you where you are; serve him there.

verseByVerse.quote: Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him. This is my rule in all the churches. Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision. For neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but keeping the commandments of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The life the Lord has assigned. Here is the governing principle of the whole chapter. Two verbs carry it. “Assigned” means apportioned, dealt out: God has given each person their place in life. “Called” points to the moment God called them to faith. Your circumstances are not an accident you must escape before your real Christian life can begin. They are a distribution, made by someone, on purpose.

This is my rule in all the churches. Not a special rule for Corinth, or a concession to its peculiar troubles, but the way Paul teaches everywhere (4:17).

In the flow. At first sight verses 17–24 wander away from marriage into circumcision and slavery. In fact the whole chapter turns on them: the married need not leave their marriages (vv. 1–16), the unmarried need not rush into one (vv. 25–40), and here Paul states the principle beneath both. The language of calling takes the reader back to 1:26: what matters is not the position God found you in but the God who called you in it.

Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Paul reaches for the test case of circumcision, and it is a shrewd choice, because it was among the most emotionally loaded status markers in his world. Some Jews under Greek influence had surgery to disguise their circumcision, to avoid mockery at the public baths and gymnasiums where men exercised naked (1 Maccabees 1:15). A Jewish believer among Gentile Christians might feel his circumcision embarrassing now. Paul says: a Jewish believer need not become a Gentile.

Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision. A Gentile convert, on the other hand, might feel a second-class member of a faith with Jewish roots, and be tempted to acquire the mark. A Gentile believer need not become a Jew (Galatians 5:2–6). The identity you brought with you is not the problem.

Keeping the commandments of God. A startling statement, since circumcision was itself a commandment. Paul probably means the moral commandments, the law of love, which applies to all: in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love (Galatians 5:6), and a new creation (Galatians 6:15). God does not accept anyone because he keeps the commandments; he accepts sinners for Christ’s sake, through faith (Galatians 2:16). But the person he accepts is given a new heart, and a new heart wants to obey (John 14:15).

The assignment the Son accepted. No one was ever given a harder assignment than the one Jesus received from his Father, and no one ever served so faithfully in it. He spent some thirty hidden years in a carpenter’s house in Nazareth, a town people mocked (John 1:46), then a short ministry among the poor, then a cross. Yet he could say at the end, I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do (John 17:4). Every Christian tempted to think that real life is somewhere else serves a Lord who did his Father’s will in the place he was put, and whose obedience there is counted to his people.

The obstacle we imagine. If I were married. If I were single. If I had the other job, the other health, the other church: then I could serve God properly. Paul’s answer is that the life you are in is the life you were assigned. There is no arrangement of circumstances in which obedience becomes easy, and none in which it becomes impossible (Philippians 4:11–12).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians can never change their circumstances: Paul is about to tell a slave to take his freedom if he can (v. 21), and he has told the burning single person to marry (v. 9). The principle is contentment, not paralysis.

Does this mean I should not leave a job that is wrong for me, or a sinful one? No. If your work requires you to sin, you must leave it, as tax collectors stopped cheating and soldiers stopped extorting when they repented (Luke 3:12–14). If it is lawful but you have a good opportunity to move, you are free to take it, prayerfully and without guilt. What Paul forbids is the restless conviction that God cannot use you until your situation changes, and the habit of making the next change the precondition of obedience. Ask two questions: is this situation sinful? If not, am I free and wise to change it? And meanwhile, serve Christ wholeheartedly where you are.
verseByVerse.note: Some Jews under Greek influence had surgery to hide their circumcision.

verseByVerse.quote: Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called. Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it. (But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it. Paul applies his principle to the hardest case in that society. A bondservant is a slave. It is a jarring sentence to a modern ear, and it should not be softened prematurely. Perhaps a third of people in Corinth were slaves, and the church contained many such people. Roman slavery was not based on race; people became slaves through war, debt or birth, and many, especially in the cities, could hope to be freed in time. Some slaves were educated professionals: doctors, teachers, managers of estates. But slaves had no legal rights and could be badly treated, beaten, sold and used. Paul tells them not to let their status trouble them, and he can say that only because of what he is about to say in the next verse about who they actually are: the Lord’s freedmen (v. 22). You are fully a Christian, with full dignity before God.

If you can gain your freedom. The ESV notes that the sentence can also be read make use of your present condition instead, meaning stay a slave even if offered freedom. The ESV’s main reading is more likely: freedom is better, so take it if you can. Manumission was common in that world. And Paul goes on at once to say do not become slaves of men (v. 23), which would make little sense if he meant them to refuse liberty.

Neither quietism nor indifference. Paul does not say slavery is good, or that a slave should refuse liberty out of piety. He says two things at once, and both are needed: your condition does not define you, and if you can be free, be free. Lose the first and nothing can be borne until it is fixed. Lose the second and you get the far uglier thing that actually happened in history: this text quoted by slaveholders to tell slaves that Christianity required them to stay put and be content. The parenthesis in this verse refutes it. It is honest to admit that the New Testament also tells Christian slaves to serve their masters well (Ephesians 6:5–8), and that slaveholders abused those words too; Paul was speaking to people who had no power to change Roman law, not blessing the system.

A Lord who took the slave’s form. Paul can tell a slave not to be troubled because of who his Lord is. The Lord of glory took the form of a doulos himself (Philippians 2:7). He was sold for thirty pieces of silver, the sum the law of Moses set as compensation for a slave gored to death (Exodus 21:32; Matthew 26:15), and he died by crucifixion, the death Rome used above all for slaves and rebels. No status can put a believer beneath the notice of a Saviour who chose the lowest one.

Where Christians differ: did the Bible approve of slavery? Some say the New Testament approved of slavery because it did not demand its abolition. This commentary’s view: The New Testament did not call for violent revolution, but it planted principles that undermine slavery: all humans bear God’s image; slave and free are equal in Christ (Galatians 3:28; Colossians 3:11); masters must treat slaves justly, knowing they have a Master in heaven (Ephesians 6:9); slave-trading is condemned (1 Timothy 1:10); and here slaves are encouraged to gain freedom. Christians like William Wilberforce rightly drew on these truths to fight for abolition. The race-based chattel slavery of later centuries, built on kidnapping, was condemned by the law of Moses itself (Exodus 21:16). The New Testament’s way with this institution was not endorsement but undermining. Paul sends Onesimus, probably a runaway, back to his master with instructions to receive him no longer as a bondservant but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16). Those sentences, believed, dissolve the thing from within, and eventually did.

What about the circumstances I cannot change? For the ordinary reader the transfer is straightforward, and it applies to any circumstance you did not choose and may not be able to change: the job you are stuck in, the illness, the family situation, the years that are not going the way you planned. Paul’s counsel is neither resignation nor restlessness. Do not let it define you, and if a door opens, walk through it without guilt. Contentment is not the refusal of a better situation. It is the freedom to live well in this one while the door stays shut. Pray for the change; take lawful steps toward it; and meanwhile refuse to let it tell you who you are.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the second sentence can also be read “make use of your present condition instead.” Slaves could sometimes buy or be granted their freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: For he who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord. Likewise he who was free when called is a bondservant of Christ. You were bought with a price; do not become bondservants of men. So, brothers, in whatever condition each was called, there let him remain with God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A freedman of the Lord. A freedman is a freed slave. A Roman freedman still owed duties to the patron who had freed him, and bore his name; here the patron is the Lord. The slave who becomes a Christian is freed from sin, guilt and death. He owns nothing, he may be sold next month, and he is, in the only sense that finally matters, a free man, with the freedom Jesus promised when he said that those the Son sets free are free indeed (John 8:36).

A bondservant of Christ. The free person who becomes a Christian is now Christ’s slave. His word now settles what you do with your time, your money and your body, and his approval is the only one you finally need (2 Corinthians 5:15). Both halves are conversions of status, in opposite directions: each man had received what the other had, and there was nothing left to rank.

You were bought with a price. Paul used the phrase a chapter earlier of the body (6:20); here he uses it of the whole self. Christ’s purchase is the slave market’s transaction and utterly unlike it. The price was not silver but himself: the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). He bought slaves in order to free them, and free men in order to make them his, and the price was so great that no other owner can ever have a claim.

Do not become bondservants of men. Taken literally, it warns against selling yourself into slavery, a common way of escaping debt; and more deeply, do not let human opinions or powers control you spiritually. A slave may belong to a master in Corinth and be, in his soul, a free man who serves Christ. A free citizen may answer legally to nobody and be entirely enslaved: to opinion, to advancement, to the fear of what people will think.

The fear of man. Few readers are legally owned, and many are servile about something. The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (Proverbs 29:25). It is the settled habit of arranging your life around other people’s approval: softening a conviction because of who is listening, taking on more than you should because you cannot bear to disappoint, measuring yourself daily by an audience you did not choose. Paul forbids it on the ground of ownership rather than self-respect: you are not for sale, because you have already been bought. If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ (Galatians 1:10).

There let him remain with God. The third statement of the principle (vv. 17, 20, 24). “With God”: in his presence, before him, with him. A slave with God is better placed than an emperor without him.

How do I serve Christ at work if my boss is the one I answer to? You do the work your employer gives you, honestly and well, but you do it for a different Master. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward (Colossians 3:23–24). In practice that means working when no one is checking, refusing to lie or cut corners even when it is expected, treating colleagues with respect, and accepting unfair treatment without bitterness while pursuing any just remedy available. If your employer requires you to sin, you must refuse, because he did not pay for you. Christ did.

For worship. The One who paid for us is the strangest of owners. He bought us with his own blood, and then he calls us not servants but friends (John 15:15). He has promised that when he returns he will dress himself for service, have his servants recline at table, and come and serve them (Luke 12:37). There is no freedom like belonging to him, and no slavery like belonging to anyone else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–40 — The Unmarried, the Betrothed, and the Widows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To the unmarried and engaged Paul gives counsel, not command. Because of the present distress and the shortness of the time, staying single has real advantages for undivided devotion to the Lord; but whoever marries does not sin. A widow may remarry, only in the Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
Eschatological Relativisation and Christian Freedom

Paul’s “as though” clauses are a great relief to a believer under pressure. No good and no loss in this age has the last word. Marriage, mourning, rejoicing, buying: all are real; none are final. The person who holds them that way is not less engaged with life but more free in it, because their ultimate security is not invested in any of them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s counsel to the betrothed (“do not seek a wife”, v. 27) and to the widow (“she is happier if she remains as she is”, v. 40) was given “in view of the present distress”, the pressures of the short time between Christ’s comings. Now: The time is no less short for us. The counsel to hold earthly goods and relationships lightly, in undivided devotion to the Lord, still applies.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the betrothed, I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy. I think that in view of the present distress it is good for a person to remain as he is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning the betrothed. The marker again, and a new question from their letter. “Betrothed” is literally virgins: unmarried young women, probably those engaged to be married, and by extension the young unmarried generally.

In the flow. Verses 8–9 spoke to the unmarried and the widows in general; now Paul answers a question about the young who have never married, especially engaged couples. He applies the rule of verses 17–24 and adds reasons of its own, and through it all runs one refrain: whoever marries does not sin (vv. 28, 36).

I have no command from the Lord. Jesus had not spoken directly on this, so Paul gives his considered judgement. He is as careful here as over mixed marriages (v. 12). There is a difference between what God has clearly commanded and the wise application of Christian principle to a situation Scripture does not directly address. A teacher who blurs the two, presenting his own judgment with the authority of a command, is doing something Paul refuses to do even when he is confident.

By the Lord’s mercy trustworthy. Paul’s trustworthiness is not a quality he claims for himself. It is mercy received from the Lord Jesus, who met him on the Damascus road while he was hunting Christians. He had been a blasphemer and persecutor, but he received mercy (1 Timothy 1:13–16), and stewards must be found faithful (4:2), the same Greek word. The steward is trustworthy because the Master was merciful. So when Paul gives his judgment here, the reader hears the counsel of a man Christ remade, and that is why it carries weight (v. 40).

The present distress. The word means necessity, pressure, and may refer to famine, persecution or the general trouble of the last days. There is evidence of grain shortages in Corinth around this time, and hostility toward the young church was real. We cannot be certain which he meant, and his reasoning holds under any of them. He is not laying down a timeless rule that Christians should not marry. He is giving situational counsel in view of a particular pressure.

How do I decide something Scripture does not settle? There is a quiet permission in this paragraph for anyone facing such a decision. A great many of the choices that actually shape a life, whom to marry, whether to marry, which work, where to live, when to move, are not commanded either way. Christians often want them to be, and go looking for a verse or a sign that will remove the responsibility of choosing. Paul’s example is more freeing than that. He weighs the circumstances, applies the principles, reaches a judgment, states it as a judgment, and leaves the other person free. So: rule out what Scripture forbids; ask what love and wisdom commend; seek counsel from mature believers; consider the circumstances honestly; pray; and then decide, trusting that God guides those who seek him even when no voice speaks (Proverbs 3:5–6; Romans 14:5). That is what wisdom looks like when there is no command, and Christian maturity is largely made of it, since most of life is lived in exactly that territory.
verseByVerse.note: The “present distress” may refer to famine, persecution or the pressures of the last days.

verseByVerse.quote: Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if a betrothed woman marries, she has not sinned. Yet those who marry will have worldly troubles, and I would spare you that.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. If you are married, or engaged, do not try to get out; and if you are free from a wife, do not rush to find one, given the present distress. The principle of verse 17 applied once more: do not make a project of changing your situation.

You have not sinned. Then, immediately and emphatically, the qualification: marriage is not sin. He says it twice, once for each party. A man who has spent much of the chapter commending singleness is anxious that nobody should conclude that marrying is a failure, and he will not have his preference turned into a burden on anyone’s conscience. That instinct is rare: a strong personal conviction, argued for, and then repeatedly protected from becoming a rule for those who will decide differently.

Worldly troubles. Literally, trouble in the flesh, the word used of persecution and hardship: the pressures and anxieties of married and family life, especially in hard times. Paul is honest in a way that teaching about marriage sometimes is not, when it stops at the wedding. Marriage doubles the number of people whose suffering you feel as your own, and exposes you to losses you would not otherwise have known. And I would spare you that is affection, not disparagement: a pastor who has watched people carry things, wishing they did not have to.

Does free from a wife include the divorced? Some read it that way, but the paragraph is about the betrothed and the unmarried (v. 25), so Paul is most likely thinking of those who have not yet married or have been widowed. Remarriage after divorce is settled not by this verse but by verses 10–15 and Matthew 19:9, on the grounds of adultery or desertion. And persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion; the elders should help judge such a case.

Honesty is a kindness. To the single reader, this honesty removes the fantasy that marriage is where the difficulty ends, a fantasy that makes singleness heavier and marriages more disappointing than they need to be. To the married reader who is in the middle of the trouble, the illness, the strain, the years of difficulty with someone you have promised not to walk away from, it says that you have not discovered a defect in your marriage. Paul told you this would be part of it, in writing, in advance.

The Bridegroom who chose the trouble. Paul would spare his readers trouble in the flesh. But the gospel tells of a Bridegroom who did not spare himself. The Son of God took our flesh knowing exactly what trouble it would bring, and took to himself a bride whose troubles were her sins. He loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25), bearing her griefs and carrying her sorrows to the cross (Isaiah 53:4). Every married person who finds that loving a spouse means feeling another’s suffering as one’s own has been given a small share in what he chose freely, and without limit.

On a Tuesday. If you are thinking of marriage, talk with a married couple a decade or two ahead of you and ask them honestly what was hard, and what carried them. If you are married and in a hard season, say to your spouse this week: this is what Paul said it would be, and I am still here.

verseByVerse.quote: This is what I mean, brothers: the appointed time has grown very short. From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none, and those who mourn as though they were not mourning, and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, and those who buy as though they had no goods, and those who deal with the world as though they had no dealings with it. For the present form of this world is passing away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The appointed time has grown very short. “Appointed time” is the decisive season rather than clock time: the season between Christ’s first and second comings. “Grown very short” (synestalmenos) means compressed, drawn together, a verb that could be used of furling sails as a ship nears harbour.

As though they had none. Five clauses in the same startling form, which taken flatly would be monstrous. Paul cannot mean neglect your wife: he has already insisted in this chapter that spouses owe each other themselves (v. 3). He means not letting marriage become their ultimate concern. That is a mercy to marriage itself. A husband or wife asked to be your saviour, the one who finally makes life worth living, will buckle under a weight only God can carry; a spouse loved as a gift, and not worshipped as a god, is free to be simply a husband or a wife. Marriage is for this age only; in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matthew 22:30).

Mourning and rejoicing. Grief and joy are real, but not final. Paul cannot mean suppress your grief; he himself writes of sorrow upon sorrow (Philippians 2:27). The Christian mourns, but not as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13), and rejoices without clinging. Grief is included not because it is unimportant but because it, too, has a horizon.
