The thing you mourn is real and the mourning is right, but it is not the last word about the person you have lost. There will be a morning when the arrangement in which that loss was possible has passed away.

Buying and dealing with the world. Buy, but hold possessions loosely: you are a steward, not an owner. “Have no dealings” means use fully, use up. Use the world, its goods and systems, but do not be absorbed by it.

The present form of this world. “Form” is outward shape, the way things are currently arranged, like a scene in a play before the set is changed. The world as it now is will not last (1 John 2:17). What is passing is the shape, not the substance: creation itself will be set free, not discarded (Romans 8:21). Marry, grieve, celebrate, buy and work, and do not let any of it become the thing you are ultimately living for.

Why the time is short. The season was shortened by something that had already happened. Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (15:20), and the harvest the firstfruits promise is on its way. The new creation has already begun in him (2 Corinthians 5:17), so the present arrangement of the world is already giving way. That is why these things are held loosely: they belong to an age whose end was announced on the morning of the resurrection, and whose replacement is already alive in the risen Lord.

Did Paul think Christ would return in his lifetime? He did not know, and he never set a date. He taught that the day would come like a thief in the night (1 Thessalonians 5:2) and was always to be expected, and in other letters he speaks calmly of his own death (2 Corinthians 5:1–8; Philippians 1:23). The appointed time has grown very short because, since the resurrection, the church has been living in the last days, and every generation since has lived with the end in view. He also taught that certain things must happen first, such as the rebellion and the revealing of the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:1–4), so the nearness he preached was never a date. That is not a mistaken timetable. It is the posture every generation of Christians is called to: watchful, unhurried, with lamps lit.

verseByVerse.quote: I want you to be free from anxieties. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Free from anxieties. That is Paul’s stated motive for everything he has been saying about singleness, and it should govern how the rest is heard. He is not trying to recruit ascetics; he is trying to spare people worry.

The things of the Lord. Here “anxious” is used positively: concerned for, devoted to. The single person can give full attention to the Lord’s work. The argument is refreshingly practical: it is about time and attention, not about which state is holier.

How to please his wife. Worldly things here are not sinful things, but the things of ordinary life: providing, caring, household concerns, the legitimate, time-consuming business of a shared life in this present arrangement. The point is not that marriage is spiritually inferior, but that marriage takes attention, and attention is finite. The single Christian has one set of claims on his time; the married Christian has two, and the second is a person with her own needs, opinions, tiredness and hopes. That is not a defect in marriage. It is marriage.

Undivided devotion that cared for a mother. The Lord Jesus is the one life in which devotion never divided. He always did the things that pleased his Father (John 8:29). Yet hanging on the cross, at the very height of his obedience, he saw his mother standing there and gave her into the care of the disciple he loved (John 19:26–27). Care for family was not a rival to his devotion; it was part of it. In Christ, pleasing the Lord and caring for one’s own belong together.

To each reader. To the single reader, particularly one who did not choose it: this is Paul naming something real that you already possess, and it is not a consolation prize. You have a freedom of movement and attention that is genuinely useful to God. That does not remove the loneliness, but your situation is not merely an absence; there is something in your hands. To the married reader: the division of interests is not a failure of devotion to repent of. The attention you give your spouse is not stolen from God; it is the form your obedience takes. What Paul asks is honesty that the cost exists, rather than years of low-grade, unexamined guilt that your capacity for other things has narrowed.

Is it wrong to be anxious, then? Jesus told us not to be anxious about our life (Matthew 6:25), and Paul tells us to be anxious about nothing but to pray about everything (Philippians 4:6). Here, though, Paul uses the same word for legitimate concern: the care a man rightly has for his wife and the care a single believer has for the Lord’s work. The difference is between care carried to God and care that has replaced God. Concern for your family is right; anxiety that forgets your Father knows what you need is not. Bring the concern to him and let him carry the weight.

verseByVerse.quote: and his interests are divided. And the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman is anxious about worldly things, how to please her husband. I say this for your own benefit, not to lay any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and to secure your undivided devotion to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His interests are divided. Pulled in two directions, the Lord and his wife, and both legitimate. And the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit: devoted to God, set apart for his service, in her whole person. In a world that defined a woman almost entirely by her household, he assumes an unmarried Christian woman has her own devotion to the Lord, her own concerns and her own spiritual vocation. The married woman, likewise, is anxious about how to please her husband, and that too is legitimate.

Not to lay any restraint upon you. This sentence rescues the chapter from every misuse it has suffered. The word behind “restraint” is vivid: brochos, a noose or halter, the loop thrown over an animal to bring it under control. Everything he has said about the advantages of singleness is counsel for the reader’s benefit, not a standard by which anyone is to be measured, and certainly not a rule the church may impose.

Undivided devotion to the Lord. “Undivided devotion” means attending on someone without distraction, unlike Martha, who was distracted with much serving (Luke 10:40). This phrase is the goal of the whole chapter. Not singleness. Not marriage. Devotion.

Betrothed to one husband. Devotion to the Lord is devotion to a person. I feel a divine jealousy for you, he writes, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ, and he fears they may be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2–3). The unmarried woman of this verse is a living picture of what the whole church, married and single, is called to be: a bride waiting for her Bridegroom with an undivided heart.

The noose thrown anyway, in both directions. What Paul forbade is precisely what happened, for centuries. The chapter was read as establishing celibacy as the higher path and marriage as the concession for the weak: a two-tier Christianity with the unmarried at the top. And the same danger now runs in the opposite direction. In many churches the noose is thrown over the single. An unmarried adult is treated as a problem to be solved, quietly excluded from a church life assumed to be about families, and made to feel that his or her life has not properly started. That is a restraint Paul forbids just as firmly.

So which is better, marriage or singleness? Paul has refused that question repeatedly and in as many ways as he can find. The question is what undivided devotion looks like for the person you actually are, in the situation the Lord has assigned you. For one reader that will mean a freedom of time and movement to be spent rather than hoarded. For another it will mean loving one person faithfully for a lifetime in a way nobody outside the house will ever see. Neither is the higher path. Both are the same devotion, and the God who assigned them is not comparing.

On a Tuesday. Look at your church through the eyes of its single members this week. Are they invited into homes, trusted with leadership, asked about their work and their walk with God rather than only about whether they are seeing anyone? Fix one thing.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks that he is not behaving properly toward his betrothed, if his passions are strong, and it has to be, let him do as he wishes: let them marry—it is no sin. But whoever is firmly established in his heart, being under no necessity but having his desire under control, and has determined this in his heart, to keep her as his betrothed, he will do well. So then he who marries his betrothed does well, and he who refrains from marriage will do even better.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Toward his betrothed. These three verses are among the more obscure in the letter. The older reading takes them of a father deciding whether to give his virgin daughter in marriage; the ESV notes this possibility, and the KJV, which speaks of giving her in marriage (v. 38), leans that way. The other, which the ESV follows, takes it of a man and the woman he is engaged to, deciding whether to proceed with the marriage. The second fits the context better (v. 25) and the language of strong passions more naturally. But a reader who meets a different rendering in another Bible is not meeting an error.

Let them marry, it is no sin. Once more Paul removes the guilt from the decision before anyone can attach it.

Firmly established in his heart. The conditions are all internal, and all mark a free decision rather than a suppressed one. Firmly established: settled, not wavering. Under no necessity: not driven by pressure from anyone. Having his desire under control: genuinely able, not merely determined to try. Vows extracted from the young, imposed by an institution, or undertaken as a spiritual achievement meet none of Paul’s three conditions.

Good and better. To remain engaged but not marry, in view of the present distress, is also good. Better here is not morally better, but more advantageous in that situation. Both verbs are positive: good and better, and the better is the practical advantage he set out in verses 32–35, in the circumstances he named in verse 26.

The engagement that will end in a wedding. Every Christian engagement sits inside a larger one. God promised his people long ago that he would betroth them to himself for ever, in righteousness and justice, in steadfast love and mercy, in faithfulness (Hosea 2:19–20), and the New Testament shows that promise kept in Christ, who has a betrothed church and is coming for her (Revelation 19:7). He does not behave improperly toward his betrothed or keep her waiting without cause; the delay is patience, so that more may be gathered in (2 Peter 3:9). Human engagements may end in a wedding or in a kind farewell. His will end in a wedding, and the waiting will be forgotten in the joy.

What it does not mean. It does not mean marriage is morally inferior. Paul says marrying does well. Nor does it give a modern engaged couple a reason to drift in a long engagement with no end in view. In a world where engagement is not a legal bond, the principle is simply this: decide prayerfully, keep yourselves pure, and do not keep each other waiting without cause.

We are engaged, but one of us is now unsure. What should we do? Take it seriously and slowly, and speak honestly. An engagement is a serious promise, and it should not be broken lightly or by a sudden mood. But it is not yet a marriage, and it is far better to end an engagement than to enter a marriage one of you cannot enter in good faith. Pray together and separately; talk with a pastor or a wise married couple who know you both; ask whether the doubt is about this person, about marriage itself, or about fear. If you end it, end it kindly, take responsibility, and do not leave the other in uncertainty. If you go on, go on gladly, as Paul says: it is no sin.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “betrothed” is literally “virgin,” and that the passage can also be read of a father deciding whether to give his daughter in marriage.

verseByVerse.quote: A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bound as long as he lives. Marriage is lifelong (Romans 7:2). The verb is a different one from the word used of the deserted believer in verse 15, who is not enslaved.

Free to be married. Death ends the marriage bond. The widow is free, and Paul says so without qualification or any suggestion that remarriage would be a lesser choice. Widows have often been made to feel that remarrying would betray the person they buried. Scripture attaches no such shame to it. Remarriage after a spouse’s death is honourable, and Paul elsewhere positively counsels younger widows to marry (1 Timothy 5:14).

Free to belong to another. Paul uses this same law in Romans to explain the gospel. A wife is bound to her husband while he lives, but if he dies she is free to marry another; likewise, he says, you have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God (Romans 7:2–4). Joined to Christ by faith, the believer shares in his death, so the law that once condemned him has no more claim on him. Every believer has passed through a death into a new marriage. And this one can never end the way verse 39 says every earthly marriage ends, because the Husband has already died and risen, and death no longer has dominion over him (Romans 6:9).

Only in the Lord. “Only in the Lord” means to a fellow believer. The freedom is real and it has one boundary: she may marry whom she wishes, provided he belongs to Christ. A Christian may not marry an unbeliever (2 Corinthians 6:14). This applies to all believers, not only widows. It is one of the few places in the chapter where Paul gives a command rather than a judgment, and it stands out against the freedom around it: whom you marry, when, and whether, are all left open; this one boundary is drawn.

Why only in the Lord? The reason is not snobbery about outsiders, which would sit very oddly in a letter that has just told believers to stay married to unbelievers, and will tell them to accept dinner invitations from pagans (10:27). The reason is what marriage is. If it is a union of two whole persons at every level, then a marriage in which the deepest thing about one of them is not shared by the other is divided at the root: not impossible, not without love, but permanently unable to be what marriage is for. Put it concretely, because this is one of the decisions on which young Christians most often reason badly. It means the person you marry will be the one you cannot pray with about your child’s illness. It means every Sunday is negotiated. It means the thing that matters most to you is a subject you learn to leave alone, and that leaving it alone becomes a habit, and habits of that kind do not stay confined to Sundays.

Two different situations. If you are already married to an unbeliever, whether you married before conversion or after, Paul’s instruction is emphatically to stay, and God’s blessing is on that household (v. 14). What he addresses here is a decision still to be made. And if you married an unbeliever in disobedience, you are still married; repent of the disobedience, not of the marriage, and live in it faithfully under verses 12–16.

What about dating? Since dating is the road to marriage, a Christian should not begin a romantic relationship with someone Paul’s rule would forbid him or her to marry. The relationship is the first step, and a heart once given does not easily turn back. Someone already in such a relationship should be honest that it cannot go where it is heading, and end it kindly. And the rule is not satisfied by a partner who merely calls himself a Christian. Only in the Lord means someone whose life shows that he belongs to Christ: who loves the Lord, is part of a church, and wants to grow. Do not marry someone in the hope that he will become a believer afterwards.

On a Tuesday. If you are single and hoping to marry, tell a friend you will marry only in the Lord, and ask them to hold you to it when your heart is tempted otherwise. If you know a widow or widower, do not assume what they should do; ask how they are, and support whichever path they take in the Lord.
verseByVerse.note: “Only in the Lord” means to a fellow believer.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She is happier. Paul gives his opinion one last time, and one last time he labels it as an opinion. “Happier” is the word behind the Beatitudes, blessed. Not holier, not more useful, not more pleasing to God: more blessed, given the present distress (v. 26) and the undivided devotion singleness allows (v. 35).

I too have the Spirit of God. A touch of irony toward the great claimants of the Spirit. But the sentence does real work. Paul has carefully distinguished the Lord’s command from his own judgment (vv. 10, 12, 25, 40), and a reader might conclude that the judgment parts are his private view, take it or leave it. This clause forbids that. Even in what he calls his opinion, he is writing inspired Scripture.

Is everything in this chapter binding on me, then? It is all God’s word, but not all of it is a command, and Paul has told you which is which. Where he speaks as the Lord’s command, as on divorce (vv. 10–11) and marrying only in the Lord (v. 39), you must obey. Where he gives his judgment, as on whether to marry or stay single in the present distress, you receive it as inspired, wise counsel that God wants you to weigh seriously, and you remain free to decide either way without sin, because he says so (vv. 28, 36, 38). Both kinds of word are Scripture; that is exactly why you may trust both the commands and the freedoms.

Looking back over the chapter. This chapter has told a church full of people at every stage of life, married, single, widowed, divorced, deserted, enslaved, engaged, married to unbelievers, that not one of them is in the wrong place. And every one of those words rests on Christ. The body is honoured because he redeemed it. The slave is free and the free man is a slave because both were bought with a price (v. 23). The time is short because he is risen and coming. Assigned by him, called by him: not left over, not settled for. In chapters 8–10 Paul will again refuse to bind consciences where God has not spoken, and will ask the free to give up their rights for others (8:9–13): the same freedom, governed by the same love.

For worship. The circumstances you are in tonight, the marriage that is hard work, the house that is quiet, the person you are still waiting for, the person you have buried, were distributed by someone who has never yet given anybody the wrong life. The Lord of this chapter had nowhere to lay his head, was deserted by everyone he loved, and died unmarried and childless, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief (Isaiah 53:3). He took that portion to give us his: the Spirit who guarantees our inheritance, a room in his Father’s house (John 14:2), and a share in the joy of the Bridegroom who will present his whole church to himself in splendour.

The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord.<sup>33</sup>But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife,<sup>34</sup>and his interests are divided. And the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman is anxious about worldly things, how to please her husband.<sup>35</sup>I say this for your own benefit, not to lay any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and to secure your undivided devotion to the Lord.<sup>36</sup>If anyone thinks that he is not behaving properly toward his betrothed, if his passions are strong, and it has to be, let him do as he wishes: let them marry—it is no sin.<sup>37</sup>But whoever is firmly established in his heart, being under no necessity but having his desire under control, and has determined this in his heart, to keep her as his betrothed, he will do well.<sup>38</sup>So then he who marries his betrothed does well, and he who refrains from marriage will do even better.<sup>39</sup>A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord.<sup>40</sup>Yet in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.

8.title: Knowledge, Idols, and Love for the Weak
8.overview:
The next question from the Corinthians’ letter is about food offered to idols. In a Greek or Roman city, most meat came from animals sacrificed at temples: part was burned for the god, part went to the priests, and much of the rest was eaten at banquets in the temple dining rooms or sold in the meat market (the macellum, whose inscription has been found in Corinth). Temples were also the restaurants and party venues of the city. For a Christian, refusing every such meal could mean cutting yourself off from trade guilds, family celebrations and civic life.

Some Corinthian believers, proud of their knowledge, argued that idols are nothing and there is only one God, so they could eat anywhere. Paul agrees with their theology, and gives one of the most important statements of Christian belief: one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ. But knowledge without love puffs people up. Not every believer has that confidence; some, long used to idols, still feel that eating such food is worship, and if they follow the example of the “strong” against their conscience, they are damaged. A believer for whom Christ died must not be ruined by another’s freedom. So Paul would rather never eat meat again than cause a brother to fall. (Chapter 10 will add that actually taking part in idol feasts is forbidden.)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Knowledge Puffs Up, Love Builds Up
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul sets down the rule for handling knowledge, love builds up, and then agrees with the strong party’s theology, confessing one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Christological Shema and the One Lordship

In vv. 5–6 Paul takes Israel’s confession of the one God (Deuteronomy 6:4) and shares its words between the Father, the one God from whom are all things, and Jesus Christ, the one Lord through whom are all things. Both are given the work of creation, which belongs to God alone. This is not two gods, nor a lesser, created Son; it is the Shema opened to include the Son within the one God of Israel, which is what the Council of Nicaea later defended.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The “strong” at Corinth were the theologically confident, who knew the idol was nothing. Their knowledge was real, and so was their pride. Now: Those who love the doctrines of grace can make correctness a platform for contempt. Paul’s question still applies: are you known by God? (v. 3).

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning food offered to idols: we know that “all of us possess knowledge.” This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 8–10 answers another question from the Corinthians’ letter: may Christians eat food that has been offered to idols? Paul agrees with the theology of the strong, and in doing so writes one of the highest confessions of Christ in the New Testament (v. 6). But knowledge puffs up; love builds up (v. 1), and a brother for whom Christ died must not be ruined by another’s freedom (v. 11).

The setting. Trade guild dinners, birthday parties and civic festivals were often held in temple dining rooms, because civic life, trade, family celebration and religion were not separate departments. A Christian who refused all such meals could lose business, friends and social standing. So the question was live, and it divided the church.

Now concerning food offered to idols. Another question from their letter. The word eidōlothyta, idol-sacrifices, has a sneer built into it; pagans called the same food sacred offering. Paul opens not by answering the question but by quoting the confident party, probably another Corinthian slogan: we all possess knowledge. They were not wrong about the facts.

Puffs up, builds up. The key principle of chapters 8–10. Physioō is the inflation word Paul has used repeatedly of this church (4:6, 18–19; 5:2): something swollen with air, like a balloon, larger than its substance justifies. Oikodomeō is the building word from chapter 3: laying one course on another, like a house, until something stands. Both make a thing bigger. Only one makes it stronger. Knowledge held without love becomes pride.

Does not yet know as he ought. The very confidence that you have understood a matter is itself the evidence that you have not understood it as you should, because knowing as one ought includes knowing what knowledge is for. True knowledge of God humbles and produces love. If I understand all mysteries and all knowledge, but have not love, I am nothing (13:2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean knowledge is bad, or that Christians should not study theology; Paul is about to teach some of the deepest theology in the letter. The problem is never too much truth; it is truth held in a closed fist.

A warning for readers of theology. There is a version of the Christian life that consists almost entirely of acquiring correct positions, on grace, on election, on baptism, and then holding them against people who have not yet arrived. Underneath, the pull is often not love of the truth but love of being the one who is right, and that is the old trust in oneself, now dressed in doctrine: I am safe, and better than others, because I understand. The Reformed tradition is not exempt; if anything it is exposed, because its doctrines are genuinely clarifying and the clarity is genuinely enjoyable. Paul’s verdict on the man who uses them to look down on others is not that his doctrine is wrong. It is that he does not yet know as he ought.

So should I stop arguing for what I believe is true? No. Paul argues hard throughout this letter, and truth matters enough to contend for (Jude 3). The question is not whether you speak but why and how. Speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15), aiming at the other person’s good rather than at winning; listen before you correct; distinguish the doctrines on which the gospel stands from the ones on which faithful Christians differ; and be willing to lose an argument rather than a brother. If you notice that you enjoy someone else being wrong, stop and pray before you say anything more.

On a Tuesday. Take the doctrinal position you hold most firmly and most enjoy holding, and ask what it has built: not what it has settled in your own mind, but who has been strengthened by your holding it. If nobody comes to mind, the thing may still be true, and it has been inflating rather than building. Bring that to the Lord who knew everything and spent it all on building his people; he gives the love that knowledge lacks (Romans 5:5).

For worship. All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ (Colossians 2:3). Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, he rose from supper, took a towel and washed his disciples’ feet (John 13:3–5). He knew that Peter would deny him before Peter knew it, and he washed Peter’s feet too. The knowledge of God he gives is a knowledge that kneels.
verseByVerse.note: Much of the meat sold in the market had first been offered in a pagan temple; temples also had dining rooms used for banquets and celebrations. The quoted phrases are probably Corinthian slogans.

verseByVerse.quote: But if anyone loves God, he is known by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is known by God. The natural completion would be: if anyone loves God, he knows God. Instead the direction reverses: not your knowing, but God’s. Paul makes the same turn to the Galatians, correcting himself mid-sentence: now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God (Galatians 4:9). The deepest reality is not our knowledge of God but God’s knowledge of us: his loving, choosing, personal knowledge (2 Timothy 2:19; Romans 8:29). We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

The full Hebrew weight. “Known” here is the language of relationship, of choosing, of intimate acquaintance: before I formed you in the womb I knew you (Jeremiah 1:5); you only have I known of all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2). And it puts the weight in the right place. Knowledge that puffs up is knowledge of which I am the subject: my grasp, my position, my achievement. The moment the sentence turns round, the whole basis of that inflation is removed.

I know my own. Jesus takes this divine knowing onto his own lips. I am the good shepherd, he says; I know my own and my own know me, and I lay down my life for the sheep (John 10:14–15). He calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3). And he speaks its terrible opposite to people rich in religious knowledge and activity, who had prophesied and done mighty works in his name: I never knew you (Matthew 7:22–23). So to be known by God is, concretely, to be known by Christ: to be one of the sheep whose name he says, whose sins he carried, for whom he gave his life.

I feel I understand so little. Does God know me? This verse was written for you. Some Christians live with a low, persistent anxiety about their grasp of God. They read, and forget what they read; their theology feels thin next to other people’s; and underneath is the suspicion that their standing with God is proportional to how well they have got hold of him, and that their hold is not very good. Paul takes the whole question away. The security of your relationship with God has never rested on the firmness of your grip. It rests on his. You are known, and you were known before you knew anything, and nothing about the quality of your understanding alters it. The one mark Paul looks for is not knowledge at all: if anyone loves God. Do you love him, however feebly? Then he knows you.

And how do I know whether I love God? Not chiefly by the strength of your feelings on a given day. Love for God shows itself in wanting him, coming back to him when you have strayed, grieving over sin because it offends him, delighting in his word even when you understand little of it, loving his people, and wanting to obey: if you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15). Peter, after failing badly, could only say, Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you (John 21:17). That is enough. And even weak love is a sign of something stronger beneath it: his love for you came first.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that “an idol has no real existence,” and that “there is no God but one.” For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords”—
verseByVerse.commentary:
An idol has no real existence. Paul agrees with the strong party without reservation, probably quoting another of their slogans. The wooden thing in the temple is not a god. There is nobody behind the statue, and the meat that passed in front of it has not been altered in any way (Isaiah 44:9–20; Psalm 115:4–8).

In the flow. Verse 4 picks up the question verse 1 left. In verses 4–6 Paul grants everything the strong believe about God; from verse 7 he shows that being right about God does not settle how to treat a brother. The same pattern runs through chapters 8–10 and ends in the summary: do all to the glory of God, and give no offence (10:31–32).

No God but one. The confession of Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4), the bedrock of Israel’s faith and now of the church’s. And yet there are so-called gods in heaven and on earth. In heaven, Zeus, Apollo; on earth, deified emperors: real as objects of worship.

Many gods and many lords. In one sense they exist: people worship them, and they hold real power over people’s lives. “Lords” was a title for mystery-religion deities like Serapis, and for the emperor. Zeus had no existence; the worship of Zeus was one of the most powerful forces in that society.

The one true image. Every idol is an attempt to give God a face: something carved, visible and near, that a worshipper can stand in front of. The second commandment forbade Israel to make one (Exodus 20:4), not because God cannot be known but because nothing a carpenter carves could show him. And then God gave his own image. Christ is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15); whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9). What every temple in Corinth was groping after, the Father has given in his Son. The idol is nothing pretending to be God. Jesus is God, come near.

Nothing, or demons? A careful reader will notice a tension here, and it should not be smoothed over. Two chapters later Paul will say something that sounds like the opposite: what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God, and he does not want the Corinthians to be participants with demons (10:20). So which is it? Both, and the two statements answer different questions. In what it is, the idol is nothing: no deity corresponds to it, and the food is not contaminated. But spiritually, idolatry is not therefore harmless, because a real enemy is happy to occupy the space a false god vacates. The image is empty; the worship is not. That is why Paul can say in chapter 8 that the meat is neutral and in chapter 10 that attending the temple feast is participation in something evil. It was never the meat.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that other religions are harmless paths to the same God. There is one God, and the gods of the nations are not him.

How idolatry works now. That distinction is exactly how idolatry works today. Few of us are tempted by a statue. But the things we organise our lives around, money, career, a child’s success, the good opinion of others, a political cause, are in themselves nothing of the kind we treat them as, and the devotion given to them is real and does real damage. An idol is usually a good thing that has been asked to do a job only God can do. The money does not steady you. The career does not justify you. The child cannot bear the weight of being your reason for living.

How can I tell if something has become an idol? Ask what you cannot imagine being content without; what you most fear losing; what you run to for comfort when you are low; where your money and spare thoughts go without effort; and what makes you angriest when it is threatened. A good thing has become an idol when losing it would feel like losing your life, or when you would disobey God to keep it. The remedy is not usually to throw the good thing away, but to put it back in its place under God, to thank him for it, and to find in him what you were asking it to give.

Isaiah’s carpenter. Scripture’s mockery of idols is pastoral. Isaiah’s carpenter burns half a tree to roast his dinner and bows down to the other half, asking it to save him (Isaiah 44:14–17). The comedy is compassion: a man is asking firewood to do what only God can do. Those who make them become like them (Psalm 115:8).

Who are we to call other people’s gods nothing? We would have no right to, if Christians had worked it out for themselves and were boasting of their own insight. But the claim is not that we are cleverer than the worshippers of Corinth. It is that the one true God has made himself known, in his word and finally in his Son, to people who were themselves idolaters until he found them (1 Thessalonians 1:9). Humility is not saying that every claim is equally true; it is receiving the truth as a gift we did not deserve. And the same verse that denies the idols denies our pride too, because the Christian has nothing he did not receive (4:7).

parallels.desc: the LORD our God, the LORD is one

verseByVerse.quote: yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet for us there is one God, the Father. Its force is invisible unless you know what Paul is quoting.

From whom are all things and for whom we exist. The Father is the source of all creation, and its goal. We exist for him: from him and through him and to him are all things (Romans 11:36).

And one Lord, Jesus Christ. Paul expands Israel’s confession “the LORD is one” to include Jesus. Devout Jews recited the Shema morning and evening (Deuteronomy 6:4), and were ready to die rather than compromise it. In the Greek Bible it contains two crucial words: theos, God, and kyrios, Lord, the standard rendering of the divine name. It stands for God’s own personal name (Exodus 3:14–15). Paul takes them and applies God to the Father and Lord to Jesus. He has not added a second deity; he has just insisted that there is no God but one. He has put Jesus inside the confession, distributing its own words between Father and Son. He thought the divine name belonged to Jesus so naturally that he can say it in passing, in a discussion about meat.

Through whom. Of the Father: from whom and for whom, the source and the goal. Of Christ: through whom, the agent of creation and of our new existence. All things were made through him (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2). And through him we exist as new creatures, redeemed. In the Old Testament only God creates, and creation is here assigned to Jesus without qualification.

Where Christians differ: the deity of Christ. Groups such as Jehovah’s Witnesses argue that this verse distinguishes Jesus from the one God, making him a lesser being. This commentary’s view: Paul is not separating Jesus from the one God of Israel but including him within it. He divides the words of the Shema between the Father and the Son, and gives the Son the divine work of creation. This is one of the earliest Christian confessions of the Trinity in seed form. The Father and the Son are distinct persons, but one God, with the Holy Spirit (the Nicene Creed; the Westminster Confession 2.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 2.3).

Why does this belong in an argument about meat? Paul is not making a doctrinal excursion. The strong party’s freedom rests on this: if all things are from the Father and through the Son, then a piece of meat cannot belong to anybody else. It was made by Christ. Passing it in front of a carved image does not transfer the title. The earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof (Psalm 24:1; 10:26). And that is a more cheerful doctrine of creation than many Christians actually hold. There is a strain of piety that treats the physical world as spiritually suspect, food, pleasure, beauty, the body, as though holiness consisted in wariness. Paul’s answer is that every good thing came through Christ and belongs to him, and that the enemy has never made anything and cannot own what he did not make.

How do I explain the Trinity simply to a friend? Say what Scripture says, without pretending to explain everything. There is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4). The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and they are not three gods but one God in three persons, who speak to one another and love one another (Matthew 3:16–17; 28:19). This verse shows it in miniature: Israel’s one God, confessed now as Father and Lord Jesus. Avoid analogies like water, ice and steam, which suggest one person in three modes. It is a mystery, not a contradiction, and it is precisely what makes the gospel possible: the Father sent the Son, the Son gave himself, and the Spirit brings us to both.

On a Tuesday. Take one ordinary good thing today, a meal, a walk, the face of someone you love, and say over it: this came from the Father, through the Son, and it is for him.
verseByVerse.note: Paul expands Israel’s confession “the LORD is one” to include Jesus Christ as the one Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — The Weak Brother and the Limits of Freedom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Being right about God does not settle how to treat a brother. Some believers’ consciences have not caught up with the truth, and the strong must not use their freedom to lead such a brother, one for whom Christ died, into sin. Paul’s own resolve closes the chapter.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Weak Brother and the Limits of Christian Freedom

The “weak brother” is not a permanent rank but a pastoral description of someone whose conscience has not yet caught up with the freedom the gospel gives. The strong keep their freedom but must think about its effect on others: Christ, “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9), is the pattern for laying down a genuine freedom out of love for the weak.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The question was how the mature should use their freedom without damaging the less free. Now: The applications range from alcohol where an alcoholic is in the room to entertainment and worship styles with real associations for some. The principle is constant: love for the weak sibling takes precedence over the exercise of genuine freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: However, not all possess this knowledge. But some, through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. Food will not commend us to God. We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not all possess this knowledge. In theory, all believers know there is one God, but not all have absorbed it deeply enough to feel free. Correct theology is not evenly distributed, and the strong must reckon with that.

Former association with idols. The word means habit, being used to something. These are converts out of paganism, and not long out. For most of their lives that meat had been part of a religious act. Their minds now accept that the idol is nothing. Their instincts have not caught up, and instincts formed over a lifetime do not dissolve because a doctrine has been explained. When they eat, something in them registers the act as betrayal.

Weak and defiled. Weak means not strong enough to be free; defiled means stained. If they eat against their conscience, they feel guilty, and in fact they sin, because they act against what they believe is God’s will: whatever does not proceed from faith is sin (Romans 14:23).

The doctrine of conscience. The conscience is not infallible. It judges our actions against the standard we actually hold, and that standard can be over-scrupulous or simply mistaken, as it is here, since the food is harmless. And yet a conscience that is wrong must still not be violated. The man who eats while believing it wrong is defiled, not by the food but because he has trained himself to act against his own conviction, and that lesson does not stay confined to meat. So a mistaken conscience is not to be overridden but instructed, slowly, by Scripture, until conviction and truth line up; until then it is to be respected even in its error.

Food will not commend us to God. Probably another slogan of the strong, which Paul accepts. Eating is spiritually neutral, so the strong lose nothing by giving it up, and the whole argument that follows swings on that point.

What does commend us to God. If food cannot bring anyone nearer to God, something else must, and the whole New Testament names it. The verb means to present before God, and Paul uses it elsewhere of Christ’s work: he has reconciled you in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless before him (Colossians 1:22). Mark tells us that Jesus himself declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and he could do so because the barrier between us and God was never on the plate. It was our sin, and he took it away. So neither eating nor abstaining moves a believer one inch nearer the Father. We have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Ephesians 2:13), and nothing on any table can add to it.

Am I the weak one or the strong one? Most of us are both, in different matters. You may be free about a glass of wine and troubled about Sunday shopping, or the other way round. On any given question, the strong believer is the one who rightly understands that Scripture leaves it free; the weak believer is the one whose conscience still forbids what God allows. Neither is a permanent rank. The strong must not despise; the weak must not judge (Romans 14:3). Both must grow: the weak in understanding, the strong in love.

Where it applies today. There are Christians who cannot do things that other Christians do freely, a drink, a film, a Sunday activity, a form of music, not because Scripture forbids it but because their history makes it impossible for them. The former alcoholic, the convert from a religion where certain foods were sacred, the believer who came out of the occult and cannot bear certain images: these are today’s weak brothers. The mature response is neither to mock the scruple nor to pretend it is a command of God, but to recognise that a real person is carrying a real formation, and to be gentle with it.

For worship. The Lord is gentle with consciences. A bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench (Isaiah 42:3). He does not drag his weak children forward faster than they can walk; he carries the lambs in his arms and gently leads those that are with young (Isaiah 40:11). And he cleansed his people’s consciences with his own blood so that they could serve the living God without fear (Hebrews 9:14).

verseByVerse.quote: But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak. For if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols?
verseByVerse.commentary:
This right of yours. “Right” means authority, liberty, a genuine entitlement, and Paul concedes it is theirs. What he questions is not whether they may, but what happens when they do. Nobody sets out to trip anyone: the strong Corinthian is simply exercising a liberty in front of his brother without thinking about the effect.

Eating in an idol’s temple. The strong were not only eating idol meat at home but attending meals in temple dining rooms; archaeologists have found such rooms at the temple of Asclepius in Corinth. Not the marketplace or a private dinner, both of which Paul will permit (10:25–27), but the most public and most religiously loaded venue available. The strong believer sits there, convinced the god is nothing, enjoying his freedom and quite possibly enjoying the demonstration of it. And the weak brother walks past and sees him.

Will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols? “Encouraged” is literally built up, the same word as love builds up (v. 1), now used with bitter irony. The strong think they are building up the weak by showing freedom, but they are building them up to sin. The weak man is indeed built up: emboldened to do a thing his conscience still condemns, on the strength of another Christian’s example. He has been constructed into a wall that will fall on him.

How influence actually works. The damage is not done by argument. The weak brother simply watched somebody he respected doing it, concluded it must be all right, and did it against his own conviction. That means every Christian is teaching all the time, whether or not they intend to. The younger believer in your church is not principally learning from what you say about holiness. He is learning from what he watches you do with your evenings, your money, your speech when you are annoyed, and your freedom.

The only stumbling block allowed. The gospel has an offence of its own: Christ crucified is a stumbling block to Jews (1:23). That stumbling block is God’s; no Christian may remove it by softening the cross. But no Christian may add another beside it. Jesus said that whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in him to sin would be better drowned in the sea (Matthew 18:6). He guards the weakest believers fiercely. The strong man has put a second stone in the road, his own, and the God who placed the first will not have his little ones tripped by the second.

What it does not mean. It does not mean eating in a temple is fine as long as no weak brother sees. In chapter 10 Paul will say that eating at temple feasts is in fact participating with demons (10:20–21). He is answering the strong on their own ground first, and will go further later.

How do I know whether my freedom will trip someone? It cannot be answered in the abstract, which is why Paul gives no list. The same action is fine in one setting and destructive in another, and the only way to tell is to know the people you are among. Love here requires attention. Ask who is present, what their history is, how young they are in the faith, and whether they are likely to copy you against their own conscience. When you do not know, you can ask them gently. And when you are unsure, it is rarely a loss to hold back. The strong Corinthian’s failure was not chiefly theological. He had not looked round the room.

verseByVerse.quote: And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died. Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This weak person is destroyed. “Destroyed” is the ruin word, the one used of perishing. Paul is not describing embarrassment but a man being wrecked, as the habit of overriding conviction spreads to matters where the conviction was right. That is how people are destroyed: not usually by one decision, but by a series of small permissions. The very knowledge the strong were proud of becomes the weapon that ruins him.

The brother for whom Christ died. The supreme reason, and the phrase that ends the argument. On one side, a man’s liberty to eat a particular piece of meat: genuine, defensible, correct. On the other, a person so valuable that the Son of God went to a cross for him. The weak brother’s whole hope hangs on that cross (1 Peter 2:24), exactly as the strong man’s does. Will you not give up a meal for him? The strong Corinthian was thinking about a principle, and he was right about the principle. He was not thinking about a person, and the person had a price attached that made the principle look very small.

Wounding their conscience. The word means striking, beating. To push a weak conscience is to beat it.

You sin against Christ. The offence does not stop at the brother. Christ is so united to his people that sin against them is sin against him (Matthew 25:40, 45; Acts 9:4). Believers are limbs of his body (6:15). The risen Christ said the same to Saul of Tarsus: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? The man who wrote this verse had been on the wrong side of that sentence. The strong man thought he was handling a brother’s scruple; he was handling the holy Lord of the church, whose eyes are like a flame of fire (Revelation 1:14).

Where Christians differ: can a brother for whom Christ died perish? Many sincere Christians, Arminians especially (who hold that Christ died equally for every person and that a true believer can finally fall away), take this verse as proof that Christ died for some who will finally be lost. This commentary’s view: Paul describes the real tendency of the strong person’s action: it would lead the brother to ruin. The warning is real. But Scripture also teaches that Christ’s death infallibly saves those for whom he died (Romans 8:32–34; John 10:15, 28), and God uses warnings like this one as means to keep his people. The point is that the strong should treat every brother as someone precious enough for Christ to die for. This is consistent with definite atonement and the perseverance of the saints. Definite atonement means that Christ died to save, actually and certainly, the people the Father gave him; perseverance means that every true believer will be kept by God and will go on believing to the end. Paul is not inviting speculation about whether the weak brother will finally be saved. He is telling the strong that their freedom could push someone toward ruin, and that this is a sin against Christ (Romans 14:15, 20). God keeps his sheep, and one of the ways he keeps them is through brothers who heed warnings like this one.

No private injuries. There is no such thing as a private injury within the church. The sharp remark, the cold shoulder maintained for two years, the person you have quietly written off: none of it stops with them. Christ counts what is done to his people as done to himself, which is a terrifying thought for the offender and an immeasurably comforting one for anyone who has been on the receiving end. Not are you right? but: what did the person you are about to run over cost him?

I think I have caused someone to stumble. What should I do? Confess it to God, and receive his forgiveness; Christ died for your sin against your brother too. Then, where it is wise, go to the person, own what you did without excuse, and ask their forgiveness (Matthew 5:23–24). Stop the thing that was harming them, at least in their presence. If they have fallen into sin because of your example, help them back gently, and carry them in prayer. Do not drown in guilt: the Lord who warns is the Lord who restores, and he can use even this to teach you love.

On a Tuesday. Put the name of the person you find most difficult in your church into this phrase, the brother for whom Christ died, or the sister, and say it aloud. It changes the temperature of everything.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If food makes my brother stumble. “Stumble” means cause to fall into sin. Paul does not conclude with a policy. He concludes with himself.

I will never eat meat. “Never” is emphatic in the Greek: never, to the end of the age, and not just idol meat but any meat, if it would cause a brother to fall. Paul is willing to give up a right entirely for love’s sake. Having told the strong what they should consider, he ends with what he himself will do. It is much harder to resent a man who has already gone further than he is asking you to go. And the readiness was costly. Meat was a rare pleasure in that world for a working man like Paul, and he declares himself ready to give it up for good, should it ever be needed, for a weaker Christian whose name he may not even know. Chapter 9 shows how he has given up other rights for the gospel.

As I am of Christ. The argument that begins here runs through chapters 9 and 10 and ends with a sentence that tells us where it came from: be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (11:1). Paul gives up meat because his Lord gave up far more. Christ did not please himself (Romans 15:3). And writing to Rome on this same question of food, Paul sets the two side by side: do not let what you eat destroy the one for whom Christ died (Romans 14:15). A meal set against a cross: the comparison settles itself.

Does this give the most easily offended person a veto? No, and this guard is needed, because the verse can be turned into an instrument of exactly the opposite kind. Read carelessly, it puts the most easily offended person in any congregation in complete control. If anyone’s disapproval obliges everyone else to stop, the church is governed by whoever is prepared to be upset, and every genuine liberty can be shut down by someone announcing that they find it a stumbling block. That is not what Paul is describing, and the difference is in the passage. His weak brother is not someone who disapproves; he is someone in danger of being led into sin against his own conscience and destroyed by it (vv. 10–11). Being scandalised is not the same as being tripped. A man who says I disapprove of what you are doing is making a criticism; a man who is about to act against his own convictions because of your example is in danger, and only the second is in view here. Nor does Paul suggest the weak should stay weak. Romans 14, the fullest treatment of the same question, puts obligations on both sides: the strong must not despise the weak, and the weak must not pass judgment on the strong (Romans 14:3). Neither is given the whip hand. And where someone insists on a scruple as a rule for the whole church, as the circumcision party did, Paul resists them to the face (Galatians 2:11–14). What is left, when both errors are excluded, is something harder than a rule and better: a willingness to lose a genuine right for the sake of a particular person, decided case by case, by people who are paying attention to each other.

On a Tuesday. Name one freedom you value that you could set aside this week, for one particular person, without any loss to your soul: the drink at a meal with a friend who is fighting addiction, the film when the young people are watching, the sharp joke in front of someone fragile. Set it aside quietly, without announcing your sacrifice. That is the love of the Lord who did not please himself, and his Spirit grows it in you.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>Now concerning food offered to idols: we know that “all of us possess knowledge.” This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up.<sup>2</sup>If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.<sup>3</sup>But if anyone loves God, he is known by God.<sup>4</sup>Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that “an idol has no real existence,” and that “there is no God but one.”<sup>5</sup>For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords”—<sup>6</sup>yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.<sup>7</sup>However, not all possess this knowledge. But some, through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled.<sup>8</sup>Food will not commend us to God. We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do.<sup>9</sup>But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak.<sup>10</sup>For if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols?<sup>11</sup>And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died.<sup>12</sup>Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.<sup>13</sup>Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble.

9.title: Rights Surrendered: The Apostle as Slave to All
9.overview:
Chapter 9 can look like a digression from idol food, but it is Paul’s example. He has just said he would give up meat rather than harm a brother; now he shows that he lives that way. As an apostle he has every right to be supported by the churches, and he proves it from common life, the law of Moses, the temple and the command of Jesus. Yet he has used none of these rights in Corinth, because he would rather die than give anyone a reason to say he preached for money.

His freedom is spent in serving others: he has made himself everyone’s slave to win as many as possible, adapting in everything except the gospel itself. Then he turns to the Isthmian Games, held just outside Corinth. Athletes train hard for a wreath that withers; Christians run for a crown that lasts, and so Paul disciplines himself, lest after preaching to others he should be disqualified.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul first establishes that the right he is about to give up was really his. He is an apostle, and the Corinthian church is the proof. Then he builds the case for being supported by those he serves: from the soldier, the farmer and the shepherd, from the law about the threshing ox, from the priests who ate from the temple, and finally from the command of the Lord himself. In the middle of the case comes the surprise: he has not used this right, but puts up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The right of ministers to be supported

Paul argues from the lesser to the greater: if God’s law protects an ox at the threshing floor, how much more the people who labour in the gospel. The principle that the labourer deserves his wages runs through the way God made the world, and the Lord Jesus confirmed it by command (Luke 10:7; 1 Timothy 5:18). So the Reformed churches have rightly held that supporting ministers properly is a matter of obedience, not charity.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Travelling teachers of rhetoric in Corinth charged for their lectures, and some Corinthians seem to have thought an apostle who took nothing was not worth much. That is why Paul defends the right even while refusing to use it. Now: The principle cuts both ways: congregations should support their ministers generously, and ministers should never let money shape what they preach. A preacher who does not depend on his hearers’ approval is free to say what they need to hear.

verseByVerse.quote: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are not you my workmanship in the Lord? If to others I am not an apostle, at least I am to you, for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 9 is Paul’s personal illustration of the principle of chapter 8: give up your rights for the sake of others. The strong in Corinth insisted on their right to eat. Paul, an apostle, has far greater rights: to be supported financially, to bring a wife on his travels, to stop working with his hands. He proves them from common sense, the law of Moses, temple practice and the command of the Lord himself (vv. 1–14). Yet he has given them all up, so as not to hinder the gospel, and his reward is to preach free of charge (vv. 15–18). He has made himself a slave to all, all things to all people, to win some (vv. 19–23). Finally, the athlete in training: the Christian life demands self-discipline, so that we win the imperishable prize and are not disqualified (vv. 24–27). Through it all shines the pattern of Christ, who though free made himself the servant of all to win a people for God.

Not a digression. A reader coming from chapter 8 may wonder why Paul suddenly defends his apostleship. Paul has just asked the strong to surrender a genuine right for a weaker brother, and resolved never to eat meat if it made his brother stumble (8:13). Now he shows that he has done the same on a far larger scale, and to do so he must first establish that the right was genuinely his. You cannot admire a man for refusing something he was never entitled to.

Am I not free? Free as the strong claimed to be (8:9). The question has been at issue since 6:12. Paul has the same freedom, and more.

Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Some in Corinth questioned Paul’s apostleship. An apostle had to have seen the risen Lord (Acts 1:21–22). Paul saw him on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:3–6; 1 Corinthians 15:8), and he treats that as an appearance of the risen Christ no less real than those given to the Twelve.

Are not you my workmanship in the Lord? Then the fourth question, and it is the one that lands. The Corinthian church itself is proof of his apostleship. It exists because of his ministry. The people questioning his credentials are his credentials. There would be no church at Corinth to hold an opinion about Paul if Paul had not come to Corinth. Every person in the room who was sitting there rather than in a temple was evidence, and the argument is unanswerable because the jury is the exhibit.

The seal of my apostleship. A seal (sphragis) authenticated a document, like a signature or a wax stamp: the mark that proved it was what it claimed to be. Their conversion is God’s seal confirming Paul’s apostleship.

The Lord behind the seal. Twice in two verses Paul adds the words in the Lord, and they carry the argument. Paul planted and preached, but it was the risen Christ who opened hearts in Corinth, as he had first laid hold of Paul himself outside Damascus. A seal is pressed by the owner, not by the messenger who carries the letter. So when Paul points to the church, he is pointing past himself to Jesus our Lord, alive and at work. A congregation of former idolaters is not evidence that Paul was impressive. It is evidence that Christ is risen.

The wound underneath. Paul is defending himself to people he led to Christ, and anyone who has invested years in someone who later questioned their motives will recognise the pain. The questions have heat in them. But he does not withdraw, write them off, or reduce his commitment to them. He is about to explain how much he has given up for the very people examining him.

Are there apostles today? Not in this sense. An apostle in the sense Paul means had seen the risen Lord and been sent by him in person (15:8; Acts 1:21–22). No one can meet that now, and Paul says the risen Lord appeared to him last of all (15:8). The office belonged to the church’s foundation, which was laid once (Ephesians 2:20), and it continues in the only way it can: through the apostolic writings in Scripture. The word is sometimes used today loosely, of missionaries or church planters, and in that sense it is harmless. Many faithful churches that call a missionary or church planter an apostle mean only this modest sense, and they deserve to be heard charitably. But anyone claiming apostolic authority to add to Scripture or to rule the churches should be refused. We have the apostles; they speak to us in the New Testament.

On a Tuesday. If you are carrying the hurt of ingratitude from someone you served, ask what you have done since. The natural movement is to protect yourself: to give less, care less, keep a little back. Paul’s answer to being doubted by his own converts was to go on spending himself on them (2 Corinthians 12:15), and to write them, a few chapters later, the chapter on love the church has treasured ever since.
verseByVerse.note: An apostle had to have seen the risen Lord. A seal authenticated a document.

verseByVerse.quote: This is my defense to those who would examine me. Do we not have the right to eat and drink?
verseByVerse.commentary:
My defense. The words are legal. “Defense” (apologia) is the speech for the defence, a legal reply. “Examine” (anakrinō) means cross-examine, the same word Paul used at 4:3, where he said it was a very small thing to him to be judged by them or by any human court. Some critics were questioning Paul, perhaps because he refused payment, which they took as a sign he was not a real apostle.

Indifferent about himself, not about the trust. In chapter 4 he refuses to be tried by the Corinthians; here he mounts a defence. The difference is what is at stake. About his own standing he was serenely indifferent; the Lord is the judge. But his apostleship is the authority by which the gospel came to them, and if it can be dismissed then so can everything he taught. So he defends the office while remaining unmoved about the man. There is a great deal of criticism a Christian should simply let go, and reaching for a defence is often vanity dressed as principle. But some things are not yours to surrender: the truth you taught, a work God gave you, the safety of people in your care. Be indifferent about yourself, and not indifferent about the trust.

Silent for himself, plain for the truth. Paul’s rule has a pattern older than Paul. When Jesus stood accused before the high priest, he gave no answer for himself; like a sheep before its shearers he was silent (Isaiah 53:7; Mark 14:60–61). Yet when he was asked directly whether he was the Christ, the Son of the Blessed, he answered plainly, I am (Mark 14:61–62), because the truth about who he was was not his to surrender. He let his reputation be torn to pieces and would not let the truth be. When Paul defends his apostleship while shrugging at his own reputation, he is walking in his Master’s footprints.

Do we not have the right to eat and drink? Now the case begins, and it opens at the most basic level. The first right: to receive food and drink at the church’s expense. “We” includes Barnabas and others. “Right” (exousia) is the key word of chapters 8–9, the same word used of the strong Corinthians’ liberty in 8:9, which is precisely the link Paul is building. And the claim is modest. Not a stipend, not a house, not a position. Food and drink. The apostle to the Gentiles is establishing, at length and against opposition, that he would have been entitled to his dinner. And in Corinth he chose to go without, knowing hunger and thirst (4:11), rather than claim it.

When should I defend myself against criticism? First, ask honestly whether the criticism is true, in whole or in part; if so, receive it as a gift and change. If it is false and only your pride is hurt, you can usually let it go and leave your reputation with God (1 Peter 2:23). But if a falsehood threatens the gospel, the people in your care, or a work God has entrusted to you, then speak: calmly, truthfully, without attacking back, and preferably to the person directly. And whatever you do, do not let the hurt shrink your love for the critic.

For worship. He to whom the cattle on a thousand hills belong (Psalm 50:10) was hungry in the wilderness and had nowhere to lay his head, and took no wage for the bread of life he gave away. And the Lord who went without has promised a day when he will dress himself for service, have his servants recline at table, and come and serve them himself (Luke 12:37). The Master who could have demanded every meal will spend eternity feeding his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Do we not have the right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A believing wife. Literally, a sister, a wife: a Christian wife, travelling with him at the churches’ expense.

As do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? Three things in that sentence repay attention, and the first is easily missed: Peter (Cephas) was married, and his wife travelled with him on ministry, supported by the churches. It is no surprise if you have read the Gospels: soon after calling Peter, Jesus heals his mother-in-law (Mark 1:30–31), and a man does not have a mother-in-law without a wife. Paul mentions it here as the normal arrangement. Second, the brothers of the Lord. Paul refers to them as a known group with a recognised ministry, as Luke does (Acts 1:14). They were Jesus’ half-brothers, James, Joses, Simon and Judas (Mark 6:3), who came to faith after the resurrection (John 7:5; Acts 1:14). James became the leader of the Jerusalem church and wrote a letter in our Bible; Jude wrote another.

The brothers of the Lord. These men grew up in the same house as Jesus and watched him at the carpenter’s bench, and while he walked among them they did not believe in him; Mark records that his family once set out to seize him, saying he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21). What changed them was the resurrection: the risen Christ appeared to James (15:7). The brother who had doubted became a pillar of the Jerusalem church, and in his own letter he calls himself not the Lord’s brother but a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ (James 1:1). Kinship with Jesus saved no one. Faith in the risen Lord saved even his own family.

Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living? Third, only Barnabas and I. Paul worked with his hands (Acts 18:3; 20:34), and this verse tells us Barnabas did the same. Are they the only ones without the right to be supported? It is the one mention of Barnabas in this letter, and it is affectionate. These two were the exception, the pair who supported themselves by their trades rather than drawing on the churches. And it is quietly moving that Paul names him. By now the two had parted company after a sharp disagreement over John Mark (Acts 15:36–39). Writing to a church that may never have met Barnabas, Paul reaches back and puts them in the same sentence as fellow labourers who made the same sacrifice. He does not pretend the split never happened, and he does not let it edit the record. He is capable of remembering honourably a man he could no longer travel with, and of asking, later, for the very Mark they quarrelled over, because he was useful (2 Timothy 4:11).

Where Christians differ: married ministers and the brothers of the Lord. The Roman Catholic Church requires celibacy of most of its priests, and teaches that Mary remained a virgin for life, so that the brothers of the Lord were cousins or children of Joseph by a previous marriage. This commentary’s view: This verse shows that the apostles, including Peter, whom Rome regards as the first pope, had wives. Church leaders may marry (1 Timothy 3:2). Requiring celibacy of ministers has no basis in Scripture. As for the brothers of the Lord, the natural reading is that they were sons of Mary and Joseph, born after Jesus (Matthew 1:25; 13:55–56). Mary is to be honoured as blessed among women, but nothing in Scripture requires her perpetual virginity. It is worth saying without heat: those who hold the tradition do so out of reverence for the Lord’s mother, which is not a bad motive. But it is not what the words naturally say, and probably not what a first-century reader would have assumed.

I have fallen out with a fellow Christian. How should I speak of him now? Like Paul speaks of Barnabas: truthfully and honourably. You do not have to pretend the disagreement never happened, or that you were wrong if you were not. But you can refuse to let the quarrel rewrite the good you once did together, speak well of him where you honestly can, refuse to gossip, pray for him, and keep the door open. Paul and Barnabas differed sharply over a judgement, not over the gospel, and both went on serving Christ. Some separations of that kind are not sin; bitterness about them always is. If reconciliation is possible, pursue it.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your pastor’s marriage and family. A minister’s wife and children often carry burdens no one sees; do one practical kindness for them this month.
verseByVerse.note: Peter (Cephas) was married, and his wife travelled with him. The Lord’s brothers included James and Jude.

verseByVerse.quote: Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard without eating any of its fruit? Or who tends a flock without getting some of the milk?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard without eating any of its fruit? Three questions, three trades, one point. Soldiers were paid and supplied by the state. Paul begins his case not with Scripture but with what any Corinthian already knows. Nobody funds his own military service. The farmer eats from his crop. Nobody plants a vineyard and then buys grapes.

Or who tends a flock without getting some of the milk? The shepherd drinks from his flock. In every trade in the world, the worker eats from the work. And the three are not chosen at random. Each has an old association with ministry, and all three pictures are used elsewhere of it. The soldier: no soldier gets entangled in civilian pursuits, since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him (2 Timothy 2:3–4). The vineyard and the farmer: Israel is God’s vineyard through the Old Testament (Isaiah 5:1–7), and Paul has already called the church God’s field (3:6–9; 2 Timothy 2:6). The shepherd: the standing image for those who lead God’s people, from Ezekiel 34 to Peter’s charge to shepherd the flock of God (1 Peter 5:2). So Paul has quietly described the ministry three times while appearing to talk about ordinary occupations. Gospel work is warfare, cultivation and care, and the labourer in each is fed by what he tends.

The chief Shepherd pays his shepherds. Behind the soldier and the shepherd stands Christ. The one who enlisted every gospel worker is the Lord Jesus. And the flock a pastor tends is not his own: it is the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood (Acts 20:28), and when the chief Shepherd appears he will give his under-shepherds the unfading crown of glory (1 Peter 5:4). That is why the labourer may expect to be fed from the flock, and also why he must never fleece it. The sheep belong to the one who died for them, and he is the one who pays his shepherds.

Starting from common life. Paul opens not with revelation but with what everybody can see, and moves upward: Scripture comes next, and the Lord’s command last. It is the same instinct that made his Lord talk about seeds, lamps, coins and sheep. The world is God’s, and ordinary things carry the shape of spiritual ones.

I have served for years and see no fruit. Is it wasted? No. The fruit of Christian service is often slow, hidden and later than we would like, and some of it will only be seen on the last day. God does not measure your work by visible results but by faithfulness, and he has promised that your labour in the Lord is not in vain (15:58). Keep planting. Ask God honestly for fruit and for the grace to wait for it. Ask a trusted friend whether anything should change in how you serve. But do not mistake slowness for failure. Many of the people you have taught and prayed for will one day tell you what you never knew you did.

verseByVerse.quote: Do I say these things on human authority? Does not the Law say the same? For it is written in the Law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain.” Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Does he not certainly speak for our sake? It was written for our sake, because the plowman should plow in hope and the thresher thresh in hope of sharing in the crop.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do I say these things on human authority? Does not the Law say the same? Common sense has made the case; now Paul grounds it in Scripture. Not just common sense: Scripture says it too.

The threshing ox. Deuteronomy 25:4 is an unlikely verse to reach for. Oxen walked over the threshing floor, or pulled a sledge over it, to separate grain from husk, and the grain was right there under their feet all day. A tight-fisted farmer might tie the ox’s mouth shut. God’s law forbade it: the animal doing the work eats from the work.
