Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Paul’s startling aside. Read flatly it sounds like a dismissal of animal welfare, and it must not be taken that way, because Scripture will not have it. Paul does not mean God does not care about animals (Psalm 145:9; Jonah 4:11). This is the God who feeds the ravens and clothes the lilies, who knows when a sparrow falls, who ends the book of Jonah by remarking that Nineveh contained much cattle, and whose law commands rest for the working animal on the Sabbath (Luke 12:24, 27; Matthew 10:29; Exodus 23:12). Whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his beast (Proverbs 12:10). God is very much concerned for oxen. Paul is using a form of argument his readers would recognise, in which a rhetorical question sets aside the lesser matter to reach the greater. The sense is: is this only about oxen? He means that the law’s deeper purpose is not merely about oxen.

Does he not certainly speak for our sake? It was written for our sake. The principle behind the law: workers should share in the fruit of their labour. It expresses a principle God built into the world about labour and its fruit, and if he applies it to a beast at a threshing floor then he certainly applies it to a man in a pulpit. If that applies to oxen, how much more to people. This is an argument from the lesser to the greater. Paul uses the same verse for elders’ pay in 1 Timothy 5:18.

In hope. Hope is what makes labour possible. A man breaking ground in February sees nothing but mud, and what keeps him going is a harvest he cannot yet see. Take away the expectation and the ploughing stops. In a letter that has already said the growth belongs to God alone (3:6–7), this is a great comfort. The Christian teaching a class, visiting the housebound, or raising children in the faith is a ploughman working in hope, and the hope rests on a God who arranged the world so that even an ox eats while it works.

Sower and reaper rejoice together. That hope has its fullest form in the Lord’s own words. Looking at a Samaritan town coming out to meet him, Jesus said that the reaper is already receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together (John 4:35–36). The crop every gospel worker hopes to share is Christ’s harvest: the field is his, the growth is his, and his labourers are promised a share in his joy. The Lord of the harvest (Matthew 9:38) does not muzzle his workers. He feeds them now, and on the last day he will bring them into the joy of the harvest home.

How should I read the Old Testament laws, then? As Paul does here. He does not treat Deuteronomy as an archive of obsolete regulations. He treats it as written for our sake, addressed ultimately to the church (10:11; Romans 15:4). That does not mean every civil or ceremonial law is binding on Christians in its original form; the sacrifices are fulfilled in Christ, and Israel’s civil laws belonged to a nation. But every law reveals something of God’s character and wisdom, and usually a principle that still applies. So ask of any Old Testament command: what does this show about God? What principle of love to him or to neighbour lies under it? And how is it fulfilled in Christ? All Scripture is profitable (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

On a Tuesday. Pick one short Old Testament law this week, perhaps in Deuteronomy 22 or 24, and read it with Paul’s questions: what does this show about God, and what was it written for our sake to teach?
verseByVerse.note: Oxen threshing grain walked over it on the threshing floor; the law let them eat as they worked.

parallels.desc: you shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain

verseByVerse.quote: If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you? If others share this rightful claim on you, do not we even more? Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right, but we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you? Spiritual seed, the gospel, yields a material harvest, financial support. The exchange is stated as plainly as it can be, and the disproportion is the argument. Paul gave them the gospel: the knowledge of God, the forgiveness of sins, eternal life. In return he might reasonably have expected dinner. A small return for a great gift (Romans 15:27; Galatians 6:6).

If others share this rightful claim on you, do not we even more? Other teachers in Corinth were receiving support. Paul, their founder, has a stronger claim. That is very often how it goes: the man who founds the work at his own expense watches his successors receive what he went without.

Nevertheless. The surprise, and the hinge of the chapter. Everything since verse 3 has built the case, and here it is surrendered, not used at all. This is the point for the strong.

We endure anything. “Endure” (stegō) is a word for covering and so bearing up, like a roof holding under rain; it is the same word as love bears all things (13:7). Paul is describing not a preference but a load. “Obstacle” (enkopē) means a hindrance; the related verb could be used of cutting up a road to stop an advance, so a roadblock is a fair picture. In Corinth travelling teachers of rhetoric (sophists) commonly charged for their lectures, and people knew the pattern: an impressive man arrives, gathers an audience, takes their money, moves on. Had Paul accepted support, he would have been placed in that category on the first day, and everything he said would have been heard as a sales pitch. So he made tents and preached for nothing, and the message arrived without a price tag.

A message that cannot be sold. Paul calls it the gospel of Christ, and the content of that gospel explains his refusal. Its message is that the Son of God laid down every right he had, glory, honour and at last his own life, for people who could pay him nothing: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). A preacher who insisted on his rights while announcing that would contradict his sermon with his life. Paul’s tent-making was not only good strategy. It was the gospel made visible. The way the message is carried should look like the message: a Saviour who gave, proclaimed by people who give.

What it does not mean. It does not mean it is wrong for ministers to be paid. Paul defends the right and accepted gifts from other churches (2 Corinthians 11:8–9; Philippians 4:15–16). He refused it in Corinth for the gospel’s sake.

The principle under the practice. Paul gave up a genuine right not because it was wrong but because of what people in his setting would conclude. So the question for anyone who serves is not whether you may have a payment, a recognition, a position or a defence of your reputation. It is whether, in the eyes of the people you are trying to reach, having it would put something across the road. It might be the right to be thanked, to win the argument with a colleague who does not believe, or to keep your evening for yourself when a neighbour needs help.

Should Christians today avoid anything that looks like making money from the gospel? We should avoid anything that makes the gospel look like a product for sale. That means churches and ministries should be scrupulously honest with money, open in their accounts, modest rather than lavish, and never imply that God’s blessing can be bought (Acts 8:20). Preachers who live in luxury on the gifts of the poor, or promise wealth in return for donations, put exactly the roadblock Paul feared across the road. But fair support of faithful workers is not that; it is obedience. The test is whether money serves the gospel or the gospel serves money.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple, and those who serve at the altar share in the sacrificial offerings? In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The temple. Two final arguments, and Paul has saved the strongest for last. The first is from the temple. In Israel, the priests and Levites lived from the offerings and tithes (Numbers 18:8–32; Deuteronomy 18:1–5), and those who served at the altar ate portions of the sacrifices (Leviticus 7:6–10). They received no allotment of land; the LORD himself was their portion. It was not charity. It was the system God designed, and it lasted for centuries. Pagan priests did the same.

The Lord commanded. The final and highest argument: the Lord Jesus himself said that the labourer deserves his wages (Luke 10:7; Matthew 10:10), when he sent out his messengers to stay where they were welcomed, eating and drinking what was provided. And Paul quotes that same saying in a later letter alongside Deuteronomy, apparently under the one heading the Scripture says (1 Timothy 5:18), a striking sign of how quickly the words of Jesus were received with the authority of the Old Testament itself.

An altar we eat from. Hebrews takes the same picture one step further. The priests ate from the altar they served; Christians, it says, have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat (Hebrews 13:10). That altar is Christ’s sacrifice, and what believers feed on there is Christ himself, received by faith. So the minister of the gospel is not a priest living off sacrifices he offers. He is a fellow guest at a table Christ has spread, and his whole work is to point others to the same food. The church supports him because the Lord commanded it, and it does so as people who have all been fed for nothing at one altar.

A command widely neglected. The practical conclusion should be stated plainly, because it is a matter of obedience. The Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should live by it. It is not the minister’s job to raise it, which is precisely the difficulty, since the one person who cannot comfortably make this argument is the one it concerns. Congregations are often careless here without ever intending unkindness. A minister’s pay is set once and quietly left behind by the cost of living. His housing is arranged so that he will retire with nothing. He is expected to look adequately prosperous and not to appear to want anything. Nobody decides any of this; it simply happens, in churches full of people who would be shocked to think they had disobeyed a command of Christ. And the principle runs beyond the paid minister to anyone the church leans on: the person who does the accounts, keeps the building, runs the young people’s work, and is thanked in general terms once a year.

Both edges. But the chapter cuts the other way too, and both edges must be kept. Paul establishes the right and then refuses it. So the minister who reads these verses and feels aggrieved has taken half the chapter. The freedom being described here is not the freedom to be well paid; it is the freedom Paul secured by declining payment, the freedom of a man who can say anything from a pulpit because nobody in the room is keeping him. That is the balance: let the church be generous as a matter of obedience, and let the preacher hold it loosely enough that it never once shapes a sermon.

How much should I give to my church? The New Testament does not set a percentage for Christians; it asks for giving that is regular, proportionate, cheerful and sacrificial (16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:3; 9:7). Many believers take the tithe, a tenth, as a sensible starting point and give more as they are able. Give first to the church where you are fed, since this verse makes that a duty, and then beyond it. Give in a planned way rather than only from what is left over. And if your circumstances are very tight, give what you can, gladly; the widow’s two coins were more than all the rest (Mark 12:43–44).

For worship. The Levites had no inheritance in the land, because the LORD was their portion (Numbers 18:20), and that is now the inheritance of every believer: the LORD is my chosen portion and my cup (Psalm 16:5). The Lord who commanded that his messengers be fed is the one who fed five thousand on a hillside and cooked breakfast for his tired disciples on the shore after he rose. He is our great High Priest, who does not live on what we bring him, but gives us himself.

parallels.desc: the priests’ portion

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Becoming All Things to All People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul explains why he preaches for nothing. Preaching itself is a charge laid on him, so it gives him no ground for boasting; his one freely chosen offering is to give the gospel away without charge. More widely, he has made himself everyone’s servant: as a Jew to Jews, as one outside the law to Gentiles, weak to the weak, yet always under the law of Christ. He does it all for the gospel, so as to share in its blessings with those he reaches.
verseByVerse.theology:
Adapting to people without changing the gospel

All things to all people has been badly misused, as a reason to adjust the gospel itself until it gives no offence. Rightly understood, it means being willing to change the container, the customs, the language, the point at which a conversation begins, while keeping the content the same. Keller’s ministry in Manhattan was one long application of this: learning to speak the language of educated secular professionals, earning a hearing, and then preaching to them the same crucified Christ Paul preached in Corinth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s examples, as a Jew, as under the law, as outside the law, as weak, match the divisions of his own missionary world. He was flexible in form and immovable in content: the Damascus road had made him a prisoner of the message, and everything else could be negotiated. Now: Every missionary and every church faces the question where fitting in becomes giving in, and it needs constant discernment. But treating our own cultural form of Christianity as if it were the gospel is a failure too.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have made no use of any of these rights, nor am I writing these things to secure any such provision. For I would rather die than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting. For if I preach the gospel, that gives me no ground for boasting. For necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not a hint. Paul has just spent twelve verses proving he is entitled to support, and he can hear how it will sound: a hint, a man angling. So he closes the door: he has refused, and he is not asking them to start paying him now.

I would rather die. The sentence is so emphatic that the Greek actually breaks off mid-sentence, which translations tidy up. Paul is agitated, and it is worth asking what has moved him so much. His boast (kauchēma) is not in himself, nor pride in his self-denial, but in being able to preach without charge. It is the one thing in his ministry he can call his own offering, and the next verse explains why he needs one.

Necessity is laid upon me. Preaching itself is no basis for pride, because he has no choice about it. “Necessity” (anankē) is compulsion, a necessity laid on a man from outside. It is a revealing sentence about Paul himself. He was going the other way, with letters in his pocket authorising arrests, and he was stopped in the road and turned round and given a commission he had not applied for (Acts 9:15; 26:16–18). So he cannot boast in preaching, any more than a conscript can boast of enlisting. And woe to me is the language of the prophets. Like Jeremiah, who resolved to stop speaking and found the word was like a fire shut up in his bones (Jeremiah 20:9), Paul cannot hold it in; he would be under God’s judgement if he refused.

The love that compels. What, in the end, was the necessity? Not a rule Paul was afraid of breaking but a Person he had met. Writing later to the same church, he names it: the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all (2 Corinthians 5:14). The arrest outside Damascus was the beginning, but what kept the pressure on, year after year, was the cross. A man who has understood that Christ died for him cannot keep the news to himself, any more than a man pulled from a burning house can stay quiet about the fire while his neighbours sleep. So woe to me is not the complaint of a reluctant employee. It is the cry of a man who knows that silence would betray the One who loved him and gave himself for him (Galatians 2:20).

One thing that was his to give. Within the compulsion Paul found one thing that was his to give: he could preach for nothing. That was not commanded. That was his, freely chosen, and he says he would rather die than have it taken from him. It is a window into a heart. Here is a man who has been given no choice about the central thing in his life, and who has responded not with resentment but by searching out something extra he could give, and then guarding it fiercely, because it was the only present he had.

Does every Christian have this necessity to share the gospel? Not every Christian is called to be a preacher or an apostle, and Paul’s commission was unique. But every Christian has been entrusted with the gospel in some measure, and is to be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in him, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). The church as a whole is under the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19–20). For most believers this means speaking naturally of Christ to family, friends and colleagues, praying for opportunities, living so that the question is asked, and supporting those sent to preach. You need not feel guilty that you are not Paul; but you should not be silent either.

On a Tuesday. Think about the necessities of your own life, the job that pays, the family that needs you, the health you have, which are easy to meet with grumbling or joyless compliance. Paul found, inside the thing he could not choose, one thing he could, and made that his offering. You cannot choose the work; you can choose to do it excellently when nobody checks. You cannot choose the illness; you can choose what people find when they visit. The necessity is not the enemy of joy. It is the field in which a freely given thing becomes possible.

For worship. The gospel came to Paul as an arrest, and that is the glory of it. Christ did not wait to be sought by the man breathing threats against his church. He came after him, knocked him to the ground, opened his eyes, and laid on him a necessity that became his joy. That is how sovereign grace works: it does not ask our permission to save us, and the chains it puts on us are the only freedom we have ever known.

parallels.desc: a burning fire shut up in my bones

verseByVerse.quote: For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward, but if not of my own will, I am still entrusted with a stewardship. What then is my reward? That in my preaching I may present the gospel free of charge, so as not to make full use of my right in the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of my own will. Paul works out the logic of his position. A volunteer could expect wages.

A stewardship. A steward (oikonomos) was a household manager, entrusted with his master’s affairs; often a slave, not paid but obliged (4:1). Given a charge he did not seek, he has no claim to wages; he is simply obliged to be faithful with what was handed to him. So is Paul with the gospel.

What then is my reward? That in my preaching I may present the gospel free of charge. Paul asks the question himself, and the answer is unexpected. His reward is not something he receives. It is something he gives up. The wage he draws is the privilege of not drawing a wage: the joy of giving the gospel away, as it was given to him.

Not making full use. Paul’s reward is precisely in not using his rights. He has discovered that the pleasure of refusing a genuine entitlement is greater than the thing itself would have been. He is not gritting his teeth through a sacrifice. He is describing something he enjoys.

More blessed to give. It is not a peculiarity of his temperament; it is the logic of the gospel working its way into a man’s appetites. Every Christian believes in principle that it is more blessed to give than to receive, and finds it surprising in practice: the anonymous gift, the favour that will never be known, carries a quiet gladness that receiving the same amount would not have produced. Paul organised a whole ministry around that discovery.

My food is to do his will. The Lord Jesus lived this before Paul did, and the saying about giving is his: Paul quotes it as the words of the Lord Jesus (Acts 20:35). Tired and hungry at a well in Samaria, Jesus gave living water to a woman others seem to have shunned, and when his disciples urged him to eat he said, my food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work (John 4:34). The giving fed him. His whole life was given away, and the reward he looked for was not payment but a people. Paul’s strange wage, the joy of handing the gospel on for nothing, is a share in Christ’s own joy: the joy of the Son who gave everything and never once wished it back.

Is it wrong to serve God hoping for a reward? No. Jesus himself promises reward to those who give, pray and fast in secret (Matthew 6:4, 6, 18), and Hebrews says that whoever comes to God must believe that he rewards those who seek him (Hebrews 11:6). What is wrong is serving for the reward of human praise, or imagining that we earn salvation. The rewards Scripture holds out are gifts of grace, given by a Father who delights to honour what his own Spirit produced in us. And the greatest reward, as Paul found, is joy in God himself and in giving as he gives. To want that is not selfish; it is to want what God wants for you.

On a Tuesday. Give something away this week in such a way that nobody can return the favour or record the credit, and do not tell anyone (Matthew 6:3–4). The reluctance comes at the moment of deciding; the gladness comes afterwards, and it is a small share in the joy of the Son who gave everything.
verseByVerse.note: A steward was a household manager, entrusted with his master’s goods.

verseByVerse.quote: For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win more of them. To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews. To those under the law I became as one under the law (though not being myself under the law) that I might win those under the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Free, yet a servant. The sentence is built as a deliberate contradiction. Free (eleutheros): no one owns him, the word the whole chapter opened with. Yet he made himself a slave (douloō) to everyone, and the verb is not passive; nobody did this to him. A free man walked into servitude on purpose, because it was the only way to reach people. That is precisely the pattern of Christ, who took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7) and came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Christian freedom, in the New Testament, is never chiefly freedom from obligation. It is the capacity to take on obligations that nobody could have imposed on you.

To win. “Win” (kerdainō) is a business word, gain, and it appears five times in verses 19–22.

As a Jew. Paul was a Jew, but in Christ he no longer depended on Jewish identity. Yet with Jews he kept Jewish customs: he took a vow (Acts 18:18) and joined in temple purification (Acts 21:23–26). Timothy had a Greek father, and Luke says Paul circumcised him because of the Jews of that region, who all knew it (Acts 16:3): it was done freely, for access, not for salvation.

Under the law. With people living by the law of Moses, he lived by it too, out of love. But he was not under the law as a covenant or a means of righteousness (Romans 6:14; Galatians 2:19), because Christ had already made him right with God (Romans 10:4). When he kept Moses’ rules, it was a courtesy that opened doors, never a price paid for heaven.

Timothy and Titus. Set beside Timothy’s circumcision another episode. When certain men insisted that Titus, a Greek, must be circumcised as a condition of acceptance, Paul refused absolutely: to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved (Galatians 2:3–5). The same operation, opposite answers, and the difference is the whole doctrine of adapting to a culture in one comparison. When the question was how do I get near these people? Paul was endlessly flexible. When the question was what must a man do to be accepted by God? he would not concede a syllable, to anyone, ever. That is the line, and it is a clean one. Everything about the container may be adjusted: language, custom, diet, dress, the order of a service, the point at which you begin a conversation. Nothing about the content may be adjusted: the holiness of God, the reality of sin, the necessity of the cross, the call to repentance and faith.

Flexibility in both directions. Paul’s flexibility ran both ways, which is the part we tend to forget. He became as a Jew to Jews and as one outside the law to Gentiles. He was not simply relaxing his own standards to reach the worldly; he was also taking on restrictions he did not personally need, in order to sit with the scrupulous. Both cost him something. Adapting that only ever moves in the direction of greater personal liberty is usually not gospel adaptation at all.

So how far should I adapt to reach my friends? As far as love requires and holiness allows. Learn their language, not only literally but in the words and questions that matter to them. Be at home in their homes and on their ground. Give up preferences that put them off without serving the gospel: your church jargon, your music, your habits, even lawful pleasures in their presence if they would stumble. But never join in sin to be accepted, never hide the hard parts of the gospel, and never let fitting in become the goal. If you find you have adapted so long that you have never mentioned Christ, you have stopped doing what Paul did.

For worship. To the Jews he became a Jew: when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). The eternal Word learned a language, a trade and a village’s customs. He was circumcised on the eighth day, kept the feasts, paid the temple tax, and ate with Pharisees and with tax collectors. He came down to where we were, all the way down, and he did not change the truth by one word to make it easier. Every missionary who crosses a culture walks in footprints he left first.

verseByVerse.quote: To those outside the law I became as one outside the law (not being outside the law of God but under the law of Christ) that I might win those outside the law. To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Outside the law. Those outside the law are the Gentiles. With them, Paul did not keep Jewish food laws or customs; he ate with them (Galatians 2:12–14).

Under the law of Christ. The safeguard sits inside the text: Paul immediately makes clear that he is nothing of the kind. He was under the law of Christ (ennomos Christou, in-lawed to Christ): the moral will of God as taught and fulfilled by Christ, summed up in love (Galatians 6:2; John 13:34). Freedom from Moses’ ceremonies is not freedom from God’s moral law. And the law of Christ is not a lighter code. It is the whole of what love requires, defined by his own life, and by the measure of the cross it is heavier. A man may eat what he likes and still be under an obligation that reaches to laying down his life.

To the weak. The weak of chapter 8. The Jew and the Gentile are cultural categories; the weak are the people with tender consciences, the easily damaged. Paul does not merely accommodate them; he joins them. He does not stand at a distance being patient with the scrupulous; he stands where they stand. We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves; for Christ did not please himself (Romans 15:1–3).

All things to all people. To save is to be God’s instrument in their salvation. Two things guard the famous phrase from abuse. The first is the purpose clause, repeated in four verses: that I might win, that I might save. The flexibility is not general amiability or a strategy for avoiding conflict, and a man who adapts endlessly and never gets round to the gospel is using Paul’s words as cover for the opposite. The second is the modesty of some. Paul has adapted at real cost in every direction, and he expects some. That word protects the evangelist discouraged by a small response and the one who thinks the right presentation would bring everybody. You spend yourself, God gives the growth (3:6), and some are saved.

If God has chosen his people, why does Paul work so hard to save some? Because God’s choosing is the reason evangelism succeeds, not a reason to stop. God ordains the means as well as the end, and the means is the preaching of the gospel (Romans 10:14–17). Paul knew the Lord had many people in Corinth (Acts 18:9–10), and that was why he stayed and preached there for eighteen months. Election does not make his effort pointless; it guarantees it will not be in vain. Christians who understand election differently agree with this much: the gospel must be offered to everyone. We do not know who the elect are, so we offer Christ freely to all, plead with them to be reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20), and trust God to open hearts as he opened Lydia’s.

The opposite failure. This passage is misused to justify a Christianity that has stopped saying anything difficult. But a common failure in conservative churches is the reverse: treating our inherited cultural form, the music, vocabulary, dress and assumptions, as though it were the gospel, and regarding anyone who does not fit it as not really interested. Paul dismantled his own preferences for people he wanted to reach. The question is not only whether we will compromise the gospel, but whether we will be inconvenienced for it.

Is being all things to all people just people-pleasing? No, and the difference lies in the heart. The people-pleaser changes in order to be liked; his deepest need is approval, and he cannot bear disapproval. Paul changed in order to win people for Christ, and he could bear any disapproval, which is why the same man who ate with Gentiles also opposed Peter to his face (Galatians 2:11). If I were still trying to please man, he wrote, I would not be a servant of Christ (Galatians 1:10). The test is simple: are you willing to say the thing that will make them dislike you, when love requires it? Only someone secure in Christ’s approval is free to adapt without being swallowed.

On a Tuesday. Pray for one person you would love to see saved, and ask what being all things to them would mean this week: an evening on their ground, a question about their life, a willingness to be bored or uncomfortable for them, a plain word about Christ when the moment comes.

verseByVerse.quote: I do it all for the sake of the gospel, that I may share with them in its blessings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A fellow partaker. “Share” (synkoinōnos) is a fellow partaker, and the little word with changes the picture. Paul is not standing outside the gospel handing it to others. He is inside it with them, a fellow sinner saved by grace, receiving the same thing he offers, dependent on the same mercy. He is not a functionary distributing a benefit he does not need, but a beneficiary given the job of telling others where he found it.

Called into the fellowship of his Son. What are the blessings Paul wants to share? Not a set of benefits that could be detached from a person. At the start of this letter he told the Corinthians that God had called them into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord (1:9), and the word there, koinōnia, shares its root with Paul’s word here. The blessing of the gospel is Christ himself: forgiveness in his blood, righteousness in his name, life in his life. So Paul does everything so that he and his converts may have Christ together. Preacher and hearer receive the same Saviour, in the same way, by the same grace.

The danger of handling holy things. This corrects something that can happen to anyone who works with the things of God for long enough. The minister’s Bible becomes raw material for Sunday; the Sunday school teacher only reads to prepare; the parent’s faith becomes entirely a matter of passing something on; the long-standing member hears every sermon as an assessment of the preacher. The tell is a change in how you hear: you listen to a sermon and think, that would help so-and-so. In itself that is love. The danger is when it becomes the only way you receive anything, and the thought this is about me stops arriving altogether. Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching (1 Timothy 4:16).

How do I keep the gospel fresh for myself when I have known it for years? Go back to it as a sinner, not as an expert. Confess specific sins regularly, so that forgiveness stays real rather than theoretical. Read Scripture sometimes with no task in view, asking only what God is saying to you. Sing the great hymns about the cross and mean them. Spend time with new believers, whose wonder is contagious. Take the Lord’s Supper as a hungry man, not as a spectator. And pray Paul’s own prayer, that you may know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:19). The gospel does not grow old; we grow dull, and the Spirit is able to wake us again.

For worship. There is enough in Christ for every preacher and every hearer, every apostle and every slave, and none of them will ever reach the bottom of it. The man who had seen the risen Lord and planted churches across the empire still came to the same fountain as the newest convert at Corinth, with the same empty hands, and found it full. The Lord does not keep one mercy for the leaders and another for the led. His mercies are new every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23), and on every one of those mornings he gives himself whole to each of his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–27 — The Discipline of the Athlete
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to the athletic games the Corinthians knew well. Athletes train with strict self-control for a wreath that withers; believers run for a crown that lasts. So Paul runs with aim and disciplines his own body, so that the preacher does not himself fail the test.
verseByVerse.theology:
Assurance and effort: the perseverance of the saints

The warning of verse 27 is not a threat to the final security of true believers. It is one of the means by which God keeps them. The God who keeps his people does so through their disciplined effort, not instead of it, and those who truly belong to him take the warning seriously, run hard, and so show that their calling is real.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians lived beside the Isthmian Games, and Paul’s comparison would have stung a little: athletes trained more earnestly for a passing prize than many Christians did for an eternal one. Now: Some Christians are wary of any talk of spiritual discipline, fearing that it sounds like earning salvation. Paul’s picture answers the fear: grace produces effort, and the free gift of the gospel makes the runner willing to run hard.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it. Every athlete exercises self-control in all things. They do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? The image would have needed no explanation at Corinth. The Isthmian Games, among the great festivals of the Greek world, were held every two years at the Isthmus just outside Corinth, under the city’s management. Many reading this letter had seen the athletes train, had watched the races, and knew exactly what the prize looked like. In a race, only one wins.

In the flow. Why does Paul turn to athletics here? He has just said he does everything so that he may share in the gospel’s blessings himself (v. 23), and the race shows that this is not automatic: running to the end takes self-denial. That ties chapter 9 to chapter 8, since the strong were being asked to deny themselves for their brothers, and it leads straight into chapter 10, where Israel all ate the same spiritual food and yet most fell in the wilderness. The strong Corinthians thought their knowledge made them safe; Paul’s answer is that anyone who thinks he stands must take care lest he fall (10:12).

So run. A guard is needed at once, because the analogy has a limit Paul plainly does not intend. The point is not that only one Christian is saved; that would contradict everything in the letter. The point of comparison is the manner of running, not the number of winners. Run wholeheartedly, like a man who means to win, rather than like someone jogging round because attendance is expected.

Self-control. “Self-control” (enkrateuomai) comes from the same root as the self-control the Spirit grows in believers (Galatians 5:23). Athletes trained for ten months, with strict diet and discipline; at Olympia they swore to it. Nobody turned up on the day. They say no to many good things for the sake of the prize.

A perishable wreath. What strikes Paul is the disproportion between the effort and the prize. At the Isthmian Games, the winner’s crown was made of pine, or in some periods of dried wild celery. It soon decayed. Ten months of denial, and the reward was a handful of leaves that browned within a week and was thrown out. Men gave years to that.

An imperishable. Our crown is eternal life and glory: the crown of righteousness, the crown of life, the unfading crown of glory (2 Timothy 4:8; James 1:12; 1 Peter 5:4). If athletes sacrifice so much for a wilting wreath, how much more should we? The rebuke is aimed at us, not the athletes. People will discipline themselves ferociously for a marathon, a qualification, a business or a physique, and find prayer and Scripture impossible, and the difference is not the time available.

Looking to Jesus. The New Testament’s other great race passage tells the runner where to look: run with endurance the race set before you, looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross (Hebrews 12:1–2). Christ is not only the one who hands out the prize at the end. He ran the course first, under a discipline no athlete has known: forty days in the wilderness saying no to bread, a lifetime saying no to every shortcut, and a garden where he prayed, not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). His self-control was perfect, and it was all for us: where our discipline falls short, his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). The Christian runs because his forerunner has already finished (Hebrews 6:20), and the course is marked by his footprints.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is earned by effort. The prize is given by grace. But the Christian life is not passive; grace trains us to strive (Philippians 2:12–13; Titus 2:11–12). Some Christians are so anxious not to fall into works-righteousness that any talk of discipline sounds to them like a threat to grace. This passage settles it. Nobody supposes an athlete’s training earns him the right to enter the stadium. The training is what a man does because he is in the race, not in order to be admitted to it.

What does spiritual training actually look like? Ordinary, regular, deliberate practices that put you where God has promised to meet you. Daily Scripture reading and prayer, at a set time if possible. Faithful attendance at the Lord’s Day worship, the preaching and the Lord’s Supper. Memorising verses. Occasional fasting. Generous giving. Honest friendship with a believer who can ask you hard questions. Saying no to things that dull you, often your phone or your screen. None of these earns anything; all of them are means of grace. Start small and keep going: train yourself for godliness, for it holds promise for the present life and for the life to come (1 Timothy 4:7–8).

For worship. The crown that awaits the Christian does not wilt, because the One who gives it does not change. The Isthmian victor wore celery until it withered; the King of glory wore thorns for a day, so that his people might wear a crown of life for ever. In John’s vision the elders cast their crowns before the throne, because they know whose victory it really was, and they sing: worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honour and power (Revelation 4:10–11).
verseByVerse.note: The Isthmian Games, second only to the Olympics, were held near Corinth every two years. Winners received a wreath of pine or dried celery.

verseByVerse.quote: So I do not run aimlessly; I do not box as one beating the air. But I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not aimlessly. “Aimlessly” means without a clear mark. Two negatives here, and both describe activity without contact: the runner with no finish line in view, the boxer throwing punches at nothing. Effort is being expended; nothing is happening.

Beating the air. A shadow-boxer swings at nothing. That is a fair description of a good deal of religious life. Someone can be busy in a church for thirty years, attending everything, tired from it, and still shadow-boxing. Paul’s alternative is not more energy. It is aim.

I discipline my body. “Discipline” (hypōpiazō) literally means to give a black eye. Paul treats his own body’s sinful desires as an opponent in the ring. “Keep under control” (doulagōgeō) means lead as a slave. Having just called himself a servant to all (v. 19), he now makes a servant of his own body. His body serves him, not the other way round. That must not be misread as contempt for the body. This is the apostle who has called it a temple of the Holy Spirit and said that the Lord is for it (6:13, 19). He is not describing the self-punishment of a man who thinks flesh is evil. He is describing an athlete’s relation to his own appetites: the body is a magnificent servant and a ruinous master, and the training consists in keeping it in the right position.

Bought with a price. Why should a man land blows on his own appetites? Because his body is no longer his own. Paul has told this church that their bodies are members of Christ and that they were bought with a price, so they are to glorify God in their bodies (6:15, 20). The price was Christ’s own body, given on the cross. So self-discipline for the Christian is not self-improvement. It is keeping what Christ bought for the purpose he bought it. And the fight is not hopeless, because sin’s ownership was broken when our old self was crucified with him (Romans 6:6). The craving still shouts, but it no longer has the right to be obeyed, and the believer who strikes it is siding with his rightful Owner.

Disqualified. “Preaching” (kēryssō) is the herald’s word; at the Games the herald announced the rules and called the contestants. “Disqualified” (adokimos) means failing the test, rejected as counterfeit. Paul applies the word to himself, and it is sobering. The danger he names is specific and his own: after preaching to others. The peril of the herald is that he handles the truth so constantly that he stops being handled by it, and can describe repentance without repenting, competently, for years. Behind the warning stands the holiness of God, who is not impressed by a man’s gifts or his platform: on that day many will say, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name? (Matthew 7:22). God looks for a heart that trembles at his word (Isaiah 66:2), and an apostle is not exempt.

Where Christians differ: could Paul lose his salvation? Some take this as proof that even an apostle could fall away and be lost. Others say disqualified means only losing a reward. Both readings are held by sincere believers who take the warning to heart. This commentary’s view: Paul knows that a person can preach to others and yet prove not to be genuine (Matthew 7:22–23). So he takes his own holiness seriously. The warning is real, and is one of the means God uses to keep his people persevering. True believers will not finally be lost (Romans 8:30; Philippians 1:6), but they persevere by heeding such warnings, not by ignoring them. Assurance and diligence go together (2 Peter 1:10). Scripture is emphatic that those whom God justifies he also glorifies, that no one can snatch Christ’s sheep from his hand (John 10:28), and this letter itself grounds the Corinthians’ security in the faithfulness of God, who will sustain them to the end (1:8–9). The warning is not idle machinery; it is one of the instruments, and it works precisely by being taken seriously. A man who reads this and thinks that could not happen to me has misunderstood it. A man who reads it and disciplines himself is the very man the warning was written to preserve. The fence at the cliff edge is not useless because nobody has gone over.

This frightens me. How can I know I will not be disqualified? Look away from yourself to Christ, and then look honestly at your life. Your safety rests on his faithfulness, not on the strength of your discipline: he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). The very fear that makes you want to take holiness seriously is a sign of life; hypocrites rarely worry about this. So rest in his promises, and respond to the warning as Paul did, by fighting real sins with real means. Confess them, flee temptation, keep company with believers, and keep coming to Christ. The person who goes on trusting him and fighting sin, however imperfectly, is not the one this verse is about. A sin you both love and hate, and keep fighting, is not proof that you are disqualified; the fight itself is the Spirit’s work in you (Galatians 5:17).

On a Tuesday. Most of us know which bodily appetite most often wins: food, sleep, lust, the phone, anger that runs through the body before the mind can stop it. Paul’s picture suggests that the fight is won less by heroic resolutions than by aim, and by the Spirit, through whom we put to death the deeds of the body (Romans 8:13): knowing the one opponent, and landing ordinary blows against it again and again. And if you teach or lead others, it is a mercy to have a trusted friend who will ask about your own holiness, not only about your ministry.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are not you my workmanship in the Lord?<sup>2</sup>If to others I am not an apostle, at least I am to you, for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.<sup>3</sup>This is my defense to those who would examine me.<sup>4</sup>Do we not have the right to eat and drink?<sup>5</sup>Do we not have the right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas?<sup>6</sup>Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living?<sup>7</sup>Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard without eating any of its fruit? Or who tends a flock without getting some of the milk?<sup>8</sup>Do I say these things on human authority? Does not the Law say the same?<sup>9</sup>For it is written in the Law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain.” Is it for oxen that God is concerned?<sup>10</sup>Does he not certainly speak for our sake? It was written for our sake, because the plowman should plow in hope and the thresher thresh in hope of sharing in the crop.<sup>11</sup>If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you?<sup>12</sup>If others share this rightful claim on you, do not we even more? Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right, but we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ.<sup>13</sup>Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple, and those who serve at the altar share in the sacrificial offerings?<sup>14</sup>In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel.<sup>15</sup>But I have made no use of any of these rights, nor am I writing these things to secure any such provision. For I would rather die than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting.<sup>16</sup>For if I preach the gospel, that gives me no ground for boasting. For necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!<sup>17</sup>For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward, but if not of my own will, I am still entrusted with a stewardship.<sup>18</sup>What then is my reward? That in my preaching I may present the gospel free of charge, so as not to make full use of my right in the gospel.<sup>19</sup>For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win more of them.<sup>20</sup>To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews. To those under the law I became as one under the law (though not being myself under the law) that I might win those under the law.<sup>21</sup>To those outside the law I became as one outside the law (not being outside the law of God but under the law of Christ) that I might win those outside the law.<sup>22</sup>To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some.<sup>23</sup>I do it all for the sake of the gospel, that I may share with them in its blessings.<sup>24</sup>Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it.<sup>25</sup>Every athlete exercises self-control in all things. They do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable.<sup>26</sup>So I do not run aimlessly; I do not box as one beating the air.<sup>27</sup>But I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified.

10.title: Israel’s Warning, the Lord’s Table, and the Glory of God
10.overview:
Paul completes his answer about idol food. The strong in Corinth felt secure: they were baptised, they shared the Lord’s Supper, they knew idols were nothing. Paul answers with Israel’s story. The whole generation that left Egypt had God’s gifts, the cloud, the sea, the manna and the water from the rock, which Paul says was Christ himself. Yet most of them died in the wilderness through idolatry, sexual immorality, testing God and grumbling, and their story was written as a warning for us. Whoever thinks he stands should take care, and the faithful God always provides a way through temptation.

So: flee idolatry. The Lord’s Supper is a real sharing in Christ, and no one can share both the Lord’s table and the table of demons. Then come practical rules: market food may be eaten without questions, and a meal at an unbeliever’s home with thanks, unless someone points out that the food was sacrificed. In everything, do all to the glory of God, and seek the good of others so that they may be saved.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells the story of Israel in the exodus. All of them had the same privileges, the cloud and the sea, food and drink from God, and Christ himself present with them; yet most of them died in the wilderness. Their sins are examples written down to warn the church: craving, idolatry, sexual immorality, testing Christ and grumbling. So anyone who thinks he stands should take care not to fall, and the section ends with a promise: God is faithful, and with every temptation he provides the way out.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ in the wilderness

When Paul says that the rock was Christ (v. 4), he means that the Son of God was already present and at work among his people before he was born of Mary, giving the water that Israel took for granted. The same Christ who died on the cross went with Israel through the desert. So the Old Testament is not a story from which Christ is absent: he is there in promise, in pattern and in person.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians who were eating idol food in pagan temples needed to hear that feeling secure is not the same as being safe. Israel had more visible privileges than any of them and still fell. Now: A Christian who trusts in baptism and regular communion as automatic guarantees, without faith and watchfulness, is making Israel’s mistake. The Lord’s Supper and baptism are real means of grace, not charms.

verseByVerse.quote: For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 10 completes Paul’s answer about food offered to idols. The strong Corinthians felt safe: they had knowledge, baptism and the Lord’s Supper. But Israel in the wilderness had their own baptism and their own spiritual food and drink, with Christ himself present, and most of them fell through idolatry, immorality, testing God and grumbling. So let anyone who thinks he stands take care, and trust the faithful God who provides a way of escape (vv. 1–13). Flee idolatry: the Supper is a real participation in Christ, and you cannot share the Lord’s table and the table of demons (vv. 14–22). Eat market meat and a neighbour’s dinner freely, but yield for another’s conscience, and do all to the glory of God (vv. 23–33). Through the whole chapter walks one Person: the Rock who followed Israel, the Lord whose table is spread for his people.

Do not be unaware. Paul has just described himself as an athlete who could still be disqualified (9:27). Now he says, in effect: this is not a nightmare I invented; it happened, to a generation as privileged as any that ever lived. The formula marks something important (12:1; Romans 11:25), and here it has a hard edge. The Corinthians prided themselves on being aware: on knowledge (8:1), on insight, on having worked out that an idol is nothing. Paul does not attack their knowledge. He tells them there is a piece of history they have not factored in.

That our fathers. Paul is writing to a mostly Gentile church, and he calls the wilderness generation our fathers. That is not a slip. The church is the continuation of the people of God; whoever belongs to Christ is Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:29), and Israel’s history is the church’s family history. A Corinthian dock worker who had never seen Jerusalem was being told that Moses was his ancestor and the Red Sea was part of his story.

Under the cloud. Count the word all: five times in four verses. Paul is not describing a spiritual elite; he is describing every last person in the camp, including the many who would never reach the land. The pillar of cloud is overhead, a visible column of the presence of God, guiding them by day and standing between them and Pharaoh’s army by night (Exodus 13:21; 14:19–20). Ahead, the sea has stood up on both sides. They walk out on the seabed on dry ground, and the water that drowned the Egyptian army does not touch them (Exodus 14:21–22). Cloud above, water on either hand: they are, says Paul, surrounded, and he uses the word for baptism to say so.

Baptised into Moses. It is a striking phrase, and it needs unpacking, because it is not water baptism. Israel did not get wet; the Egyptians did. To be baptised into someone is to be bound to that person, so that his deliverance becomes your deliverance and his story becomes the story you live inside, just as Christians are baptised into Christ and joined to him (Romans 6:3). Israel came out of that sea belonging to Moses, their leader and mediator, in a way they had not belonged to him when they went in. They had a mediator, a rescue, a covenant sign and a visible sign of God’s presence. If church membership, the font and the table could save anyone, that generation was safe, and that is exactly the point Paul is setting up.

Baptised into a person. Paul tells the Red Sea story in the vocabulary of Christian baptism on purpose. The heart of it was never the water but the person: Israel was bound to Moses; believers have put on Christ (Galatians 3:27). Yet the two mediators are not equals. Moses was faithful in God’s house as a servant; Christ is faithful over it as a son (Hebrews 3:5–6). Moses could lead the people through the sea, but he could not give them new hearts, and he himself died outside the land. Christ does more than walk ahead of his people: he joins them to himself, so that what is his becomes theirs. That is why the warning that follows is so sharp. A rite can be had without him; he cannot be had without faith.

Who this passage is for. It is for the man who was sprinkled as a baby and has the certificate in a drawer, the woman baptised in a river at seventeen, the family that has not missed a Sunday in a decade. Paul’s point is not that these things are worthless; he calls them spiritual food and drink. His point is that Israel had the equivalent of every one of them, in a more spectacular form than any church has seen, and it was possible to have the lot and perish anyway. The cloud did not make anyone love God. It only made him impossible to ignore.

Does this passage settle how baptism should be done? Not directly, and it is wise not to make it carry more than it does. Israel was neither immersed nor sprinkled; they walked through on dry ground. Paul uses the word baptism for union with a mediator, not for a method. This commentary holds to believer’s baptism by immersion on other grounds: the New Testament pattern of baptising those who repent and believe (Acts 2:41; 8:12), and the picture of burial and rising with Christ (Romans 6:4; Colossians 2:12). Our paedobaptist brothers, who baptise the children of believers, read the covenant differently, and we honour them as fellow servants of the same Lord. What both sides agree on here is the point Paul is making: no form of baptism, however it is done, can stand in for faith.

On a Tuesday. Take stock of your own privileges honestly: the Christian home, the good church, the Bible on the shelf, the baptism and the table. Thank God for every one of them. Then ask the question this passage is about to press: has all of this led me to trust and love Christ himself, or has it only made him familiar?

parallels.desc: the pillar of cloud
through the sea on dry ground

verseByVerse.quote: and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Spiritual food and drink. The privileges keep coming, and now they are edible. The food is the manna from heaven (Exodus 16); the drink is the water from the rock (Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11). Paul sees them as Israel’s equivalent of the Lord’s Supper, which is why he describes them in the same breath as their baptism. Spiritual here does not mean immaterial. The manna could be gathered in a jar, and it went bad if you hoarded it. The water from the rock was wet. The word means supplied by the Spirit: food and drink that no farmer grew and no well yielded, arriving because God sent them, and pointing beyond themselves to Christ, the true bread from heaven (John 6:31–35). For forty years a nation woke up in a desert that grows nothing and found breakfast on the ground, until the day they ate the produce of Canaan and it stopped (Joshua 5:12).

The Rock that followed them. Is Paul repeating a Jewish legend? A Jewish tradition, found in writings of roughly this period and later, had a well or rock literally travelling along behind Israel. Paul does not endorse that. Water came from a rock at Rephidim near the beginning of the journey (Exodus 17:6) and again at Meribah near the end of it, nearly forty years later (Numbers 20:11). The rocks were different rocks in different places. What followed them was not a stone; it was the One who gave the water, and he was there at both ends of the wilderness and every dry mile in between.

The Rock was Christ. Why call him the Rock at all? Because that is God’s own name in the song Moses sang over this very generation: the Rock, whose work is perfect; the Rock that bore you, whom you forgot (Deuteronomy 32:4, 15, 18; compare Psalm 78:35). And at Rephidim the LORD said he would stand before Moses on the rock (Exodus 17:6). Paul takes a divine title out of the Old Testament, a title reserved for the LORD, and lays it on Jesus of Nazareth without a word of apology. This is not borrowing an image; it is identifying a person, and it affirms both Christ’s deity and his eternal pre-existence: that he is God himself, not a creature, and that he was alive and at work long before he was born of Mary. Paul will say the same again: Israel put Christ to the test (10:9; some manuscripts read the Lord there, but Christ is the best-supported reading).

How could Christ be with Israel centuries before he was born? Because the Son did not begin to exist in Bethlehem. He is the eternal Word who was with God and was God in the beginning (John 1:1), through whom all things were made. At Bethlehem he took a human nature to himself; he did not come into being. Before that, he was already at work among his people. Jesus himself said that Abraham rejoiced to see his day, and that before Abraham was, I am (John 8:56–58). So when Israel was led, fed and watered in the desert, the Son was not watching from a distance and waiting for his turn. He was the one doing it. The God of the Old Testament and the Saviour of the New are not two characters. They are the same Lord.

Before there was a manger, there was a rock in a desert. The Son of God stood in a waterless place beside a people who had already decided he was not worth trusting, and opened a spring for them. He fed men who would soon grumble at him again, and gave drink to throats that would soon complain against him. Centuries later he stood up in Jerusalem at the Feast of Booths, the feast that remembered those wilderness years, and cried that anyone who thirsts should come to him and drink (John 7:37). It was the same voice and the same offer. Only now the One who had been hidden behind the rock was standing in the open.

On a Tuesday. Read the wilderness stories in Exodus and Numbers looking for him. When the manna falls and the water flows, you are watching Christ provide for people very like you. And when you are in a dry place yourself, remember who stood on the rock. He has not stopped giving water in deserts.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition told of a rock that followed Israel through the wilderness; Paul says the true source of their water was Christ.

parallels.desc: bread from heaven
water from the rock

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not pleased. Everything turns on one word, nevertheless. All had the privileges; most perished. Paul says most, and the word is almost a mercy, because the arithmetic is worse than it sounds. Of the fighting men who came out of Egypt, two entered the land: Caleb and Joshua (Numbers 14:29–30). Two. Out of a muster of more than six hundred thousand men of fighting age (Numbers 1:46). And note the restrained phrase: God was not pleased. He does not rage. He is simply not pleased, and a generation ends.

Overthrown. The verb is a picture word, taken from Numbers 14:16: katestrōthēsan, strewn, scattered, laid out flat, bodies spread across a desert floor. On the figures Numbers gives, that is something like forty funerals a day, for thirty-eight years. And every one of those people had been under the cloud. Every one had walked through the sea. Whatever the signs God gave them did, they did not do this.

Privilege is not armour. The confident Corinthians had concluded that spiritual privilege was insulation: that a man who had been baptised, who ate at the Lord’s table and had the Spirit, was beyond serious spiritual danger. Paul answers with a graveyard. He does not deny that the privileges were real. He denies that they were armour.

They ate the manna and died. Jesus himself drew this line from the wilderness to his own person. Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, he told the crowd, and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die (John 6:49–50). Every one of the bodies strewn across that desert had eaten bread from heaven that morning. The manna kept them alive for a day; it could not give them life. What they lacked was not another miracle but the One the miracle pointed to. That is the difference Paul is pressing on Corinth: the Supper is not a charm, but Christ himself, received by faith, is a life no wilderness can take away.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that all who died in the wilderness went to hell. Moses died in the wilderness under God’s displeasure, and Moses is on the mountain of transfiguration (Deuteronomy 34:5; Luke 9:30). Miriam and Aaron died there too, and they were God’s servants. To be shut out of Canaan was a real and terrible judgment, but Canaan is not a picture of heaven in any simple way, and Paul is not conducting an inquest into individual souls. He is making one point, and it is enough on its own: privileges without faith and obedience do not protect from God’s judgment, and God’s manifest favour to a group is no guarantee about any particular person in it.

Were these people ever truly God’s? Some were, and many were not, and that is exactly the danger. Israel was a covenant people, but not everyone inside it had faith. The letter to the Hebrews explains what went wrong: the message they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united by faith with those who listened, and they were unable to enter because of unbelief (Hebrews 3:19; 4:2). The church today is the same kind of mixture. It is possible to sit among God’s people, sing their songs and share their table, and never have trusted Christ yourself. The answer is not to doubt every Christian around you, but to make sure of your own heart: to come to Christ himself, not merely to his people. And if you fear you may be one of those outsiders, the fear itself shows that you want him, and he has promised rest to all who come (Matthew 11:28).

Was God not harsh to let a whole generation die in the desert? It can sound so, until the story is read whole. That generation had watched the plagues, the sea and the manna, and still, as God said, put him to the test ten times and would not obey his voice (Numbers 14:22). Even then the judgment came slowly: thirty-eight years in which the manna still fell six mornings a week, the cloud still led, and their children were raised to enter the land. God is not cruel. He is holy, and he is patient far beyond anything we would be. The real question is not why he judged them, but why he bears with any of us, and the answer is that he has not ignored sin but dealt with it, in his Son (Romans 3:25–26).

For worship. The God who was not pleased with most of a nation opened the heavens over the Jordan and said of one man, This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased (Matthew 3:17). Everything that generation lacked, he possessed: faith that never failed, obedience that never wavered, love for the Father that never cooled. And the favour that rests on him rests on everyone who is in him. Those who could never please God in themselves are accepted in his Son, and the displeasure that strewed bodies across the wilderness fell, in the end, on the one body on the cross.

parallels.desc: your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness

verseByVerse.quote: Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Examples for us. The word is typoi, types, patterns: a mark or impression, like the one a die leaves when it stamps a coin. These events really happened, and God shaped them so that the pattern pressed into them would still be legible centuries later. The Old Testament is not raw material we are cleverly applying. It was struck this way on purpose.

In the flow. Verses 1–5 told the story; verse 6 says why it was told. From here to verse 10 Paul works through four of Israel’s sins, idolatry, sexual immorality, testing Christ and grumbling, and each had its echo in Corinth. Verse 11 will repeat this verse’s point, and verse 12 will land it: let anyone who thinks he stands take heed. And the whole history serves the question of chapters 8–10, whether a Christian may eat in an idol’s temple. Israel too thought a meal was only a meal.

Craving. Paul reaches past the four sins he is about to list and names the thing underneath them. It was not, first of all, that Israel worshipped a calf or slept with Moabites. It was that they craved. The Greek is epithymētas kakōn, cravers of bad things. One of the first great collapses in the wilderness was a food riot. They despised the manna and wanted fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic (Numbers 11:5), and they wanted them so badly that they said out loud they had been better off as slaves. God gave them quail until it came out of their nostrils, sent a plague, and the place was named the Graves of Craving (Numbers 11:4–34). The Corinthians’ craving for temple meals is the same thing in a toga. Desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin (James 1:14–15).

Not by bread alone. Moses explained the manna in one sentence: God let his people hunger and fed them with manna, that he might make them know that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD (Deuteronomy 8:3). Israel failed that lesson at the Graves of Craving. Israel was God’s son (Exodus 4:22); centuries later the true Son was led into the wilderness and was hungry, and the devil offered him bread on his own terms. Jesus answered with that very verse (Matthew 4:4). Where the cravers demanded what God had not given, he went without rather than reach for it. He is the one Israelite who learned what the manna was teaching, and he learned it for a people who never had.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament stories are merely moral fables. They are history that teaches. Nor does saying the Old Testament was stamped for us license treating every detail as a code to be cracked: the scarlet cord, the number of the pillars, the colours of the curtain. That kind of reading turns Scripture into a puzzle and the interpreter into a genius, and it produces sermons that could not have been preached by Moses. Paul’s typology (reading Old Testament events as patterns God placed there for his later people) is disciplined and it is moral: here is a people with advantages, here is what they did with them, here is what happened, and you are made of the same material. The pattern is not hidden. It is the plain sense of the story, pressed on a later generation. And the reason it presses is not that history repeats itself but that human hearts do. The desert is gone. The craving is not.

Is it wrong to want things? No. God made us creatures of desire, and he gives us good things richly to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). Wanting food, love, rest, children or useful work is not sin. The problem in the wilderness was not appetite but what the appetite did. It wanted bad things, or good things on its own terms; it despised what God had given in order to demand what he had not; and it valued the gift above the Giver, to the point of preferring Egypt. A useful question is whether a desire can be brought to God in prayer and left with him. A desire that sulks when God says wait, or that would rather have the thing without him than him without the thing, has become craving.

On a Tuesday. Think back over the last week and ask: what did I want that I would have been embarrassed to pray for out loud? Not what did I do, but what did I want. Then bring that desire to God by name, and ask him for contentment with what he has given.

parallels.desc: the graves of craving

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be idolaters as some of them were; as it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Idolaters. The first of the four wilderness failures, and Paul picks the one everybody knows: the golden calf (Exodus 32), at the very foot of Sinai, weeks after the people had heard God speak the commandments.

To eat and drink. Paul quotes the line from Exodus 32:6 about the meal because the Corinthians are arguing about meals. They ate a sacrificial feast before the calf and then played. But look closely at what the calf actually was. Israel did not decide to swap the LORD for a Canaanite deity. Aaron built the calf and then announced that tomorrow would be a feast to the LORD (Exodus 32:5). They kept the name. They kept the God. What they changed was the terms: they would have him visible, manageable, on their own schedule, in a form they had chosen. That is idolatry, and it is a religious sin, committed in a worship service, by people who would have described themselves as devout.

Rose up to play. Play is the polite translation of a Hebrew word that covers dancing, revelry, and what happens after the dancing. Exodus notes drily that the people had broken loose (Exodus 32:25). This is exactly what happened at Corinthian temple feasts: eating, drinking and immorality, in that order. Worship on your own terms first, and the bed follows; Peor would show it again.

Today’s idols. Nobody in the reader’s street is casting calves out of earrings. But an idol, as Tim Keller put it, is a good thing that has become an ultimate thing: anything you look to for what only God can give. To find yours, finish this sentence honestly: if I lost this, life would not be worth living. Whatever fills that blank is receiving worship. It may be a wholly good thing: a marriage, a child, a reputation, a ministry. Good things make the strongest idols, because nobody thinks to suspect them. Another test is plainer: where the spare money goes, where the free hours go when nobody is watching, and what you think about in the ten minutes before sleep. A person’s theology is on his lips. His worship is in his diary and his bank statement.

Stop feeding the rival. Paul does not tell the Corinthians to manufacture a stronger devotion to God. He tells them to stop feeding a rival. Nobody has ever loved God more by trying harder to feel it; hearts warm to God when the thing that was absorbing the heat is set down. That is why Paul’s command a few lines later is flee from idolatry, a thing you can actually do on a Monday, rather than feel differently, which no one can do by command (10:14; 1 John 5:21).

The mediator who could not pay. After the calf, Moses went back up the mountain to make atonement. He asked God to forgive the people, and if not, to blot him out of the book he had written. God refused: whoever had sinned against him, he would blot out of his book (Exodus 32:30–33). Moses loved them enough to offer himself, and it was not enough, because he was a sinner too and could not stand in their place. The offer that failed on Sinai succeeded on Golgotha. Christ, who had no sin of his own, bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). Idolaters are not saved by a better resolve but by a better Mediator.

Can I worship the true God in a wrong way? Yes, and that is the calf’s lesson. Aaron’s people meant the LORD, and they were still idolaters, because they worshipped him in a form he had forbidden (Exodus 20:4–5). It is possible to believe the right God exists and still shrink him down: to a God who only comforts and never commands, or who agrees with my politics, or who exists to make my plans succeed. The safeguard is simple to state: let God define himself, from his own word, and worship him the way he has revealed. Whenever I find myself thinking, my God would never, it is worth checking whether that sentence comes from Scripture or from me.

parallels.desc: they sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play

verseByVerse.quote: We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sexual immorality. The second of the four sins. The episode is Numbers 25, at Baal of Peor, and Paul chose it deliberately, because it is this chapter’s exact problem in Old Testament dress. Read how it starts: the Moabite women invited the people to the sacrifices of their gods, and the people ate and bowed down to their gods (Numbers 25:1–2). It began with an invitation to dinner. The meal came first; the immorality came second; the idolatry was in both. A Corinthian believer accepting a temple invitation would have said he was only eating. Israel said the same, and twenty-four thousand of them were buried.

Twenty-three thousand. Twenty-four thousand, says Numbers, and there is the difficulty, because Paul writes twenty-three. It deserves a straight answer, because a thoughtful reader will notice it. First, the two texts are not making the same claim. Numbers gives a total for the whole judgment: those who died by the plague were twenty-four thousand (Numbers 25:9). Paul adds a phrase Numbers does not have: in a single day. The chiefs of the people were also executed by judicial sentence (Numbers 25:4–5), and the plague ran until Phinehas stopped it. A day’s toll inside a larger total is not a contradiction of the total. Second, both figures are round. Ancient reporting rounds, and rounding to the nearer or the lower thousand is no more an error than saying a stadium held forty thousand when the turnstiles read 40,412.

The rough edge left standing. Other explanations are offered too: that Paul was rounding down, or counting only the first day of the plague. These are reasonable, and believers can hold Scripture true while admitting that we do not know exactly how Paul reached his figure. What the difference does show is that no one has smoothed the two texts into agreement. Paul knew Numbers well and wrote to a clever church; the small difference has been left standing, the mark of real writers handling real records.

The body that belongs to the Lord. Paul has already told this church why Peor matters for a Christian, and the reason is Christ. Your bodies are members of Christ, he wrote; shall I take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price, so glorify God in your body (6:15, 19–20). Israel at Peor were the LORD’s people by covenant and gave themselves to the Moabite gods with their bodies. A Christian’s body has been purchased by the death of the Son of God and joined to him by his Spirit. Sexual sin is never only a private matter between two people. It takes something that belongs to Christ and hands it to another.

Is this verse a sentence on me if I have already fallen into sexual sin? No, it is a warning, and warnings are given so that people can turn back.
