Paul wrote this to a church in which some had been sexually immoral, and only four chapters earlier he told them: such were some of you, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God (6:11). Justified means declared righteous by God, the guilty verdict cancelled for Christ’s sake; sanctified there means set apart as God’s own and made holy. The judgment at Peor fell on people who went on in their sin without repentance. For anyone who turns to Christ, the judgment has already fallen on him. Confess it plainly to God, break off whatever is feeding it, and if others have been wronged, seek to put it right. Then stand up as one who is forgiven, because you are.

On a Tuesday. Peor began with a dinner invitation. Ask what the dinner invitation is in your life: the friendship that has started to feel secret, the late conversation, the app, the habit of looking. Decline the invitation, and you will rarely face the bed.
verseByVerse.note: Numbers gives 24,000 as the total who died in the plague; Paul speaks of those who fell in a single day.

parallels.desc: Israel and the Moabite women

verseByVerse.quote: We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did and were destroyed by serpents,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Testing Christ. The third sin. The verb is ekpeirazō, to test out, to try to the limit: to push God to see how far you can go before he acts. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read the Lord here, and a few read God; the ESV follows the reading with the strongest early support, and it is the reading a scribe was least likely to invent: a copyist puzzled by Christ in the wilderness might soften it to the Lord, but would hardly sharpen the Lord into Christ. So it is very probably what Paul wrote, and it says the same thing verse 4 said: Christ was with Israel in the wilderness, and the one they were provoking in Numbers 21 was the Son of God.

Serpents. Israel is on a long detour around Edom, and they speak against God and Moses: why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? There is no food and no water, and we loathe this worthless food (Numbers 21:4–5). The worthless food is the manna. They are complaining about the miracle. Fiery serpents come into the camp, people die, and the remedy God gives is a bronze serpent on a pole: look at it and live. Jesus took that image and applied it to himself: as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life (John 3:14–15).

What it is to test Christ. It is not doubt, and it is not asking hard questions; God is patient with both. Testing is defiant presumption, treating his patience as a margin you are entitled to spend, daring him to do something about your sin. Israel had watched him split a sea, and they were probing to see whether he would really follow through on his threats.

The forgiveness factored in. Have you ever done something while quietly counting on being forgiven for it, the forgiveness factored in beforehand, part of the calculation, the cross treated as an allowance? That is not weakness. Weakness falls and is horrified. This is the sin of the confident, which is why it is in a chapter written for people who thought their knowledge kept them safe.

One more sign. Testing has a second form, quieter and commoner: the demand for one more sign. If God would just make this unmistakable, I would obey. Israel had a pillar of fire and asked for evidence. More proof has never yet produced obedience in anybody, because the problem was never the quantity of evidence. Jesus met this exact request in his own wilderness with the exact answer: you shall not put the Lord your God to the test (Matthew 4:7). Where Israel failed the test in the desert, the true Son passed it.

Is it testing God to ask him for guidance or a sign? Not when it is asked humbly. Asking God for wisdom is commanded, and he gives generously (James 1:5). Gideon’s fleece is often cited, but God had already spoken to Gideon plainly, and the fleece was a weak man’s request for reassurance, which God graciously granted rather than a method to copy (Judges 6:36–40). The sin is demanding a sign as the price of obeying what God has already made clear. If Scripture has spoken, the faithful response is to obey, not to ask for a second opinion. Where Scripture leaves the choice open, pray, seek counsel, use the mind God gave you, and trust him to guide.

For worship. Israel spent his patience as if it were theirs to spend, and it was his all along. When the bill for all that provoking finally came due, he paid it himself. The Christ they dared in the desert was dared again at the cross: come down now, and we will believe. He did not come down. Because he stayed, a rebel poisoned by his own defiance has only to look to him and live. There has never been a sinner too far gone for that cure, and never one who looked to him and was turned away.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the Lord.”

parallels.desc: fiery serpents among the people

verseByVerse.quote: nor grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nor grumble. The fourth sin, and of the four this is the one that looks out of place. The word is gongyzō, to mutter, to complain under the breath, a word that sounds like what it describes. Yet grumbling is the sin that killed more of that generation than any other. It was grumbling at the report of the spies that shut the door on the whole nation (Numbers 14:1–4, 29). Perhaps the Corinthians were grumbling against Paul.

The Destroyer. Paul probably has in mind the scene after Korah’s rebellion: when the ground had opened (Numbers 16:31–33), the people grumbled about it the next day, and a plague killed fourteen thousand seven hundred (Numbers 16:41–49). The Destroyer (olothreutēs) is the destroying angel, probably the same figure who passed through Egypt on the night of the Passover (Exodus 12:23; Hebrews 11:28), now walking through Israel’s own camp.

Why God takes it so seriously. Because grumbling is never really about the food. It is a verdict. Every complaint carries an unspoken clause: this arrangement is wrong, and I would have arranged it better. Underneath it lies a claim to the throne: I want a God who runs the world to my plan. The complaint was not that God had failed to provide; it was that his provision was beneath them. Grumbling is the sound a heart makes when it has reviewed God’s management and found it wanting. It is also the most respectable sin in the list. A man can grumble his way through forty years of Sundays, about the music, the preacher and the young people, and be thought a pillar. Israel grumbled their way to a desert grave and never once thought of themselves as rebels.

Grumbling at the true bread. John records the wilderness sin repeated face to face with Christ. When Jesus said, I am the bread that came down from heaven, the Jews grumbled about him (John 6:41), and he answered, Do not grumble among yourselves (John 6:43). The crowd had just quoted the manna in the wilderness (John 6:31), and they muttered at the true bread exactly as their fathers had muttered at the shadow. It was the same verdict: God’s provision is beneath us. And the same verdict was passed most loudly at the cross, the arrangement that looked like the worst management in history and was God’s wisdom for our salvation (1:23–24).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we cannot express sorrow or lament to God. There is a world of difference between grumbling and lament. Around a third of the Psalms are laments, and some of them are savage: how long, O LORD, will you forget me for ever (Psalm 13:1)? God did not merely tolerate those words; he put them in the hymn book and gave them to his people to sing. So the difference is not the presence of pain in the sentence, and it is not the volume. The difference is direction and address. Lament is spoken to God, and it stays in the room with him; it argues, weeps, and will not leave. Grumbling is spoken about God, to everyone except him. Israel in Numbers 11 did not pray. They stood in their tent doorways and talked to each other.

The tell. It is simple and it is worth knowing: when something is wrong, who hears about it first? If the answer is God, that is a sufferer. If the answer is anyone else, that is a grumbler, and the way out is not to suppress the complaint but to redirect it, which is what the Psalms are for.

Is it grumbling to say my job is hard or my church has problems? Not in itself. Describing a hard thing truthfully is not a sin, and some problems need to be raised so that they can be fixed. The question is the spirit and the destination. Raising a concern with the person who can address it, for the sake of the good, is love. Repeating it to everyone else, with a shrug of contempt, for the pleasure of being aggrieved, is grumbling. One builds; the other corrodes. And a heart that has stopped noticing God’s gifts will find something to complain about in any job and any church on earth.

For worship. The Destroyer passed over every house marked with blood on the night of the Passover, and he passes over still. Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed (5:7), and those sheltered under him are safe from the judgment their grumbling deserved. And the Son himself, given a cup more bitter than any wilderness hardship, did not mutter. He said, not my will but yours be done. His contentment in the Father’s will, perfect to the end, is counted to grumblers who trust him.

parallels.desc: the destroyer

verseByVerse.quote: Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Warning patterns. Paul repeats the thought of verse 6 so that nobody misses it. Then come two large claims. The first is about the Old Testament: it was written down for our instruction. The word nouthesia means warning, admonition, the kind of correction a father gives. It was not merely preserved or made available but written with us in view (Romans 15:4; 2 Timothy 3:16). When Moses set down the account of the quail, the calf and the serpents, God intended it to be read by a Gentile believer in a Greek port centuries later, and by whoever is reading it now. The Old Testament is still the Christian’s book.

The end of the ages. The second claim is about where we are standing. Literally, the ends of the ages have arrived at us. Christians live at the climax of history, where all the previous ages meet their fulfilment in Christ (Hebrews 9:26). The old age and the age to come overlap, and we are living in the overlap. What does that mean? The age to come is the new creation God promised, and it has already broken in, because Christ is risen and the Spirit has been given (2 Corinthians 5:17); but the present evil age of sin and death has not yet ended (Galatians 1:4). The decisive act has happened: the Passover Lamb has been sacrificed (5:7), and the tomb is empty. And the world is not yet put right. This makes the warnings weightier, not lighter. Israel had the shadow and fell. We have the substance. They had a rock in the desert; we have the crucified and risen Son and his Spirit living in us. Greater light is a greater privilege and a greater accountability, in that order and always together.

Does the end of the ages mean Christ will return very soon? It means the last days have already begun, and they began with Christ’s first coming (Hebrews 1:2; Acts 2:17). The whole period between his ascension and his return is the last days. Nobody knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36), and Scripture forbids date-setting, but every generation of Christians lives at the end of the ages and must be ready. Scripture does name things that will come first, such as the final rebellion of 2 Thessalonians 2:3, but they are not a timetable to calculate, and they never make his coming less near. His return will be one public, visible event, when he comes to raise the dead and judge the world, not a secret coming in stages. Many Christians who expect a secret rapture before the final coming love the Lord’s appearing just as sincerely; this commentary holds to one visible return because passages such as Matthew 24:30–31 and 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17 describe the gathering of believers as loud, public and at the end. So the right response is not to calculate but to watch: to live each ordinary week as people who may see him before it ends.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take heed. The whole history has been building towards this sentence, and it is not aimed at the struggling man who knows he is weak. It is aimed at the one who thinks that he stands; the verb means supposes, presumes, takes it as settled. In Corinth that was the confident believer with the correct doctrine of idols, sitting down to dinner in a temple and quite sure the theology covered him. Self-confidence is the danger. Peter is the classic example: though they all fall away, I will not (Mark 14:29–31). Within hours he was warming his hands at the enemy’s fire.

In the flow. Therefore gathers up verses 1–11: the privileged generation, its four sins, the graves, and the reminder that all this was written for us. Paul closes the history not with a threat but with a call to watchfulness, and in the very next sentence with a promise (v. 13). In his argument warning and comfort belong together: the warning keeps the confident from presuming, and the promise keeps the frightened from despair. Both prepare for the command of verse 14: flee from idolatry.

The one who prayed for Peter. Luke records what Jesus said to Peter at the table that night, just before the boast: Simon, Satan has demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (Luke 22:31–32). Peter fell, exactly as the warning said he could. But he was not lost, because his standing had never rested on his own confidence. It rested on the prayer of Christ. That is the deepest answer to this verse. The one who thinks he stands is leaning on himself and will go down; the one who knows he could fall is driven to lean on the Saviour who always lives to intercede for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

Can a true Christian finally be lost? The question a Reformed reader will feel immediately should be answered rather than dodged. If Christ says no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28), why the warning? The answer is that the warning is not an alternative to being kept. It is one of the ways God keeps his people. He does not preserve his own by making them immune to danger while they sleep through it; he preserves them by waking them up. Paul writes work out your own salvation with fear and trembling and then, in the same breath, for it is God who works in you (Philippians 2:12–13). Both halves are true and they are not in tension. The alarm that gets a family out of a burning house is not evidence that the fire brigade failed; it is how they were saved. This verse is an alarm, and God has been using it to keep people on their feet for two thousand years. Christians in other traditions read such warnings as showing that a believer can finally fall away, and they are right that the warning is meant in earnest; the difference is over what it is for.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should live in fear of losing salvation. It means overconfidence is dangerous, and humble watchfulness is the mark of the true believer. A true Christian may fall into grievous sin for a time, as David and Peter did, and suffer for it; but those whom God has truly called he keeps, and they are restored (the Westminster Confession 17.1, 3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 17.1, 3).

The frightened reader. If this verse frightens you, it is already doing its work, and you are not the person it is warning. The one in danger is the one who reads it and feels nothing, who assumes at once that it is about somebody else in the congregation. The man most likely to fall down the stairs is the one who says he could walk them in the dark.

The quiet kinds of confidence. The confidence Paul names is not usually loud. It rarely says I could never fall. It says that a certain sin is not in one’s temperament, that a friendship which would look questionable in someone else is fine here, that a habit which flattened another Christian is manageable with better theology. Each is the sentence of a man walking a wall in the dark, telling himself he knows where the edge is.

On a Tuesday. Take heed, not by working up anxiety about your standing, which helps nobody, but by doing the ordinary things a person does who knows he could fall: stay near the means of grace, keep short accounts (confess each sin to God as soon as you see it), tell someone the truth about yourself, and stop rehearsing the sins you have decided you are no longer capable of (compare 9:27; Romans 11:20). The means of grace are simply the ordinary ways God has promised to strengthen faith: his word read and preached, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the company of his people (Acts 2:42).

verseByVerse.quote: No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Common to man. And then, immediately, the promise: Paul will not leave a frightened Christian there for a single sentence longer. Temptation (peirasmos) covers testing, trial and temptation, and the context here is the pull toward sin. Common to man is anthrōpinos: human-sized, the sort of thing human beings get. This is the first mercy of the verse, and it goes straight to a private ache: the conviction that mine is different, a freakish thing that would horrify anyone I told. It is not. Other people have faced it and overcome, and some of them are sitting in your row. The loneliness is a lie, and it is the lie that keeps the sin fed, because a thing you believe is unique is a thing you will never say out loud.

God is faithful. Then the ground of the promise, and it is not you. It is the same phrase that closed the opening thanksgiving of this letter, and there it was tied to Christ: God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord (1:9). The faithfulness that sets the limit on your temptation is the faithfulness that joined you to his Son, and it guards what belongs to him. And look at what that Son faced. In Gethsemane he could have appealed to his Father for more than twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:53), and he would not, because that way out of suffering would have been a way out of his Father’s will. He went on to the cross rather than turn aside, the one man never overcome, and the faithful God keeps his people in that Son’s victory.

Not beyond your ability. This is not a description of your strength. It is a limit God imposes and polices, as he set limits on Satan with Job (Job 1:12; 2:6). He stands at the gate of every trial that comes at you and decides how much of it gets through. He knows our strength, and he will not allow more than his grace can enable us to bear.

The way of escape. The word is ekbasis, a way out; many picture a mountain pass that lets an army get clear of a valley it should never have marched into. With every temptation, God makes an exit. For the Corinthians, the way out of idolatry was to flee (v. 14). In practice the door is usually further back than people look for it: the escape is nearly always upstream. It is the second drink, not the twelfth. It is the reply typed at eleven at night, not the affair eighteen months later. It is the decision about what the laptop does after everyone else is asleep, not the moment of looking. Track any fall backwards and you will find the door standing open at a point that felt utterly harmless at the time.

Able to endure it. The goal is not always removal of the trial but endurance through it. Sometimes the escape God provides is a road out, and sometimes it is the strength to stand in the fire without bowing. Both are the way of escape. Both come from the same faithful God (Hebrews 2:18; 2 Peter 2:9).

Where Christians differ: can believers be overcome? Some take this verse to mean believers never actually fall into sin, or that if they do, they were never really tempted beyond ability. This commentary’s view: God always provides a way to resist, so no believer can say, I had no choice. When believers sin, it is because they did not take the way out, not because God failed. This verse does not promise that believers never fall, but that they never have to. And it promises that God’s faithfulness will see them through (the Westminster Confession 17.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 17.3).

If there was always a way out, am I not guiltier? It is the objection an honest reader raises at once: if there was always a door, then every time I sinned I could have not sinned, and that only makes me guiltier. Yes. That is exactly what the verse says, and pretending otherwise would be no kindness. There was a door. But look at who is standing beside it. The same sentence that removes the excuse names God as faithful, and a God faithful enough to have built the door is faithful enough to forgive the man who walked past it (1 John 1:9). The verse takes away the alibi and hands over the Father in the same breath.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God never gives us more than we can handle in suffering. That popular saying is not in the Bible, and Paul himself flatly denies it about affliction: he was so utterly burdened beyond his strength that he despaired of life itself (2 Corinthians 1:8–9). God does give his children more grief than they can carry. That is often the point of it, because the next line is that we might rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead. So if you are reading this with a diagnosis in your hand or an empty chair at your table, this verse is not telling you that your load has been measured to fit your shoulders. The promise is about temptation to sin: God will always enable us to resist, by his grace.

Does God tempt me, then? No. God tests his people, to prove and strengthen their faith, as he tested Abraham (Genesis 22:1); but he never entices anyone to sin. Let no one say when he is tempted, I am being tempted by God (James 1:13). The same Greek word can mean a test or a temptation, and the same event can be both: God means it for our strengthening while the devil and our own desires mean it for our fall. Joseph’s brothers meant evil, and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). So in every pull toward sin, you can know that God has set its limit, is present in it, and has a purpose of good for you through it.

What if I genuinely cannot see a way out? Then the way out may be closer than you think and smaller than you expected. Very often it is simply to leave: the room, the conversation, the screen. Often it is to tell someone, today, because sin grows in secret and weakens in the light. Sometimes it is to pray out loud, short and honest: Lord, help me now. And when the escape is not removal but endurance, as with a long-standing desire that does not go away, the way out is to keep saying no, one day at a time, with others alongside you. You do not have to see the whole road. God has promised there is one, and he is faithful.

On a Tuesday. Ask while you are calm: for the temptation I know is coming this week, where is the pass out of the valley, and what would I have to decide today to be standing in it? God has promised the way of escape, and the Spirit who raised Jesus lives in you to give the strength to take it (Romans 8:11). He has not promised to carry you through a door you refuse to look for.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — The Lord’s Table and the Demons’ Table
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul gives the command, flee from idolatry, and then the reason. The Lord’s Supper is a real sharing in Christ’s body and blood, and the one loaf makes many believers one body. Israel’s sacrifices bound the worshipper to the altar in the same way. The idol is nothing, but what pagans sacrifice is offered to demons, and no one can share both the Lord’s table and theirs without provoking the Lord to jealousy.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Supper as participation

Paul’s word for the cup and the bread, a participation (koinōnia) in the blood and body of Christ, does not explain how Christ is present, but it insists that he is. Something real happens at the table: believers truly share in Christ and what he has done. Following Calvin rather than Zwingli, Reformed teaching has held that Christ is truly present by his Spirit, giving himself to be received by faith.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: For some Corinthians, dinners at a temple were part of the civic and business life their livelihood depended on, so flee idolatry would have cost them something real. Now: Some parts of cultural and civic life still carry a meaning that a Christian cannot share, and they are not always obvious. Paul’s two tables give the test: what am I actually taking part in when I take part in this?

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, my beloved. My beloved, from a man who has just spent thirteen verses on graves in the desert. He is not a prosecutor. He is a father, and the sternness and the tenderness come from the same place; only someone who loves you tells you the graveyard story.

Flee from idolatry. Then the command, and it is the way of escape God promised a sentence earlier. What Paul does not say is telling. Not study idolatry. Not manage it, negotiate with it, or test how close you can get. Not develop a mature theology of it, which is precisely what the strong Corinthians had done. Flee. The verb (pheugō) is a present imperative, keep on running, make it your standing policy, and it is the same verb he used in 6:18 about sexual immorality. Those are the only two things in this letter that Paul tells the church to run away from, and it is not an accident that they are the two that Corinth’s temple culture served up in the same room. For the Corinthians, it meant: stop attending temple feasts.

Where courage runs. Christians are told to stand and fight almost everywhere else: resist the devil, put on the armour, endure hardship. Here, no. Here courage looks like running, and staying to fight would be folly. Joseph did not reason with Potiphar’s wife or explain his convictions; he left his garment in her hand and got out of the house (Genesis 39:12). There is no medal for how long you stayed in the room.

Running towards someone. Flight in Scripture is never only away. It is always towards. John ends his first letter by naming the one we run to before he names what we run from: we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ; he is the true God and eternal life. Little children, keep yourselves from idols (1 John 5:20–21). The idol is left behind because something better has been found. The Corinthians were not being told to leave the temple and stand in an empty street. They were being called from a dinner with demons to the table of the Lord Jesus, and from a god of stone to the living Christ who had bought them.

Sensible people. Sensible (phronimoi) means wise, thoughtful, and the Corinthians prided themselves on wisdom. Paul appeals to it. Having given a flat command, he now hands them the argument and invites them to check his working. It is a model for anyone who teaches: he does not want compliance without conviction.

What fleeing looks like when the temple is gone. It looks like boring, practical measures people are embarrassed to admit they need. Deleting the thing rather than resolving to use it better. Taking the other road home. Not being alone in that house. Telling one person the truth so that the secret has a witness. Handing over the card, the password, the key. None of it is glamorous, and all of it works where resolutions do not, because it removes the opportunity instead of relying on a will that has already proved unreliable.

Is that not avoidance rather than victory? The objection comes quickly: should a mature Christian not be able to stand in the room? But that question has the shape of the Corinthian error, which was to treat strength as something to be demonstrated. Scripture never asks anyone to prove he can stand beside an idol. The mature response to a fire is not to practise standing in it. Fleeing is the victory; it is simply a victory that gives nobody a story to tell.

Should I get rid of objects connected with my old life? Often, yes. When the Ephesians came to faith, those who had practised magic brought their books and burned them publicly, though they were worth a fortune (Acts 19:19). Objects have no power in themselves, and Paul has said so (8:4). But things that were used in false worship, occult practice or a besetting sin can be a standing invitation back, and getting rid of them is a clear, simple act of turning. There is no need to be superstitious about ordinary things with an odd history. The question is whether this object keeps a door open that Christ has closed.

verseByVerse.quote: The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cup of blessing that we bless. A phrase from the Jewish table: the cup of wine drunk with a prayer of thanksgiving at the end of a meal, especially at Passover. That is the cup the Lord took in his hands in the upper room, on the night a Passover meal became the first Supper, and made it the cup of the new covenant (11:25). That we bless means: over which we give thanks to God.

Is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? Both questions in this verse are rhetorical, expecting the answer yes, and Paul needs that yes, because his whole argument about temple meals depends on a prior conviction: that eating and drinking at a table can be a real sharing in what the table represents. If the Lord’s Supper is only a memory exercise, then a temple dinner is only a dinner, and the strong Corinthians are right. The word he uses is koinōnia: participation, sharing, communion, having something in common with. The English word fellowship has been worn down until it means coffee after the service; the Greek word means a genuine joint holding, the way business partners hold a firm. Paul says the cup is a joint holding in the blood of Christ. To drink it is to share in the benefits of his shed blood: forgiveness and the new covenant.

The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? To eat the bread is to share in Christ himself, crucified for us. He did not hand his people a symbol of a distant event and leave them to remember it as best they could. He gives himself.

One bread, one body. Then the sentence a divided church needs most. One loaf, shared by all, torn, and everyone eats from the same torn loaf. The Supper expresses and strengthens the unity of the church. The phrase body of Christ shifts its meaning between verse 16 and verse 17: from Christ’s crucified body to the church, his body. The one makes the other. Those who share in the body given for them become the body that belongs to him. That is a hard image to hold while maintaining that you are of Paul and he is of Apollos (1:12). The bread on the table is the standing argument against every faction in the room. You cannot eat from one loaf with someone all month and claim to have nothing to do with him. The unity of the church is not something we manufacture by agreeing with each other; it is something we receive by all being fed by the same Lord.

Where Christians differ: what happens in the Lord’s Supper? It is worth answering carefully, because a reader has probably heard three answers and been told the differences are enormous. Roman Catholics teach transubstantiation: the bread and wine become the actual body and blood of Christ. Lutherans teach that Christ’s body and blood are present in, with and under the bread and wine. Many evangelicals hold a memorial view: the Supper is only a reminder. Those who hold it rightly guard against superstition, and many of them find great blessing at the table. This commentary’s view: The bread and wine remain bread and wine (11:26–28 still calls it bread). But the Supper is more than a memorial: Paul calls it a real participation in Christ, and a reminder is not a participation. The Reformed view, taught by Calvin, is that Christ is truly present by his Spirit, and believers, by faith, really feed on Christ spiritually, receiving him and all the benefits of his death. Christ’s body is in heaven, but the Spirit lifts us up to commune with him (the Westminster Confession 29.7; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 30.7). Christ is truly present, not physically but spiritually, and truly given to faith.

Not nothing and not magic. Calvin was content to say he experienced the thing more surely than he could explain it. What that means at the table is this: when you eat, you are not performing a memory. You are receiving, by faith, the Christ who died, and he is giving himself to you as certainly as the bread is in your hand. The Christ who is present is a risen and ascended Christ who is not brought back down to be offered again, because the offering was made once for all (Hebrews 10:12).

If Christ is not physically present, is the Supper only symbolic after all? No. Spiritual does not mean imaginary or less real. The Holy Spirit is the most real presence in the world; he is how Christ dwells in his people at all. In the Supper the Spirit truly unites believers to the living Christ, and faith truly receives him, as truly as the mouth receives the bread. The bread is a sign, but it is not an empty sign; God uses it as a means of grace, to nourish faith, deepen assurance and draw us closer to Christ and to each other. That is why the Supper is to be received often and with expectation, not treated as an occasional add-on to the sermon.

Who should come to the table? Those who have trusted Christ and been baptised as believers, who belong to his church, and who come in repentance and faith. This commentary places baptism on profession of faith before the table, following the order of Acts 2:41–42; churches that baptise infants differ on the order, not on the need for faith. It is not for the unbeliever, because the whole meal is a participation in Christ, and you cannot share in someone you have refused. But it is also not a prize for the spiritually accomplished. It is food for the hungry. The weak Christian who is fighting sin and trusting Christ should come; that is exactly who the bread is for. Paul will say more about coming in a worthy manner in 11:27–32.

On a Tuesday. At the next Lord’s Supper, come expecting to meet Christ. Feed on him by faith, and look around at the one body you belong to. If there is someone in that room you are refusing to be reconciled to, the bread is asking you a question. Begin to put it right before you eat.
verseByVerse.note: “The cup of blessing” was the Jewish name for a cup of wine drunk with thanksgiving at a meal, including the Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: Consider the people of Israel: are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? What do I imply then? That food offered to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider the people of Israel. Literally, Israel according to the flesh: the nation in its worship. Paul is building a case with three tables: the Lord’s, Israel’s, and the demons’. The principle is that eating from a sacrifice puts you in league with the altar it came from.

Are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? The Old Testament practice behind this is the peace offering, and it is worth knowing, because many modern readers assume every sacrifice was burnt whole. It was not. In the peace offering, part went up on the fire to God, part went to the priest, and the rest was eaten by the worshipper and his household in a meal on the spot (Leviticus 7:15–16; Deuteronomy 12:17–18). It was a shared dinner with God as host. Nobody in Israel thought of it as a snack with religious decoration. To eat there was to be counted in, sharing in the worship, in fellowship with the God to whom it was offered.

We have an altar. Paul sets Israel’s altar beside the Lord’s table because the same logic runs through both. At Israel’s altar the worshipper ate from a sacrifice and was counted in. At the Lord’s table believers share in the body and blood of Christ (10:16), the one sacrifice that is never repeated. Hebrews says it plainly: we have an altar (Hebrews 13:10). Christ has made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). We do not eat in order to make peace. We eat because he has made it, and to eat is to be counted in with him.

What do I imply then? That food offered to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything? Paul steps in front of an objection before it is raised. He knows exactly what the clever ones in Corinth will say: you told us in chapter 8 that an idol has no real existence and there is no God but one, and now you are treating idol meat as though it were charged with something. His answer, coming in the next verse, is not a retreat. He still holds what he said in 8:4. He is not about to concede that the idol is real after all. He is about to say that what pagans sacrifice, they offer to demons. The Corinthians had started from a true premise and drawn a wrong conclusion, and a great deal of confident Christian foolishness lives in that gap.

What about halal or other religiously slaughtered meat today? The principles of this chapter answer it. Meat sold in an ordinary shop or served at a friend’s table, even if a prayer was said at its slaughter, is simply food that belongs to the Lord (vv. 25–27); a Christian may eat it with thanks and does not need to investigate. What a Christian should not do is take part in a religious act: eat it as part of a festival offered to another god, or in a way that would be understood, by those watching, as joining in their worship. And if someone at the table makes a point of its religious meaning, and eating would confuse him or another believer, verse 28 applies: decline quietly, for his sake.

For worship. On the mountain of the covenant the elders of Israel beheld God, and ate and drank (Exodus 24:11). That has always been his heart: not merely to be obeyed from a distance, but to eat with his people. The holy God, who could have kept sinners at the bottom of the mountain for ever, keeps setting tables for them. He fed Israel at the altar, he feeds the nations now at the table of his Son, and he will sit down with his whole redeemed people at the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9), where no one will ever be sent home hungry again.
verseByVerse.note: Worshippers ate part of many sacrifices, sharing a meal with God.

verseByVerse.quote: No, I imply that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God. I do not want you to be participants with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Offered to demons. The correction is precise. The strong Corinthians reasoned: the idol is nothing, therefore there is nothing at the altar, therefore the meal is empty of spiritual content. Every step of that but the last is right. Nothing at the altar is not the same as nobody at the altar. The statue is only stone, yet somebody is receiving what is offered, and it is not God: demons (daimonia). Paul is not inventing this. He is quoting the same song of Moses he drew on in verse 4: they sacrificed to demons that were no gods, to gods they had never known (Deuteronomy 32:17). The Old Testament had already said both halves, no gods and demons, and held them together without embarrassment.

Participants with demons. Participants (koinōnoi) means partners, sharers: the same family of words as the participation in Christ in verse 16. Deliberate participation in false worship is spiritual adultery.

Is any of this still live? The question a modern reader will have should not be left hanging. The temples are museums now. But the impulse to reach past God for power or knowledge on terms he has not authorised has never gone out of fashion, and it is currently doing extremely well. The card reading booked as a laugh, the app that gives the daily horoscope, the ancestor shrine kept in the corner because the family expects it, the ceremony entered into on holiday because it seemed rude to decline. In every case the reasoning is the Corinthian reasoning: it is nonsense, so it is harmless. Paul’s answer is that the first clause does not deliver the second.

Do thoughtful people still have to believe in demons? Jesus did, and he was not a credulous man. He spoke soberly about Satan and cast out demons as part of his work (Mark 1:34; Luke 11:20). Some suggest he was simply speaking the language of his time, but he did not hesitate to correct popular beliefs elsewhere (Mark 7:13; John 9:2–3). Scripture does not ask us to see a devil behind every misfortune, and it has none of the lurid fascination of a horror film. It simply says that there are created spiritual powers opposed to God, and that false worship is not empty but is a service they are glad to receive. For the Christian the main note is not fear but confidence: these powers are real, and they are already under the feet of the risen Christ (Ephesians 1:20–22).

Where is the line? Being present is not the same as taking part. A Christian may attend a friend’s wedding in a temple or a family funeral with rites he does not share, as a guest who loves the people there. He may not join in the worship itself: bowing to the image, offering incense, reciting the prayers, or eating what is presented to him as offered to the god (v. 28). Practices that are religious in their very content belong on the same side of the line, such as yoga built around chants and devotion to Hindu deities, even when it is sold as exercise; simple stretching is not the issue. When family pressure comes, the believer can explain gently that he honours them and will be there, but that he worships Christ alone.

You cannot. Temple feasts included cups of wine poured out to the god. Not may not, but cannot. Paul is not laying down a rule that could in principle be broken discreetly. He is describing an impossibility, the way no one can be faithful to two husbands at once. The attempt does not produce a double portion. It produces the loss of the first.

Two tables. Invitations to dine at the couch of the lord Serapis survive on papyrus from Roman Egypt, most of them a little later than Paul, and they show how naturally pagans spoke of a meal hosted by a god. Paul takes that kind of language and sets beside it the table of the Lord, a phrase from the prophets for the Lord’s altar (Malachi 1:7, 12). Two tables, two hosts, two loyalties. Divided loyalty is impossible.

The cup that bought you. Why can a Christian not hold both cups? Because of what the first cup is. On the night he was betrayed the Lord Jesus called it the new covenant in my blood (11:25). It is not a neutral drink he lends his guests; it is the pledge of a covenant sealed with his own life, and the guest at the Lord’s table has been purchased by the host (6:19–20). To lift the demons’ cup is not merely to add a second loyalty. It is to offer what Christ has bought to his enemy.

What about Halloween, or Christmas trees with pagan roots? The line in this chapter is participation in worship, not the distant history of a custom. Most customs in any culture have tangled origins, and a thing that was once religious can become simply ordinary, as the market meat did (v. 25). A Christmas tree in a Christian home worships no one. The question to ask of any practice is what it means now, to the people doing it and watching it: is it plain fun, or is it a celebration of death, the occult or a spiritual power other than Christ? Christians will draw these lines in slightly different places, and Romans 14 asks them not to despise one another for it. But nobody should take part in anything that is, in its present meaning, a rite offered to another power.

parallels.desc: they sacrificed to demons that were not God

verseByVerse.quote: Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Two short questions, left unanswered because they answer themselves. The first is from the song of Moses: they stirred him to jealousy with strange gods, and provoked him with their idols (Deuteronomy 32:16, 21). Israel did it, and was judged. Jealousy sounds like a vice, but there are two jealousies. One is envy: wanting what belongs to somebody else. That is never in God, and never can be, since everything is already his. The other is the jealousy of a husband for his own wife, and it is not a defect in him but the proof that the marriage is real (Exodus 20:5; 34:14). A man who watched his wife leave with another man and felt nothing would have stopped loving her long ago. God’s jealousy is of that second kind. He has bound himself to a people, and he will not be treated as one option among several. His jealousy is not petty, but holy love that will not share his bride with rivals.

The jealous Lord has a name. In this chapter the Lord whose table it is (v. 21) is the Lord Jesus, and the Lord we must not provoke is most likely the same Lord. Paul does here what he did with the Rock (v. 4) and the testing in the desert (v. 9): he takes words that the song of Moses spoke of the LORD and speaks them of Christ. So the jealousy is the jealousy of a bridegroom. Paul writes to this same church: I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2). The one who would be provoked by a Christian at a demons’ table is not a distant deity but the Bridegroom himself.

Are we stronger than he? The second question is flatter and more frightening, and it is aimed at the strong in Corinth. You think you are strong. Are you stronger than God? Paul has just filled thirteen verses with corpses in the wilderness, so the reader knows what the question is doing. It asks a congregation of the confident whether they have thought about who it is they are provoking. There is a way of using Christian freedom that is not really freedom at all but a small experiment in whether God will actually do anything.

Test it against the alternative. Suppose God were not jealous. Suppose he watched his people give their affections to whatever caught them, and felt nothing. That God would be easier to live with, and he would be worth nothing, because his tolerance would be the measure of his indifference. Nobody has ever been comforted at a graveside by a deity who did not much mind.

Does God’s jealousy mean he resents the good things I love? No. He gave them to you. God is not jealous of your wife, your children, your garden or your work; he is jealous for your heart, that it should love him first, and love all these as his gifts. In fact, the things we love are safest when they are not our gods. A child who is loved as an idol is crushed by the weight of being someone’s whole meaning; a child who is loved under God can be loved freely. God’s jealousy guards our joys rather than competing with them.

For worship. Is he strong? Yes: look at the wilderness. Does he care? Yes: look at the jealousy. A god who was strong and did not care would be a terror. A god who cared and was not strong would be a tragedy. The idols are neither, and neither is anyone else who has ever been worshipped. But our God is both. To be loved by someone who will not share you is a fearful thing and a safe thing at once. Cold gods let you drift. This one comes after his own. He is jealous because the cost of getting his people was his own Son, and he does not shrug about what his Son has bled for.

parallels.desc: they have made me jealous with what is no god

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–33 — Do All to the Glory of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul answers the Corinthian slogan: not everything that is lawful builds others up, so seek your neighbour’s good. Food from the market may be eaten without questions, because the earth is the Lord’s, and so may a meal in an unbeliever’s home. But if someone points out that the food was offered in sacrifice, decline for that person’s sake, while staying free before God. The section ends with the principle that covers it all: do everything to the glory of God, and give no needless offence, so that many may be saved.
verseByVerse.theology:
To God alone be glory, in ordinary life

The Reformers’ watchword soli Deo gloria, to God alone be glory, has one of its roots in verse 31. A meal, a conversation, a day’s work can be an act of worship when it is received from God and done for him. So the Reformed churches have taught that all of life is lived before God, and that the line people draw between sacred and ordinary parts of life does not hold.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Verses 25–28 gave the Corinthians practical wisdom for daily life. Ask no questions at the market, which spared them needless scruples; take care at the dinner table, which protected the weak and the unbeliever. Both were shaped by God’s glory and others’ good, not by personal preference. Now: Do all to the glory of God is not a slogan but a habit: asking, in any situation, how this act or this conversation can honour him.

verseByVerse.quote: “All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful,” but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The slogan again. It was quoted first at 6:12, and it is very probably the Corinthians’ own line, the sort of thing a church says when it has learned grace and is enjoying it. Paul now turns from the temple to the question of meat at home and in the market. He does not delete the slogan. He puts a comma after it. Twice.

Helpful, and building up. The two tests he attaches are not is it permitted. Is it helpful: does it get anyone anywhere? And does it build up (oikodomeō), a construction word, the same root as edification: does anyone end up stronger because you did it? That is the test of love (8:1). Both questions have someone else in them. The lawfulness question can be answered alone in a room. These cannot. The picture, used all through the letter, is of a congregation as a structure going up, course by course, where the question about any action is not merely whether it damages anyone but whether it adds a stone. A great deal of Christian liberty is defended on the grounds that it hurts no one. That is a lower bar than the one in this verse.

The neighbour’s good. This one short sentence governs everything from chapter 8 to chapter 11. Love looks to others’ interests (Philippians 2:4), and Paul means it more radically than it is usually applied. The usual version is: enjoy your freedom, but be considerate. Paul’s version puts the neighbour’s good in the driving seat, not the passenger seat. And for some Christians freedom itself becomes the idol: being the one who knows better, who is not bound by the scruples of lesser believers. A liberty that must be shown off to be enjoyed has stopped being a gift and become a badge.

Christ did not please himself. Paul grounds this same rule in Christ when he writes to Rome: let each of us please his neighbour for his good, to build him up. For Christ did not please himself (Romans 15:2–3). The Son of God was the one person who had every right to seek his own good, and he sought ours instead, all the way to the cross. The whole gospel is this verse lived out by God: the Lord of all did not look to his own interests, but to the interests of people who had nothing to offer him. A Christian who gives up a liberty for a brother is not inventing a sacrifice. He is copying, in a very small way, the shape of the life that saved him.

How do I know whether something builds up? Ask three questions about the people actually involved. Will this help them trust and obey Christ more, or make it harder? Will it draw them toward the church and its fellowship, or push them away? And would I be glad for them to copy me in this? You will not always know the answer, and you are not responsible for every possible reaction of every possible person. But when you know that a particular brother or sister would be hurt or misled, love lets that knowledge decide. And the question works positively too: building up is not only refraining from harm, but looking for the word, the visit or the gift that will strengthen someone.

verseByVerse.quote: Eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising any question on the ground of conscience. For “the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The meat market. After all that solemnity, a relaxed instruction, because Paul protects the over-scrupulous as much as the over-confident. The word is makellon, the covered meat and fish market at the centre of the city; excavators at Corinth have turned up an inscription naming one. Some of the meat on those slabs, perhaps much of it, had come from a temple, since sacrifices produced more carcasses than the priests and worshippers could eat and the surplus was sold on.

Without raising any question. A conscientious believer could spend his life interrogating butchers. Paul’s ruling is not ask, and then decide, but do not ask. Once it has left the temple, it is just food. There is pastoral kindness in that. For a certain sort of person the investigation never ends, and a conscience kept permanently on duty does not become holier, only more exhausted. Sometimes the godly course is to close the question rather than to research it, and to eat the dinner in front of you with thanks.

The Lord owns the earth. Paul gives the reason from Psalm 24:1, a verse later Jewish teachers cited as the reason to give thanks before eating. The idol does not get to change the ownership of a cow. A false priest can mutter over a carcass all afternoon and not transfer the title; the beast belonged to God when it was born, belonged to God on the altar, and belongs to God on the slab. Nothing in the world has been successfully stolen from its Maker.

The Lord who owns the market. In Psalm 24 the owner is the LORD. In this letter Paul has already named him: there is one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist (8:6). The cattle on the Corinthian slabs were made through Christ, and in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:16–17). That is why the believer may eat without fear. He is not eating in enemy territory, picking his way through things that belong to other gods. He is eating at the table of his own Lord, who made the meat, rules the market and redeemed the man who buys it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean contradicting verses 14–22. There, the issue was taking part in temple worship; here, it is buying ordinary meat. One guard is needed, or this freedom will be stretched into something Paul has just forbidden. There is a difference between eating a piece of meat with a history and taking a seat at a rite: between buying a chop that once passed an altar and going to the altar. The first is a question about property, and God owns everything. The second is a question about allegiance, and no one may hold two. Paul is not inconsistent; he is drawing a line, and the line falls exactly where participation begins.

Does this mean Christians may eat any food at all, including what the Old Testament forbade? Yes. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and God taught Peter the same lesson in a vision (Acts 10:13–15). The food laws of Moses were part of the old covenant’s marking out of Israel, and they pointed to a holiness that Christ has now brought. So a Christian may eat pork, shellfish, or anything else with thanks. What remains is the law of love: if your eating would harm a brother, you may choose not to (Romans 14:20–21). And what remains is the call to self-control; freedom to eat anything is not a licence to be ruled by the stomach.

parallels.desc: the earth is the LORD’s and the fullness thereof

verseByVerse.quote: If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you are disposed to go, eat whatever is set before you without raising any question on the ground of conscience. But if someone says to you, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience—
verseByVerse.commentary:
An invitation to dinner. Paul assumes without argument that Christians will be invited to dinner in unbelievers’ homes, and may accept. This is a private home, not a temple, and there is no list of precautions. Fleeing idolatry is not the same as avoiding idolaters; he has already said so in this letter, and bluntly: to avoid them entirely you would need to go out of the world (5:10). Disposed to go (thelō, if you want to) leaves the decision genuinely open. Some invitations are not wise for a given believer at a given time, and Paul does not pretend otherwise. But the default is yes.

Whatever is set before you. The manners at the table are simple. Do not interrogate your host; enjoy the meal, as Jesus told his disciples to eat what was set before them (Luke 10:8). A guest who cross-examines his host about the origin of the lamb is not being holy; he is being a poor guest, and the gospel is not served by it.

The Lord who accepted invitations. Paul’s relaxed instruction is the pattern of Jesus himself. He went to dinner with Levi and his tax-collector friends, with Zacchaeus, and with Pharisees who were watching him closely (Luke 5:29; 19:5; 14:1). He was called a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners (Luke 7:34), and he did not stop going. He sat at those tables not because he approved of everything said there, but because he had come to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). A Christian at an unbeliever’s table is not on dangerous ground in himself. He is walking where his Lord walked.

If someone says. Then the one situation that changes everything. The word is hierothyton, sacred offering, the polite pagan word, rather than the Jewish and Christian word for idol-food used elsewhere; it sounds like something said at the table, perhaps by the host, perhaps by another guest, perhaps half as a test of the Christian. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, repeat at the end of verse 28 the line the earth is the Lord’s; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles omit it.

Do not eat it. Nothing about the meat has changed. The information has. Once somebody has put it into words, the meal has become a statement, and it will be read as one: that the Christian approves of idol worship, or does not take his faith seriously. The speaker may be a young believer watching to see what freedom looks like, or a curious pagan guest. Either way, a person has just told you that this matters to him, and Paul’s instruction is to let it matter. The conscience in view is the other person’s (v. 29). Put the fork down. Say nothing pious. That is a useful principle well beyond first-century meat: the moment someone signals that a thing is loaded for him, your liberty stops being the only fact in the room.

How to decline. First, do it quietly. Paul gives no speech to accompany the refusal; a Christian who declines the dish and then explains at length why he is entitled to eat it but is graciously abstaining has kept the meat and taken the credit as well. Second, do not shame the host. The whole manoeuvre is for the sake of someone else’s conscience, and a refusal delivered as a verdict on the household undoes the very thing it was meant to protect.

What is the modern equivalent? The clearest one is alcohol. A Christian is free to drink wine in moderation; Scripture calls it a gift that gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15), and drunkenness, not drinking, is the sin. But if you are at a meal with a friend who is fighting alcoholism, or with a young believer who has just come out of a drinking life and says so, the situation has changed. Your glass is no longer only a glass. Leave it empty that evening, without fuss or explanation, and enjoy his company. You have lost nothing, and he may have gained a great deal.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not mean your conscience, but his. For why should my liberty be determined by someone else’s conscience? If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not mean your conscience, but his. This looks at first like Paul contradicting himself: he has just said do not eat, and now he asks why anybody else’s conscience should govern him. The resolution is in this clause. Your own conscience is clear; you abstain for the other person’s sake.

For why should my liberty be determined by someone else’s conscience? Whether Paul is voicing the strong believer’s objection or speaking for himself, he agrees with it: in principle, my freedom is not ruled by others’ scruples. I am still free before God. What he surrenders in verse 28 is the use of his freedom on that occasion. What he refuses to surrender here is the freedom itself, and the verdict on it. His conscience is not remade by his neighbour’s. He does not walk away from that dinner thinking he was nearly defiled, or that the meat was in fact unclean after all. He walks away free, having chosen not to spend his freedom in front of someone it would injure.

If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks? Denounced (blasphēmeō) is spoken against, slandered. If I thank God for food, how can anyone condemn me? Paul’s point is that he gives up his freedom voluntarily, not because the other person’s conscience binds his, but to avoid having his good thing spoken of as evil (Romans 14:16). And there is a small warmth in with thankfulness. Paul’s instinct at a table is to give thanks, which is what a man does who believes verse 26: that the food, the evening and the world belong to God. He is not defending a right to indulge. He is defending a right to be grateful without apologising for it (Romans 14:22; 1 Timothy 4:4–5).

Two opposite disasters. Getting this wrong produces two opposite disasters. Collapse the distinction one way and you get the Christian who bulldozes: my liberty is real, therefore I will exercise it, and if that ruins you, learn some theology. Collapse it the other way and you get a church governed by whoever is most easily upset, where every scruple anyone raises becomes binding on everybody, and the strongest conscience in the room is the narrowest one. Paul will not have either. Love limits what I do with my freedom. It does not hand my conscience over to a committee.

The free Son who paid the tax. Matthew tells of a moment when Jesus did exactly what Paul is describing. Collectors of the temple tax asked Peter whether his teacher paid it. Jesus pointed out that kings do not tax their own sons: then the sons are free. However, not to give offence to them, he sent Peter to find a coin in a fish’s mouth and pay for them both (Matthew 17:24–27). The Son of the house owed nothing, said so plainly, and paid anyway. He gave up the use of his freedom without for a moment giving up the freedom itself. And the brother for whose sake a Christian yields is never a mere obstacle: he is the brother for whom Christ died (8:11).

Who is the weaker brother I should give way to? Not simply anyone who disapproves of me. In Paul’s argument the weak brother is someone who might be drawn, by my example, into doing what his own conscience still condemns, and so be damaged in his faith (8:10–11). That is very different from the person who has turned his own preferences into rules for everybody and is merely annoyed by my freedom. Jesus did not yield to the Pharisees over hand-washing or healing on the Sabbath (Mark 7:1–13; 3:1–6); when people try to bind consciences with man-made rules as if they were God’s law, love may require standing firm (Galatians 2:3–5). The question is always: would my action wound a fragile believer, or only offend a critic?

A rule the anxious can live by. When you give something up for the sake of another Christian, you are not conceding that he was right and you were wrong. You are not adding a rule to your own life, and you need not feel guilty about the thing next Tuesday when he is not there. Charity is not the same as agreement, and giving way is not the same as being convinced. A conscience that quietly takes on every restriction anybody around it holds ends in a Christian who cannot enjoy anything and cannot say why, serving other people’s opinions rather than God. Paul’s way is harder and cleaner: know that you are free, and then choose, in this room, on this evening, for this person, not to use it.

verseByVerse.quote: So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, whether you eat or drink. Three chapters about butchers, dinner parties, weak brothers and demons come down to one sentence broad enough to cover a life. Paul could have begun with prayer or preaching. He begins with chewing and swallowing, the most unremarkable thing a body does, and says that this too can be done to the glory of God. If eating qualifies, nothing is excluded.

Or whatever you do. Everything: work, rest, play, speech, spending, sleep. The line between sacred and ordinary bits of life does not survive this verse. There is no part of a Tuesday that is off the map.

Do all to the glory of God. The governing purpose of the Christian life. To glorify God (doxa) is to show his worth, to honour him, to make him look as great as he is. The Westminster Shorter Catechism begins here: man’s chief end is to glorify God and enjoy him for ever (Q. 1). No part of life is outside this. The Reformers stressed that ordinary work and meals are as sacred as prayer when done for God; the milkmaid and the minister serve the same Lord.

The one whose food was his Father’s will. Only one life has ever fully kept this verse. When his disciples urged him to eat, Jesus said, My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work (John 4:34). At the end he could say to the Father, I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do (John 17:4). Every meal he ate, every road he walked and every hour at the carpenter’s bench was done to the glory of God. Our eating and drinking will never be that pure. But those who belong to him are being remade in his likeness, and the life that perfectly glorified God is counted to them as their own. That is what Scripture means when it speaks of righteousness credited to us: God treats the believer as having his Son’s obedience, because he is joined to him by faith (2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). We do not glorify God in order to be accepted; we glorify him because in Christ we already are.

What has to be true of a plate of food for it to glorify God? To the glory of God is exactly the sort of phrase that can be repeated for years without meaning anything, so let it be spelled out. That it is received rather than seized: taken as a gift from a hand, not a right that was owed. That it is eaten with thanks, spoken and meant, since everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4). That it is enjoyed and not worshipped; there is a way of eating that is really an attempt to be comforted by something that cannot comfort. That it is not taken at someone else’s expense, which is the whole burden of this chapter. And that the one eating is content for God to be looking, which is a test that can be run on any activity in about four seconds.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we must be constantly thinking about God in every second. A surgeon glorifies God by concentrating on the operation, not by thinking about theology during it. It means our whole life is offered to him, done in a way that honours him.

How do I glorify God in a dull job or a long day of chores? By doing it well, honestly and for him. Paul told slaves, who had the dullest and hardest work in the ancient world, to work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, because it is the Lord Christ they were serving (Colossians 3:23–24). The spreadsheet, the nappy, the shelf-stacking and the commute are not interruptions to the Christian life; they are where most of it happens. Do the work with integrity, treat the people around you with kindness, give thanks for the strength to do it, and rest when the day is done, trusting God with what is left undone. Nobody sees most of it. God does, and he is glorified by it.

On a Tuesday. Take the last hour of yesterday and ask what would have had to change for it to have been offered to God. Very often the answer is nothing about the activity and everything about the aim. The Christian does not need a different life to have a life full of worship; he needs the one he has, turned in a different direction.

verseByVerse.quote: Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God, just as I try to please everyone in everything I do, not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they may be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give no offense. Give no offence (aproskopoi) means not causing stumbling, putting no unnecessary obstacle in anyone’s way. Paul names three groups and covers the whole world: the Jew, the Gentile and the church. He circumcised Timothy for the sake of the first (Acts 16:3), lived as one outside the law among the second (9:21), and would give up meat for ever for the sake of the third (8:13).

Please everyone. This clause raises a genuine problem. To the Galatians Paul wrote that if he were still trying to please man, he would not be a servant of Christ (Galatians 1:10). They are the same principle applied to opposite motives. In Galatians, the pleasing was a way of buying safety: certain men wanted to avoid persecution for the cross (Galatians 6:12), so they trimmed the message and kept their position. The object of that exercise was themselves. Here the pleasing is not people-pleasing for approval but accommodating for their good (9:19–22). The difference shows in where it leads: the people-pleaser gives way when giving way keeps him liked, while Paul gave way when it brought others nearer to Christ, and was beaten for the gospel he would not bend (2 Corinthians 11:24–25).

Not my own advantage. Here the object is stated outright. The goal is the salvation of others, and Paul’s whole life is shaped by it. He yields his preferences, his diet, his rights and his dignity to remove every obstacle between a person and Christ, and he will not yield one syllable of the gospel to remove an obstacle between himself and trouble.

As I am of Christ. Paul’s very next sentence tells us where he learned this: be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (11:1). Not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, is a portrait of the Lord before it is a portrait of the apostle. Though he was in the form of God, he made himself nothing, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:6–8). Paul’s changed diet and given-up rights are a small copy of that great descent, and so is every Christian’s.

What it does not mean. It does not mean avoiding the offence of the cross (1:23). The gospel itself offends; we must not add needless offence of our own.

How far can I adapt to win people? As far as you like in everything that is truly indifferent, and not an inch in what God has commanded or forbidden. Paul changed his diet, his customs, his manner and his timetable for the sake of others; he would not change the gospel, join in sin, or hide the cross. So learn the culture of the people you love, eat their food, speak their language, enjoy their company, and drop the habits of your own background that are mere preferences. But never pretend to agree with what Scripture calls sin, and never soften the message so that Christ sounds less necessary. Adaptation is for the sake of the message, never at its expense.

On a Tuesday. The next time you soften something, delay something, or leave something unsaid, ask who the accommodation is actually for: whether the other person is nearer to being saved, or you nearer to being comfortable. The two look identical from outside and are opposites inside.

10.text: <sup>1</sup>For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea,<sup>2</sup>and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,<sup>3</sup>and all ate the same spiritual food,<sup>4</sup>and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ.<sup>5</sup>Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.<sup>6</sup>Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did.<sup>7</sup>Do not be idolaters as some of them were; as it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.”<sup>8</sup>We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day.<sup>9</sup>We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did and were destroyed by serpents,<sup>10</sup>nor grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer.<sup>11</sup>Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come.<sup>12</sup>Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.<sup>13</sup>No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.<sup>14</sup>Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.<sup>15</sup>I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say.<sup>16</sup>The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?<sup>17</sup>Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.<sup>18</sup>Consider the people of Israel: are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar?<sup>19</sup>What do I imply then? I do not want you to be participants with demons.<sup>21</sup>You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.<sup>22</sup>Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?<sup>23</sup>“All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful,” but not all things build up.<sup>24</sup>Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor.<sup>25</sup>Eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising any question on the ground of conscience.<sup>26</sup>For “the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.”<sup>27</sup>If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you are disposed to go, eat whatever is set before you without raising any question on the ground of conscience.<sup>28</sup>But if someone says to you, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience—<sup>29</sup>I do not mean your conscience, but his. 11.title: Head Coverings and the Lord’s Supper
11.overview:
Chapters 11–14 deal with problems in the church’s gatherings. The first concerns how men and women appear when they pray or prophesy. In the Roman world clothing and hair sent strong signals: a respectable married woman covered her head in public, and going uncovered could suggest immodesty or rebellion, while men did not cover their heads except in some pagan rites. Some Corinthian women, perhaps reasoning that in Christ such distinctions no longer mattered, were praying uncovered. Paul answers from creation and from the order of headship, God, Christ, man, woman, while insisting that in the Lord men and women depend on each other.

The second problem was worse. The Lord’s Supper was eaten as part of a shared meal in a wealthy member’s house, and the host’s friends ate the best food early while latecomers, often slaves who had worked all day, arrived to little or nothing. Paul says this is not the Lord’s Supper at all. He repeats what he received from the Lord, reminds them that the meal proclaims Christ’s death until he comes, and warns that eating in an unworthy way brings the Lord’s discipline. They must examine themselves, and wait for one another.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul begins with praise for holding to what he taught them, and then sets out the order of headship: Christ the head of every man, the husband the head of his wife, God the head of Christ. From it he argues about head coverings in worship, drawing on creation, the angels, and the ordinary sense of what is fitting. In the middle he places the balance: in the Lord men and women depend on each other, and all things are from God. He ends by refusing to let the matter become a fight.
verseByVerse.theology:
Headship, order and the Trinity

Paul models the relationship of husband and wife on the relationship of the Father and the Son (v. 3), and this is one of the most debated texts in the doctrine of the Trinity. Most Reformed theologians have understood the head of Christ is God to describe the Son’s willing submission in his mission of salvation, not a lower rank in his being, since the Son is fully God. Either way, Paul takes the order within God’s own life as the pattern for an order between equals in the church’s worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In Corinth a married woman praying with her head uncovered could be read as immodest, or as rejecting the order of marriage, and that would harm the church’s witness. Now: In most Western settings a head covering no longer carries that meaning. The principle remains: worship should honour God with fitting dignity, and the difference between male and female is a gift to be honoured, not erased.

verseByVerse.quote: Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Chapter 11 opens Paul’s teaching on public worship, which runs to chapter 14. Verse 1 closes the argument begun at 8:1: imitate Paul as he imitates Christ. Then come two problems. First, praying and prophesying (vv. 2–16): some wives, it seems, were throwing off the head covering, in that culture the sign of a married woman’s honour.
