Paul answers from an order rooted in creation: Christ is the head of every man, the husband of his wife, God of Christ; yet in the Lord men and women depend on each other completely. Second, the Lord’s Supper (vv. 17–34): the rich ate their fill while the poor went hungry. Paul recites what the Lord handed down: the bread and cup proclaim his death until he comes. So examine yourselves, and wait for one another. Over both halves stands the Son who gladly does his Father’s will, and who on the night he was betrayed broke bread for those who would desert him.

Be imitators of me. The word is mimētai, from which we get mimic. Read on its own it sounds like the most arrogant sentence in the letter. But look at what Paul has just finished describing, because that is what he is offering to have copied: a man who gave up his right to be paid (9:12), his right to marry (9:5), his right to eat what he liked (8:13), and his right to be understood, so that people who were not his responsibility might be saved (9:19–23; 10:33). He is not saying admire me. He is saying watch what I gave up, and do that.

As I am of Christ. The second clause governs the first. It is the qualification and the source. Paul is not the original; he is a copy being held up, and he is careful to say so. The pattern is the Son of God, who did not please himself (Romans 15:3), who had every right there is and used none of them for himself, who emptied himself and took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:5–8). Paul is one step nearer in the chain, close enough to be seen. Imitate Paul only so far as he imitates Christ.

How the Christian life is learned. Nobody learns to be a Christian from a definition. People learn it the way they learn a trade or an accent: by being near someone who does it, long enough to catch it. That is why the most important thing an older believer can offer a younger one is not advice but a visible life at close range (Philippians 3:17; 1 Thessalonians 1:6). It also sets the terms for what follows: how men and women appear in worship, and a supper where the rich humiliated the poor. Both are questions about whether a congregation will lay down its rights for others in the room, and Paul has put the answer at the top of the page.

Is it not dangerous to tell people to follow a man? An objection worth meeting, because it is a good one. The history of the church is littered with the wreckage of ministries built on a personality, and this very congregation had already split into fan clubs: I follow Paul, I follow Apollos (1:12). Paul knew that better than anyone; he had spent four chapters demolishing it. The safeguard is in the second half of the sentence, and it is a safeguard anyone can apply. Follow a Christian only as far as he is following Christ, and no further, which means you must know Christ well enough to see where the line falls. That is the difference between a disciple and a fan. A fan goes wherever his man goes. A disciple watches his man and keeps checking the pattern against the Master, and is ready to stop the moment the two diverge.

Whom should I learn from? Not the most gifted person available, and not the most confident. Look for the one whose life shows the marks Paul has just described: rights not used, comfort spent on other people, a willingness to be thought less of. Gifts are impressive and they can be counterfeited. That pattern cannot. And if you cannot think of anyone near you, do not give up. Ask God to bring someone into your life; spend time with the older members of your church whom nobody notices; read the lives of faithful Christians from the past. Very often the person you need is already sitting a few rows away, and has simply never been asked.

On a Tuesday. Live so that someone younger can learn from you. If a new believer copied your week exactly, what would he learn about Christ?

verseByVerse.quote: Now I commend you because you remember me in everything and maintain the traditions even as I delivered them to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I commend you. Praise first, in a letter that has not been generous with it and is about to become severe again in fifteen verses. Perhaps the Corinthians’ own letter claimed that they remembered his teaching, and Paul accepts the claim generously before correcting them. There is a real compliment in it: this congregation, for all its arrogance, still cared what its founder thought. A church that has stopped listening cannot be corrected; it can only be left. Paul writes the rest of this letter because he believes these people will still hear him. The most dangerous position is not being wrong (the Corinthians were wrong about a great many things) but reaching the point where nobody is permitted to say so.

The traditions. Whatever else was wrong in Corinth, and the list is long, they had not thrown out the deposit. The word traditions makes some Christians uneasy, because it has been used to smuggle in doctrines the Bible does not teach, but Paul owns it without embarrassment. Paradosis means something handed over: a parcel passed from one pair of hands to the next. Delivered (paradidōmi) is the technical term for passing on authoritative teaching, and he uses the same verbs in verse 23 about the Lord’s Supper and in 15:3 about the gospel itself: I received and I delivered. What is being handed on here is not a set of customs invented by the church but a deposit that came from Christ through the apostles, and is now preserved in the New Testament. That is the difference that matters. A tradition is trustworthy when you can trace the parcel back to a hand that had the right to fill it.

When tradition and the Bible pull apart. There is a rule here for that vexed question. Paul’s own test is simply whether the parcel came from the Lord: I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you (v. 23). Where a practice can be traced to that source it is binding, however inconvenient. Where it cannot, it may be genuinely valuable, since the church’s accumulated wisdom is not nothing, but it can never be made a test of obedience. Many congregational quarrels would end quickly if the parties sorted their practices into those two boxes first.

A chain of hands. Everything the Corinthians had, they had been handed, and so has every Christian since. Nobody has worked out the gospel from first principles; it reached each of us through somebody: a mother, a preacher, a friend who would not let the subject drop, a translator who died for the privilege. That is what a tradition is when it is healthy: not a dead weight but a chain of hands, and the only question that matters is whether you intend to be one of them.

The Lord who was handed over. Paul’s verb for handing on the teaching is the very verb he uses, twenty verses later, for what happened to Jesus: on the night when he was betrayed, literally handed over (v. 23). The Father handed over his Son (Romans 8:32); the Son handed himself over for us (Galatians 2:20). So the tradition is not merely a message about Christ. At its heart is Christ himself, given up into the hands of sinners, and every faithful handing on of the gospel since is the passing along of that one great gift. What the church guards is not its own heritage. It is the Son of God, delivered for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Romans 4:25).

On a Tuesday. Think of the people who handed the gospel on to you, and thank God for them by name. If any are still living, tell them.
verseByVerse.note: “Traditions” means the teaching Paul had handed on to them.

verseByVerse.quote: But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The head of every man. Before any of the difficult application, Paul lays down the framework, and it needs handling slowly because a great deal is loaded onto the word head. The Greek is kephalē. In English, head has largely collapsed into one meaning: the boss. In Greek it carried more than that. It could mean the source of something, the way we still speak of the head of a river; it could mean the one who leads or represents; and in a body it is the part without which the rest cannot live. In this context head means one with authority and responsibility, as in Ephesians 1:22 and 5:23. Some argue it means only source. Both ideas may be present, since verses 8–9 speak of origin. But in Paul’s usage, headship includes leadership.

The head of a wife is her husband. Is Paul speaking of husbands and wives, or of men and women generally? The ESV notes that the same Greek words can mean woman and wife, man and husband, and translators differ. The context, with its focus on the married woman’s head covering, suggests husband and wife. Headship in Scripture is a marriage relationship (Ephesians 5:23), not a rule that every woman is under every man. But the passage applies it in the church’s worship, where the order of creation shapes how all men and women take part. The husband has a God-given responsibility to lead his wife in love (Ephesians 5:23–25).

The head of Christ. The sequence Paul gives shows why the word head cannot mean what the world means by boss. The Son, as incarnate Mediator, submits to the Father (15:28; John 5:19, 30; 14:28). What does that mean? A mediator is one who stands between two parties to bring them together, and Christ is the one mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5); incarnate means that he took a real human nature, body and soul, without ceasing to be God. In that role, sent by the Father to save us, the Son obeys. Yet the Son is fully equal with the Father (John 1:1; 10:30; Philippians 2:6). This is the key to the whole passage. Whatever this verse means, it cannot mean that a head is superior in worth to what it heads, because the third clause would then make Christ inferior to God, and the New Testament will not allow it. The Son is the exact imprint of God’s nature (Hebrews 1:3), in whom the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9). If the head of Christ is God can stand alongside I and the Father are one, then headship and equality are not rivals. Paul has picked the one relationship in the universe where perfect equality and willing order are both beyond dispute, and he has made it the model. Christ is not less than the Father because he submits to him; a wife is not less than her husband because she submits to him. Order is not the enemy of equality; it is the shape love takes when two equals are doing something together, and the Son’s submission was not the loss of his dignity but the display of it.

Where Christians differ: headship. Egalitarians (those who hold that no role in home or church is limited by sex) argue that head means only source, and that Christ’s coming abolished all role distinctions between men and women. Many hold this out of a sincere concern for the dignity of women and a careful reading of texts such as Galatians 3:28, and they serve Christ faithfully. This commentary’s view: Paul grounds this order in creation (vv. 8–9), not in culture or the fall, and compares it with the relation of the Father and the Son. Men and women are equal in worth, dignity and salvation (Galatians 3:28; 1 Peter 3:7). But God has given husbands the responsibility to lead their families, and qualified men the responsibility to lead and teach in the church (1 Timothy 2:12–13). This is the complementarian view: equal in being, distinct in role. Husbands must lead as Christ leads: by sacrificial love, not domination.

Where Christians differ: does the Son submit to the Father eternally? Christians differ over how far this reaches into the eternal life of God. Most Reformed theologians have been careful here: the Son’s submission is real, and it belongs to his mission, the sending, the incarnation, the obedience unto death, rather than being a subordination of nature within the Godhead, since the Father and the Son share one undivided divine essence. Others have argued for an eternal ordering of persons in authority and submission. It is a discussion worth conducting with great care and very little heat. This commentary’s view: of those two views, the first is the more likely. Scripture plainly shows the Son submitting to the Father in his mission (15:28; John 5:19), but it never makes him anything less than fully God (Philippians 2:6). His submission belongs to the work of salvation he freely undertook, and it is no subordination of his being.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every woman must submit to every man. The headship here is in marriage (and, by extension, the church), and it gives no cover to harshness or abuse (see on verses 8–9).

Does headship mean the husband always gets the final say? In the rare case where a decision must be made, the two cannot agree, and nothing sinful is involved, yes: someone must bear the responsibility, and God has laid it on the husband. But a marriage that is constantly reaching for the final say has already gone wrong. Headship is first a responsibility, not a casting vote: to pray for his wife, to take the lead in loving, apologising and serving, to protect and provide, to care for her soul. A wise husband listens long, seeks his wife’s counsel as a gift from God, and very often defers to her judgment gladly. And no husband may ever ask his wife to sin; her first obedience is to Christ (Acts 5:29).

For worship. The head of Christ is God, and the Son has never resented it. The eternal Son, equal with the Father in power and glory, came gladly to do his Father’s will, and said, I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29). There was no grasping in it, and no loss. And Christ, the head of every man, exercises his headship by laying down his life. The order of heaven is an order of love, from the Father who sends to the Son who obeys to the Spirit who glorifies the Son. What a God, whose very greatness is displayed in giving, and whose authority looks like a towel and a basin and a cross.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the same Greek words can mean “woman” and “wife.”

verseByVerse.quote: Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head, but every wife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, since it is the same as if her head were shaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His head covered. Why would a covered head dishonour a man? In public worship, a man covering his head would dishonour both his physical head and his spiritual head, Christ. The likeliest background is the Roman custom in which a man leading pagan worship drew his toga over his head; a Christian man doing the same would look like a priest of the idols. Paul’s concern is what the sign said in that setting. Whether a man wears a hat in church today is a matter of courtesy, not of this text.

Her head uncovered. In that culture a married woman’s head covering signalled her modesty and her honour as a wife; to remove it in public could suggest she was unattached or immoral. Her physical head and her husband were both shamed. Two things are established in this sentence, and the first is easily missed because it is assumed rather than argued. Women are praying and prophesying in the Corinthian assembly, out loud, and Paul does not object. He objects to how they are dressed while doing it. That is a striking thing to find in a letter often thought to silence women, and it needs to be held onto: the apostle’s correction here presupposes their audible participation and corrects only its manner. To pray uncovered, he adds, is the same as if her head were shaven, and a shaved head was a sign of disgrace for a woman, perhaps associated with punishment for adultery or with certain pagan practices.

Before the face of his head. The sentence only works because of verse 3: a man’s head is Christ. Whatever a man does with his own head in worship says something about the Lord he stands before. If he prayed dressed like a priest of the idols, he would be honouring another altar in the presence of the one Lord who bought him. And a Christian man needs no priest’s gesture at all, because he has a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, through whom he may draw near with confidence (Hebrews 4:14–16; 10:19–22). So the question of the covering is never really about cloth. It is about whose worship this is: the worship of Christ, in his presence, on his terms.

Garments speak. The second thing established here is that appearance in worship carries meaning. Paul assumes that what a person wears on his or her head in the assembly says something, and that saying the wrong thing brings dishonour. Every culture has clothing that speaks, which is why nobody wears a swimming costume to a funeral. Paul is not inventing the fact that garments talk. He is asking what these particular garments were saying in that room.

How can chapter 11 assume women speak, and chapter 14 tell them to be silent? This raises the hardest question in the chapter, and it should be answered here rather than left to ambush the reader three chapters on. Paul was not a fool, and the letter was probably read aloud in one sitting; whatever he meant, he did not think he was contradicting himself three chapters later. The resolution lies in noticing what kind of speech chapter 14 is actually discussing. That passage sits inside a paragraph about prophecy being weighed by the congregation (let the others weigh what is said, 14:29), and it ends by telling the women to ask their questions at home (14:35). It is regulating a particular activity in a particular part of the meeting: the public sifting and cross-examination of prophecies, an exercise of governing judgment over the congregation’s teaching. That is a different thing from praying and prophesying, which chapter 11 takes for granted that women do. So the two passages are addressing two activities, not one, and the seeming contradiction comes from reading silent as absolute when Paul has already shown, in this very verse, that he does not mean it absolutely. This will be taken up again where it is written, at 14:34.

Where Christians differ: women praying and prophesying. How does this fit with 14:34 (women should keep silent in the churches) and 1 Timothy 2:12? This commentary’s view: Women may pray and contribute in the church’s life, and in New Testament times some prophesied (Acts 21:9). What is reserved for qualified men is the authoritative teaching and judging of doctrine in the gathered church (14:29, 34–35; 1 Timothy 2:12). This commentary holds, with many Reformed churches, that prophecy as new revelation belonged to the church’s apostolic foundation (Ephesians 2:20) and ceased when the canon of Scripture was complete; many faithful brothers and sisters believe it continues, and they deserve a respectful hearing. On that view, since prophecy as new revelation has ceased, the question today concerns praying, sharing and teaching; women serve in many ways, but the office of elder and the authoritative preaching of the church belong to qualified men.

So what may a woman do in church today? A great deal, and churches that hold this verdict should say so as loudly as they say the limits. She may pray aloud in the gathering, read Scripture, share what God has taught her, lead in song, give testimony, and use every gift of mercy, administration, hospitality and wisdom God has given her. She may teach women and children, as Titus 2:3–5 commands the older women to do, and she may, like Priscilla with her husband, explain the way of God privately to a man who needs it (Acts 18:26). What she does not do is hold the office of elder or bring the church’s authoritative preaching. That is not a judgment on her gifts, many of which may exceed those of the men in the room. It is the shape God has given his household.
verseByVerse.note: In that culture a married woman’s head covering signalled her modesty and married status. Christians differ on how the principle applies today.

verseByVerse.quote: For if a wife will not cover her head, then she should cut her hair short. But since it is disgraceful for a wife to cut off her hair or shave her head, let her cover her head. For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, but woman is the glory of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cut her hair short. Paul argues by reduction: if she is going to abandon the sign, she may as well go the whole way and take the shears to her hair, and everyone in Corinth knew what that meant, which is why the argument works. A shaved or cropped head on a woman in that world was a mark of disgrace; it seems to have been associated with women advertising a rejection of ordinary respectability. It is the ancient equivalent of saying that if you are going to leave the wedding ring at home, you may as well announce what its absence implies. And since that would be shameful, Paul concludes, let her keep the covering.

The image and glory of God. Verse 7 gives the theological reason, from Genesis 1:26–27: man was made in God’s image and reflects God’s glory.

The image who came. What does it mean to be the image of God? An image is a likeness that represents the one it resembles, as a king’s statue stood for him in a distant province. Humanity was made to show the world what God is like. Sin defaced that likeness in all of us, men and women alike. Then the New Testament names the one who bears it perfectly: Christ, who is the image of God (2 Corinthians 4:4), the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15). He is not a copy that faded. He is the original likeness, and believers are being renewed after the image of their Creator (Colossians 3:10), predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:29). Every man and woman in that Corinthian room was being remade to look like Jesus.

But woman is the glory of man. What is not said matters. Paul does not say that the man is the image of God and the woman is not. Genesis, which he has in mind, is explicit: God created man in his own image, male and female he created them (Genesis 1:27). Both bear it equally, and Paul knew that text better than his critics do. What he changes is the second noun. Man is the glory of God; woman is the glory of man. Glory here means that which honours and displays another: the honour that is reflected back. She was made from man and for him (vv. 8–9), and she brings him honour, as an excellent wife is the crown of her husband (Proverbs 12:4; Genesis 2:23).

A glory veiled before a greater one. His argument is about what should be on show in worship: when the church gathers, God is the one being honoured, so nothing should visibly compete for that honour. The man, unveiled, reflects God. The woman, in that culture, reflected the honour of her husband, and Paul asks that this reflection be gently covered while God is being worshipped: not because it is shameful, but because it is glorious, and this is not the hour for it. Every other glory in the room dims when God is being praised. The covering is not a muzzle or a badge of inferiority. On this reading it is the veiling of a genuine glory in the presence of a greater one, which is exactly what the seraphim do with their wings in Isaiah’s temple, covering their faces before a holiness that outshines them (Isaiah 6:2).

Is it wrong for a woman to have short hair today? Not in itself. Paul’s argument depended on what a cropped head meant in Corinth: disgrace, or a public rejection of being a wife. In most cultures today a short haircut on a woman says nothing of the kind. The principle that remains is that women and men should not try to erase the God-given difference between them, and should not use their appearance to make a statement against the order God has made. A woman with short hair who is glad to be a woman and honours her husband is not breaking this verse. A man or woman who styles themselves deliberately to blur the line between the sexes is going against its grain, whatever the length of their hair.

For worship. Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up, and John tells us whose glory it was: Isaiah saw his glory and spoke of him (John 12:41). The King enthroned in that temple, whose train filled it, is Jesus. Man and woman together, a single portrait in two colours, are only reflections; he is the radiance of the glory of God (Hebrews 1:3). And the wonder is that this glory did not stay behind the wings. It took flesh, walked into rooms like the one in Corinth, and shines now into ordinary hearts in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

verseByVerse.quote: For man was not made from woman, but woman from man. Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woman from man. Paul now goes back to Genesis 2. He is not appealing to Corinthian manners or to what the neighbours will think, but to how human beings were made, before there was a culture to have opinions about it. The first fact from the garden is that the woman was taken from the man: alone among human beings, neither formed from the dust as Adam was nor born as everyone since has been, but built by God out of the body of another, from Adam’s side (Genesis 2:21–23).

Woman for man. The second fact is that she was made for him, in answer to the first thing in the creation account that God calls not good: it is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him (Genesis 2:18).

From and for, read as Genesis reads them. Both facts have been used badly. From does not mean lesser. Eve came out of Adam’s side, and Adam’s response was not to assert rank but to break into what is often called the first poetry in the Bible: this at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh (Genesis 2:23). And for does not mean an instrument. The word Genesis uses for the woman’s role is helper (Hebrew ʿēzer), and it is worth knowing that the same Hebrew word is used most often in the Old Testament of God himself helping his people: our help and our shield (Psalm 33:20; 121:2). It is not a word for a subordinate assistant but for one who comes to the aid of somebody who cannot manage alone. It describes a role, not inferiority.

What Paul is establishing. His point is narrow, and he guards it himself. He is grounding headship in creation, which means the difference between men and women is not a social construction that a sophisticated congregation may dispense with. It reflects God’s design, and it is therefore not the church’s to abolish. He is not establishing rank in worth, and his next sentence makes sure nobody thinks so: in the Lord, woman is not independent of man nor man of woman (v. 11).

A mystery hidden in the garden. Why does the order of Genesis 2 matter so much? Because it was never only about Adam and Eve. Paul quotes the same chapter elsewhere, a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and then says that this mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). The first marriage was drawn as a picture of the last. Christ is the husband who came for his bride, and the church is the bride made for him, joined to him as members of his body, loved by him (Ephesians 5:25, 30). That is why the from and for of these verses cannot be shrugged off as ancient custom: they are lines in a portrait of the Son and his people.

How this text has been misused. Something has to be said here, because pretending otherwise would be dishonest and would leave a wounded reader unhelped. Verses like these have been quoted by men to justify treating their wives as inferiors, to shut down every disagreement, and in the worst cases to demand submission to cruelty. That is not a misapplication at the edges; it is the exact reverse of what the passage teaches, and it is wickedness. The measure of headship in the New Testament is never the authority a man may claim. It is the death a man must die: husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). That is the standard, and it is a standard that ruins domineering before it starts. Christ’s headship over the church consisted of washing feet, absorbing insult, and being executed for people who had contributed nothing. Any man who quotes 1 Corinthians 11 to get his own way has picked up a verse about the Trinity and used it as a stick, and he will answer for it. Order in the Bible always runs downhill in service. It never runs downhill in privilege.

What if my husband is harsh or abusive? Then hear this clearly: nothing in this passage requires you to endure abuse, and no faithful church will ask you to. Headship is a calling to self-giving love, and a man who threatens, hits, controls or terrorises his wife has abandoned it. Your safety, and your children’s, comes first. It is right to leave a dangerous home, to call the police where a crime has been committed, and to tell your pastor or elders, who should protect you and confront him, not counsel you to go back and submit harder. Abuse is a grievous sin against God and against you. Whether a marriage broken this way may end in divorce is a further question, to be worked through with your elders in the light of Scripture’s teaching on adultery and desertion (the Westminster Confession 24.5–6). This commentary holds that persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion, and the elders should help judge each case; but separation for safety is never disobedience to this text.

On a Tuesday. Husbands, measure your headship by Ephesians 5:25 this week: what would it cost you to love your wife as Christ loved the church, today, in one specific thing? Do it, by the Spirit he has given you, and when you fall short, as every husband does, rest in the Husband who never has. Wives, thank God that your role as helper is the very word he uses of himself. And if you know a home where this passage is being used as a weapon, do not stay silent; speak to someone who can help.

parallels.desc: a helper fit for him; she shall be called Woman

verseByVerse.quote: That is why a wife ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A symbol of authority. Two puzzles in one short verse. The first is the phrase rendered a symbol of authority. The Greek says simply that she ought to have authority on her head. The older reading takes the covering as a sign of her husband’s authority over her. But the words can just as naturally be read another way: the covering is her authority, the thing that gives her the standing to pray and prophesy in the assembly, under that order. On that reading the veil is not a leash but a licence. It marks her as a woman in her rightful place doing a rightful thing, and it answers in advance anyone who might object to her praying aloud. That reading fits the flow: Paul has been assuming since verse 5 that she prays and prophesies, and this is the garment that makes it unexceptionable.

Because of the angels. The second puzzle is one of the most contested phrases in Paul’s letters. The plain point first: on any likely reading, the church worships in the sight of heaven. Four readings have been offered. A widely held one today takes the angels as the appointed guardians of the created order. They are present when the church worships, they observe God’s order in the church (4:9; Ephesians 3:10; 1 Peter 1:12), and to overturn that order deliberately in a worship service would be a visible affront to the very servants charged with upholding it. A second, with a long history, sees them as fellow worshippers: the church joins a heavenly assembly where angels worship with perfect reverence (Psalm 138:1 in the Greek reads, before the angels I will sing your praise; compare Isaiah 6 and Revelation 4 and 5). A third reading, the oldest, appeals to the strange episode of Genesis 6 and the Jewish traditions built on it, in which angels fell through desire for women; on this view the covering was protective. This reading was common in the early centuries, but it requires a speculative account of angels that the text does not supply. A fourth notes that the law was given through angels (Galatians 3:19), so their presence would call for the order the law required.

Where the ordinary reader should land. The first two readings are the most defensible, and they share a conclusion: a Christian congregation at worship is not alone in the room. That is a bracing thing to carry into a Sunday morning: the singing is overheard, the reverence is observed, and the company is far larger and far older than the one you can see (Hebrews 12:22).

What the angels are watching. What do angels see when they look at a congregation? Paul tells us elsewhere: through the church the manifold wisdom of God is now made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places (Ephesians 3:10), and Peter says the good news of Christ’s sufferings and glories is something into which angels long to look (1 Peter 1:12). The angels have no Saviour of their own; none of them was ever redeemed. So when sinners bought by Christ’s blood gather in his name, men and women in their God-given order, praying to the Father through the Son, heaven’s servants are watching the one thing they could never experience and never tire of studying: grace.

Should I pray to angels, or try to sense them? No. Angels are fellow servants, not objects of worship or prayer; when John fell at an angel’s feet, he was told at once to get up and worship God (Revelation 22:8–9). Scripture never invites us to seek contact with them, and an interest in angels that crowds out Christ is a road away from him (Colossians 2:18). What it does give us is a comfort and a dignity. The comfort is that they are ministering spirits sent out to serve those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14). The dignity is that ordinary Sunday worship, in a small hall with a weak organ, is watched by heaven.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of “because of the angels” is uncertain; angels were thought to be present at worship and to guard God’s order.

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman; for as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not independent. And there is the guard, placed by Paul himself, in case anyone should take verses 8 and 9 and build a wall out of them. Nevertheless is the hinge. Everything just said about the garden stands, and it does not entitle anybody to independence or superiority. The sentence cuts both ways with deliberate symmetry. In the Lord, in Christ’s new community, men and women need each other completely. Neither sex is a complete account of humanity, and neither can conduct its life as though the other were an optional extra.

Born of woman. Then Paul makes the point with a piece of homely wit. Yes, the first woman came out of a man. And every man since has come out of a woman, his mother. If anyone wants to argue about origins, the ledger balanced itself in the second generation and has stayed level ever since. Every man who has ever lived, including the ones in Corinth arguing about veils, was carried, delivered and fed by a woman. The dependence runs both ways.

All things are from God. The last clause closes the account entirely. The whole arrangement traces back past both of them to the one who made the pair and gave them to each other, which means neither party has grounds for a boast, since neither invented himself.

In the Lord. The phrase to hold on to is in the Lord. What does it mean? To be in the Lord is to be joined to Christ by faith, so that what is true of him is counted true of you. A believing husband and a believing wife stand before God on exactly the same ground: both were dead in sin, both were bought with the same blood, both are clothed in the same righteousness, and they are heirs together of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7). Christ did not die for men a little more than for women. So the order of creation is not cancelled in him; it is the old order now lived inside a new atmosphere, the atmosphere of a shared rescue. Sin turned difference into domination, and the curse said as much on the way out of the garden (Genesis 3:16). In Christ the difference remains and the domination has no place. Some Christian teaching about men and women quotes verses 8 and 9 loudly and lets verses 11 and 12 fall silent. Paul wrote all four, a few seconds apart, and the church is not free to keep only the half that suits it (Galatians 3:28; Ephesians 5:21).

What it does not mean. It does not mean headship is cancelled in the Lord. Paul holds both: an order of headship and a deep mutual interdependence.

What dependence looks like when it is working. In a marriage it is a man who genuinely does not know what he thinks until he has heard his wife, and says so out loud in company. In a congregation it is a church whose men would notice within a fortnight if the women stopped, and are honest enough to admit that much of what holds the place together is being done by them. Dependence is not a compliment paid at an anniversary. It is a thing you can see in who gets consulted before a decision.

What does this mean for single people? Everything Paul says here applies to you as fully as to the married. You are not half a person waiting to be completed. You belong to a church in which men and women depend on one another as brothers and sisters, mothers and fathers in the faith, and you have gifts that the rest of the body cannot do without. A single woman is not under the headship of every man in the congregation; she is under Christ and the shepherding of her elders, as the men are. And the single man or woman can often show this mutual dependence most freely, in friendships, hospitality and service across the whole family of God.

For worship. The difference between men and women is not a problem the church has to solve, nor a weapon either side may pick up. It is a piece of God’s workmanship, made deliberately, by someone who could have made us all identical and did not want to. He looked at what he had made, male and female, and called it very good before either of them had done anything at all. And when the Son came to redeem them both, he was born of a woman (Galatians 4:4): the eternal Word, through whom all things were made, carried, delivered and fed by a mother in Bethlehem. The God from whom all things come came to us that way.

verseByVerse.quote: Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a wife to pray to God with her head uncovered? Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair it is a disgrace for him, but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For her hair is given to her for a covering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a wife to pray to God with her head uncovered? Once again Paul refers a matter to the congregation’s own judgment rather than settling it by decree, exactly as he did at 10:15. He appeals to their sense of what is fitting (prepō). He has given the theology; now he asks them to look at the thing itself and see whether it fits.

Nature itself. A modern reader will object that nature does no such thing: hair grows on everyone, and plenty of cultures have thought long hair splendid on a man. The objection is fair, and the answer is that Paul is not making a biological claim. The word (physis) covers the natural order of things as people generally sense it, the settled instinct of a people about what is fitting. In the Greek and Roman culture of Paul’s day, long, carefully dressed hair on a man was widely associated with effeminacy, though there were exceptions, such as some philosophers. Paul is pointing at a shared sense of the fitting and saying that even that untutored instinct is pushing in the same direction as his argument. It is a supporting consideration, not the foundation; the foundation was laid in verses 3 and 8 to 12.

Long hair. Long hair was considered a woman’s beauty and dignity, one of her recognised glories. The last clause has caused endless discussion. Some have concluded that Paul means the hair is the covering, and that no cloth was ever in view. That reads oddly against verse 6, where cutting the hair short is the alternative to covering the head rather than a way of doing it; the two cannot be the same thing if one is offered as the substitute for the other. The better sense is that nature itself gives women a covering, a God-given picture of the very thing the head covering signifies. Nature already drapes a woman’s head, and the fabric follows the pattern that the Creator drew first.

The kind of argument this is. Paul appeals to Christ, to creation, to the angels, and now to the ordinary human sense of what is seemly. He is not embarrassed to use the last of these. Christians sometimes speak as though only a proof text may be consulted, but the apostle here treats the shared instincts of decent people as a real witness: not the highest one, and never one that may overrule Scripture, but not nothing either (Romans 2:14–15).

Whose handwriting nature is. Why should nature teach anything at all? Because nature has an author, and the New Testament names him. All things were made through the Son, and without him was not any thing made that was made (John 1:3); by him all things were created, and in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:16–17). The grain of the world, including the difference between man and woman and the instinct that some things suit one and not the other, was cut by the hand of Christ. So when Paul appeals to nature he is not stepping outside the gospel to borrow a pagan argument. He is reading the handwriting of the same Lord who wrote Scripture, faint where Scripture is clear, but his.

Is long hair on a man therefore a sin? Scripture sets no hair length for men; the Nazirite let his hair grow long as a mark of devotion (Numbers 6:5). Paul’s concern is what a hairstyle signalled in Corinth: a man presenting himself as a woman. Where a style carries no such meaning, it is a matter of conscience and taste, and no Christian should judge another by the length of his hair.

Where Christians differ: must women wear head coverings today? Some churches require head coverings in worship today; most do not. This commentary’s view: The principle is permanent: the distinction between men and women, and the husband’s headship, rooted in creation, should be honoured in worship. The specific form, a head covering, was the cultural expression of that principle in first-century Corinth, where an uncovered married woman sent a message of shame or rebellion. Where coverings carry no such meaning, the principle should be expressed in other ways: modest dress, and clear distinctions between men and women. Christians who wear coverings out of conviction should be respected.

What about dress more generally? The same principle reaches further than hair. The law of Moses forbade a man to wear a woman’s garment or a woman a man’s (Deuteronomy 22:5), and the concern was the same: not a particular cut of cloth, but the blurring of the line God drew between the sexes. What counts as masculine or feminine dress varies a great deal between cultures and centuries; trousers on a woman in many countries today are simply women’s clothes. So the question is not whether an item matches a rule from another time and place, but whether, here, it says I am glad to be the man or woman God made me, or says the opposite. And modesty applies to both sexes: dress for worship and for life in a way that does not draw attention away from God to yourself.

On a Tuesday. If you have felt pressure, from the world or from your own heart, to resent the body God gave you, bring that to him honestly; he made you on purpose, and he does not make mistakes. And be slow to judge other Christians over matters of dress and hair where Scripture has left room.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such practice, nor do the churches of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone is inclined to be contentious. The last word on the subject, and it is not another argument. It is a door closing. Contentious (philoneikos) means fond of quarrelling, loving to win arguments, and Paul expects some to argue.

No such practice. The phrase is deliberately compact in the Greek, and both readings end in the same place. If it means the practice of contentiousness, Paul is saying: we do not do fighting about this, and neither does any other church. If it means the practice of women praying with uncovered heads, he is saying: no church anywhere does what you are proposing, so the innovation is yours alone. Either way the appeal is to the shared life of the churches, and either way it lands on the person who wants a fight: Corinth must not go its own way.

The Lord who did not need to win. The love of winning has no place in the church because it has no place in Christ. He had every argument on his side and every right to press it, and when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). He did not come to win a debate with his people. He came to lay down his life for them. It is the mind Paul asks of every church, as he wrote to Philippi: do nothing from rivalry, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves, because this was the mind of Christ Jesus, who emptied himself (Philippians 2:3–7). A contentious Christian is defending his own corner. His Lord gave his corner away.

Are Christian women meant to cover their heads in church today? This brings the passage to the question every reader has been waiting for, and it deserves an answer rather than an admiring description of how difficult it is. Begin with what does not change. The theology of verses 3 and 8 to 12 is rooted in the Trinity and in creation, and neither of those is a first-century custom. That men and women are equally God’s image, genuinely different, mutually dependent, and ordered in relationship to one another is not up for revision, and a congregation that quietly erases the difference between men and women has departed from Paul, whatever it is wearing. Now what does change. The visible sign is a different matter, and Paul’s own way of arguing suggests as much. He reasons from what is disgraceful, from what nature suggests, from what the churches do: the vocabulary of things that are legible in a particular place and time. A sign works only if people can read it. In first-century Corinth an uncovered head in worship said something specific and everyone in the room heard it. In most Western congregations today a hat says nothing whatever, and a woman who wore one to make Paul’s point would find that nobody received the message, which is the one thing a symbol must do.

So, practically. Where the covering is still meaningful, and there are cultures and congregations where it plainly is, wear it, and let nobody sneer at those who do; they are obeying Scripture in a way their neighbours can read. Where it is not, the principle must find a form that people can actually see: a church where men and women are equally welcome to pray and are not embarrassed to be different from one another; where the distinction is treated as a gift rather than an awkwardness to be managed; where dress and manner in worship are chosen with an eye to what honours God rather than what displays the wearer. And in either case, verse 16 governs: whatever conclusion a Christian reaches, he is not permitted to become contentious about it. The apostle who has just spent fifteen verses on the matter ends by refusing to let it become a battlefield.

What if my conviction differs from my church’s practice? Then follow your conscience quietly, and do not make it a cause. A woman who believes she should cover her head may do so in a church where few do, and the church should welcome her gladly. A woman who does not believe it is required should not be pressed to cover by the opinions of others. What neither may do is treat the other as less faithful, or turn the question into a campaign. That is exactly the contentiousness this verse shuts the door on. If the difference becomes a constant source of strife, talk to your elders with humility, and remember that the unity of the church is a weightier matter than this sign.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–22 — Divisions at the Lord’s Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now Paul has no praise for them: their meetings are doing more harm than good. The church is divided along the lines of rich and poor, and at the very meal that proclaims Christ’s death some go hungry while others get drunk. That, says Paul, is not the Lord’s Supper; it despises God’s church and shames those who have nothing.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Supper and the equality of the gospel

Paul’s answer comes from the cross. The Supper proclaims the Lord’s death (v. 26), the death of the Son of God who became poor for our sake and gave one body for all his people. A Supper that ranks people by wealth is not merely unkind; it contradicts what the meal itself declares. No one can share rightly in the body and blood of Christ while despising the members of his body around the table.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Roman patronage ranked even a shared meal: the wealthy ate better food in the inner room, and dependants got less outside. The Corinthians had brought that arrangement straight into the church. Now: The Lord’s Supper is still a place where the gospel’s welcome is either shown or denied. A church where wealth, race or education decides who is welcomed and who is overlooked has made the Corinthian mistake.

verseByVerse.quote: But in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse. For, in the first place, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you. And I believe it in part, for there must be factions among you in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not commend you. Earlier in the chapter Paul wrote, I commend you (v. 2). Now he takes it back, and the echo is deliberate. Whatever they had held on to, they had lost the thing that mattered most.

For the worse. Paul is not saying the meetings were dull or badly run. He is saying that these people would have been better off staying at home. There is such a thing as a church service that leaves people further from God than it found them, and an apostle says so in writing.

Divisions. The cause is named at once. Divisions (schismata) is the word of 1:10, but here the divisions are social: rich and poor.

Divided at his table. What made this so grave? They were dividing at the one place built to proclaim that Christ had made them one. He died to break down the dividing wall of hostility and create in himself one new man in place of two (Ephesians 2:14–15), and he prayed on his last night that his people might be one, as he and the Father are one (John 17:21–22). In Christ there is neither slave nor free (Galatians 3:28). To split the church into the comfortable and the overlooked, at a meal that announces his death, is to contradict with the seating what the bread says with its breaking. Their divisions were not a failure of manners. They were a denial, in public, of what the cross had done.

And I believe it in part. That last phrase is a model of pastoral care. Paul neither swallows the report whole nor dismisses it. He has heard something, perhaps again from Chloe’s household (1:11), and he refuses both to pretend it is nothing and to convict them of everything alleged. Any pastor who has had to weigh what one member says about another will recognise the discipline in that short phrase.

There must be factions. Then a genuinely hard sentence. Factions (haireseis) is the word from which heresies comes: parties, sects. This is not approval; Paul has been attacking factions since chapter 1. He speaks with irony and realism about how God works even through what he hates. Trouble sorts people. When a congregation splits along the lines of money or personality or taste, it becomes visible who was there for Christ and who was there for the circle, and the sorting is not an accident but a providence. God permits the fracture and uses it as a sieve. What does the must mean, then? Not that God likes factions, but that in a church of forgiven sinners living in a fallen world they will come, and God rules over them for his own ends, as Jesus said that temptations must come, yet woe to the one by whom they come (Matthew 18:7). And there is comfort in it: a church going through an ugly season is not outside God’s hands. The word for genuine (dokimoi) was used of coins and metal that had been tested and approved. Nobody discovers what an alloy is made of while it sits on a shelf. It is found out in the fire, and a divided church is a furnace (1 John 2:19).

Should I leave a church that is divided? Usually not at the first sign of trouble, and never simply to escape discomfort. The passage gives three things to do instead. Do not conclude that God has abandoned the place; verse 19 says he is at work in the very thing that feels like collapse. Do not join a party, because the sifting is precisely between those who are for Christ and those who are for a camp. And ask the uncomfortable question that this verse presses: when the fire came, what did it show that I was made of? There are times when leaving is right: when the gospel itself is denied, when abuse is covered up, or when the leaders will not be corrected by Scripture. But most church troubles are a call to stay, pray, speak truthfully and seek peace. A season of trouble in a church is often the time when a person first finds out what he was actually attached to.

On a Tuesday. The next time you hear a report about another member, do what Paul did: believe it in part, refuse to repeat it, and if it matters, go to the person.

verseByVerse.quote: When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat. For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk. What! Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I commend you in this? No, I will not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The Lord’s Supper was eaten as part of a shared meal, sometimes called the love feast (Jude 12), in the homes of wealthier believers. Houses excavated near Corinth help us picture the room: a dining room, the triclinium, held perhaps nine or a dozen reclining on couches; everyone else would have been in the courtyard, the atrium. Roman writers describe hosts who gave their high-status friends the best food and wine and lesser guests lesser fare, and few thought this shocking. The poor, the slaves and labourers, probably came when their work let them, which was late. They walked in to find the meal eaten, the good wine gone, and their brothers in the inner room flushed and full.

Not the Lord’s supper. It is a devastating sentence to write to a church. These people gathered as a church (v. 18), probably on the first day of the week (16:2; Acts 20:7). They took bread and a cup. They said the words. And the apostle tells them that whatever they were doing, it was not the Lord’s Supper. The Lord’s meal had become a private party, and the thing had lost the right to its own name.

Goes ahead. The verb (prolambanō) means takes beforehand, or devours, and the result is told in flat words.

Whose supper it is. The name says everything Corinth had forgotten. It is the Lord’s supper: his table, his bread, his rules of hospitality. And the Lord, at his own last supper, did not recline while others served. John tells us that he rose, tied a towel round his waist and washed his disciples’ feet, the work of the lowest slave in the house, and then said, I have given you an example (John 13:4–5, 15). The host of this meal took the place the Corinthians gave to their late, hungry slaves. A supper where the first-comers feast and the last-comers starve may use his words, but it cannot carry his name.

Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Then the anger breaks out, and Paul does not tidy it. The question opens with an exclamation, What!, a cry of sheer disbelief. Four questions follow, one after another, and they are not gentle. If you want a private feast, have it at home.

Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? The sharpest word falls here. Not on the drunkenness, bad as that is, but on those who have nothing. A man who arrives late and hungry and watches the meal end without him has been told something about his worth, and he has been told it at the table where Christ’s death for him is being celebrated. That is what Paul cannot bear. Their behaviour despised the church, God’s people, and shamed the poor. Social snobbery at the Lord’s table is contempt for God’s church. The Corinthians thought they were having a slightly untidy dinner. They were preaching, in actions, the opposite of the gospel they said with their mouths.

What shall I say to you? Shall I commend you in this? No, I will not. No praise.

The world’s seating plan. The sin is not really greed. It is the effortless importing of the world’s seating plan into the church. Nobody in that house had to decide to humiliate the poor; they only had to do what everyone in Corinth did, and let the ordinary arrangements stand. That is how it usually happens. Congregations rarely resolve to grade people by money or accent or schooling. They simply fail to notice that the surrounding culture has already done it for them, and do nothing to interfere (James 2:1–4). Beneath it lies an old idol of the heart: the need to be seen as someone who matters. Corinth fed that need with couches and good wine. The gospel meets it another way: the only verdict that finally counts has already been given at the cross, and it was given to rich and poor on exactly the same terms (Romans 3:22–24).

Where does this happen today? Rarely at the communion table itself, and often everywhere around it. It happens at the coffee after the service, when the same circles form every week and the visitor stands alone with a cup. It happens when the church’s leaders are all drawn from one profession or one class, when the poorer members are served but never invited home, when the young families and the elderly never speak, when people from another country or another race are welcomed politely and never befriended. None of it is deliberate. All of it says, as Corinth did, that some here matter more than others. The remedy is not guilt but attention: look for who is on the edge, and go and stand there.

What if I am the one left out? Then know that the apostle is on your side, and so is the Lord whose table it is. Paul’s anger in these verses is anger on behalf of people like you. Your place at Christ’s table does not depend on whether anyone made room for you at the coffee urn; it was bought with his blood, and he does not grade his guests. It is still right to speak to an elder about how the church welcomes people, gently and honestly, and it is often worth taking the first step yourself towards one other person. But do not let other people’s neglect persuade you that you do not belong. You belong to Christ, and therefore to his body.
verseByVerse.note: The Lord’s Supper was eaten as part of a shared meal. The wealthy, free to arrive early, ate and drank before poorer members — often slaves — could come after work.

parallels.desc: your love feasts

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–34 — The Institution of the Lord’s Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul hands on what he received from the Lord: the words Jesus spoke over the bread and the cup on the night he was betrayed. Every time the church eats and drinks, it proclaims the Lord’s death until he comes. So to eat in an unworthy manner, despising Christ’s body, is a serious matter, and the Lord had been disciplining the Corinthians for it. They must examine themselves, and the remedy for the divided meal is simple: when they come together, they must wait for one another.
verseByVerse.theology:
The real presence: the Reformed understanding of the Supper

Calvin, working closely with this passage, taught that Christ is truly but spiritually present in the Supper. He rejected both the Roman Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation (that the bread and wine are changed into Christ’s body and blood) and Zwingli’s view that the Supper is only a symbol. Paul’s language of participation (10:16) and proclamation (11:26) supports this: at the table Christ truly gives himself to be received by faith, and the soul is fed through the Spirit.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians turned the Supper into a meal ranked by class, and that showed they had not grasped the gospel. Anyone who understands that Christ died for the rich and the poor alike cannot eat well while his brothers go hungry at the same table. Now: The Lord’s Supper is one of the church’s plainest proclamations of the gospel, which is why abusing it is so serious, and why a church gathered as equals around the cross is a sign to the world.

verseByVerse.quote: For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, “This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Received from the Lord. Paul stops arguing and starts reciting, in the words for handing on tradition (v. 2; 15:3), and from the Lord means the teaching originates with Jesus himself, passed on through the apostles. This is probably the oldest written account we have of that night, written about AD 54, before any of the Gospels, within about twenty-five years of the event, and already worn smooth by use in the churches.

The night when he was betrayed. Not on the night of the Passover, though the Gospels set it in the Passover season; not on the eve of the crucifixion, though it was. Paul fixes the Supper to the moment of treachery, because that is the point. On the night he was handed over to death, he handed this meal to his church. A man who had eaten with him for some three years had already taken money to hand him over (Matthew 26:14–16), and on that night Jesus broke bread for his friends, none of whom would stand by him either. The Supper was not instituted in a season of loyalty. It was given on the worst night in the history of friendship, a real night in a real room, which is precisely why an unfaithful Christian may still come to it.

Given thanks. The Greek word is eucharisteō, which is where the old name Eucharist comes from. Jesus followed the Passover pattern of giving thanks over bread, and he gave thanks for it knowing what the bread meant and what the next day held.

Which is for you. Two small Greek words, hyper hymōn, carrying the whole gospel. Not merely a body broken, but a body broken for: on your behalf, in your place, instead of you. His body was given in death for us, in our place. This is what substitution means: he in our place. And he said it to a room that, on Luke’s account, still held the man who had sold him (Luke 22:21), as well as the man who would deny him and the others who would run.

In remembrance of me. Remembrance (anamnēsis) is not just recalling, but calling to mind in a way that makes the past event present in its power, as Israel remembered the Exodus at Passover (Exodus 12:14; Deuteronomy 16:3). At every Passover a Jewish father told his children that this is what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt (Exodus 13:8), though he had never been there. So the Christian at the table does not merely recall a death long ago; he takes hold of it as his own.

Where Christians differ: This is my body. Roman Catholics take is literally: the bread becomes Christ’s body (transubstantiation), while continuing to look and taste like bread. Lutherans say Christ’s body is present in, with and under the bread. Zwinglians say it is purely a symbol, a vivid memorial of something now absent. This commentary’s view: Jesus was physically present, holding the bread, when he said it; the disciples could not have understood him to mean the bread had become his body. Jesus often spoke in metaphors: I am the door, I am the vine (John 10:9; 15:1). The bread signifies his body. But it is not an empty sign: through it, by the Spirit and through faith, believers truly receive and feed on Christ (10:16; the Westminster Confession 29.7; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 30.7). Christ is spiritually and really present to faith.

Two observations that need no degree. The words This is my body have divided the church for five hundred years, and the question is what the small word is is doing. Two plain observations help enormously. First, the body the sentence referred to was passing the plate, so nobody at that table can have heard it as a statement of chemistry. Second, this is how he regularly talked: the door, the vine, the light, the road, and nobody thinks he was made of timber. So the bread stays bread, and something entirely real is happening, because represents is far too thin a word for what the previous chapter called a participation in the body of Christ (10:16). The Reformed answer holds both, and it is not a compromise but the only position that keeps Paul’s own two statements in the same hand. What that means at the table is not a puzzle: the believer who takes the bread is receiving Christ, truly, by faith, through the Spirit, and the receiving is as real as the crumbs.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Supper is a re-sacrifice of Christ. He was offered once for all (Hebrews 9:25–28).

What should I actually do in my mind while I eat? Look back, look in, look around, and look forward. Look back to the cross: this body was given for me, in my place. Look in, with honest faith: I have nothing to bring, and I receive him gladly. Look around at your brothers and sisters, who eat the same bread and are one body with you. And look forward to the day he will eat it new with you in his kingdom. You do not need to feel something dramatic. You need only to take what is given, trusting the one who gives it. The Lord’s Supper is not a test of your concentration; it is his gift to your faith.

For worship. He knew the kiss that was coming, the trial, the whip, the nails, the darkness and the forsaking, and he lifted bread to his Father and gave thanks. The hands that broke it were the hands through which all things were made (John 1:3), and before the next sunset they would be nailed open. He did not wait for his friends to prove faithful before he gave himself to them. He put his body into their hands first, in bread, and then gave it on the cross for the same men who ran. That is what he is like still. Every time his table is spread, the Lord of glory serves himself to guests who have deserved nothing, and he does it gladly.
verseByVerse.note: This is probably the earliest written account of the Lord’s Supper, earlier than the Gospels.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way also he took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
After supper. A small detail that probably tells us which cup this was. The Passover meal, as later Jewish sources describe it, moved through a sequence of cups, and the one taken after the main course, the third cup, came to be called the cup of blessing, the same phrase Paul used at 10:16. For centuries Israel had kept the Passover year by year in memory of a rescue from Egypt. On this night the host picked it up and quietly transferred it to himself.

The new covenant. No phrase in the Old Testament was more loaded with hope. Jeremiah had promised a day when God would make a new covenant, not like the one Israel broke, in which he would write his law on hearts rather than stone, everyone would know the LORD, and he would remember their sin no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34). The disciples probably knew the passage. Jesus tells them, holding a wine cup, that it arrives with his own death. Covenants in that world were cut with blood: Moses sprinkled the people with the blood of the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 24:8). This one is sealed by the blood of one of the parties, poured out to secure the other party’s faithfulness as well as his own (Hebrews 9:15–22). That is not how human covenants work.

What is a covenant? A covenant is a binding relationship with promises, sealed by an oath or a sacrifice. It is more than a contract, because it binds persons, not merely services; it is the kind of bond marriage is. God’s covenants are his gracious commitments to his people: I will be your God, and you shall be my people. The old covenant at Sinai depended on Israel’s keeping it, and Israel broke it. The new covenant does not fail like that, because Christ has kept its terms for us and his blood has paid for every breach. Its promises are forgiveness, a new heart, and knowing God personally. When you drink the cup, God is renewing his pledge to you: all this is yours in my Son.

As often as you drink it. This is the nearest thing the New Testament gives to a rule about frequency, which is to say, no rule at all, only the assumption that it will be often. What the phrase does exclude is a Supper kept so rarely that it becomes an occasion rather than a meal; the Lord assumed his people would need feeding regularly, and he was not wrong about them.

Where Christians differ: how often? Some churches hold the Supper weekly, believing that was the apostolic practice (Acts 20:7). Others hold it less often, to preserve its solemnity. This commentary’s view: Scripture does not command a frequency. The early church seems to have celebrated it each Lord’s Day, and Calvin wished for weekly communion. Frequent celebration is a great blessing, as long as it is done with understanding and self-examination, not mechanically.

What should the cup contain? Jesus used the Passover fruit of the vine (Matthew 26:29), which in his day was wine, and wine is the fitting element. But the New Testament gives no rule about the vessel, and a church that uses grape juice for the sake of a recovering alcoholic or a troubled conscience has not broken the Supper. Nor does the Supper need to be a full meal: Paul tells the Corinthians to eat at home if they are hungry (11:34), separating the ordinary meal from the Lord’s table.

On a Tuesday. You belong to the new covenant: your sins are forgiven and remembered no more. Live in that freedom today. When an old sin rises in your memory to accuse you, answer it with the cup: God has promised to remember it no more, and he sealed that promise in blood.

parallels.desc: a new covenant

verseByVerse.quote: For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You proclaim. Paul adds his own comment to the tradition he has just recited, and it draws the Supper in two directions at once. In passing, Paul still calls it bread after the words of institution. Backwards first. The verb (katangellō) is the word for announcing, publishing, preaching. The Supper is not a private devotional moment with the eyes closed; it is a public announcement, made with hands and mouths rather than words. Augustine called the sacraments visible words, and the Reformers loved the phrase. A sacrament here means one of the two ordinances Christ gave his church, baptism and the Supper: signs by which he shows his promise to the eye and confirms it to faith (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 28.1; 30.1). A congregation eating together says something, out loud, to everyone watching: that a man died, that his death is the whole hope of these people, and that they are not ashamed of it. It is a sermon that even the illiterate can preach and no one can misquote. And it preaches one part of the story: not the teaching, not the miracles, not the example, but the death. Bread broken, wine poured: the symbols will not be repurposed.

Until he comes. Then forwards. Three words that turn the meal around. The Supper looks back to the cross and forward to the return. It is provisional, a meal for the road between, and it will one day stop, not because it failed but because it will have been overtaken by the thing it pointed to. Christ himself said he would not drink of the fruit of the vine again until he drank it new in his Father’s kingdom (Matthew 26:29; Revelation 19:9). So every communion service is a table with an empty place at it, not because Christ is absent, for he gives himself to faith at every Supper, but because he is not yet here in the body, and every celebration is a prayer: Our Lord, come (16:22).

A meal of joy and of hunger. That is why the Supper suits the way a Christian actually feels. It gives real food and it leaves you wanting a fuller one; it says the rescue has happened and it says the party has not started yet. Anyone who has taken the bread and cup in a season of grief knows the strange fitness of it: this act of worship does not require you to pretend everything is well, because it is built around a death and a waiting. Communion is designed to leave a person unsatisfied. Not because the food is poor but because it is a foretaste, and a foretaste is meant to make you hungry for the meal. That ache at the table is not a failure of devotion. It is the sacrament working.

What if I feel nothing at communion? Then you are in good company, and you have lost nothing. The Supper does not work by the strength of your feelings but by the faithfulness of Christ, who gives himself to faith whether faith feels warm or cold. A starving man is nourished by bread even when he is too tired to taste it. Come, take, and believe the promise attached to it; that is all that is asked. Over time, many find that the quiet, repeated meal does its work below the surface, steadying faith in a way no single moment could. And sometimes the dryness is itself a call to come with more expectation: to prepare during the week, to read the passages beforehand, and to pray for eyes to see him.

For worship. The death we announce belongs to a man who is not dead. He died and is alive for evermore, and he holds the keys of death (Revelation 1:18). Every loaf broken in every church for two thousand years has been a pledge in his own hand, and he has never broken a promise. And when he comes, he will do the most astonishing thing of all. He told his disciples that the returning master would dress himself for service, have them recline at table, and come and serve them (Luke 12:37). The Host who broke bread on the night he was betrayed will wait on his people at the wedding supper of the Lamb.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In an unworthy manner. This verse has probably kept more Christians away from the Lord’s table than any other sentence in the Bible, usually by being read backwards. The crucial word is an adverb. Paul does not write whoever is unworthy. He writes whoever eats in an unworthy manner. The word describes the manner, not the person; the KJV’s unworthily is the same adverb, describing how one eats, not who one is. That distinction is the difference between a table and a locked door. And it has to be so, because nobody has ever been worthy of the body and blood of the Son of God. That is the entire reason the body was broken. A Supper for the worthy would be a Supper for nobody, and Christ did not institute it in a room of worthy men; he handed it to a table of deserters. It is for sinners who trust Christ.

What is an unworthy manner? Paul is not speculating; he has spent six verses describing it. It is what was happening in Corinth: coming to the table while treating the people at it with contempt, despising the poor and treating the meal carelessly. Eating well in front of the hungry. Taking the sign of a death that levelled everybody, and using the occasion to display that you are not level with them at all.

Guilty concerning the body. Guilty (enochos) means liable, answerable. To treat the Supper with contempt is to handle the holiest thing in the world carelessly, and to be answerable for it: to sin not merely against a ritual but against the Lord himself, whose body and blood the bread and cup set forth. Israel learned at the ark what careless hands mean near the holy God, when Uzzah reached out and died (2 Samuel 6:6–7). The God of the ark is the God of this table, and he has not become less holy.

Who should hesitate. So the person who genuinely should hesitate at the table is not the one who feels unworthy. It is the one who has an unhealed contempt for a brother and intends to keep it. It is the person carrying a grudge into the queue, or nursing a sin he has decided not to give up, and reaching for the bread as though none of that were in the room with him.

If you have stayed in your seat. If you have read this verse and stayed in your seat because you knew yourself too sinful to come, hear this plainly: you have understood your own heart correctly and this verse wrongly. The table is not a reward for the clean. It is food for the starving, and a sense of your own unworthiness is very close to the qualification. Christ came to call not the righteous but sinners, and he invites the hungry to come and eat without money and without price (Matthew 9:12–13; Isaiah 55:1).

What if there is a sin I keep falling into? Then come, provided you are fighting it and not keeping it. There is a world of difference between the believer who hates his besetting sin, confesses it again and again, and keeps asking Christ for help, and the person who has made peace with a sin and intends to go on in it. The first is exactly who the Supper is for; it is given to strengthen weak faith in the fight. The second should not come until he has repented. If you are unsure which you are, the fact that you are asking with a troubled heart is usually a sign of the first. Speak to a pastor if it helps, confess the sin to God before you eat, and receive the bread as the pledge that Christ’s body was given for this sin too.
verseByVerse.note: “Unworthy manner” refers to how they were eating — despising the poor — not to whether the individual was worthy.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Examine himself. Examine (dokimazō) means test, prove, the same root as Paul’s word for the genuine, tested believers in verse 19: metal tested in the fire. And the shape of the sentence is the pastoral point: examine yourself, and so eat. The point of self-examination is not to keep away, but to come rightly. It is the way you come. Paul assumes the person who has examined himself will be at the table, not in the car park. A whole tradition of self-examination has grown up which ends in abstaining, leaving sincere Christians with their hands in their laps for years, taking their exclusion as seriousness. It is a misreading, and it deprives the very people the meal was made for.

What am I actually looking for?
