Not a morbid inventory of every failure since the last Supper; that is introspection, and it ends where introspection always ends, with the self at the centre of the picture and Christ somewhere in the background. The examination Paul has in view is short and it faces outwards. A few questions will do it. Do I trust Christ, and not myself, for my standing before God? That is the first, and if the answer is yes, however shakily, the door is open. Am I repenting of known sin? Is there anyone in this room I am refusing to be reconciled to? That is the one Corinth failed, and if there is, deal with it, because the Lord himself said to leave the gift at the altar and go and settle it first (Matthew 5:23–24). Am I coming to honour Christ and his body, to receive rather than to perform? That last one catches the respectable.

Ten looks at Christ. Where does honest self-examination lead? Away from yourself. Robert Murray M’Cheyne advised that for every look at yourself you take ten looks at Christ, and that is exactly the movement of this verse: the test ends in eating, and what is eaten is the sign of Christ given for you. You look in long enough to see that you have nothing, and then you look up at the one who is everything: the Lamb who in every respect was tempted as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), and whose perfect obedience is counted as yours. The examination does not ask whether you are good enough. It asks whether you are resting on the one who is.

Where Christians differ: who may come to the table? Some churches practise open communion, inviting anyone; others closed communion, inviting only members of that church or denomination. This commentary’s view: The table is for baptised believers who trust Christ, are not under church discipline, and examine themselves. Churches should explain this clearly and invite all such believers, whatever their congregation. Unbelievers and those living in unrepentant sin should be lovingly warned not to partake (Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 173). This is called fencing the table.

A fence around a fire. The table belongs to the Lord, not to the church that sets it out. To say openly and warmly who it is for, with the warning of verse 27 attached, is not a gate to keep the wrong people out. It is a fence around a fire, which is what you build when something is precious and hot.

What about children who profess faith? In a church that holds believer’s baptism, as this commentary does, the order is baptism first, then the table. When a child gives a credible profession of faith, understands in a simple way what the gospel and the Supper mean, and shows the beginnings of a changed life, the elders and parents may well judge it right to baptise him, and then to welcome him to the Lord’s table. The age differs from child to child, and no church should rush or refuse it for the sake of a rule. Our paedobaptist brothers, who baptise infants, usually admit children to the Supper after a public profession of faith, and so arrive at a similar place by a different road. What both agree on is that the Supper is for those who can examine themselves and discern the body.

On a Tuesday. Before the next Supper, take time to examine yourself in prayer, a day or two ahead rather than in the thirty seconds while the plate approaches. Ask the questions, confess what needs confessing, forgive whoever needs forgiving, send the message that needs sending. Then come gladly.

verseByVerse.quote: For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Discerning the body. Everything turns on what the body means here, and the context has already answered most of it. (Some later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read the Lord’s body; the earliest have simply the body.) Discerning the body may mean recognising the Lord’s body in the Supper, understanding what it means, or recognising the church as Christ’s body, which the Corinthians were despising by humiliating the poor (v. 22; 10:17). Both fit the context; perhaps Paul means both. The Corinthian failure was not a defective theory of the elements. It was that they could not see the church. They ate in front of hungry members and did not perceive that those members were the body of Christ, the very thing Paul has been saying since 10:17, that the one loaf makes the many one body, and will say again at length in chapter 12. To fail to discern the body is to look around a congregation and not see Christ’s own people there.

Judgment on himself. The word for judgment (krima) is not the word for final condemnation, though the King James Version rendered it damnation; for that Paul uses a stronger verb, condemned (katakrinō), in verse 32. It means a verdict, a sentence handed down: not necessarily eternal condemnation, but God’s judgment in the form of discipline, as the next verse shows. For the believer it is a Father’s correction, not a judge’s condemnation: when we are judged by the Lord, Paul says, we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world (v. 32).

Look up. That makes the practical test easier than the theology. Before the plate reaches you, look at the row in front and the row behind, and ask whether there is anyone there you are quietly writing off: the tedious one, the difficult one, the one who has been rude to you, the one whose politics you find intolerable, the one who has less money or less education than you and whom you have never once invited home. Those people are the body of Christ. Failing to see it is what this verse calls eating judgment.

The modern danger. There is a further application that our own age needs more than Corinth did. The modern danger at communion is not that we despise the poor member across the aisle; it is that we have forgotten he is there at all. Communion has quietly become a private transaction: head bowed, eyes shut, the congregation an incidental crowd. Paul assumes a meal where people look at each other, around one loaf that makes one body (10:17). To receive it as though the person beside you were scenery is to miss the point more gently than the Corinthians did, but to miss it nonetheless. Discerning the body is not only refusing to despise; it is bothering to notice.

Do I need to understand the theology of the Supper perfectly to discern the body? No. You need to know what it is about and whom it is for: that the bread and cup set forth Christ’s body and blood given for sinners, that he gives himself to faith through them, and that everyone who eats with you is one body with you in him. A child or a new believer can grasp that. What the verse warns against is not limited understanding but careless contempt: eating as though the meal were ordinary, and as though the people around you did not matter.
verseByVerse.note: “Discerning the body” may mean recognising the Lord’s body in the Supper, or recognising the church as his body.

verseByVerse.quote: That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died. But if we judged ourselves truly, we would not be judged. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Weak and ill. Paul makes a direct connection between how this church was behaving at the table and the sickness and deaths in its membership: God’s discipline had come in the form of illness and even death. Died is literally fallen asleep, the Christian word for believers’ death (15:18, 20). He does not soften it and neither should any commentary. But it must be handled with great care, because the wrong lesson drawn from this verse has caused enormous and needless pain.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every illness is a punishment for sin. Scripture warns against that assumption. It does not license anyone to look at a sick Christian, or a sick child, and go hunting for the hidden fault. Jesus faced that assumption head on and demolished it. Asked whose sin had caused a man’s blindness, he answered that it was not that this man sinned, or his parents (John 9:2–3). Told about Galileans killed by Pilate and eighteen crushed by a falling tower, he asked whether his hearers thought the victims were worse sinners than everyone else, and answered his own question: no (Luke 13:1–5). The whole book of Job exists to destroy the theory that suffering is a reliable index of guilt. But it does mean that God sometimes disciplines his people through physical affliction.

A specific diagnosis, not a general theory. What Paul has here is a specific diagnosis, given by an apostle about a particular congregation whose particular sin had a particular consequence. He could name the cause because he wrote as an apostle, under the inspiration of the Spirit. Nobody today has that information about anybody else’s illness, and to imitate the diagnosis without the revelation is cruelty with a Bible verse attached. So if you are reading this from a hospital bed, or after a funeral, take the plain sense of the whole passage: this text is not an accusation aimed at you. If God has something to say to you, he is well able to say it, and he does not do it in code.

If we judged ourselves truly. What the verse does teach is that God takes his table seriously enough to intervene, and that his interventions with his own children are not punishments. Verse 31 offers the simple way of avoiding them. Judged ourselves (diakrinō) means discerned, assessed, the same root as discerning in verse 29. If we examined ourselves honestly and repented, God would not need to discipline us. Honest self-appraisal now spares the need for correction later. The person who deals with his own sin is not dealt with.

Disciplined. Verse 32 gives the doctrine that makes the whole passage bearable, indeed comfortable. Disciplined (paideuō) means trained, as a father trains a child (Hebrews 12:5–11). God’s judgment on his people is fatherly correction, not final condemnation. Two different things are named in one sentence, and they must never be confused. Discipline belongs to sons; condemnation belongs to the world. God does not punish his children for sin in the sense of making them pay for it, because the punishment fell somewhere else, on a hill, once. What he does with his children is train them, and training hurts.

Not condemned. The purpose of discipline is to keep believers from final condemnation. Read the logic and it is astonishing: God let believers in Corinth become ill and let some of them die, in order that they should not be condemned with the world. Even the death of some Corinthian believers was discipline, taking them home rather than letting them go on dishonouring Christ; they were not condemned. Even the severest thing in the passage is a rescue. The hand that struck was holding on (Revelation 3:19).

Does God still discipline believers with sickness today? He may, but you can almost never know that a particular illness is discipline, and you should never conclude it about someone else. Most sickness in a Christian’s life is simply part of living in a fallen world, and God uses it to draw us nearer to him rather than to correct a specific sin. The right response to any illness is not a frantic search for hidden guilt but the ordinary, healthy practice of verse 31: ask God honestly whether there is anything he wants to show you, confess what he brings to mind, and then rest in his fatherly care. Pray for healing, use the doctors he has provided, and trust that whatever he allows, he means for your good (Romans 8:28).

Is it not cruel for God to discipline with sickness and death? From a stranger settling scores it would be. But Paul says he does it as a Father, and for one purpose: so that his children are not condemned with the world. A father who pulls his child roughly back from the edge of a cliff is not cruel, even if the child is bruised. Sin at the Lord’s table was carrying the Corinthians towards ruin, and God loved them too much to let them go quietly. And the God who disciplines is the God who spared not his own Son, but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32). He does not bruise his children from a safe distance. He took the condemnation himself.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another— if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home—so that when you come together it will not be for judgment. About the other things I will give directions when I come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wait for one another. After the warning and the discipline, the remedy is a single short command. The verb (ekdechomai) means wait for, and some scholars argue that here it also carries the sense receive, welcome. There is a lesson in the smallness of it. Paul has taken the Corinthians to the upper room, to the return of Christ and to graves in their own congregation, and what he asks is that they sit still until the slaves get off work. That is what repentance usually looks like: not a programme, but a small, slightly inconvenient change on the next occasion. And the ones asked to wait are not the poor, who were already waiting, but the comfortable, the ones with the leisure to arrive early. They are told to hold their hunger for an hour so that the meal can begin together. The cost falls on the people with something to give up, which is the direction love always travels in this letter (8:13; 9:19; 10:24).

Eat at home. Paul is drawing the distinction the Corinthians had lost. There is nothing wrong with a good dinner; there is something badly wrong with treating the Lord’s table as one. The church meal is not for satisfying appetite at others’ expense. When the church gathers, what you do at that table is not about you at all.

Welcomed, so welcoming. Why should the comfortable wait? Because Christ waited for them. Paul’s reasoning everywhere is that believers treat one another as the Lord has treated them: welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God (Romans 15:7). Not one person on those Corinthian couches had arrived at Christ’s table early, on his own merit, with something to offer. Each had come in late and empty from the courtyard of the world, and found the Son of God had kept a place for him. To make a hungry slave wait outside the meal that celebrates that welcome is to forget your own arrival.

When I come. A quiet ending, and a reminder that a letter is not the whole of pastoral care. There were other matters, perhaps about the Supper, and Paul would not settle them at a distance; some things need a face. He is coming, and they know it, and that expectation is itself part of the correction. Not everything was written down, but everything necessary was (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

In the flow. These verses close the chapter’s second half the way it began, with the church coming together (vv. 17, 33). Paul has moved from the divided tables of verses 17–22, to the words of the Lord, to the warning and the discipline, and he lands on one plain command: wait for one another. And the theme does not end here. The body that Corinth failed to discern at the table is the body chapter 12 will unfold, one body with many members, each needed by the rest, where the weaker parts are indispensable (12:22).

What does waiting for one another look like in a church today? It looks like a hundred small courtesies that say: you matter here. Holding the service until the bus from the care home arrives. Keeping a seat for the latecomer with three small children. Making sure the food at the church lunch reaches the back table before seconds are offered at the front. Not starting the meeting before the person who works shifts can get there. Choosing, at the Supper itself, to receive the bread together rather than as isolated individuals. None of these is dramatic. All of them preach the same sermon that a Corinthian host preached when he put his bread down and waited.

For worship. Picture a wealthy Corinthian on his couch, hearing footsteps in the courtyard, putting the bread back down until the man with the calloused hands has come in and sat beside him. Nothing grand happened in that room, yet the death of the Son of God was preached in it, by two men starting to eat at the same moment. And behind that small courtesy stands a vast patience. The Lord of glory has been setting his table for centuries, in cathedrals and in kitchens, and he has not yet closed the door. He is not slow, as some count slowness, but patient, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). The Host is still waiting for his last guests.

But since it is disgraceful for a wife to cut off her hair or shave her head, let her cover her head.<sup>7</sup>For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, but woman is the glory of man.<sup>8</sup>For man was not made from woman, but woman from man.<sup>9</sup>Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.<sup>10</sup>That is why a wife ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels.<sup>11</sup>Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman;<sup>12</sup>for as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God.<sup>13</sup>Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a wife to pray to God with her head uncovered?<sup>14</sup>Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair it is a disgrace for him,<sup>15</sup>but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For her hair is given to her for a covering.<sup>16</sup>If anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such practice, nor do the churches of God.<sup>17</sup>But in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse.<sup>18</sup>For, in the first place, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you. And I believe it in part,<sup>19</sup>for there must be factions among you in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognized.<sup>20</sup>When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat.<sup>21</sup>For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk.<sup>22</sup>What! Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Do this in remembrance of me.”<sup>25</sup>In the same way also he took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”<sup>26</sup>For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.<sup>27</sup>Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord.<sup>28</sup>Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.<sup>29</sup>For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.<sup>30</sup>That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died.<sup>31</sup>But if we judged ourselves truly, we would not be judged.<sup>32</sup>But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world.<sup>33</sup>So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another—<sup>34</sup>if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home—so that when you come together it will not be for judgment. About the other things I will give directions when I come.

12.title: One Body, Many Gifts, One Spirit
12.overview:
Paul turns to another question from their letter: spiritual gifts. The Corinthians were especially impressed by dramatic gifts, above all speaking in tongues, and treated them as marks of superior spirituality. Their pagan background explains some of this: Greek religion prized ecstatic experience, from the trance of the prophetess at Delphi to the frenzy of the worship of Dionysus, and being carried away was taken as a sign of the divine. Paul begins with a test that has nothing to do with excitement: the Spirit always leads people to confess that Jesus is Lord.

The gifts are many but the giver is one, and every gift is given for the good of the whole church, not for display. Then Paul takes up the picture of the body, a common image in ancient politics for a community whose members must cooperate. In Corinth it had a local twist: at the temple of Asclepius, the god of healing, worshippers left clay models of the body parts they wanted healed, hands, feet, eyes, ears, and many have been dug up. The church is one body with many parts, and no member can do without the others. The chapter ends by pointing to a better way still, the way of love.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Gifts of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before listing a single gift, Paul gives the test of the Spirit’s work (what is said about Jesus) and names the source of every gift: one Spirit, one Lord, one God. Every believer is given some gift, as the Spirit wills, for the good of others.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Trinitarian Source of All Gifts

In verses 4–6 Paul assumes the Trinity in passing, without stopping to argue for it. Reformed teaching on spiritual gifts has grounded them here: they are not the Spirit’s work apart from Christ, but the common work of Father, Son and Spirit. That guards against two opposite mistakes, making much of the Spirit and little of Christ, and neglecting the Spirit’s present work. Every genuine gift is the work of the triune God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians were competing for the most impressive gifts and using them as social standing. Grounding every gift in the one God removes the competition at its root: no one can boast of a gift the Spirit gave as he willed. Now: The same rivalry can run in different directions: some churches prize dramatic gifts over quiet ones, others prize intellectual gifts such as teaching over practical ones. Paul’s list refuses both rankings.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed. You know that when you were pagans you were led astray to mute idols, however you were led.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Chapters 12 to 14 answer the Corinthians’ question about spiritual gifts. They prized the spectacular gifts, tongues above all, as badges of spiritual rank, and it was dividing the church. Chapter 12 lays the foundation. The test of the Spirit’s work is not ecstasy but the confession that Jesus is Lord (vv. 1–3). One Spirit, one Lord and one God give many gifts, each for the common good, as the Spirit wills (vv. 4–11). The church is one body, all baptised by one Spirit into Christ, and every part is needed, the weaker most of all (vv. 12–26). Not all have the same gift; desire those that build up most, and Paul will show a better way still: love (vv. 27–31).

Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers. The phrase now concerning (7:1; 8:1) signals that Paul is answering a question the Corinthians put to him in writing. What follows is the longest treatment of the subject in the Bible, three chapters with a hymn in the middle. Spiritual gifts is literally spiritual things or spiritual people (pneumatika), perhaps the Corinthians’ own word for the gifts they valued and the people who had them. Paul will soon use a different word, charismata, grace-gifts (v. 4), shifting the focus from spirituality to grace. They thought they knew about spiritual things; Paul says they need teaching.

Mute idols. Out of all he could have said about their old gods, Paul chooses one detail: they could not speak. The word (aphōna) is mute, voiceless. The Old Testament says it with something close to contempt: they have mouths, but do not speak (Psalm 115:5; Habakkuk 2:18), and on Carmel four hundred and fifty men shouted all day at a silence (1 Kings 18:26–29). Picture one of those temples: incense, drums, a crowd, and a statue with painted eyes that has never said a word. The priest interprets, the oracle is ambiguous, and nobody can check what comes out of the ecstasy, because the god in the room has no voice.

However you were led. Led (agō) means carried off, swept along by forces beyond their control. Pagan worship in Corinth was not dull; it involved real ecstatic states, frenzy, trance and utterance, for example in the cults of Dionysus. The Corinthians had seen impressive spiritual phenomena long before they heard of the Holy Spirit, and had arrived in the church already trained to believe that the more overwhelming an experience, the more divine it must be. They were grading the Spirit’s gifts by the standard of the temple they had left. But the Holy Spirit does not work by mindless compulsion; the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets (14:32).

Intensity is not evidence. Something can be powerful, sincere, moving, and entirely unconnected to God; the idols were mute, but the worship in front of them was not quiet. Being carried away is not proof of the Holy Spirit, then or now.

How can people of other religions have powerful spiritual experiences? Because human beings are made for God and are deeply spiritual creatures, and because there are real spiritual powers in the world besides the Holy Spirit (10:20). Ecstasy, visions, healings and trances are reported in many religions, and Scripture never pretends otherwise; Pharaoh’s magicians copied some of Moses’ signs (Exodus 7:11, 22). So the presence of a spiritual experience settles nothing by itself. A Christian should neither be impressed by such things nor frightened of them, but should ask Paul’s question: what does this say about Jesus Christ? The Spirit of God always points to him.

Are emotions in worship wrong, then? Not at all. The Psalms shout, weep, dance and clap; the early church was filled with joy; and a Christian who is moved to tears by the love of Christ is responding rightly. Paul is not against feeling. He is against using feeling as the measure of God’s presence. The healthiest worship engages the mind and the heart together (14:15): it understands what it is singing, and it feels the weight and wonder of it. Strong emotion that rises from the truth about Christ is a gift. Strong emotion pursued for its own sake is the temple of Dionysus with Christian words.

Idols that cannot speak, and a Shepherd who calls. Paul’s contrast is between being driven and being spoken to. The Corinthians had been swept along towards gods with no voice. Now they belong to a Lord who leads by speaking: the sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out (John 10:3). In the temple the crowd was carried along and nobody knew where; in the church the risen Christ calls each of his people by name, and they follow because they know whose voice it is (John 10:27). And the Spirit’s work is to bring people to confess that voice as Lord (v. 3).

On a Tuesday. Think of the most powerful spiritual experience you have had, and ask what it left you believing about Christ, and how it changed the way you live. That is the measure of it.

For worship. The idols were mute because there was nothing in them. The Son of God was silent because he chose to be. He who spoke the stars into being stood before his accusers like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, and opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7). He kept silence under the charge, the scourge and the nails, so that people who had spent their lives before gods that never answered might hear a God who calls them by name. The Word made flesh went quiet at the cross, and because he did, he will never be silent towards his people again.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I want you to understand that no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says “Jesus is accursed!” and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I want you to understand. The first test of genuine spiritual activity moves the question from the experience to the content: not how did it feel, but what did it say about Jesus?

The curse. Accursed is anathema. Whether anyone in Corinth actually shouted it is debated. Perhaps someone in an ecstatic state had said it and the church was shaken. Perhaps unbelievers in the synagogues were cursing Jesus and pressing Christians to do the same, as Paul himself once did (Acts 26:11). Perhaps Paul is naming the worst thing imaginable in order to establish the principle at its extreme. Whatever the source, the rule holds at both ends: the Spirit never speaks against Christ, and no one comes to confess Christ without him.

Jesus is Lord. This is the sweeter half. Jesus is Lord was one of the earliest Christian confessions (Romans 10:9; Philippians 2:11). Anyone can pronounce the syllables. Paul means the confession of a person who has truly handed over the running of his life to a crucified Jew from Nazareth, and owns him as God and master. That sentence, meant, cannot be manufactured by good arguments, a strong upbringing or an emotional evening. It is the fingerprint of God on a human heart. By nature the mind is blind to the glory of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:4–6): a person may admire Jesus and even defend him, but he will not bow to him until the Spirit gives him new birth (John 3:3–5). So every believer who confesses Jesus as Lord has the Spirit. There are no second-class Christians without him.

The accursed one is the Lord. Put the two cries side by side and the gospel stands between them. To the synagogue a crucified man was under God’s curse, for the law said a hanged man is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23), and many think that is where the cry Jesus is accursed came from. The gospel does not deny the curse. It explains it. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). He hung where the curse falls so that those who trust him would never bear it. So the Spirit does not teach a believer to say that Jesus was never under the curse. He teaches him to look at the one who bore it, and call him Lord.

What does Lord mean here? More than master or sir. The Greek word is kyrios, and it is the word the Greek translation of the Old Testament used for the name of God himself, the LORD. To call Jesus Lord in a church full of Jews and Gentiles who read that Bible was to give him the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9–11). It was also costly. In the Roman world the cry was Caesar is Lord, and Christians who refused to say it, or who said Jesus instead, were sometimes killed for it. So the confession means three things at once: Jesus is God, Jesus has the right to rule me, and Jesus outranks every other power that claims my loyalty.

How do I know I am not simply talked into this? It is a question that troubles thoughtful Christians more than they usually say, and here is one honest place to look. If Christ is genuinely your Lord, not merely your preference or your heritage, then according to this verse somebody did that to you, and the somebody was the third person of the Trinity. The most ordinary Christian confession in the world is a supernatural event.

The practical use of the test. Corinth wanted a way to tell the Spirit’s work from spiritual theatre, and Paul gives one that needs no special insight: listen to what is being said about Jesus. The Spirit’s whole business is to glorify Christ (John 16:14). So a movement, teacher or book that makes much of the Spirit and little of Christ has failed the only test the New Testament gives, however remarkable the phenomena; and a quiet congregation where Christ is honoured and trusted has passed it (1 John 4:2–3).

On a Tuesday. Say it today, slowly and meaning it: Jesus is Lord. Then ask what in your week he is not yet allowed to rule, and hand it over; the Spirit who taught you to say it is at work in you to make it true.

For worship. The Spirit is the least self-advertising person in the universe. He is like a floodlight trained on a building at night: doing all the work, entirely unlooked at, and content that what people see is the building. And the building he lights is a cross. He shines on the place where the Son of God hung under the curse, and shows it to be a throne. Glory to the Spirit who glorifies Christ, and glory to the Christ whom every tongue will one day confess as Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
verseByVerse.note: “Jesus is Lord” was one of the earliest Christian confessions.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Varieties of gifts. Three sentences with the same shape, and the shape is the argument: variety on one side, sameness on the other, three times over. Paul is showing where the unity comes from. Varieties (diaireseis) means distributions, allotments. Gifts is charismata, from the word for grace: a gift is grace made specific, grace with a shape. Grace is God’s kindness to people who have not deserved it, and a gift is that same kindness given a definite form in a particular person: the ability to explain a passage clearly, to open a home to strangers, to sit with the dying. Peter calls those who use them stewards of God’s varied grace (1 Peter 4:10).

Varieties of service. Service is diakoniai, where we get the word deacon: a gift is not an ornament but a job. The gifts are for serving, under one Lord, Jesus.

Varieties of activities. Activities is energēmata, from which we get energy: workings, effects. It is God actually doing something through a person, not a talent the person owns and operates. God the Father works through all.

The Trinity. The same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, laid out in one breath in a paragraph about church squabbles, and Paul does not stop to explain or defend it. The doctrine of the Trinity is sometimes called a late invention of the bishops at Nicaea in AD 325. The careful vocabulary did come later, but the pattern is here, some twenty-odd years after the crucifixion, so settled in the apostolic mind that it can be used in passing in a letter about who is showing off in church. Each person of the Trinity is involved in every gift, and unity in diversity in the church reflects unity in diversity in God.

Why the competition collapses. Put the three nouns together and the Corinthian competition collapses on the spot. If a gift is grace, nobody earned it. If it is service, it was never given for display. And if it is God working, then boasting about it is as odd as a chisel congratulating itself on the furniture.

In the flow. These three verses give the source of every gift, and Paul states it before he lists a single gift, so that the list in verses 8–10 is read with the Giver already in view. The order shapes the whole chapter. Unity comes first and variety second, because the variety flows out of the one God and cannot rightly be turned against him. Everything Paul says later about the body, its many members and its one life (vv. 12–26), is these three sentences worked out in a congregation.

The same Lord, who came to serve. Every diakonia in the church is rendered to Jesus, and Jesus is the one who turned service from a slave’s job into a glory. To disciples arguing about rank, as the Corinthians were, he said, I am among you as the one who serves (Luke 22:27). The Lord whom all the services honour is himself the great Servant, who washed feet and then gave his life. A gift used to climb above other people is a service offered to that Lord in a manner he never once used himself.

Should I pray to the Holy Spirit? You may, and the church has done so for centuries in hymns such as Come, Holy Ghost. The Spirit is fully God, and he may be worshipped and addressed. But the ordinary pattern of New Testament prayer is to pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18). And Paul’s three sentences quietly settle the worry behind the question, whether attention paid to one person is attention withheld from another. There is no dividing them up, because they are never working separately. The gift in your hands was given by the Spirit, is a service rendered to the Lord, and is God at work in you. One act, three persons, no seams. Whomever you address, you are speaking to the one God.

On a Tuesday. When the gifted people in a congregation gather, is the conversation about what God is doing, or about who is doing it? Paul’s three sentences make the second sort of conversation not merely uncharitable but incoherent. Next time you talk about your church, speak of what God has done before you speak of who did it.

For worship. Within the life of God there has never been a moment of competition. The Father is not diminished by the Son’s glory; the Spirit does not resent being the one nobody looks at; nothing in that fellowship has ever needed to be negotiated. And out of that life, unhurried, unthreatened, entirely at peace with itself, came a world, and a cross, and a church full of quarrelling people in a Greek port, handed grace with a shape and set to work. Every gift in every church, the ones most unlike ours included, has flowed from that same overflowing life of Father, Son and Spirit.
verseByVerse.note: Spirit, Lord and God appear together: the gifts come from the triune God.

verseByVerse.quote: To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To each is given. Two words in this verse settle questions that trouble many Christians. To each: not to the impressive, the ordained or the articulate. This was a church of slaves, dockworkers and people Paul had called not wise, not powerful, not of noble birth (1:26), and every believer in it had received a manifestation of the Spirit. There are no giftless Christians. And is given: received, not earned.

Nobody simply attends. Many people quietly reason: I am not a teacher, I do not sing, I have never led anything, so I am one of the ones who simply attends. This verse says that is not a category. It does not say every Christian has a prominent gift. It says every Christian has one.

The manifestation of the Spirit. Manifestation (phanerōsis) means display, showing. Each gift is a way the Spirit shows himself at work. When a member of your church comforts the grieving well, or keeps the accounts honestly, or explains a passage so that it opens, you are watching the invisible Spirit become visible.

For the common good. There is the purpose, and it ruins gift competition permanently. The word (sympherō) means for benefit, what helps. A gift is not a personal enrichment, a spiritual souvenir or evidence of standing. It is given to one person for the benefit of others, the property of the congregation held in his hands for a while. A gift used for self-display has been used for the opposite of its purpose. This is the key to chapters 12–14.

Anointed for others. The pattern was set in Christ before it was given to the church. When the Spirit came upon Jesus at his baptism, the first thing the Gospels record is a refusal to serve himself: hungry in the wilderness, he would not turn stones into bread for his own need (Matthew 4:3–4), though later he fed five thousand. In Nazareth he read out what the Spirit was for: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor (Luke 4:18). He never used the Spirit’s power for his own comfort or display. The gifts in a church are that same anointing shared out among his members, with the same direction: outward.

How do I find out what mine is? That is the practical question every honest reader wants answered, and it is usually left vague when it should not be. Not, in the first place, by introspection. The New Testament does tell a Christian to examine himself, but about his standing before God and his conduct at the Lord’s table (11:28; 2 Corinthians 13:5), never about which gift he has been given. Gifts are discovered in use, not in analysis. Four things will do more than any questionnaire. First, start serving something, anything the church actually needs, and notice what happens. Second, watch for the thing that leaves other people strengthened rather than merely impressed; that is the mark of a gift as against a talent. Third, ask two or three Christians who know you well and will tell you the truth, because gifts are far easier to see from outside than from inside. Fourth, notice what you keep being asked to do; congregations are usually better at spotting gifts than the people who have them. And notice what is not on that list: whether you enjoy it, and whether you are naturally good at it. Both are useful signs and neither is decisive. This is a manifestation of the Spirit, not a personality test, and the Spirit has been known to work through people who found the work difficult all their lives.

What if I am too old, ill or worn out to do anything? Then your gift has not been taken away; it may simply have changed shape. Some of the most fruitful members of any church are those who can no longer leave the house: who pray through the church list every morning, who write a card to the grieving, who telephone the lonely, who receive visitors with such faith and patience that the visitors go home strengthened. Suffering borne with trust in Christ is itself a ministry to everyone who sees it (2 Corinthians 1:3–6). The common good does not require energy. It requires a member who belongs to the body and is still, in whatever way is left, offering what God has given.

verseByVerse.quote: For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The utterance of wisdom. The list begins, and Paul offers no definitions, which suggests the Corinthians knew what he meant. The utterance of wisdom is a word of wisdom (logos sophias): something said, not merely possessed. Wisdom in this letter is not cleverness; the wisdom of God is a crucified man (1:23–24; 2:6–7). So this gift is the ability to speak God’s wisdom into the situation in front of you. Everyone has met it: the believer who is not especially learned but who, in a crisis, says the one sentence that helps.

The utterance of knowledge. A word of knowledge (logos gnōseōs) is its companion: grasping the truth of God and being able to put it into words that hold. It is the ability to explain the truths of the faith, probably close to teaching. The Corinthians loved knowledge (8:1); Paul reminds them that even knowledge is a gift, not an achievement.

Faith. Every Christian has saving faith, so Paul must mean something more: a particular God-given confidence for a particular thing, the believer who is certain God will provide for a work while everyone else is doing sums, and is proved right. It is the faith Jesus described as moving mountains, an image Paul uses in the next chapter (13:2; Matthew 17:20).

Gifts of healings. Both nouns are plural in the Greek, which is itself instructive. Not the gift of healing, a standing power a man carries around, but gifts of healings: particular acts of mercy, given occasion by occasion, the ability to bring God’s healing in specific cases, as the apostles did (Acts 3:6–8; 5:15–16; 28:8).

Jesus Christ heals you. That is what Peter said to Aeneas, paralysed for eight years (Acts 9:34), and it tells us whose healing the gifts of healings were. The apostles never claimed the power as theirs: his name, by faith in his name, has made this man strong (Acts 3:16). Luke calls his Gospel an account of all that Jesus began to do and teach (Acts 1:1), and the healings in Acts are the risen Lord continuing it. Matthew roots Jesus’ own healings in the cross: he took our illnesses and bore our diseases (Matthew 8:17; Isaiah 53:4). Every healing of his people is a fruit of the cross.

What it does not mean. It does not mean this is a complete list of gifts, or that each person has only one. Paul gives several lists, all different (Romans 12; Ephesians 4; 1 Peter 4).

Does God still heal? Yes. He is not less able than he was, and Christians should pray for the sick expectantly and without embarrassment, because they are told to: James tells the sick to call the elders to pray over them (James 5:14–15). That is different from a gift by which a person could heal at will, as the apostles did to confirm their message (Acts 5:15–16; 2 Corinthians 12:12). That sign gift belonged to the apostolic foundation and has ceased with it. This is the cessationist conviction (that such sign gifts ceased with the apostles), held because Scripture ties them to the apostles’ own ministry (2 Corinthians 12:12); continuationist brothers and sisters, who believe the gifts continue, read the evidence differently, and their eagerness to pray for the sick is a rebuke to cold hearts. A sign gift is a power given to mark out a messenger as truly sent by God, as the signs given to Moses were, so that Israel would believe the Lord had appeared to him (Exodus 4:1–5); the apostles’ healings did exactly that, as the Lord bore witness to the word of his grace by signs and wonders done by their hands (Acts 14:3). So a believer should pray for the sick with confidence in God, and treat claims to a healing ministry with caution, testing them by Scripture and by what actually happens.

And does he always? Plainly not, and the New Testament is remarkably candid about it. Paul left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). Epaphroditus nearly died, and Paul calls his recovery a mercy rather than an entitlement (Philippians 2:27). Timothy had a recurring stomach complaint and got advice about wine, not a healing (1 Timothy 5:23). And Paul himself asked three times for his own thorn to be removed and was told no, with a reason: my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). That is enormously important for anyone who has prayed and not been healed, or who has been told that the failure was theirs. If the apostle who raised a young man from the dead at Troas (Acts 20:9–12) could not heal his own friend or himself, then unhealed sickness in a Christian is not evidence of a lack of faith. It is evidence that the gifts are given as he wills, and that the will in question is wiser than ours.

What is the difference between a spiritual gift and a natural talent? Sometimes very little on the surface, and a great deal underneath. God gives natural abilities to everyone, believers and unbelievers alike: a good mind, a fine voice, a head for figures. A spiritual gift is an ability the Spirit gives or takes up and uses, in a believer, for building up Christ’s body. Often the Spirit takes a natural talent and turns it to new ends, so that a teacher becomes a teacher of the word. Sometimes he gives what was never there before. The real difference is in the fruit: a talent impresses, a gift strengthens. When people go away from your service closer to Christ, rather than merely admiring you, the Spirit is at work.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the sick in your church this week, by name, expecting God to hear; and tell one of those who explain the faith clearly how their words helped you.

verseByVerse.quote: to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the ability to distinguish between spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues. All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Miracles. Five more gifts, three of which chapter 14 treats at length. The working of miracles is literally workings of powers (energēmata dynameōn): acts of power beyond healing, such as Paul striking Elymas blind (Acts 13:11) or raising Eutychus (Acts 20:9–12).

To another prophecy. Prophecy in the New Testament is not mainly prediction. It is speaking a message revealed by God for the church’s strengthening, encouragement and comfort (14:3), and it could lay bare the secrets of a heart (14:24–25). Paul assumes it must be tested: let the others weigh what is said (14:29), which no one would say about Scripture. So prophecy in Corinth stood under the apostolic word and never beside it, and no congregational prophecy of this kind ever added a line to the Bible.

Distinguishing between spirits. The companion gift, and its presence in the list is telling: Paul assumes that not everything claiming to be from God is from God, and that some believers were given a nose for the difference. It is discerning which messages and powers are from God and which from false spirits (1 John 4:1), since prophecies needed testing (14:29). The public test is the one Paul gave at the start of the chapter, the confession that Jesus is Lord (v. 3); this is the discernment that goes with it.

Tongues. Speaking in languages one has not learned, by the Spirit, as at Pentecost (Acts 2:4–11). These were the gifts Corinth prized most and understood least. Paul includes them without a hint of scorn, and says he speaks in tongues more than any of them (14:18). Yet tongues and their interpretation come last, here and again in verse 28, perhaps deliberately, since the Corinthians ranked them first.

Interpretation. The ability to explain what was spoken in a tongue, so the church could understand (14:13, 27–28).

Every gift with one subject. One name runs through all five of these gifts. The miracles of Acts were done in the name of Jesus. The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy (Revelation 19:10). The test for discerning spirits is whether a spirit confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh (1 John 4:2). And when tongues were first heard at Pentecost, the crowd heard the mighty works of God in their own languages (Acts 2:11), and Peter explained that the risen Jesus, exalted at God’s right hand, had poured out what they saw and heard (Acts 2:33). The Spirit hands out the gifts as he wills, but he has only ever had one message.

As he wills. The closing sentence governs the whole chapter. The Spirit wills (bouletai): he is a person with a will, not a force to be switched on. No one can demand a particular gift or boast in having one. That is a rebuke to anyone who thinks a gift reflects credit on its holder. And it is a comfort to anyone who has begged for a gift, not received it, and been told by someone confident that the fault lies in his faith. The distribution is the Spirit’s free act, and he has never given anybody grounds for despising a Christian who lacks something.

Where Christians differ: do the miraculous gifts continue? Continuationists hold that all these gifts are available today, and they have real reasons: Paul gives them for the common good (v. 7), tells the church to desire them and not to forbid them (14:1, 39), and says they will pass away when the perfect comes (13:10), which many take to be Christ’s return. This commentary’s view: The gifts of miracles, healings, prophecy and tongues served as signs confirming the apostolic message while Scripture was being given (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). With the foundation of apostles and prophets laid and the canon (the complete collection of Scripture) closed, these revelatory and sign gifts have ceased as ordinary gifts in the church. God still heals in answer to prayer and does wonders as he pleases, and the gifts of wisdom, knowledge, faith, discernment, teaching, serving and mercy continue. This cessationist view (that these gifts ceased with the apostles) is held charitably toward continuationist brothers and sisters, with whom we share the gospel.

Held with charity. Christians have differed over this for centuries, and both convictions are held by people who love the Bible and each other. The cessationist view rests on the church being built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), a foundation laid once; continuationists answer that the foundation was the apostles’ teaching, not every gift that came with it. What this verse settles, whichever way a reader lands, is that no one may look down on another Christian over it. The Spirit apportions as he wills, and that clause has never yet been amended by a committee on either side.

What about Christians today who say they speak in tongues? Treat them as brothers and sisters, not as suspects. Many love Christ deeply, and the experience they describe is sincere. A cessationist will believe that what they experience is not the New Testament gift of real languages given as a sign, but a form of prayerful speech or devotion; a continuationist will see it differently. Both can agree on what Paul himself requires in chapter 14: that nothing in the church should be unintelligible without interpretation, that everything must be done decently and in order, and that no gift may ever be made the badge of the Spirit’s presence (12:30). Where those rules are kept, the disagreement need not divide fellowship in the gospel.

What if someone says God told me? Listen carefully and humbly, and test it. God does guide his people, by his word, by wise counsel, by the circumstances he arranges, and by the Spirit’s inward work in their hearts and consciences. But an impression is not a revelation, and it never carries the authority of Scripture. If what someone believes God told them contradicts Scripture, it is not from God. If it agrees with Scripture, its authority comes from Scripture, not from the impression. And no one may bind your conscience with a word they say God gave them about your life. The canon is closed, and in it God has given us everything we need for life and godliness (2 Peter 1:3; 2 Timothy 3:16–17).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul gives the gifts a picture: the church is one body, joined by one Spirit to Christ. He speaks first to the member who feels he does not belong, then to the member who thinks he does not need the others, and ends with a body whose members suffer and rejoice together.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Body of Christ: Church and Salvation Joined

The body is not only a useful picture of community life. The church is the body of Christ because the Spirit has baptised every believer into union with the crucified and risen Lord (v. 13). The union is real, which is why the suffering of one member is felt by the whole (v. 26). Paul’s whole ethic of community rests on it: you can no more be indifferent to a fellow member’s suffering than your hand can ignore the pain in your foot.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The competition over gifts had produced both contempt (those with prized gifts dismissing the rest) and despair (the rest feeling shut out). Paul answers both: the despairing are told they belong; the contemptuous are told they need those they despise. Now: Every church has members who look impressive and members who look marginal by the world’s standards. Both were placed by the same God, and the body needs both.

verseByVerse.quote: For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—Jews or Greeks, slaves or free—and all were made to drink of one Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One body, many members. The image arrives, and Paul will spend the rest of the chapter on it. The body was a familiar picture in ancient political writing for a united society, but Paul gives it a twist of his own.

So it is with Christ. The sentence does not end as anyone expects. The natural conclusion is so it is with the church. Paul writes so it is with Christ. The church is not merely like a body; it is his body (v. 27; Ephesians 1:22–23), so united to him that it bears his name. The risen Lord said it to a man on the Damascus road who had never laid a finger on him personally: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). Saul had been arresting Christians; Christ counted it as an assault on himself. The man who heard that sentence is the man writing this one.

Baptised into one body. In one Spirit, or by one Spirit. The words all and one answer a question many Christians have been troubled by: is there a second experience after conversion, a baptism in the Spirit, which some believers have and others lack? Paul’s sentence is hard to get round. He writes it to a church whose spiritual life was a shambles, with factions, gross immorality, lawsuits and drunkenness at the Lord’s table. If any congregation could have been called second-class in the Spirit, it was this one, and he says all of them have had it. Baptism in the Spirit, in this verse, is what happened to every Christian when he became one: the entrance, not the upgrade. It is the Spirit’s work of uniting us to Christ, of which water baptism is the sign. Being united to Christ means that what is true of him becomes true of us: his death counts as our death to sin, and his risen life now flows into us (Romans 6:5; Galatians 2:20).

Jews or Greeks, slaves or free. These were the deepest divisions of that world, ethnic and religious, social and economic. The Spirit does not abolish the differences; a Jew was still a Jew and a slave still went back to his master. He does something better. He puts them in one body, so that the differences remain and stop being walls (Galatians 3:27–28; Ephesians 2:14–16).

Made to drink. The Spirit is like water poured out and drunk, the picture the prophets and Jesus himself used (Isaiah 44:3; John 7:37–39). All believers have drunk deeply of him; he is not sprinkled on the surface but taken in.

In the flow. Verse 13 gives the reason the picture is true: every believer has been joined by the same Spirit to the same Christ. The rest of the chapter works the picture out in two directions, first for the member who feels he does not belong (vv. 15–20), then for the member who thinks he does not need the others (vv. 21–26). And it serves the whole letter. A church split into the party of Paul, the party of Apollos and the party of Cephas (1:12) is told what it already is: one body, because Christ is not divided (1:13).

Where Christians differ: baptism in the Spirit. Pentecostals often teach that baptism in the Spirit is a second experience after conversion, evidenced by speaking in tongues. This commentary’s view: Paul says all believers, including the immature Corinthians, were baptised in the one Spirit into the one body. Spirit baptism happens at conversion; it is the Spirit’s work of joining us to Christ and his body. It is not a second blessing for some. Believers may and should seek to be filled with the Spirit continually (Ephesians 5:18), which is different from the once-for-all baptism in the Spirit.

The hunger behind the question. Something else should be said just as clearly, because brothers and sisters who use the phrase differently are usually reaching for something real. Scripture plainly teaches fresh, powerful fillings of the Spirit after conversion. The believers filled in Acts 2 are filled again in Acts 4 (Acts 4:31), and Christians are commanded to go on being filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), a continuous thing, not a single event. So the hunger behind the question is right and should not be shamed. A Christian may and should ask for more of God. What he need not ask for is admission to a body he has already been baptised into.

Then what is water baptism for? If the Spirit joins us to Christ at conversion, water baptism is the outward sign the Lord commanded for those who have been joined to him (Matthew 28:19). It pictures what the Spirit has done: washing, death to the old life, burial and rising with Christ (Romans 6:3–4). It is the believer’s public confession of faith and his entrance into the visible church. It is also a means God uses to strengthen faith and assure his people that they belong to him. That is why this commentary holds that baptism belongs to those who have professed faith in Christ, following the 1689 London Baptist Confession, while honouring paedobaptist brothers who baptise the children of believers. Paedobaptists (those who baptise infants) see baptism as the sign of God’s covenant promise to believers and their children, as circumcision was in Israel; this commentary holds that the New Testament joins the sign to repentance and faith (Acts 2:38, 41), yet gladly owns them as members of the one body this verse describes. Baptism does not make anyone a Christian. It is how the Lord marks out those who are.

On a Tuesday. Look at the Christian you find most different from yourself, in background, race, class or politics: the Spirit has put you in one body with him. Treat him like it.

verseByVerse.quote: For the body does not consist of one member but of many. If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body. And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many members. Diversity is essential to a body. Paul now gives the body a voice, and the first thing it says is a complaint about itself.

The foot’s complaint. Paul addresses the discouraged first; the proud come at verse 21. The image was familiar: the Roman Menenius Agrippa was said to have calmed a rebellion of the common people with a fable of the body’s members refusing to feed the stomach. Listen to the foot’s logic. It has admired what the hand can do, concluded that it cannot do any of it, and drawn the inference: therefore I am not really part of this. That feels like humility. It is in fact a verdict passed on God’s arrangement by a body part that has decided it knows better.

No less a part. Paul answers with a shrug. The foot’s membership is not a matter of the foot’s opinion. Feelings of not belonging do not detach anybody from Christ’s body, any more than a man’s low view of his own left foot detaches it from his leg. Belonging was settled by the Spirit’s baptism (v. 13), and it is not reopened every time a member feels unimpressive.

Whose body it is. The foot talks as if the body were a club with membership depending on qualifications. But the body is Christ’s (v. 27), so who belongs in it is his to answer, and he has answered: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). The discouraged member argues from his gifts: I cannot do what the hand does, so I cannot be his. The gospel argues from Christ: he called you, he joined you to himself, and he does not disown what he has joined. That is why Paul does not reassure the foot about its abilities. Its place never rested on them.

Comparison looks upward. The foot did not compare itself to a foot. It compared itself to a hand, which makes the comparison useless and painful at once. Nobody is discouraged by comparing himself with someone doing the same job; discouragement comes from measuring yourself against a gift you were never given and treating the shortfall as a personal failing.

The quiet withdrawal. The foot in this picture does not merely feel bad. It withdraws. People who conclude they do not belong stop offering, stop coming forward, and eventually stop coming; and because they leave slowly and apologetically, nobody chases them. If that has been your drift, the answer is not a compliment but a fact: your leaving would not make you any less a part of the body, and it would leave the body without a foot. And the discouraged rarely announce themselves; they say they are busy that week. So asking a quiet member what he is finding hard, and meaning the question, is not small talk. It is body maintenance.

What if my church really does not seem to want me? Sometimes the problem is not the foot’s feelings but the body’s neglect, and it is right to say so. If you have offered to serve and been passed over, or been made to feel unwelcome, that is a failure the church must answer for, and verses 21–26 are written to it. But the answer to being overlooked is rarely to withdraw. Speak to an elder honestly and without bitterness; ask where help is actually needed; look for the people on the edges like yourself and befriend them. If after real effort a church persistently refuses to receive you, it may be right to seek another, but go to belong somewhere, not to belong nowhere. You are a member of Christ’s body, and you need a local expression of it, as it needs you.
verseByVerse.note: The body was a familiar image in ancient politics for a united community.

verseByVerse.quote: If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing? If the whole body were an ear, where would be the sense of smell?
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing? Paul argues by absurdity, and the absurdity should land. Picture a body that is one enormous eye: not a better body but a helpless monster, unable to hear a shout or smell smoke. That is what Corinth was trying to become. If tongues were the true mark of the Spirit, the ideal congregation would be one where everybody speaks in tongues and nothing else happens. A church where every member has the same gift is not a super-church. It has lost the ability to do everything that gift does not do.

If the whole body were an ear, where would be the sense of smell? Diversity is not a problem to be fixed; it is necessary. The argument works just as well against the opposite error, which is more common in sober congregations. A church where everyone is a teacher is a church that talks and never visits. A church of activists is one that never thinks. A church that has quietly decided which sort of Christian it approves of, and every church has one, is a body growing a second eye where an ear should be. The point is not that variety is pleasant. It is that variety is functional. God did not scatter different gifts around a congregation for the sake of interest. He did it because the work requires all of them, and no member has been given a gift that makes the others optional.

Senses the eye does not have. Hearing and smell are not other ways of doing what the eye does; they know what the eye cannot know. An eye cannot detect a gas leak. A church with a narrow range of gifts is not merely less varied but less aware. The pastoral instinct that notices a family in trouble, the practical one that notices the accounts drifting, the discerning one that notices a teacher beginning to say something slightly wrong: these are different senses. That is why the members a church finds least congenial are so often the ones it most needs. The person whose questions are awkward and whose concerns are always about what nobody else is worried about may be the congregation’s sense of smell, and a body that silences him will not notice the smoke.

The measure of Christ’s fullness. There is a deeper reason why one gift will not do. The body is built up, Paul tells the Ephesians, until we all attain to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ (Ephesians 4:13). The church is meant to grow into the likeness of its Head, and its Head is not a one-gift Lord. In Jesus the teacher and the healer, the one who wept and the one who rebuked, the one who noticed a widow’s two coins and the one who overturned the tables, lived in a single life. No member can show all of that. A church that is all eye can only ever show one feature of his face; it takes the whole body, every gift working, to grow up into him.

Is it wrong for a church to be made up mostly of one kind of person? It is not wrong for a church to reflect the place where it is; a village church will look like its village. But it is wrong for a church to be content to be one kind of person, or to arrange itself so that others feel they do not fit. The gospel creates a people out of every tribe and language and nation (Revelation 7:9), and the local church is meant to be a foretaste of that. A church that finds it has become all one age, one class or one background should ask, without despair, whom it has been failing to reach or keep, and pray and work to widen its welcome.

For worship. He who planted the ear, does he not hear? He who formed the eye, does he not see? (Psalm 94:9). The God who made every sense needs none of them, for he hears and sees all things without organ or effort. And this God, in whom nothing is lacking, has chosen to make his church out of members who each lack almost everything, and through their many differences to display his manifold wisdom to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places (Ephesians 3:10). A congregation of people unlike one another, held together by one Lord, is a sight the angels study with wonder.

verseByVerse.quote: But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose. If all were a single member, where would the body be? As it is, there are many parts, yet one body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God arranged the members. Here is the answer to the discouraged foot, and it is not encouragement but doctrine. The verb (tithēmi) is deliberate placement: the word for setting something where you have decided it should go. And Paul makes it personal: each one of them, not the body in general with individuals falling where they may. Your place in the church is God’s decision, not an accident.

What that means for an ordinary Christian. The gift you have was chosen for you. The gift you do not have was withheld on purpose. The congregation you are in, with its particular needs and gaps, is the place you were set down. As he chose echoes the Spirit who gives as he wills (v. 11): it is God’s sovereign choosing applied to who does what on a Sunday. And it cuts both ways. To the person proud of his gift: you were handed it, and a man proud of a present has misunderstood the transaction. To the person who wishes he were somebody else: your wish is a complaint about the placement, and the one who placed you knew exactly what he was doing.

A smaller life than you would have chosen. There is a particular ache this speaks to: the sense of having been assigned a smaller life than the one you would have chosen: a quieter role, a less visible service, a set of abilities that will never be remarked on. That is not a mistake in the distribution. The body has parts nobody has ever photographed, and it dies without them.

The Son who took the place appointed for him. No one has ever accepted an arrangement as Christ did. The eternal Son took the place his Father appointed: a manger in Bethlehem, a workshop in Nazareth, and some thirty years of which the Gospels record almost nothing. His neighbours knew him as the carpenter (Mark 6:3). He did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped (Philippians 2:6), and at the end he could say to the Father, I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do (John 17:4). Whoever resents the smallness of his place serves a Lord who spent most of his earthly life in a smaller one, and called it obedience.

If all were a single member, where would the body be? A single member is not a body.

Many parts, one body. Then the closing line, the whole doctrine of the church in a handful of words. Not many parts that ought to become one, but many parts that already are. Unity is not the church’s achievement but its starting condition, and everything Paul asks of the Corinthians is that they stop contradicting what is already true of them (Ephesians 4:3–4).

What it does not mean. It does not mean you cannot grow in your gifts or seek new ways to serve. Nor is God arranged a licence to refuse anything you have not been specially equipped for. Plenty of what a church needs done is not a gift at all; it is simply obedience, and it is required of everyone. Every Christian is commanded to give, to pray, to show hospitality, to speak the truth in love, to bear with difficult people, and to tell others about Christ, whether or not any of it comes easily. Nobody is excused from the ordinary duties on the grounds that generosity is not his gifting. Gifts describe how you will serve most fruitfully. They never describe the limits of what you will do. A hand that declines to help because carrying is properly the shoulder’s work has misread the whole chapter.

Should I move churches if my gifts are not being used? Rarely for that reason alone. God placed you, and the first question is whether you have offered what you have where you are. Gifts are often not used because nobody knows about them, and the remedy is to speak to your elders and start serving where help is needed, even in ways that are not your strongest. Some of the best gifts in a church grow out of years of doing whatever needed doing. There can be good reasons to move: a family move, a church that has departed from the gospel, or a real call to serve elsewhere. But a restless search for the congregation that will appreciate me is usually the foot talking again, and the place God has set you down deserves more patience than that.

On a Tuesday. God has put you exactly where he wants you in his church, and his Spirit works in you there. Name one need in your church that is not a gift of yours but simply a duty, and do it this week.

verseByVerse.quote: The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have no need of you. Now the other failure. The first speech was the discouraged member talking about himself; this one is the impressive member talking about somebody else. The speakers are the eye and the head, the noble parts, the ones in the portrait. The ones dismissed are the hand that does the work and the feet that do the walking. It is a precise little satire on Corinth, where the members with visible gifts had concluded that the rest of the congregation was decorative.

Cannot. The word to weigh is cannot. Paul does not say the eye should not say it, or that it is unkind. He says the eye cannot, because the statement is false. An eye that announces it has no need of hands will be needing those hands within the hour, and needing them without ever noticing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean head here refers to Christ, the head of the church. Paul is using the physical body as an analogy.

How contempt works in a church. It is seldom spoken. It is expressed by omission: who gets consulted, who gets invited, who is treated as background, a conversation that stops when a certain person joins it. And the impressive members are the ones warned here because the temptation to despise belongs almost entirely to the gifted, the busy and the capable, who can generally manage without help and so come to believe that they do.

The Head who knelt at the feet. The church has a true Head, and he answered the eye’s sentence before Corinth ever spoke it. At the last supper, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, Jesus rose from supper, tied a towel round his waist, and washed his disciples’ feet (John 13:3–5). The one man with every right to say I have no need of you knelt at the lowest part of the body and did a slave’s work. Then he said, I have given you an example (John 13:15). A church whose Head did that has no room for an eye that looks down on a hand.

What does repentance look like here? Not a warmer feeling about people you find tedious; feelings are not directly available to the will, and trying to manufacture them produces condescension, which is worse. Something more practical is required. Ask a member you have overlooked for advice about something that matters to you, and then take it. Put a name you have never put there onto the list of people whose opinion you seek. Sit somewhere else. Discover, by asking rather than assuming, what a person you had filed as marginal actually does with his week. Contempt is broken by finding out that the sentence was false, and the only way to find that out is to need the person and see what happens. The eye cannot argue itself into valuing the hand. It has to try picking something up.

On a Tuesday. Whose absence next Sunday would make the least difference to you? Ask what would actually stop if that person stopped; if you do not know, that is itself the answer, so go and find out. None of us has valued every member as the Head has. He did it perfectly, for us, his obedience is counted as ours, and he washes the eye that looked down too.

verseByVerse.quote: On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, and on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor, and our unpresentable parts are treated with greater modesty, which our more presentable parts do not require. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The weaker parts. Paul turns the world’s ranking upside down with an observation anybody can check on his own person. The strong parts are the ones on show: arms, shoulders, face. The parts you cannot survive without are soft, hidden and defenceless: heart, lungs, brain, tucked behind bone because they could not take a blow. In the church, those who seem weakest may be the most vital: those who pray, the faithful elderly, the quietly serving.

Less honourable parts. We clothe some parts more carefully; honour here may well mean clothing. This is Paul’s second observation and a delicate one: we spend more effort covering what is unpresentable than displaying what is presentable. Our unpresentable parts are covered with special care, while the face needs none; a man will leave his face bare in all weathers and would not dream of leaving the rest of himself so.

God has so composed the body. Composed (synkerannymi) means blended, as a painter mixes colours. This is not sentiment about the underdog. It is the design: God built compensation into the arrangement, so that members with no natural standing receive an honour given rather than earned, as he chose what is low and despised in the world (1:27–28). A congregation that honours its unimpressive members is not being nice. It is being accurate.

Honour given to the one who lacked it. God composes the body this way because it is how he has always worked, and the cross is where he did it most. His Son took the place of no honour at all. He was stripped, mocked and hung up outside the city, enduring the cross and despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2). He humbled himself to the point of death, even death on a cross; therefore God has highly exalted him and given him the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:8–9). Greater honour to the part that lacked it is the shape of the gospel before it is the shape of the church, and a congregation that honours its overlooked members is copying what God did with Jesus.

Who are they? Be concrete, because vagueness here costs somebody something real. They are the housebound woman who has not been in the building for three years and has prayed for half the congregation by name. The man with a learning disability whose questions in the Bible study slow everybody down. The elderly member whose memory has gone, who cannot follow the sermon, and who is still, on this verse, a load-bearing part of the body. The person who cleans up afterwards. The one who is simply hard work.
