What does greater honour look like in practice? It looks like the overlooked being given the best, not the leftovers. Visiting the housebound as faithfully as the leaders are consulted. Asking the elderly to pray for specific things and then telling them how God answered. Making the building accessible before making it impressive. Thanking, by name and in public, the people who clean, count and set up. Seating the person with a disability where he can take part, not where he is out of the way. Listening to the slow question in the Bible study as though it might be the most important one asked, because it may be. Honour is not a feeling; it is attention, time and place given on purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another. If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That there may be no division in the body. Here is the purpose of the arrangement, stated as God’s aim. Division (schisma) is the word of 1:10 and 11:18. The unity of a church is not a project the members dreamt up; it is what God was after when he handed out the gifts. Its positive form is that the members may have the same care for one another: care (merimnaō) is the word for anxious concern, each member concerned for the others, equally.

If one member suffers, all suffer together. Paul does not say the members ought to suffer together. He says they do: it is how bodies work. Stub one toe in the dark and the whole organism reacts: the breath catches, the eyes water, the hands reach. Nobody has to persuade the shoulder to care about the foot, and the body does not hold a meeting about whether the injury is serious enough. It responds because the foot is not somebody else. When one believer suffers, the whole church should feel it (Romans 12:15; Hebrews 13:3).

A body with nerve damage. So the question this verse puts to a congregation is not, are you sympathetic enough? It is a diagnosis: are the nerves working? A church where a member can lose a job, a marriage or a child while the rest carry on undisturbed is not merely unkind. It is a body with nerve damage, where the signal is sent and nothing arrives, and that is not cured by exhortation.

The Head feels it first. The body suffers together because its Head does. Of the LORD and his people in the days of the exodus, Isaiah wrote, in all their affliction he was afflicted (Isaiah 63:9), and in Christ that sympathy took flesh. The pain of the least member registers in heaven. We have a High Priest who is able to sympathise with our weaknesses, tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), who wept at the grave of a friend he was about to raise (John 11:35). A congregation learns to feel with its members because it is joined to a Lord who already does.

If one member is honored, all rejoice together. This is the harder half in practice. It is often easier to weep with those who weep than to rejoice with those who rejoice. Sympathy costs time; gladness at another’s success costs you the comparison. When someone else gets the thing you have prayed for and not received, the child, the recovery, the post, the body’s health is measured by what happens in you at that moment, more accurately than at any funeral.

How does a body come to feel what its members feel? Not by resolving to. Nerves are built out of information, and the practical form of this verse is unglamorous: knowing people’s names, knowing what is happening in their lives, and asking again the following week. Suffering that nobody knows about cannot be shared, and a great deal of the suffering in most congregations is invisible because nobody has ever asked a second question. And the sharing runs in both directions, and neither direction is optional. A member who tells nobody anything has, with the best intentions, cut his own nerve. Privacy is not a Christian virtue in a body; it is how a limb goes numb. Letting people know that you are struggling is not weakness or self-indulgence, and this verse quietly requires it, because a body cannot suffer together with a member who has determined to suffer alone. That need not mean telling everyone; one or two trusted brothers or sisters, or an elder, is where most of us begin.

How can I rejoice when I am envious? Honestly, and by bringing the envy to God rather than pretending it is not there. Name it to him: Lord, I wanted that, and she has it, and it hurts. Then remember that the body’s blessing is your blessing; when another member is honoured, you are honoured in him, because you are not somebody else. Thank God for the specific good thing he has given that brother or sister, out loud if you can, and then do something kind for them. Gladness often follows the act rather than preceding it. And bring your own unanswered longing back to the Father who sees it; his love for you has not been reduced by his kindness to someone else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–31 — Varieties of Gifts: The Greater Gifts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul brings the picture home: this congregation is Christ’s body. He returns to the gifts, now ranked with the ministry of the word first and tongues last, shows by a string of questions that no gift is given to all, and points ahead to a better way.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ordering of Gifts and the Priority of Love

The numbered list in verses 28–30 shows that Paul does rank the gifts, not because some are better in themselves but because some build up the whole church more directly. Apostles and prophets laid the foundation; teachers explain it; the other gifts serve the body in many ways. The more excellent way of chapter 13 is not one more gift above tongues and prophecy. It is the love that makes the use of any gift excellent.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinth had turned the order upside down, treating tongues, which without interpretation builds up only the speaker, as the most prestigious gift. Paul puts it last. He does not dismiss tongues; he reorders their values, so that gifts that build the church outrank gifts that build only the speaker. Now: A gifted teacher who uses his gift to impress rather than to build up has missed what gifts are for. The more excellent way is open to every Christian who puts his gift under love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it. And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are the body of Christ. Paul lands the metaphor, and the verb is the one to watch: you are. Not you should be, or will be if you sort yourselves out. To this congregation, factional, arrogant, drunk at communion, tolerating scandal, the apostle says: you are the body of Christ. The identity comes first and the instructions afterwards, the order the New Testament always uses. Then individually members of it. You are not the body on your own, and you are not swallowed by it either. A hand in a body is more itself, not less.

In the flow. Verse 28 returns to the gifts with which the chapter began, but now in an order, and the order points ahead. Word ministries stand first and tongues last, which prepares for chapter 14, where Paul will rank prophecy above tongues because it builds up the church (14:1–5). And the questions of verses 29–30 will show that no gift, however it is ranked, is given to everybody.

What it means to be his body. The phrase is familiar enough to sound like a slogan. A body is how a person is present and how he acts. So Paul means at least three things. First, you belong to him, as a hand belongs to a man, and his life flows into you by his Spirit (Ephesians 4:15–16). Second, he acts through you: the Lord who promised to be with his people to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20) goes on doing his work through them. Third, he remains distinct from you and over you. The church does not replace Christ or become him; he is the Head, and the body takes its orders from him (Ephesians 1:22–23; Colossians 1:18).

First, second, third. Appointed (tithēmi) is the same word as verse 18. This list is numbered, which the earlier one was not, and the numbering is doing something. The first three all have to do with the word of God: apostles, the foundational witnesses of Christ who received and delivered it (Ephesians 2:20); prophets, those who spoke revelation in the early church; and teachers, who explain it. These three word ministries come first because everything else in a church is built on what God has said, and they build the church most. Take the word out and the rest is activity.

Helping and administrating. Two items are easily overlooked. Helping (antilēmpseis) means practical aid to those in need, and Paul puts it in the same list as miracles and healing. Administrating (kybernēseis) is a nautical word for what a ship’s pilot does: steering, leadership and guidance. So the person who keeps the accounts straight, arranges the rota and makes sure the widow gets visited is exercising a gift of the Holy Spirit, named by the apostle alongside the spectacular ones. And tongues come last. The Corinthians had the order upside down.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that those with lower-ranked gifts are less valuable as persons. The ranking concerns how much each gift builds up the church (14:5).

If God appointed first apostles, are there apostles today? The office as Paul describes it had conditions attached that cannot now be met: an apostle had seen the risen Lord (9:1) and was commissioned directly by him, and the apostles together are called the foundation of the church, with Christ as the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). A foundation is laid once; a building with a permanent foundation-laying department has a serious problem. So the office in that sense closed. The word also has a broader use in the New Testament, a sent one, a messenger of the churches (2 Corinthians 8:23), and that work has never stopped: church planters and missionaries doing today what Paul did at Corinth. Christians who use the title for such people usually mean the second thing, and the disagreement is often smaller than the vocabulary makes it sound. What verse 28 does settle is the order: the word that founds the church comes first, and every later gift is measured by it.

And prophets? The prophets named here stand with the apostles as part of the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20; 3:5). They brought God’s revealed word to the churches before the New Testament was complete. That foundational, revelatory office has ceased with the closing of the canon. Continuationist brothers often distinguish these foundational prophets from a humbler, ongoing gift of prophecy that must always be weighed (14:29); this commentary does not think the New Testament draws that line clearly enough to build on, but it recognises that careful and godly readers hold it. What continues is the ministry of the word: preachers and teachers who do not receive new revelation but faithfully explain and apply the revelation God has given once for all. When a sermon pierces your heart and you feel that God has spoken to you, he has, but through his written word, not beside it. That is why this commentary reads the third item on the list, teachers, as the living heir of the first two.

verseByVerse.quote: Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Seven questions, and in Greek each is framed to expect the answer no. Paul is not wondering aloud. He is closing a door. Not everyone has the same gift. Do all work miracles? Do all possess gifts of healing? No.

Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret? The sixth question is the one Corinth cared about. Do all speak with tongues? No. Not every Christian speaks in tongues. That single syllable dismantles the whole system the church had built: the idea that one gift is the badge of the Spirit’s presence and that the believers without it are in the lower division. If the Spirit had intended tongues as the mark of genuine Christianity, he would have given it to everyone. He has not, and the fact that he has not is itself the argument.

Where Christians differ: tongues as the evidence of the Spirit. Some Pentecostal groups teach that speaking in tongues is the necessary evidence of being baptised in the Spirit, often because in Acts tongues accompanied the Spirit’s coming (Acts 2:4; 10:46; 19:6), and many who hold it have known real blessing. This commentary’s view: Paul’s question expects the answer: no, not all speak in tongues. Yet all were baptised in the Spirit (v. 13). So tongues cannot be the required evidence of Spirit baptism. The evidence of the Spirit is confessing Jesus as Lord (v. 3) and the fruit of the Spirit, above all love (Galatians 5:22–23; 1 Corinthians 13).

The Corinthian error in other clothes. Any church which makes a particular gift the test of spiritual seriousness has fallen into the Corinthian error, whatever the gift. Some do it with tongues; others with doctrinal precision, evangelistic boldness, emotional expressiveness in worship, or a particular pattern of daily devotions. In every case the same sentence answers it. Do all? No.

A release for the discouraged. There is a mercy in that no which the discouraged reader should take. The seven questions are usually read as a rebuke to the proud, and they are. But turn them round and they are a release for everyone who has spent years feeling second-rate in church. You were never meant to be able to do all of it. The Spirit did not distribute the whole list to anybody, and the apostle writing the sentence does not make himself the standard. There has only ever been one person who could do everything, and the whole point of the body is that he chose to do it through thousands of people who cannot.

On a Tuesday. If you have been measuring your Christian life by a gift you do not have, put the measuring stick down. Measure it instead by verse 3 and by chapter 13: do you confess Jesus as Lord, and are you growing in love?

For worship. There was one work that was never shared out. When it came to bearing the sin of the world, no apostle stood beside him, no prophet spoke for him and no healer eased him; all the disciples left him and fled (Mark 14:50). The redemption that could not be divided he finished by himself, and then he rose, sent his Spirit, and divided everything else among fishermen and slaves and housewives and tentmakers, so that none of them could manage without the others, and none of them could manage without him. Glory to the Head who did alone what only he could do, and does the rest through his body.

verseByVerse.quote: But earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But earnestly desire the higher gifts. At first this looks like a contradiction. Paul has spent thirty verses saying the Spirit apportions as he wills, and now he tells them to want the higher gifts. But the two sit together, as they always do in Scripture. God is sovereign over who is saved, and we pray for the lost; he is sovereign over daily bread, and we ask for it. Sovereign distribution makes desire safe, because we are asking a Father who will not give a stone to a child who asks for bread (Matthew 7:9). Earnestly desire (zēloō) means be zealous for, and the command is plural: Paul is telling a congregation what to want for itself. Some read the verb as a statement: you are eagerly desiring the supposedly greater gifts, but I will show you a better way. Either way, the next clause redirects them.

What higher means. After everything said about eyes and feet, it cannot mean more impressive. It means more useful to others: the gifts that build up the church most, such as prophecy and teaching. Paul spells it out at 14:5: the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, because prophecy builds up the church. A gift ranks higher in proportion to the good it does the person sitting next to you, and by that measure the faithful visitor of the sick outranks a great deal that gets applauded.

A still more excellent way. A great hinge in the letter. More excellent (kath’ hyperbolēn) means beyond comparison. Everything is set for Paul to name the top gift, and he does not. He steps off the ladder, because the more excellent way is not a gift distributed to some and not others. It is the way in which all gifts must be used: love, required of everybody, available to everybody, and without which the whole list is worth nothing. They wanted to know which gift was best. Paul is about to tell them the question was wrong, and that a man may exercise every gift with power and be nothing whatever.

The way has a face. Paul’s verb is I will show you: not describe, define or commend. He is about to put something in front of them and let them look, which is why chapter 13 reads less like an argument than a portrait, sentence after sentence of what love does and does not do. And the portrait is recognisable. There has been exactly one life that was patient, kind, not envious, not boastful, not irritable, bearing all things and enduring all things to the end. The more excellent way has been walked, once, from Bethlehem to Golgotha, by Jesus Christ.

So should I pray for spiritual gifts? Yes, in the way Paul means. Pray, with your church, for the gifts that build others up: for wisdom to counsel, clarity to teach, compassion to visit, generosity to give, faith to persevere, and for God to raise up faithful preachers and leaders. Pray for these not as trophies but as tools, asking how you can be more useful to the people around you. And pray above all for love, because without it every gift is noise. The Father delights to give good gifts to those who ask him, and the best gift of all, the Holy Spirit, he has already given (Luke 11:13).

12.text: <sup>1</sup>Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed.<sup>2</sup>You know that when you were pagans you were led astray to mute idols, however you were led.<sup>3</sup>Therefore I want you to understand that no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says “Jesus is accursed!” and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit.<sup>4</sup>Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit;<sup>5</sup>and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord;<sup>6</sup>and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone.<sup>7</sup>To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.<sup>8</sup>For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit,<sup>9</sup>to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit,<sup>10</sup>to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the ability to distinguish between spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues.<sup>11</sup>All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills.<sup>12</sup>For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ.<sup>13</sup>For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—Jews or Greeks, slaves or free—and all were made to drink of one Spirit.<sup>14</sup>For the body does not consist of one member but of many.<sup>15</sup>If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.<sup>16</sup>And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.<sup>17</sup>If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing? If the whole body were an ear, where would be the sense of smell?<sup>18</sup>But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose.<sup>19</sup>If all were a single member, where would the body be?<sup>20</sup>As it is, there are many parts, yet one body.<sup>21</sup>The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.”<sup>22</sup>On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable,<sup>23</sup>and on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor, and our unpresentable parts are treated with greater modesty,<sup>24</sup>which our more presentable parts do not require. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it,<sup>25</sup>that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another.<sup>26</sup>If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together.<sup>27</sup>Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it.<sup>28</sup>And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues.<sup>29</sup>Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles?<sup>30</sup>Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?<sup>31</sup>But earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way.

13.title: The Most Excellent Way: Love
13.overview:
This famous chapter is often read at weddings, but it was written to rebuke a quarrelsome, proud church that valued spectacular gifts above everything. Paul sets it between his teaching on gifts in chapters 12 and 14, as the more excellent way in which every gift must be used. The Greek word for love here, agapē, was rare in ordinary Greek; the Christians filled it with new meaning from the love God showed in Christ. Read the chapter with Jesus’ name in place of love and it describes him; read it with your own name and it shows how far you fall short.

It moves in three steps. Without love, even the greatest gifts and sacrifices are worth nothing. Love is then described in action, and almost every phrase corrects something in Corinth. And love lasts, while the gifts are partial, suited to the present age, and will give way at Christ’s return to seeing God face to face.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul sets the greatest gifts and the greatest sacrifices beside a single test. Without love, the gift is noise, the gifted person is nothing, and the sacrifice gains nothing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Form of All Virtues

Aquinas, following Augustine, called love (caritas) the form of all virtues: the quality without which no virtue is truly virtuous. Paul’s three sentences make the same point: gifts without love are not merely incomplete but cancelled. Reformed teaching has grounded this in the law of love (Matthew 22:37–40): the whole law is fulfilled in love, so the whole Christian life, including the use of spiritual gifts, finds its goal and its measure in love. A gift not used in love has been cut off from its own purpose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian who spoke in tongues in a public meeting, leaving the congregation untaught and only himself built up, was the noisy gong in practice: the gift was real, the love was absent, and the gift had become noise. Now: The preacher who loves the sound of his own voice more than his hearers, the theologian who loves winning arguments more than the person he argues with, the worship leader who loves the experience he creates more than the people he leads: all are producing noise, not music.

verseByVerse.quote: If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 13 is the most famous chapter on love ever written, but it is not a wedding poem. It is a rebuke to a gifted, proud, divided church, set in the middle of Paul’s teaching on spiritual gifts (chapters 12 to 14). It moves in three steps. Without love, even the greatest gifts and sacrifices are worthless (vv. 1–3). Love is then described in action, fifteen verbs that hold up a mirror to the Corinthians (vv. 4–7). And love lasts forever: the gifts belong to this age and will pass away when the perfect comes, when we shall see face to face; faith, hope and love remain, and the greatest is love (vv. 8–13). The word throughout is agapē, the self-giving love God showed in Christ.

The setting. Chapter 12 taught that the Spirit gives different gifts to the members of one body, as he wills, for the common good, and it ended with the promise of a still more excellent way (12:31). Here it is, and chapter 14 will apply it to the church’s meetings. So chapter 13 is not a detour into poetry. It is the hinge of the whole argument.

Tongues of men and of angels. Paul starts at the top, with the gift the Corinthians prized most. Not merely every human language, but the speech of angels: he grants his readers more than they were claiming, and then demolishes it. He writes I, not you. He puts himself in the dock first, which is how a pastor rebukes a church he loves.

Is there an angelic language? Paul is reaching for the most extreme case he can imagine, as he does in the next verse with all mysteries and faith that could remove mountains. He is not describing a language he or anyone else spoke, though some at Corinth may have believed their ecstatic speech was exactly that. When angels speak in Scripture, they speak words people understand (Luke 1:13; 2:10), so the verse gives no ground for an unintelligible heavenly tongue. Some continuationist believers take the phrase more literally, as a hint that a tongue might not be a human language; that is possible, but it is a great deal to build on a sentence that begins with if. The point is the argument from the greater: if even the speech of angels would be worthless without love, so is everything less.

But have not love. Love (agapē) is not mainly a feeling, but a self-giving commitment to another’s good, defined by God’s love in Christ: God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:9–10). The noun was uncommon in ordinary Greek; the Greek Old Testament had begun to use it, and the New Testament filled it with new content. At its simplest, agapē is choosing another person’s good and paying for it yourself. It is measured not by what it feels but by what it gives, and the measure of it is a cross.

A noisy gong. The choice of instruments is not random. Instruments like these sounded in the pagan cults the Corinthians had come out of, especially the cults of Cybele and Dionysus: bronze, loud, resonant, and carrying no words. Many in that congregation had heard such cymbals crash in a temple courtyard, and Paul is telling the man proud of his tongue that his gift, exercised without love, makes the same sound. A gong is not silent. It is the loudest thing in the room, and that is the trouble with it: it fills a space, everyone turns round, and afterwards nobody can say what it said.

Prophetic powers. The stakes rise. Prophecy, the gift Paul ranks highest and which chapter 14 will rank above tongues (14:1, 5). Understanding all mysteries and all knowledge: not a great deal of theology but the whole of it, without gaps.

All faith. Not saving faith here but wonder-working faith (12:9), the Lord’s own image for the largest faith imaginable (Matthew 17:20). Paul has listed the speaker, the prophet, the theologian and the miracle-worker, and he is about to put them all in the same column.

I am nothing. The verdict is not the one anyone expects. Paul does not say that such a man has less than he thinks, or that his ministry is diminished. He says I am nothing: not my gift is nothing, but I am. The failure is not in the performance; it reaches back to the performer. A gifted person without love is spiritually zero. A man can be a first-class instrument and not be a Christian at all, and the gifts will not tell him which he is.

The gifts are no evidence about the man. That is a sobering thing to put to anyone who serves in a church, and it should be put personally rather than left in the air. It is entirely possible to preach well, pray in public with feeling, know your Bible thoroughly, give generously of your time, be thanked for all of it, and be nothing. The gifts are given as the Spirit wills (12:11), which means they say more about the Giver than about the man holding them. Judas was sent out with the Twelve with authority to heal (Matthew 10:1–4), and nobody at the Last Supper suspected him even as he left (John 13:27–30). Our Lord warned that many will say on that day that they prophesied and cast out demons in his name, and he will say he never knew them (Matthew 7:22–23). Yet the people in that warning are untroubled and sure of themselves. A believer who reads this verse and fears for his own heart is showing the very tenderness they lacked, and the remedy for that fear is not more gifts but Christ, who loves the loveless into love.

What it does not mean. It does not mean gifts do not matter. Paul has just urged them to desire the higher gifts (12:31), and he will say it again (14:1); the church needs them. It means gifts without love have no value before God and no value to the man who has them.

How can I tell whether my service is done in love? Ask who it is for. Love serves the person in front of it; pride serves its own reputation. A few honest tests help. Would I still do this if no one ever thanked me or knew it was me? Am I glad or deflated when someone else does it better? Do I notice the people I serve, their names and burdens, or only how it went? When the work is criticised, do I care first whether people were helped, or whether I was hurt? No one passes these perfectly. The point is not to stop serving until your motives are pure, which would mean never serving at all, but to bring the mixed motives to Christ and ask him to make love the reason.

For worship. There was once a man with every gift in this list and more. He spoke as no man ever spoke, he knew what was in every heart, and his faith did not move mountains only because he had made them. And not one word he ever said was noise, because every word was love. He did not use his gifts to be admired; he used them to heal lepers, feed crowds and raise a widow’s son, and then he laid them all down and went to a cross. The more excellent way is not a technique. It is the way he walked, all the way to Golgotha, for people who had nothing to offer him but their need.
verseByVerse.note: Gongs and cymbals were loud instruments used in pagan worship.

verseByVerse.quote: If I give away all I have, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I give away all I have. Paul has finished with the gifts and moves to the deeds, and he goes straight to the two that no one has ever been able to top. The first is total divestment. Not generous giving; the verb (psōmizō) means to dole out in morsels, to feed, and suggests parcelling out everything you own, piece by piece, to feed the poor, until there is nothing left.

To be burned. The second is martyrdom. A man walks into the fire rather than deny his Lord. These are the summit of Christian devotion, the two acts no congregation would dare to question. Paul questions them.

A note on the text. A reader comparing translations will meet a difference here. The ESV, like the KJV, reads to be burned, and notes that some manuscripts read deliver up my body that I may boast. Two Greek words differing by a letter or two lie behind the phrase; several of the oldest manuscripts read boast, and the NIV and NRSV follow them. Burned fits the idea of martyrdom; boast fits the Corinthian pride, and is almost bleakly appropriate to the point: a sacrifice offered so that one has something to say about it. Either way the sentence works, and the meaning is the ultimate sacrifice of self.

I gain nothing. It is possible to do the most extreme thing a human being can do and have the wrong reason for it. A man may give away his fortune because he cannot bear to be thought ordinary. A man may go to the stake because his own consistency has become the thing he worships, or because he cannot face what climbing down would cost him in front of people who are watching. Sacrifice proves that something mattered more than comfort. It does not prove what. Our Lord warned against giving to be seen by others (Matthew 6:1–4). This is religion used as self-salvation: the sacrifice offered as a payment, so that God or the onlookers will owe the giver something. The irreligious man keeps his life for himself; the religious man may give his life away and still be keeping it for himself. The gospel undoes both, because the one sacrifice that gains anything before God has already been made, by Christ, and it was made in love.

Nothing, and then nothing gained. The phrase has been quietly changed. In verse 2 it was I am nothing; here it is I gain nothing. The first was about what a man is; this is about what he takes away with him. A whole life could be poured out, admired, written up, and yield its owner precisely nothing at the end, because the only currency that will still be legal tender on that day is love.

He loved us and gave himself up. Paul’s own words for the cross join exactly the two things this verse pulls apart. Walk in love, he tells the Ephesians, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Ephesians 5:2). The giving up and the love were never separated in him. Here, in Paul’s imagined case, a man hands over his body and there is no love in it, and the result is nothing. At Golgotha a Man handed over his body and there was nothing in it but love, and the result was a redeemed people. Every human sacrifice is weighed against that one, and it is the love in it, not the size of it, that God regards.

But if love is the one thing that counts, and I find little of it in me, what do I do? The answer is not to try harder to feel it, and the chapter never suggests that. Love is not generated from a standing start; it is received and then returned. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). So the road to more love runs through more knowledge of his love: dwelling on the cross, on what he forgave you, on how fully he knows you and loves you anyway (v. 12). Ask him for it plainly, because it is the fruit of his Spirit (Galatians 5:22). And then do the loving thing while the feeling lags; affection very often follows obedience rather than going before it.

Should I stop giving until my motives are pure? No. Our motives this side of glory are always mixed, and if we waited for pure ones we would never give a penny or lift a finger. Keep giving and keep serving, and bring the mixture to God. Ask him to purify your heart as you go. The warning of this verse is not against giving; it is against trusting the giving, as though the size of the sacrifice could stand in for love or earn us something before God.

On a Tuesday. Look at your giving, of money and of time. Is any of it arranged so that it will be noticed? Give something this week in a way that leaves no trace of your name, and thank God that he sees in secret.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “deliver up my body [to death] that I may boast.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now Paul describes love in action, mostly by what it does not do, and almost every phrase holds up a mirror to Corinth.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as a Portrait of Christ

Put Jesus Christ in place of love in verses 4–7 and the sentences remain true. Christ is patient: he bore with his disciples for three years, and he endured the cross. Christ is kind: he touched lepers, welcomed children, ate with sinners. Christ does not insist on his own way: “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). He bears all things, believes all things (his trust in the Father was perfect), hopes all things (the joy set before him, Hebrews 12:2), endures all things (the cross). Love is not only a command to be obeyed but a Person to be united with, and as Christ is formed in us (Galatians 4:19), his character becomes ours.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s list is a mirror held up to Corinth, and every church that reads it should use it as a diagnosis, not only as an aspiration. Where is the envy? The boasting? The resentment carried from meeting to meeting? The delight when a rival stumbles? Now: One of the strongest witnesses a church can give is not an argument but a fellowship that actually loves like this, bearing, believing, hoping and enduring. The watching world knows what love looks like, and it is waiting to see whether the church shows it.

verseByVerse.quote: Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love is patient and kind. Now the portrait. In Greek every item is a verb, not an adjective. Paul does not say love is a patient thing; he says love acts patiently, behaves kindly, refuses to envy. This is not a description of a feeling. It is a description of conduct, which means it can be checked.

Patient. The word (makrothymeō) is a compound of long and anger: love has a long fuse. It is not the patience of waiting for a bus but the patience of putting up with people who wrong you, the same word family the New Testament uses of God bearing with sinners for centuries (Romans 2:4; 2 Peter 3:9). The measure of it is not how you behave the first time someone irritates you but the fortieth.

And kind. The word (chrēsteuomai) means to show kindness, to be gracious, actively doing good to others. The pair belongs together. Patience is what love does not do; kindness is what it does. Patience endures injury; kindness repays it with good. It is possible to endure someone indefinitely while giving them nothing at all, and there are marriages and churches held together on exactly those terms. Patience alone is endurance. Patience with kindness is love.

Love does not envy or boast. Put those two side by side and something surfaces. Envy (zēloō, to be jealous) is what this disease does when the other person has it; boasting is what it does when you have it. They look like opposites and they are the same illness in two positions, and the illness is the habit of measuring yourself against other people. The Corinthians envied one another’s gifts (3:3) and boasted in their gifts and leaders. The word behind boast (perpereuomai) is a rare one that means something like a windbag: the man who parades himself, who cannot let a story pass without improving his own part in it. Love rejoices in others’ blessings and has no need to advertise its own.

It is not arrogant. The verb is physioō, to be puffed up, inflated with air, and this is Paul’s signature word for Corinth. He has used it about their factions (4:6), about the men who thought he would not come (4:18–19), about their pride over the scandal in chapter 5 (5:2), and about their knowledge of idols (8:1). Now it appears in the list of what love is not, and Corinth would have recognised the word instantly. Love is humble because it is not the centre of its own attention.

A portrait of Christ. Every quality in this list was perfectly shown by Jesus, and only by him. Put his name in place of love and the sentences remain true: Jesus is patient and kind; Jesus does not envy or boast; he is not arrogant. He was patient with disciples who argued on the road about who was greatest, kind to a woman everyone else despised, and he never once paraded himself. Paul does not name him here, and he does not need to: anyone who has read the Gospels knows whose love this is. Put your own name in, and you see how far you fall short, even on your best day. Yet his perfect love was lived in your place, and by his obedience the many are made righteous (Romans 5:19), so the mirror does not condemn you.

Am I meant to read my own name into this list? Yes, but as a mirror and not as a ladder. The list is not a set of rungs by which to climb into God’s favour; Christ has done that for you. It is a description of what his love looks like as it grows in his people. So read it with your name in, honestly, and let it drive you to him. Then read it with his name in, and rest. The Christian who does both is not crushed by the standard and is not careless about it either.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love tolerates everything, or that patience means never addressing a wrong. It means love responds to others with patience, kindness and humility, even when it has to say hard things.

On a Tuesday. Picture the person you find hardest in your congregation or your family, and read the items again with that person’s name after each verb. Am I long-tempered with him? Do I actively do him good? Am I glad when he does well? Love in this chapter is never a general benevolence toward humanity; it always has a name attached (1 John 3:18). God has borne with you far longer, and his Spirit is at work in you: be patient and kind to that person today, in one specific act.

parallels.desc: love covers all offences

verseByVerse.quote: or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or rude. Four more, and every one of them is a photograph of the Corinthian church. The word (aschēmoneō) means to behave disgracefully, in a way that is unseemly, that shames. The Corinthians were behaving shamefully at the Lord’s Supper, where some went hungry while others were drunk (11:21–22), and in their worship. It is striking to find manners in a list of Christian virtues, and it should give pause to the believer who prides himself on being blunt. Rudeness is not a personality type in the New Testament; it is a failure of love. There is no gift, no calling and no strength of conviction that entitles a Christian to make another person feel small in front of others.

It does not insist on its own way. Literally, love does not seek its own things, and it is close to the phrase Paul used at 10:24 and again at 10:33 (Philippians 2:4). This is the whole argument of chapters 8 to 10 compressed into a single phrase, and it is the hardest item on the list, because insisting on one’s own way rarely feels like selfishness from the inside. It feels like being right. The strong at Corinth were right about idols, were insisting on their rights, and were destroying people with it.

It is not irritable. The word (paroxynomai) gives us paroxysm; it means sharpened, provoked to a flash, easily angered, touchy. Everyone knows what this looks like: the person a whole household reads before speaking, the man whose mood determines the temperature of a room. It is usually treated as a temperament rather than a sin, and Paul files it here.

Or resentful. The Greek is sharper than the English. Literally, love does not count up the wrong (logizetai to kakon). The phrase is an accountant’s: love does not reckon up the evil, does not enter the wrong in a ledger. And that is precisely what resentment is: not the memory of an injury, which is involuntary, but the keeping of it in a place where it can be produced later. Anyone can find out whether he is doing this. When a quarrel starts, does a list arrive? Are you able, without any preparation, to give the date and the wording of things said to you years ago? Nobody has that at his fingertips by accident. It is there because it was filed.

The ledger and the gospel. Behind the accounting image lies the gospel, which is why Paul reached for it. Logizomai is the very word used for righteousness being credited to believers in Romans 4, and of God not counting our trespasses against us (Romans 4:8; 2 Corinthians 5:19). The Christian is a person whose own ledger has been cancelled, not reduced, not suspended, cancelled, and who is therefore in no position to keep one on anybody else. For you, that means God will never produce your sins against you, not on the last day and not on a bad Tuesday, because Christ has paid for every one of them (Romans 8:1, 33–34). Forgiveness is the closing of an account you were entitled to keep open.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love ignores serious sin or abuse. Love confronts sin for the person’s good (Galatians 6:1), and it may need to remember facts for the sake of protection or justice (see v. 7). Keeping no record of wrongs is not the same as pretending nothing happened. But love does not nurse grudges, rehearse injuries, or hold them in reserve as weapons.

If I forgive, do I have to trust him again straight away? No. Forgiveness and trust are different things. Forgiveness is releasing the debt: you give up the right to punish, to repay, to keep the account open. It can be given at once, because Christ has forgiven you. Trust is rebuilt over time by changed behaviour, and wisdom may require boundaries while it is rebuilt, especially where someone has been harmed or is at risk. A wife can forgive a husband’s betrayal and still need time, honesty and counsel before trust returns. Forgiveness says: I will not hold this against you. It does not say: nothing has consequences.

What if the memory keeps coming back? Remembering is not the same as resenting. You cannot command your memory, but you can decide what to do when it arrives. When it comes, do not rehearse it, add to it, or imagine the speech you would make. Hand it back to God: Lord, I gave you this; I give it again. Pray for the person, even briefly. Many Christians have to forgive the same wrong many times before the feeling follows the decision, and that is not failure; it is what forgiving looks like in real life.

On a Tuesday. Is there a record of wrongs you are keeping against someone? Name the person and the item, bring it to God, and close the account, as he has closed yours.

verseByVerse.quote: it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It does not rejoice at wrongdoing. A single verse, and it exposes something hard to admit. Wrongdoing (adikia) is unrighteousness. Paul is not only talking about approving of sin. He is talking about the small, private pleasure that rises when something bad turns out to be true about somebody else. The verb is to be glad. And it is very hard to deny, because it is so quick: the flicker of satisfaction at hearing that a colleague’s promotion has fallen through, that a critic’s marriage is in difficulty, that a preacher you found insufferable has been found out. Nobody chooses that flicker. But the fact that it arrives uninvited is exactly what makes it such an accurate reading of the heart.

At Corinth it had a public form. The church had been arrogant about a case of gross immorality in its membership, a man living with his father’s wife, instead of mourning (5:2), and the factions were probably cheering when a rival group came off badly. But the private form is the commoner one, and it is the one this verse catches. Love takes no pleasure in sin, whether its own or others’.

But rejoices with the truth. The positive is not the balance we would have written. The opposite of rejoicing at wrongdoing ought to be grieving at wrongdoing. Paul writes rejoices with the truth instead, and the truth is almost personified: love and the truth standing side by side, glad about the same things. Love is glad when truth prevails, the truth of the gospel and truthful living. Which settles a question that comes up constantly in Christian life: whether love and honesty are in tension, so that being loving means going quiet about what is true. This verse says they are allies. Love does not celebrate a wrong even when the wrong is convenient; it does not suppress a truth even when the truth is awkward. A love that requires lies is not love, and a truth-telling that takes pleasure in the damage is not truth-telling either (Ephesians 4:15; 2 John 1–3).

Gossip. There is a practical form of this sin that is seldom called what it is. Nobody says “I am glad this happened to him”. What people say is that they only mention it so that you can pray. The verse supplies a way of telling the two apart. Ask whether you would be disappointed to discover the report was false. If the correction would come as a relief, the interest was love. If it would come as a small deflation, the interest was the flicker.

So when may I speak about someone else’s sin? When speaking serves the person or protects others, and when you are speaking to someone who needs to know. Go to the person first where you can (Matthew 18:15). Speak to elders when the matter concerns the church’s care, and to the proper authorities when someone is in danger or a crime has been committed; love never hides abuse. Ask a wise friend for counsel without dressing the story up. What love does not do is pass the story along to people who can do nothing about it, add colour to it, or enjoy the telling. A useful question before you speak: is this person part of the problem or part of the solution?

How is the flicker killed? Not by scolding yourself for having it, which only drives it out of sight. It dies when the other person stops being a competitor, and he stops being a competitor when you genuinely believe that God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose (12:18). A man who is certain his own place was given him has nothing to gain by another man losing his.

On a Tuesday. When you hear of someone’s sin this week, refuse to enjoy it and refuse to repeat it; pray for him instead. And when you next catch the flicker, confess it at once, simply, and thank God that he did not rejoice at your wrongdoing.

For worship. God has never once been glad at our fall. He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). When the son came home from the far country, the father did not savour the rags or rehearse the waste; he ran. And the Son of God is the Truth in person (John 14:6). In him love and truth are not rivals but one face. He told the woman at the well the whole truth about her life, and she went back into the town to tell everyone about him, because the one who knew it all had not rejoiced over her sin but come to take it away.

verseByVerse.quote: Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love bears all things. Four verbs, each with all things attached, and the effect is of a wall that will not come down. Bears (stegō) is related to the word for a roof: it can mean to cover, to keep the weather off, and so also to put up with. Paul used the same word of himself: we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel (9:12). Love puts a roof over the person it loves, so that his failures are not exposed to everybody. That is not the same as pretending they are not there; it is refusing to broadcast them. Love covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8; Proverbs 10:12) means that love does not repeat the story, and carries burdens instead.

Believes all things. Not gullibility, but a readiness to think the best, to give the benefit of the doubt where doubt genuinely exists. Love reads the other person generously and assumes the better explanation until it cannot. It does not assume the worst motives.

Hopes all things. When the evidence has run out, love goes on expecting God to do something with a person. It does not give up on people, because it trusts God’s power to change them. It is the parent still praying for a son twenty years after the last conversation.

Endures all things. The word (hypomenō) means to remain under a weight rather than get out from under it, to stand firm under pressure. Love keeps going when it is hard, persecuted or rejected. Love does not leave when loving becomes expensive. Christ endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2).

A guard on these four verbs. These four have been used to do great harm, and must be guarded. Bears all things has been quoted at a woman to persuade her to keep silent about what is being done to her at home. Believes all things has been quoted to a congregation to persuade it that a credible allegation must be a misunderstanding. Endures all things has been used to send people back into danger. That is not what Paul means, and the proof is in his own letter. This is the man who, eight chapters earlier, told this church to put a man out of the fellowship for his sexual conduct and not even to eat with him (5:11–13). He names Alexander the coppersmith and warns Timothy about him (2 Timothy 4:14–15). He rebuked Peter to his face, publicly (Galatians 2:11). The apostle who wrote verse 7 did all of that, and he did not think he was contradicting himself.

What love does with wrongs. So the four verbs describe what love does with the wrongs it suffers, not what it does with the wrongs it discovers. Love will absorb an insult without publishing it. Love will not absorb an assault and call it patience. Believing all things means refusing to assume the worst about a person’s motives; it has never meant refusing to believe a victim, and using this verse to silence one turns it exactly on its head. Where someone is being hurt, love’s roof goes over the person being hurt, and the wrongdoer is brought into the light, which is itself the most loving thing that can happen to him. Abuse is never to be tolerated or covered, and a person in danger should seek safety and help at once, from the church’s leaders and, where a crime has been done, from the police. Leaving danger is not a failure of love.

Does hoping all things mean I must believe a person will change? It means you never write anyone off as beyond God’s reach, and you keep praying for them. It does not mean you must pretend change has happened before it has, or put yourself back in harm’s way on the strength of a promise. Hope rests on God, not on the other person’s words. You can hope for a man’s repentance with all your heart and still wait to see its fruit before you trust him again (Matthew 3:8).

For worship. Love covers a multitude of sins, and there is one love that covered sin not by hiding it but by bearing it. He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24), and so of everyone who trusts him it can be said, blessed are those whose sins are covered (Romans 4:7). He put the roof over us at the cost of standing under the storm himself. He endured the cross to the end. And the love that held then holds still: he will bear with his people all the way home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns from love’s conduct to its permanence. The gifts the Corinthians prized are partial and will pass away when the perfect comes; faith, hope and love remain, and love is the greatest.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gifts Pass, Love Remains

The passing away of prophecy, tongues and knowledge is often taken as the foundation of the cessationist argument (that these gifts belonged to an age of incomplete revelation). Whether the perfect means the completed New Testament, the maturity of the church, or the return of Christ has long been debated; but Paul defines his own terms in verse 12, where then is when we see face to face and know fully even as I have been fully known. Since no one began to see God face to face when the canon closed, this passage by itself does not settle the question; the stronger arguments for cessation, which this commentary holds, are made from Ephesians 2:20 and Hebrews 2:3–4.

What the passage does settle is the order of things: the gifts are for now, and love is for now and for ever. A church that pours its energy into the spectacular while neglecting love has it backwards, and that is true of every party to the argument.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians who prized tongues above all else were investing in something that would not survive into the coming age, while neglecting the one thing that would. Now: A church rich in programmes, gifts and activity but thin in love has the Corinthian problem in modern dress. Every tradition, charismatic, Reformed or liturgical, can produce churches that are impressively gifted and loveless, and Paul’s word to all of them is the same: love never ends.

verseByVerse.quote: Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love never ends. The portrait stops and the argument resumes, and the hinge is the word never. The verb behind ends (piptō) means to fall, the way a leaf falls, or a flower, or a building. Everything else in the chapter has a collapse in its future. Love does not. It will never fail or become obsolete; it will continue into eternity, because God is love (1 John 4:8).

Prophecies will pass away. Three things are named, and they are precisely the three the Corinthians had been ranking: prophecy, tongues, knowledge. Pass away (katargeō) means to be done away with, rendered inoperative, put out of use. Of tongues Paul says they will cease (pauō), which simply means to stop.

Knowledge will pass away. The same word as for prophecy. Our present partial knowledge will be replaced by full knowledge. Paul says all three have an expiry date, and this is a hard thing to say to a church that had built its whole status system on them. The gifts they were fighting over were, on the apostle’s own account, temporary equipment.

Why the gifts pass away. The reason is not that the gifts are inferior. They came from the Spirit, they were given for the common good, and Paul will tell this church to desire them earnestly and not to forbid them (14:1, 39). They pass away because they are the equipment of a journey, and journeys end. A map is a wonderful thing. Nobody consults one after arriving. That point should survive every argument over this passage. Whatever a Christian concludes about when these gifts pass away, the apostle’s reason for raising the subject was not to settle a timetable. It was to tell a church obsessed with the temporary that it had its heart set on things with a shelf life, while neglecting the one thing that will still be standing when the sun burns out.

The last sermon. The most gifted preacher who has ever lived will one day preach his last sermon, and there will never be any need for another. Every translation, every commentary, every sermon series, every one of these words will be as obsolete as a candle at noon. And the smallest act of love done by the least-noticed believer in the congregation will still be there, because it belongs to what is coming rather than to what is passing (1 Peter 1:24–25).

Does the different verb for tongues mean they stopped first? One detail of the wording is often pressed into service. Paul uses one verb of prophecy and knowledge, they will be rendered inoperative, and a different verb of tongues: they will cease, in a form that can suggest ceasing of themselves. Some have built on that the claim that tongues were to stop of their own accord at an earlier point than the other two. It is a slender foundation for a large conclusion; Greek writers use that form loosely, and Paul’s three clauses are plainly parallel in force. A doctrine should not be hung on a verb ending. The case for the cessation of these gifts, which this commentary holds, rests on other ground: the once-for-all foundation of apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20) and the signs that confirmed their message (Hebrews 2:3–4).

What it does not mean. It does not mean knowledge itself ends in heaven. We will know more, not less (v. 12). It means the present gift of partial knowledge will give way to something far greater, as starlight gives way to the sun.

Why is love the exception? Not because love is more useful. It is that the other three are things we do in a world where God is not yet seen, while love is what God is (1 John 4:8). Prophecy exists because we cannot see him; knowledge exists because we do not yet know him as we will; tongues exist because we are still on the road. Love existed before there was a road, in the giving between Father, Son and Spirit, and it will still be there when the road has been rolled up. On earth it was seen in the Son, who, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end (John 13:1).

verseByVerse.quote: For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know in part. Even the best present gifts give only partial understanding. Paul includes himself: the apostle who received revelations knew in part.

But when the perfect comes. The perfect (to teleion) is the complete, the goal reached, the end for which a thing exists. It most naturally refers to the completion of all things at Christ’s return, when we see him face to face (v. 12).

The partial will pass away. When the complete arrives, the incomplete is no longer needed. The candle is not despised when the sun comes up. It is simply no longer lit.

The question everyone asks. Christians have long argued over this verse, and it deserves a straight account. What is the perfect, and when does it come? On the answer hangs, for many, whether prophecy, tongues and healing continue today. Three answers have been given: the completed New Testament, so that once the last book was written the church no longer needed revelatory gifts; the maturity of the church, grown out of its infancy; or the return of Christ and the state of things that follows.

Where Christians differ: what is the perfect? Some cessationists (who hold that the revelatory and sign gifts have ceased) argue that the perfect is the completed New Testament canon (the finished collection of Scripture’s books), so that tongues and prophecy ceased when Scripture was finished. Continuationists (who hold that all the gifts continue) argue that since the perfect is Christ’s return, the gifts must continue until then. This commentary’s view: The perfect is best understood as the return of Christ and the age to come, when we will see face to face and know fully. This verse says that these gifts will certainly end by then; it does not say whether some of them might end sooner. The case for the cessation of the revelatory and sign gifts rests on other texts: the foundational and unrepeatable role of apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), the confirmation of the apostolic message by signs (Hebrews 2:3–4), and the closing of the canon (Jude 3).

Why the perfect is Christ’s return. Paul himself defines his terms two verses later. Then we shall see face to face; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known (v. 12). Whatever else may be said, no Christian began to see God face to face when the book of Revelation was finished, and nobody alive knows God as fully as God knows him. The then of this passage is not a date in the first century. It is the day we see him. That has to be said even though it cuts against a conclusion some careful and beloved teachers have drawn, because honesty about a text matters more than tidiness. This passage does not, by itself, prove that the miraculous gifts ended with the apostles.

The case on other ground. But it would be equally dishonest to leave the impression that the case for their ceasing rests on this verse, because it does not, and the men who have made that case were not careless readers. Their argument runs on other ground. The apostles and prophets are called the foundation of the church, with Christ as the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid once. The signs and wonders of the first generation are described as God bearing witness to a message declared by those who heard the Lord (Hebrews 2:3–4), which suggests a purpose tied to that generation. The faith was once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3). Scripture is sufficient, and a church expecting fresh revelation is exposed to every confident voice. And there is the honest observation that what is called prophecy or tongues in many places today bears little resemblance to what is described in Acts, where tongues were known languages (Acts 2:6–11). B. B. Warfield argued the case a century ago, and in our own day John MacArthur has argued it with conviction and love for the Word. These are serious arguments made by serious men, and they deserve a serious answer rather than a sneer.

The other side, fairly stated. The answer from the other side is also serious. Paul told this church plainly, do not forbid speaking in tongues (14:39), and told another church, do not quench the Spirit, do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:19–21). Those are commands, and continuationist brothers point out that no verse explicitly announces their repeal. And the observation that today’s claimed gifts often look nothing like the New Testament’s may, they argue, be an argument for testing them rather than for abolishing the category. They add that in Corinth, unlike at Pentecost, no one present understood a tongue without interpretation (14:2), so Pentecost may not be the only pattern. Cessationists answer that commands addressed to churches with living apostles and prophets assume conditions that no longer hold, as the instructions about apostolic visits do. Godly men such as Wayne Grudem have held the continuationist view, and Martyn Lloyd-Jones was open to it; they have loved Christ and his word.

So where should an ordinary believer land? The cessationist case, made on that other ground, is the stronger, and it is the one followed here: the apostles and prophets were a foundation laid once, the signs attested their message, and the Scripture they gave is complete. Three further things can be said with confidence, and they are enough to live by. First, whichever conclusion a Christian reaches, this passage forbids him to look down on a brother who reached the other one; the chapter it sits in is about love, and a man who wins this argument uncharitably has lost the chapter. Second, no gift is the mark of the Spirit’s presence; that was settled at 12:3, and the mark is the confession that Jesus is Lord. Third, and this is Paul’s actual point, all of it is partial. Both sides of this debate are arguing about equipment for a journey that is nearly over, and the chapter was written to say so.

If the gifts have ceased, does God still heal and guide today? Yes. Cessationism does not mean God has stopped working. It means the particular gifts by which the apostles and prophets received new revelation and confirmed it with signs were for the foundation period. God still answers prayer, and he still heals the sick, sometimes in ways no doctor can explain; James tells us to call the elders and pray (James 5:14–15). He still guides his people, through his word, wise counsel, providence, and the Spirit’s illumination of Scripture. What he does not do is add new revelation to the Bible. A strong impression in prayer may be used by God, but it must be weighed by Scripture and never treated as his voice with the authority of Scripture.

What should I do if my church, or a friend, believes the gifts continue? Love them, and keep the main thing the main thing. Many continuationist believers are sound on the gospel, love the Bible, and put cessationists to shame in prayer and evangelism. Be clear about what you believe and why, but do not make it a test of fellowship among those who confess Christ crucified. Two things are worth watching for in any setting: whether claimed words from God are tested by Scripture and treated as below it, and whether Christ and the gospel stay at the centre. Where those hold, there is real unity to enjoy.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Scripture is partial or imperfect. Scripture is complete and sufficient for this age (2 Timothy 3:16–17). But our knowledge, even with Scripture, is partial compared to seeing Christ. The map is perfect; our reading of it is still the reading of travellers.
verseByVerse.note: “The perfect” most naturally refers to the completion of all things when Christ returns.

verseByVerse.quote: When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I gave up childish ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I was a child. An illustration, and it is regularly misused as a rebuke, as though Paul were telling the Corinthians to stop being childish, which he does elsewhere (3:1; 14:20) but not mainly here. Read it in its place: he is explaining what he means by partial. There is nothing wrong with the child’s speech. A three-year-old naming things is not lying. His thinking is real thinking, his reasoning is real reasoning, and within its own scale it works perfectly well. It is simply small. He is not mistaken about the world; he has less of it. That is right for a child.

Childish ways. Gave up is katargeō again, the same word as pass away in verses 8 and 10. The present gifts are like childhood speech compared with the maturity of the age to come. There may also be a gentle rebuke in the background: the Corinthians, proud of tongues, were acting like children.

True knowledge on a child’s scale. That is what Paul says about our present knowledge of God, and it is a wonderfully balanced thing to say. It rules out two errors at once. It rules out the confidence that imagines our theology has God taped, that the systems and the creeds have got him mapped and there is nothing left to be astonished by. And it equally rules out the fashionable humility that says nothing can really be known, that all our talk of God is guesswork. The child does know his mother. He simply does not yet know what she gave up for him, what she fears at three in the morning, or what she was like at twenty. So the Christian’s knowledge of God is true knowledge, and it is knowledge on a child’s scale. What comes next is not a correction of it but a growing up into it.

A quiet comfort. Nobody blames a child for being a child. The smallness is not a fault to be repented of; it is a stage to be outgrown, and the outgrowing is not something a child achieves by concentrating. It happens to him. Growing up is done to us, and so is this: when he appears we shall be like him (1 John 3:2).

Firm and light. What is required, then, is conviction held firmly and carried lightly: believing what God has said with your whole weight, and holding your conclusions on the harder questions knowing that you are, at present, three feet tall. A church divided over prophecy and tongues is a nursery of children shouting about a subject on which every one of them speaks like a child. That is not an argument for indifference. It is an argument for the patience this chapter describes.

How do I know which convictions to hold firmly and which lightly? Hold most firmly what Scripture states most clearly and what the church has confessed together through the ages: the Trinity, the deity and humanity of Christ, his atoning death and bodily resurrection, justification by faith alone, the authority of Scripture, his return. On these, a Christian stands without apology. Hold more lightly the conclusions that depend on harder texts and on which faithful Bible-believing Christians have long differed, such as the details of the gifts, church government, or the order of end-time events. Believe them, teach them, but do not treat the brother who differs as an enemy of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a mirror dimly. Corinth was famous for its bronze, and mirrors in that world were polished metal; many readers of this letter had looked into one. They did not work like ours. A bronze mirror gives you back a darkened, slightly warped version of a face: recognisably you, and never quite you. The phrase translated dimly (en ainigmati) is literally in a riddle, which is where the word enigma comes from. That is our present sight of God. Not blindness. We see him truly, through his word and works, but indirectly, like a reflection: a face in dark metal, and a riddle that is genuinely about him.

But then face to face. Scripture does not leave that phrase vague; it is the hope of the whole Bible in three words. God spoke to Moses mouth to mouth, clearly and not in riddles (Numbers 12:8), and Paul’s word for dimly echoes that verse. Yet when Moses asked for the one thing more, please show me your glory, he was told, you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live; he was put in a cleft of rock, covered with a hand, and allowed to see the back of God going past (Exodus 33:18–23). The reason was not distance but holiness. Sinful man cannot stand before the unveiled purity of God; even Isaiah, seeing only the edge of his glory, cried woe to himself as a man of unclean lips (Isaiah 6:5). That is the high-water mark of the old covenant. The greatest prophet in Israel’s history asked to see God’s face and was refused it. And the last page of the Bible says of ordinary redeemed people, without ceremony: they will see his face (Revelation 22:4). What Moses was not given, the least believer in the congregation is promised. That means something will have happened to him first: he will have been made holy, washed in the blood of the Lamb, so that the sight which would have undone him becomes his joy (Hebrews 12:14; Revelation 7:14). We shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). This is what the church has called the beatific vision, which means the sight of God that makes us blessed: seeing him will be our full and final happiness (Psalm 16:11; 17:15). It is the great hope of the Christian.

Whose face will we see? The face of God in Christ. The glory of God has already shone in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6), and on that day we will see the Son, risen and glorified, with the marks of the nails still on him (John 20:27; Revelation 5:6), and in him we will see the Father (John 14:9). We will not see the divine essence with bodily eyes, for God is spirit and infinite; but we will know him directly, without veil or riddle, in the face of the Lamb, as fully as creatures can.

Then I shall know fully. Know fully (epiginōskō) is to know thoroughly. Our knowledge will be complete, not infinite as God’s is, but without the distortions and gaps of the present.

Fully known. Then the last clause, and it is a tender one. God already knows us completely (8:3; Galatians 4:9). In every merely human love we are caught in one of two positions. Either you are loved by people who do not fully know you, who love a version of you assembled from your better hours, or you are known by someone who has seen the worst and whose affection you can feel adjusting itself. The fear that runs underneath most human relationships is the same fear: if they knew everything, they would not stay. It is why people edit themselves in company, and why being loved often fails to settle anything. Paul writes, of God, I have been fully known. Past tense, already accomplished. There is no discovery still to come, no file not yet opened, nothing that will emerge in the last hour and change the verdict. The one who knows the whole of it, the thing you have never told anyone, the thing you would not put in a prayer, is the one who set his love on you before you had done anything at all.

The ground of the whole chapter. And that is the ground of everything this chapter has asked for. A person who is fully known and fully loved has nothing left to protect, and a person with nothing to protect can afford to be patient, kind, unenvious, and free of the ledger. Love like this is not squeezed out of the loveless by effort. It leaks out of people who have stopped being afraid of being found out.

Will we recognise one another? Scripture gives good reason to think so. If our knowledge then is fuller, not emptier, we will not know less than we do now. The disciples recognised Moses and Elijah on the mountain (Matthew 17:3–4); the risen Jesus was known by those who loved him; Paul expects to glory over the Thessalonians at Christ’s coming (1 Thessalonians 2:19). The relationships of grace are not erased but perfected. And every face we know will be turned the same way, toward his.

What happens to believers who die before that day? They are with the Lord at once, consciously and gladly. To be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), and to depart and be with Christ is far better (Philippians 1:23). They do not sleep in unconsciousness, and there is no purgatory between. Yet the fullest face to face waits for the resurrection, when Christ returns and body and soul are reunited in glory (15:51–54).

On a Tuesday. Think of the thing you most fear being known about you. Bring it to God in prayer, by name, and remember that he knew it before you told him and loves you no less. Then, in one relationship this week, stop protecting yourself a little: admit a fault, ask forgiveness, let yourself be seen. People who are fully known by God can afford it.

For worship. The Son of God knew exactly what he was buying. He looked at the whole record, not the edited version, the whole of it, and went to the cross for it anyway, so that on some morning still ahead he could stand in front of the people he died for with nothing hidden on either side, and be looked at. That is what he wanted. Not servants at a distance, but a face to face. You are fully known by God, and fully loved, and one day you will see him. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matthew 5:8).
verseByVerse.note: Mirrors were made of polished metal and gave a dim, imperfect reflection; Corinth was famous for its bronze work. The ESV notes that “dimly” is literally “in a riddle.”

parallels.desc: with him I speak mouth to mouth, clearly, and not in riddles

verseByVerse.quote: So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith, hope, and love abide. Paul has just said that prophecy, tongues and knowledge will fall. Now he names three things that will not. Abide (menō) means to remain, to last. The three appear together all over Paul’s letters: your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope (1 Thessalonians 1:3; 5:8; Colossians 1:4–5). And they map the Christian life onto time. Faith takes hold of what God has done. Hope leans forward to what he will do. Love does the present tense. Between them they cover everything a believer has.

But the greatest of these is love. At first sight the last clause is odd. Why is love greater? Faith saves; love does not. Faith is how a sinner is justified, that is, declared righteous by God for Christ’s sake, and Paul of all people is not about to demote it. The answer is in the word abide. Consider what happens to each of the three when Christ returns. Faith is trusting a God you cannot see, and on that day you will see him, so faith will have become sight (2 Corinthians 5:7).
