Hope is waiting for what has not yet arrived, and on that day it will have arrived, so hope will have become possession (Romans 8:24). Neither is lost; each is swallowed by its own fulfilment. Some careful readers think faith and hope remain in glory in a changed form, as endless trust in God and glad expectation of more of him; even on that reading love is greatest, for the reason the next paragraph gives. Love alone arrives unchanged. There is nothing love turns into, because there is nothing better than love to turn into. It is the only thing in the Christian life that will be doing in eternity exactly what it does now, which is why practising it is the one activity of this life that is not preparation for something else.

The deepest reason. Faith and hope are things creatures do; God has neither. He does not trust, because he knows, and he does not hope, because he holds. But God is love (1 John 4:8, 16): not merely loving, but love itself, in the unbroken giving between Father, Son and Spirit that was going on before there was anything else at all. Love is greatest because love is the one item on the list that is a description of God.

If love is greater, does it save us? No. We are justified by faith alone, not by our love. Faith is not the greatest virtue, but it is the empty hand that receives Christ, and Christ’s righteousness is what saves (Romans 3:28; 5:1). Love is the fruit, not the root. A faith that produces no love is dead (Galatians 5:6; James 2:17), but even the believer’s best love is imperfect, and if we had to stand on our love we would fall. We stand on Christ’s love for us, received by faith, and that love then begins to love through us.

If love is what matters most, why do Christians make so much of doctrine? Because love needs to know what is true in order to do good. A friend who warmly waves you onto a bridge he knows is down has not loved you, however kindly he smiles. The love of this chapter rejoices with the truth (v. 6), and it is defined by a historical event, God sending his Son to die for sinners (1 John 4:9–10); take away the truth about Christ and love shrinks to a warm feeling that cannot save anyone. The opposite mistake is just as real. Correct doctrine held without love is the noisy gong of verse 1. The Christian aim is not truth or love but both: truth spoken in love (Ephesians 4:15).

Three ways of holding on to Christ. Faith, hope and love are not three free-standing virtues. When Paul thanks God for the Thessalonians’ faith, love and hope, he names where all three are fixed: in our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Thessalonians 1:3). All three have the same object. Faith rests on what Christ has done. Hope waits for Christ to appear. Love is Christ’s own love, poured into his people and flowing out through them. So the three that abide are three ways of holding on to one Person, and the chapter that began by pricing the gifts ends by pointing past every gift to him.

In the flow. This verse closes the chapter and opens the next. Chapter 14 begins by telling the church to pursue love and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts (14:1): the gifts are to be used, but in the way this chapter has shown. The three words also run through the rest of the letter. Faith and hope will carry chapter 15, where Paul defends the resurrection on which both rest (15:14, 19), and the letter ends with one instruction for everything: let all that you do be done in love (16:14). Corinth’s troubles, from factions to lawsuits to the Lord’s Supper, were at bottom failures of love, and this verse names the cure.

On a Tuesday. At the end of today, ask not just: did I believe? did I hope? But: did I love? Name one person you loved well today and thank God for the grace that did it; name one you did not, and confess it, and plan one concrete act of love for that person tomorrow. Then go to sleep resting in his love, not yours: only he has ever loved perfectly, and he did it for you.

13.text: <sup>1</sup>If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal.<sup>2</sup>And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.<sup>3</sup>If I give away all I have, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing.<sup>4</sup>Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant<sup>5</sup>or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful;<sup>6</sup>it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth.<sup>7</sup>Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.<sup>8</sup>Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away.<sup>9</sup>For we know in part and we prophesy in part,<sup>10</sup>but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.<sup>11</sup>When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I gave up childish ways.<sup>12</sup>For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.<sup>13</sup>So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.

14.title: Prophecy, Tongues, and the Order of Worship
14.overview:
Having shown that love is the way all gifts must be used, Paul applies it to the Corinthians’ worship, which had become noisy and confusing as many people spoke in tongues at once. His test is simple: what builds up the church? Only what is understood can do that, so prophecy, spoken in ordinary language, is worth more in the meeting than a tongue no one can interpret, and a visitor should be able to follow what is said and add his Amen.

Then come practical rules: speakers in turn, tongues only with interpretation, prophecy always weighed, and women not taking part in that weighing. The ground of it all is the character of God, who is a God of peace, not disorder, and Paul presents his instructions as the Lord’s command.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love is the aim, and among the gifts prophecy is to be preferred, because it speaks to people in words they understand and so builds up the church, while an uninterpreted tongue reaches God alone.
verseByVerse.theology:
Understanding Comes Before Building Up

Paul’s governing rule for the church’s worship, that it must be understood, has deep roots. The God who speaks is a God who makes himself known; the Word became flesh to be heard and understood. Worship that puts the word of God out of the people’s reach works against the grain of the incarnation. The Reformers’ insistence on worship in the people’s own language, against the Latin Mass, applied exactly this principle: if the people cannot understand what is said and done, they cannot be built up.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian preference for tongues in the meeting was driven by the same status-seeking that produced the factions: tongues was the impressive gift. Paul’s preference for prophecy puts the good of all above the spectacular. Now: The same test reaches beyond tongues: sermons full of jargon and services no newcomer can follow fail it too. Does the person who attends understand what is happening, and is he being built up?

verseByVerse.quote: Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy. For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God; for no one understands him, but he utters mysteries in the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 14 applies the love of chapter 13 to the Corinthians’ worship. Their gatherings were chaotic: many speaking in tongues at once, with no interpretation, so that no one understood and outsiders thought them mad. Paul’s principle is that everything in worship must build up the church, and only what is understood can build up. So prophecy, which speaks God’s word intelligibly, is greater than uninterpreted tongues (vv. 1–5); pray and sing with the mind as well as the spirit (vv. 6–19); tongues without interpretation are a sign of judgement on unbelievers, while prophecy convicts them and brings them to worship (vv. 20–25). Then come rules: two or three speakers, one at a time, with interpretation and weighing; women are not to take part in judging what is said; and all things done decently and in order, because God is a God of peace (vv. 26–40).

In the flow. Chapter 12 showed that every gift comes from one Spirit for one body; chapter 13 showed the way all gifts must travel, which is love; chapter 14 brings both truths into the meeting room. The key word is the one Paul planted at 8:1: knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. A church proud of its gifts had forgotten what they were for, and this chapter answers in one word: building up.

Pursue love. Two commands, and both matter. After a chapter saying that gifts without love are worth nothing, the obvious inference would be to stop caring about the gifts. Paul heads that off at once. Love is not an alternative to gifts; it is the way gifts are to be used. Pursue (diōkō) is a word for chasing, used of hunters and pursuers: chase it down, run after it.

Especially that you may prophesy. Earnestly desire is the verb behind our word zeal. So the Christian is to be zealous about both, and there is a definite order: love first, gifts within it. Love does not cancel gifts; it directs them. Then the whole chapter’s argument in one phrase. The reason is simple, and it will not change: prophecy can be understood by the people in the room, and so it builds them up.

Love first, because love is his. Why must love come before the gifts? Because the love of chapter 13 is not an ideal Paul invented. It is a portrait of Christ. Patient, kind, not insisting on its own way, bearing all things: that is how the Son of God used every power he had. He could have turned stones into bread and would not do it for himself (Matthew 4:3–4). He healed people and then told them to keep quiet about it. He had all authority and spent it washing feet and carrying a cross. So the order of this verse is the shape of his life. Gifts are tools; love is the likeness of the Son, and that likeness is what God is making in his people (Romans 8:29).

Not to men but to God. Without interpretation, a tongue is addressed to God, in prayer or praise, not to the congregation. That is why Paul will describe it as praying, singing and giving thanks (vv. 14–16) rather than as teaching.

Mysteries in the Spirit. Understands is literally hears: no one grasps it. Mysteries here are not riddles. They are the things of God, spoken in a form the listeners cannot open. In the Spirit (or in his spirit, as the ESV notes) means by the Spirit’s enabling.

What tongues were. The chapter assumes a knowledge we no longer have. The Greek word is simply tongue (glōssa), the word for a language. At Pentecost the gift produced recognisable human languages: visitors each heard the mighty works of God in his own language (Acts 2:6–11). In Corinth no foreigner present knew the language, so no one understood, and a separate gift of interpretation was required. Four things can be said with confidence. It was genuine speech, given by the Spirit. It was addressed to God, not to the congregation. It was unintelligible to hearers unless interpreted. And it was never the badge of a real Christian or the proof of an advanced one.

Where Christians differ: what were tongues? Some think the Corinthian tongues were ecstatic, non-human speech, pointing to 14:2, where no one understands the speaker, and to the tongues of angels (13:1); others that they were real human languages as at Pentecost. This commentary’s view: At Pentecost, tongues were known human languages, understood by foreigners (Acts 2:6–11). Paul’s own analogy here is foreign languages (vv. 10–11), and interpretation means translation. So the most natural reading is that tongues were real languages the speaker had not learned. Paul’s mention of tongues of angels (13:1) is a hypothetical extreme, not a description of the gift.

Not the mark of the Spirit. What cannot be said is that tongues are the sign of a Spirit-filled Christian. That was settled two chapters ago: not all speak with tongues (12:30), and the mark of the Spirit is the confession that Jesus is Lord (12:3). Corinth had made a distinction out of a distribution, and the whole chapter is a patient dismantling of it.

Is the private prayer language some Christians speak of today the same thing? This commentary holds that it is not. The tongues of the New Testament were real languages, given by the Spirit as a sign gift belonging to the apostolic foundation of the church, and there is no warrant in Scripture for a separate private prayer language for later believers. Many sincere Christians who practise something they call tongues love Christ deeply, and they should be treated as brothers and sisters, not mocked. They can point to verses 4 and 28, where the speaker builds himself up and speaks to himself and to God, and they are right that Paul allowed such speech; this commentary’s judgement is that he was describing a gift of his own day, not promising it to every later believer. But no Christian needs such an experience to pray fully and freely. The Spirit helps every believer in his weakness and intercedes for him (Romans 8:26), and you may pour out your heart to your Father in your own words. A sign gift means a gift whose chief purpose was to mark the apostles’ message as God’s own, as signs and wonders did (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). The apostolic foundation means the once-for-all laying of the church’s base by the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20): a foundation is laid once, and then the house is built on it.

verseByVerse.quote: On the other hand, the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Speaks to people. Here is the contrast that governs the chapter. Tongues speaks to God; prophecy speaks to people, in their own language. Both are real, both were given by the Spirit, and only one of them does anything for the person in the next seat.

For their upbuilding. Paul defines prophecy not by its source, or by how it feels, or by whether it predicts anything, but by its effect, and that gives the church a usable test: look at what happened to the people who heard it. Upbuilding (oikodomē) is the builder’s word, the key word of the chapter (vv. 3, 4, 5, 12, 17, 26): the congregation is a structure going up, and this speech adds a course of stone.

And encouragement and consolation. Encouragement (paraklēsis) belongs to a verb for calling someone to your side, and in use it means putting strength into a person, whether by urging or by comfort. Consolation (paramythia) is the plain word for what you say to the grieving.

The test of the effect. Prophecy as most people imagine it is dramatic, predictive and slightly alarming. Prophecy as Paul describes it leaves a congregation stronger, braver and comforted. A word that leaves people frightened, confused, or impressed with the speaker has not passed this test, whatever it claimed about its source.

Another Helper. Paul’s word for encouragement belongs to a family Jesus himself used. In the upper room he promised his disciples another Helper, the Paraklētos, the one called alongside (John 14:16). Another, because they had already had one: Jesus had been walking beside them for about three years, putting strength into the weak and comfort into the grieving, and John later calls him our advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1), the same word. The Spirit’s work, Jesus said, would be to bring to their remembrance all that he had said to them (John 14:26). So the words that build up, urge on and console are never the speaker’s own invention. At their truest they are Christ’s words, carried by his Spirit into a room that needs them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean prophecy was only encouragement and never correction. It could expose sin (vv. 24–25). And it does not mean prophecy is the same as preaching, though they share these purposes. Preaching expounds a text that is already given. Prophecy in this chapter was something said into a particular room on a particular day, which then had to be weighed by the others (v. 29), a thing no one would ever say about Scripture. So whatever else must be settled about this gift, it was subject to Scripture and never an addition to it.

If prophecy has ceased, what does this verse ask of me? A great deal. What is not in dispute is that these three effects are wanted, and that any Christian may aim at them. Even a believer entirely certain that the gift itself has ceased may take verse 3 as a description of what preaching should do and what his conversation after the service ought to do. Somebody in the room this Sunday needs to be built up, somebody needs courage, and somebody needs consoling, and the words that do it, drawn from Scripture, are the nearest thing to this verse that most of us will ever handle (1 Thessalonians 5:11; Hebrews 3:13).

verseByVerse.quote: The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself, but the one who prophesies builds up the church. Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy. The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets, so that the church may be built up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Builds up himself. The first half is easily heard as a sneer, and it is not one. Paul is not saying the tongue-speaker is being selfish. He is stating a fact about what the gift did: the speaker might be edified in some way, perhaps through the experience of praising God, even without understanding the words. But that is not the purpose of gifts, which are for the common good (12:7). The problem is not the gift. It is the setting. Corinth had taken something that built up the individual and made it the centrepiece of the gathering, and the gathering exists for a different purpose: the one who prophesies builds up the church, everyone in the room.

Even more to prophesy. Paul does not despise tongues. But he does not mean all will (12:30); it is a wish, like his wish that all were single as he was (7:7). He is not removing anything but reordering it, which is the harder and better kind of correction.

Unless someone interprets. Greater here means more useful to the church. And there is the qualifier that shows exactly where the ranking comes from. Interpreted tongues are no longer inferior to prophecy, because interpreted tongues do what prophecy does: the room understands and is built up. So the greatness Paul is measuring is not in the gift itself; it is a question of how many people benefit.

So that the church may be built up. The test for everything, and it reaches further than tongues: the sermon full of allusions the congregation cannot catch, the prayer meeting a newcomer could not join, the music pitched where only the musicians can sing it. The activity may be excellent, and the same question decides the matter: is anyone else being built by this, or only the one doing it?

Christ did not please himself. Paul uses this same building word in Romans and grounds it in a Person. Let each of us please his neighbour for his good, to build him up, he writes, for Christ did not please himself (Romans 15:2–3). That is the deepest reason why a gift that edifies only its owner cannot be the centrepiece of worship. The Son of God had every right to please himself, and he chose the road that pleased his Father and saved his people. A church that measures its gatherings by whether others are built up is not adopting a technique for good meetings. It is being shaped like its Lord, whose whole life was spent for the good of people who could give him nothing.

Is it wrong to go to church for what I get out of it? Not wrong, but incomplete. You should come hungry, wanting to be fed by the word and to meet God, and he delights to feed you. But this chapter adds a second reason for being there: the others. Every believer comes as a member of a body, with something to give as well as something to receive (12:7). The two are not rivals. The Christian who comes to serve is very often the one who goes home most fed, and the one who comes only to consume is often the first to complain that he got nothing.

parallels.desc: would that all the LORD’s people were prophets!

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul presses the point with pictures (a flute, a bugle, a foreign language) and with his own example, to show that speech no one understands helps no one, and that worship must engage the mind as well as the spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
Worship as the Act of a Body

Paul’s insistence on understanding rests on what a Christian gathering is: not a private experience shared by many individuals at once, but one body built up together. Worship is not only my meeting with God in the presence of others; it is our meeting with God as a body. That requires understanding: no one can say Amen to what he cannot follow, and a congregation’s Amen is the sign that the body is truly worshipping together.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The enthusiasts for tongues were bringing a private practice into the meeting without asking whether the rest could take part. Paul’s five words against ten thousand are not a sum to calculate but a principle to live by: ask whether what is done can be received and answered by the whole church. Now: The principle applies to any part of worship that puts the experience of some above the building up of all.

verseByVerse.quote: Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Suppose I come. Paul courteously puts himself in the frame. He does not say that when you speak in tongues you are useless. He says: suppose I turn up and do it.

How will I benefit you. The same question, whose advantage is served, governed the argument about idol meat (10:23, 33). Paul is not asking whether an activity is spiritual, permitted or sincere, but whether anyone is better off.

Unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching? Four things he could bring instead, and they are not four synonyms. Revelation is something disclosed by God; knowledge is grasp of the truth; prophecy is that truth spoken into this room now; teaching is the patient explanation that makes it hold. Revelation and prophecy are messages from God; knowledge and teaching are the explanation of truth. Between them they describe how the word of God actually reaches a congregation, and every one of them has this in common: the hearer understands.

All four in one Person. Behind the argument lies the character of God. Our God speaks. He is not the mute idol of 12:2. He made the world by speaking, he gave a book, and when he came in person he came as the Word. And the four things Paul could bring all meet in Jesus Christ. He is the revelation of the Father (Matthew 11:27). In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). He is the Prophet Moses promised, to whom the people must listen (Acts 3:22). And the officers sent to arrest him came back saying that no one ever spoke like this man (John 7:46). Everything about him leans toward being understood, so a form of worship that makes God’s truth inaccessible to the people present is running against the grain of who he is.

The Reformation and the ploughboy. That conviction did real work in history. It is why the Reformers fought for services in the language of the people, and why William Tyndale vowed that a boy driving the plough would one day know more of the Scriptures than the learned cleric he was arguing with. A Latin liturgy in an English village failed this verse as an uninterpreted tongue failed it in Corinth: the words true and beautiful, and the man in the back row going home with nothing.

Things that are nobody’s fault. The same test can be turned on things done with no bad intent at all. A preacher who quotes Greek without translating it, a prayer full of phrases only someone raised in church would know, a hymn whose language was ordinary in 1780 and is now a puzzle: each leaves somebody outside the conversation. The remedy is small: explain the word, give the reference, say what you mean. And Paul asks about benefit, not interest. A congregation can find a sermon interesting and go home with nothing to believe more firmly and nobody comforted. Somebody stronger by the end is the test.

On a Tuesday. When you explain your faith to a friend this week, drop the church words and say it in the language you would use about anything else that mattered to you.

verseByVerse.quote: If even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp, do not give distinct notes, how will anyone know what is played? And if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle?
verseByVerse.commentary:
If even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp, do not give distinct notes, how will anyone know what is played? Two pictures. The first is a flute or a harp producing notes that do not resolve into a tune. An orchestra tuning up is a wonderful noise and nobody hums it on the way home. No individual sound is wrong; what is missing is the shape that makes sound into music. That is what uninterpreted tongues do to a service.

And if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle? The second picture is sharper, because it has consequences. A bugle in a camp was not decoration; it was command. Different calls meant advance, retreat, gather, stand to. And an army only marches if the call is distinct. A bugler who blows something ambiguous does not produce a slightly confused response; he produces a camp of men looking at each other while the enemy comes over the ridge.

From taste to survival. The change of image is the point. The flute makes indistinctness a matter of aesthetics; the bugle makes it a matter of survival. A congregation that cannot make out what is being said cannot obey it. So for anyone who speaks to God’s people, clarity is a duty rather than a style preference. A sermon that is admired and not understood has failed as the bugle failed: nobody can say what they are to do on Monday. The Levites in Nehemiah’s day read from the Law clearly and gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading (Nehemiah 8:8).

The silver trumpets. The trumpet image was not a figure of speech to Israel. God gave Moses two silver trumpets with a fixed code: both blown together summoned the whole congregation, one alone summoned the chiefs, an alarm set the camps on the east moving (Numbers 10:1–7). Lives were arranged around the certainty that the same sound meant the same thing every time. Which is why muddled teaching is more serious than it feels, and the people most damaged are those with the least background: the new believer, the visitor, the man who came in troubled and needed one clear sentence and was given a beautiful fog.

The one clear note. What is the note every Christian voice must sound distinctly? Paul told this church: I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified (2:2), and he names the tune at 15:3–4: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day. A church may be uncertain about many secondary things and survive. It cannot be uncertain about him. A man who does not know whether his sins are forgiven cannot get ready for any battle, least of all the last one. And Christ himself never sounded an uncertain note. The crowds were astonished, because he taught them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes (Matthew 7:29).

What if I am not a gifted speaker? Clarity is not eloquence. It is saying one true thing in a way the listener can take home. You do not need a fine voice or a large vocabulary; you need to know what you mean and say it plainly. Before you speak about Christ, ask yourself: what is the one thing I want this person to understand? Then say that, in ordinary words, and stop. Some of the clearest witnesses in the church have been people who would never call themselves speakers at all.

For worship. There is a trumpet that will give no uncertain sound. The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God, and the dead in Christ will rise first (1 Thessalonians 4:16). No one on that day will wonder what the call means. The sleeping saints of every century will hear it and stand up. Our Captain gives his soldiers a plain word now, and he will himself sound the call that gathers his whole army home.
verseByVerse.note: A trumpet sounded signals to soldiers in battle.

verseByVerse.quote: So with yourselves, if with your tongue you utter speech that is not intelligible, how will anyone know what is said? For you will be speaking into the air. There are doubtless many different languages in the world, and none is without meaning, but if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker and the speaker a foreigner to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not intelligible. Intelligible (eusēmos) means clear, distinct, easily recognised. Paul applies the pictures to Corinth.

How will anyone know what is said? For you will be speaking into the air. There is the phrase that sums up the whole chapter, and it is more desolate than it first sounds. Speaking into the air: wasted words, like a boxer beating the air (9:26). Not speaking nonsense, and not speaking wickedly. Speaking real words that reach nobody: sound going out into an empty room and simply dispersing.

None is without meaning. A generous concession first. Languages here (phōnai) is literally voices, sounds. Every human language is full of poetry and law and love and grief to somebody, and Paul is not saying tongues were gibberish. The problem is never the language. It is the gap.

A foreigner. The word for foreigner is barbaros, and its origin is a small piece of Greek snobbery. It is probably imitative: to a Greek ear, foreign speech sounded like bar-bar-bar, so a foreigner was a barbarian, a person who made noises. Anyone who has stood in a hospital corridor in a country whose language he does not speak knows the feeling: surrounded by meaning, cut out of all of it. The comparison also supports the view that tongues were real languages.

Strangers in God’s house. Now put that feeling in a church. The gift Corinth prized most was producing, in the person three feet away, the loneliness of a stranger in a foreign country, in the one place on earth where nobody is supposed to be a foreigner. Christ died to end exactly that. Those who were once far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ; he himself is our peace, who has broken down the dividing wall, so that we are no longer strangers and aliens but fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Ephesians 2:13–14, 19). Jews and Greeks, slaves and free were baptised into one body (12:13). The cross tore down a wall, and Corinth had found a way to rebuild it out of syllables, and was proud of it.

Any church can manufacture barbarians. A congregation that would never dream of the Corinthian error can do it through unexplained jargon, in-jokes, a way of praying outsiders cannot join, and assuming everyone knows where the book is kept. None of it is malicious. All of it says to the person standing at the back: you are not from here.

How can our church help a newcomer not feel like a foreigner? Small things do most of the work. Say who is speaking and what is happening next. Give page numbers and Bible references, and explain a word like justification or communion the first time it is used. Make sure someone sits with a visitor, shows him where to find the reading, and talks to him afterwards about something other than the weather. Invite him for lunch. Each of these says what Paul wants said: you are welcome here, and this is meant for you too.

verseByVerse.quote: So with yourselves, since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive to excel in building up the church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eager for manifestations of the Spirit. A model of correcting people without crushing them. Literally, Paul says you are zealots for spirits. He takes their eagerness as given and does not condemn it. He could have said: your appetite for spiritual experience is the whole problem, calm down. Instead he turns their hunger round: you want the Spirit’s manifestations, so excel at the thing his manifestations are for.

Strive to excel in building up the church. Excel (perisseuō) means to abound, to overflow, to have more than enough. Paul takes the Corinthian instinct to outdo one another and does not abolish it either. He gives it a new field. If you must compete, compete at this: who can do the most good to the people in this room. In this league table the people at the top are the ones nobody has been counting: the member who has quietly rebuilt the confidence of a family going through a bad year is winning, and does not know there is a competition.

The test. It can be applied to any activity in a church. Not was it spiritual? Not did I feel God in it? Simply: who is stronger because of it? If no one is, the thing may still be innocent, but it has not yet been what this verse is asking for. And the test exposes a quiet idol. Corinth’s appetite for spiritual display was, at bottom, a hunger to be somebody: religion used to win standing. The gospel ends that hunger by giving us a standing we could never win, for in Christ we are already loved, chosen and made holy (1:2, 30), and people who no longer need to be impressive are free to be useful.

Zeal for his house. There was once zeal pointed exactly where Paul points the Corinthians’. When Jesus drove the traders out of the temple, his disciples remembered that it was written, zeal for your house will consume me (John 2:17; Psalm 69:9). His zeal was not for experiences but for the house of God, and it consumed him in the plain sense: it took him to the cross. And the house he cared about is now the church, God’s temple made of people (3:16). So when Paul tells eager Corinthians to excel in building up the church, he is asking them to want what their Lord wanted, and to spend their zeal where he spent his.

A word for the flat. There is a warning here for the opposite temperament too, and sober congregations have their share of it. Some Christians are eager for nothing at all. They have never longed for more of God, never asked him for anything they could not arrange themselves, and mistake their flatness for maturity. Paul does not commend that. He says be eager about the right thing, which assumes the eagerness is there. So the verse asks two questions. Am I eager? And is my eagerness pointed at the people around me? This is not a word against the grieving or the depressed, whose flatness is suffering rather than choice; the Lord is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18), and he does not ask them to manufacture feelings.

How do I find out what I can do to build up my church? Start where you are and with what is in front of you. Ask your elders where there is need, and offer to fill it. Notice what others thank you for, and what you find yourself caring about when no one asks you to. Pray for the people around you, one face at a time, and you will soon see what they need. Most building up is done in ordinary ways: a meal taken round, a child taught, a hand held at a funeral, a verse given at the right moment. Faithfulness in small things is how gifts are discovered.

On a Tuesday. Somewhere in your church this week is a family having a hard time that nobody has noticed. Eagerness for God, pointed the right way, looks like a meal on their doorstep or a message asking how they really are.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful. What am I to do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pray that he may interpret. The instruction is practical: if you have the one gift, ask God for the other, so that what you are doing can be shared and the tongue can benefit others.

My mind is unfruitful. My spirit is the inner person moved by the Spirit. Mind (nous) is the understanding. Unfruitful (akarpos) means producing no fruit, no understanding for himself or others. It does not mean the speaker is in a trance and not responsible; Paul’s next sentence says I will four times, which is a man deciding what to do. Unfruitful means the mind is producing nothing anyone can pick up.

What am I to do? Paul’s conclusion follows, and it is neither of the two answers people usually reach for.

With my mind also. Both, not a choice. Worship should engage the whole person, heart and understanding. Paul refuses the two great mistakes about worship in a single sentence. The first mistake is to want the spirit without the mind: worship as pure experience, where thinking is felt to interrupt the feeling, where the aim of a service is a state and doctrine is an obstacle to it. The second is to want the mind without the spirit: worship as instruction only, correct and cold, where a congregation could sing about the blood of Christ with the expressions of people reading a timetable, and where any warmth is suspected of being manipulation. Both are amputations, each usually adopted as a reaction against the other, and Paul will have neither.

Singing with the mind. He applies the rule to singing as well as praying, which is where most Christians meet it. Singing with the mind means singing words we understand and mean, letting the word of Christ dwell in us richly as we sing (Colossians 3:16; Ephesians 5:19). Anyone who has arrived at the end of a hymn with no memory of the middle verse knows how possible it is to sing with neither. Older translations render Psalm 47:7 as sing ye praises with understanding (KJV), and the Hebrew word there probably means a skilful or thoughtful song.

The whole man at prayer. The Lord Jesus prayed exactly as this verse asks. In Gethsemane he offered up prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears (Hebrews 5:7), and no prayer was ever more deeply felt. Yet the same prayer was entirely clear: not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). And the long prayer of John 17, spoken aloud in front of his disciples, is the mind at prayer at its fullest, every sentence weighed and understood. Spirit and mind were never at war in him. The one true worshipper the world has seen worshipped with all of himself, and that is the pattern Paul is restoring to Corinth.

I often feel nothing when I sing. Is my worship worthless? No. Feelings rise and fall with tiredness, health and grief, and God does not measure worship by them. What he asks is that you mean what you sing, that you sing truth with your mind engaged and your will offered to him. Sometimes that is all a weary believer can give, and it is a true offering. Keep singing truth, and pay attention to the words. Very often warmth returns as the mind is filled with what God has done, and on the days it does not, the Spirit still carries your praise to the Father.

On a Tuesday. Before the service, read the words of what you are about to sing. During the prayers, mean the Amen. Afterwards, ask what was said. That is praying with the mind, and it does not cost a Christian one degree of warmth.

For worship. Christ sang with his mind and his spirit. On the night he was betrayed, after the Supper, he sang a hymn with his disciples, very likely the psalms that end the Passover (Matthew 26:30), and he meant every word: the LORD is my strength and my song; I shall not die, but I shall live (Psalm 118:14, 17). And now, risen, he sings the Father’s praise in the midst of his people (Hebrews 2:12), and our poor worship rises to the Father carried inside his. He made us whole people, and he redeems us whole.

verseByVerse.quote: Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit, how can anyone in the position of an outsider say “Amen” to your thanksgiving when he does not know what you are saying? For you may be giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not being built up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit. Praising God in a tongue. Paul brings the argument down to one word, and it is a word every congregation says without thinking about it.

Say Amen. Amen is Hebrew, and the church took it over from the synagogue without translating it, which is itself a small marvel: the same syllables have been said by God’s people for some three thousand years. It means something firm, reliable, sure: so be it. It was the congregation’s response to prayers (Nehemiah 8:6; Psalm 106:48). When one person prays aloud and the congregation says Amen, they are not being polite. They are signing the prayer. It becomes theirs. And Paul’s word for the outsider (idiōtēs) means an ordinary person, uninstructed, someone occupying the position of the uninitiated: the enquirer, the newcomer, the person who came because a friend asked him.

When he does not know what you are saying? You cannot say Amen to what you do not understand. So the outsider who cannot say Amen has not merely missed a nice moment. He has been excluded from the congregation’s prayer: present at it, unable to join it. The one guest in the building who most needed to be included has been quietly left out by the thing everyone else found most exciting.

Giving thanks well enough. Paul concedes the point completely. The thanksgiving is real, and God has heard it. But it fails in its public purpose, and in a gathering of the church that is decisive.

Sincerity is not the test. It is possible to do something in a church service that is entirely genuine and God-directed and still wrong, because of who else was in the room. Sincerity is not Paul’s criterion anywhere in these three chapters. The criterion is always the person next to you.

The Yes beneath every Amen. Why can a congregation say Amen to a prayer so firmly? Because of what it rests on. All the promises of God find their Yes in Christ, Paul writes, and that is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory (2 Corinthians 1:20). A Christian’s Amen is not a hopeful guess that God might do what was asked. It is a signature under promises that Christ has already secured by his death and resurrection. That is why the outsider matters so much here. He is the one person in the room who most needs to hear those promises in words he can follow, so that one day he too may say Amen through Christ.

Should I say Amen out loud in church? Yes, if your church’s practice allows it, and most do. The congregation’s Amen is a biblical act, and saying it aloud is a way of joining the prayer and encouraging the one who led it. Where a church’s custom is quieter, a silent Amen from the heart is still yours to give. What matters is that you have followed the prayer and mean it. If a prayer contains something you cannot agree with, you are not obliged to sign it; but for most prayers, an honest Amen is one of the simplest ways to share in worship.

On a Tuesday. Remember the last time you took part audibly in a gathering: a prayer, a reading, a comment in a study, a testimony. Could a nervous newcomer with no church background have said Amen to it, and known what he was agreeing to?
verseByVerse.note: “Amen” (“so be it”) was the congregation’s response to prayer and thanksgiving.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.
verseByVerse.commentary:
More than all of you. This verse stops the argument from being a caricature. Paul is not criticising tongues out of jealousy or lack. He had the gift abundantly, more than the congregation most famous for it, and his attitude is not tolerance but gratitude. Every rule in this chapter comes from someone who prized the thing he was regulating.

In church. In church: in the gathered congregation. Paul is asking what belongs in a public gathering, and the same activity can be excellent in one setting and out of place in another. Instruct (katēcheō, from which we get catechise) means to teach. He is not praising brevity for its own sake, but speech that lands somewhere. The measure is not length but transfer: whether something that was in one head is now in another.

Ten thousand words. Ten thousand (myrioi) is the largest Greek number word, and the ratio is a deliberate absurdity: five against ten thousand, two thousand to one. He is not proposing a calculation. He is saying that in the assembly, comprehensible speech and incomprehensible speech are not on the same scale at all: that five intelligible words which teach somebody outweigh an entire evening of the other.

Five words. Five words is one short sentence. In English, Christ died for our sins (15:3) is exactly five, and it is fitting that the sentence which best suits Paul’s number is about Christ, because the instruction that builds a church is always, in the end, instruction about him. A single plain sentence about the Saviour, understood by a struggling believer, is worth more in a church than a display that lasts all night. Any Christian can manage five words. There is real freedom in this for anyone who has felt he had nothing to offer. You do not need a platform, a gift you can name, or a way with an audience. Five plain words that instruct one person are, on the apostle’s own scale, worth more than the most impressive thing that happened in Corinth that year.

Where did Paul speak in tongues, then? He has just spent seventeen verses saying the gift does not belong in the assembly without interpretation, so his use of it must have been chiefly elsewhere: perhaps in his own prayers, perhaps in his mission among people of other languages, where tongues could function as at Pentecost. The text does not tell us. What it does tell us is that the apostle who travelled constantly, was beaten, imprisoned and shipwrecked, and carried the anxiety of all the churches, gave thanks for every gift God had given him and used each for its purpose.

For worship. Fewer than five words were enough on the lips of our Lord. It is finished, he said (John 19:30), and in Greek it was one word, tetelestai, a word that holds the whole gospel. He did not need ten thousand words to save us. He spoke the word of the cross, and the word of the cross is the power of God (1:18). The Word made flesh said in one word what ten thousand could never add to.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul calls for mature thinking and turns to Isaiah, where foreign speech was a sign of judgement, to show what each gift does to an outsider who walks in: uninterpreted tongues leave him outside, while plain prophecy can lay bare his heart and bring him to worship.
verseByVerse.theology:
Worship and Witness

Paul’s concern for the unbeliever who walks into the meeting shows that the church’s worship is not only for the converted. A congregation that worships so that the outsider is addressed, convicted and drawn to worship is doing something a meeting full of tongues cannot do. That does not make evangelism the main purpose of the gathering, which is the glory of God, but it does mean that worship of the living God, when it is understood, reaches outward.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian meetings were apparently chaotic, with several speaking in tongues at once and no interpretation. Paul’s use of Isaiah turns their pride upside down: uninterpreted tongues are a sign linked with God’s judgement, not his favour. Now: A church whose worship is closed to the outsider, whether through uninterpreted experience, theological jargon or customs no newcomer can read, is failing the unbeliever who walks through the door. The word of God should be what disturbs him, not the confusion of the proceedings.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature. In the Law it is written, “By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.” Thus tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, while prophecy is a sign not for unbelievers but for believers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not children in your thinking. Corinth thought itself spiritually advanced, and Paul tells them they are behaving like toddlers, drawn to whatever is loudest and shiniest. Their fascination with tongues was childish (13:11).

Infants in evil. He adds the one respect in which he does want them childish: be as innocent as a baby about evil, the sort of person who has to have wickedness explained to him, but grown up in your understanding (Romans 16:19; Matthew 10:16).

In the flow. Having shown that only what is understood can build up (vv. 1–19), Paul now asks what each gift does to the outsider who walks in. Verses 21 and 22 bring in Scripture, and verses 23 to 25 show it happening in a Corinthian room. The argument of the whole letter is here in miniature: the Corinthians thought themselves wise and grown up (3:1–3, 18), and Paul shows them that a truly mature mind cares whether the outsider understands.

In the Law it is written. The Law here means the Scriptures, for the quotation is from Isaiah, and the setting must be known. Isaiah is preaching to the drunken leadership of Israel, and they mock him: his plain speech sounds to them like baby talk, a string of nonsense syllables (Isaiah 28:9–10). Very well, says God: if my clear word through a prophet is only babble to you, you shall have a message you genuinely cannot understand. He means the Assyrian army, whose foreign speech would soon be heard in their streets (Isaiah 28:11–12). Moses had warned of the same: a nation whose language you do not understand (Deuteronomy 28:49). Unintelligible language was the judgement: the sound of God no longer speaking to them in words they could follow.

A sign for unbelievers. The Isaiah background unlocks this verse. Paul does not mean tongues are a good way to reach unbelievers. He means they function as in Isaiah: the mark of people who are outside, hearing sounds that carry nothing to them, a sign of judgement, not of welcome. When unbelievers hear tongues they cannot understand, it confirms them in their unbelief and alienation. At Pentecost, tongues also signalled that the gospel was going to the nations, and many interpreters see in them a warning too, that judgement was coming on the generation that refused its Messiah (Acts 2:40).

A sign for believers. Prophecy is a sign for believers in the opposite way: the mark of a God who is present with his people, showing his favour, and speaking to them in words they understand. And as verses 24–25 show, it also brings unbelievers to faith. That is why verse 23 can say that unbelievers walking into a room full of tongues will conclude the church is mad. That is not a contradiction of verse 22; it is the demonstration of it. The sign does exactly what Isaiah said such a sign does: it leaves the outsider outside.

A famine of hearing. Here is a sobering thing for any church, quite apart from tongues. One of the most fearful judgements God brings on a people is not fire but unintelligibility: a famine of hearing the words of the LORD (Amos 8:11), a pulpit full of noise, a religion that has stopped saying anything. That can happen to a congregation without anybody deciding it, and the people inside are usually the last to notice.

The stone in the same chapter. The oracle Paul quotes holds something more. A few verses later, speaking to the same scoffers, God says that he has laid as a foundation in Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, and whoever believes will not be in haste (Isaiah 28:16). The New Testament knows who that stone is. Paul applies it to Christ, over whom unbelieving Israel stumbled (Romans 9:32–33), and Peter does the same (1 Peter 2:6). So the strange tongues of judgement and the cornerstone of mercy stand in one chapter of Isaiah. Those who mocked God’s plain word were left with babble; those who trust the stone he has laid will not be put to shame. The clearest word God ever spoke is a Person.

What does it look like to be mature in thinking? It means weighing things by Scripture rather than by how impressive they are. A child is drawn to noise and novelty; a mature believer asks what is true, what builds up, and what honours Christ. It means being able to hold a disputed question patiently, to distinguish what is central from what is secondary, and to resist being swept along by whatever is exciting this year. And it goes with innocence about evil: the mature Christian is not the one who knows the most about sin, but the one who knows the most about Christ.

On a Tuesday. Since you have been washed and made holy in Christ (6:11), guard your innocence: turn away this week from one thing you watch or read that makes you knowing about evil.
verseByVerse.note: “The Law” here means the Scriptures. In Isaiah, foreign speech — the Assyrian invaders — was a sign of judgment on those who refused to listen.

parallels.desc: by people of strange lips and with a foreign tongue the LORD will speak to this people

verseByVerse.quote: If, therefore, the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your minds? But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all,
verseByVerse.commentary:
If all speak in tongues. The whole church: perhaps the gathering of all the house churches in one place. All speaking in tongues: the chaos Paul is correcting.

And outsiders or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your minds? Paul asks them to picture their own meeting through the eyes of someone standing at the door. Someone has come, perhaps a neighbour, perhaps a husband who finally agreed to come once. He steps in, and every person in the room is speaking words he cannot understand, all at the same time. What does he conclude? Out of your minds (mainomai) means mad, raving, like the frenzy of pagan cults he knew. Not that the doctrine is false; he has not heard any doctrine. He will simply decide that these people are unhinged, and he will go home, and he will not come back. And here is the sting: he was never given the chance to reject Christ. He rejected a room. Paul assumes that unbelievers may walk into a Christian gathering, and worship should be understandable to them when they do.

The offence of the cross and the offence of a shambles. The objection is always available that the world finds the gospel foolish anyway. It does; Paul said so at 1:23. But there is a difference between the offence of the cross and the offence of a shambles, and this chapter exists to say that a church may not confuse the two. If people are put off, let it be by Christ crucified, and not by the fact that nobody explained anything.

But if all prophesy. The second scenario. It is not one gifted speaker doing the work: if all speak God’s word intelligibly, one by one (v. 31), the whole congregation is speaking words that build up, encourage and console.

He is convicted by all. Convicted (elenchō) is a courtroom word: exposed, shown his sin. It is the word Jesus used for the Spirit’s work: he will convict the world concerning sin, because they do not believe in me (John 16:8–9). So the conviction that falls on the visitor is never finally about the church’s opinions. Through the plain words of ordinary believers the Spirit brings him face to face with Jesus, and with his own refusal of him.

He is called to account by all. Called to account (anakrinō) is another: examined, searched. Nobody has singled him out; the congregation is talking about God to each other, and the truth spoken plainly does its own work on a man who came in only to keep somebody company. He came to observe and finds himself on trial, which is what always happens when the word of God is intelligible in a room (Hebrews 4:12–13).

An ordinary mechanism. Nothing here requires a special word of knowledge about the visitor. It requires a congregation plainly saying true things about God to one another, and a man who happens to be in the room. The conviction is the word’s own work, not the speaker’s insight. That is a comfort to anyone who feels evangelism requires a technique he lacks. The best thing a congregation can do for the friend it has finally persuaded to come is not to arrange something special, but to be, that Sunday, a people who mean what they say and say it in words he can follow.

Should our services be changed to suit visitors? Not their substance, but their clarity. The church must not water down the gospel, drop the hard parts of Scripture, or turn worship into entertainment to keep outsiders comfortable; that would remove the very word that converts them. But everything should be done so that a visitor can follow it: plain language, explained terms, readings he can find, and a warm welcome. Aim for a service that a believer finds deeply nourishing and a stranger finds understandable. Those two aims are not rivals; the clearest worship serves both.

On a Tuesday. Invite an unbelieving friend to church, and pray that God will speak to him through his word.

verseByVerse.quote: the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The secrets of his heart are disclosed. This is what Paul wants a service to do, and it is more ambitious than most of us expect on a Sunday. The unbeliever feels: this is about me; God knows me. Disclosed, brought into the light, and chiefly to himself. Anyone who has sat under plain preaching and felt himself described knows what this means. Nothing supernatural need be assumed about the speaker. The word of God walks into a man’s private rooms and turns on the lights, and he stops hearing about people in general and starts hearing about himself.

Falling on his face. Not nodding. Not thoughtfully agreeing. This is the posture of awe and surrender, of a man who has met something and lost his footing: the posture of Ezekiel by the river, of John on Patmos, of every person in Scripture who found himself unexpectedly in the presence of God. What brings him down is not the atmosphere of the room. It is the holiness of God pressing close, the God before whom Isaiah cried that he was lost, because his eyes had seen the King, the LORD of hosts (Isaiah 6:5).

God is really among you. This is the sentence Paul wants said about a congregation. Not these people are warm, or that was a fine argument, or they made me feel welcome, good as those are. He wants the visitor to walk out having concluded that God was in the building. The goal of worship is that outsiders recognise God’s presence: not through chaos or showmanship, but through his word convicting hearts.

The nations coming in. The words the visitor speaks are not new. Surely God is in you, and there is no other, is what Isaiah promised would one day be said by outsiders about Israel, foreigners bowing down and confessing that God was there and nowhere else (Isaiah 45:14). Zechariah foretold ten men from the nations taking hold of the robe of a Jew and saying they had heard that God was with him (Zechariah 8:23). Paul takes those promises and lays them on a house church in a Greek port. The nations coming in has begun, and it is happening in an ordinary room, one man at a time.

Immanuel in a front room. How can a visitor say truthfully that God is among a roomful of Corinthians? Because God has come among us in a Person. Immanuel, God with us, was the name given to the child (Matthew 1:23). The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). The Lord promised that where two or three are gathered in his name, there he is among them (Matthew 18:20), and since Pentecost his Spirit makes the gathered church God’s temple (3:16). So the outsider’s cry is not a compliment on the atmosphere. It is the literal truth about a congregation that meets in Jesus’ name, discovered by a man who came in a stranger.

Say something true, and let God be extraordinary. The thing most likely to convert a visitor is not the excellence of the arrangements, the music or the welcome, though none should be neglected. It is a congregation talking plainly about a God who is actually there. Corinth thought the way to impress an outsider was to show him something extraordinary. Paul says the way is to say something true, and let God be extraordinary.

What it does not mean. It does not mean prophecy is the only way unbelievers are converted. The preaching of the gospel does the same today, and the Spirit uses the plain word of Scripture in every age to lay hearts bare and bring sinners to their knees.

Does God want me to feel exposed in church? He wants you to be known, so that you can be healed. Being searched by the word can be painful: a sermon names the sin you hoped was hidden, and you feel as if everyone can see. But the purpose is never to shame you; it is to bring you to the One who already knows and has come to forgive. The visitor in this verse is not crushed and sent away. He falls down and worships. Conviction is the doorway, and on the other side is mercy. When the word finds you out, do not run; confess, and come to Christ.

Is this not just emotional manipulation? A fair question, because churches have sometimes worked up feelings with music, lighting and pressure, and called the result conviction. But look at what Paul describes. Nothing here is staged: there is no appeal, no mood, no pressure, only ordinary people speaking God’s truth plainly, one at a time. Manipulation works on the emotions by going around the mind. This works by going through the mind: the man understands what is said, and what he understands is true about him. That is why the result is not a passing thrill but worship of God. The word of God judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart (Hebrews 4:12), and it needs no help from technique.

For worship. There has never been a service anywhere that God attended reluctantly. He is the God who searches hearts, and the God who receives the sinner on his face. The woman at the well said, come, see a man who told me all that I ever did (John 4:29), and she said it not as a confession of shame but as an invitation. Christ is the one before whom every secret will be disclosed, and the one who has borne every secret sin of his people. To be found out by him is to be found by him.

parallels.desc: God is with you only
we have heard that God is with you

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–40 — Orderly Worship and Final Rules
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns the principle into rules for the meeting: tongues and prophecy in turn and in limited number, tongues only with interpretation, prophecy always weighed, and women not taking part in that weighing. He grounds it all in the God of peace and in the authority of the Lord’s command, and ends by holding eager desire and good order together.
verseByVerse.theology:
God as the Ground of Ordered Worship

Orderly worship rests on the doctrine of God: he is not a God of confusion but of peace (v. 33). Father, Son and Spirit live in eternal, loving and ordered fellowship, so worship that is chaotic misrepresents the God being worshipped, and worship that is ordered, understood and shared by all shows something of what he is like. The Reformers held this as more than a preference: they reformed worship in Geneva and Zurich from the conviction that it should reflect the character of the God it addresses.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian meeting was apparently chaotic: several tongues at once, no weighing of prophecies, and a general air of competitive display. Paul’s rules (two or three, in turn, with weighing) are not red tape but pastoral wisdom about how a church can actually benefit from the gifts God has given it. Now: Decently and in order guides every part of church life, from Sunday worship to members’ meetings to pastoral care. Order is not the suppression of the Spirit; it is the setting in which his gifts can be received and used by the whole church.

verseByVerse.quote: What then, brothers? When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. Verse 26 turns the principle of verses 1–25 into practice, and the rest of the chapter follows its rule: tongues (vv. 27–28), prophecy and its weighing (vv. 29–33), women in that weighing (vv. 34–35), and the authority behind it all (vv. 36–40). The love of chapter 13 now takes the shape of a Sunday meeting.

What then, brothers? Paul turns to practical instructions, beginning with a rare description in the New Testament of what a church meeting looked like.

Each one has. A picture of early Christian worship, with many participating. A hymn (psalmos, perhaps a psalm or a new song), a lesson (didachē, teaching), a revelation (a prophecy), a tongue, and its interpretation. Each one has: people arrived with something. It is a room of contributors, not an audience, and for all their disorder Paul does not put a stop to it. He regulates what he finds, in a single clause.

Let all things be done for building up. The rule for everything (oikodomē). Not let all things be done sincerely, or reverently, or with excellence. For building up. The phrase that has governed the whole chapter, and it is measured on other people.

The word of Christ dwelling richly. What were these hymns and lessons about? Paul answers in another letter: let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs (Colossians 3:16). The early church sang about its Lord, and some of those songs may survive in the New Testament itself (Philippians 2:6–11; Colossians 1:15–20). A Roman governor, Pliny, reported around AD 112 that Christians met before dawn on a fixed day and sang a hymn to Christ as to a god. So every contribution in that crowded room had one centre. Building up the church means building it on him, with words about him, until Christ is formed in his people (Galatians 4:19).

Where Christians differ: how should worship be ordered? Some take this verse as the model for open, participatory worship, with anyone contributing. Others hold to the regulative principle: worship should include only what God commands, led by qualified men. Brethren assemblies and many charismatic churches take the first view out of a real concern that every member should take part, and that instinct is a good one. This commentary’s view: The apostolic church had more open participation, partly because of the revelatory gifts then active. With the canon closed and those gifts ceased, the core elements of worship are those God has appointed: reading and preaching the Scriptures, prayer, singing psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, the sacraments, and giving (the Westminster Confession 21.5; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 22.5). Worship should be ordered, led by those God has called, and above all edifying. Within that, the congregation participates fully in singing, prayer and Amen.

The criterion and the format. The binding instruction here is not the format but the criterion. Paul lays down no order of service, no timings, no minimum number of contributions. He insists on one thing: that everything done should build people up. And the New Testament plainly places teaching at the centre, since it lists teachers before most other gifts (12:28) and tells Timothy to devote himself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation and to teaching (1 Timothy 4:13).

A rebuke to passivity. The picture is nonetheless a rebuke to passivity. Whatever the Sunday structure, what am I bringing? is a fair question for any Christian on the way in. It may be a conversation prepared for someone who is struggling, a burden carried into the prayers, an invitation to lunch, a heart prepared to sing and to listen. Believers come with something in their hands, and that instinct survives every difference of tradition.

What is the regulative principle? It is the conviction that God alone decides how he is to be worshipped. In ordinary life we may do whatever Scripture does not forbid; in public worship we offer what Scripture appoints. The reason is that worship is God’s, not ours to invent: Nadab and Abihu offered unauthorised fire and died (Leviticus 10:1–2), and Jesus condemned worship built on human traditions (Mark 7:7). This does not freeze every detail; the time of the service, the order of elements, the tunes and the building are matters of wisdom. But the elements themselves, reading, preaching, prayer, singing, the Lord’s Supper and baptism, giving, are what God has given, and they are enough.

On a Tuesday. On Saturday evening, read the passage to be preached if you know it, pray for one person you will see, and decide whom you will speak to after the service.

verseByVerse.quote: If any speak in a tongue, let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn, and let someone interpret. But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent in church and speak to himself and to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two or at most three. The rules, and they are strikingly specific for a man who has just affirmed the gift so warmly. A maximum number: two, or at the outside three, in one meeting, which implies that Corinth had been running many more. Not a whole service of tongues. And each in turn: one at a time, not all together, which implies they had been speaking over one another.

And let someone interpret. Always with interpretation, without which the whole thing stops. If interpretation is what makes tongues useful, a congregation should want interpreters and pray for them (v. 13). Paul’s rules are not designed to reduce the gift to nothing. They are designed to make it useful.

Keep silent in church. No interpreter, no tongue. If a person can be told to wait his turn, then he is able to wait his turn, as Paul says outright at verse 32. The Spirit does not seize people and make them speak against their will. Any claim to a spiritual experience that cannot be paused when the elder raises his hand has already been answered by this verse.

To himself and to God. Quietly, in his own heart. This is not a dismissal. The tongue-speaker without an interpreter is not told his gift is bogus; he is told where it belongs. What it may not do is take up the congregation’s time producing nothing for anybody.

Is this the room? That is a model for how a church should handle a great many things that are good in themselves and unsuited to the assembly. A believer’s favourite doctrine, his particular burden, his favourite emphasis, the experience that changed his life: none of these need be denied to be given their proper place. The question is never only is this real? The question is also is this the room?

The love of restraint. Two or three, and no more, even of a good thing the Spirit gave. A congregation’s time is finite, and somebody with something real to offer will go home without offering it. That is not a tragedy; it is what happens in a room with other people in it. Restraint of that kind is a form of love, and it has a source. Paul tells another church to look not only to their own interests but also to the interests of others, and grounds it at once in Christ, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself (Philippians 2:4–7). The One who had the most right to the floor gave it up for us. Holding back a good word for another’s sake is a small likeness of him.

What should a church do today if someone stands up and speaks in a tongue? The elders should act gently and by Paul’s own rules. A church that holds, as this commentary does, that the gift has ceased will not make room for it in its services, and will explain why kindly and privately. But even a church that allows it is bound by this chapter: no more than two or three, one at a time, always with interpretation, and silence otherwise. Whatever is said must be weighed by Scripture. And the person concerned should be treated as a brother or sister, not shamed in front of others.

On a Tuesday. Self-control is a fruit the Spirit grows in you, not a feat of willpower. In your next church meeting or Bible study, let someone else speak first, and leave one good thing unsaid if the time is better given to another.

verseByVerse.quote: Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said. If a revelation is made to another sitting there, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let two or three prophets speak. Prophecy gets the same numerical limit as tongues, and then something tongues did not get.

Weigh what is said. Weigh (diakrinō) means to sift, to evaluate, to discern. Prophecy in the Corinthian assembly was to be examined by the congregation. New Testament congregational prophecy was not automatically accepted; it had to be tested against apostolic teaching (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21; 1 John 4:1). That one instruction settles more about the nature of this gift than any definition could.

Nobody weighs Scripture. Nobody sifted Isaiah to see how much of him to keep. If a prophecy in this room was to be tested by the people listening, then this gift was not on the same footing as the written word of God, which is not weighed but obeyed. And a man who claims to speak for God in a way that places him beyond examination has misunderstood what he is claiming. Thus says the Lord, said in a manner that forbids questioning, is precisely what this verse rules out.

How is it weighed? Four questions do most of the work. Does it agree with Scripture? Anything that does not is finished at once, whatever accompanied it. Does it exalt Christ, or the speaker? Does it build up, encourage and console, which is what Paul said prophecy does (v. 3)? And what is the speaker like: is this a person whose life commends what he says? The Bible never asks anyone to accept a spiritual claim without examination, and the Berean Jews are commended precisely for checking an apostle against the Scriptures (Acts 17:11).

The spirit of prophecy. Why is it a test to ask whether a word exalts Christ? Because Christ is what prophecy was always about. The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy, the angel told John (Revelation 19:10). Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, the risen Lord interpreted to his disciples in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27), and he said the Spirit would glorify him, taking what is his and declaring it (John 16:14). So weighing a word is finally asking whether it leads to him. And there is one Prophet whose words no congregation weighs. On the mountain the Father said of him: This is my beloved Son; listen to him (Mark 9:7).

Let the first be silent. One speaker at a time: if something is given to a person sitting down, the one on his feet stops. No one has the floor by right. And the mark of a man who is truly hearing from God is that he does not mind sitting down.

One by one. Taking turns allows everyone with a word to give it, and everyone to benefit. There is the purpose again, and both halves matter. Learning without encouragement produces a congregation that is informed and flat. Encouragement without learning produces one that is cheerful and hollow. Paul asks for both from the same activity, which is a high standard and the right one.

Is there prophecy today? The gift of prophecy, like tongues, belonged to the apostolic foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20), and with the completion of Scripture it has ceased. Continuationist Christians read this very verse the other way: because congregational prophecy had to be weighed, they say, it never stood level with Scripture, and so it can continue without threatening a closed Bible. That is a serious argument, and this commentary answers it by noting that these prophets still spoke revelation (v. 30), which is what the apostolic foundation supplied once for all. That does not make this passage useless. When someone says the Lord told him something, the church still has to weigh it, and the tests are the ones Paul’s instruction implies: does it agree with Scripture, does it exalt Christ, and does it build up? An impression may be sincere and even wise, but it is never a word that binds anyone’s conscience. The voice that binds the conscience is the voice of God in Scripture.

What should I do when a Christian friend says God told him something about me? Listen graciously, and then weigh it. Thank him for caring enough to speak. Ask whether what he says agrees with Scripture and whether it is wise; talk it over with your elders or a mature believer if it matters. If it is a call to repent of something Scripture forbids, take it seriously, because it may be God’s word to you through Scripture whatever the friend calls it. If it is a claim about whom to marry, where to move, or what will happen, you are not bound by it. Your guide for life is the Bible, and you need not fear disobeying God by setting aside a word that Scripture does not give.

parallels.desc: test everything

verseByVerse.quote: and the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of confusion but of peace. As in all the churches of the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Subject to prophets. This answers the defence that has been offered ever since: I could not help it; the Spirit came on me. Paul’s answer is that the prophet is in charge of his own mouth. Prophets could control when and whether they spoke, or Paul’s rules would be unenforceable.

The Spirit’s signature. Here is how the Holy Spirit works, over against every counterfeit. The pagan oracle was possessed; the priestess at Delphi was thought to be seized by the god, and her loss of control was taken as the proof of the god’s presence. The Holy Spirit does not do that. He never overrides a person; he restores him to himself. Self-control is the last item in the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23), and a spiritual experience that removes it is not evidence of more of the Spirit but of something else altogether. The man from whom Jesus cast the legion was found sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind (Luke 8:35). That is the Holy Spirit’s signature.

Not a God of confusion. Confusion (akatastasia) is disorder, the word used of riots and political upheaval. Paul does not settle order by taste or custom but by the character of God. Worship is meant to be a true statement about the one being worshipped; a congregation in uproar is making a false one.
