Worship preaches before the sermon starts: the way a church behaves when it meets tells onlookers what its God is like. A room where everyone shouts at once says that God is restless and careless of others; a room where people listen, wait and make room for one another says that he is the God of peace (Romans 15:33).

Peace with a face. The God of peace is not an abstraction. He came in Christ, who stood up in a boat in a storm and said to the sea, Peace! Be still! (Mark 4:39), who told frightened disciples that he was leaving them his peace (John 14:27), and who made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). The peace of a well-ordered gathering is a small echo of that greater peace. People reconciled to God through his Son can wait their turn, sit down when another rises and listen without fear, because the deepest confusion of all, war with God, has been ended.

Peace is not the same as quiet. This sentence has been used to smother things it was never aimed at. Order is not the same as predictability. A church can be so orderly that nothing ever happens in it, where no one would weep, or stay behind, or say anything not on the sheet. That congregation has not obeyed this verse; it has merely avoided the problem it addresses. Paul is regulating a fire, not a filing cabinet, and he ends the chapter by forbidding them to put the fire out (v. 39).

As in all the churches of the saints. This phrase may end the sentence about God’s peace, or begin the next about women, as the ESV takes it. Either way, Corinth is reminded that it is not the only congregation in the world, and that its practice is not its own invention.

But what about when people in the Bible were overwhelmed by God? They were often overwhelmed in awe: Isaiah cried woe is me, John fell at Christ’s feet as though dead (Revelation 1:17). But they were never turned into puppets. Isaiah answered here I am, send me; John was raised up and told to write, and he wrote clearly. Being deeply moved by God is right and good, and tears in worship are no disorder. What Paul rules out is the claim that the Spirit makes a person act against his own control and against the order of the church. The Spirit humbles us, but he never dehumanises us.

verseByVerse.quote: the women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says. If there is anything they desire to learn, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women should keep silent in the churches. Few passages in the Bible are harder. The difficulty is not the culture. It is Paul. Three chapters ago he regulated how women should be dressed when they pray and prophesy in the assembly (11:5), and he did not object to their doing it. A man does not give guidance for how women should pray aloud in church and then forbid them to open their mouths. So this cannot be total silence, and any reading that makes it the flat opposite of 11:5 has gone wrong somewhere.

Look where these verses sit. The context is the weighing of prophecies (v. 29). That weighing was a public, judicial act: the assembly sitting in judgement on what had been said, testing a claim to speak for God. Women should not take part in that public judging and questioning, which carried teaching authority over the congregation.

As the Law also says. No single verse is quoted. Most likely Paul means the order of creation in Genesis 2, which he cites elsewhere for the same principle (11:8–9; 1 Timothy 2:13), and which stands in the Law in the sense of the five books of Moses. The principle is headship, not culture alone. Headship means the responsibility God gives a man to lead, protect and serve in love, as Christ leads his church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:23–25). It is a calling to responsibility, not a claim to greater worth.

Ask their husbands at home. And look at what verse 35 regulates: asking questions. The instruction is not addressed to praying or prophesying at all; it is addressed to the cross-examination and questioning that went with the weighing. Wives questioning or challenging prophets, perhaps their own husbands, in public would undermine order and headship. Paul directs their questions to the home, assuming women should learn. And the practical setting fits the ancient room, where most women had far less schooling than the men, and where an honest question called across a courtyard could stop the meeting. So when Paul adds that it is shameful for a woman to speak in church, speak carries the sense of the public judging and questioning just described.

Four readings. Interpreters have offered four. Some have taken it as a universal ban on women speaking in church; that founders on 11:5, and also on the fact that Christians who hold it do not actually apply it: the women in such congregations sing, confess the creed, and answer Amen. Some have suggested the two verses were not written by Paul at all, noting that a few manuscripts place them after verse 40. That displacement is real and worth knowing, but every manuscript we possess contains the verses somewhere, so they cannot simply be removed. Some read verses 34 and 35 as a Corinthian slogan that Paul quotes in order to demolish it in verse 36. It is an ingenious reading, but the letter gives no signal that a quotation has begun, and verse 37 calls what he is writing the Lord’s command. The reading that fits the passage best takes it from its own context, in the paragraph about weighing prophecy.

Where Christians differ: women’s silence. Some take this as an absolute ban on women speaking at all in church. Others say it was a cultural rule for disruptive Corinthian women and no longer applies, or even that it was not written by Paul. Many who take these views are egalitarians (Christians who hold that every ministry in the church is open to men and women alike), and they hold them out of love for Scripture and a sincere wish to honour the women God has gifted, like those who prayed, prophesied and laboured beside Paul. This commentary’s view: The verses are in all the manuscripts, though a few move them after verse 40. Since Paul allows women to pray and prophesy (11:5), this is not a ban on all speech, but on women taking the role of authoritatively judging prophecy and teaching in the gathered church, which belongs to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:11–12). This is the complementarian position. Women may sing, pray, testify, and serve in countless ways. The principle is grounded in creation, not merely culture.

Read that way, the two passages agree. A woman may pray and prophesy in the assembly (11:5). She is not to exercise the congregation’s governing judgement over the church’s teaching. That judgement belongs to the same ordering of men and women that Paul roots in creation elsewhere (1 Timothy 2:12). This commentary holds this reading because it lets 11:5, 14:29 and 1 Timothy 2:12 all stand as written. Egalitarian brothers and sisters who read the passage otherwise deserve to be heard with respect, not suspected of setting Scripture aside, and the two sides share far more than divides them: the same Saviour, the same Bible, and the same concern that no woman be silenced by cruelty.

What does this mean for a church today? The restriction concerns the authoritative teaching and judging of doctrine in the gathered church, which Paul elsewhere reserves to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12). It does not forbid women to pray aloud, read Scripture, sing, give testimony, teach other women and children (Titus 2:3–5), or speak in a members’ meeting. And since prophecy has ceased, the part women once played in praying and prophesying (11:5) is now their full share in the church’s prayer and praise.

And women with no husband to ask? Paul’s point is to keep the meeting orderly, not to keep women from learning. A single woman, a widow or a wife whose husband does not believe should be taught by the elders and by other mature believers, as every member should. Many churches give opportunity for questions after the service or in classes, and that fits Paul’s concern exactly.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women are less intelligent or spiritual, or that their questions are unwelcome. Paul wants them to learn. The same apostle wrote that in Christ there is neither male nor female (Galatians 3:28), greeted Junia as well known to the apostles (Romans 16:7), and honoured Priscilla, Phoebe, Euodia and Syntyche for their labour alongside him (Romans 16:1–4; Philippians 4:2–3). Equal in worth and in Christ; different in calling within the church and the home.

A misuse to refuse. This passage has been used to shame women into silence far beyond anything Paul wrote, and that misuse has done real damage. A congregation where women are afraid to speak at all has not obeyed this text; it has ignored chapter 11. And headship in Scripture is never a licence for control. It is the self-giving love of Christ for his church (Ephesians 5:25). A husband who uses this verse to belittle or dominate his wife has turned it upside down, and abuse is never to be tolerated or covered in the name of submission.

Why would God give men and women different roles if they are equal? Because difference is not inequality, and the Trinity shows it. The Son is fully equal with the Father, yet in the work of salvation he gladly does the Father’s will (11:3; John 6:38). Ordered roles among equals are not a scar on creation but part of its beauty. God made man and woman both in his image (Genesis 1:27), and he gave them to each other as partners with different callings, so that the home and the church might picture Christ and his bride. The man is called to lead by laying down his life, the woman to honour that leadership freely, and both to serve. Where this is lived in love, it is not a cage but a dance.

On a Tuesday. Husbands, be ready to discuss Scripture with your wives at home. Make your home a place of learning together: ask your wife what she took from Sunday’s sermon, and listen. Sisters, ask your questions, and do not let anyone tell you that your understanding of God does not matter; it matters to him.

For worship. The Lord Jesus let Mary of Bethany sit at his feet and listen to his teaching, and when her sister complained he would not send her back to the serving: she had chosen the good portion (Luke 10:39–42). He opened the deepest truths about worship to a Samaritan woman at a well (John 4:21–24), and on the morning of his resurrection he sent a woman to tell his brothers that he was alive (John 20:17–18). The Lord who orders his church cherishes every daughter in it as an heir with her brothers of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7). He is the Teacher who has never once turned away a woman who wanted to learn.
verseByVerse.note: Paul has already assumed that women pray and prophesy in worship (11:5). Interpreters differ on what speaking is forbidden here; many take it as the public judging of prophecies just mentioned (v. 29).

verseByVerse.quote: Or was it from you that the word of God came? Or are you the only ones it has reached?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or was it from you that the word of God came? Two questions, dripping with irony, and they are the sting in the tail of the whole chapter. This verse tells us what Paul thought the Corinthians’ real problem was. It was not tongues. It was independence. Behind every fault in this letter lies a congregation that had come to believe it was the centre of things: that its practices were its own to invent, its judgements its own to make, and its founder’s instructions a matter for consideration.

Or are you the only ones it has reached? Did the gospel start here? Are you the only place it has got to? Both answers are humiliating and both are obvious. The word of God came to Corinth from somewhere else, brought by a man who had received it himself, and it had already reached a great many other cities where the churches did not do what Corinth was doing. They were one church among many, receiving the same word, and must follow the same practice. The link with verse 33 is exact: as in all the churches of the saints, and now, are you the only ones? Paul is placing this congregation back among its peers. Whatever they had concluded about worship, they had concluded it alone, and that alone was a warning sign.

The word has a source. The answer to Paul’s first question is that the word of God came from Christ. The risen Lord told his apostles that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47), and Paul insists that what he delivered to Corinth he had first received (15:3), not from any man but through a revelation of Jesus Christ (Galatians 1:12). So a church that treats the apostolic word as its own to revise is not merely proud. It is putting itself in the place of the Lord who spoke it. Every congregation stands at the far end of a line that begins with him, and its freedom is the freedom of a receiver.

Novelty is worth examining. Paul’s question is not an argument for mere conformity. Truth is not decided by counting congregations, and there have been moments, the Reformation among them, when a few were right and the many were wrong. But a church that finds itself doing something no other body of Christians anywhere has thought necessary should at least ask whether the Spirit really has told it alone. The same Spirit is at work in the church in the next town, and in the churches of the last twenty centuries.

Private certainty. There is a humility in this for individuals too. The believer convinced that he has seen something in Scripture that the whole church has missed is occasionally right and is usually a man who has been reading alone for too long. Paul’s questions are worth asking of any private certainty: did this begin with me, and am I the only one it has reached?

How do I tell faithful conviction from mere novelty? Ask three questions. First, does Scripture plainly teach it, read in context, or am I building on one verse? Second, have faithful Christians in other times and places, people who loved the Bible as much as I do, seen it too? The creeds and confessions are a great help here. Third, would my elders and wise believers in my church recognise it, or am I hiding it from them? Not every old view is right, and not every new insight is wrong. But a conviction that cannot be found in Scripture plainly, has no friends in church history and must be kept from the church’s leaders deserves deep suspicion.

For worship. The word of God came to Corinth. Somebody carried it over land and sea to a city with a bad reputation and no interest in it, and Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord together with his entire household, and many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptised (Acts 18:8). Nobody in that congregation had generated a word of it, and no Christian since has either. There is no self-made believer. Every one of us stands somewhere downstream of an empty tomb, reached by a word that was running toward us before we were born, sent by the Father, bought by the Son and carried by the Spirit. We did not invent it. We received it, and that is grace.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks that he is a prophet, or spiritual, he should acknowledge that the things I am writing to you are a command of the Lord. If anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone thinks he is a prophet. Paul supplies the test he knew would be needed, for those most confident of their own spirituality would be the ones to object.

A command of the Lord. So he sets a trap and states it openly. Do you consider yourself a prophet? Do you consider yourself spiritual? Then here is how that claim is checked: you will recognise that what I am writing is the Lord’s command. Any spirituality that arrives at a different conclusion from apostolic instruction has failed at the only point where it could ever have been tested. A true prophet will recognise apostolic authority, and any prophecy that contradicts the apostle is false.

A large claim about this letter. Paul does not present these chapters as his best judgement, his temperament, or a policy for a difficult congregation. He calls them a command of the Lord. That is the apostolic authority the whole New Testament rests on: not that these men were wise, but that they were sent, and that what they wrote to the churches carries the weight of the one who sent them. The Lord here is Jesus, and it was he who told his apostles that whoever receives the one he sends receives him (John 13:20). To refuse Paul’s instructions on worship is to refuse Christ’s. A sceptic may hear in this a leader’s bid for power. But the man who writes it had been beaten, imprisoned and left hungry for this word (2 Corinthians 11:23–27), and he puts himself under it as fully as he puts Corinth: if even he, or an angel from heaven, preached a different gospel, he says, let him be accursed (Galatians 1:8). Paul is not claiming that the word belongs to him. He is insisting that he belongs to the word. Peter already counted Paul’s letters with the other Scriptures (2 Peter 3:15–16). This shows that the apostolic writings, now our New Testament, stand above all claimed revelation.

He is not recognised. Short and cold. Not recognised by God, or by the church as a true prophet. The manuscripts vary slightly here between he is not recognised and let him not be recognised (the KJV’s let him be ignorant follows the second), and either way the man is outside the circle he was claiming to lead. He wanted to be acknowledged as a prophet, and he is not acknowledged at all.

A self-refuting claim. The principle settles the commonest form of spiritual manipulation. Whenever anyone claims an authority, an insight or an experience that places him above correction from Scripture, this verse answers him. The claim refutes itself. A genuine work of the Spirit will always submit to the word the Spirit gave; the test is not whether a man sounds spiritual, but what he does when the Bible contradicts him.

How do I run this test on myself? Everyone has a place where Scripture cuts across something he wants: a grudge, a habit, a plan, an opinion held for thirty years. The question is what happens in that moment. A man who reaches for a reason why the passage does not quite apply to his own case has just learned something about the real source of his convictions, whatever else he believes about the Bible. And there is mercy in Paul’s verb. He says the spiritual man should acknowledge this, should come to see it, the way one recognises a face. He does not say he will agree at once, or without a struggle. Recognition can take a while. Bring your struggle to God honestly and keep reading until you bow.

On a Tuesday. Name one place where the Bible is currently cutting across your will, and pray today for the grace to yield. None of us bows perfectly, but Christ bowed perfectly in your place (Romans 5:19), and his Spirit works in you to will and to work (Philippians 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: So, my brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But all things should be done decently and in order.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Earnestly desire to prophesy. Two commands and a governing principle, and their balance is the point. Earnestly desire is the verb Paul opened with. After a chapter of regulation he does not want a subdued church but one hungry for the gift that builds people up.

Do not forbid. That is a command, and it is placed exactly where a lesser writer would have put a ban. Tongues, rightly used with interpretation, were a genuine gift then. Having restricted the practice, he forbids the church to forbid it. He knows what happens when a congregation is corrected about an excess: it swings, and the next generation treats the thing as an embarrassment.

Decently and in order. Two expressions, one from the drawing room and one from the parade ground. Decently (euschēmonōs) is fittingly, beautifully, with dignity. In order (kata taxin) is in proper order, like soldiers in ranks. The final word on worship. It is often quoted by people who want a quiet church, but verse 39 stands in front of it. Order is what Paul wants around the fire, not instead of it.

Where Christians differ: does do not forbid tongues apply today? Continuationists argue that churches today must not forbid tongues, since the command stands in Scripture with no stated end, and they take it as seriously as any other. This commentary’s view: Paul’s command applied when the gift was active. If the revelatory and sign gifts have ceased with the apostolic age, as this commentary holds because they confirmed the apostles’ once-for-all foundation (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 2:3–4), the question is whether present-day phenomena are the same gift. Cessationists believe they are not. Churches should neither mock nor exclude continuationist believers, and all should agree on the principles here: everything must be understood, edifying, tested by Scripture, orderly, and done in love.

How does a church that believes tongues have ceased obey this command? By recognising that Paul was protecting a gift then active, and by holding the conclusion that it has ceased with humility rather than scorn. Even for those who conclude, as is argued here, that the sign gifts belonged to the apostolic foundation, this sentence should temper the way the conviction is held. The instinct to shut down anything that cannot be controlled is not a Christian virtue, and it is not what this apostle did with a church that had abused almost every gift it had. He regulated, and then he protected. In practice, elders should test any claim to tongues by Paul’s own rules in this chapter: speakers in turn, never more than two or three, always with interpretation, and silence otherwise (vv. 27–28). And earnestly desire to prophesy is obeyed today by longing for the clear, Spirit-given proclamation of the word that builds the church up.

In the flow. Verses 39 and 40 gather up the chapter in two lines: verse 39 repeats its opening call (v. 1), and verse 40 sums up its rules (vv. 26–35). They also close the whole answer about spiritual gifts that began at 12:1. And they clear the ground for the next chapter, where Paul turns from how the church speaks to what it must always say, the gospel of first importance: Christ died for our sins, was buried and was raised (15:3–4). Orderly, understandable worship exists so that this message can be heard.

The fire and the grate. That is the balance the whole chapter has been holding: a church that is neither chaotic nor cold, where the Spirit’s work is wanted and not feared, where what happens can be understood by a stranger at the back, and where every single thing is measured by whether anybody was built up. Corinth had the fire and no grate. Many congregations since have had a beautiful grate and no fire.

Order around a miracle. Fire and order were never at odds in the Lord himself. When five thousand hungry people were on a hillside and he was about to feed them from five loaves, he first had them sit down in groups on the green grass, by hundreds and by fifties (Mark 6:39–40). Then the bread was blessed, broken and given out, everyone ate and was satisfied, and the leftovers were gathered up. Power and order, abundance and arrangement, in the same afternoon. That is the shape Paul wants for every gathering: life and order together, because both come from the same Lord, who still feeds his people through his word.

How can a cessationist church keep from becoming cold? By remembering that cessationism concerns certain gifts, not the Spirit himself. The Spirit is as present and powerful in the church today as at Pentecost: he convicts, regenerates, comforts, sanctifies, and makes the word come alive. A cessationist church has every reason to be warm, because it believes the Spirit speaks fully and sufficiently in Scripture. Pray for his blessing on the preaching, expect conversions, sing with heart and mind, and love one another fervently. The great revivals under Whitefield and Edwards, and the preaching of Spurgeon, came through men who looked for no new revelation, and they were not cold.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your church’s gatherings this Sunday: for the preacher to be clear and full of the Spirit, for the singing to be heartfelt and true, for visitors to understand, and for everything to be done in love. Then come with your own heart prepared, as part of the answer to that prayer.

For worship. Underneath it all is the God of verse 33: not a God of confusion but of peace, whose own life is perfect order and perfect love at once, who has never had to choose between liveliness and dignity. He gave gifts to men when Christ ascended on high (Ephesians 4:8–13), so that a room full of ordinary people might be built up into something that will last after every tongue has fallen silent. And on the last day the whole redeemed creation will worship him in perfect order and unbounded joy, ten thousand times ten thousand, every voice distinct and every voice one, crying that the Lamb who was slain is worthy (Revelation 5:11–12).

14.text: <sup>1</sup>Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy.<sup>2</sup>For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God; for no one understands him, but he utters mysteries in the Spirit.<sup>3</sup>On the other hand, the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation.<sup>4</sup>The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself, but the one who prophesies builds up the church.<sup>5</sup>Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy. The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets, so that the church may be built up.<sup>6</sup>Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?<sup>7</sup>If even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp, do not give distinct notes, how will anyone know what is played?<sup>8</sup>And if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle?<sup>9</sup>So with yourselves, if with your tongue you utter speech that is not intelligible, how will anyone know what is said? For you will be speaking into the air.<sup>10</sup>There are doubtless many different languages in the world, and none is without meaning,<sup>11</sup>but if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker and the speaker a foreigner to me.<sup>12</sup>So with yourselves, since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive to excel in building up the church.<sup>13</sup>Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret.<sup>14</sup>For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful.<sup>15</sup>What am I to do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also.<sup>16</sup>Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit, how can anyone in the position of an outsider say “Amen” to your thanksgiving when he does not know what you are saying?<sup>17</sup>For you may be giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not being built up.<sup>18</sup>I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you.<sup>19</sup>Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.<sup>20</sup>Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature.<sup>21</sup>In the Law it is written, “By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.”<sup>22</sup>Thus tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, while prophecy is a sign not for unbelievers but for believers.<sup>23</sup>If, therefore, the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your minds?<sup>24</sup>But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all,<sup>25</sup>the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you.<sup>26</sup>What then, brothers? When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up.<sup>27</sup>If any speak in a tongue, let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn, and let someone interpret.<sup>28</sup>But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent in church and speak to himself and to God.<sup>29</sup>Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said.<sup>30</sup>If a revelation is made to another sitting there, let the first be silent.<sup>31</sup>For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged,<sup>32</sup>and the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets.<sup>33</sup>For God is not a God of confusion but of peace. As in all the churches of the saints,<sup>34</sup>the women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says.<sup>35</sup>If there is anything they desire to learn, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.<sup>36</sup>Or was it from you that the word of God came? Or are you the only ones it has reached?<sup>37</sup>If anyone thinks that he is a prophet, or spiritual, he should acknowledge that the things I am writing to you are a command of the Lord.<sup>38</sup>If anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized.<sup>39</sup>So, my brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.<sup>40</sup>But all things should be done decently and in order.

15.title: The Resurrection of the Dead
15.overview:
Some in Corinth were saying there is no resurrection of the dead. That fitted Greek thinking well. Many Greeks regarded the body as a prison for the soul; a philosophical pun called the body (sōma) a tomb (sēma). Salvation meant the soul escaping, not the corpse rising, and the Athenians laughed when Paul spoke of resurrection (Acts 17:32). In one of Aeschylus’ tragedies the god Apollo says that once a man has died and the dust has soaked up his blood, there is no rising again. The Corinthians probably still believed in Christ’s resurrection and in some spiritual life after death, but not in the raising of their own bodies.

Paul answers in four stages: the facts of the gospel and its witnesses; what follows if the dead are not raised; God’s plan, with Christ the firstfruits and the last Adam reigning until death is destroyed; and the resurrection body, sown like a seed and raised in power. It ends at the last trumpet, with death swallowed up in victory and labour in the Lord never in vain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Resurrection of Christ: The Apostolic Testimony
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reminds the Corinthians of the gospel they received and stand in: the early creed of Christ’s death for our sins, his burial, his rising on the third day, and the list of those who saw him, ending with Paul himself, the least of the apostles and what he is by the grace of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection as the Foundation of Salvation

The creed Paul hands on is among the earliest Christian statements we have; he received it before he wrote the letter. Both the death and the rising are in accordance with the Scriptures, with Psalm 16:10, Isaiah 53 and Hosea 6:2 the likeliest passages in view. The two belong together. The resurrection is not an isolated miracle but God’s vindication of the atoning death. Without the resurrection the death has no declared meaning; without the death the resurrection has no saving content. Together they are the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: When Paul spoke of the resurrection at Athens, some mocked and some wanted to hear more (Acts 17:32), the usual Greek reaction. In the Platonic tradition a raised body was not an upgrade but a step back into the very thing the soul hoped to escape, and Paul argues straight against that instinct. Now: Today the objection is usually put in scientific terms: dead bodies do not rise. Paul’s answer is the same as then, the witnesses. The question is not whether bodies normally rise but whether this body, on this morning, was raised by the God who made bodies in the first place.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I would remind you, brothers, of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, in which you stand, and by which you are being saved, if you hold fast to the word I preached to you—unless you believed in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 15 is the Bible’s fullest teaching on the resurrection. Some in Corinth, shaped by Greek thought that saw the body as worthless, denied that believers will be raised bodily. Paul answers in five movements. The gospel rests on Christ’s bodily resurrection, attested by Scripture and by hundreds of eyewitnesses (vv. 1–11). If the dead are not raised, faith is empty and sins unforgiven (vv. 12–19). But Christ has been raised, the firstfruits; as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive, and he reigns until death itself is destroyed (vv. 20–28). The hope explains how believers live and risk (vv. 29–34). The resurrection body will be the same person transformed, like a seed and its plant, bearing the image of the last Adam (vv. 35–49). At the last trumpet death is swallowed up in victory, so labour in the Lord is not in vain (vv. 50–58).

The setting. Some at Corinth were denying the future resurrection of the dead (v. 12). Greeks generally believed the soul might survive, but bodily resurrection seemed absurd; when Paul spoke of it at Athens, some mocked (Acts 17:32). Some Corinthians may also have thought that they had already been raised spiritually and needed nothing more (4:8; 2 Timothy 2:18). Fourteen chapters of correction are behind Paul now: factions, immorality, lawsuits, marriage, idol meat, head coverings, the Supper, the gifts. Here he turns to the thing all of it rests on, and his tone changes completely.

I would remind you. Remind (gnōrizō) is to make known again. The foundation of this whole chapter is material they already had and had stopped standing on. The Corinthians were not short of information; they had been taught by Paul for eighteen months (Acts 18:11) and by Apollos after him. What they needed was for somebody to walk them back to the first thing and make them look at it again. Very little of what steadies a believer in a hard year is new to him. It is the old thing, remembered at the right moment, by someone who troubled to say it again.

Which you received, in which you stand. Four verbs in this sentence, and together they are a small map of the Christian life. The gospel was preached: it came from outside, as news; nobody worked it out. It was received: taken by faith, as a gift is taken, which is the only posture available to a man being given something. It is what they stand in: the present tense of it, the ground under their feet, and Paul chooses that verb for a congregation that had been standing on its gifts, its wisdom and its teachers. And by it they are being saved, a present continuous: salvation is not only something that happened at a meeting years ago but something still going on, to be completed in the resurrection. So God forgave and accepted them the day they believed, and that is settled for ever (Romans 5:1); but he is still at work rescuing them from sin’s grip day by day, and one day he will rescue their bodies from death itself (Romans 8:23).

The gospel is a person. What the Corinthians received was not first a set of ideas but Christ himself. Paul says it in another letter in exactly these terms: as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him (Colossians 2:6). The ground they stand on is not their grasp of a doctrine but a finished work, his death and his rising (vv. 3–4), as solid as an empty tomb. And the One by whom they are being saved is alive to finish it: he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25). Every tense of salvation in this verse has the same subject. He saved, he holds, he will complete.

If you hold fast. Hold fast (katechō) is to keep a firm grip. In vain (eikē) is without cause, without result. The clause can badly frighten a Christian troubled about his own perseverance, so read what Paul actually says. He does not say you will lose what you have if you slip. He raises the possibility that some of them believed in vain: a profession that never had anything living in it. If the resurrection were false, their believing would be pointless; and if they let go of this gospel, they would show their faith was empty. That is a different thing from a believer falling out of God’s hand, which this apostle elsewhere says is impossible (Romans 8:38–39).

Holding fast is evidence, not cause. In the New Testament, holding fast is not the cause of being kept; it is the evidence of it. The people God keeps are the people who keep going, and he keeps them by making them keep going. So this clause is not a threat held over a frightened Christian; it is a question put to a comfortable one. And it has a searching form: not do you remember believing? but are you still holding on? The mark of a real faith is not the vividness of its beginning but the fact that it is still there (Colossians 1:23; Hebrews 3:14).

I am afraid I might not hold on. What then? The fear itself is a good sign. People who have truly let go of Christ are rarely troubled about it. Your holding on is not a matter of gritting your teeth; it is a matter of looking at Christ, and he holds you far more firmly than you hold him. No one will snatch his sheep out of his hand (John 10:28–29). So when you feel your grip weakening, do not stare at your grip. Go back to the gospel in verses 3 and 4, read it, pray it, and take the Lord’s Supper with his people. Faith is strengthened by being fed, and its food is Christ.

For worship. We did not find the gospel; it found us. God sent it across seas and centuries until it reached our door, and then he opened our hearts to receive it. He set our feet on his Son, and the ground has never moved: a cross that has been borne, a tomb that stays empty. Blessed be the God who keeps those who hold fast, by holding them.
verseByVerse.note: Some at Corinth were denying the future resurrection of the body; most Greeks thought the body was left behind at death.

verseByVerse.quote: For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Delivered and received. Two words here are worth more than they look. Received and delivered are the standard vocabulary for handing on a fixed tradition, word for word, without adjustment: the same pair Paul used of the Lord’s Supper at 11:23. Paul is not composing here. He is reciting something he was given, and it stands at the very heart of the gospel.

How early is this creed? That matters more for the historical question than almost anything else in the New Testament. Paul is writing a little over twenty years after the crucifixion, around AD 54. But he did not invent this formula; he received it, which means it was already in circulation and already fixed when he was taught it, most likely in his first years as a Christian, perhaps when he spent two weeks with Peter in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:18), within a very few years of the event. This is not a legend that grew over generations. It is a summary that was being recited by Christians while many who had seen these things were still alive. Now the clauses, and each is load-bearing.

Christ died for our sins. The little word for (hyper, on behalf of) means on our account, and with Isaiah 53 standing behind the whole creed it carries substitution: in our place. Sin is a real offence against a holy God, and its just sentence is death (Romans 6:23); God does not pretend it away. So the Son took the sentence himself, and the punishment that brought us peace fell on him (Isaiah 53:5). A death without that word for is a tragedy; with it, it is an exchange.

In accordance with the Scriptures. The phrase appears twice, once for the death and once for the rising: this was not an emergency. Isaiah had described a servant pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, who would see his offspring and prolong his days after making his soul an offering for guilt (Isaiah 53:5–12). The plan is older than the crime.

He was buried. The oddest item on the list. Why include it in a summary this compressed? Two reasons. It settles that he was actually dead: there was a body, and men carried it, and it was heavy. And it means the resurrection was bodily: the body placed in the tomb was the body raised, leaving the tomb empty. A burial means a tomb, and a tomb has an address, and Jerusalem is a small city. The claim was placed where it could be checked.

Raised on the third day. Note the passive. Was raised (egēgertai) is perfect tense: God raised him, and he remains raised. The resurrection is the Father acting on the Son, his answer to the cross and his verdict on it. On the third day: a specific, historical date, counted the way the ancient world counted, where any part of a day was a day. Jesus died on Friday afternoon, lay in the tomb through Saturday, and rose early on Sunday. The three days and three nights of the Jonah sign (Matthew 12:40) is the same span in a common Jewish idiom, not a stopwatch.

In accordance with the Scriptures. The rising too was foretold. The psalmist had said God would not let his Holy One see corruption (Psalm 16:10), which Peter preached at Pentecost (Acts 2:27). The servant of Isaiah, after his death, would see his offspring and prolong his days (Isaiah 53:10–12). Hosea had spoken of God raising his people up on the third day (Hosea 6:2), and Jesus himself pointed to the sign of Jonah (Matthew 12:40).

Where Christians differ: the meaning of Christ’s death. Some see Christ’s death mainly as an example of love, or as a victory over evil powers, and reject the idea that he bore the punishment for sins. This commentary’s view: Christ died for our sins. Scripture presents his death as many things, including example and victory, but at its heart it is penal substitution: he stood in our place, bearing the penalty of God’s just wrath against our sins, so that we might be forgiven and declared righteous (Isaiah 53:5–6; Romans 3:25–26; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13). This is of first importance.

Why is the gospel news rather than advice? Because it tells what God has done, not what you must do to reach him. Advice says: try harder, and you may get there. News says: it has been done; believe it. Most religions finally offer a kind of advice. The Christian gospel is a report of three events, a death, a burial and a resurrection, and an announcement of what they mean: your sins can be forgiven, because Christ has borne them. The commands of the Christian life are real, but they follow the news. You do not obey in order to be accepted; you obey because in Christ you have been.

On a Tuesday. Learn these two verses by heart this week, so that you can say the gospel to anyone in a breath, and then say it to one person who needs to hear it.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 3–5 are an early summary of the faith that Paul had received — within a few years of the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And that he appeared to Cephas. The witness list begins, and it begins with a scandal. Cephas is Peter, and the last thing the reader knows about Peter is that he stood by a fire in a courtyard and swore three times that he had never met the man. All four Gospels record it. And he is first on the list. Luke preserves the same detail: when the two from Emmaus got back to Jerusalem, the others told them the Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon (Luke 24:34). Nobody records what was said in that meeting, which is a mercy; some conversations are not for publication. But the fact of it is here, in one of the earliest Christian creeds we possess: the first apostle the risen Christ went to was the man who had denied him.

Tell his disciples and Peter. The angel at the tomb had already signalled it. Go, tell his disciples and Peter (Mark 16:7), and those two extra words are the gospel in miniature. Peter had disqualified himself and would have said so. Somebody made sure his name was spoken separately, in case he assumed the message was for the others and not for him. On the shore of Galilee the restoration was completed, three questions for three denials, and a commission: feed my sheep (John 21:15–17).

Then to the twelve. A careful reader stops, because at that point there were not twelve. Judas was dead, and Thomas was absent from the first appearance (John 20:19–29). The answer is that the Twelve had become a title rather than a headcount, the way a regiment keeps its number after a bad year. John uses it the same way, calling Thomas one of the twelve (John 20:24). The apostolic group as a whole saw him.

A rough edge that rings true. A man polishing a story would hardly leave a countable discrepancy in the second line of his creed. He writes the eleven, as Luke does when he is being precise (Luke 24:33). The rough edge is the mark of a formula in use among people who were there and knew perfectly well what it meant.

Could the disciples have been mistaken or deceived? Consider what the alternatives require. Hallucinations are private experiences; they do not happen to groups in the same form, and they do not eat fish or invite touch. A stolen body would not explain why the men who knew where it was went to their deaths saying he was alive. Legend takes generations to grow, and this creed was fixed within a few years. And the disciples were not expecting a resurrection; they were hiding behind locked doors. Something turned frightened men into bold witnesses within weeks, in the very city where he was buried, where anyone could have produced a body if there was one. The simplest explanation is the one they gave: he appeared to them.

For worship. He did not go to the Sanhedrin, or to Pilate, or to the crowd. He went back to his friends, and the first name on the list is the one who had let him down worst. If you have failed him, he still comes to you. The risen Christ does not begin with the loyal. He begins with the man who has to be told twice that he is still wanted, and he goes and finds him first. Such is the Shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine, and such is the love that rose from the dead.
verseByVerse.note: Cephas is Peter. “The twelve” was the title of the group even when only eleven were present.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
More than five hundred. A mass appearance, perhaps the meeting on the mountain in Galilee (Matthew 28:16–17), though Scripture does not say where it happened. It is recorded nowhere else in the New Testament, which is itself striking: Paul knows more than the Gospels chose to write down.

Most of whom are still alive. That is not a devotional remark. It is an invitation. Many of the five hundred could still be questioned when Paul wrote, more than twenty years later, and the letter was going to a port city with constant traffic to Palestine. Paul is in effect saying: several hundred people saw this at once, and you may go and ask them. A man inventing a story would hardly point to a crowd of living witnesses. He would locate his miracle somewhere quieter.

Fallen asleep. This is the Christian word for believers’ death: the body lies down for a while, and there will be a waking at the resurrection.

Then he appeared to James. This is James the brother of the Lord, who ended up leading the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13–21; Galatians 1:19; 2:9) and, according to early Jewish and Christian sources, was stoned to death around AD 62. The Gospels record, without embarrassment, what he thought before that: not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5), and his family once went out to seize Jesus, saying he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21). Nobody is harder to convince that a man is the Son of God than the brother who grew up in the same house and watched him be an ordinary older brother for some thirty years. James went from that to leading the mother church and dying rather than take it back, and this verse is the whole explanation. The brother who once thought him mad would open his letter by calling himself a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ (James 1:1).

Then to all the apostles. Perhaps at the ascension (Acts 1:3–9), including a wider group beyond the Twelve.

He showed himself. None of these witnesses went looking for the risen Christ and found him. In every case he came to them: he presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days (Acts 1:3), to the crowd on the hillside and to one sceptical brother in private. The evidence for the resurrection is, at bottom, the risen Jesus deciding to be seen.

Why are the women not on the list? One thing the list does not contain is worth explaining, since a modern reader will notice it. All four Gospels say the women found the tomb empty, and Matthew and John record that they were the first to see him (Matthew 28:9; John 20:14–18). Paul is assembling something like a legal brief, and in that world a woman’s testimony carried little weight in a court, which is precisely why the fact that the Gospels kept the women in is such powerful evidence of honesty. Nobody constructing a case puts his least admissible witnesses at the front. They did it because that is what happened. And the Lord himself chose a weeping woman, Mary Magdalene, to be the first to see him and to carry the news to the apostles.

Where Christians differ: soul sleep. Some take fallen asleep to mean that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. This commentary’s view: Sleep describes the appearance of the body in death and the certainty of waking. But Scripture teaches that the souls of believers go immediately into the presence of Christ, conscious and at rest, awaiting the resurrection of the body (Luke 23:43; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23; Revelation 6:9–11; Westminster Confession 32.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1).

Where are my Christian loved ones now? With Christ, consciously and gladly. When a believer dies, his soul goes at once to be with the Lord, which Paul calls far better (Philippians 1:23). There is no waiting room of unconsciousness and no purgatory of cleansing; Christ’s blood has cleansed them fully. They are at rest, free from sin and pain, in the presence of Jesus. Their bodies, meanwhile, rest in the grave, still united to Christ, waiting for the resurrection. So you grieve the parting, but you do not grieve as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). They are more alive now than they ever were with you.

On a Tuesday. When someone asks why you believe, start where Paul starts: with the people who saw him, among them a brother who once thought him mad. And pray for the sceptic in your own family; the risen Christ still changes the hardest hearts by showing himself alive.
verseByVerse.note: Many of the five hundred could still be questioned when Paul wrote. James is the Lord’s brother, who had not believed during Jesus’ ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Last of all. The resurrection appearances ended with Paul.

One untimely born. The word (ektrōma) is blunt in Greek: an abnormal birth, a miscarriage or a premature birth, one that came violently and out of season. It may have been a name his opponents used for him, the runt, and if so he has picked it up and put it in his own creed, because it fits. The Twelve had some three years of walking beside Jesus, being taught and prepared. Paul had none of it. He was on a road with warrants in his bag, travelling to arrest people, and the risen Christ intercepted him mid-journey (Acts 9:3–6), outside the normal time of the appearances. He was not raised into apostleship; he was seized into it.

The least of the apostles. True humility, with no performance in it. Paul never forgot what he had been. Later he calls himself less than the least of all the saints (Ephesians 3:8) and, later still, the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). The longer he walked with Christ, the smaller his estimate of himself became. That is the normal arithmetic of grace, and it runs the opposite way from the arithmetic of religion.

I persecuted the church. He had hunted, imprisoned and helped kill believers (Acts 22:4; 26:10–11; Galatians 1:13). Luke shows what it looked like: witnesses laying their garments at his feet while Stephen was stoned (Acts 7:58); Saul entering house after house, dragging off men and women to prison (Acts 8:3); still breathing threats and murder as he set out for Damascus (Acts 9:1).

Why are you persecuting me? The words the risen Christ spoke on that road show what Paul’s crime really was. He had been hunting men and women, and Jesus said, I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting (Acts 9:5). The Lord so binds his people to himself that a blow struck at the least of them lands on him. That is why Paul calls it the church of God: it was not a sect he had harassed but the body of the risen Lord. And it is why the forgiveness is so staggering. The man Saul had wounded was the One who forgave him, and the church he had ravaged was the body he was sent to build.

Humble, but not self-cancelling. What he never does, though, is say he is not an apostle. The commission was not his to resign; it was given. A Christian can hold two things at once: an honest low estimate of himself, and a settled certainty about what God has said about him. Losing either produces a distortion, arrogance on one side, false humility on the other.

A hard fact for the sceptic. There is evidence in this verse as well as autobiography. Paul’s own conversion is one of the harder facts for a sceptic to place. Here is a trained, motivated, well-connected opponent, actively destroying the movement, with everything to gain by continuing, and he changes sides, loses his standing, and spends thirty years being beaten and imprisoned for the thing he was suppressing. Something happened on that road. He says he knows what it was.

Can someone who has done terrible things really be forgiven? Yes, and Paul is the proof; so do not write anyone off as too far gone, either. He was complicit in murder and had violently persecuted Christ’s people, and Christ not only forgave him but made him an apostle. He says Christ did it precisely so that he might be an example to those who were to believe (1 Timothy 1:16). There is no sin so dark that Christ’s blood cannot wash it, for those who turn to him. Forgiveness does not erase every earthly consequence, and it does not make the past unimportant; Paul never forgot it. But it removes the guilt before God entirely. If you are carrying a past you cannot bear to look at, bring it to the One who met Saul on the road.

For worship. Whatever else grace is, it is not a general kindliness. It is specific enough to walk out onto a road and stop a man who is on his way to arrest more of the family. The risen Lord could have struck him dead. Instead he called him by name, and the man who held the coats at Stephen’s stoning wrote nearly half the books of the New Testament. The grace of our Lord overflowed for him (1 Timothy 1:14), and it overflows still, for the worst of sinners.
verseByVerse.note: “Untimely born” describes an abnormal birth — Paul’s sudden, late calling.

verseByVerse.quote: But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me. Whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By the grace of God. One of the most compressed sentences in Paul, and it holds together two things that people are forever pulling apart. Everything Paul is, apostle, Christian, forgiven sinner, is God’s free gift: not the apostleship, not the conversion, not the endurance, and not the letters are self-made. Everything traces back to an unearned kindness that intercepted him when he was going the other way. That is what grace means: not a reward for the deserving, nor help for those who are doing their best, but God’s favour given to people who deserve the opposite. Christ died for us while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8), and Paul had been the worst of them.

Not in vain. In vain (kenē) is empty. Grace is never inert; where it truly lands, it does something.

I worked harder. That sounds, on the face of it, like the boast he has just disowned, until the last clause takes it back without cancelling it. Grace does not make people lazy; it makes them work.

Not I, but the grace of God. Even his hard work was grace at work in him. Do not resolve that tension by choosing a side; Paul refuses to. Grace is not an alternative to effort; grace is what produces the effort. It is the same grammar as work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:12–13), and it answers two opposite mistakes.

The grace that is with me. Grace in Paul is never a substance or a force; it is the Lord himself, present and at work. He describes the same labour elsewhere as toiling with all the energy that Christ powerfully works within me (Colossians 1:29). The power that kept him going was the power of the risen Christ, who had said, apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:5), and who told him in his weakness, my grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:9). So the sentence that began with grace ends with a companion: the grace of God that is with me. Paul was never working alone, and neither is any servant of Christ.

Two mistakes about grace. The first hears grace and concludes that effort is unspiritual: that a Christian should wait to be moved, and that trying hard is a form of unbelief. Paul worked himself to exhaustion, through many a sleepless night (2 Corinthians 11:27), and he did not think so. The second hears work and quietly begins keeping score, measuring itself against other Christians and pleased with its own diligence. Paul had a genuine claim to that comparison, and he made it in the same breath as its cancellation.

I or they. After all that autobiography, it does not matter which apostle said it. The Corinthians had been dividing over exactly this, Paul, Apollos, Cephas (1:12), and here is the man himself waving the question away. The messenger is not the point. What was preached is the point, and it was the same from all of them.

In the flow. With that line Paul ends the chapter’s first movement. Verses 1–11 establish what nobody in Corinth disputed; verse 12 turns that common ground into a question, and the rest of the chapter argues from this fixed point, that Christ has been raised, to the future it guarantees for his people.

How do I work hard without trusting my work? Work as a son, not as a hired hand. A hired hand works to earn his wages; a son works because he already belongs to the family and loves his father. Begin each task by remembering that you are already accepted in Christ, so that nothing rides on your success for your standing with God. Then pour yourself into the work, asking for his strength. When it goes well, thank him; it was his grace. When it fails, confess any sin and rest; your acceptance never depended on it. That is how a Christian can be both tireless and at peace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — If Christ Has Not Been Raised
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul follows the denial to its end: if the dead are not raised, Christ is not raised, and everything else falls with him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection as the Confirmation of the Atonement

Verse 17 ties the resurrection to the atonement. Christ’s death atones; his resurrection declares the atonement accepted. That is why Christ was raised for our justification (Romans 4:25): the resurrection is the Father’s yes to the Son’s sacrifice. Without it, Good Friday is a tragedy; with it, Good Friday is the turning point of history.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian denial probably owed something to the Platonic split between soul and body: if the soul is what matters and it survives death, why would God put it back into a body? Paul answers that this misunderstands both salvation, which redeems the whole person, body and soul, and what happened to Christ, whose body was raised, not merely his spirit. Now: A milder form of the same position appears whenever Christians treat the soul going to heaven as the whole story. For Paul the resurrection body is the destination; the soul’s time with the Lord before the resurrection is the waiting room.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? At last the actual problem, and the inconsistency in it. Some in Corinth were denying the resurrection of the dead: not, apparently, the resurrection of Jesus, which they seem to have accepted, but the idea that the rest of us will be raised bodily.

Why it felt reasonable to them. It was not stupidity. Educated Greeks had a low view of the body. The soul was the real self; the body was its container and, for many, its prison, and there was a well-worn play on words for it, sōma sēma: the body is a tomb. On that view death is not the enemy but the release. Immortality of the soul, gladly; but God putting you back into a body was not salvation but re-arrest. So the Corinthians were perhaps trying to keep the parts of the faith they liked and file the rest under the crude expectations of Jewish converts.

The reasoning is exact. Paul’s reply is to show that the thing they wanted to keep cannot survive the thing they wanted to drop. Resurrection of the dead is the category. Christ’s resurrection is an instance of it. If the category is impossible in principle, no instance of it happened, including that one. You cannot say such things do not occur, except once. Christ’s resurrection and ours stand or fall together.

Not even Christ. Everything Paul says next hangs on one man. Jesus had staked his own claims on this event: he told his disciples plainly that he must be killed and after three days rise again (Mark 8:31), and he said of his body, destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up (John 2:19). The resurrection is the Father’s answer to those claims. Jesus was declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4). So the question in Corinth was never a side issue about the afterlife. If the tomb is still occupied, Jesus was wrong about himself, and a teacher wrong about the one thing he most insisted on cannot be the Lord. If it is empty, he is everything he said he was.

Preaching and faith in vain. Empty: not mistaken in a detail, but containing nothing at all. Faith is only ever as good as the thing it rests on, and if the thing is not there the sincerity of the resting changes nothing.

The easier letter Paul did not write. What Paul does not do here is what most of us would do. He does not tell the doubters that their faith can survive without the doctrine, or offer a version of Christianity that keeps the ethics, the community and the comfort and quietly drops the miracle. A faith that can be adjusted to fit whatever a generation finds credible has no power to contradict that generation, and therefore nothing to offer it. Christianity does not claim that believing is good for you. It stakes everything on an event, says so out loud, and offers to be checked.

Is it wrong to have doubts about the resurrection? Doubt is not the same as unbelief. Thomas doubted, and Jesus came to him and showed him his hands (John 20:27). If you have questions, bring them into the light: read the accounts in the Gospels, read a careful book on the evidence, talk to your pastor, and pray, Lord, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24). Paul’s own method is to invite inquiry, not to forbid it. The resurrection has been examined by sceptics for two thousand years, and many careful people, some of them sceptics, have found the evidence stronger than they expected. What would be wrong is to settle into doubt as a comfortable place, or to treat the resurrection as optional. It is the centre.

On a Tuesday. When a doubt comes, do not ask first how you feel; ask what happened in Jerusalem on the third day.

verseByVerse.quote: We are even found to be misrepresenting God, because we testified about God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if it is true that the dead are not raised. For if the dead are not raised, not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Misrepresenting God. The logic gets worse at every step. Literally, we are found to be false witnesses of God. If there was no resurrection, then the apostles have not merely been mistaken. They have been going round the Mediterranean telling people that God did something he did not do: putting words in his mouth, attaching his name to a fiction. They are liars, and liars about God.

True or a lie. There is no middle ground, and Paul does not say the gospel is worth believing regardless. People do not usually die for what they know to be a lie, and the apostles suffered for this testimony, many of them, by early accounts, to the point of death.

Futile. Paul repeats the condition of verse 13 and adds a new word: futile (mataia), useless, without result.

Still in your sins. Then the worst consequence, and not the one most people would guess. Why should it follow? If the death is what pays for sin, why does the rising matter to the accounting? Because a death, by itself, tells you nothing about whether it worked. Two men were crucified beside him and their deaths paid for nobody. What the cross needed was a verdict: a public act by which the Father declared that the sacrifice had been received and the debt cleared. That is what the resurrection is. Jesus was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Romans 4:25). Justification is the courtroom word: God acquits the guilty, not because they have improved, but because the righteousness of his risen Son is reckoned to them (2 Corinthians 5:21). Without it, there is no proof that sin has been dealt with.

The receipt. Think of it as a receipt. A man may pay an enormous debt and the payment does the work; but until the paper comes back stamped, the debtor has no way of knowing whether it went through. The empty tomb is the stamp. On Friday the price was paid. On Sunday the Father put it in writing, in a form that could be walked into and looked at.

A chapter about assurance. This turns the chapter into one about assurance and not only about the afterlife. The Christian troubled about whether his sins are really forgiven is pointed, by this verse, away from his own feelings and toward a garden outside Jerusalem. The question is not whether you feel forgiven but whether the tomb is empty. Paul does not say that without the resurrection a Christian would feel unforgiven. He says you are still in your sins: a statement about the actual position, not the impression of it. Which cuts both ways, and the second way is the comfort. If the objective fact governs when the news is bad, it governs when the news is good. The believer who feels nothing on a grey Tuesday is not less forgiven than on the day he first wept over his sin. The tomb did not become less empty overnight.

What if I still feel guilty after I have confessed? Feelings of guilt can linger long after God has forgiven, through habit, through a tender conscience, through the accuser’s whispers, or through consequences that remain. Do not measure your forgiveness by your feelings. Measure it by Christ: he was raised, so the payment was accepted. If there is something still to put right with another person, put it right. Then tell your conscience what God has said: if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9). Faithful, because he promised; just, because Christ has paid. The feelings will often follow the truth in time.

For worship. The Father has spoken his verdict over the cross, and it cannot be reversed: it is God who justifies; who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died, more than that, who was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us (Romans 8:33–34). The One who paid is alive to say so, and he says it before the throne every day. No accuser can reopen a case the Judge himself has closed, and no debt can be demanded twice. Glory to the risen Saviour, whose life is the proof of our pardon.

verseByVerse.quote: Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Perished. The argument stops being abstract. There were graves in Corinth with Christians in them, members of that congregation whose families were still in the room when this letter was read out. Fallen asleep says the condition is temporary; Paul now removes that, for the sake of the argument. If there is no resurrection, believers who have died are not asleep but finished, and every Christian funeral is a lie. A doctrine can be discussed as an idea in a room full of healthy people. Take it to a graveside and you find out what it is.

Asleep in Christ. The word sleep for a believer’s death goes back to Jesus himself. Of Jairus’ daughter he said, the child is not dead but sleeping, and they laughed at him (Mark 5:39); of Lazarus, our friend has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him (John 11:11). He could call death sleep because he could end it with a word. And the two little words in Christ say why the name still holds after he has ascended. The believer’s union with him is not broken by the grave; neither death nor life can separate us from his love (Romans 8:38–39), and God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:14). The dead in Christ are asleep because the One who wakes the sleeping holds them.

Most to be pitied. Not we are still better off, or at least the ethics are good and the community is warm. If this life is all there is, the Christian has made the worst bargain of anyone alive. He had grounds for saying so. He had given up his standing, his safety and his comfort; he would later list the beatings, the shipwrecks, the hunger and the sleepless nights (2 Corinthians 11:23–28). If there is no resurrection, that is not nobility. It is a man who threw his one life away on a rumour. Christianity is true, or it is pitiable.

A comfortable Christianity indicted. The verse quietly indicts the kind of Christianity that values the faith for what it does now: it steadies a family, shapes the week, provides friends and a moral framework. All of that is real, and a religion which delivers those things and nothing else is a pitiable arrangement. This faith is not primarily a way to live. It is a claim that a dead man is alive, and everything else follows from that or falls with it.

Does this mean the Christian life is miserable now? No. Paul is not saying believers are wretched in this life; he wrote elsewhere of joy, peace and contentment in all circumstances (Philippians 4:11–13). He is saying that the sacrifices of the Christian life only make sense if Christ is raised. The joy is real, but much of it is the joy of hope: the gladness of people who know where they are going. Take the destination away and the road becomes foolish. Keep it, and even suffering can be borne with joy, because it is working for us an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17).

On a Tuesday. This week, do one thing that would be foolish if the tomb were still full: give away something you would rather keep, forgive a debt, or speak of Christ where it will cost you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But in fact Christ has been raised. Paul sets out God’s plan: Christ the firstfruits, Adam and Christ as the two heads of humanity, the order of the resurrection, Christ’s reign until death is destroyed, and the end, when the Son hands the kingdom to the Father so that God may be all in all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Adam and Christ, and the Scope of Redemption

The comparison of Adam and Christ (as in Romans 5:12–21) is central to Paul’s teaching on both sin and salvation. Adam stands at the head of everyone born of him, and his sin brought death to all who are in Adam, which is every human being by natural birth. Christ stands at the head of his people, and his obedience, death and resurrection bring life to all who are in Christ, which is every believer by new birth. The scope is parallel but not identical: in Christ shall all be made alive refers to all who are in Christ, not to every human being. And the life Christ brings is at least as real as the death Adam brought.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians who had buried members of their church needed to know that those deaths were sleep awaiting a harvest, not permanent loss, and the firstfruits gave them an image they knew from Israel’s worship. Now: A Christian stands at a believer’s graveside with the same confidence: the firstfruits have already appeared, and the rest of the harvest is as certain as the God who gave the pledge.

verseByVerse.quote: But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in fact. Two words in Greek (nyni de, but now), and they turn the whole chapter. Paul has spent eight verses in a nightmare of his own construction: empty preaching, futile faith, unforgiven sin, dead friends gone for ever, a life thrown away. And then, without argument, he simply steps out of it. Not if, but in fact. The corridor of horrors was hypothetical. He was never in any doubt about the way out. Christ is risen.

The firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. The image is agricultural and liturgical at once, and every Jewish reader knew it. On the day after the Sabbath following Passover, a single sheaf of the new barley was cut and brought to the priest and waved before the LORD (Leviticus 23:10–14). One sheaf, in a field still standing. It was not the harvest; it was the promise of the harvest, given to God first, and the sheaf in the priest’s hands was the proof that the field would be reaped. On the most likely reckoning, that ceremony fell on the very morning Christ rose.

The first of a series. The image changes the category of the resurrection completely. It is not a stand-alone wonder that happened to one exceptional person, best admired from a distance. It is the first of a series. Nobody waves a sheaf over an empty field. The resurrection of Jesus is God’s public statement that the harvest of the dead has begun, and it therefore says something about every Christian grave that has ever been dug: ours will follow.

By a man. Death came through Adam’s sin (Genesis 3; Romans 5:12). Christ had to be truly human to undo what a human did.

In Adam, in Christ. Paul’s way of thinking about the human race is one of representation. Two men stand at the head of two humanities, and what each did counts for everyone belonging to him. Adam sinned, and death entered and spread to all who are in him, which is everybody, by birth. Christ obeyed, died and rose, and life comes to all who are in him, united to him by faith, by new birth.

Where Christians differ: will everyone be saved? Universalists read all in both halves the same way: as all die in Adam, all humans will be saved in Christ. This commentary’s view: The two alls are defined by in Adam and in Christ. All who are in Adam die; all who are in Christ, those who belong to him (v. 23), will be made alive to glory. Paul is not saying every human will be in Christ. Scripture is clear that some will rise to judgement and eternal punishment (John 5:28–29; Matthew 25:46; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). Paul here speaks only of the resurrection to life.

Whichever man you are joined to. Whichever man you are joined to, his outcome is yours. Nobody is standing on his own. Which is bad news read one way and the best news in the world read the other. You did not choose to be in Adam and you cannot argue your way out of it; the evidence is that you are going to die. But the same principle that ruins you is the principle that saves you, because being in Christ works exactly the same way: not by achievement, but by belonging (Romans 5:17–19).

How do I know I am in Christ and not only in Adam? You come to be in Christ by faith: by turning from your sin and trusting him as your Saviour and Lord. The Spirit unites you to him, and his death, his righteousness and his resurrection life become yours. If you are trusting Christ, however weakly, you are in him; faith is the hand, and Christ is the treasure it holds. Look for the fruit as well: a new love for him, a new hatred of sin, a desire for his people and his word. These do not make you his; they show that you are. And if you are not sure, come to him now. He has never turned away anyone who came.

On a Tuesday. Next time you pass a churchyard, remember the sheaf. The harvest has begun. And if you have a Christian grave to visit, go and stand by it this week and say: firstfruits.
verseByVerse.note: The firstfruits were the first sheaf of the harvest, offered to God as a pledge of the whole harvest to come — at the time of the Passover festival.

verseByVerse.quote: But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ. Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and every authority and power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
