But each in his own order. Order (tagma) is a military word: a rank, a division, a company of soldiers moving in sequence. Paul is not being vague about the future; he is saying it has a shape and the shape has stages.

Christ the firstfruits. The first has happened. Christ’s resurrection is already accomplished, a fixed point in history behind us rather than in front of us.

Those who belong to Christ. The second is still to come. At his coming (parousia, arrival, the word for a king’s visit to a city), all believers will be raised. And notice the definition of the group. Not those who achieved something, or understood something, or belonged to the right party in Corinth. Those who belong to Christ: the sole qualification is ownership, and it runs the right way round. They are his.

Then comes the end. The end (to telos) is the goal, the consummation of history. A mediator is one who stands between two parties to bring them together, and Christ alone can stand between God and sinners, because he is both God and man (1 Timothy 2:5). The whole long campaign, the incarnation, the cross, the empty tomb, the centuries of the church, the resurrection of the dead, is a mission with a completion, and it ends with the Son handing the finished work to his Father, like a commander reporting to the one who sent him. And what is handed over is not a ruin salvaged from a fire. It is a kingdom: complete, every enemy dealt with and every subject alive.

Every rule and authority. Every power opposed to God: human rebellion, death itself, and the spiritual forces behind the visible ones, the powers the Christian actually wrestles with (Ephesians 6:12). Not reformed, not negotiated with, not accommodated. Abolished.

A steadiness for anyone reading the news. The powers that look permanent, the regimes, the ideologies, and the darker things behind them, are on a list, and the list has a completion date. None of it will survive the arrival of the King, and none of it will require a second campaign (Colossians 2:15).

Where Christians differ: the millennium. Premillennialists see a gap between his coming (v. 23) and the end (v. 24), filled by a thousand-year earthly reign of Christ. This commentary’s view: The most natural reading is that the end follows Christ’s coming directly. Christ is reigning now (v. 25), from heaven, and will reign until his return, when the dead are raised and death is destroyed. This is the amillennial view: the millennium of Revelation 20 describes Christ’s present reign during the church age. There is one return of Christ, visible and public, not a secret rapture followed by a later coming.

The case on both sides. Premillennial Christians, many of them careful students of Scripture, read the word then as leaving room for an interval: Christ returns, raises his people, and reigns on earth for a thousand years before the end. They point to Revelation 20:4–6, where the saints came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years, and note that Paul’s word can mark a gap, since a long time has already passed between Christ’s resurrection and his coming. Amillennial Christians answer that Paul places the resurrection of believers at his coming and then the end, and the next verses say Christ must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet, the last being death (vv. 25–26); and death is defeated at the resurrection itself (vv. 54–55). If death is destroyed at Christ’s coming, there is no room after it for a further age in which death still reigns. That is why the amillennial reading is the more likely: Christ reigns now, and his coming brings the resurrection, the judgement and the end together. Christians who expect a thousand-year reign, or a rapture before it, love his appearing as truly as anyone; the difference is about the order of events, not about whether he comes.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s rule ends. He hands the kingdom over in the sense that his mediatorial work is complete, but he reigns forever with the Father: of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:33; Revelation 11:15).

If Christ is reigning now, why is the world still so evil? Because his reign is a campaign still under way. He has already won the decisive battle at the cross and the empty tomb, and he now rules from the Father’s right hand, gathering his people from every nation by the gospel and restraining evil. But the enemies are not yet all under his feet, and his people still suffer, as he did. The New Testament holds both together: he reigns, and we wait. The evil you see is real, but it is not winning; it is on borrowed time, and its end is already set. Meanwhile his kingdom grows like a mustard seed, quietly, in every place where sinners bow the knee to him.

On a Tuesday. When the news frightens you this week, name the thing that frightens you and add three words: until he comes.

verseByVerse.quote: For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must reign. From Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse the New Testament quotes and echoes more often than any other: the LORD says to my Lord, sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool. Christ is reigning now, at the Father’s right hand (Ephesians 1:20–22; Hebrews 10:12–13), and must (dei) means it is God’s plan. The reigning Christ is at this moment putting his enemies under his feet, one after another, and he is working his way toward the grave.

The last enemy. Destroyed (katargeitai) means abolished, rendered powerless. Look at what death is called. Not a doorway, not a natural transition, not a part of the circle of life, not a friend who comes at the end of a long day. An enemy, and the last one standing after everything else has fallen. Christ has already defeated it by his resurrection; at his return it will be abolished entirely (Revelation 20:14; 21:4).

In the flow. Why must the end of verse 24 wait? Verse 25 gives the reason. Christ is reigning now, and the end comes only when his reign has done its work. Verse 26 then names the last enemy, and so brings the argument back to Corinth. Those who deny the resurrection of the dead are, without knowing it, leaving death undefeated and Christ’s reign unfinished. A gospel with no resurrection has a King who never wins his last battle.

Permission to hate death. That single word enemy is worth more to a grieving Christian than a great deal of what is said at funerals. There is a religious way of speaking that tries to make peace with death: that says it is only a change of address and a believer ought to be serene. The Bible calls death an enemy, and it gives the mourner permission to hate it. The Lord himself did. On his way to the tomb of Lazarus, knowing he would call him out alive that same day, Jesus wept (John 11:35), and the word John uses of him a moment earlier suggests something closer to indignation than sorrow (John 11:33). He was not weeping about the outcome; he was standing in front of the enemy itself, doing to a family he loved what it does to everybody.

What death does. Be concrete, because vagueness here helps nobody. Death takes a person who was in the room and makes the room empty. It ends the conversation in the middle. It takes a hand that has been held for fifty years and makes it cold in an hour. It leaves a chair, a coat, a voice on an old recording that is now unbearable to play. So the Christian is not asked to pretend. He is asked to believe that the enemy is on a schedule: not tamed, not made bearable, but destroyed, and last, because everything else goes first.

Is it a lack of faith to be afraid of dying? No. Death is an enemy, and it is natural to shrink from it; our Lord himself was in agony in Gethsemane. What faith does is not remove every fear but give it a horizon. For the believer, death has lost its sting (v. 55): it cannot separate you from Christ, and it will not keep you. Many Christians fear the process of dying more than death itself, and that fear can be brought honestly to God in prayer. He has promised to be with you in the valley (Psalm 23:4). Very often those who have feared most find, when the hour comes, that grace is given for it.

On a Tuesday. If you are grieving, you do not have to pretend. Tell God that you hate what death has done, and then tell him that you believe it is on a schedule. If someone near you is grieving, do not hurry them toward serenity; sit with them, and remind them, when the time is right, that death is the last enemy, and it will be destroyed.

For worship. There will come a day on which there is no death anywhere in the universe, and no one will ever again have to be told that someone has died. The Son of God went down into the enemy’s own territory, let it do its worst to him, and walked out on the third day carrying its defeat. Glory to the King who must reign, and who will not lay down his sceptre until the last grave is empty.

parallels.desc: until I make your enemies your footstool

verseByVerse.quote: For “God has put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when it says, “all things are put in subjection,” it is plain that he is excepted who put all things in subjection under him. When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All things under his feet. The quotation is from Psalm 8:6, and the psalm is not, in the first place, about the Messiah. It is about human beings: what is man that you are mindful of him? And yet God has crowned him with glory and put all things under his feet (Psalm 8:4–6). It is creation’s job description for the human race, given in the garden and abandoned there. Adam was made to rule the world under God and instead handed it over. Paul applies the psalm to Christ, and the logic is the one running through this whole chapter. Christ is the last Adam, the true human being, doing at last what humanity was made for (Hebrews 2:6–9). Psalm 8 has not been wrenched out of context; it has finally found a man it fits.

He is excepted. Paul states the obvious because it needs stating: the Father is not among the things subdued.

The Son himself will also be subjected. This sentence has troubled readers for centuries, because it appears to make the Son permanently lesser. It does not. What is described is not the Son’s nature but the completion of his mission. He was sent; he came; he obeyed; he died; he rose; he reigns; he subdues; and when the work is finished he presents it all to the Father and takes his place in the order he willingly took when he was sent. The Son who is the exact imprint of the Father’s nature (Hebrews 1:3) does not become less divine by handing over a completed kingdom. It is the same Son who said, in a garden, not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42).

That God may be all in all. That is the goal of history: God’s rule complete and unchallenged, filling everything (Ephesians 1:23; Colossians 3:11). It means a universe with nothing left in it that is not filled with God: no corner where he is absent, nothing between him and his people, and nobody anywhere having to go looking for him. Every place where a believer has felt God to be distant will have been abolished, along with distance itself.

In the flow. Verse 28 is the summit of the chapter’s central section. Paul has climbed from Christ’s rising (v. 20), through the order of the resurrection (vv. 23–24) and the reign of Christ (vv. 25–27), to the goal of everything: God all in all. In verse 29 he comes straight back down to Corinth and to the way Christians live, as if to say that a hope this large must show in ordinary choices.

Where Christians differ: is the Son inferior to the Father? Arians, ancient and modern (followers of Arius, a fourth-century teacher who held that the Son was created), use this verse to argue that the Son is a lesser being. This commentary’s view: The subjection here is of the Son as incarnate Mediator, in his role of redemption, not of the Son in his divine nature. In his divine nature, the Son is equal with the Father, of the same substance (John 1:1; 10:30; Philippians 2:6). In his role as Mediator, he submits to the Father’s will (John 6:38). This is the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity, as summarised in the Nicene Creed and in the Westminster and 1689 Confessions (Westminster Confession 2.3, 8.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 2.3, 8.2).

Will we still see and worship Jesus when God is all in all? Yes, forever. The Son does not disappear into the Father at the end. He remains the God-man, with his risen body, and the Lamb is on the throne in the new Jerusalem (Revelation 22:1, 3). God is all in all precisely in and through Christ: the glory of God is its light, and its lamp is the Lamb (Revelation 21:23). The handing over of the kingdom is not Christ stepping aside; it is the Son presenting his finished work to the Father, so that the whole of creation rings with the praise of Father, Son and Spirit. We will worship the Lamb who was slain for all eternity.

parallels.desc: you have put all things under his feet

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–34 — The Logic of Resurrection Living
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul argues from practice: the baptism for the dead, his own daily danger, and the party-goer’s creed all show that how people live depends on whether the dead are raised. He warns against the company that is leading them astray.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection and the Ground of Christian Living

If there is no resurrection, a life of self-denial, risk and suffering for others makes no sense, and the man who says let us eat and drink is simply being consistent. Paul’s own life is an argument for the resurrection: his willingness to face death daily makes sense on no other footing.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Fighting with beasts at Ephesus may be literal or a picture of violent opponents; either way it was real mortal danger, and Paul asks what it was for if the dead are not raised. Now: The missionary in a dangerous field, the pastor who will not trim his convictions, the church member who gives up promotion for the sake of integrity: each life of this kind makes sense only if the resurrection is true.

verseByVerse.quote: Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf? Why are we in danger every hour?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? Verse 29 is probably the most puzzling sentence in the letter, and it is often said that more than forty interpretations have been suggested. It is worth being honest about that rather than pretending to a certainty nobody has.

In the flow. With verse 29 Paul comes back to the line of argument he left at verse 19. Verses 12–19 showed what follows for belief if the dead are not raised; verses 20–28 broke in with what is true instead, Christ risen and reigning. Now verses 29–34 add a second kind of argument, from practice: what people do at Corinth, and what the apostles suffer, makes sense only if the dead will rise.

Three readings worth knowing. The plainest sense of the Greek is that some people at Corinth were being baptised as proxies for relatives or friends who had died unbaptised, hoping it would do the dead some good. Early writers such as John Chrysostom knew of such practices among heretical groups and condemned them. A second reading takes for as because of: new converts were being baptised because of the dead, moved to faith by a believer whose hope had held to the end, or longing to be reunited with believing loved ones. A third takes it as baptism with one’s own coming death and resurrection in view. Whatever it was, Paul does not endorse it; he uses it to show the inconsistency of those who deny the resurrection.

If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf? Whatever it was, it only made sense if there was a resurrection. What can be said with certainty is how Paul is using it, and that is the part that matters. He is not teaching it. He does not say you or we but they: he holds the practice at arm’s length, neither endorsing nor attacking it here, and simply points out that whatever it is, it makes no sense at all unless the dead have a future. His argument is that the Corinthians’ own behaviour contradicts their stated theology. That is worth noting as a method, because it is a fair one. People are often better than their opinions, and one honest way to answer a bad idea is to show the person that he does not actually live as though it were true. Nobody grieves as if the dead were nothing. Nobody attends a funeral and behaves like a man who thinks a machine has stopped.

Buried with him in baptism. Whatever the Corinthian practice was, Christian baptism itself is a sign that only makes sense if the dead are raised, because it is a picture of Christ’s own death and rising. We were buried with him by baptism into death, Paul writes, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life (Romans 6:4). Jesus himself called his coming death a baptism he must undergo (Luke 12:50). So every baptism in Corinth, going down into the water and coming up out of it, preached the empty tomb. A church that baptised and denied the resurrection was acting out the gospel with its hands while denying it with its mouth.

Why are we in danger every hour? Paul turns to his own life. Why would the apostles risk death constantly if there were no resurrection? The second argument runs to the end of verse 32. It is the same question turned on himself: what am I doing, if there is nothing after this?

Where Christians differ: baptism for the dead. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints practises proxy baptism for the dead, based on this verse. This commentary’s view: Paul mentions the practice without endorsing it, and notice he says people, not we. Nowhere else does Scripture teach it. The New Testament is clear that each person must believe for themselves, and that after death comes judgement, with no second chance (Hebrews 9:27; Luke 16:26). Baptism is for those who personally repent and believe. (Christians who baptise the infants of believers agree that no one can be baptised on behalf of the dead.)

Holding a passage loosely. Two things are worth carrying away from a verse this obscure. First, it is possible to hold a passage loosely without holding the Bible loosely. Not every sentence in Scripture yields its meaning easily, and saying so is honesty rather than doubt. The doctrine of the resurrection does not rest on verse 29; Paul’s case runs perfectly well without our knowing what the practice was. Second, a caution about the opposite error. A whole teaching has been built by one movement on this single obscure verse, against the plain sense of the rest of Scripture, which nowhere suggests that anything can be done for the dead by the living. A doctrine erected on one difficult sentence is a building on a very narrow footing.

Can I do anything for a loved one who died without Christ? Nothing can change a person’s state after death; Scripture gives no second chance and no way for the living to alter it (Hebrews 9:27). That is a hard truth, and it is right to grieve it honestly. But remember two things. You do not know what passed between that person and God in their last hours, and the thief on the cross shows how late grace can come. And the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). Leave them with him. What you can do is pray for the living, and speak of Christ to those who are still within reach of the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of “baptized on behalf of the dead” is disputed; most likely some Corinthians were being baptized as proxies for the dead. Paul mentions the practice without approving it, only to show that it assumes a resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day! What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
I die every day. A solemn oath, and not first a devotional phrase about self-denial. Paul is describing his working conditions: he faced the threat of death daily (2 Corinthians 4:10–11; 11:23–27), and a man in that position needs a reason. He swears to it, oddly, by my pride in you, staking the claim on the one thing this difficult congregation would recognise as valuable: that he is proud of them. Even in the middle of an argument he tells them that.

What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? Fighting with beasts at Ephesus is probably a picture of fierce human opposition, since a Roman citizen was unlikely to be thrown to animals, and Paul does not mention it in his list of sufferings (2 Corinthians 11:23–27). Some link it with the riot of Acts 19 (Acts 19:23–41), though the letter was probably written before that riot; more likely it refers to the many adversaries Paul mentions (16:9), opponents who acted like wild animals. Either way the sense is the same: he had been in a place where he did not expect to come out alive. What do I gain? That is the honest question, and it deserves an honest answer. Nothing. If the dead are not raised, Paul has purchased absolutely nothing with his life, and he says so without flinching.

To die is gain. Paul’s own letters give the other half of the answer, the one he holds when the dead are raised. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain (Philippians 1:21). Whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ, that I may gain Christ and be found in him (Philippians 3:7–9). So the question what do I gain? has one answer if the tomb is full, nothing, and another if it is empty: the Lord himself. Paul did not risk the beasts for a principle or a cause. He risked them for a Person, and because that Person is risen, every danger faced for him was an investment, not a loss.

Let us eat and drink. The quotation is from Isaiah 22:13, and it is not a joke. Isaiah described a city under siege that ought to have been weeping and repenting, and instead threw a party. It is the philosophy the ancient world had already worked out and ours has rediscovered: if this is all there is, get what you can before the lights go out. And Paul does not sneer at it. He treats it as the rational position for a man with no resurrection. If death is the end, a life of self-denial for other people’s benefit is not admirable but a waste, and the person eating and drinking has understood the situation better than the martyr.

But many people with no hope of resurrection live generous lives. Does that not prove Paul wrong? No. Paul is not saying that unbelievers cannot be kind; plainly many are, and some put Christians to shame. He is saying that their kindness has no ground in their creed. If death ends everything, self-giving love is a beautiful habit with nothing underneath it, and people who live that way are living better than their beliefs, as the Corinthians were in verse 29. The Christian can give his life away for a reason: the One who gave his life away first was raised, and nothing given for him is lost (v. 58).

Is it selfish to serve God for the sake of heaven? Not if heaven is God himself. The reward the Bible holds out is not a payment unrelated to the work, like money for a chore; it is the natural end of loving God: being with him, seeing his face, enjoying him forever. A man who marries for love is not mercenary because he looks forward to his wedding day. Jesus himself endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). To want Christ, and to be willing to lose everything else to gain him, is not selfishness. It is the very thing we were made for.

For worship. The Lord Jesus did not eat and drink because tomorrow he would die. He took bread and a cup, and gave them away, because tomorrow he would die for us. He laid down his life, and he took it up again, and because he lives, every life laid down for him is gathered up and kept. Because he is risen, self-denial is wisdom and martyrdom is victory.
verseByVerse.note: Fighting with beasts at Ephesus is probably a picture of fierce human opposition; a Roman citizen could not normally be sent to the arena.

parallels.desc: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived: “Bad company ruins good morals.” Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning. For some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be deceived. The proverb is a line from the Greek poet Menander’s comedy Thais, probably a common saying by his day. Paul does the same at Athens with the poets (Acts 17:28) and in Titus with a Cretan (Titus 1:12): truth is truth wherever it turns up. But consider what a sentence about company is doing in an argument about the resurrection. It tells us something Paul assumes and we often do not: people do not usually reason their way into a false belief. They drift into it, in company, over time.

How faith is usually lost. Many Christians who abandon what they believed did not do it in a library. It happened gradually, through friendship, through the desire to be thought reasonable by people they admired, through a slow adjustment of what could comfortably be said aloud. Nobody decides to stop believing in the resurrection. He starts spending time where it is quietly assumed to be embarrassing, and after two years he finds he has moved. Paul is not commanding a retreat from the world; he has already ruled that out (5:10). He is pointing at the confident deniers inside the church and telling the congregation to stop finding them impressive. If you recognise some of that drift in yourself, the fact that it troubles you is a sign of life: Paul’s word is wake up, not give up.

Wake up. Wake up (eknēphō) is what you say to a man sleeping it off: sober up, come round. Wrong beliefs about the future had made them spiritually drunk, and wrong doctrine was already producing wrong living. It is an extraordinary thing to say to a congregation that thought itself the most spiritually advanced in Greece. He does not tell them they are mistaken. He tells them they are not properly conscious.

No knowledge of God. No knowledge (agnōsia) is ignorance, and it is ironic for a church that prided itself on knowledge. That is the diagnosis under the error. Behind the denial of the resurrection is not a difficulty with biology but an inadequate view of God: a God not big enough to raise the dead, which is to say not the God who made the world out of nothing. To deny the resurrection is to know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God (Matthew 22:29).

The God who raised Jesus. In the New Testament, God is named by what he did on the third day. Paul names him as the one who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord (Romans 4:24), and the knowledge of his glory shines in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). That is why denying the resurrection is not a small error about the future but ignorance of God himself: it leaves out the deed by which he has made himself known. Eternal life, Jesus said, is to know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). To know God is to know him as the Father of the risen Son.

To your shame. It is the second time in the letter Paul has used that phrase (6:5). A church full of knowledge, and some of its members do not know God.

How do I keep unbelieving friends without being pulled away? Be the influence rather than the influenced. Jesus ate with sinners, but he set the direction of the conversation. Keep your roots deep: be in the word daily, be in church weekly, and have Christian friends close enough to notice if you drift. Be honest about your faith early in a friendship, so that it is not something you have to hide. Watch for the warning signs: finding your convictions embarrassing, laughing at what grieves God, wanting their approval more than Christ’s. And if a particular friendship is steadily dragging you into sin, love may require distance. The goal is to win them, not to become them.
verseByVerse.note: “Bad company ruins good morals” is a line from the Greek poet Menander.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul answers the question how the dead are raised and with what body: through the picture of a seed, the variety of bodies God has made, four contrasts between the body sown and the body raised, and the two Adams whose images we bear.
verseByVerse.theology:
Continuity and Transformation in the Resurrection Body

The church has always confessed the resurrection of the body, not merely the survival of the soul, and Reformed teaching has held firmly to it. Paul’s seed holds both truths: continuity, since seed and plant are one living thing at different stages, and transformation, since the plant’s glory exceeds anything visible in the seed. The body that is buried, with its own history and scars, is the body that will be raised. Christ’s own resurrection is the pattern: the body that was crucified was raised, still bearing the wounds (John 20:27), and yet transformed into glory.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Greek objection was that the body is the problem, and salvation is the soul set free from it. Paul will not accept those terms. The body is God’s good creation and is destined for resurrection; the problem is not having a body but mortality and corruption. Now: Whenever the goal of salvation is pictured as the soul leaving the body behind for ever, the Corinthian problem is back. The goal is the new creation: raised bodies on a renewed earth, in the presence of God.

verseByVerse.quote: But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” You foolish person! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But someone will ask, how are the dead raised? Now the real objection, and Paul lets the sceptic put it in his own words. It is not a stupid question. Bodies decay, are burned, are lost at sea and scattered so completely that not a molecule stays in place. Where exactly is the body that is going to be raised?

With what kind of body do they come? And what would such a body be like? The same decaying body? That sounded absurd to Greeks.

You foolish person! Foolish (aphrōn) means without sense. It is sharper in English than in Greek, and Paul is not calling him stupid for asking. The word describes someone reasoning without taking into account what he already knows: a man who has the answer in his own back garden and has not looked at it, and has not reckoned with the power of God.

Unless it dies. Here is the answer: the analogy of a seed. Every farmer in the ancient world, and every gardener since, has watched this happen. You take a hard dry seed and bury it in the ground. That is a funeral. It goes into the dark, and if you dug it up a fortnight later you would find it soft and rotting. And out of that comes a green shoot, then a stalk taller than the seed ever was, carrying thirty seeds of its own. The objection assumes that burial is the end of the story. The seed says otherwise, in every field the objector has ever walked past. In the only process any of us can observe, death is the doorway to new life. Burial is sowing.

A grain of wheat. Jesus said exactly this about himself, days before it happened: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). He was talking about his own burial, and about a harvest that would include the man asking this question.

Evidence from a seed. Paul could have answered from revelation; he had been caught up into the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2–4). He answers from a seed. God has arranged the world so that the hardest thing a person has to believe is acted out every spring in front of him, in mud. The resurrection is not an alien intrusion into a universe that runs on other principles; it is a pattern written into creation from the beginning, applied at last to the thing that matters most.

Does it matter whether a Christian is buried or cremated? It does not matter to God’s power; he will raise the cremated as surely as the buried, the lost at sea as surely as those in the churchyard. Many Christians, following the pattern of Scripture and of Christ’s own burial, prefer burial, because it pictures the sowing of a seed and honours the body as something God will raise. Others choose cremation for good reasons, and they do no wrong. What matters is that the body is treated with respect, and that the funeral speaks plainly of the hope of the resurrection.

For worship. The God of the harvest is the God of the resurrection. Every spring he preaches it in the fields, and on one spring morning he did it in a garden: in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb (John 19:41). The Seed went into that ground on Friday, and on Sunday Mary, weeping, supposed the man in front of her to be the gardener (John 20:15). The risen Lord was standing in the garden, the first of a crop that will cover the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain. But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A bare kernel. Paul presses the picture, and its two halves answer the two halves of the objection. First, a seed looks nothing like the plant. Hold one in your hand: small, brown, dry, hard and unremarkable. Nothing in it suggests a green stem or a field moving in the wind; if you had only ever seen the seed, you would think the plant a wild story. So the question with what kind of body do they come? has an answer, and part of it is: not one you could work out from what goes into the ground. The resurrection body is not an improved corpse. It stands to the buried body as harvest to seed-time: continuity and transformation, the same life in a different form.

As he has chosen. God is the one who gives the new body, and that quietly settles the question of molecules and scattered atoms. The wheat plant is not built only out of the material of the seed; the seed is spent, and the plant is made of soil and rain and air. Continuity is not a matter of the same particles being reassembled. It is the same God attending to the same person. So a Christian may lay to rest a body ruined by illness, or burned, or lost at sea, or long since gone to dust, and none of it is an obstacle. The God who made the first body out of the ground has never been short of material, and he knows exactly where every one of his people is.

The body he has chosen. We are not left to guess what God has chosen, because he has done it once already. The body laid in the garden tomb was the body that came out of it, leaving the grave empty and the linen behind; and yet that same body came and stood among the disciples behind locked doors (John 20:19) and could never die again. Paul says plainly that this is the pattern: the Lord will change our weak bodies to match his own body of glory (Philippians 3:21). The seed God has already raised is his own Son, and every believer’s harvest will be shaped like his.

Its own body. Wheat becomes wheat. So each person will be raised as himself, recognisably the same, but transformed. This is a promise of particularity: not one generic glorified shape issued to everybody, but its own. It answers a fear people rarely put into words, that whatever is raised will not really be me, that eternity means being absorbed into something general, a soul among souls. Barley does not come up wheat.

Will I still be me? Yes. The resurrection is not the creation of a new person who happens to carry your name. It is you, body and soul, raised and made whole. Your soul has been with Christ since death, and on that day it will be reunited with your body, the same body, transformed. Your history, your relationships, the work of grace in you will not be erased. The risen Jesus was recognisably Jesus; he knew Mary by name and she knew him by his voice. So it will be with you, except that everything sin and death have spoiled will be gone.

verseByVerse.quote: For not all flesh is the same, but there is one kind for humans, another for animals, another for birds, and another for fish. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not all flesh is the same. A second analogy. Paul now widens the lens, and the argument is doing something specific: it is dismantling the assumption that the word body can only mean one thing.

Humans, animals, birds and fish. The list echoes Genesis 1. Look around, he says. A man’s flesh and a fish’s flesh are both flesh and they are not remotely alike; the bird that can live in the air and the fish that would drown in it are both embodied creatures. God the Creator is able to make bodies of every kind suited to every sphere.

Heavenly and earthly. Heavenly bodies are sun, moon and stars; earthly ones are plants and animals and men. Each has its own splendour (doxa, glory, brightness), and their glories are of different orders altogether.

Sun, moon and stars. Even among the heavenly bodies, no two lights are the same. The point is that God has never worked with one template. A God with this much range in what he has already made is not likely to be stuck for a design when he comes to raise the dead. The objector at verse 35 was assuming that a resurrection body would have to be the same sort of thing as the body he currently has, and that assumption is the whole of his difficulty.

Through him all things were made. The New Testament names the Maker of all this variety. All things were created through him and for him (Colossians 1:16), and without him was not any thing made that was made (John 1:3). The One who made flesh for fish and birds, and fixed every star in its own glory, is the Son, and the same Son is the one who will raise the dead: as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will (John 5:21). The design of the resurrection body is in the hands of the Craftsman of the universe. He has never yet run short of ideas.

Difference is God’s habit. Star differs from star in glory. Difference is not a defect in God’s workmanship; it is his habit. He made a church of eyes and ears and feet (12:17), and a sky in which no two lights are matched. A congregation that had been ranking one another by a single measure is being shown a night sky.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that believers will become stars, or that there will be ranks of glory among the saved based on merit, though some interpreters have taken it that way. Paul’s point is about God’s creative power. He is answering the question with what kind of body do they come? (v. 35), and the illustration is about kinds, not ranks. Scripture does speak elsewhere of rewards that differ (3:12–15), but every raised believer will bear the image of the man of heaven (v. 49).

Will there be rewards in heaven? Yes, but not the kind that make anyone envious. Scripture speaks of reward for faithful service (3:14; Matthew 25:21), but every reward is itself grace, for even our good works were prepared by God (Ephesians 2:10). No one will be second-class in glory, and no one will begrudge another; the elders in Revelation cast their crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:10). Every believer will be filled to the brim with joy, though the vessels may differ in size. The greatest reward of all is the same for everyone: Christ himself.

On a Tuesday. Look at your church with the eyes you turn to the night sky: stop measuring your brothers and sisters by a single standard, and thank God for one person this week who is gloriously unlike you.

For worship. A tentmaker writing to a quarrelling church about a hard doctrine stopped in the middle of it to look up. The God whose ordinary handiwork filled that sentence is the Son who made it all, and who came down into his own creation, slept in a fishing boat on a lake he had made, and rose to make a new one. He determines the number of the stars and gives to all of them their names (Psalm 147:4). He knows the names of those who sleep in him, and he will call each of them out by it.

verseByVerse.quote: So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So is it with the resurrection. The comparisons stop and the promises begin: four contrasts (vv. 42–44), and each of the first three names something a reader has felt.

Imperishable. Perishable (phthora) is decay, corruption; imperishable (aphtharsia) is incorruption. The present body is on a schedule of decay and everyone knows it. The knee goes, the eyes go, the name of somebody you have known for forty years will not come. Whatever is done to slow it, and there is nothing wrong with slowing it, the direction is fixed. The resurrection body will not be kept young by effort. It will have nothing in it that can wear out.

Raised in glory. This is the honest one, and anyone who has sat with the dying knows what Paul means. There is very little dignity at the end: being washed by strangers, a body that will not obey, a mind that says the wrong word, a person who was formidable and is now frightened of the stairs. Death does not merely end a life; it humiliates it first. Into that Paul writes raised in glory, the same word used of the splendour of God himself. The body that was carried out of a ward with a sheet over it comes back radiant (Matthew 13:43).

Raised in power. Weakness is the daily one, and it is not only the sickbed; it is the ordinary ceiling every person lives under: wanting to help and being too tired, wanting to stay and having to sleep, wanting to do the good thing and finding that the body will not carry the will that far. Every human being alive is limited by an instrument that cannot keep up with him. Raised in power means the instrument will be equal to the person at last.

Sown. Look at the verb governing all three. Not disposed of, not lost, not stored. Sown, which is a thing done by a farmer, on purpose, with a harvest in mind. Christians have buried their dead for two thousand years in that word’s shadow. A grave, on Paul’s account, is not a full stop but a planting.

He was sown first. Every one of these contrasts happened first to Christ. He was sown in dishonour: stripped, mocked, spat on and hung naked on a cross, then taken down by friends and laid in a borrowed grave. He was sown in weakness: crucified in weakness, Paul writes elsewhere, but he lives by the power of God (2 Corinthians 13:4). And he was raised imperishable: Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again (Romans 6:9). So these contrasts are not a theory of what might happen to bodies. They are a description of what has already happened to one body, and a promise that his people will go the way he went.

How should I care for my body now if it will be raised? With gratitude and respect, but without idolatry. Your body is not a prison to escape but a temple of the Holy Spirit (6:19) and a seed of glory. So feed it, rest it, exercise it, and do not abuse it with drunkenness or sexual sin. Care for the bodies of others too, the sick, the elderly, the disabled, because God will raise them. But do not worship youth or beauty, and do not despair as the body declines. Its weakness is not the end of the story. The wrinkles and the aches are the dishonour of the sowing, and the harvest is coming.

On a Tuesday. Visit someone whose body is failing, in a hospital, a care home, or their own front room, and treat them with the honour due to one who will be raised in glory.

verseByVerse.quote: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is sown a natural body. The fourth contrast, and the one most often misunderstood, so it must be handled carefully. Natural (psychikos, soulish) describes a body animated by ordinary human life, suited to this age (2:14): breath, blood, appetite, sleep.

It is raised a spiritual body. A spiritual body is a real body wholly empowered by the Spirit, not a body made of spirit. It does not mean a ghost, a mist, or a soul that has escaped its container. Spiritual (pneumatikos) describes what governs and empowers it, not what it is made of; Paul uses the same word of spiritual people (2:15), who are not made of spirit. So the resurrection body is not less physical than the present one. If anything it is more so: more solid, more alive, more capable, because everything that drags at the body has been removed.

One such body was examined. We are not guessing, because one such body exists and was examined. The risen Christ told them to touch him, and said that a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have (Luke 24:39). He ate broiled fish in front of them (Luke 24:42–43), which reads exactly like a man proving a point, and when Thomas needed evidence, he offered the wounds (John 20:27).

He kept the scars. That last detail answers a question people carry and rarely ask. The one resurrection body we have any information about is marked, permanently, by what was done to it. Glorification did not erase the history; it healed it and kept the record. Whatever that means for the rest of us, it means the risen life is not an amnesia. The Lamb in heaven stands as though it had been slain (Revelation 5:6).

Where Christians differ: a physical resurrection? Some say the resurrection body is immaterial, a spirit body, and that Jesus’ resurrection was spiritual rather than physical. This commentary’s view: Christ’s resurrection body was physical: he ate, was touched, had flesh and bones and the marks of his wounds (Luke 24:39–43; John 20:27). The tomb was empty. Ours will be like his (Philippians 3:21). The spiritual body is physical, but transformed and wholly governed by the Holy Spirit (Westminster Confession 32.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.2).

Will we know one another? The disciples knew him, sometimes at once, sometimes after a moment, and always in the end, and Paul assumes throughout his letters that Christians will be reunited and will recognise each other (1 Thessalonians 4:17–18; 2 Corinthians 4:14). Love does not end (13:8), and the people we have loved in Christ will be ours to love forever, more truly than now.

What about bodies wrecked by disease, dementia or disability? Verse 38 has already answered it: God gives it a body as he has chosen, and what is raised is raised imperishable, in glory, in power (vv. 42–43). Nothing that the fall put into a body is going to be raised with it. The child who never walked will run; the mind lost to dementia will know and praise and remember; the body broken by illness will be strong. And what age? Scripture does not say, and it is better to admit that than to invent. What it does say is enough: the body will be like his (Philippians 3:21). That is the whole promise, and it is a great deal more than a description.

For worship. He did not leave his body in the grave like a shell. He came out in it, glorified, and took it with him into heaven, where a man with scarred hands now sits on the throne of the universe. The Spirit who raised him dwells in his people already, the pledge that the same Spirit will give life to our mortal bodies (Romans 8:11), and is at work in them now. Blessed be the Lord who redeems the body and does not discard it, and who has gone ahead of us in ours.
verseByVerse.note: A “spiritual body” is a real body wholly empowered by the Spirit, not a body made of spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus it is written, “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first man Adam. Paul goes back to Genesis 2:7: a living soul (psychē zōsa), the word behind natural body. He received life; God breathed it into him and he stood up. Everything about the first man is on the receiving end: he was made from dust he did not gather, given breath he did not take, and put in a garden he did not plant.

A life-giving spirit. Not merely alive: a source. Christ is the head of the new humanity (Romans 5:12–21), and by his resurrection he became the giver of life through the Spirit. Adam received life; Christ gives it (John 5:21; 6:63). The first Adam was a vessel; the last Adam is a spring. That is why the resurrection of Jesus is not simply the best example of resurrection but its cause. He does not stand at the head of the queue. He is the reason there is a queue.

What life-giving spirit means. Spirit here does not mean Christ is no longer bodily, nor that he turned into the Holy Spirit; the two remain distinct persons throughout Paul’s letters (2 Corinthians 13:14). It means that the risen Christ, in a body wholly alive with the Spirit, now gives life: he pours out the Spirit (Acts 2:33) and will raise his people by that same Spirit. Note also the title. Paul can call him the second man (v. 47), but here he calls him the last Adam, so that no one expects a third. The human race has had two representatives and will have no more. Everything after Christ is a matter of which of the two you belong to.

First the natural. Verse 46 looks like a small logical aside and is doing real work. The order of history is first the natural, Adam and this age, then the spiritual, Christ and the age to come. It runs against the instinct of every religious person who has ever wanted to skip a stage. The dust comes before the glory, the natural body before the spiritual one, the long unremarkable life before the transformation. That is a rebuke to the Corinthian error, which was to believe they had already arrived, already reigning, already beyond the ordinary business of bodies and patience (4:8). Paul says the spiritual comes later, at the resurrection.

Seed first, harvest afterwards. And it is a comfort to anyone who suspects his own Christian life is too plain to be real. The plainness is not a sign that something has gone wrong; it is the appointed order. Nobody gets the second without going through the first, and the Lord himself did not (Hebrews 5:8; Philippians 2:8–9): some thirty years in a carpenter’s shop came before about three years of ministry. If the last Adam took the natural first and did not complain about the ratio, nobody else is being short-changed. There is no shortcut past the natural into the spiritual, only the appointed sequence, and God is not in a hurry.

My Christian life feels ordinary. Am I missing something? Probably not. Most of the Christian life is meant to be ordinary: daily prayer and Scripture, weekly worship, faithful work, patient love at home, small acts of service. That is not second-rate Christianity; it is the natural before the spiritual, the seed before the harvest. If you are trusting Christ and walking with him, you are not missing a secret level. Seek more of him, certainly, and do not settle for coldness. But beware of anyone who promises a shortcut to glory now. The glory is coming, and it is far greater than any experience this life can give.

parallels.desc: the man became a living creature

verseByVerse.quote: The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven. As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven. Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man of dust. Two men, two origins, and two families that look like their heads. Genesis says so and does not apologise for it: God formed the man of dust from the ground (Genesis 2:7), and told him after the fall that to dust he would return (Genesis 3:19). Every person carries the evidence. We are made of the same elements as the soil in the garden, we require constant maintenance from that soil in the form of food and water, and in the end we go back into it. There is a reason the funeral service says what it says over a grave: dust to dust.

The second man is from heaven. Not made of different material: he had a real body, born of a woman, that got tired and hungry and bled. He is from heaven in origin: he came from somewhere, which no other human being has ever done. Christ came from heaven, and his risen body belongs to the heavenly realm. The KJV, following later manuscripts, reads the second man is the Lord from heaven; the earliest lack the Lord, so most modern Bibles omit it.

The image of the man of heaven. Image (eikōn): we were born in Adam’s likeness (Genesis 5:3), and we know its features intimately: mortality, weakness, the pull toward what we know is wrong, the face in the mirror getting older. Nobody had to be taught to bear that image. The second is as certain as the first. Note the tense: we shall also bear, flat future, no condition attached. This is what Paul says in Romans, that those God foreknew he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:29), and what John says in one line: we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Predestined means that God settled it beforehand: the end of the believer’s story was decided by him before the story began, and it cannot be undone.

A note on the text. Many manuscripts, including most of the oldest, read let us bear, making it an exhortation; the ESV note mentions this. The two Greek words differ by a single vowel that sounded much the same when read aloud, so copyists could easily confuse them. The future we shall fits the context of the resurrection better, and it is the reading the argument requires, which is why most translations print it.

The gap closes. The man you have wanted to be and the man you are have never once been the same man; every Christian carries an internal record of the gap. On that day it closes. Not by lowering the standard, and not by gradual improvement finally arriving, but because the likeness of Christ, worked into his people slowly and against resistance, will be completed in an instant and will hold. There will be nothing left in you that he would have to overlook.

If I will bear his image then, why try to be like him now? Because the Spirit is already at work forming that image in you, and you are called to cooperate with him. We all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). The resurrection completes what sanctification begins. Sanctification is the Spirit’s patient remaking of a forgiven sinner, until heart and life grow like Christ’s. And the hope itself is a motive: everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure (1 John 3:3). You do not become like Christ in order to be saved; you become like him because you are saved, and the finished likeness is promised.

For worship. The Son of God came down from heaven and bore our image all the way to the grave, so that we, the men of dust, might bear his. He did not wait for us to become presentable; he wore the family likeness of Adam while it was still marked by death, and then he rose in a likeness death cannot touch. We know whose face we will wear, and whose face we will see. Glory to the Man from heaven, who has made the children of Adam the brothers of the King.

parallels.desc: you are dust

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul discloses the mystery of the last trumpet, when the dead are raised and the living changed in an instant, and death is swallowed up in victory. He gives thanks for the victory God gives through Christ, and draws the conclusion: stand firm and abound in the Lord’s work, for it is not in vain.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection as the Foundation of Present Labour

The chapter ends not with heaven but with work (v. 58). The resurrection gives hope for the future and also gives weight to the present: every act of love, faithfulness, service and endurance offered to Christ belongs to a creation that will be renewed, not thrown away. Herman Bavinck’s great theme was that grace restores nature: the resurrection does not cancel creation but redeems and glorifies it.

Anthony Hoekema makes the same point in his study of biblical eschatology: the resurrection is the guarantee that present labour is not in vain, because the God who raised Christ will also raise and renew the creation in which that labour was performed. The resurrection does not make the present world irrelevant; it makes it eternally significant.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians needed to hear that their dead were not lost, that their own work was not futile, and that the God who raised Christ would finish what he had begun in them. This hope is what lets love bear all things and endure all things (13:7). Now: Every generation asks whether a life means anything beyond its short span. Paul’s answer is yes, because the God who raised Jesus from the dead wastes nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Flesh and blood. The phrase is a Hebrew phrase for human nature in its present weak, mortal state (Matthew 16:17; Galatians 1:16), not a slur on physical existence, which Paul has spent fifteen verses defending. Bodies as they now are, mortal and corruptible, must be changed. It is not a moral judgement but a statement about fitness. You do not go deep-sea diving in a jacket.

He shared our flesh and blood. The phrase points to the wonder underneath the whole chapter. The Son of God, who had always possessed the kingdom, took the very nature that cannot inherit it. Since the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Hebrews 2:14). He entered mortal flesh, died in it, and was raised in it, changed, so that he now stands in the kingdom as the firstfruits, flesh and bone made imperishable (Luke 24:39). The change Paul announces is not a general upgrade for the human race. It is his people being made like him.

A mystery. A mystery in Paul is never a puzzle; it is a truth previously hidden, something that could not have been worked out and has now been disclosed by God. He is about to say something the church did not know.

We shall not all sleep. Here sleep means what it has meant all through the chapter: to die. Now the new information. The chapter so far has assumed the pattern of death and resurrection: sown, then raised. But not every believer will die. There will be a generation of Christians alive when Christ returns who will never be buried at all. They will not miss the transformation; they will reach it by a different road.

All changed. All believers, dead and living: changed (allassō) is exchanged, as one garment is exchanged for another.

Did Paul expect to be alive when Christ returned? He writes we because he speaks as one of the living church, which is always to be ready, and he did not know the day (1 Thessalonians 5:1–2). Elsewhere he speaks just as calmly of his own death (2 Corinthians 5:1–8; Philippians 1:21–23). We means believers generally; Paul did not know whether he would be alive then. He was not mistaken about a date; he never set one.

One with Thessalonica. Paul’s teaching here joins hands with what he had written to Thessalonica: the Lord descending with a cry of command and the sound of the trumpet, the dead in Christ rising first, and then those who are alive being caught up together with them to meet the Lord in the air (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). Christians of every persuasion share nearly all of it: that Jesus Christ will return personally, visibly and bodily; that the dead in Christ will be raised and the living transformed, in an instant and at his initiative; and that no believer of any generation will be left out.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the resurrection body is not flesh. Jesus’ risen body had flesh and bones (Luke 24:39). It means our bodies must be changed from mortality to immortality.

Will believers who are alive at his coming miss anything by not dying? No. They will not miss the resurrection; they will receive the same transformation in a different way. And those who have died will not be disadvantaged either: the dead in Christ rise first (1 Thessalonians 4:16). Both groups meet the Lord together, and both are changed into his likeness. Whether the Lord comes in your lifetime or you go to him first, you lose nothing. Either way, you will be with him and like him.

On a Tuesday. Live today as if he might come before evening, not in fear, but in readiness: with sins confessed, quarrels made up, and your face turned toward the sky.

verseByVerse.quote: in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a moment. Paul reaches for two measures of time and both of them mean the same thing: there will be no process. In a moment translates en atomō: in an uncuttable instant. It is the word from which we get atom, and it meant the smallest thing that cannot be divided further. Paul is saying the change will happen in a slice of time too thin to have parts.

In the twinkling of an eye. The homelier version of the same idea. As fast as a blink, or faster: the flicker, the involuntary movement of the eye that is over before it has been noticed. The change will not be gradual.

The slowest and the fastest work of God. This is not what anyone would have guessed. Everything else in the Christian life is slow. Sanctification takes decades and moves backwards on many days. Grief takes years. Prayers are answered over a lifetime, or not visibly at all. A believer’s whole experience trains him to expect God to work at the pace of growing things. And then this: no preparation, no gradual improvement. A woman who has spent eleven years unable to leave her chair is in the next instant not merely well but imperishable. A man in a churchyard since 1840 whose stone is illegible is in the same instant standing.

At the last trumpet. A trumpet announced great acts of God and summoned his people (Exodus 19:16; Joel 2:1). In Israel trumpets summoned the assembly and called the camp to move (Numbers 10:1–10), and announced a new king (1 Kings 1:34). This one does all three at once. The last trumpet signals the end of history and the return of Christ (Matthew 24:31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16), and it is last because there will never again be anyone who needs calling.

The dead will be raised. First the dead are raised, then the living are changed (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17), and all together meet the Lord. Note who is doing what. The dead do not rise by their own power; they will be raised, the same passive that was used of Christ at verse 4. Nobody in that vast company contributes anything to his own resurrection. They are called, and they come, because the voice that calls them is the voice of the Son of God himself: all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out (John 5:28–29). It is the voice that once said, Lazarus, come out (John 11:43).

Where Christians differ: the rapture. Many dispensationalists (Christians who divide history into distinct eras and expect a separate future for national Israel) teach a secret rapture: Christ will come invisibly to take believers away before a seven-year tribulation, and then return again visibly later. This commentary’s view: Paul says this happens at the last trumpet, which suggests the end, not a stage before further events. The New Testament describes one return of Christ, visible, public and glorious (Matthew 24:27, 30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; Revelation 1:7), at which the dead are raised, the living changed, and all are judged. There is no secret rapture. Believers will be caught up to meet the Lord in the air, to welcome him as he comes, and then be with him forever.

The case fairly stated. Christians who hold a pre-tribulation rapture point to promises that believers are not destined for wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9) and will be kept from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world (Revelation 3:10), and many of them love the Scriptures and read them with great care. Others, including amillennial, postmillennial (expecting the gospel to bring a long age of blessing before Christ returns) and historic premillennial Christians, see one coming. They note that Paul ties this moment to the last trumpet, the public trumpet of Christ’s coming (Matthew 24:31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16), and to the resurrection that ends death (vv. 54–55). The word for meeting the Lord in the air was used of citizens going out to meet an arriving king and escorting him into the city, not of being taken away from it. That is why the more likely reading is one coming of Christ, visible to all, at which the dead are raised and the living changed together. It is a poor use of a promise this size to make it the occasion of a quarrel among people who are all waiting for the same trumpet.

Will there be one resurrection or two? One general resurrection, at Christ’s return. Jesus said an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgement (John 5:28–29). Paul spoke of a resurrection of both the just and the unjust (Acts 24:15). This chapter dwells on believers, because its purpose is comfort and hope; but the same trumpet that raises the saints to glory summons all to judgement (Matthew 25:31–46). That is why the gospel is urgent now. Premillennial Christians see two resurrections a thousand years apart in Revelation 20:4–6; this commentary takes the first resurrection there as the believer’s new life with Christ now, with one bodily resurrection at his return.

For worship. The certainty of that morning does not rest on the strength of anyone’s faith. Everyone in the churchyard will be raised by the same voice, at the same instant, with the same ease. The believing dead of every age, apostles and martyrs, mothers and children, the forgotten saints of a thousand village churches, will stand up in a moment, imperishable, and look on the face of their King. He who was laid in a tomb will open every tomb, and the last trumpet will announce him.
verseByVerse.note: A trumpet announced great acts of God and summoned his people.

verseByVerse.quote: For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality. When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put on the imperishable. The verb is put on (endyō), the word for getting dressed. Paul does not say the perishable body is discarded and a better one issued. He says it is clothed, and the thing underneath is still there (2 Corinthians 5:2–4). That is the difference between resurrection and replacement. The same man who has struggled and prayed and failed and hung on is going to be dressed in immortality, and it will be him inside it. And this perishable body, Paul writes: not the perishable, but this, the body we have now. One imagines him gesturing at himself as he dictated, a man with a scarred back and perhaps failing eyes, saying: this one.

Immortality. Immortality (athanasia) is deathlessness. Only God has immortality in himself (1 Timothy 6:16); he will give it to his people.

Immortality brought to light. If only God has immortality, how will mortals receive it? Through the One who is both. Paul says it in his last letter: our Saviour Christ Jesus abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel (2 Timothy 1:10). The immortality the saints will put on is not a quality they develop but the life of the risen Christ shared with them. He went into death as a mortal man and came out of it never to die again, and he is the first human being ever to wear what Paul here describes. On that day his people will be dressed in what he already wears.

Must. Press the word must: the language of necessity, not of likelihood or hope. Necessary to whom? Not to us; nobody here arranged anything. It is necessary because God has purposed a new creation and determined that his people will live in it, and a perishable body cannot. The obligation sits on his side. He has bound himself by his promise, and he is the God who keeps his word.

Swallowed up in victory. The quotation is from Isaiah 25:8, and Isaiah is describing a feast. On his mountain the LORD will make for all peoples a feast of rich food; he will swallow up the veil spread over all nations; he will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces (Isaiah 25:6–8). Swallowed up (katapinō) is gulped down, devoured. Death is not defeated in a negotiated settlement. It is taken in and gone, the way the sea takes something and closes over it. The thing that has swallowed every human being who ever lived is itself swallowed at last.

The faces. The detail that most people need is the one about the faces. God is not described as issuing a decree about grief. He is described as coming close enough to wipe tears off individual faces with his own hand, which is what he is doing at the end of the Bible too (Revelation 21:4). Whatever else that day contains, it contains a God who has come near enough to touch the people who have been crying.

How do I hold on to this when I am grieving? Slowly, and with help. Grief does not obey arguments, and God does not ask you to stop grieving; he promises to wipe away tears, which means there will be tears to wipe. Read these verses aloud, even when they feel far off. Let others pray for you when you cannot pray. Visit the grave, if it helps, and say there what Paul says here. Mourn honestly, and keep company with the hope of the feast. The day is coming when the Lord will lift your face with his own hand, and the person you have lost in Christ will be at the table.

On a Tuesday. If you know someone who is grieving this month, send them Isaiah 25:8 with one line telling them you are praying.

parallels.desc: he will swallow up death forever

verseByVerse.quote: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting? Paul turns and speaks to death directly, and the tone is not respectful. He is quoting Hosea (Hosea 13:14), where the questions probably call up death’s plagues against unfaithful Israel; Paul, standing on the far side of the empty tomb, turns them into a taunt song over defeated death: the sort of thing shouted after an enemy who has been beaten and is being watched off the field. Where is your victory? Death has had a total record. It has never lost a single engagement in the history of the world; every person it has come for, it has taken. And Paul stands in front of it and asks what it has won.

The sting. Then the word to concentrate on: sting, the barb of a scorpion or a bee, the part that can actually kill you. The old illustration is still the best one. A honeybee that has stung has left its sting behind. It can still fly at your face and make a grown man leave a picnic, but it cannot hurt you, because the thing that made it dangerous is gone, and a child who knows that will stand still while it buzzes round his head. That is the Christian’s position. Death may still frighten, but it cannot destroy believers. (The KJV reads O grave in the second question, and puts sting first, following later manuscripts; the earliest have death twice.)

The sting of death is sin. Paul explains the mechanism rather than leaving it as a picture. Death is the wages of sin (Romans 6:23). What makes death terrible is not that it ends the body; animals die and it is sad, but not frightening in this way. What makes it terrible is that it is the doorway to judgement for a guilty person. Sin gives death its barb, and Christ removed the barb by bearing our sin.

And the power of sin is the law. The law gives sin its power, by exposing it, condemning it, and even provoking it (Romans 7:7–13). The law is not the villain; it is holy, righteous and good (Romans 7:12). But it turns wrongdoing into a documented offence: it names it, measures it, and pronounces the sentence, and so gives sin its legal force.

Follow the chain backwards. Death is fearful because of sin. Sin has its power from the law. And Christ has dealt with both: he kept the law we broke and bore the curse it pronounced (Galatians 3:13). So sin has no power to condemn believers, and death has no sting. It is still an enemy. It cannot destroy a Christian, and it never will. This has a consequence for the religious person who hopes his good record will see him through death. Trying harder to keep the law cannot draw death’s sting, because the law is what gives sin its power to condemn; leaning on it is leaning on the prosecution’s case. Only the One who kept the law for us and bore its curse can disarm it.

What about those who die without Christ? For them death keeps its sting, because their sin remains on their own account. Death is then not a doorway to rest but to judgement, and Scripture warns plainly of conscious, eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). That is why the gospel is not a pleasant extra but the most urgent message in the world. The sting is drawn only for those who are in Christ, who has borne their sin. If you are not yet trusting him, come to him now, while death is still at a distance. He receives all who come. And if you are grieving someone who seemed to die without him, you do not know all that passed between that soul and God at the end; leave them with the Judge of all the earth, who will do right (Genesis 18:25).

On a Tuesday. Say Paul’s taunt aloud at the end of a hard day, and again when you hear bad news from a doctor.

For worship. Death drove its sting into the Son of God, and the sting stayed in him. He took into his own body the curse of the law and the wages of sin, and he exhausted them, until there was no condemnation left for anyone who is in him. Death still buzzes at us, but its barb is in the cross. O death, where is your sting? It was spent on Golgotha, and the Lord of life has gone out into the morning with his people following behind.

parallels.desc: O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting?

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But thanks be to God. The proofs are finished, the objections answered, and Paul does the only thing left: he gives thanks (Romans 7:25).

Who gives us the victory. Read the verbs. Nobody in the sentence wins anything. The victory is given, handed over as a present, to people who were not on the field. Every Christian who will ever be raised was, at the decisive moment, dead in trespasses and sins, and had contributed nothing to the outcome except the problem. And the tense matters: gives. Present. God is giving us the victory now, over sin, death and the law, to people still in perishable bodies, still burying their friends, still afraid of the diagnosis. The thing has been settled and the settlement is in force.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ. The channel is named, as it always is in Paul: through his death, which removed sin’s sting, and his resurrection, which defeated death. Not through our grasp of the doctrine, our steadiness under pressure, or the quality of our dying. Christians have died well and Christians have died badly, frightened, confused, heavily medicated, saying nothing memorable, and it makes no difference to the outcome, because the victory was won by somebody else. Paul uses a stronger form of the same word in Romans: in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us (Romans 8:37). Not merely surviving the engagement, but coming out of it with more than was taken in.

What does victory look like on a hard day? It rarely looks like triumph. It looks like a believer who falls and gets up again, who confesses sin instead of hiding it, who keeps praying when prayer feels empty, who weeps at a graveside and still sings the hymn. Victory in Christ is not the absence of struggle but the certainty of the outcome. You may feel defeated and still be more than a conqueror, because the battle that decides everything has already been won. On the hardest days, do not look for the feeling of victory; look at the One who gives it, and thank him.

For worship. He was dead. Properly dead, pronounced dead by soldiers who did this for a living and knew when a job was finished (John 19:33–34), then wrapped with spices and shut behind a stone by friends with no expectation whatever of seeing him again. Everything that has ever terrified the human race had done its complete work on him, and had done it with the full cooperation of the authorities, the crowd, and his own friends. And on the first day of the week he rose, and left the cloth that had been on his head folded up in a place by itself, and went out into a garden where a woman was crying, and said her name (John 20:7, 15–16). Thanks be to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, my beloved brothers. Fifty-seven verses of the highest doctrine in the letter, and the conclusion is about Monday. After rebuking them throughout the letter, Paul calls them beloved. He does not say: therefore look forward to heaven. He says: therefore get on with it. The very next words of the letter make the same point: chapter 16 opens with a collection of money for poor believers in Jerusalem (16:1). From the last trumpet Paul turns straight to the offering, because the resurrection is meant to be lived out in ordinary things.

Steadfast, immovable. Steadfast (hedraios) is firmly seated; immovable (ametakinētos) is not to be moved. Two words meaning much the same thing, laid one on the other for weight: not shifted by false teaching or hardship. This is the answer to a church that had been blown about by every teacher, every fashion and every clever argument all through this letter.

Always abounding. Abounding (perisseuō) is an overflow word: not managing or doing one’s bit, but more than is required, spilling over the edge.
