A man is being told to spend himself in a body he has just been told is perishable, on the ground that it is going to be raised. The doctrine does not produce detachment from this life. It produces holy recklessness in it. Nor is the strength his own: the Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in him (Romans 8:11), and the overflow comes from that spring.

Your labour is not in vain. The clause the whole chapter has been travelling toward. Labour (kopos) is toil to exhaustion. Not in vain (ou kenos, not empty) is the word that has haunted this chapter: if Christ is not raised, the preaching and the faith are empty (v. 14); Paul’s grace was not empty (v. 10). Now it lands where the reader lives. Because Christ is risen, nothing done for him is wasted.

In the Lord. The words in the Lord carry the whole promise, and the Lord’s own story shows why. Isaiah gives the Servant of the LORD a sentence every tired believer has felt: I have laboured in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing, and yet my right is with the LORD (Isaiah 49:4). Jesus lived that. Some three years of preaching ended with his friends scattered and his body in a tomb, and on Friday evening it looked like the most wasted life in history. On Sunday the Father answered. Because his labour was not in vain, nothing done in him can be. The work of his people is joined to the One whose work God vindicated by raising him from the dead. Nor does the promise wait for flawless work, for none of ours is; it is offered in the One whose obedience was perfect and is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), and God accepts it for his sake (1 Peter 2:5).

Not in vain, concretely. It is the sort of promise that evaporates when left general. The mother who has prayed for a son for thirty years and watched him get worse. The man who taught a Sunday class of eight children for a decade and has no idea what became of any of them. The woman who nursed a husband through seven years of dementia, thanked by nobody, remembered by a man who did not know her name. The missionary who gave forty years to a place and left it with three converts and a small building. Every one of them has looked at what they have to show for it and thought: that was nothing. And every one of them has been wrong, on the authority of this verse. Not your labour will probably bear fruit eventually, but your labour is not in vain: the work itself is not lost, because it was done in the Lord, and what is done in the Lord belongs to a world that is not going to be thrown away but raised.

What counts as the work of the Lord? Far more than church activities. It includes preaching, evangelism and serving in the church, certainly. But it also includes any work done in the Lord: for his sake, in faith, by his strength. Changing a nappy, filling in a spreadsheet honestly, caring for an elderly parent, visiting a lonely neighbour, praying in secret, raising children in the faith. Paul told household slaves, whose work no one praised, to do it with all their heart as for the Lord, because the Lord himself would repay them (Colossians 3:23–24). The question is not whether the task is religious, but whether it is done in him.

On a Tuesday. Take the task that most feels like nothing, the one no one notices, and do it today as an offering to the risen Christ.

15.text: <sup>1</sup>Now I would remind you, brothers, of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, in which you stand,<sup>2</sup>and by which you are being saved, if you hold fast to the word I preached to you—unless you believed in vain.<sup>3</sup>For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures,<sup>4</sup>that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures,<sup>5</sup>and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.<sup>6</sup>Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep.<sup>7</sup>Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles.<sup>8</sup>Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me.<sup>9</sup>For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.<sup>10</sup>But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me.<sup>11</sup>Whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed.<sup>12</sup>Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?<sup>13</sup>But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised.<sup>14</sup>And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.<sup>15</sup>We are even found to be misrepresenting God, because we testified about God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if it is true that the dead are not raised.<sup>16</sup>For if the dead are not raised, not even Christ has been raised.<sup>17</sup>And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.<sup>18</sup>Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished.<sup>19</sup>If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.<sup>20</sup>But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.<sup>21</sup>For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead.<sup>22</sup>For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.<sup>23</sup>But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ.<sup>24</sup>Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and every authority and power.<sup>25</sup>For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet.<sup>26</sup>The last enemy to be destroyed is death.<sup>27</sup>For “God has put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when it says, “all things are put in subjection,” it is plain that he is excepted who put all things in subjection under him.<sup>28</sup>When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all.<sup>29</sup>Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf?<sup>30</sup>Why are we in danger every hour?<sup>31</sup>I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day!<sup>32</sup>What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”<sup>33</sup>Do not be deceived: “Bad company ruins good morals.”<sup>34</sup>Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning. For some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.<sup>35</sup>But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?”<sup>36</sup>You foolish person! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.<sup>37</sup>And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain.<sup>38</sup>But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body.<sup>39</sup>For not all flesh is the same, but there is one kind for humans, another for animals, another for birds, and another for fish.<sup>40</sup>There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another.<sup>41</sup>There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory.<sup>42</sup>So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable.<sup>43</sup>It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.<sup>44</sup>It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.<sup>45</sup>Thus it is written, “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit.<sup>46</sup>But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual.<sup>47</sup>The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven.<sup>48</sup>As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven.<sup>49</sup>Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven.<sup>50</sup>I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable.<sup>51</sup>Behold! 16.title: The Collection, the Plans, and the Farewell
16.overview:
After the end of chapter 15, the letter comes down to practical matters, which is itself a lesson: the hope of the resurrection is what makes ordinary faithfulness not in vain. First comes the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem (described more fully in 2 Corinthians 8–9): regular, proportionate giving on the first day of the week, carried by messengers the church itself chooses.

Then Paul’s travel plans. He is writing from Ephesus, where a wide door has opened amid much opposition, and he plans to stay until Pentecost before coming through Macedonia to Corinth, perhaps for the winter, when sea travel stopped. Timothy must be made welcome, and Apollos will come later. Five brisk commands follow, with a word of honour for the household of Stephanas and the three men who brought the Corinthians’ letter. The letter ends with greetings, Paul’s own signature, a solemn warning, the ancient prayer Maranatha, and grace and love.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Collection for the Saints
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul gives instructions for the collection for the believers in Jerusalem and for carrying it there honestly.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Collection as a Gospel Act

Paul’s fullest teaching on the collection, in 2 Corinthians 8–9, grounds generosity in the grace of Christ, who though he was rich became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9). The collection is not a tax but a sharing in the pattern of the cross: material help given freely across economic and ethnic lines, showing that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek. Gentile churches supporting the Jewish church in Jerusalem put Romans 15:27 into practice: those who have shared Israel’s spiritual blessings serve Israel’s poor with material ones.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jerusalem church was poor, perhaps because of the famine of Acts 11:28, or because Jewish believers were cut off from the family and trade networks that had supported them. The collection was an act of solidarity across the deepest social divide of the ancient world. Now: Regular, proportionate, planned giving is still the wisest pattern for Christian giving, and tying it to the first day of the week makes it part of the church’s worship.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the collection for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also are to do. On the first day of every week, each of you is to put something aside and store it up, as he may prosper, so that there will be no collecting when I come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 16 brings the letter to a practical close, and it is no less spiritual for being practical: the hope of chapter 15 is lived out in ordinary faithfulness. Paul gives instructions for the collection for poor believers in Jerusalem: regular, proportionate, planned giving each Lord’s Day, carried by trustworthy people (vv. 1–4). He shares his travel plans, commends Timothy and explains Apollos’s delay (vv. 5–12). He gives a burst of short commands: be watchful, stand firm, be courageous and strong, do everything in love, and honour those who serve, like the household of Stephanas (vv. 13–18). Then come greetings, a holy kiss, his own signature, a solemn warning, the ancient prayer Maranatha, and a closing word of grace and love (vv. 19–24).

The setting. The collection was one of the great projects of Paul’s life. The believers in Jerusalem were poor: there had been famine (Acts 11:28–30), and Jewish believers who confessed Christ were often cut off from the family and trade networks that had supported them. So Paul spent years gathering money from Gentile congregations around the Aegean for a Jewish church most of them would never meet, and he risked his freedom delivering it (Romans 15:25–31). It was not for his own ministry. The gift expressed the unity of Gentile and Jewish believers in one body.

The collection for the saints. Another topic from their letter (now concerning, 7:1). After the resurrection, money. The transition only looks jarring. Paul has just spent fifty-eight verses proving that the dead will be raised, and the very next thing he mentions is a hardship fund for a church some eight hundred miles away. The resurrection does not lift Christians above the practical. It sends them back into it with open hands.

As I directed the churches of Galatia. Corinth was not alone. The churches of Galatia, Macedonia and Achaia were all taking part (2 Corinthians 8–9). Four things follow in one sentence, and together they are one of the New Testament’s most practical paragraphs on giving.

On the first day of every week. It is regular. Sunday, the day of Christ’s resurrection: the church gathered for worship on that day (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10), and Paul ties the setting aside to it. The next words, put something aside and store it up, are literally by himself, and may mean the money was laid by at home until Paul came; either way the gift was tied to the day of resurrection. This is one of the earliest pieces of evidence that the first day had become the Christian day of worship.

Giving on resurrection day. The day was chosen for a reason. The first day of the week was the day the women found the tomb empty (Mark 16:2), the day the risen Lord stood among his disciples and said, Peace be with you, and the day he came to them again eight days later (John 20:19, 26). So every coin set aside in Corinth was set aside on the day that proved that labour in the Lord is not in vain (15:58), and that the poor saints in Jerusalem would rise with their givers. Generosity is what resurrection hope looks like when it reaches the purse.

Is Sunday the Christian Sabbath? Faithful Christians answer differently, and both views deserve a fair hearing. Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8), hold that the fourth commandment still stands as a moral law, with the day changed to the first day of the week in honour of the resurrection: the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, to be kept holy in worship and rest. Other Christians, including many Baptists and Reformed believers, see the Sabbath as a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), and hold that while the apostolic habit of meeting on the first day is wise and good, no day binds the conscience as the Sabbath did (Romans 14:5–6). This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10), and that the Lord’s Day is his gift: Christians gladly set the first day apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom, not as a binding law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). Readers should know that here this commentary parts company with the 1689 Confession it follows on baptism, which holds the first view; that view is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. Both agree that the Lord’s Day is the day of the church’s worship, and that it is a gift to be treasured rather than a burden to be minimised.

Each of you. It is personal: not the wealthy patrons or whoever feels moved. Everybody, rich or poor, gives, deliberately and not on impulse.

As he may prosper. It is proportionate: the sum is not fixed but scaled to income. That single phrase protects the poor from a demand they cannot meet and prevents the rich from discharging the duty with something they will not notice. Generous giving flows from God’s generosity to us (2 Corinthians 9:8).

No collecting when I come. And it is planned in advance, so that Paul’s arrival is not the occasion of a scramble or a high-pressure appeal. He does not want his visit remembered as the week they were asked for money.

Where Christians differ: tithing. Some teach that Christians are bound to give exactly a tenth, as under the law; others that no standard applies. This commentary’s view: The New Testament does not command a fixed percentage. It calls for regular, proportionate, generous, cheerful giving, in response to grace (2 Corinthians 9:6–7). The tithe is a helpful starting point and a biblical benchmark, and many Christians rightly give more. Giving is part of worship on the Lord’s Day.

Why Paul names no figure. Paul had every opportunity to name a figure here and in two whole chapters on giving (2 Corinthians 8–9), and he never does. As he may prosper is deliberately not a number, and it is harder rather than easier, because a fixed percentage can be paid and forgotten while a proportion has to be rethought whenever circumstances change. And when Paul wants to move people to generosity he appeals not to a rule but to a Person: you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). The Christian does not give a percentage of his income to a cause. He gives, out of what he has been given, to people who have less, because that is precisely what was done for him, and the One who did it did not calculate a proportion.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving earns God’s favour. It means grace makes us generous. The religious heart is tempted to give in order to feel safe with God; the irreligious heart holds on to its money because money feels like safety. The gospel frees both. In Christ you already have a treasure that moth and rust cannot touch (Matthew 6:19–21), so you can give without trying to buy anything, and without fear of running out.

What if I am in debt or can barely pay my bills? Then give something, however small, and give it gladly; as he may prosper protects you from a demand you cannot meet. The widow’s two coins were worth more in Christ’s eyes than the gifts of the rich (Mark 12:41–44). God does not want you to neglect your family or your honest debts to give (1 Timothy 5:8). Pay what you owe, live simply, ask for wise help with your budget if you need it, and give regularly what you can. As your circumstances improve, let your giving rise with them. The habit matters more than the amount.

On a Tuesday. Sit down this week with your income in front of you, pray, and set a figure for your giving, in proportion to what God has given you; and include in it something for believers in need beyond your own church.

For worship. The Lord of glory owned the cattle on a thousand hills (Psalm 50:10), and he was laid in a manger, and later in a borrowed tomb, so that beggars might inherit a kingdom. Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift (2 Corinthians 9:15), and blessed be the God who loves a cheerful giver because he is one.
verseByVerse.note: The collection was for the poor believers in Jerusalem. The first day of the week is Sunday, the day Christians met.

verseByVerse.quote: And when I arrive, I will send those whom you accredit by letter to carry your gift to Jerusalem. If it seems advisable that I should go also, they will accompany me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those whom you accredit. A quietly important note for any ministry that handles money. Accredit (dokimazō) means to approve after testing. Paul, an apostle with every right to be trusted, does not carry the money himself. The funds travel in the hands of men the Corinthians themselves have chosen and accredited, so he will never be alone with the money. It is their gift, and they appoint its escort.

Your gift. Gift (charis) is the word for grace. Giving is an act of grace (2 Corinthians 8:1, 6–7): it begins in God’s grace to us, and it carries grace to others. Grace here is kindness given to people who did not earn it. The Corinthians had received forgiveness for nothing, and now they pass on, in coins, a small share of that kindness to poor believers who can never repay them.

If it seems advisable. Even whether the apostle travels with the delivery is left open. In the end, Paul did go, with representatives from several churches (Acts 20:4; 24:17).

A debt to Jerusalem. Why Jerusalem? Paul explains to the Romans: if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings (Romans 15:27). The greatest of those blessings is a Person. From Israel, according to the flesh, came the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever (Romans 9:5). So Greek money travelling to a Jewish church was the thanks of the nations for a Jewish Messiah: Corinthians who had received the Son of David sending bread to his poor kinsmen. Every coin in that box said that the wall between Jew and Gentile was down, and that Christ had made both one (Ephesians 2:14).

Financial integrity. Paul explains elsewhere: we take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man (2 Corinthians 8:20–21). Note the two audiences. A ministry must be honest before God, and also visibly, checkably honest before people who are not obliged to think well of it.

Apostolic practice. This is not modern governance imported into the Bible. Many a scandal could have been prevented by following a verse written in the fifties: more than one person responsible, two signatures, an audited account, a treasurer who is not the preacher, and no one, however trusted, ever alone with the cash. Not because Christians are suspected, but because the gospel is worth protecting from suspicion.

How can I know whether a ministry I give to is trustworthy? Ask the questions Paul’s practice answers. Is more than one person responsible for the money? Are the accounts audited and the figures available to givers? Do the leaders live in a way that matches what they ask of others? Is the ministry accountable to a church or a board that can say no? Does it tell you plainly what your gift will do? A trustworthy ministry will welcome such questions, as Paul did. A ministry that is offended by them, or that pressures you to give quickly and emotionally, has given you your answer.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul shares his travel plans, held under the Lord’s permission, and explains why he is staying in Ephesus for now. He asks the church to welcome Timothy and reports that Apollos will come later.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Missionary Network and the Unity of the Gospel

Paul’s travel plans are more than logistics. The early churches were not independent congregations operating in isolation but a network bound together by the gospel, apostolic ministry, financial sharing and personal friendship. Paul’s letters are part of that network: the apostle present at a distance through what he wrote.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s care for Timothy’s welcome and his easy mention of Apollos as a brother show the warmth and shared work of early Christian ministry. Now: Christian ministry is easily treated as a competition. Paul’s warmth toward Apollos, whose admirers had been used as a weapon against him, shows the largeness of a heart shaped by the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: I will visit you after passing through Macedonia, for I intend to pass through Macedonia, and perhaps I will stay with you or even spend the winter, so that you may help me on my journey, wherever I go. For I do not want to see you now just in passing. I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Macedonia. Paul’s plan: from Ephesus, through Macedonia (northern Greece: Philippi, Thessalonica), then south to Corinth (Acts 19:21; 20:1–3).

Spend the winter. Sea travel stopped in winter; to winter somewhere was to be stuck there until spring. He did eventually spend three months in Greece (Acts 20:3), where he probably wrote Romans. And there is warmth in it: Paul is proposing to be shut in for months with the most difficult church he has.

Help me on my journey. Help on my journey (propempō) means to provide for a missionary’s travel: food, money, companions. Paul was willing to receive this kind of help from them, even though he refused payment for his preaching (9:15–18).

Not just in passing. That is what a man says about people he loves, not about a problem he is managing.

If the Lord permits. Paul makes detailed plans: a route, a season, a length of stay. There is nothing unspiritual about a diary. But every plan he makes sits under a clause. James puts it more sharply: you do not know what tomorrow will bring; you ought to say, if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (James 4:14–15). It is not a superstitious formula to be attached to sentences. It is a settled awareness that the diary is a proposal and not a contract.

The Lord of the itinerary. In Paul’s letters the Lord is almost always Jesus. The apostle’s winter plans sit under the will of the risen Christ, the same Lord whose Spirit had once barred the road into Bithynia and sent him instead across to Macedonia (Acts 16:7–10). That is the comfort inside the clause. The one who may overrule the diary is not chance, nor a distant deity, but the Shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep and now directs his servants’ movements for the good of his churches. A plan changed under his hand is never a wasted winter.

When plans change. In fact it did not go as written. Paul’s movements changed, and he had to answer the charge of being unreliable in his next letter (2 Corinthians 1:15–2:1). If the Lord permits has to be meant in advance, so that when the year goes differently there is something already in place to stand on.

How do I hold plans loosely without being unreliable? Make your plans carefully, keep your word wherever you can, and tell people honestly when circumstances change. Saying if the Lord permits is not an escape clause for breaking promises lightly; Paul was grieved when he was thought unreliable. It is a humble admission that God governs the future and you do not. So plan, commit, and work hard at what you have promised. When God’s providence closes a door, through illness, a change at work or a family need, accept it without bitterness, explain it kindly to those affected, and trust that his plan is better than yours.

For worship. The Lord Jesus did not visit us in passing. He came and stayed, and dwelt among us full of grace and truth, and he has promised to be with us always, to the end of the age.

verseByVerse.quote: But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Until Pentecost. Pentecost fell fifty days after Passover, in late spring. Paul wrote this letter in Ephesus, probably in the early months of the year.

A wide door. Two facts about the same situation, joined by and. A door is an opportunity for the gospel (2 Corinthians 2:12; Colossians 4:3; Acts 14:27). Wide and effective (energēs, active, powerful): work that works, that gets somewhere. Ephesus was proving fruitful, and Luke records what that looked like: two years of daily teaching, the word spreading through the whole province of Asia, sorcerers burning their books in public (Acts 19:9–10, 19–20). He is staying because something is actually happening, and he can tell the difference between motion and progress.

Many adversaries. The same city, the same season. Within a short time the silversmiths would start a riot that filled the theatre for two hours and could have cost him his life (Acts 19:23–41). Paul does not write but there is opposition, as though the second clause qualified the first. He writes and. The adversaries are part of the report, and they are not a reason to leave; they are named in the same breath as the reason to stay.

The servant and his Master. Paul’s and is the pattern Jesus himself announced. If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you, he told his disciples (John 15:20), and: in the world you will have tribulation, but take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33). The widest door of all was opened through the fiercest opposition of all. Herod and Pilate, the nations and the people gathered against the Lord’s Anointed, and did what God’s hand had planned beforehand (Acts 4:27–28), and the cross they raised became the way of salvation for the world. So an apostle who finds adversaries crowding round an open door is not off course. He is walking where his Master walked.

Reading circumstances the right way round. It is easy to read the two facts the wrong way round. A door opens, resistance follows, and the resistance is taken as proof that the door was not from God. Paul assumes the opposite. Where the gospel is advancing, something pushes back. Opposition is not a sign that God has closed the door; often it means the door is open, and the absence of opposition may only mean that nothing has been disturbed.

How do I tell an open door with opposition from a closed door? The rule cuts both ways, and both halves are needed. Not every difficulty is proof that you are on the right road; some obstacles are God closing a door, and Paul himself was once forbidden by the Spirit to go where he intended (Acts 16:6–7). But opposition by itself never disqualified an opportunity. The test is not the size of the difficulty; it is what the difficulty is made of. Opposition from people who do not want the gospel to advance is evidence that it is advancing. A closed road, an exhausted body, a family that needs you at home, a door that simply will not open however hard it is pushed: those are different, and a wise Christian reads them differently, with prayer and the counsel of others.

For worship. Christ is the one who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens (Revelation 3:7). He set before his church an open door, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. The riots of Ephesus came and went, the temple of Artemis fell into ruins, and the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily (Acts 19:20). The Lord who opens wide doors is stronger than every adversary.
verseByVerse.note: Pentecost fell fifty days after Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: When Timothy comes, see that you put him at ease among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am. So let no one despise him. Help him on his way in peace, that he may return to me, for I am expecting him with the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put him at ease. Paul is sending a young man into the hardest congregation he has, and he writes ahead. At ease (aphobōs) is without fear. The Corinthians could be intimidating. Timothy was young, and Paul would later have to tell him to let no one despise him for his youth (1 Timothy 4:12). He seems to have been prone to timidity; Paul writes elsewhere about his tears (2 Timothy 1:4) and tells him that God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control (2 Timothy 1:7). Corinth graded people by eloquence and presence, and before long some there would say that Paul’s own bodily presence was weak and his speech of no account (2 Corinthians 10:10).

The work of the Lord. The safeguard Paul offers is not a claim about Timothy’s gifts. He does not say Timothy is a fine preacher, or more capable than he looks. He says: he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am. The same work. That is the whole credential. Timothy carries Paul’s authority as his representative (4:17). Paul cuts across confidence, accent and bearing with a question about what a man is doing.

Let no one despise him. Not for his youth, and not for his temperament; and send him back to Paul in peace, provided for.

The work of a crucified Lord. Timothy’s only credential is the work of the Lord, and this letter has already said what kind of Lord that is. God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong (1:27), and the centre of the gospel is Christ crucified, the weakness of God that is stronger than men (1:25). The Lord himself had no form or majesty that we should look at him (Isaiah 53:2). So a church that despised Timothy for being unimpressive would be despising the very pattern of the gospel it had believed. An unimposing young man doing the work of the crucified Christ is not an awkward exception in the kingdom. He is what it looks like. Underneath the habit of grading preachers lies a quiet idol: we want leaders who make us look impressive. The gospel takes that need away, because our standing comes from Christ, and he is not ashamed of us.

A word for every Timothy. For anyone who has felt too young, too quiet, too unimpressive for the room: timidity is not a disqualification. It is a thing the family is supposed to make allowances for.

What does putting someone at ease actually look like? It is work, and somebody has to decide to do it. Not merely refraining from crushing someone, but actively setting him at ease: being the person who goes over first, who asks the question that lets a nervous newcomer talk about something he knows, who does not leave him standing at the edge of a room with a cup in his hand. Learn his name and use it. Introduce him to one other person. Thank a young preacher for something specific in his sermon rather than offering a critique at the door. Pray for him, and tell him you are. Every church has a Timothy in it on any given Sunday. The command is not to admire him. It is to go and put him at ease.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy was young and perhaps timid.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning our brother Apollos, I strongly urged him to visit you with the other brothers, but it was not at all his will to come now. He will come when he has opportunity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning our brother Apollos. A short verse, remarkable in three directions. Perhaps the Corinthians had asked for Apollos to come. He is the other name in the faction fight, I follow Paul, or I follow Apollos (1:12), the eloquent Alexandrian (Acts 18:24) whose admirers had been used as a stick to beat Paul with. Four chapters were spent dismantling that party spirit. And here is Paul, at the end of the same letter, calling him our brother Apollos.

I strongly urged him. That is the first remarkable thing. Paul and Apollos were not rivals, whatever the factions in Corinth thought (3:5–9), and Paul is actively trying to send his supposed rival to the church that prefers him.

Not his will to come now. The second remarkable thing is that Apollos said no, and Paul reports it without complaint and without appealing to his authority to overrule him. Apollos may well have had a good reason, and the obvious one is staring out of the text: a church divided into a Paul party and an Apollos party is not helped by the arrival of Apollos (1:12). Staying away may have been the most loving thing he could do, and it would have cost him a warm welcome. The Greek may also mean that it was not God’s will for him to come now.

When he has opportunity. The third remarkable thing: no coolness, no door shut. Two servants of the same Lord disagreeing about timing, and the friendship entirely intact. A great deal of damage in churches would be avoided if Christians could learn to let a no be a no without treating it as a verdict on the relationship.

Is Christ divided? How could the two men at the centre of a party quarrel stay friends? Because neither of them was the centre. When Corinth said I follow Paul, and I follow Apollos, Paul answered: Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? (1:13). And later: all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s (3:21–23). Two servants who both belong to the one Lord do not need to compete for a church that belongs to him too. Our brother Apollos is what the gospel sounds like when the Saviour, and not the preacher, is the one being followed.

Christian freedom among leaders. Even an apostle did not command Apollos. Christian workers are fellow servants, not a chain of command (3:5). Apostolic authority was real, and Paul had just used it heavily in this letter. But it did not extend to running another man’s diary. Where Scripture commands, there is no discretion; where it does not, a Christian is free to weigh a matter and reach a different conclusion from someone he respects, and neither man has sinned.

How do I find God’s will when Scripture does not settle a decision? The way Apollos did. He did not receive a revelation telling him to stay where he was. He weighed a request from a man he respected, considered the situation, formed a judgement, and acted on it, and the New Testament records the outcome without a hint that he should have waited for something more supernatural. So where the Bible speaks, obey it. Where it does not, pray, use the mind God gave you, take advice (Proverbs 15:22), weigh the good of other people, and decide. Then get on with it, trusting God’s providence to overrule your mistakes. You do not need a sign to do a wise and lawful thing.

On a Tuesday. If there is a Christian whose no you have taken personally, release it this week; let it be a no and not a verdict.

For worship. The Lord Jesus never once competed for a following. When the crowds were about to take him by force and make him king, he withdrew to the mountain by himself (John 6:15), and he did not seek his own glory (John 8:50). Every servant who stays away so that a church may love Christ more than it loves him is walking in his steps. One plants, another waters, but God gives the growth (3:6–7). Blessed be the Lord of the harvest, whose servants are brothers and not rivals, and to whom alone belongs the glory.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul gives five short commands, then honours the household of Stephanas and the three men who had refreshed him, and tells the church to recognise such people.
verseByVerse.theology:
Courage and Love in Christian Character

The commands of verses 13–14, watchful, firm, courageous, strong, and then loving, hold together what Paul has asked for all through the letter: the courage to stand for the truth, as he has done in every hard section, and the love that is patient and kind and bears all things (chapter 13). Neither is Christian without the other. Together they describe Christ himself, who drove the money-changers from the temple and wept on the way to Lazarus’s tomb.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians needed watchfulness against false teaching, firmness against the pressure to conform, courage to exercise church discipline, and strength to bear the cost of faithfulness, and they needed all of it held in love, or it would make them cold and harsh. Now: A church that is watchful and firm but unloving becomes a fortress, not a family. A church that is loving but neither watchful nor firm becomes sentimental and cannot stand.

verseByVerse.quote: Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be watchful. Five commands, fired off like an order of the day. Watchful (grēgoreō) is a sentry’s word: stay awake, keep looking. Watch for Christ’s return (Matthew 24:42), and against danger and false teaching. It is the same verb Jesus used in Gethsemane to men who could not manage an hour (Mark 14:34–38). Corinth had been asleep too, arrogant rather than mourning over gross immorality in its membership (5:1–2).

Stand firm in the faith. Not in your faith: in the faith, the thing believed, the deposit handed over, the gospel especially as defended in chapter 15. Do not be shaken (15:58). The ground is not the church’s to renegotiate, and the pressure to move it is constant and usually reasonable-sounding.

Act like men. One word in Greek (andrizomai), built on the word for a man, and it means: be courageous, be mature, behave like an adult. The Greek Old Testament often uses it on the eve of battle, in the charge to be strong and courageous (Joshua 1:6–7; 2 Samuel 10:12), and God said it to Joshua as he faced a task far bigger than himself. Here it is addressed to the whole church, men and women: be brave and mature, not childish (14:20). In short: grow up and show some nerve, the nerve of people whose God is with them wherever they go (Joshua 1:9).

Be strong. Be strong (krataioō) is passive in form: be strengthened. The strength is not manufactured; it is received from a Person. Be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might, Paul tells another church (Ephesians 6:10), and when he himself pleaded for a thorn to be removed, the risen Christ answered: my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). So a frightened church is not told to find courage in itself. It is told to lean on the Lord who has already overcome death, as chapter 15 has just shown, and to stand in his strength. It is borrowed courage, and the lender never runs short.

Done in love. And then the fifth, which changes everything. Take the first four alone and you get a Christian everyone has met: watchful, immovable, courageous, strong, and impossible to be near. Vigilance without love becomes suspicion. Firmness without love becomes rigidity. Courage without love becomes belligerence, and there is a species of contender for the faith who is right about everything and has never comforted anyone. Take the fifth alone and you get a church so anxious to be loving that it will not stand anywhere or say a hard thing. Paul wants all four, soaked in the fifth. Only Christ has ever held that balance, and his perfect obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19); the love asked for here is the fruit of his Spirit, growing in us (Galatians 5:22).

In the flow. The five commands sum up the whole letter. Be watchful answers a church that had slept through scandal (5:1–2) and thought it could not fall (10:12). Stand firm in the faith points back to chapter 15, where the resurrection itself had been doubted. Act like men answers people Paul had to call infants (3:1). Be strong answers a church that thought itself strong already (4:10) by pointing it to the Lord’s strength. And do everything in love sums up chapter 13, and the rule laid down in 8:1 that knowledge puffs up but love builds up.

What does it mean for a man, in particular, to act like a man? The command is to the whole church, but it lands with special weight on men, because Scripture calls husbands and fathers to lead their homes and qualified men to lead the church (11:3; 1 Timothy 3:1–7). Biblical manhood is not swagger or control. It is courage in the service of others: standing firm in the truth, protecting the weak, taking responsibility instead of blaming, leading in prayer and in repentance, and laying down your life as Christ did for his bride (Ephesians 5:25). A man who uses strength to dominate or harm has not acted like a man in Paul’s sense; he has acted like a child with a weapon. Many faithful Christians read these passages differently and open every office to women; this commentary holds the complementarian reading (men and women equal in worth, with different callings in home and church) because Paul grounds the pattern not in the customs of his day but in creation (11:8–9; 1 Timothy 2:13), and it honours those who differ as brothers and sisters.

On a Tuesday. Think of one place where you have gone quiet out of fear, and speak; and one place where you have been firm without kindness, and soften.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I urge you, brothers—you know that the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints— be subject to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I urge you. After fifteen chapters of problems, Paul points at some people who were getting it right.

The first converts in Achaia. Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its capital. First converts is literally firstfruits (aparchē), the same word used of Christ in 15:20: among the first in southern Greece to believe. (A few had believed at Athens shortly before, Acts 17:34, so Paul may mean the first household to believe, or simply the firstfruits of his work in the province.) Stephanas and his household were God’s first sheaf in Achaia, with a whole province still to be gathered. Paul had baptised this household (1:16), one of the very few he remembered baptising personally. And they had been at it ever since.

Does the household of Stephanas show that infants were baptised? It is sometimes cited for infant baptism, because Paul baptised the household (1:16). But the description here, a household that had devoted themselves to the service of the saints, describes believers, and nothing in either passage mentions children. The other household baptisms in Acts are likewise households that heard, believed and rejoiced (Acts 16:34; 18:8). This commentary, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, holds that baptism is for those who personally repent and believe. Our paedobaptist brothers (those who baptise the infants of believers), who read the households in the light of the covenant promise to believers and their children, are honoured and beloved fellow servants, and we gladly labour alongside them.

Devoted to the service of the saints. The verb is the striking thing. Devoted (tassō) means they appointed themselves, posted themselves to the duty. Nobody rostered them. They saw what the church needed and put themselves into the gap, apparently for years and without a title.

Be subject to such as these. Then the instruction nobody expects, in a congregation that had spent the whole letter arguing about status. Paul does not tell them to admire Stephanas, but to follow the people who have proved themselves by serving, not the most gifted speaker or the most confident. Leadership in the church is earned by service, not demanded by status. And the word for labourer means someone who works to the point of exhaustion: the qualification is simply that a person has worn himself out for the church.

Greatness turned upside down. Be subject to the servants: that is not a Corinthian idea, or a Roman one. It is Christ’s. When his disciples argued about which of them was the greatest, he told them that the kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, but among you the leader must be as one who serves, and he pointed to himself: I am among you as the one who serves (Luke 22:24–27). The household of Stephanas had simply taken him at his word. A church that follows people like them is not lowering its standard of leadership. It is adopting the Lord’s own standard, set by the one who served his people all the way to the cross.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone who serves automatically holds office. Elders are to be appointed according to the qualifications of Scripture (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). It means faithful servants deserve respect and should be followed.

Should I wait to be asked before serving? No. Stephanas did not wait. Churches are full of people whose gifts are real and whose service never begins, because nobody approached them and it felt presumptuous to volunteer. This verse quietly removes the excuse: the household Paul holds up as the model appointed themselves, and the apostle commends them for exactly that. Speak to your elders, see a need, and fill it. And a warning for those who are already serving. What Paul commends is not the work; it is the direction of it. They devoted themselves to the service of the saints: to people, not to a programme, a building, or a set of arrangements. You can be exhausted by church activity and never once have served a person.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece.

verseByVerse.quote: I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus, because they have made up for your absence, for they refreshed my spirit as well as yours. Give recognition to such people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus. These three men probably brought the Corinthians’ letter to Paul in Ephesus (7:1), a crossing of some two hundred and fifty miles by sea, and would carry his reply.

Made up for your absence. Their presence brought the church to him. He had been missing them: not the letter, not the news, but them.

They refreshed my spirit. Refreshed (anapauō) is to give someone rest, the way a weight is taken off. Paul was in Ephesus with a wide door and many adversaries, carrying, by his own account, the daily pressure of anxiety for all the churches (2 Corinthians 11:28). Into that came three men from a difficult congregation, and he says they rested him. Some people bring life and encouragement wherever they go (Philemon 7). There is no record of Fortunatus preaching or Achaicus writing anything. What lifted the weight off an overloaded apostle was some ordinary Christians turning up.

Give recognition to such people. Honour them: notice them, and say so out loud. Every congregation has its Stephanas, and the reason they are rarely thanked is not unkindness but that quiet service is almost invisible by design: the work only becomes noticeable in the week it stops.

The traffic runs both ways. The letter has been a torrent of correction flowing from Ephesus to Corinth. Here, for a moment, it flows the other way: a half-grown church sent three men across the sea, and they rested the apostle who was correcting them. Nobody is only a recipient in the body of Christ. Paul says as much to the Romans about a visit he was hoping for: that we may be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith, both yours and mine (Romans 1:12). He did not want anyone thinking the traffic went one way.

Refreshed in Christ. When Paul asks the same kindness of Philemon, he adds two words: refresh my heart in Christ (Philemon 20). The rest Christians give one another is Christ’s own care, passed from hand to hand within his body; through these three visitors the Head of that body was caring for his apostle. That is why the smallest visit can carry so much: the one who comes in Christ’s name brings more than himself.

How can I refresh a pastor or missionary who is carrying too much? You do not need a gift for it. Go and see them. Take something. Stay a while, but not too long. Say the encouraging thing you have thought and never said, and be specific: a sermon that helped, a visit that mattered. Pray for them and tell them you are praying. Offer a practical help that removes a burden rather than adds a meeting. Protect their day off. It sounds too small to matter, and Paul put three men’s names in Scripture for doing it.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person whose arrival makes your week lighter. Very likely they have no idea. They are doing for you what Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus did for Paul, and it would cost you one sentence to tell them.
verseByVerse.note: These three men probably brought the Corinthians’ letter to Paul.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter closes with greetings from Asia and from Aquila and Prisca, the holy kiss, Paul’s own signature, a solemn warning, the prayer Maranatha, and grace and love.
verseByVerse.theology:
Maranatha: The Church’s Prayer for Christ’s Coming

The Aramaic can be divided maran atha, our Lord has come, or marana tha, our Lord, come. Its place, after the warning and before the blessing, and its echo in the last prayer of the Bible, Come, Lord Jesus (Revelation 22:20), favour the prayer. A church that has the cross at its centre (chapters 1–2), loves without condition (chapter 13) and proclaims the resurrection (chapter 15) lives with this prayer on its lips: the One who died and rose is coming again.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: An Aramaic prayer kept untranslated in a Greek letter to a Gentile church is a small, moving piece of evidence that Jewish and Gentile believers prayed the same prayer in the same words. Now: Christians in every tradition and century have prayed for the Lord to come. To pray it is to join the whole church across time, watching and waiting for the One whose coming makes all things new.

verseByVerse.quote: The churches of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca, together with the church in their house, send you hearty greetings in the Lord. All the brothers send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The churches of Asia send you greetings. Greetings, and they are a map of the early church. Asia was the Roman province around Ephesus, where churches had sprung up through Paul’s ministry and that of his fellow workers: Colossae, Laodicea, Hierapolis (Colossians 1:7; 4:13). Churches, plural: a whole province of congregations that had not existed a few years earlier.

Aquila and Prisca. The church in their house, because for some two centuries there were no dedicated church buildings: a front room, some benches, a table, and a family willing to have people tramping through every week. Aquila and Prisca deserve to be known. They were a couple, tentmakers like Paul, expelled from Rome when Claudius drove the Jews out, who took him in when he arrived in Corinth after Athens (Acts 18:1–3). They moved to Ephesus with him (Acts 18:18–19), and there took the eloquent Apollos aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately (Acts 18:26): two tentmakers correcting a brilliant preacher, privately, and he took it. And Paul says elsewhere that they risked their necks for his life (Romans 16:4). They are always named together, and Prisca is usually named first, which was not the ordinary order.

Hearty greetings. They knew the Corinthians well, having worked there with Paul for eighteen months, and all the brothers in Ephesus join them.

A holy kiss. The family greeting of believers (Romans 16:16; 1 Peter 5:14). After all the divisions, this command is pointed: be reconciled and show it. It was the ordinary affectionate greeting of that world, and Paul’s addition is the important word: holy. In that room a slave and a slave-owner greeted each other this way. A Jew and a Greek did. The rich patron and the dockworker who arrived late for the supper did. The greeting was the one moment in the week when the world’s seating plan was visibly suspended, and it was holy because the people exchanging it had been made holy in Christ Jesus (1:2). Made holy means set apart for God: they now belonged to him, and to one another, because they belonged to his Son. A slave and his master could greet each other as brothers because both had been bought with the same price (7:22–23). The cross had already torn up the seating plan; the kiss simply showed it, and much of the fight of this letter comes down to who you are willing to greet warmly on a Sunday morning.

So what should I actually do in a culture that does not kiss? Greet people. Warmly, in whatever way your place counts as warm: a firm handshake, a hug where it is welcome, a smile and a name remembered. And greet the ones you would not naturally have crossed the room for: the visitor, the elderly widow, the awkward teenager, the person you quarrelled with last month. Be pure and considerate in it; holy means no one should feel uncomfortable or used. That is the whole instruction, and a congregation can be transformed by ten people obeying it for a month.

On a Tuesday. If you have a home, ask God how it might be opened to his people, for a meal, a Bible study, or a lonely student on a Sunday afternoon.

For worship. The Father has gathered children from every nation into one household, and he has given them front rooms to meet in until he gives them a city. A tentmaker’s house in Ephesus and the new Jerusalem are the same family’s home at different stages. His people greet one another as family because in his Son they are family, and the Son is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). He is the Father of the great household, who sets the lonely in families (Psalm 68:6).
verseByVerse.note: Churches met in homes.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With my own hand. The pen changes hands. Letters were normally dictated to a trained secretary, and Paul used one; the man who took down Romans signs his own name in it (Romans 16:22). Now the apostle takes the pen himself, and the script on the papyrus would have visibly changed. He does this at the end of several letters as a signature, to prove the letter was genuine (Galatians 6:11; Colossians 4:18; 2 Thessalonians 3:17), and once he draws attention to it: see with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand (Galatians 6:11).

The seal of a real correspondent. Forged letters were a real problem, and Paul had to warn one congregation not to be shaken by a letter seeming to be from us (2 Thessalonians 2:2). His handwriting was the seal, and a congregation that knew his hand could check.

What the last lines are. There is more in it than security. He has picked up the pen in order to write a warning, a prayer, and two declarations of love to a church that had given him as much grief as any. He did not save his own handwriting for the easy people.

The marks of Jesus. When Paul took the pen at the end of Galatians, the large letters were followed by this: I bear on my body the marks of Jesus (Galatians 6:17). The hand that signed this letter belonged to a man who had been flogged, beaten with rods and stoned for Christ (2 Corinthians 11:24–25). Those scars were a surer seal than any handwriting, because they showed whose he was. His authority never rested on his pen or his eloquence. It rested on the risen Lord who had met him on the Damascus road, sent him, and marked him as his own, so that the letter in Corinth’s hands came, through Paul, from Christ.

Does it matter that Paul used a secretary? Not for the authority of the letter. A secretary wrote down what Paul dictated, and Paul read and signed it; the words are Paul’s, and through Paul, the Lord’s (14:37). God inspired the Scriptures through the ordinary means of the ancient world, papyrus, ink, scribes and couriers, and he kept every word he intended. The verse is a reminder of what these documents physically were. Not a leather-bound book with gilt edges. A roll of papyrus, dictated over days, carried by hand across a sea, read aloud to a room of people who had been waiting for it, and at the bottom of the last sheet, larger and less tidy than the rest, the writing of a man they knew.

On a Tuesday. Write a note by hand this week to someone who has hurt you or whom you have found hard, with one line of genuine blessing, as Christ blessed you when you were hard to love.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters and added a closing greeting in his own handwriting as a mark of authenticity.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed. Our Lord, come!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let him be accursed. One of the hardest sentences in the letter. Love here is phileō, warm affection. Accursed is anathema: devoted to destruction, handed over to the judgement of God. It is not a temper; it is a formal declaration, and Paul writes it in his own hand. Lack of love for Christ is not a small matter. All who have no love for Christ, whatever their spiritual gifts or knowledge, are outside the kingdom.

What the verse does not say. Begin with what it does not say, because a tender conscience will misread it within seconds. It does not say if anyone does not love the Lord perfectly. It does not say if anyone’s love has grown cold, or if anyone struggles to feel anything in church, or if anyone has doubts. Every believer who has ever lived would be under that sentence, including the man writing it. It says has no love. None. Paul is describing the person for whom Jesus Christ is a matter of complete indifference: who may be in the congregation, may be perfectly orthodox, may know the arguments and enjoy the debates, and has no affection for him at all. That, and not weakness, is what falls under this word.

But it should not be softened. Paul is saying that the final question is not whether a person knows the right things about Jesus. This whole letter has been written to a congregation stuffed with knowledge and gifts, and here at the end the apostle names the one thing that cannot be substituted for. Christianity is not agreement. It is love for a Person, and there is no version of it in which that is optional. Why so severe? Because the holy God has one beloved Son, and he wills that all should honour the Son just as they honour the Father (John 5:23). Indifference to Jesus is not a neutral position. It is a cold shoulder turned to the dearest treasure of heaven.

Our Lord, come! Then, immediately, the other sentence, and Paul leaves it in Aramaic. The ESV notes that Our Lord, come! translates Maranatha: Marana tha, our Lord, come! (Revelation 22:20). Here is a Greek letter to a Greek-speaking church, and this one phrase is left untranslated because everyone already knew it. The letters can also be divided Maran atha, our Lord has come, but the Greek prayer of Revelation 22:20, Come, Lord Jesus, favours reading it as a prayer; and the KJV prints Anathema Maranatha together as though one curse, when they are two separate sayings. It was probably a prayer of the earliest, Aramaic-speaking church in Jerusalem, among the oldest recorded prayers of the church, and it is two words long. And it shows something astonishing: Jewish believers, who would never pray to a mere man, were praying to Jesus as Lord, a powerful witness to his deity from the very beginning.

Is it not harsh to curse people simply for not loving Jesus? Not loving one teacher among many would hardly deserve it. But if Jesus is the Lord who gave himself for sinners, then to have no love for him is to refuse the only rescue there is, and God’s judgment simply confirms what that person has chosen (John 3:18–19). Paul is not calling for anyone to be harmed, and he is not speaking out of personal spite. He is stating how things stand, and in the same breath he prays for the Lord’s coming. And the door stays open while he waits: Christ himself became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), so that anyone who turns to him, however cold he has been, will find no curse left to bear.

I am afraid I do not love Christ enough. Am I under this curse? No, and the fear is itself the answer. Nobody who has no love for Christ is troubled by a verse about not loving Christ. The people this sentence describes read it and feel nothing whatever, which is precisely the diagnosis. Your love will always be smaller than it should be, and smaller than his love for you. Do not try to manufacture feeling; look at him. Read of his life and death, think on what he has forgiven you, and ask the Spirit to pour God’s love into your heart (Romans 5:5). We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Love for Christ grows as we gaze at Christ.

On a Tuesday. Tell the Lord Jesus that you love him, in your own words, today, and pray for one person you know to whom he is a matter of complete indifference.

For worship. The prayer of the first believers is still the last prayer in the Bible, in Greek this time: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus (Revelation 22:20). It stands beside his own promise, surely I am coming soon, and the church has been praying it for two thousand years, until one day it will be answered in a moment. The One we pray to is the One who first loved us, who became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), so that no anathema remains for anyone who loves him. The curse and the hope sit side by side in this verse, and between them stands the cross.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Our Lord, come!” translates Maranatha, an Aramaic prayer of the earliest church.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grace at both ends. The letter opened with grace (1:3) and closes with it. Everything in between, the factions, the immorality, the lawsuits, the idol meat, the head coverings, the disgraceful supper, the tongues, the denial of the resurrection, rebuke and teaching alike, is enclosed by grace at both ends and flows from it. Whatever this church was, it was a church, and Paul never once wrote to them as though they were not.

My love be with you all. Then the last line, unique among Paul’s letters: a tender final word to a congregation that had given him as much pain as any. They had split into parties over teachers, questioned whether he was an apostle at all, tolerated a scandal that shocked pagans, sued each other in front of the city, and got drunk at the Lord’s table while poor members went hungry. He answered every one of their questions at length, softening almost nothing. And then he took the pen and wrote, in his own hand: my love be with you all. All. Not the ones who had stayed loyal. Not the party that still called itself his. The whole quarrelsome congregation, including the men who thought him a fool. Love, from chapter 13, is the last word.

In Christ Jesus. The last words say where such a thing comes from, because it does not grow in human ground. Paul had no natural stock of affection for people like this, and neither has anybody else. What he had was a share in the love of the One who had looked at a world exactly this arrogant, this divided and this ungrateful, and had not withheld himself from it.

Amen. So be it. Many manuscripts, followed by the KJV and the ESV, end with it, while some early ones leave it out; either way it is the right last word.

How do I love someone I have had to correct? Let the correction serve the love, not replace it. Before you speak, pray for the person and remind yourself of the grace you have received. Correct what is wrong plainly, as Paul did, without exaggeration or contempt. Then say, and show, that you are still for them: stay in touch, speak well of them to others, and be quick to rejoice in any change. If they reject what you said, keep loving them anyway, as Christ has kept loving you. A rebuke wrapped in grace and sealed with love is one of the kindest gifts one Christian can give another.

I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits.<sup>8</sup>But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost,<sup>9</sup>for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.<sup>10</sup>When Timothy comes, see that you put him at ease among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am.<sup>11</sup>So let no one despise him. Help him on his way in peace, that he may return to me, for I am expecting him with the brothers.<sup>12</sup>Now concerning our brother Apollos, I strongly urged him to visit you with the other brothers, but it was not at all his will to come now. He will come when he has opportunity.<sup>13</sup>Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong.<sup>14</sup>Let all that you do be done in love.<sup>15</sup>Now I urge you, brothers—you know that the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints—<sup>16</sup>be subject to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer.<sup>17</sup>I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus, because they have made up for your absence,<sup>18</sup>for they refreshed my spirit as well as yours. Give recognition to such people.<sup>19</sup>The churches of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca, together with the church in their house, send you hearty greetings in the Lord.<sup>20</sup>All the brothers send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss.<sup>21</sup>I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand.<sup>22</sup>If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed.
